8910: ə dobrè a sjà mòjš li pɤ̀rvo da ni raskàžeš
OK. And now, can you first tell us
8912: kakvò si slùšala ot màjka si od bàba si
what you heard from your mother, your grandmother,
8915: ot stàrite xòra za sèlutu kàk e bilò zesèleno
and from old people [here] about how the village was settled?
10000: ... that means that the people are hungry.
10006: nèmə li də dədèš də sə nəjədɔ̀t ili də sə nəjədèm
"Aren't you going to give them [enough] to eat their fill?" – to eat our fill?
10023: Over there by the road, do you see ...
10029: vìždəm žinàta vìždəm vìždəm ama məgl'àwo
I see the woman [over there], I see [her], I see, but [only] dimly.
10030: dèto predè səs xùrka tàm i vretèno
... the one who is spinning over there with distaff and spindle?
10032: Did you spin when you were young?
10038: prid'ɑ̀h am prid'ɑ̀ i təkɛ̀ tə i
I used to spin, and weave.
10041: vlɑ̀čajmi i prid'ɛ̀jmi kɑ̀k rɑ̀botɛ̀hmi kɑ̀k n'èma da predɛ̀
We used to card and spin. Ah, how we used to work! How could I not spin?
10042: fùrka ìmam, i pred'ɛ̀w i pred'ɛ̀ i tečɛ̀
I have a distaff; I used to spin, and I spin and weave [now too],
10043: i žènew i i tɛ̀j žèneše i sìčko
and I used to reap – like this – and she used to reap, and everything.
10072: ami da ni raskàžeš togàva za golèmite pràznici za kurbàn.bajràm tùkə
[Can] you tell us, then, about the major holidays here, [for instance] "Kurban-Bayram"?
10080: zə kurbàn.bəjrɛ̀mə əgà dòjdeše zəbrujɔ̀t dèsetnə dène zəbrujɔ̀t
[To know] when Kurban-Bayram was coming they count ten days.
10085: kurbənlɔ̀ci hrànet enəgà gi zəkòl'et əgà dòjde bəjrɛ̀m gi zəkòl’ət
Then they feed up the sacrificial animals and slaughter them when Bayram comes.
10091: kədènu n'èmət ədìn in bràf agə zəkòl’ət dènu zə umrɛ̀ti
[For] those who have no animal to slaughter, others [who] slaughter to honor the dead
10096: zəkòlet z’ɔ̀mət tə gu rəsprudədɔ̀t nə dɛ̀l nə dɛ̀luve
take [it on themselves] to distribute [the meat] out in parcels
10101: i dènu sə nè klàli kurbənlɔ̀ci gu rəzdədɔ̀t nə vrìt
to those who [weren't able] to make sacrifice. They distribute it out to everyone.
10107: pàk nɛ̀kuj pàk z’ɔ̀me tə gu svərì i rùkne komš’ii nə
And someone will take it on themselves to cook it, and invite neighbors,
10113: sə gudì sufrɔ̀ də gu izedɔ̀t bəjrɛ̀mə i rəməzànə gànu
[and] prepare the table [for everyone] to eat the Bayram sacrifice. And when Ramazan comes,
10118: pàk enəgà dàvət kulàci pekɔ̀t sìč’ku də vɛ̀rvət də dàvə al:àh hùbəvu
they give out breadstuffs and bake everything so they’ll believe, that Allah gives good,
10123: də sə žìvi də sə ràdvət də sə
that everyone may live and rejoice, and –
10216: àš’ur’ ìmə vərɔ̀t enəgà sìč'ku ut sɛ̀kəkvu zberɔ̀t tə vər’ɔ̀t
They cook ashur then [too], pulling together things from everywhere to cook it up,
10222: i gu rəzdàvət kutrìnu sə nəbòžni kutrìnu vɛ̀rvət
and give it out. Those who are pious [that is], those who believe.
10225: [As for] the one who doesn't believe –
10248: i to edìn mèsec e tovà ramazàna nalì
10253: ədìn mɛ̀səc rəməzàn i i rəməzàn meždu mə
Ramadan [lasts] a month. And it's between –
10256: nàj prèš’ rəməzàn rəž’ìp š’əbàn rəməzàn
Well, first there’s Ramazan. [in sequence:] “Razhip, Shaban, Ramazan” (Arabic names)
10262: enəgà sə guvɛ̀ klàn’ə se sìč’ku sə mòli zə zə d’yn’ɔ̀
At that time you fast and do ritual prayers; everyone prays for the world.
10267: zə zə sòə svɛ̀t i zə drùgijət sə mòliž' zə hùbəvu
You pray [both] for this world and for the other, for well-being,
10270: oti nə d’yn’ɔ̀sə də živɛ̀eš’ hùbəu i nə drùgijət svɛ̀t
so that you’ll [be able] to live well in this world, and in the other world;
10274: pàg də t’i̥ e hùbəvu òti tàm š’e f ednà zèm’ə
so it'll be good for you there too. Because it's in a single earth that
10279: š'e ni zəròv'ət ut č'ètirite stràni prɤ̀s š'e e
they'll bury us. From all four sides, there'll be only soil.
10283: kəkvò š'e e əl:àh znàe vrìtem əlàh də dàvə hùbəvu sə mòlime
Only Allah knows how it will be. We pray that Allah should grant good to all.
10286: n’è jɛ̀ ti kàzvəm jɛ̀ səm tìj mə mène rùkət də pòskàzvəm
We – I tell you, I’m – [People] call on me to tell [them]
10290: es’è elè səm nəbòžnə mlògu jɛ̀ ne vɛ̀rvəm
how pious I am. I don’t believe [in that way of doing things].
10294: jɛ̀ è gi kàrəm i deč'ìš'tətə i vnùč'etətə də vɛ̀rvət
I work to make my children and grandchildren believe,
10299: də nə pràət lòš’u də də uvəž’ɛ̀vət hòrətə
not to do anything bad, to respect people,
10301: Yes, that's right. That's how it should be.
10306: də nèmə grɛ̀š'ki də vìdiš' gə ədìn čuvɛ̀k də mu pumògneš'
That there be no errors. That if you see someone [in need], you help him,
10310: nè də ìeš pòsle də mu se prismìvəš' i
not [just] to go off and later make fun of him
10312: də mòž’e də mu pumògneš’ də gu səž’əlìš’
when you could have helped him, and felt pity for him.
10315: tə tə i tèbe əl:àh də dəde hùbəvu
[If you do all this], then Allah will give you well-being.
10403: kàk se kàzva tovà koèto se slàga oddòlu da težì
What do you call that thing you put underneath to weigh it down?
10406: [OK, that's the] wool on the distaff, and this?
10408: ne mù li slàgate nèkoj pɤ̀t ednò takòva da težì oddòlu
Don't you sometimes put some sort of thing underneath to weigh it down?
10409: əm n'àkoj slɑ̀ga ama ɑ̀z ne slɑ̀gam
Some people do, but I don't put [anything there].
10453: išlà səm išlà səm sɤs govèda z volòve ìmašemo
Oh, I did, I did! I went out with the cows, and we also had oxen.
10454: pa me ubòde edɤ̀n jà gi pasèm pa do livàdutu
And one gored me. I was taking them to pasture, out to the meadow
10455: ta da se napasè òn kìmnu vàrdi se od mùe
to graze, and he gave a shake to ward off the flies.
10456: kìmnu i jà òp ta na rodzìte mu se ukačì
He gave a shake and whoops! There I was up on his horns!
10458: Gave a shake [how]? With his tail?
10460: jà sɤm detè učenìčka è sɤs ə ɤm komšìk'a ni bèše
I was a child, a schoolgirl, and this neighbor of ours was there too –
10462: pak vamìlija smo bèomo dvème decà è tòlki smo
we were family, in fact. [There] were two of us, [just] kids, just this big.
10507: pa me vànu vòlɤt ta me prenèse jà ne smèem
And the ox took me up and carried me across – I didn't dare
10513: da rovèm če me ostài pa če me s ròdzi namùška
start to cry, [for fear] that he'd drop me and poke me with his horns.
10520: jà mirùjem onò vodà bèše golemà nèkvo valè dɤ̀š
So I stayed quiet. The water was very high, it had rained a lot.
10525: òn òp ta preko vodùtu me prenèse i me òstai vòlɤt
And just like that, the ox carried me across the water and left me.
10530: a onà si nò kvò stànu kvò stànu jà ne smèem
And she said, "Ah, what happened? What happened?" [But] I didn't dare
10535: da se obàdim če da ne bì da me mirùjem
speak up for fear that he'd – that he – So I kept calm
10537: če če me utrepàl vòlɤt tùj pod mìšku
that – that this ox had struck me here under my arm.
10538: xàjde àjde ìdemo si oddòle mi oddòle ìdemo po tòo pùt
So, OK, we went up from [there]. We were going up along that road.
10539: kat pìpnu onò mi mòkro tùj pod mìšku bolì me
And when I touched [myself], it was wet here in my armpit! It hurt,
10950: be ràbuta še ìmə i sled nàs
Well, there will be work after us ...
10954: Did your mother do the three-day fast?
10962: də trimìr'ə o [unintelligible] wòs'em gudìn səm trimiròsələ b'èz l'àp
Ah, do the three-day fast! [unintelligible] I did it for eight years. [I went] without bread
10966: trì d'èn'ə pək ìnək pùstuvete si b'àhə pùstuve i sià pàk
for three days. But otherwise, fasts were [regular] fasts. Even now
10969: ne blàžə pàg gà dòjde p'ètək gà dòjde pùs šə zgòvejə
I don't break the fast. And when Friday comes, when the fast comes, I’ll fast,
10972: š ìə də sə kònkəm i tugàs še jàm
I'll go to take communion and then I’ll eat.
10977: The Easter one is the most important. Easter –
11049: ami təkwòs n'àkoj bòlči zəvərtèli zə zə pò tèšku̥
Well, some [add] a small bolt [to make it] heavier.
11121: These people seem to have fallen out of the sky!
11167: za brəšnòtu tìe segà kətu tùra: təkà f ednò kurìtce i se
About flour. When they put [it] in a small trough, then –
11316: Atidžè bàba Atidžè na kòlko godìni
Atidzhe. Granny Atidzhe, how old are you?
11738: i tì kɤdè si živ'àla s'à
11744: jà sɤm živ'àla vɤv durlìite osemnàese godìni
I lived in Durliite for eighteen years.
11753: i pòsle se ožènix ta bèx tùka vɤf ednɤ̀ maalɤ̀ parapàndofci
And then I got married, and I was here in a district [called] Parapandovtsi.
11758: presèlia ni ta ni zbràa tùka ta ma:nàxme onàa maalɤ̀
And they moved us, gathered us together, and we abandoned that district,
11770: predì vɤv àm ednò vrème sɤ sɤbìraxte li se
Earlier on in – in the old days, did you get together
11776: with people from the other village?
11779: čàkaj segà da vìdime tùka a žètvata tùka kàk ja pràvexte
Wait a minute. Let’s see about the harvesting. How did you do that?
11798: kugàtu lètneš'e dɔ̀š màlku nìje izlìzəhme nəgòre tə nəhòdəhme gɔ̀bi
When it would rain a bit, we’d go out up there and look for mushrooms.
11804: jəd'ɛ̀hme gi pɔ̀rž'ehme gi sə zvɛ̀hme gi sərn'èli
We’d eat them, we’d fry them. We called them “surneli” (parasol mushrooms).
11811: ìmə i drùgi gɤ̀bi kutrìtu sə jəd'ɛ̀hə nìj gi kàzvəhme č'ervenùš'ki
There are other mushrooms which people ate. We called them “blood redcaps”.
11819: t'ɛ̀ izlìzət fəf nuèmvri dekèmvri kugàtu sə nəpujì hùbəvu zem'ɔ̀nə
They come up in November or December, when the ground is well watered
11839: fč'èrə zɔ̀h m'ɔ̀su r'ɛ̀zəh m'ɔ̀su gòtvime m'ɔ̀su əmə
Yesterday I took [some] meat and sliced the meat. We cook with meat but [now]
11847: də stàne vlàžnə tugàf izlìzət pr'ez dekèmri m'ɛ̀sec
so it gets moist. They come up then, in the month of December.
11851: à da napràite golèmo sèloto tùka
Ah, in order to make the village here bigger.
11853: à i na drùgo mèsto ne sì živ'àla
And you haven’t lived any other place?
11854: e ne sɤ̀m odìla za živòt ne sɤ̀m odìla
I haven’t gone [away], I haven’t gone [anywhere] all my life,
11855: odìla sɤm vɤf Sòfia čèteri godìni
[except] I went to Sofia [for] four years.
11877: n'èmə nəpr'ɛ̀šnit'e nòž'uve də gu udr'ɛ̀ž'eš izvednɔ̀š' r'ɛ̀ž'eme
there aren’t these old-time knives to cut it up at one stroke. We slice
11883: r'ɛ̀ž'eme zòrle gu udr'ɛ̀zvəme gòtvim'e m'ɔ̀sunu tùrime gu
and slice and cut it all up [only] with difficulty. We cook the meat, we put it
11891: f hàrkumənə vəzvərì gà sɔ̀dnehme nemòj pìtə kàk əd'ɛ̀hme
in a cauldron and it boils. When we sat down [to eat], don’t ask how we ate!
11905: n'è sejɛ̀hme i rɔ̀š' i pš'enìcə i ječ'emìk i càrevicə
We would plant rye and wheat and barley and corn.
11912: ž'ɔ̀nehme gu sìč'ku səs sɔ̀rpuve ələ be jɛ̀ce trùdnu
We reaped all of it with sickles, it was really hard [work].
11921: sejɛ̀hme fəsùl' l'ɔ̀štə ələ ne stànvəš'e pò izìdəhə gu pìl'etə
We planted beans. And lentils, but they didn’t make it. The birds ate it all,
11930: izìdəhə gu sɔ̀rni ne ustànvəš'e zə nàs l'ɔ̀štə
the deer ate it all. There weren’t any lentils left for us.
11939: [С въже ли го носехте в къщи?]
[Did you use a rope to carry things back home?]
11947: ìštəm də mi dunes'èš vɔ̀ž'e wòti sə zəd'ɛ̀vəme dərvà fəsùl' l' e bilò
[I'll say] “I want you to bring me a rope” because we’d tie up wood, beans, whatever.
11957: š'ìkəl'ki hòdim tə zbìrəm'e zə də ìməme zimɔ̀skə pòtvətkə i bòrnə
We go gather oak-apples so we’ll have fire-starter and kindling for the winter.
11963: ələ gu nòsim'e nə gərbuv'èse kòjtu n'èmə məgàre nə gərbɔ̀n
But we carry it on our backs. Whoever doesn’t have a donkey – on his back.
11978: kòjtu ìmə məgàre fpr'ɔ̀gne kərùčkənə ìde si tə si nətvàri
Whoever has a donkey harnesses up the carriage and goes off to load it up.
11986: kòjtu n'èmə məgàr'e nòsi nə gərbɔ̀n nə vɔ̀ž'e i si dunìsəme
Whoever doesn’t have a donkey carries it tied to his back. And we bring
11988: sìč'ku nə vɔ̀ž'e i š'ìkəl'ki i bòrnə sìčku si nòsim
everything tied up – oak-apples, kindling – we carry it all.
12011: emi na dvanàes gòdin me e zavèl baštà mi
Well, [I was] twelve years old [when] my father took me [there].
12023: màjka mi bèše bòlna g'oturùmen pa ìmax sestrà pò golèma
My mother was sick, not able to get about, and I had an older sister.
12050: sedèla sɤm za trìese na trìe za trìese dèna za šejsè lèva
I stayed there thirty – thirty days [to earn] sixty levs,
12056: i sɤm gledàla na evrèite decàta
and I looked after the children of [some] Jews.
12069: ta òra ta sɤm odìla u calapìško pòle čèteri godìni
and plow. And I went to Tsalapishko field for four years,
12074: ot ə calapìško pòle ta žɤ̀nem pa nàše tù̥kə̥
from Tsalapishko field and we reap at our [field].
12083: e n tovà òdene kàk mu vìkaxte na ro romanìja li
And how did you call that traveling – to – to Thrace?
12097: emi s sɤberè ni nèkoj se kàzvaše dragomànin mɤ̀š
Someone got us together, he was called the manager,
12104: odgovàra za nàze sɤberèm se po pet.šesnàese dùši momìčeta momčèta
responsible for us. We get together, fifteen or sixteen boys and girls,
12109: tòj ni sòpšti elàte če e za žɤ̀tva nìe otìvame
[and] gets word to us – “Come [help in] the harvest.” We go off,
12117: srèšnat ni na pàzardžik sɤs karùci zakàrat ni
and they meet us at Pazardzhik with carriages and take us off,
12123: ta si ostàim bagàše i na drùgata sùtrin na polèto
and we leave our things and the next morning it’s off to the field.
12126: Do you go there on foot?
12140: du ixtimàn otìdem pèši ot ut ixtimàn natàm si òdime
We go to Ihtiman on foot, and we go from Ihtiman to there,
12145: tàm ni srèšnat vèče na gàrata slèzem na plòv na pazardžik
they meet us there at the station. We get off at Plov- at Pazardzhik
12150: i karùcite ni čèkat čorbadžìite tòj nè e sàmo edìn
and the carriages await us, and the landowners. Not just one,
12156: tìa òdea po desetìna dùši̥ grùpi
they came in groups of ten or so.
12164: sèki si e fanàl čorbadžìata i dòde li mu
Each one found his landowner, and when he goes over to him,
12167: tòj si go vìka da vrɤvì da mu žɤ̀ne
he calls them to move out and reap for him.
12174: edèm česnòf.lùk i skačkìva izvàra ìmaše i ednà pèsen
We eat garlic and old curds [like in] this song –
12181: dnèska na žègata sàmo česnòf.lùk sɤs takìva gavànki è dṛ̀veni
Today in the heat only garlic in these bowls, these wooden [ones].
12187: sčùkat česnòf.lùk i ocèt kùsame ta se trèpeme
They mash up garlic, [mix it] with vinegar, we scoop it up as we can.
12194: i tò takà trepère žègata kato glèdaš ama nìe žɤ̀nem
And the heat is such that it shimmers when you look [out]. But we reap
12198: ednò kàk žɤnà takà padnà i
and one [girl] was reaping and fell down
12206: dobrè a kàk se narèždate da žɤ̀nete tàm
OK. And how do you arrange yourselves to do the reaping there?
12211: emi ednà do drùga fànem si čekɤ̀m ot tùk do tùk i
We line up next to each other, check the reaping space from here to here –
12214: Is it “chekŭm” (reaping space) that you call it?
12219: We go along, go along the “chekŭm”, the “postat”
12229: pu pu gràždanski e postàt po
12242: That’s the way it is in Belitsa speech.
12248: i kòj opredèl'a kòlko da bɤ̀de širòk čakɤ̀mɤ
And who determines how wide the reaping space will be?
12255: emi kòlko sme čovècite tòlkova kàram às drùgia kàra do mèn
However many we are, that’s what I take on, and the one next to me takes
12262: tòlko i takà po tòlkova si fànem kòj
that much, and that’s how much each one takes.
12263: če ednàkvo šte zìmame ednàkvo še kàrame
Since we all get paid the same, we'll [each] take on the same amount.
12269: a ednà tì a tì a ne znàeš znàeš
And one – You don’t know her. [Do] you know
12274: from Parapandovtsi? Do you know her?
12281: ne pòmna da sam ne pòmna be mòže da a znàm
I don’t recall that I – I don’t remember. Maybe I know her,
12285: ama ne znàm tòčno kojà e ama segà
but I don’t know exactly which one she is.
12291: Oh, she died a long time ago.
12293: odàvna ama sestrà li ti bèše
Ah, long ago. But was she your sister?
12297: t'à mi nè e sestrà komšìjk'a mi bèše
No, she’s not my sister, she was my neighbor.
12303: ami ìskam da ti kàža če
What I wanted to tell you is that she was
12306: bèše dèset godìni pò stara od mène
12312: i sme otišlè f calapìško pòle
and we’d gone off to Tsalapishko field,
12317: because this man is asking me ...
12323: da si bɤ̀brem i žɤ̀neme s sɤ̀bo stojànof ud durlìite
... to talk [about it]. So we were reaping with Sŭbo Stoyanov from Durliite,
12331: tòj sedèše pri dòktorete pri zɤbolèkarete glàdni ot po
He lived near the doctors and dentists ([they were] hungry from – ),
12334: ama segà e počìnal i tòj tòj žɤ̀ne i jà žɤ̀na
but he’s dead now. So he – he’s reaping and I’m reaping,
12340: ama odrèže pa drème pa tùka
She cut [one stalk] but she was drowsing, and [fell] here …
12345: i kato ne mòže a žɤ̀ne nìe a potkarvà:me sɤs sɤ̀bo
And since she can’t reap, Sŭbo and I were pushing her [awake],
12350: tòj ottùk jà ottùk i ednò plàdne
he from here, I from here. And one afternoon
12357: kato a zarèza:me kòlko ottùk do
when we notched her off the amount from here to …
12363: … there, all the way to the street, ...
12369: ostàvim a zɤt nàze̥ t'à vìka
... we left her behind, and from behind us she said –
12375: tìe ne sɤ̀ a čùle tàa dùma
they didn’t hear what she said –
12384: t'à se ispràvi pa vìka mòja bràt nètko
she stands up and says “My brother Nedko” –
12388: t'à rèče takà rɤcète pa vìka bàjčo nètko
she did like this with her hands, and said “Brother Nedko!
12393: jà da ne sɤ̀m došlà tùk da nòsa na kùrvite vòda
Have I just come here to bring water to whores
12398: ta da sèda po òrata a pa bàjčo kàže
and to sit and chat?” And then her brother said,
12403: jà vi ne mèšam gospodìno sèki si odgovàra za nègo
“I’ve got your number, Gospodina. Each is responsible for himself.”
12408: a čorbadžìata ni bèše mnògo àren vìka èj dìke
And our landowner was a really good man. He said, “Hey Dika,
12413: ne sè sṛdì če sa te ostàvile
don’t get angry that they left you behind."
12417: This thing keeps on listening, doesn’t it?!
12421: a be tì segà ne pìeš da vìkaš tòlkova
Hey, now you’re not drinking and you don’t shout so much!
12426: He doesn’t give you [anything] to drink!
12434: nèma da pìeš ta da vìkaš
… [and so] you don’t drink or  shout!
12439: mi pògledni vìka po tèp kòlko snòpe sɤm vṛzàl a pa
But just look,” he said, “how many sheaves I’ve tied off for you, and then
12452: pògledni po tèx kòlko sɤm vṛzàl nèmu si e tovà
look how many I tied off for them.” That’s his job.
12459: tòj če dnèska nèma ùtre šte ni vṛ̀zva rɤkòjkite po baškɤ̀
There’s nothing today [so] tomorrow he’ll tie off the bundles separately
12466: da vìdi kòj kàk žɤ̀ne kato zème da plàšta təkà plàštə
to see who reaped what, so as to know what to pay when it’s time to pay.
12479: togàva ni plàštaa na dèn šeesè lèva a nèi dàdoa četìrese
At that time they were paying us sixty levs a day, but they gave her forty.
12485: ta nasèkade sɤm odìla za mɤ̀ka i za teglò
So everywhere I’ve gone it’s been pain and hardship.
12491: àrno ne sɤ̀m takà čorbadžìjski živòt živeàla
I haven’t lived the nice landowner’s life.
12499: pa segà čovèk me e ostàvil stanàa dvàese i trì godìni
And now it’s been twenty-three years [since] my husband’s left me.
12505: sɤm pri štèrka pri zèt zèt'a stanà čèteri gòdin
I’ve been with my daughter and son-in law, and [now] it’s been four years
12525: gerg’òvden tuk f selòtu gu praznùvahme
We used to celebrate St. George's day here in the village.
12533: jà kətu mlədèš kəto ergèni nie nàš'te mòmi
[When] I [was] a young man, we bachelors [together with] the local unmarried girls
12540: gu prəznùvəhə prəznùvaà go òpštu mlədeštà zbìraà se
celebrated it. All the young people celebrated it. They gathered together.
12546: kvo pretstavl'àvəše tùkə gerg’òvden gerg’èvden kətu du ùtre
So what was St. George's day like here? On the day after St. George's day –
12553: i se nə nə utsɛ̀jə gu tàm utsɛ̀ja gu i
then they sift it, they sift it there and [then]
12562: nə əlìn'd'en' hòd'əhm'e pu trì d'èn'ə nə l'uvàtkit'e igràehme hòru səs
On St. Elias’ day we went to the meadows for three days. We danced the horo, [wearing]
12570: gerg'èvden e nə šèsti nəlì a nə pèti večertà
St. George's day is on the 6th [of May], isn't it? So on the evening of the 5th,
12577: mumìte zbìra: cvet'à zdràvec eglìče è
the girls gather flowers – geraniums and primroses, [things that grow
12584: pu pu mesnostà udvɤnkə pu pulètu i gu pràva: nə č'itki̥
locally outdoors in the fields – and then they make bouquets of them.
12590: pràvejà gu f č'ùp sìčkite̥ mòmi puudɛ̀lno f
They used to make these [and put them] into a large pot. All the girls in each
12596: məəlà nə sɛ̀kujə məəlà puudɛ̀lnu č'ùp si pràva:
neighborhood do this, each neighborhood makes its own flower pot.
12603: i s kətu nətòpa: tuvà cvɛ̀te f č’ùpu i večertà gu upɛ̀va:
And when they put the flowers in the pot, in the evening they sing [and]
12607: upɛ̀va: upɛ̀va: prez noštà gu iznàs’a: udvɤ̀nkə
sing [and] sing over [each pot] and then at night they carry them outdoors
12615: də gu pečè lunàtə̥ nìə pə ergènite prez təvà vrɛ̀me
to bathe them in the moonlight. We bachelors, meanwhile,
12619: prez nuštà òdim dèbimè gu dɛ̀ sə gu
go out during the night to spy it out, [to find out] where they have –
12630: dɛ̀ sə gu ustìli č’ùpu i òdim i gu ukrədèm
where they have left the flower pot, and we go and steal it.
12638: ukrədème gu ut tìjə səjà i kətu ukrədèm na tàa məəlà č'ùpə
We steal it from them; when we steal the flower pot from that neighborhood,
12645: u drùgətə məəlà mumìte se rədùva: če ì sə ukrəlì
the girls in the other (= our) neighborhood cheer [us] that their [pot] got stolen.
12651: ergènetò sə ukrəlì ot onàa məəlà nə mumìte
The bachelors have robbed the girls in the other neighborhood of their
12658: č’ùpu i sega nèmə nə šò də pɛ̀jɛ i t'è
flower pot, and now there's nothing left to sing over. So [then] they,
12664: pud nɛ̀kəkəf nàčin nìe se prinùdime
[that is] we (the bachelors), find some way to give in,
12671: dədème sì gu pà tìjə pɛ̀ejɛ ìgra:
and we give it (= the flowerpot) back [to them], and then they sing and dance,
12678: фùsti səs ə ərmelìcit'e tɔ̀pən'ə č'ùkəš'e nìe rìpkəhme
folk aprons with decorative coins. The drum would beat and we would jump about
12686: kòlkutu mòž'eme trì d'èn'ə sigà kəkvò də kàž'e n'èmə n'è elìn'd'èn'
as much as we could for three days. Now what can I say? There’s neither St. Elias day
12695: n'èmə nì nì svir'àn nìtu igràjət nìtu nìštu nìe si sme bàbise nəuč'èni
nor is there music playing nor do they dance – nothing at all. We grannies are accustomed
12702: nəuč’èni svir'ànə də si igràime vìd'ehme si ràptətə hòd'əhme si nìe
to dancing to live music. We would see to our work, and we would go
12710: nə del'èku nəh rəvništà tàm si kus'ɛ̀hne četìrise tuvàrə zbìrəhme
far away to the plains, and there we’d mow, and gather up forty loads.
12716: s'ɛ̀nu si zbìrəhme səs mùl'ətətə tuvàr'əhme si s'ɛ̀nu duhòdəhmè si
We’d gather up the hay and load the hay onto the mules, and come home –
12725: nìe sìč'kit'e pràznici gi tàč'ehme sigà ni tàčet ž'ɛ̀lku zə mlàdit'e
We observed all the holidays. Now they don’t observe them. A pity for the young people!
12735: ìd'e pràznikət ìd'e əlìn'd'en' ìd'e p'ètrud'èn' ìd'e svità nid'ɛ̀l'ə
[and then] comes the holiday. St. Elias’ day, St. Peter’s day, Holy Sunday –
12745: əv'èlckutu vr'ɛ̀me beše drùgu hùbəvu beše v'ɛ̀rnu žə rukɔ̀t
It was different in the old days. It was good. Truly! [People] will say
12753: n'è e bilò lòšu bilò e hùbəvu hùbəvu beše si
that it wasn’t bad, it was good. [And I affirm that] it was good for us
12763: č'i si znàehme sìčkutu i məž'uv'ète si uvəž'ɛ̀vəhme i sìč'kutu si uvəž'ɛ̀vəhme
because we knew everything, we respected our men, and we respected everything.
12770: s'egà mlàdit'e pɔ̀lnumàlu də gu ustàv'ət decà sme iskùtvəli
Now the young people are messed up, they’ll abandon it. We raised our children!
12777: nè e imàlu nì bòlnici nè e imàlu nìkəkvìčku segà kəkvò
There weren’t [any] hospitals, they wasn’t anything.  And now what?
12786: òh nì bàbətə də uvəž'ɛ̀vət nì d'àdutu də uvəž'ɛ̀vət nìe ràptime segà
Ohhh! [They’re not about to] respect either Grandma or Grandpa. “We’re working now,
12794: pərì si ìməme i stàrite hi zərìtəhə àh dà hi rìtnat
we’ve got our own money.” And they kicked out the old folks. Well, let them kick them out!
12802: tùkə nəgòre ìməme m ənə pə pə pərəklìsč'ek sv'etì dùh sə kàzvaš'e
Up here we have a – a chapel, it was called the [chapel of the] Holy Spirit.
12813: im'ɛ̀š'e hòru gul'ɛ̀mu tùkə nə pərəklìsč'ek' udgòr'e hòru sə pàk vɔ̀rnehme
There was a big dance up there at the chapel. We came back [to] the dance.
12819: hɔ̀ pàk huràtə hɔ̀ pàk hurà də igràime i də sə sm'èjem
Ah the dances! Ah, let’s dance horo again, and laugh
12824: i də sə vèselìm'e segà kəkvɔ̀ n'ìtu v'èselu ìmə n'ìtu nìštu
and rejoice. What is there now? There’s nothing joyful, [there’s] nothing at all.
12833: spumìnəmè si mìnəlìte ràbuti kəkvì sə bìli nə tr'èpeznìk' jɛ̀den'e tùr'əhə
We remember what things of the past were like. They piled food on the festive table,
12839: kərd'ɔ̀ pət'ètə i s m'ɛ̀huve gul'ɛ̀mi im'ɛ̀hme
we had cabbage, potatoes, and big skin bags [of cheese].
12846: vɔ̀rhəhm'e səs mùl'etətə ədìn hərmàn izvɔ̀rhəme gu
We threshed with mules. We finished threshing [what was on] one threshing floor,
12853: dvà hərmànə izvɔ̀rhəhme hɔ̀ pč'en'ìcə hɔ̀ uv'ès hɔ̀ càrev'ìcə fəsùl'
two threshing floors. Here’s the wheat! Here’s the oats! Here’s the corn! The beans!
12859: i gu nəvɔ̀ršvəhme i gu zbìrəme i gà v'ɛ̀e v'ɛ̀ter vejɛ̀hme gu
And we’d thresh it [all] and gather it up. And when the wind blows we’d toss it up
12864: nə veterɔ̀t i gu tvàrehme nə mùletətə i si gu dukàrvəhme
to the wind.  And we loaded it onto the mules and brought it home.
12874: nə bəìr'ə hòdehne dərvà də ber'ème suhàrje suhàrje sùhi dərvà suròvi
We went to the hills to gather wood, windfall, dry wood, and green wood.
12881: dukàrəme si gi gur'ɛ̀hme si gi nə wògən' tùkə bəž'ɛ̀ si im'ɛ̀hne
We bring them back and burn them on the fire. We had a fireplace here,
12889: ednò gul'ɛ̀mu k'utùč'e še si tùrehme àjde tùrehme də kəkètə hàrkumətə
a big log. We’d put them here and here you go! We’d put the kettle to boil.
12897: svàdbə sə pràveš'e ìdehə nəj nəpr'èš' nə junàkuvətə
[How] the wedding was celebrated: They went – first of all the hero’s (= groom’s) home.
12905: ut.tam tɔ̀rnəhə ìd'ehə u nev'ɛ̀stətə zɔ prekrìehà jə zəp'ɛ̀ehə
They set out from there, went to the bride’s to –  They covered her hair and began to sing:
12912: jèlə sə svìvə prevìvə mumà s ròdum pruštàvəj
“The fir tree bends down, bends over; the girl takes leave of her family, [singing]
12922: stàrə màjč'ice d'ètu mə si kùtilə d'èv'et gudi d'èv'et m'ɛ̀sečku
‘Dear old mother, you carried me nine – nine sweet months
12929: nə sərc'è i trì gudìnki nə rəc'è izved'ɛ̀hə jə i tìdəhə tugà
next to your heart and three sweet years in your arms.’ ” They’d lead her out and then go
12934: f č'ɔ̀rkvətə venč'ɛ̀hə jə n'èməš'e drùguš' ne putpìsvəne
to the church [where] they married her. There wasn’t any signing [of certificates] back then,
12941: venč'ɛ̀vəhə hi drùguš f č'ɔ̀rkvətə id'ɛ̀hə i putpìsvəhà i
they just married them. They went to the church and they registered them,
12959: zàednu pɛ̀eme i nìe s nìh nə òru ìgrəme pɛ̀eme
and we sing together with them. We dance the horo together, and sing.
12966: slet təvà kugà gu rəzvàla: trì dènɤ sədì č'ùpə
After that, when they take [it] apart – the flowerpot sits there three days –
12971: təkà kugà gu rəzvàla: i slet trìte d'ènə večertà
when they take it apart – after the third day in the evening
12975: kəto rəzvàləjə č'ùpu i prɤ̀ska: tàm
when they take the flowerpot apart, [everyone] there gets sprinkled [with
12979: mlədeštà ženìte se zbìrə: dètu slùša: dètu pɛ̀e:
water] – young people and women who listen and sing – they gather around
12985: prɤ̀ska: sus vudàtə i mladeštà i mumìte
and everyone gets sprinkled with water – young people, unmarried girls,
12990: i ženìte i i xòrətə kuìtu gi slùša: glèda:
and married women, people who are watching and listening.
12996: i təkà se rəzvàlijə təka prəznùvaja gerg'èvden
And that's how they took it apart, how they celebrated St. George's Day in
13003: nə vrɛ̀metu trì čètiri pèt dènə ìgra: pɛ̀aja vesèleja sе̥
the old days. They'd dance, sing, and make merry for three, four, five days.
13024: nèmaše i četvṛ̀to nèmaše i četvṛ̀to
[I] didn’t [even get to] fourth, I didn’t [get to] fourth.
13033: [Just] enough to keep my eyes open.
13042: togàj bèše stòka mìlo stòka ìmaše nì te pràštat
Back then there was livestock, dear one – livestock. They didn’t send you
13050: na učìlište od učìlišteto dòjde cɤrvèno izvèstie
to school. [Then] from the school would come a red notice (warning of a fine):
13057: ùtre da se jàviš mène me ne pùštat
“Tomorrow you must appear!” [But] they didn’t let me go,
13066: trèbe da se pùštat stòkata drùgi dèn pà ispràtat izvèstie
because the livestock had to be let out. The next day again a notice,
13073: i jà ìda tàm da zapìšad dèka səm se javìla
and I go there [long enough] for them to note down that I had appeared,
13081: And you were absent the whole week.
13089: tòku tòku u nedèlata jà dvà pati jà edìn pɤ̀t
That’s all [there was]. Either once or twice in a week.
13099: Just enough for there not to be a “red notice”.
13105: tòku carvèno izvèstie da nèma əə štò da pràime i ostarèxme
[Just] so much – to be no red notice. Yes. What can we do? And we’ve gotten old.
13109: udnemožèxme ne mòga vòda da si dònesa ne mòga
We’ve lost the ability to cope. I can’t carry water [any more], I can’t
13115: dṛ̀va da s cèpa ne mòga da gi dònesa
chop wood [any more], I can’t bring it (the wood) in, [I have to do it]
13126: èla de èla èla èla èla
Come on over! Come here, come here, come here, come here.
13138: zàpoznaj se tùka sos tìja xòra
13145: What have they come here [to do]?
13150: è de onì če ti kàžat
13155: à da ne doòždat kaj nàs
Well, they shouldn’t come here among us …
13176: [laughter]  sàmo tùka zapìsvat nèšto nèma ne tràžat pàri
[laughter] They’re only recording something, they’re not asking for money.
13197: a nìe nè ne znàeme prìkaski
13201: Ah, you know, first name, last name –
13212: sàmo da si govòrim be nìšto drùgo ne tràžim
We’re just [here] to talk, you know? We’re not looking for anything else.
13236: ja utìduf tàm ìməše təkìə l'ùde dètu mi pròba: glasɤ̀
[So] I went there. There were these people who were testing my voice
13239: with a thermo-fork ( = tuning fork), I think they call it.
13246: aha termatòne màj i tìja vìka: slùšaj mumčè
Hm, probably a thermo-fork. So these people said, “Listen, fellow,
13253: tì si ut pruvìncijàtə i mòže də tè e sràm
you’re a country boy, so maybe you are feeling shy.”
13261: vìkəm əmi smuštàvəm se sràm me e nəlì vìkəm
“Well,” I said, “I’m a bit confused, so I guess I’m feeling shy,” I said.
13266: əmə nàs ni trebùva təkɤ̀f glàs kətu tèbe
“But,” [they said], “we need the kind of voice you [have]. ”
13274: i pòsle mi rèkuə da da revà kat magàre vìkə še nəberèš
And then they told me to – to bray like a donkey. [One] said, “Take
13281: təkɤ̀f vɤ̀zdux v gɤrdìte tə sə sè.ednò revèš
this much air into your lungs, and then [let it] all [out] just as if you’re braying
13290: məgàre tì si sèlski čuvèk znàaš kàk revè məgàre
[like a] donkey. You’re a country person, you know how a donkey brays.”
13298: əbe jà i bɛ̀h vɛ̀rnu bɛ̀h mnògu gul'àm stò i trì kilugràmə
Well, I was – I was really very big. A hundred and three kilos
13304: bɛ̀h gòl i glàs ìmah gràdi ìmah
buff naked, I was – and I had [a big] voice. I had [strong] lungs.
13309: nìtu pìeh nìtu pùših čiz glàs be
I neither drank nor smoked, [so I had] a clean, pure voice.
13318: i kətu zèməh kət se izrevà vɤ̀tre kət məgàre tìjə jà rèvə
So when I let go and brayed like a donkey, [but] indoors, these – I was braying
13326: kət məgàre tàm zàlətə kuìtu xòrə se b’àə sɤbràli
like a donkey there in this hall – and these people who'd gathered,
13334: i mɤžè i ženì ut tanc'òretu tèə rìpa: tòlku visòku
men and women from the dance troupe, they are jumping so high.
13339: i jà si mìslə nə əkɤ̀lə vìkəm jà səm ùləf
And I thought to myself, I [may] be a fool
13343: šò vi rèvə kət məgàre əmə i tìjə
to be braying to you [all] like a donkey, but these people
13348: ne sɤ̀ mnògu ìtri što skàča:
who jump around [a lot] aren't very smart [either].
13357: i i nə drùgijɤ dèn vednàga zìma: rešènie də me usvubòda:
Well, [already] the next day, they decided to release me
13364: ut təvà pudelènie də me pràta: də ùčə də ìdə də ùčə
from my [military] unit and send me to study, to go and study
13369: s'è.ednò muzikàlnə əkədèmijə də də me pràta:
at some kind of music academy. They [wanted] to – to send me
13374: də ùčə vednàgə vɤf vɤf učìlišč'e də me ùča:
right off to study in – in a school where they would teach me
13383: də stànə təkɤ̀f òperen pev'èc i tòə čuvèk sɤ̀štijə pɤk
to become some sort of opera singer. And this man, the same one
13391: ud gràdevu bɛ̀še punèže bɛ̀še naš zeml'àk i bɛ̀še mnògu
from Gradevo, he was, you know, from our area, and he was really
13398: merəklìjə càlijɤ živòt č’e pumìneš rəhàt
keen [on the idea]. “You’ll live in comfort the rest of your life,” [he said]
13403: i aku ne mè uslùšəš segà da se izùčiš
“and if you don’t do what I say now, if you don’t go off to study,
13408: càl živòt k’e stràdəš i təkà si stənà
then all your life you’ll be sorry.” And that’s what happened.
13413: I didn't listen to the man. Well – [what can you do?]
13415: [Do you still thresh this way now?]
13419: nie segà si gu pòlzvame harmànɤ əmi segà
[Yes,] we use the threshing field now [too]. Now
13425: nə ərmàn kàk sə òdi nìe i segà si gu pòlzvəme tuvà
when we go to the threshing field, we use it [the same way] now.
13431: i segà si žɤ̀neme tùk pu čàsnijɤ sèktur si pusɛ̀eme
And even now, when we reap what we've sown on [our] private land –
13439: ečemìk uvès rɤ̀š vrɤšème gu sɤs kòne rəsfrɤ̀l'əme snòpite
barley, oats, and rye – we thresh it with horses. We spread the sheaves
13445: pu zeml'àtə vrɤzème dvà kun'à əlì trì əlì čètiri
around on the ground, we rope up two horses  – or three or four,
13451: zəvìsimo kòlku krəstàčki snòpe tùrim nə nə ərmànɤ
depending on how many sheaves we've spread out over the threshing floor.
13458: berème se tr i žèni i màže tri čètiri pèt šèz dùši
We gather together, women and men – three, four, five, six people,
13463: vrɤšème cèlijɤ dèn uvrɤšème gu udlɤ̀čime
and we thresh all day long. We finish the threshing, and we separate it,
13470: slàmətə nəstrənì žìttò gu zberème nə ednà kupà
the straw is on one side, and we gather the grain up into a single stack.
13475: vɛ̀emè gu pòsle s lupàtə i se udvɛ̀və žìtutu
After that, we winnow it with a shovel. You toss the grain up in the air,
13483: nə stərn nə ednò mestò pàdə žìtutu òti e tèšku pək pl'ɛ̀vətə
and the wheat falls to the si- in one area, because it's heavier. And the chaff
13488: bɛ̀ga dùvə vɛ̀terɤ vəf.stranì i təkà gu udvɛ̀eme
flies away, [because] the wind is blowing from the side. And that's [how]
13493: uvrɤšème gu udvɛ̀eme nətùrəme f čuvàlite
it's winnowed. We thresh it, and winnow it, and put it into sacks,
13498: pòsle mèleme nə vrèmetò gu jədɛ̀hme zə hlɛ̀p
and then we grind it. In the old days we ate it as bread,

14884: sìčko če izmṛ̀znat i dṛvèta si onì i dòsta issahnàa
everything, even the trees, will freeze. They’ve already withered quite a bit.
14891: dṛvètata issahnàa kajsìi čerèši sos plodò si isahnà
The trees have withered, the apricot and cherry trees, and their fruit.
14902: nè ne mòže isahnà si̥ precəftèa se raššumìja se issahnà
No! We couldn’t. It withered. The blooms fell off, they leafed out, and then dried up.
14909: Burned up – straight out. [Good only] for burning.
14914: əmxəm [sigh] a kartòfki sèexte li ili nè
Uh huh. [sigh] And did you plant any potatoes? Or not?
14925: làni na tovà mestènce štò posadìme tùka što sì sàdime izvadìme
Last year, from what we planted in this spot that we’re planting, we got
14938: dèvet kasètki kartòfi sà sɤ̀štoto mèsto posadìme
nine crates of potatoes. Now, we planted the same area
14948: e tovà e bez dɤ̀š nìštò nìšto i nèma i za sème
Well, that’s how it is without rain. Nothing! Nothing! Not even for seed!
14956: za sème trèbva se kupùva pa sa dèset lèva kìloto
You have to buy for seed, and now that’s ten levs a kilo.
14961: Where’s the end to it, [I ask you]?
14969: skɤ̀po skɤ̀po ne znàm ako ìskat decàta da kòpat da sàdat
Expensive. Expensive. I don’t know – if the children want, let them dig up and plant.
14975: od mène tòku vìkam jà sam tùka da pàza
I’ve had it. [Now] I say I’m here to make sure
14984: da nèma do pràgo trèva e tùka tṛ̀sa ə trevàta da nèma
that grass doesn’t get to the threshold. I weed away the grass so it's not
14990: do pràgo òda li si jà trevàta če dòjde do tùka
at the threshold. Once I go, the grass will come up to here.
15003: And I see that you don’t even have any livestock.
15011: nìšto nèmam tovà sam samìčka štò me glèdaš
I don’t have anything. I’m alone here just as you see me.
15015: i i i i màčka nèma dàže
And – and – and – and you don’t even have a cat.
15025: nèma nèma màčki màčki doòdat mlògo
None, none. Cats –a lot of cats come ...
15033: tùka màčki pìš zatvòreno ta kùče ne mòže da ulèzne
… here. Cats. [But I keep the door] shut so that dogs can’t get in.
15037: jà pa kùčeta mnògo mràza nèču gi
I really hate dogs, I don’t want them.
15042: i òt gi mràziš tìja psètata
And why do you hate these dogs?
15048: No [reason to like them]! They’ve got a lot of fleas.
15080: nìko mu ne dàva ni xlèp ni kadè òdi tè takà
Nobody gives him bread or anything [at all]. Wherever he goes, it’s the same.
15167: [What did you do as a shepherd?]
15175: mi kətu ufč'àr' rəbòtih pəs'àh ufc'ète i iskàrvəhne xùbəvi jàgnetə
I worked as a shepherd. I used to graze the sheep, and we raised nice lambs.
15182: gl'èdəne xùbəvu ž'ivòtnite i dàvəhne pruizvòtsvu nə nə pretprijɛ̀tietu nə a
We cared for the animals well, and gave the "products" to the firm, to the ah-
15188: àpekàtu nə t'èkezes'ètu punəč'àlu əmə i kətu č'àsnik d'e
agrarian complex, the collective farm, in principle. Even as a private [owner]
15195: pàk si beh ufč'àr' sl'et tvàskə kətu se už'ènix stànəx zeml'ed'èlec
I was a shepherd also. After that – when I got married I became a farmer.
15203: nàč'i zemed'èlie pòčnəɣ də rəbòt'e i ràbutine   du ednò izv'èsnu vr'ɛ̀me
That is, I began to work in agriculture; we worked [at that] a certain time.
15212: sl'et tvà pres č'etìres i dev'ètə gudìnə brəzùvəne t'èkezes'ètu vl'àzəne vəf
After that, in ’49 [when] we formed the collective farm, and entered into
15219: t'èkezes'ètu i pòčnəhne də rəbòtim zədrùžnu tàm i vəf n'ègu rəbòtix
the collective farm, we began to work there collectively and I worked there
15225: kətu brigədìr pɤ̀rvite gudìni sl'et tvàskə i pretsedàtel' nə t'èkezes'ètu b'èx
as a supervisor the first years. After that I was the chair of the collective farm.
15232: vəf t'èkezes'ètu tugàvə [cough] pɤ̀rvite gudìni sr'ɛ̀štəne gul'ɛ̀mi trùdnusti
During the first years in the collective we encountered great difficulties,
15239: nəlì tugàvə beš'e nìsku plət'èn trùduvijə dèn
[as] at that time a working day was paid very poorly.
15240: [Кажи ми за овчарството и такива работи.]
[Tell me about sheepherding and such things.]
15247: punəč'àlu nìe ufc'ɛ̀te kətu gi pòčneš ùtrin š'e stànem
Generally we – you start out with sheep in the morning: we’ll get up,
15252: š'e gi š'e gi nəxrànime š'e i na š'e i nəxrànime
We’ll – we’ll feed them, we’ll feed them,
15259: š'e udlɤ̀č'ime àgnetə̥tə ud'èlnu š'e dəd'èm nə màjkite də jədɤ̀t
we’ll take the lambs off separately, we’ll give food to the mothers,
15262: pu màlku punəč'àlu sl'et tvàskə nə àgneətə pàk dàvəhne
a little at the beginning, and then we gave [food] to the lambs.
15268: i gi pùštəhne nə pàš'e predìmnu tùkə se se dəržɤ̀t dərž'àə ž'ivòtnite
And [then] we let them out to graze. Here the animals were mostly kept
15275: nə nə pàš'e i bène trìmə dùš'i rəbòtnici edìnijət ustàvəš'e pri àgneətə
out in the pasture. There were three of us workers. One stayed with the lambs,
15283: drùgijət ustàvəš'e zəbìrəš'e ednɤ̀tə surìjə ufc'è nə dv'à surìi gi del'ɛ̀ne
another drove one herd of sheep – we separated the sheep into two herds –
15289: drùgijəd drùgətə surìjə ednò puč'ìstvəš'e kuš'àrətə tàm
and the other, the other herd. One was cleaning out the sheep pen there
15297: hràneš'e ˀàgneətə nə.òb'et št'ɛ̀še də i dukàrə də gi i duìme
feeding the lambs. At noon he'd take  them to [where] we milk [the sheep].
15304: dujàhne gi prenàs'əhme ml'əkòtu səs məgàretə vəf s'èlu du pùntə
We milked them, and took the milk on donkeys to the village, to the collection point
15312: kəd'ètu beše vəf s'èlutu i təkà prutìč'əš'i cal c'ɛ̀lijə sezòn
that was [located] in the village. And so went the whole season
15316: [What other animals did you care for?]
15323: əm drùgi ž'iòtni təkà surìi nè səm gl'èdəl
I didn’t look after any other animals in herds like that.
15333: tì si bilà takòva nàči si bilà tàm pastìrka
So you were – you were a shepherdess?
15354: červèn pipèr màlku tàm č ìdeš i če tòpiš če rùčaš
a bit of red pepper, and off you go! You dip [bread in pepper] for lunch;
15363: če edèš vòda jà ìma jà nèma takà bèše
you’ll eat whether there’s water or not – [and] that’s how it was.
15370: a ə znàči ta takìva bànici takìva ràboti
So then banitsa, and such things –
15381: for someone to put banitsa [in] my [lunch sack]!!  [laughter]
15391: [laughter] lèbec lèbec tvṛ̀t lèbec tòe se mèseše u ponedèlnik
[laughter]. Bread! Bread! Hard bread! It got made on Monday,
15398: pa u drùgijo ponedèlnik po ednà sèdmica lèp se pečèše
and then on the next Monday. Bread got baked [only] once a week.
15404: kàk se pe mèseše kàk se pečèše lèbo
How did they make – how did they bake bread?
15412: èe dòma si se mèsi si ìma fùrna domàšna fùrna
Ah, you knead it at home, there’s the outside oven, the oven of [our] house.
15418: kàk se mèsi tɤ̀j otnačàlo da ni raskàžeš
How do you make it? Tell us from the beginning,
15422: [starting] from the beginning when you take –
15431: Using a sieve. There was a particular –
15435: Is that how you called it?
15447: sìto otsèe se i se naprài na sredàta dùpka tùri se sòl
A sieve. You sift [the flour], you make a hole in the middle, and you put in salt.
15450: What did you sift it into?
15461: speciàlno pà nòštvi takà se kàzva nòštvi
A particular kneading trough, that’s how you call it – kneading trough.
15469: i togàj segà se sos majà mèsi togà bèše sos kvasèc
And then – now you knead it with yeast, but back then it was with starter.
15476: kvasèc odnèkade zèma od nèkoja ženà pa go pòdmesa
I get the starter from somewhere, from some woman, and then begin to knead.
15487: onà stàne pòveče tùri i òtsej tàm kòlko bràšno trèbe da è
It gets bigger, you put it in and then sift out as much flour as you need,
15496: zàmesi onò skìsne i go ràzmesi tè kòku pàničkata
and start to knead. It ferments, and you knead it into the shape of a bowl,
15501: na daskì kato gòri fùrnata ìzmeti ìščisti
on boards. And when the oven is hot you sweep it out, clean it out.
15505: s kvò ja izmìtaxte i isčìstvaxte
What did you sweep it out and clean it out with?
15511: na edìn na ednò dṛvò golèmo parcàl
With a – with a big piece of wood [and] a rag.
15520: golèm izmetè se iščìsti se tè takà nafṛ̀l'aj lèbo
A big [one]. You sweep it out, clean it out like that, and throw in the bread!
15528: vràta si ìma zàtvori zàlepi tàm kòku se pečè
There’s a door – you close it, seal it there for as long as [the bread needs to] bake,
15536: òtvori ìzvadi nàredi na daskìte zàvij pa drùgata sɤ̀buta
open [it], take [the bread] out, arrange [it] on boards, and cover [it] up. Then next Saturday –
15540: And how many [loaves of] bread did you make each time?
15552: kakvò sa tvṛ̀t netvṛ̀t če se rùčka [laughter]
… which are [to be fed]. Hard or not, it’ll be eaten! [laughter]
15571: òx jadàt ta sàmo da ìma
Ohh! They eat [it]! There just has to be some!
15588: jadàt e tùka komšìkata ònja dèn puštìla golèmoto svinčè
They eat it. The other day a neighbor let out a big pig,
15596: ta kato pognà kokòškite [sound gesture] onà òka onà òka
and it took off after the hens – (sound gesture = "look out!") – she's shouting, shouting!
15604: i a grabnà a za nogàta ne možè če a z izedèše
It grabbed the leg of a hen that couldn’t [escape], and was about to eat it up!
15608: ama ne ì li strošì nogàta
But didn’t it break its leg?
15615: ne možè da ja stròši onà m otṛčà bṛ̀že
It wasn’t able to break it. It (the hen) ran quickly away from it (the pig)
15620: ta a udarì ta a puštì
then it (the hen) struck it (the pig), and then it (the pig) let it (the hen) go.
15626: ne možè da a stròši a če ja izedèše
It wasn’t able to break it (the hen’s leg). [Otherwise] it would have eaten it up.
15634: tò ìmame drùgi živòtni nìe kàzvad gi pòrove
We have [these] other animals. People call them polecats.
15642: nòšno vre vèčer kato vèče si se prìbera
[They come at] night. In the evening when I come home,
15649: zàtvora si vratàta i kato ìzgasa làmbata i òn se prefṛ̀li
I close the gate, and when I turn out the light, it hurls itself
15655: tùka prez vratàta i če si se issère ìli tùka
here over the gate, and it’ll do a good shit either here
15664: ìli tùka da mòga da go vìda če e minàl
or here – so that I can see that it’s been by.
15671: dà kokòška pìle jajcè à gi ne pribrà
Yes. Hens, chicks, eggs – If I didn’t secure them away
15676: and it found them – [it’s] curtains [for them]!
15682: i idnò vrème pàk ìmaše li takìva pòrove
Did there used to be such polecats in the old days?
15689: pa imàlo e imàlo ama kòj gi e zabeleževàl
There were! There were! But who ever cared about them?
15694: à ne sɤ̀ gi kato zème edìn
15703: togà sme čuvàli pò nògu stòka pò nògu
Back then we kept more livestock, more [than now].
15713: segà po pet šes kukòški pògledni segà tàa a nèma
But now [just] five or six chickens each. Look around now, and it’s not here –
15724: nàmeri kogà krìlo nèkade nòga nèkade tovà elì zakòle a
find sometimes a wing here, a leg there. Either it’s killed [and eaten] it,
15733: ispìe i kṛftà i a ostàvi cèlatə̥ a kṛftà ispìe
and drunk its blood, or it’s left it whole, and [just] drunk the blood.
15753: mnògo ama e čèrno ama e čèrno ama e čèrno
Very [bad]. And it’s black – and it’s black – and it’s black!
15760: tè takà e čèrno kato go poglèdneš ləštì
So black that when you look at it, it shimmers.
15769: nògu mu bilà skɤ̀pa kòžata kòj kakò gu ubìe nèkoe
Its hide is supposedly very valuable – anyone who kills one
15774: fednàga go odère i mu prudàva kòžata
skins it immediately and sells its hide.
15780: ne gì li lov'àxa ednò vrème tìja
Didn’t they hunt them in the old days, these – ?
15787: kədè če go fàneš onò nòšno vrème
Well, how are you going to catch one?! It’s nocturnal!
15793: [It comes out] at night, not [during] the day.
15796: [Couldn’t you use] some sort of trap?
15802: kòj če mu i da tùriš kapàn ne gò znàeš
Who’ll [get] him [like that]? Even if you lay a trap, you don’t know
15808: kadè da o če mìne sèkade mìne
where it’ll pass by. It goes everywhere!
15815: tè tùka kat dòjde da sère i pùf
So it just comes, and shits, and poof!
15820: a kòj če go jà dodèka de stàna òn
Ah, who will – By the time I get up, it –
15826: è go kačùva si se u dṛvòto kačùva si se
See, it climbs up a tree. It climbs up
15831: i po čeremìdite kačùva si se sèkade
roof tiles, too. It climbs up everywhere!
15837: kràvite gl'èdəm nìə krəvàrite si ìməš'e ud'èlnu krəvàri
I tend cows. We cowherds – there was a separate [group] of cowherds
15841: kuìtu se zənimàvəhə səs krəvef'èrmətə i tè tàm nəlì
who were busy at the cow farm – and they, you know,
15848: lɤ̀č'exə tel'ètətə xrànexə gi ə edìnijət ədìnijət də kàž'e
took the calves from [their mothers] and fed them. One – that is one –
15853: hòdeš'e səs kràvite a drùgijə ustàvəš'e pri tel'ètətə xrànexə gi
went with the cows, and the other stayed with the calves [and] fed them.
15854: [What sorts of occupations were there in the village?]
15860: ami tìjə zənəjàtite vəf s'èlutu sə t'àh elì vəv ž'ivutnuvɤ̀svutu̥
Well, the occupations in the villages are these: either in animal husbandry
15866: š'e̥ si̥ ufč'àr' jelì š'e si vəf pul'evɤ̀svutu č'ufč'ìe
– you’re a shepherd – or you’re in field labor, a land worker,
15873: d'ètu mu vìkəme nìe pu.nàš'emu urèd də kàž'em ž'ènət
as we say in our [speech]. For example they plow, they reap,
15879: vòzet snòpetu nə vərš'àč'kətə gu vərš'àhə e
they transport sheaves, they thresh them at the threshing machine,
15884: e təkà prutìčəše ràbutətə vəf pul'evɤ̀svu
and that’s how work progressed in field agriculture.
15889: ìməš'e səfs'èm màlku punəč'àlu ìməš'e biul'à mnògu
There were very few. At the beginning there were many water buffaloes.
15894: predì də sə ubrəzùvə t'èkezes'ètu dukətu bene č'àsni
Before the collective farm was formed, when we were private [landowners],
15896: biul'à ìməš'e kunè ìməš'e kràvi ìməš'e təkìvə
there were water buffaloes, horses, cows, there were these –
15900: tugàvə ìməš'e bìuli mnògu kràvi ìmaše
at that time there were many water buffaloes. There were cows –
15907: kòne ìməš'e svìni ìməš'e pàk təkà pu surìjki surìjki d'ètu ìməš'e
There were horses, there were pigs in small herds, these small herds –
15911: č'àsni surìjki ìməš'e mu vìkəme nìe ìməš'e dubìtək
private herds as we call them, there were livestock.
15928: nə mnògutu grùpətə ž'ivòtni mu vìkəme mu dùməme svì
When there are many, a group of animals, we call that pi-
15930: svìni da i ìməš'e živòtni mnògu ubàč'e sl'et tvàskə
Pigs, yes. And there were a lot of animals. However after that
15936: i xòrətə ispàdnəxə lìpsəhə izmr'àhə d'ètu ìmə ednɤ̀ dùmə
people fell into poverty, they disappeared, they died out, as they say,
15939: pək i živòtnite i tìə si
15944: òx mi tɤ̀j səs svìrki i s kəvàl':i svìrehne
Well, we did play [instruments], these small pipes and end-blown flutes.
15951: svìreə də kàž'em ufčàrite əmə tuvà e nè e n'àkujə
That is, the shepherds played [them]. But that’s not some kind of,
15956: təkà vərì tə si turulìkə pudir ufc'ɛ̀te də sə zəwəvl'àvə
[a shepherd] walks along, chirps after his sheep to amuse himself.
15969: dà katèri se katèri se è tàa visòkata kɤ̀šta
Yes! It climbs! It climbs! [You see] that tall house there?
15978: tè tàm sme gi gledàli tè tè tàm po
We saw them over there. There, over –
15984: u cṛnìcata po cṛnìcata na čeremìdite dà živòtno
up the mulberry, up the mulberry, and onto the roof tiles. Yes. A beast.
15994: živòtno ednì gi vìkat pa bèlki pòro što è
A beast. [There’s] some others they call martens. The one that’s a polecat –
16003: òn e čìsto čèren bèlkata e tùka e bèla
it is pure black. The marten is white, here –
16011: tùka kor ə šìjata tùka i nadzàde bèlo
Here on the – on the throat here, and in back it’s white.
16018: i vìkaja bèlka onà bilà pò lòša
And they call it a marten. It’s supposed to be worse.
16024: On its back it’s black. Brown.
16035: təkìvə svi sviràč'i sme bilì nìe səs svìrki kəvàl':i
We were all that kind of musicians, with small pipes and end-blown flutes.
16041: i gàjdi ìməš'e nə n'àkuj tə svìrexə vətrešnustɤ̀ gəjdərž'ìi
Some had bagpipes, and played them; bagpipe players [were] in the interior,
16042: štòtu jà i kəde grənč'àr xòdih nə tàm tàm ìməš'e mumč'ètə
because when I went to Granichar, there were boys there
16050: kuìtu svìrehə gàjdi nè e gàjdə gàjdə səs
playing bagpipes. No, not the [simple] bagpipe but the bagpipe with –
16055: kəvàl':i i kəvàl':i i də gàjdətə bəškɤ̀ i kəvàlət
End-blown flutes, end-blown flutes. A bagpipe is one thing, an end-blown flute –
16056: e dà de gàjdətə bəškɤ̀ i kəvàlət bəškɤ̀
Yes indeed. A bagpipe is one thing and an end-blown flute is another.
16064: lɤ̀tə jə pràine ut dərv'ètə nəkuvàni prɤ̀k':e i slet prək
We make the [sheepfo]lds from wood. Sticks pounded [into the ground] and after the sti–
16070: tvàskə pukrìtə s rəž'ànkə i vɤ̀tre pràeni pregràdi zə də mòž'em də
it’s covered with rye straw, and inside we make dividers so we can –
16075: də sə rəspredel'èni ufc'ɛ̀te pu pu.ud'èlnu kuìtu sə uàgnenite bəškɤ̀
to separate the sheep out. The ones who’ve had lambs [go] in one place,
16080: [And what do you make the sheepfolds out of?]
16086: ne ud dɤ̀rven məter'àl dɤ̀rven məter'àl sə prài səs
[We ma]ke [it] from lumber. It’s made from lumber, with ...
16096: tìjə kəšlì sə pràvehə tugàs sə izbìrəhə pustàrumu
Sheepfolds were made back then – they'd choose according to the old custom.
16100: ednò vr'ɛ̀me usòbenu tugàvə gi izbìrəhə nə təkìvə mistà
Especially back then, they would choose them to be in places
16106: kujìtu sə tòpli kujìtu sə təkà duvàdət nə nə zàvet
that were warm, that were such, that faced – as a shelter
16112: ud vɛ̀truvetu də ne gì fàštət vɛ̀truvetu i kəš'lìte sə pràehə
from the wind, such that the wind wouldn’t get in. They built them
16115: primətìvni pàk	primətìvni sə ne sɤ̀ kətu segà də kàž'em
in a primitive manner. They were primitive, not like now, so to speak,
16119: dèt gi pràjət tuvà primətìvni sə ednɤ̀ kəšlɤ̀ š'e ìmə də kàž'em
as they make them, but primitive. There’ll be in one sheepfold, let’s say,
16129: zə də fkàrəš č'etirì:se pedesè ufcè segàšni ə pək tugàvə fkàrvəš'e
[room] to get in forty or fifty of today’s sheep. But back then you got in
16134: četrì:se pedesè kòzi flìzəhə ə ufc'ɛ̀te si lež'àə vɤ̀nkə
– forty or fifty goats went in, while the sheep lay down outside

18449: i às ne mɤ̀ sə ne mì sə žuv'èi v'èki [laughter]
I don’t feel like – I’ve had enough of living already [laughter].
18468: i pàk si ut’ìvət ìmət si blòk tàm
and then go away again. They have an apartment there.
18472: mumìčitu im b'èši pri t'àx t'è gu z’èə sigà
Their daughter was with them there. Now they’ve taken her
18476: utidòə pu mur'è i às səmìčkə
and gone off to the seacoast. And I’m [here] alone.
18480: Do you manage to do everything here all alone?
18486: I see that it’s very well cared for [here], very clean.
18490: əmči mitɤ̀ si čìstu si e
Well, I sweep, and so it’s clean.
18495: t'à e nə dividis'è gudìni nəlì vi kəzàx nèštu̥
She’s ninety years old, didn’t I tell you something [about that]?
18501: ə devedes’è gudìni pudir idìn m'èsic gi nəvɤ̀ršəm
In a month I’ll be ninety.
18511: devedes'è gudìni də ne è krəkɤ̀ sigà də mə bulì tɤ̀j
Ninety years. And if my leg didn’t hurt here now,
18515: rəcèti mi i tè əkɤ̀lə mi òšte ne sɤ̀m gu zəgùbilə
[or] my arms – [at least] I still haven’t lost my mind.
18525: əmə krəkɤ̀ mə bɤ̀rkə bulì mə
But my leg gives me trouble. It hurts.
18533: àbe kəd'è də vərɤ̀ i nə dòktur
Ah! Where [is there] a doctor I [can] go to?
18534: segà čàkəj zə svàdbətə də vi kàžə
So now, wait [and] I’ll tell you about weddings.
18536: slet tùj še vi kàžə zə cɤ̀rkvətə i kràj
After that I’ll tell you about the church, and then that’s all.
18541: a kuètu sə čùdite màlku zə cɤ̀rkvətə
Those things you were wondering about, a bit concerning the church.
18543: How do they do a wedding ceremony without the church?
18546: nè še zakačìm tùj ne flìzə segà  vəf
No, let’s put that up, it doesn’t fit inside.
18551: kàktu vi ub'əsn'àvəm tò e ud'èlnu konkrètno ìdət sigà
… as I was explaining to you, that’s separate. In actuality now they go –
18556: osòbenus nàšte dɤržàxə tùkə z'èmət pod nàem kunè
and our people were especially insistent on this – they rent horses.
18561: kun'ète gi kàg də ti kàžə səs ednɤ̀ dùmə pisk'ùli
And the horses – how shall I say it in a word? They’re tasseled.
18565: Here, [you know] what a tassel is?
18568: vrɤ̀zvət im kəkvò li ni štèš
And they tie on them whatever you want.
18575: à pudàrəci i gi z'èmət i trɤ̀gvət sigà kulònə c'àlə kòjtu ìskə
Right. And they take gifts and set out. A whole column. Whoever wishes
18580: otìvə nə venčàfkətə venčàvət gi f tr'àvnə punèže tàm cɤ̀rkvətə
goes to the ceremony. They wed them in Tryavna, because the church is there.
18584: i kəm dvà kəm jid'ìn čəsɤ̀ tr'àbvə də sə zəvɤ̀rnət
And around 2:00 or 1:00 they are supposed to return.
18593: pris tùj vrèmi kətu gi venčèjət xòrə si ìmə tàm səs t'àx
There's people there with them during the time of the church ceremony,
18598: ìdət i pràštət n'àkuj àj tùkə komìtə mu kàzvəmi èj tàm
and they send somebody, we here call him a rebel, up there
18607: ə tɤ̀j gurɤ̀tə kàktu i str'èl'ət də predizvest'ɤ̀t či ìdi tùkə
in the forest to shoot [a gun] to announce that they’re coming,
18610: če še si ìdi svàdbətə v'èče
that the wedding [procession] is on its way.
18618: kàk im kàzvəxə na tìja dètu strèl'at dètu isprevàrvət svàdbətə
How do you call those who shoot, who go on ahead of the wedding procession?
18624: I’m not able to tell you.
18627: Did they maybe call them “prèvarnitsi”?		[ritual announcers]
18633: prèvarnici ili prevàrnici koìto isprevàrvat naprèt
“Prèvarnitsi”, or “prevàrnitsi” – who race ahead to announce (“isprevarvat”).
18638: kònnici im vìkət busìlci im vìkət n'àkuj ni znàm zəštò
They're called horsemen. Some call them “busiltsi" (basil-bearers), I don’t know why.
18644: šòtu ìmə idnò ìmi i tùkə i sigà i sigà e ustànəlu
[Maybe] because that’s a [person’s] name, and now – now what’s left,
18648: what remains, is the “busiltsi”. [It’s] like a nickname.
18654: tò ottàm nòsi ìmitu si šòt bəš bəštà mu nə tòs
That’s where the name is from, because the father of that person
18664: à kònnici dà sə im vìkəli pràvilnu štòt ìskə pò inirgìčni xòrə
Ah, yes! They called them horsemen! Because it requires more energetic people.
18672: i est'èstvenu či i tò dr'èbnə ràbutə d'è əmə səopštàvət
That makes sense. Well, it's a minor job. So they announce [the news] –
18677: i ne ì znàm i sled tùj səupštàvət bɤ̀rzət
– I don’t know them – and after they announce [it], they hurry.
18681: kətu utìdi də sə venčàvə òšte ut sutrinɤ̀tə rànu
When it's time to have the church ceremony, already early in the morning
18685: tɤ̀rs'ət sə nər'àzəni dɤ̀ski dɤ̀ski pək stulòvi
they’re looking for cut boards, boards ( = to be table tops), and chairs,
18689: i s obrəzùvə trəp'èzə às ni znàjə
and a festive table is created. I don’t know
18692: v bɤlgàrijə təkà li e bilò nəfs'àkədi vìš tùj ni znàm
whether it was like this everywhere in Bulgaria – you see, this I don’t know.
18697: zbìrə sə c'àlutu s'èlo nə jàdene i nə pìene
The whole village gathers together for eating and drinking.
18702: Regardless of whether they are relatives or not?
18704: Regardless! As long as they cook [and bring] food.
18714: s'èki si gòtvi zənàs'ə ə gòtv'ət pòvečeto vəf sùxo səstujànie
Each cooks, and brings [something]. Mostly they cook foods without liquid
18716: zə də mòe sə nòsi də kàžem
so that they can be transported [more easily]. And [let me] tell [you]:
18720: uttàm ìmə idìn xùbəf ut tùrsku ròpstvu xərmàn
there’s a beautiful threshing floor [dating] from the Turkish occupation,
18724: ftòrijə xərmàn ut des'àtəkə ot ot tùrcite d'ètu e tvà
the second threshing floor from the Turkish tithing period.
18729: tòj bèši nàj putxud'àš dàže n'àkuj gu zeə z'èməd gu
It was the most appropriate [spot], and some even rent it
18732: pri svàdba ne mògət də sə rəspulòžət
for a wedding, and [even then] they can’t fill the whole area.
18736: ne gù pràat v dvòrovete f kɤ̀štata
They don’t do it in the yards of houses,
18737: so as to have the wedding at home?
18743: kujàtu kɤ̀štə pril'àgə mòži nàštə às nìj sm'e d'ès'ət dùši
You can in a house that’s appropriate. Our [family] – I – there are ten of us
18750: às səm nàj màlək àj nìj sm'e bèdni t'à b'èše ùžəs
and I am the youngest. Ah, we were poor. The [whole thing] was horrible.
18756: dušlè bugàti xòrə dušlè pretpriemàči bəštà mi sə srəmùvə
Rich people came, business people came, my father was ashamed,
18761: i vìždəš kɤ̀štətə kàk i kàktu i də è
and you see what the house is like. Well, it is what it is.
18769: òdix i mi pràvea snìmkə vìkət šìpuv'e
I went [once] and they took a picture and said [it was] bone spurs.
18776: i ut vrèmitu bɤ̀brekə mi ut t'èšku dìgəni i
And recently my kidney, from heavy lifting …
18790: snìšen mi bɤ̀brekə ut t'èšku dìgəni ud ràbutə
My kidney got displaced from heavy lifting, from [physical] labor.
18798: kulìčkə tùkə pripràəhmi t’à kɤ̀štə stàrətə tə t'à nizəpòmninə
We were working [with] a wheelbarrow here on this old house, who remembers [how old]
18806: kə tɤ̀s kɤ̀štə ut didì ud bəbì mə jə pupripràixmi i
this house is, from my grandparents – well, we rearranged it a bit and
18811: What do you do at the beginning of the autumn [season]?
18816: èsenutu vr'ɛ̀me kətu št'à: uvərš'ème tò l'ètneš'e
In the autumn when we’d do the threshing – it would be raining
18824: predi dimìtruvdèn' št'à pòčneme də s'ɛ̀eme zìmnicə ž'ìtu rɤ̀š' ečmìk
before St. Dimitri’s day – we’d begin to sow the winter grains – rye, barley –
18830: i kətu št'à zəs'ɛ̀eme št'e št'à ə dòjde zìmətə
and when we’d finish the sowing, we’d – winter would come,
18834: št'à: nòsime s kulàtə dərvà tùkə də se gr'ɛ̀em
and we’d bring wood in with the carriage, [enough] to keep us warm.
18838: i št'à sedìme i nə prulettɤ̀ pàk št'à pòčneme də s'ɛ̀me
And we’d wait, and in the spring we’d again start to sow
18843: pròletnu uv'ès ə rənì kuìtu ni ni beə nùž'ni
the spring [crops] – oats, and – food that we – that we needed.
18849: n'àkuj pɤ̀t' št'à pòjdeme s kulàtə də sm'èlime bràšnu
Sometimes we’d go with the cart to grind flour
18853: nə udenìcətə š'e z'èmeme kulà səs dvàes trìese krìni
at the mill. We’ll take the cart with fifteen or twenty bushels
18858: i primɤ̀knim tùkə zə bàbətə də m'ɛ̀si xl'àp
and drag it over here for Granny to make bread.
18860: ə nə g'òrg'udèn' št'à zèmeme ut tùkə kulàtə
And on St. George’s day we’d set off from here [with] the cart,
18865: št'à də ìdeme è nə dòlu krəj mur'ètu
and we’d go all the way down to the sea,
18870: pu skelìte tàm dètu ìmət čurbəžìite uč'àstəci də ràbutime tàm
to the wharves where the landowners have plots of land, and work there
18874: pu edìn m'ɛ̀sec dvà i št'à dòjdeme tùkə də pòčnem ž'ètvə
for a month or two. [Then] we’d come back here to begin the harvest,
18880: št'à ž'èneme tìjə dnì kətu už'èneme š'e gu vərš'èm
and we’d reap. [And on] those days when we finish reaping, we’ll thresh it.
18888: pu dv'ɛ̀ trì kràvi št'à: ìmə bìvulicə št'à də ìmə kòne
Two or three horses each; there’d be a female water buffalo, there’d be horses.
18892: ə ìməne si g'unl'učìi xòrə tə pə edni pəs'àə
And we’d have people as day-workers. Some pastured
18898: kràvite drùgi pəs'àə kònetu drùgi pəs'àə biul'àtə
cows, others pastured horses, and others pastured water buffaloes.
18902: Shepherds – what musical instruments did shepherds play?
18904: s kəvàl':e be səs svìrki s kəvàl':e
End-blown flutes, you know! Small pipes and end-blown flutes.
18908: [What did you use to make a fence?]
18918: ut kəkvì ud dərvò bè zəbìjeme ə kòl':e vəv zem'ɤ̀tə
What sorts?! Wooden, of course! We pound stakes into the ground and
18925: kuv'ème ut kòl du kòl pu dv'à dərv'ètə e pu dv'ɛ̀
hammer on, from stake to stake, two pieces of wood each, two each –
18930: pervàs se kàzvə i kuv'èm skilimìdite
they call it an a edge – and hammer on planks.
18937: ili pək ubràtnu əku nèməš skilimìdi ə zəbìjem kòl':etu
Or the reverse, if you don’t have planks. And we pound in the stakes
18942: i berèm ud gurɤ̀tə prɤ̀k':e i zəgrədìme pl'èt skilimìdi
and gather sticks from the forest and weave them in with the planks.
18946: pək segà òšte pòveč'e səs tèl' gi pràime
But now we make them even more [frequently] with wire.
18948: Each does it how he can, right?
18954: i nə d'ugènu št'à: pòm də sə nəpijèm
To the store? We’d go to have our fill of drink,
18959: f pràznik kətu sɤ̀mne utrintɤ̀ š'e se premenìme tùkə
On a holiday, as soon as it gets light in the morning we’ll dress up here
18966: də pòeme pə vəf č'èrkvətə č'e ut č'èrkvətə š'e dòem tùkə
and go to church, and after church we’ll come [back] here.
18969: š'e sə nəhrànime  tùkə št'e si puč'ìnem màlku
We’ll eat well here, and [then] we’d rest a bit.
18973: i šte pòm nə d'ugènə tàm pɤ̀len d'ugènət xòrə
[Then] we’ll go to the store. [And down] there, the store is full of people.
18976: i uttàm nə xuròtu də igràeme i də p'ɛ̀eme
From there [we’d go] to the dance area, to dance and sing
18979: i də se veselìm nə pràznikət tvà e
and make merry on [the occasion of] the holiday. And that’s it.
18980: št'à pòm nə xuròtu də əm tvà e
we’d go to the dance, to – But that’s all.
19046: det'ètu kət sə rudì pòčvəme də gu puwɨ̀vəme
When a child is born we start to wrap it up,
19052: də gu zəwɨ̀vəme də gu zəwɨ̀vəme də rəst'è zəvìtu s plenì
to swaddle it. To swaddle it so it will grow, wrappted in swaddling cloths.
19057: s plenì krəčkàtə mu nə prɤ̀slenkite ìmə pəmùk
In swaddling cloths. [At] his little feet, his little toes, there’s cotton
19063: də ne gù ub'ɨ̀və i e uvìtu uvìtu uvìtu uvìtu
so it won’t pinch him. He’s bound, bound, bound, bound –
19067: dò i tùkə krəčònkite mu sə vɤ̀rzəni
all the way to here. His little feet are tied …
19073: də rəstè štòtu ìnač'e jà nəlì vi kàzvəm zə tvà
… so that he’ll grow [straight]. Otherwise, won’t it – I tell you –
19080: əmi dnèskə trì pɤ̀ti tr'àbvə də gu rəzvìje štòtu sə pupikàvə
Well you have to unwind it three times a day, because it gets wet.
19082: How old is it [when you do this]?
19087: mɤ̀ninku be l'ehùdl'e gu vìkəmi nìe l'ehùdl'e
19093: l'ehùdl'e màlku nà kətu e tvà seà bèbe e tùkə dètu e
A little “le-hud-le”, like this baby right here.
19095: [How long do you keep it like that?]
19100: pèt š'ès m'ɛ̀scə dənò də sə fjàkne
[You swaddle it for] five or six months, in the hope that it gets strong.
19109: n'àkoe dərvò ìmələtə e tuvà təkà tòp tòp e
[On] a tree of some sort! Mistletoe is [like] a ball, a ball.
19357: gul'àmu e ìmələtə tè ne jà puteb'àvət zə nìštu
Mistletoe is big. People don’t use it for anything.
19362: ìmə zərnà tə gi berɤ̀d zə kukòškite də im fɤ̀rl'əd
It’s got seeds that they gather for the hens – to throw out to them
19366: [so] they [will] peck at [it], so [that] they [will] lay eggs.
19367: [What does it grow on most often?]
19373: We go out and pick wild fruit. You know –
19379: ednì kìseli nə kìselcite se fàštət mnògu
these sour [fruits] on wild fruit trees. There’s a lot of it on those.
19387: nə drùgu dɤ̀rvu ne hòdi sàmu nə kìselc'i'te
They don’t grow on [any] other tree, only on wild fruit trees.
19388: Do they grow [on a maple tree]?
19390: kàk à i na klenɤ̀ hòdi hòdi
What? Oh yes, they also grow on a maple [tree]. They grow [there too].
19394: On a maple tree, and on a wild fruit tree.
19398: dà nə drùgu dɤ̀rvu ne xòdi t'à sàmu nə lìpətə
Yes. It doesn’t grow on any other tree. Only on a lime tree.
19402: dà pu klen':ètu hòdi pu lìpite hòdi
Yes, it grows on maple trees, it grows on lime trees –
19403: [And what musical instruments do shepherds play?]
19411: The end-blown flute. We play the end-blown flute
19416: kəvàl svìrime kətu màl'ki se uč'àhne svìrki [whistle]
We play the end-blown flute. As kids, we learned the small pipes [whistle]
19420: ò mi tuvà vr'ɛ̀me ìməš'e tùkə č'ètiri hìl'ədi ufc'è
Ohh! At that time there were four thousand sheep here,
19424: tèə č'ètiri ìl'ədi ufc'è nìe tuvà vr'ɛ̀me nə hòdime
and these four thousand sheep – at that time we didn’t go to school.
19428: nə uč'ìlište du č'etvɤ̀rtu udel'ènie àjde s ufc'ète tàtku ti
[Only] up to the fourth grade [and then] off with the sheep! Your dad –
19434: bəštà mi š'e z'ème tujàgətə əku ne òdiš tə upàli
my father would take his staff if you didn’t go, and strike out at you
19440: dvà trì pɤ̀ti àjde zə ufc'ète pə segà n'èmə v'èče təkìvə ra
twice or thrice: “Off with the sheep, you!” But now there's no longer such –
19456: prɤ̀s kulìčkətə iskàrvəx i bɤ̀brekə mi sə snišì
I was moving dirt with the wheelbarrow and my kidney got displaced.
19462: i sigà i šìpuv'e mi sə pudm’èstiə i mnògu ràbuti i tɤ̀j
And now the bone spurs have shifted all around, and other stuff, and there it is.
19471: əmə tuvà čàk sigà kət ustər'à əmə kəd b'èše mlàdə
Well, that’s now, when you’re old. But when you were young?
19478: kəd b'àx mlàdə ràbutə ni b'àgə ut m'ène às jə vɤ̀ršə
When I was young, no work got away from me! I did it [all].
19486: stànə dèzes'è pudìr'e tikezes'è ə i tè kik sè
The state-owned farm came, and then the collective farm. [No,] the coll-
19491: tikizis’è nàj nəpr'èd gu nəpràviə pudìr'e dezes'è
they formed the collective farms first and then the state-owned farm.
19495: i tɤ̀j s'è ràbut'ehme tàm dòkəto sə pinsiunìrəm
And we worked there up until [when] I retired.
19504: əm tùkə kvò rabòtite kvì ud neštà udgl'èždət'e
And what do you do here? What sorts of things do you raise?
19512: Well, we plowed the land, you know.
19521: s'èki si ìməši pu trìis četìrise pedes’è d'èkərə imòt
Each one had three or four or five hectares of property
19534: kəkvò žìtu uv'ès pəpùr kərtòfi bòp kvòt e ni i nùžnu
What? Wheat, oats, corn, potatoes, beans. Whatever we needed,
19545: si pruizv’èždəxmi si i si pruizv’èždəxmi pudìr'e kət stànə t'èkizis'è
we produced it for ourselves – we produced it. Then when the collective farm came
19553: i səbràə dubìtəkə nə inò m'àstu də gi gl’èdə n'àkujə žinà
and they gathered all the livestock into one place for some woman to look after them,
19560: nìe utìvəme sùtrinə nəràmvəmi gi z'èməm'e i gi fpr’àgəmi i ur'èm
we would go out in the morning. We’d feed them, take them and harness them, and plow.
19566: The women, [that is]. The men work on construction.
19578: məžètu̥ òdea pək nìi žinì sə rəspràəxmi səs t'àx
The men would go off and we women would deal with them.
19583: And then everything became state-owned, the state-owned farm.
19589: i səs tràkturi pòčnəə də urɤ̀t əmə pàk òdim kət pus'èjət kərtòfi
and they began to plow with tractors. But still when we go to plant potatoes
19595: nìj òd'exm'e s'è də kupàim də žènim kət pus'èjəd žitàta i tɤ̀j
we’d go out to do all the digging, and to reap when they planted wheat, and so on.
19599: dud'ètu v'èki zəpr'èxme ne mòžem v'èki [laughter]
until we stopped.  We can’t do it any more [laughter].
19609: dà vi ə vìždaxte li se sɤs t'àx čèsto
Yes, did you see them often?
19619: əmi mlàd'i òrə kətu b'èxmi mumì irgèni ud drùgi silà ìdea
When we were bachelors and maidens, young people would come from other villages.
19626: dà ud drùgi silà ìdea fəf nàše̥tu s'èlu
Yes. They’d come from other villages to our village.
19639: kəvàl':e tùkə v grədɤ̀ št'à də ìdeme v burgàs
[They have] end-blown flutes in town. We’d go to Burgas,
19643: ìmə tàm kəvəl'ž'ìjnicə ut tàm št'àme də kùpime
there’s a flute-maker there, and we’d buy [them] there.
19652: ə kugɤ̀tu stàvəš'e nàš'ijət səbòr nə devèti àvgus tòə ìdvəš'e prəmətàretu
When we had our [village] fair, on August 9th, then peddlers would come.
19656: tvà prəmətàre nòsət svìrki nòsət kəvàl':e
[And] these peddlers brought small pipes and end-blown flutes.
19658: and we would try them out.
19664: krəstòsənu s č'ètiri stòla ud ednɤ̀tə stərnɤ̀ si sədì mumč'ètə
[They’d sit] cross-wise on four chairs. The boy sits on one side
