21259: edìn odgrìba žìtoto drùkᵊ odgòre veàčkata si ìma kòš tàm
One [of us] shovels up grain, another's up above. The winnower's got a basket,
21271: tò gu dàvəš nə màjstur' nə təkvìsə š'ivàč'i̥
You give it to a master craftsman, to these tailors [to make it up].
21278: tùkə udòlu ìmə kòžə štòtu zìmnu vrèmi də ti tòpli
There’s leather here underneath so as to keep you warm in the winter.
21281: i tùkə òkuluwrɤ̀s ìmə pək blàn':t'ȅ
And here, all around [it] there are the “blani”,
21301: vìš drùguš jadɛ̀ha grùba hranà əmə beha pò jɛki nəròdə hòrata
Look, earlier on [people] used to eat coarse food. But people were healthier.
21307: pək əzgà sladkᶤìšɤ pò drùgi i i nèma drùgučɛ̀šen čuvɛ̀k ɛ̀dar
But now sweets and other [stuff], and there’s no old-time sturdy people,
21315: i zdràf enakɔ̀f či jɛ̀ kvòt sam prekàrala tò hòdɤ
[no] healthy [ones] like then. What I lived through – when he was
21320: čètɤrɤ gudᶤìnɤ zəpàs i jɛ̀ səz decà də gu zadɛ̀vež dɛ̀kenu
four years in the reserves, and I with the children – you have to stick the kid
21326: na garbɔ̀n s l'ùlka da ìdež da žɔ̀neš
on your back in a cradle in order to go out to reap.
21332: zɔ̀meš sarpɔ̀ da sa navìdaš da žɔ̀neš slɔ̀ncetu nažìža
You take up a sickle, you bend down to reap, the sun is sizzling,
21333: ama že žɔ̀neš si nèma kàk trɛ̀bva da pudberèš
but you reap. No [other] way, you have to get started.
21342: sìčku se e pràilu ža naràmiš uràlu ž ìdeš də urèš
You did everything. You’ll take up the wooden plow and go out to plow.
21348: pək ezgà zgà nə mòžɤ da tò ne mòž dɛ̀ken də s nòsi
But now they can’t – now [a woman] can’t carry a child
21355: è tɤ̀j jnè kòž'ički ùbəvi tɤ̀j ùkuləwrɤ̀s
these nice little pieces of leather all around [it all].
21363: blànə sə kàzvə tɤ̀j e tò tɤ̀j kòžə pàk amə
It’s called “blana”. It’s leather too, but
21369: tɤ̀j dɤ̀lgu sədì səmìti kusməlàci səmàtə kòžə
it hangs down [like] separate strands of long hair, but of leather.
21373: nə gərdì tugàva gu dàva na mažɔ̀n də nòsi dɛ̀kenu
on her chest, but rather gives the child to her husband to carry,
21375: sin če ne možè tò də gu nòsi tò slàbu
my son, because she can’t carry it, she’s weak.
21381: əmə sìčku ut gulik'ɔ̀ hòg'ət gòlɤ izmɔ̀rznət
And everything [now] is poverty, [people] go around bare and freeze.
21384: pək drùguš ublɛ̀čenu sìčku ublɛ̀čenu ta tvà e
But then, [people] were dressed, everyone [was] dressed [sufficiently]. And there it is.
21391: səs vɤ̀l'nena plɛ̀na gulɛ̀ma pa to gulɛ̀ma plɛ̀na i ə
[We used] a big woolen swaddling cloth, a big “diaper”
21395: What did you use to wrap babies up with?
21400: ut vɤ̀lna istəkàta vɔ̀lnena ta če ušìta ta səs sèka
woven from wool – [It was] woolen, and each one sewn up
21406: səz gəjtàn i dɛ̀kenu gà gu puvìeš s pòvoi vɔ̀lneni
with cords, and when you wrap the child up in this woolen swaddling,
21412: gà gu uvìeš òtɤ f plɛ̀ne ta zdì pràfku
when you wrap him he sits straight because of the swaddling,
21417: podàva na veàčkata odvèem žìtoto plèvata baškɤ̀
feeding into the winnower. We winnow out the grain – the chaff separately
21420: žìtoto baškɤ̀ priberèm i tovà i pòsle vèče
and the grain separately –and we store it away and that’s it. And after that –
21423: kɤdè gi pribìrate kɤdè gi pribìraš
Where do you all store it? Where do you store it away?
21430: emi kɤdè è vɤf plèvn'a vɤf ə zìmnik vɤf mazè
Well, wherever! In the loft, in the cellar, in the basement –
21481: kvòt e pòjasa i gàštite ona nà gu putpìra
the belt and pants. See, it props him up, [the way it's]
21487: z gajtàne putplatènu tə təkò pək əzgà m'èlhi sə rudì se
lined by the cords like that. But [kids] now are soft. [The minute] it’s born,
21492: i gu tùr'ət f partàlɤ tàm i decàna si se nakvì hɔ̀
they put it into rugs. And that’s how children are now. Hah.
21498: i decàna sa nakìva mèlk'i mèlk'i plɛ̀ni mèlku
Children are soft, soft, [because] of soft wrappings.
21504: i tɤ̀j gu pràvim nə grànici pòsli gu putup'àəmi fəf vudɤ̀
and then we аrrange them in skeins. After that we soak it in water
21512: də sə upɤ̀ni tɤ̀s pr'èždə kət sə upɤ̀ni pr'èždətə i kətu isɤ̀:ni
so the yarn will stretch out. And when the yarn is stretched out, and dry,
21518: sn'èməmi jə ut ə mutuvìl'čitu i jə m'ètvəmi nə slɤ̀nci
we take it from the yarn-crutch and put it out in the sun
21525: də si isɤ duisɤ̀:ni štòtu tò ni mòži də isɤ̀:ni nə mutuvìl'čitu
to finish drying, because it can’t get dry on the yarn-crutch.
21532: mi kətu isɤ̀:ni i še si plit'èš blùzə li
Well, when it dries, you’ll maybe knit a blouse,
21537: še si plit'èš čuràpi li še s plit'èš kəkvòtu ìskəš
or you’ll knit socks, or you’ll knit whatever you want,
21543: tɤ̀j dɤ̀lgə b'àlə s nəkràjə səs č'èrnu pàk tɤ̀j
Long and white, with black on the ends.
21548: [Can] you know how beautiful [it was], all around –
21552: tò b'èši mnògu ùbu nè j kət sigàna
it was very beautiful. Not like [what they wear] now.
21556: a na glavàta slàgaxa li i nèšto
And did they put something on her head?
21560: gləvɤ̀tə pàk è tɤ̀j ìmə bəjrìš' sə təkòzvə
[On ] her head there’s a headdress. [Yes,] she does that.
21564: i ə i s'ètn'e kət utìš tùkətɤ̀j nə č'èrkvətə
And then, um, when you go off to the church,
21573: tì n'èməš nìštu ud vàs n'èməš cv'èti sàmu ìməš tùkətɤ̀j
you don’t have anything from your [family home]. You only have flowers.
21582: se krìe zimɤ̀ska stòkata go šte go jadè za stòkata
it’s kept for the winter, for the animals to eat. [It’s] for the animals.
21586: a pa nà za žìtoto prostìramè go na čèrgi
And as for the grain, we spread it out on rugs [and]
21596: [What  do you do when a  child is born?]
21607: kəkò i šə šə sə rudɤ̀j de d'àtetu še gu ukòpiš
What is it [that we do]? When the child is born, you’ll wash it,
21624: šə gu zəvɤ̀jš səs ədnɤ̀j pərcàlevi pl'àni tugà nemàše pl'àni
you’ll wrap it up in some rag wrappings – there weren’t [real] diapers then.
21636: səz zəbràtkətə tɤ̀j i səz bəj səz zəbràtkə
With a head covering, [yes]. With a head covering.
21642: tugà b'àə pərcàl'e šə gu zəvɤ̀jš i càl dè̝n d'àtetu
Then there were [just] rags. You’ll wrap it up and all day long the child
21648: i s'ètn'e tùkə kət dòiš utìvəš nə č'èrkvə
And later when you come – you go to the church.
21654: tò kòitu j ut s'èlu ut s'èlu
[If] someone’s from the [same] village [they go to the church] of the village.
21663: təkà sedɤ̀j fəf pərcàl'ete n'è̝mə kòj də gu putsušɤ̀j ud ràbutə
stays like that that in the rags. There’s no one [who can take time] from work to dry him out,
21673: pək às ud drùgu s'èlu mə dunèsəwə tùkə sə d'ìsi̥t p'i̥tnàjs' kərùci
But I was from another village, they brought me here with 10-15 carriages.
21683: i utìdujmi nə č'èrkvətə pòpu tàm ti slàgə təkòs ə inì venčilà
And we went to the church. The priest is there, he puts these wreaths on you –
21687: i tvà e i pà si rəst'è i pà izl'àze pà rəstè
and that’s all. But they grow up anyway, and get tall. They grow up.
21693: še si uputrebìš nə məžɤ̀ šə uplit'èš fən'èlə
[whatever] you can use. [For instance] you’ll knit your husband a sweater.
21696: i kàk se pletè kakvò pràexte
And how do you knit? What did you do?
21698: əm či kàk sə plit'è səs iglì ba
How do you knit?! Well, with needles, man!
21704: səs iglì dib'èli gul'èmi iglì dɤ̀lgi kətu i širòko ə pək čuràpa
With needles – big thick needles [that are] both long and wide. And for socks,
21710: səs p'èt iglì p'èt iglìčki t'à šə gi znài drugàrkətə
with five needles, five little needles. The comrade will know this, she will.
21717: ìgli zə čuràp ni znàiš li kəkvò i
Needles for socks, don’t you know what that is?
21729: drùk v žègana kakvònu si stòriš
[It’s] different in the heat – whatever you make,
21734: kvot sì si nagudìl si izràbutìlu
21742: lèšta fasùl' bòp gràx nakìva ràbotɨ kakvònu i čenìca
Lentils, beans, fava beans, peas, those sort of things like – and wheat.
21750: čèrɤn lɛ̀p sᶤìrɤne f tulùmɤ stòr'enu əmə gà udrɛ̀žeš
Dark bread, white cheese made in skin bags. When you cut off
21755: rɔ̀žen lɛ̀p fəlìja ta gu ugrɛ̀eš i s enekvà sᶤìrɤne
a slice of rye bread and heat it up with this white cheese,
21762: kəkɔ̀f bɛ hùbəf a zgà nѐ̝ma tɤštɤm'èlɤ nèma
it was so nice. But now not even a single tablecloth.
21770: sìčkunu b'e pò drùgu i urìs nemɛ̀ əm ža žə si̥ stò̝riš
Everything was different. There wasn’t any rice. But you’d make
21775: ut pšenìcana ta imɛ̀ ta gu pràvea zvɛ̀ha go trahàl'nica
from wheat – there was – they used to make – they called it a handmill,
21782: in'è ràbuti nəpràu kɤ̀k də t' kàžə tò
Some things they make – how can I tell you?
21785: tò tɤ̀j e ut ə ləmər
21794: təkòs ləmərìnə əmə t'à e ləmərìnə čìstə sr'ebrò tr'àə də j
Tin – but pure tin, it’s supposed to be [like] silver,
21799: sə iskàrə ot vugenìca tɤ̀j vèke i vartɛ̀ ta si stòriš
and it works like a mill. You rotate it, and you make
21806: enakvà tràhana za urìs nə mɛ̀stu jadɛ̀ja nəkìva grùbi hrənì
this sort of gruel, and they ate it in place of rice. Such coarse food,
21812: əmə be zdràf ə naròda càrevìčnu bràšnu ža svarìš zvɛ̀hme gu kačamàk
but the people were healthy. You’ll cook up corn flour – we called it polenta.
21817: b'èl'i nəpràu tɤ̀j səmòtu pɤ̀sro čərkòwnu təkwòs tukə ùkuluwrɤ̀s
[all] white. They make it all decorated like in a church, all around,
21824: òh ža izvàdiš tòlkiva tupàcɤ nared'ɔ̀t tugàva nemɛ̀ màsa
You’ll take so many chunks and lay them out. Back then there weren’t tables,
21828: i tùkə ìmə tɤ̀j ìmə tɤ̀j gòr'e ìmə tùkətɤj krɤ̀st
and here there’s this, and here on top there’s a cross.
21835: a sufrɔ̀ ta ga tùr'aš na sufrɔ̀na ta č tugàva izvàdiš
but rather a low “sofra”. You put it on the “sofra” and then you take out
21838: tò nəpràv'enu mnògu xùbavu à tɤ̀j idìn pɤ̀t nə tɤ̀j
It’s made up really nicely. See, one [piece goes] this way,
21847: pupèrki čùški ut kàca salamùra i hùbavu bɤlò jɛ̀lu sɤ
peppers from the barrel of brine. and it was nice. One ate well,
21851: i pò pò zdràv b'e nəròda pək ezgà zgà da mu dadɔ̀t
and people were more – more healthy. But now they give  –
21857: zgà nàa hranà da ja dadèš na dnèšnijas naròt nèma da edè
That food you give now to people today – they won’t eat it.
21864: nèma da go nakùsa nvà a nugà gu edɛ̀a i hùbavo bìlo
They won’t [find] any taste in it. But back then they ate it, and it was good.
21869: pək ezgà lìzneš màlku tùr'at tɤ slàtku nakìva ud ednò drùgo
But now you lick a bit, they put all this sugar in, and other things,
21873: i ti se e nè jɛ̀lu če nèmaš sì [unintelligible]
and you don’t feel like eating. You don’t have [unintelligible]
21879: ta tugàva nemɛ̀ takìva slatkᶤìši tɔ̀rn'em na širòka.lɤka
But back then there weren’t such sweet things. We set out for Shiroka Lŭka
21881: màjka nɨ ža tɔ̀rneš dnèska ž ìdeš do širòka.laka
(our mother) – You’ll set out today and go to Shiroka Lǔka,
21886: i ža si udrɛ̀žeš hlɛ̀p ut tòu lɛ̀p ta še gu udnesèš
you’ll cut some bread and you’ll take that bread back with you
21889: nə sèlu i gà sa vɔ̀rnɤš če vìkaš na dɛ̀kenu
to the village, and when you come back you say to the child –
21892: i tò vìka kvò mi si donèla màmo
and the child says, “What did you bring me, Mama?”
21896: and you say “Here, have some of the “priest’s bread”,
21901: če bìl blàk i tò si gu stùrilu lɛ̀ban
because it is supposed to be tasty, and the child took the bread.
21903: i i mu dadèš i tò jadè i čɤ blàk
You give it to him and the child eats it, and it’s tasty
21906: because it’s supposedly from the “priest’s bread” [laughter].
21912: hɔ̀ i vìš kàk svetɤ̀n è gu varvì varvì
Hah! Look at the world, going along like this,
21914: and look how it’s [completely] messed up.
21922: abe svetɔ̀s si kurunòu esèj sa vartì vartì vartì vartì
Ah, the world is running things. It spins and spins and spins and spins,
21925: zgà se izvartɛ̀lu dušlò svà i na svà
and now it’s all spun around to this. And to this –
21928: kò zna pàk kakvò ža dòjde
21934: nìkoj ne znàe ama ug gòspud'a sìn dušlò
Nobody knows. But it’s [all] come, my son, from the Lord.
21936: əku i za v balgàrija balgàrija ne štè da e
If it were only for Bulgaria, it wouldn’t be just for Bulgaria.
21941: vìš əf càl svɛ̀t bušùva càl svɛ̀t nì izbìrat ednì glasùvat
You see, it’s boiling all over the world. Some have elections, some vote,
21950: ta sa ne bahtɔ̀t ta sòlkuva prepàtaa tò od dè
some fight, and they [all] suffer so much. And where [did all this come from]?
21955: ud gòspud'a e dušlò sèj da sa iskaldìsat naròdas
All this has come from the Lord, the way people are exterminating one another …
21959: da sa iskaldìsat da se iskràk'at naròda
… exterminating one another, decimating the people
21963: za da ustànat pò màlku də də žuvɛ̀jat sìčkunu e nvà
so that fewer will remain to live [on the earth]. All that
21965: ud gòspud'a jə dušlò òtɤ aku e sàmu v balgàrija
has come from the Lord. Because if it was only in Bulgaria,
21967: ne štè da è a pa tò vìš nasɛ̀kade zgà
it wouldn’t be [that way]. But look, everywhere now,
21972: e kakvìtu sa daržɛ̀vi nìkoga nè e čùvalu
[all] the sorts of states no one has ever heard of!
21975: and there’s one that goes that way …
21978: azgà gi slùšaš či ne znàm kakvò pràv'at
And now you hear of them – I don’t know what all they are doing –
21980: i tùkə òkuluwrɤ̀s da sədì nə gləvɤ̀tə
… and all around here so that it fits on your head.
21983: And here are these little crosses.
21986: [It’s] made out of silver – very pretty.
21990: And after that he switches them around.
21994: i s'ètn'e tàm pòpu t'i č'it'è tə venčàvə
And then the priest says to you [the words] to marry you,
22001: tə prɤ̀steni ìməš sə m'enì səs tòju s mòju tɤ̀j təkòzwəš
and you have a rings, he switches yours with mine, you do all that.
22008: i ə krɤ̀snik utsàm utàtək ìmaš krɤ̀snik i krɤ̀snicə
And the godfather moves around – you’ve got a godfather and a godmother –
22016: i s'ètn'ə ubikàl'eš ə kət tə venč'ɛ̀jət vèč'i šə ubikàl'əš
and then you walk in a circle. After they marry you, you circle around
22021: màsətə tàm səz bìblijətə səs pòpu nəprèt čit'è
the table there with the Bible. The priest [goes] in front, he recites,
22026: i tì pudèr'e i tɤ̀j krɤ̀sniku i krɤ̀snicətə i i nìj dvàmə
you [go] after him, and then the godfather and godmother, and us two,
22031: č'itìrmə ubikàl'əš màsətə tɤ̀j kɤ̀ktu j màs:tə tùkə̥tɤ̀j ìmə bìblijə tàm
the four go around the table – it’s like a table.  There’s the Bible there
22037: nèguit'ȅ dètu č'i̥t'è knìgi pòpo i ubikàl'əš ut tri pɤ̀t'ə tɤ̀j
and his books that the priest reads from. You go around three times
22041: s'ètn'e v'èči̥ ti gi ismɤ̀kvə i kàzvə v'èč'e
and then they take them off [your head] and [the priest] says
22048: zɤ̀mə prɤ̀stent'ȅ gi menì mòjo tòjo i celùvəme rəkɤ̀
he’ll take the rings and switch them – mine, yours – and we kiss the hands
22054: i gà gu pumìsliš vìš če dušlò enakòvu kràjas slèdva tvà
and when you think on it, you see something’s come. The end is coming.
22060: a v bìblijasa pòvn'am pìše dvèhìl'adnata gudᶤìna
I remember that in the Bible it says in the year 2000 –
22064: tò s dvèhìl'adnata i dvanàesta gudᶤìna e zapìsanu v bìblijata
What’s written in the Bible is the year 2012.
22073: a nìe tùka ìmame bìblija kadènu i četè stàrecat bìblijana e tàm
We have a Bible here that the old man reads. The Bible's over there.
22081: aha tòj z'ɔ̀me če kadè nìkade ne izlìza tugàva gu četè
Ah, he takes it up to read and never goes out, he just reads it.
22087: ama vìš tò i bez učilà vìš na sèj gudᶤìni
Just look at him, no glasses. See, [even] at these [advanced] years
22092: I’ll see till the end [of my days].
22095: tugàva ni vìkat če tò mnògu si vìdɨ če jɛ̀l
They used to tell us that he sees so much because he ate
22098: mnògu čèrnɤ buruvìnki pək tìi nəlì za za zrèniet
so many blueberries. They’re good for sight, you know,
22106: i mnògu jadɤ̀t i tɛ̀h a tò kàrlak sàmo čèrni buruvìnki̥
and people eat a lot of them. In Karlak there’s only blueberries.
22110: o tò ne tònuve izìda buruvìnki
And he eats no [less than] tons of blueberries!
22114: pu càl dèn' kvò da pàk varì jadè
All day long – he walks and eats them.
22122: ednà gudᶤìna ut plòvdiv be dušlà enà dukturìca ta be duvèla mòmče
One year a doctor lady came up from Plovdiv and brought a boy
22127: f pustèle vìka kàzahà mə vìka pòčna
[wrapped in] a sheet. She said, “They told me,” she said, that he’d begun
22130: da ne mòž da vìžda kàzahà da čèrni buruvìnki
to lose his sight. They said that [he needed to eat] blueberries.
22135: ne bɛ̀ mə nèka tò bɤlò si nè e kəsuglèdu
He wasn’t! No, [in fact] it turned out that he was not nearsighted.
22142: ama z'ɔ̀lu da ne mòže da vìžda tugàf nàšte ja vòdia gòre
He’d begun to lose his sight, so our people brought her here
22148: tə dvɛ̀ tenkìi naberà čèrni buruvìnki vìka da mu dàvam
and she gathered two cans of blueberries and told me to give them to him
22153: da da jadè tà be ut plòvdif de dòkturka ta tùka spà
to eat. She was from Plovdiv, this doctor woman, and stayed over here.
22156: i ja duvèdua nàšte zberà buruvìnki̥
Our people brought her, and she gathered blueberries.
22159: And when do the blueberries ripen?
22162: Now, in the month of August.
22167: prez àvgu mɛ̀sɤc malᶤìnɤ buruvìnki ìma i čèrni i červèni buruvìnki
In August there’s raspberries and blueberries – blueberries and cranberries both.
22175: abe prɤròdata nɤ e darᶤìla sas sìčki pluduvè ama nìe ustarɛ̀hme
Ah, yes, Nature has given us all kinds of fruits. But we’ve gotten old.
22177: sùšime go kàčvame go f čuvàle s kolà
dry it. Then we load it into sacks, on the cart,
22178: and go off to the mill and grind it …
22183: Where is – where was the mill?
22185: emi tùka si ìmaše po rekìte na vòda vodenìca
Well, here along the rivers, on the water. There was a mill
22190: s kàmik šmìrgel kàmik mu kàzvaa omèlem brašnòto
with a stone that they call an emery stone. We’d grind up the flour,
22194: i edèm čèr lèp ne edèm kato segà bèl
and eat black bread. We wouldn’t eat white bread, like [they do] now.
22196: And what was sown around here?
22199: nè s kakvò se sə sèeše tùka po nìvite
No, [I mean] what got planted here in the fields?
22203: nə krɤ̀sniku nə krɤ̀snictə nə pòpu i v'èč'e̥ sme venč'èni
of the godfather, godmother, the priest – and we’re married.
22208: è ə stànə šijsè gudìni kɤ̀ktu sme venč'èni è kɤ̀ktu živèjmi nìj
It’s 60 years now that we’ve been married, that we’ve been living [together].
22215: sigà nə dvàs s'èdmi š'ə nəpràim šijsè gudini, kɤ̀ktu smi̥ dvàmə̥tə̥
Now on the 27th it’ll be exactly sixty years that we’ve been a pair.
22225: è à s'ètn'e tə pùštə utìvəš pàk krɤ̀sniku nəprèt' i tì pudèr'e
Then he lets you go, you set off again, the godfather in front and you next –
22228: tò nəlì hòdil' l'i si u č'èrkvə t'ì
You’ve been to a church, haven’t you?
22234: wòd'il'i l'i sti znàjti li č'èrkvə kəkò j
Have you [all] been? Do you know what a church is?
22240: à e tɤ̀j kət pòčniš əltàru dètu izlìzə pòpu əltàr sə kàzvə
Ah. Starting with the altar where the priest comes out, that’s called the altar.
22249: i s'etn'e tò nəl'ì ìmə svitìci tɤ̀j ùkuluwrɤ̀s
And then, you know, there are these women saints all around,
22258: svitìci təkvìsə è gul'èmi təkòs i c'əlùvəš v'èč'i nərèt nərèt nərèt tàm
these big women saints like this, and you kiss them all, all in order.
22276: ikòn'i tò switìcə j ikònə ikòn'i
Icons, that “woman saint” is an icon. Icons.
22287: ikòni i tàtək əltàrə tòj ubl'àkən ùbəu isùsə xristòs kɤ̀ktuj j
Icons. And then the altar, it is dressed nicely, with Jesus Christ on it,
22292: təkòs imə mnògu kət si əku sì òdil' nə č'èrkvə
there’s a lot [of nice things], if you– if you’ve gone to church [you know].
22298: às wòd'ə i znàm kəkò j tò kəkò n'èštu ìmə vɤ̀tr'ə
I go, and I know how it is, how there’s something inside
22303: v əltàru nəpràvu isùs ristòs kɤ̀ktu j rəspɤ̀nət nə
the altar, in fact it’s Jesus Christ crucified on –
22308: nə krɤ̀stu tàm snìmənu ud dərvò nəpràenu
on the cross, pictured there – it’s made out of wood.
22310: tò dərvò è tɤ̀j è gul'èmi ikòn' təkvìsə
it’s [from] wood – those are [really] big icons.
22314: emi po nìvite vùtrin kato dòda na nìvata i kato òbṛza
Ah, in the fields. In the morning when I go to the field and check it out,
22317: i òra sɤs volòvete dokɤde ikindìa i pòsle tùram žìtoto
I plow with the oxen until afternoon prayer. And then I put the grain
22322: vɤf ə edìn šinìk mu kàzvat tùram zìam go pod mìšnica
into what they call a “shinik”. I put it under my arm
22329: i s tàa rɤ̀ka zìmam i vṛ̀va po nasèvnicata i fṛ̀gam
and with [my other] hand, take [seed], walk along the rows, and throw it out …
22334: ot do tùka e tù pùsteno brazdɤ̀ nàsea tàa pòsle
... to [the point where] they’ve made the furrow.  I sow all of this one, and then
22339: pa pò natàtaka nasèem gu i gu zavlèčeme i si vṛvìm
we sow it further on, and rake it over, and go home.
22343: ma kakvò se sèeše ə esèn'oto žìto li e
But what did you sow [then]? Autumn wheat?
22349: esèn'oto žìto go ur nasèem i orèm i ràloto go zaròvi
[For] autumn wheat, we sow it, then plow. And the plough buries it.
22357: a lètn'oto go vlàčim sɤz branɤ̀ se kàzva  sɤs vṛ̀šina
But summer [wheat] – we rake it with what’s called a harrow, with brushwood.
22360: ja sàmo žìto li se sèeše
Um – was it only wheat that you sowed?
22366: emi žìto sàmo z žìtu čenìca kojò e za esèn'o
Well, wheat. Only grain (“zhito”); the wheat (“chenitsa”) that’s for autumn,
22372: kojò more e mòže da tràe na studɤ̀ zimɤ̀ska
that can – that can endure the cold in the winter.
22375: And we sow again in the spring.
22378: žìto i pšenìca ednò i sɤ̀što li e
22391: znàči na na rɤštà vìkate vìe žìto takà li
So that means you use the term “zhito” for rye, is that right?
22395: e žìtoto e za rɤštɤ̀ a čenìcata si e pčenìca baškɤ̀
Yes, “zhito” is for rye, and “chenitsa” is wheat. [It’s] different.
22404: baškɤ̀ ìma sème  ovèsᵊ ečemìk tò se sèe pròleti
And there’s other seeds. Oats, barley – that gets sown in the spring.
22407: tò se le èseni ne sèe dòde li aprìl
It’s not sown in the fall. When April comes
22412: nasèe se ečmìk nasèe se ovès i tò stìgne
they sow barley, they sow oats – and that can all be done
22418: jà vɤ̀jš kəkɤ̀j gi sme izgl'òdəli kəkvɤ̀j gi sme izgl'òdəli
Just look at the kind [of children] we raised – what we raised,
22426: gul'àmi məž'è̝ ìməm p'è̝t mumčètə sàmu
big men. I’ve got five of them – only counting the boys.
22431: [laughter] i tɤ̀j s iglì sə plit'è
22441: əmi təkàli sni təkàli sni əmə segà v'èki sə uništužì
Well, we used to weave. We used to weave. But now it’s already gone.
22446: stənuv'èti sə uništužìə i n'àmə stàn n'àmə nìštu n'àmə kvò də təčèm
The looms are [all] gone. There’s no loom, nothing.  Nothing [for] us to weave.
22453: sìčkutu gutòvo idì fəf məgəzìnə i še si kùpiš
Everything’s ready-made. You go to the store and buy yourself [everything].
22455: [Tell me something about the old days.]
22457: n'àmə kəkvò də təčèm n'àmə kvò də prid'èm
There’s nothing to weave, nothing to spin.
22471: əmi š eš èj tùkə niz dòln'ite məəlɤ̀i ìmə stàri nìnki
Well, you [should] go down to the lower districts, to the old grannies here,
22478: t'à še pupɤ̀jtəš t'è še ti kàžət sɤ̀jčku
[if] you ask them they’ll tell you everything.
22484: še ti kàžət è bɤ̀jrvəkìcki ràbuti d'ètu d'ètu t'è sə zəpòvnili
They’ll tell you [all] these old-time things that – that they’ve remembered.
22488: nìe sme zəpòvnili nɤ̀jštu nìe ne gla
We haven’t remembered anything. We don’t –
22491: sàmu adɤ̀jn glàs sme zəpòvnili nìe
we’ve only remembered one way of life.
22499: pu ədnovr'àmešnu si guvòrim kàtu sɤ̀j sme nəšlɤ̀j təkà si guvòrime
We speak the old-time speech. What we come across, that’s how we talk.
22506: dà òdimə nə ərmàn ə i səber'è̝me tvà žìtutu səs pl'evòwtə
Yes. We go to the threshing field. We gather up the grain and the chaff,
22512: səberè̝m gu nə kɤ̀wp i z'èmeme lupàti̥te fəf rəkɤ̀jte
we gather it into a pile, and take shovels into our hands.
22517: i še gl'òdəš iskəd'ètu ìmə v'àter tàm še istàtək
Then you look where the wind is coming from, and that’s the direction
22522: še fòrneš tò sə žɤ̀jtutu jəndàn si sə udv'àvə
you’ll throw the grain. It winnows out, off to the side
22528: [Were you the ones who built this house?]
22539: kɤ̀wpifmè jə ud ədɤ̀jn čuv'àk tòj sə iss'è̝li ə pə
We bought it from some man. He moved away, and then
22545: nìe jə kɤ̀wpime nìe si sme segà ugrədɤ̀jli drùgə
we bought it [from him]. Now we’ve built another one
22549: əmə f nèjə ne smè sed'àli
but we haven’t been living in it.
22555: seà sme fəf sàə kulìbə f sàə kulɤ̀jbə
Now, we’re in this hut. [In] this hut!
22562: əmi nə ərmàn sutrintɤ̀ stàvəš rànu
Well, [there’s work] at the threshing field. You get up early in the morning.
22570: nəsàždəš snòpete nə ərmànə gi slàgəš rəstɤ̀jləž gi ùbəvu
You put the sheaves down on the threshing field, and spread them out nice,
22576: i fpr'àgəš vulòve li šè e kòn'e li šè e
and harness up oxen if that’s [what you have], or it might be horses,
22583: məgàretə li še e kəkvò də è kəkòtu ìməš prìmer živòtnu
or if it’s a donkey – whatever! Whatever animal you’ve got,
22588: gu fpr'àgəš i pòčvəš də kàrəš nə ərmàn'e də gu vəršèš
you harness it up and start to drive it [about] the threshing field to thresh,
22593: i də sə i kətu sə svəršè i pòsle slàmətə fkàrvəš
and to – And when it’s done, afterwards you put the straw
22598: fəf pl'àvn'ətə də gu kàžem slet tùj səbìrəš žìtutu nə kùpu
into the hayloft, so to speak, and then you gather up the grain into a pile.
22602: udv'àvəš gu i pòčvəš veče kòlkutò e gu prenàs'əš
You winnow it and then begin – however much there is, you take it
22605: i gu slàgəš f əmbàrə i tvà e drùgu kvò
and put it into the barn. And that’s that. Anything else?
22606: [(When you say ‘you harness [it]’, do you say) fpryagash or fpryogash?]
22610: gu fpr'àgəš i gu fpr'ògəš sè si e ednò
Whether you say “fpryagash” or “fpryogash” – it doesn’t matter!
22616: n'àki təkà əmə n'àkuj gu pək kàzvə še gu fpr'àgə
Some [say] this [“fpryogash”] but another will say he’ll harness it, “fpryaga”.
22619: mə pučtì še gu fpr'àgəš kàzvət
But mostly it’s – you’ll harness it, “fpryagash” - [that’s what] people say.
22621: dubɤ̀jtəkà gu fpr'àgəš f ərmànə i pòčvəš
You harness up the cattle in the threshing field, and get started.
22627: jà ne sɤ̀m sàdil i lòze n'èməm təkì ràbuti
I haven’t planted vineyards. I don’t have such things,
22630: ne sɤ̀m sàdil vɤ̀jš əku ìmə gròzde də àpneme
I haven’t planted [any]. Look, if there are grapes to eat,
22636: ili n'àštu vɤ̀jnu də pìjme še pìjme əku nè n'èməme
or if there’s some sort of wine to drink, we’ll drink! If not, we won’t.
22638: But we don’t have vineyards here.
22650: i ə i s'ètn'e təkòzvəš ə v'èč'i sə wrɤ̀štəš
And so. And you do [all] this, and then you come back
22654: u kòj u mòməkə li ili u
To whom? To the [home of] the boy, or to –
22655: u mòməkə be v'èči u mòməkə u mòməkə sə wrɤ̀štəš
The boy! [You live] already [now] at the boy’s. You go back to the boy’s.
22661: ini inò wr'èmi tò sigà ìmə màsi nə unùj
In the old days – now there are tables for this –
22665: pək inò wr'èmi dàmištə hl'àf gu kàzvəmi nìj
but in the old days [it was in] the ground-flour stable – the barn, we called it.
22666: [We all gathered] in the stable there.
22674: l'àf u hl'àvu u dàmu tàm idìn gul'àm dàm ìməši
The barn. In the barn, in the stable. There was a big stable there.
22679: nìj ìməxmi gul'àmə kɤ̀štə kəd'è j t'à bèše gul'àmə
We had a big house, so it (the stable area) was big too.
22680: i k'e gu prigòtvi i tò k'e presedì tə də se
and get it ready so it can sit, so as to ...
22690: dvàase lɛ̀bə du dvàase kulàci l'ɛ̀buve əmə tè pò golɛ̀mi
… twenty breads, up to twenty loaves of bread. But they're bigger
22695: lɛ̀buv'ètu ne sà kətu tìjə màlečki unìjə sə gulɛ̀mi
[loaves] of bread. They're not like these little ones. Those are big –
22703: e tòlk'i tekà gulɛ̀mi lɛ̀buve tìjə də tràje pòveč'e
the bread loaves are this big – they['re made] to last longer.
22708: tàm kətu zèmeš də rɛ̀žeš lɛ̀bu estefà gulɛ̀mə udrɛ̀žiš si
And when you take the bread to cut it into big chunks, you cut off
22711: ut tòa lɛp se rànəjə mòže də
[chunks] from this [big] bread, and that's what people ate. It might
22717: zəkəsnɛ̀e mòž də pur'àsə əmə ud n’ègu nèma drùk
go a bit sour, it might get air holes in it, but there was nothing else.
22723: segà tràsa: təz'è segà ìma: l'ɛ̀p i glèda: də ə pò m'èk
Now people want to have fresh bread, and they make sure that it is softer,
22727: də nə jè kuràf də se jədè tə təkà
that it's not stale, that it's edible. [And that's] how it is.
22743: s'èki si ur’èši mistàtə dud'è b'èši čàsnu
Everyone plowed his own plot so long as it was private [ownership].
22755: sɤs volòve i se žɤ̀ne fsìčko zàedno
with oxen. And then it’s all reaped together.
22761: OK. [Now] you say that at the mill …
22770: nə vodenìcata šmìrgel kàmik si se vṛtì è tòlk'uo kolò
... at the mill the emery stone revolves, a wheel this big.
22775: tò si e odgòre napràveno i si pàda žìtceto po màlko
It’s made so the grains fall on it from above a little at a time,
22781: ot tùka kràj kolòto kolòto go isfṛ̀ga na brəšnò
from here by the wheel. And the wheel puts out flour.
22786: i vɤf kòšče tàm sɤbìra se tùra se f čuvàle
And everything gets gathered in a basket, and put into sacks.
22790: i kàrame i sèeme mèm mèlem mèsim
So we go out and sow and grind and knead …
22794: čèr lèp po ednà nedèl'a òpečà go f ponedèlnik pa pà
… black bread once a week. I bake it on Monday, and then again
22799: f ponedèlnik takìva samùne čèrni ama nèma azmɤ̀ da fàne mu:lɤ̀
on Monday – these dark loaves, that aren’t damp [?], that don’t get moldy
22802: i dàmu èj tùkətɤ̀j ìmə də səbirèš' i vɤ̀tr'e
This much space to gather [people]! And inside,
22805: tables all lined up [sitting] on the mangers.
22808: In the mangers? You put tables [in the mangers]?
22813: ni jè jèdentȕ tàm nər'ed'ènu kòjtu i təkòzvə
No, not [there]. The food was laid out there, whoever did [whatever].
22816: ə pək mɑ̀s:t'ȅ tò nəpràenu màsi əmə
And the tables. They were made up [as] tables, but
22819: kəkvì màsi səs məgàr:ta i i təkòs ə
the kind of tables using sawhorses and, and these –
22824: l'èsi b'e l'èsi nəl'i znàjš kəkò e tòj l'èsi
Table tops, yes! Table tops. You know what table tops are?
22827: dɤ̀l' ne znàjš kòj tə znàj
[Well,] who could guess whether you’d know that.
22831: ut dərwò nəpràenu i ut ə kurì tɤ̀j upl'èt'eni
So they’re made of wood, and of woven bark woven together [wattle-like].
22838: upl'èt'eni i dɤ̀ski n'àkəde kədèt ni stìgə tò mnògu nəròt
woven. And boards in places if it’s not enough, if there’s a lot of people.
22843: i tàm v'èč'ə s'àdəš i edèš i drùgu du dvənàjs
And then you sit down there and eat and such, till midnight.
22850: dà swədbàr:tȅ tàm tò hòrə mnògu tàm sə idè
Yes. The wedding guests [are] there, many people. That’s where you eat,
22857: tàm təkòswəš pijèš' du dvənàis č'esɤ̀ s'ètne dvənàjs č'esɤ̀ v'èč'e
hang out, drink – up to midnight. Then when it’s midnight,
22861: nèma da isɤ̀xne ami mèko i ùbavo i te tè takà
and won’t dry out but rather [stay] soft and nice. And there it is.
22867: a ìmaše li vìe da mèlite fkɤ̀šti takɤ̀v edìn màlki kàmɤk
So did you all used to grind at home with some little stone
22870: da si go vɤrtìš na rɤk na rɤ̀ka
that you’d rotate around by hand?
22876: nèma lèp nìe sedìme tùka na sènka na vɤ̀zdux
There's no bread – we’re sitting here in the shade, outdoors.
22879: That’s what these things are like.
22881: i pòsle kato go donesèš brašnòto kɤdè go pribìraš
And then when you bring the flour [home], where do you put it?
22886: emi sedì si f čuvàle turìle sme dɤskɤ̀ na do stenɤ̀tɤ
Well, it sits in the sacks. We put up a board on – near the wall
22891: vɤ̀tre fkɤ̀šti sedì si f čuvàla vɤf noštuvìte si òtsea
inside the house, and it sits in the bag. Then I sift it into the kneading trough
22897: sɤs sìtoto mèsa si onòva si sedì dodè go ìzmesa
with a sieve, I knead [that part], and the rest sits there until I finish it all.
22898: kɤdè še go tùra vɤf čuvàla si sedì
Where [else] am I going to put it? It sits in its sack.
22906: tekà i pòsle trèbva da zamèsiš xl'àp àjde da mi kàžeš
O.K. So then you need to make the bread. Tell me now
22910: recèptata za xl'àba kòjto vìe ste pràvili ednò vrème
the recipe for the bread that you used to make in the old days.
22916: emi mèsihmè go nìe sme si omèsile da kàem fčèra li
Well, we kneaded it. For example, if we made some up yesterday,
22922: onàa nedèl'a sme si omèsile ostàvilè sme è tòlčafko turtè
or we made it last Sunday, we'll have left aside this little round bit –
22926: v'èč'i sə rəspil'àvət utìvət də zəncɤ̀t krɤ̀sniku
everyone leaves. They go away, they go to see the godfather off.
22929: They accompany the godfather back home,
22936: pək bùl'kətə ustàvə səs ə unùj š'ə izvin'àvəte əmà
And the bride is left with that – you’ll [have to] excuse me but –
22939: nè nè rəzkəžì gu tvà e interèsnu
No, no, tell [us] about it. It’s interesting!
22946: bùlkətə ustàvə səz gudenìku v'èč'i tùkə
The bride stays here with her fiancé,
22951: pək ə krɤ̀sniku̥ səs swudbɑ̀r:tȅ utìvət də də nòs'ət krɤ̀sniku̥ sìčkitȅ
while the godfather and all the wedding guests go to see the godfather off.
22958: à nàči dùkətə nòs'ət krɤ̀sniku tugàvə
Ah, so it’s while they are seeing the godfather off that –
22967: bùlkətə səz gudeniku v'eč'i̥ t'àxnətə ràbutə tàm
The bride and her fiancé are already [doing] their “job” there,
22973: i ə unès kət zəncɤ̀t krɤ̀sniku̥ pàk sə wrɤ̀štət
And the others come back after they see the godfather home,
22993: i sə rəspolàgət xùbəv dèn kəto i nə xərmàna
and if it's a nice day they make up the tables [out] on the threshing floor.
23026: i pàk xurà pàk ə tùpət tɤ̀pani xò vèselo dur sɤ̀mni
and again [there’s] dancing, again the drums beat, and oh! merriment until daybreak,
23029: du du plànne nəpràu kəkò j tò
and even well into the day [depending on] how they feel.
23035: a àku nèštu ràbutətə izlèze lòšə
And if somehow the “job” comes out badly?
23040: kət jizlèzi lòšə àjde bùlkətə jə pɤ̀d'ət nə u t'àf
If it turns out badly, they send the bride back to them ( = her parents).
23046: emi tò inò wr'èmi n'èmə təkòs kəd'è š'e e
Well, in the old days there wasn’t any such thing. How could it –
23049: Hey Rachka! Where did you go?
23058: òf jà sɤm ostàvila stòka domà da stàjam da si vṛ̀va
Ah, I left the animals at home. I have to get up and go
23064: čàkaj segà sled màlko əf mlekòto da ni kàeš kàg go rabòtiš
Wait [and go] in a bit. The milk – tell us you how process it.
23066: emi mlekòto mlekòto kato ìzdoa ofcìte dnèska pèt òfci li sa
Well, milk – milk. I milk the sheep today, maybe it’s five sheep,

23203: Honor [is what] they were looking for.

the ash and coals, and then we toss [the bread] in there with a shovel,

23386: i kakvò kətu əkù slèt katu sə səberɤ̀t dvàmətə

23414: e tɤ̀j d'è ìstinski tùj ìstinsku kəd'è igràjət nə urò tò

23455: ama s'èd'əm wòs'əm decɑ̀ s'àkuj čuèk s'èd'əm wòs'əm s'èd'əm wòs'əm

seven or eight – [each one] had up to nine or ten children.

23485: takà bèše i fùrnite kòj uš kàl napràil si fùrn'a

23494: That’s how it was back then.
23496: That’s the sort of things there were.

23535: na bojadžìata sestrà mu gospodìna bàba gospodìna
the painter’s sister Gospodina? Granny Gospodina

23563: i sìrište imàlo e i magazìni imàlo e ìdem

23584: čàkaj da mìne tòzi ne čùvame dobrè takà sìrište si ìmaš

23589: sìrište si ìma akò e dèset kilà mlèko šte tùriš dvè kàpki

you’ll pour [it] into either a cauldron or a kettle,

23663: šte si go sìpeš vɤf butàlka ki tò si e bɤškɤ̀ za nèa

23667: tò si e butàlka takà tòlkova širòčka
23673: tòlkuva visòka kòlko si sìpeš mlèko i sɤz džurùl'akᵊ tojàga

23759: šte si go izbìeš s ednà vòda bìstra vɤv dvè
… you’ll wash it in clear water once or twice ...
23762: da nèma vòda pòsoli si go tùri si go f
... until there’s no water [in it]. You salt it, and put it into –
23769: nèkoga ìmaše dèlvi kàaləeni takà takòva k'ùpče mìničko tùram tàm nàpḷna gu

23772: kàk sɤm si go izmìla sɤm si go posòlila sɤm go

23799: men'àvaš tàa vòda tùraž drùga pàk si presòlvaš solčìca

23801: da si e solènko odgòre i takà

23814: tò ə m vòda štò a pùšti se kàzva sulumùr

23829: ako gò razbṛ̀kaš sɤs ə sulumùra sìreneto še zème da ti merìše

23833: a tòo kajmàk odgòre lèko šte si go fàneš

23836: šte si go fṛ̀liš šte si go očìstiš šte si go otrìeš

23840: kačènceto naòkolo dodèka e bilò mòkro
the little keg all around where it got wet.
23842: jàz sɤm vɤf sòfia sɤm mnògo rabotìla i tàm okrivèx ot sòfia
I’ve been in Sofia. I did a lot of things and I went lame from Sofia!
23846: tùka na selu kakvò da pràva

23850: And the butter is kept that way ...
23854: And that’s how these things are.

Wait? [Yes,] the bread hasn’t come, but [even] if there’s no bread

Well, may you be alive and well. Look, you’re sixty now,
23890: you [must] have granddaughters. You do have some [right?]
23895: šte zèmat da ti čorbadžìjstvat tì šte kato rečè

“I don’t know how [to do this], Grandpa, I don’t know how, Dad”
23910: But in the old days you used to weave?
23913: əmi idnò vr'èmi si təčèxmi nìj i čèrgi
Ah, in the old days we would weave rugs
23917: čèrgite zə pustìləni si təčèxmi əmxəm

23928: I just asked because I saw [your watch]

So that’s that. After that, like I told you, they’ll
23954: du ob'et v'èki igràjət pìjət təkòzwət v'èč'i sə rəspil'àwət
be dancing and drinking and such until noon, and then they’ll disperse,
23957: i v'èč'i bùl'kətə v'èč'i š si pudrèždə drèit'e v'èč'i
and the bride will have been arranging her handiwork
23973: nèjn'it'ȅ əm kɤ̀k às kəkò č'eìs səm dunèsələ ò kəkò čeìs
Her things. Oh, what a dowry I brought with me! Oh, what a dowry,
24156: kəkò n'èštu wòs'əm jurgàn'ə səm ìmələ i vəzglàvnici i č'erš'èβi
what a thing! I had eight quilts, and pillows, and sheets –
24163: kòlku č'erš'eβi ìməm às dàže ìməm òšte id'ìn
how many sheets I had! I even still have one –
24169: b'àl vɤ̀l'nen è tɤ̀j b'àlu səz b'àl pəmùk i ə təkòs
it’s of white wool, white [like] this one. And white cotton too, and such.
24173: i kəkò šə stàni às ni znàm nìkuj ni gì štè
And what will happen [to it all] I don’t know. Nobody wants them [any more].
24180: sid'ì sid'ì sìn sìn təkɤ̀f pàk təkàn
Yes, still here. And [I have] a blue one, too, woven.
24182: mnògu às ìməm mnògu drèi səm ìmələ mnògu
[There’s] a lot – I have a lot of handwork. I had a lot.
24184: às dàβəm nə nə unùj ə d'ètu d'ètu igràjət sigà
I give things [now] to those – the ones that dance now,
24189: t'ès ə  bùl'kit'ȅ nə ə stər'èškiu dòm ə stər'èškiu dòm nəlì
these – the “brides” at the old-age home. The old-age home, you know?
24193: ednò vrème si mesùvame nìe lèbu
In the old days, we would make our own bread.
24200: əmi jà fùrnədžìite ne sì li vidèl nà pekà
Haven’t you seen the outdoor oven tenders [who] bake it over there?
24204: i nìe təkà pečè:me e tekà mèsimè gu f nuštuvìte
And we [also] bake it that way. Like this: we knead it in the kneading trough,
24209: pòsle č'e gu nəmèsime nə pitàrčetə slàgəme nə ednà dəskà
and then we’ll shape it into loaves, put them on a board
24214: i pòsle pà pràve:me si ednì fudùl'č'i mu vìkəme nìe
And then we would make some smaller loaves, we call them “fudulchi”.
24220: fudùl'č'i nèkugàš zə bɤ̀rzu də stàne dukətu gurì peštà
Back then [we made] “fudulchi” because they bake fast, while the oven is heating up.
24223: ta kətu mè̝tneme lèbu f òn'e kràj
When we put the bread into one end [of the oven],
24226: də vuzìde tàm i lupàtətə mètəme f peštà
[to let them] rise, and then toss them in the oven with a peel.
24232: pèš mu vìka:me nìe nè fùrnə a peštà
We called it “pesh”. Not “furna” (outdoor oven) but “pesh” (home oven).
24246: təkòzvət nə kəf'en'ètu tàm ìmə grùpa mlàdi tɤ̀j bùl'ki
They do stuff at the café there. There’s a group of young girls [who]
24251: igràjət tàm səm in dàlə ìməv è tɤ̀j prist'ìlkə
dance there [and] I gave them – I had this apron,
24254: tùj sə kàzvə prist'ìlkə əmə l'ešt'àu b'àlu mərukìn sə kàzvə
it’s called an apron, but all shiny, of white satin [Damascene], it’s called,
24260: kuprìnə nəpràu i ròzəf i kədif'è zil'ènə sən dàlə
just like silk – pink. And I gave them green velvet.
24267: əm zəbràtki zəbràtki krepsul'ìn sət'ìn nəprə̀u s tənt'èl'i ùkulurɤ̀s
And head coverings – scarves of crepe and satin with lace around the edges:
24271: č'èt'ər' sən gi dàlə tàm nə t'àw bùl'ki də mɤ̀ təkòzvət
I gave four of these to those “brides” to do me honor.
24278: is tòo kràj se izpekà splè̝skəni təkvìjə nə tɤ̀nku
they bake at the other end. They’re flattened thin –
24283: we flatten out the bread [dough into] – “fudulchi” –
24289: dukətu se ispečè lèbu nìe hi dukətu mè̝tneme lèbu
While the bread is baking, we [take] them – when we toss the bread in,
24293: nìe hi izvàdime i jədè̝me lèbu se pečè pòsle
we take them out, and eat [them]. The bread bakes after that.
24296: tòj se pečè pòveče čəsuvè tàm i izvàždəme
It takes more hours to bake. And we take it out
24298: and then we eat [it]. That’s how it was.
24301: [In] the kneading trough. We would knead [dough] in the kneading trough,
24305: tə èj gulèmi nòštuvi slòžime brəšnòtu slàgəme sòl vodà tam
[in] a kneading trough this big! We put in the flour, add salt and water to it,
24310: brɤ̀kəme brɤ̀kəme vèčer pudmèsime də č'ìsne
and stir and stir. We knead it in the evening so it’ll ferment;
24314: sùtrin stàneme pà pretùrime brəšnò pà mèsime pà č'e č'ìsne
in the morning we get up, add flour, knead it again, it ferments again,
24316: pòsle č'e gu pràviš nə pitàrčetə
then you’ll make it into small loaves, and that’s that.
24321: i tə təvà e ednò vrème bèše sos kvàs nèməše məjà
Like that. In the old days [bread] was [made] with starter, there was no yeast.
24323: s kvàs si zəbrɤ̀kəme tàm i kətu mèsime lèbu
We mix it up with starter, and when we knead the bread,
24329: ustàime si tòledžèvu kulàčence ut xlèbə testò
we set aside a piece of bread dough the size of a small bun
24332: č'e čèkə pə zə drùgətə sèdmicə pàk də mèsime lèp
and it awaits the next week for when we make bread again.
24338: suberè̝m se ut məəlàtə kòlkutu xòrə ìma
We get together, as many from the neighborhood as have [food to cook],
24343: osòbenu gàtu ìmə kurbàn nə gerg'òvdèn
particularly when there’s a celebration. On St. George’s Day
24347: soberè̝m se pet šès dùši upàlime fùrnətə
five or six of us gather together, and fire up the large communal oven,
24351: tam peštà i izmetèm jə mùšneme təvìte vɤ̀tre
the oven there. We sweep it out, and then shove the pans inside
24355: də se ispekà jàgnetàtə vèčer izvàdimè i gutòvi
so the lambs will roast. In the evening we take them out [when] ready,
24359: nòsime f čèrkvə pòpu i prekàdi [laughter]
and carry [them] to the church for the priest to bless them. [laughter]
24360: [How do you know when it’s done?]
24365: è kàk gu puznàvəš əmi lè gu ubɤ̀rneme
How do you know when it’s ready?  Well, don’t we turn it over
24370: iscrɤ̀vi se udgòre stàne ùbəvu pèčenu
[when] it’s gotten red on top, [when] it’s nicely roasted?
24372: Later we turn it over [again] and add rice.
24378: èj nə tɤ̀z bùlkə tùkə̥tɤ̀j nàštə
And to the “bride” here, the one from our family –
24392: l'ešt'àu tò krèp kət sətìn təkòs nəpràu mnògu xùbəf plàt
Yes, shiny. Yes, all shiny. Crepe, real satin. Really nice fabric.
24396: amə kò də gi pràjə t'è bùl'kit'ȅ nàšte ni štɤ̀t
But what can I do with them? These “brides” of ours don’t want [them].
24404: i im gi dàduf tàm də igràjət əm təkàni фùsti
So I gave them to [the girls] there that are dancing.
24407: inò wr'èmi təkànu nəpràu wòs'əm фùsti səm ìmələ jà
Woven aprons, woven properly in the old days. I had eight [such] aprons.
24413: nə tɤ̀s dàduw dv'è i dàvəm nəpràu è tu̥kətɤ̀j è
I gave those [girls] two, and I am still giving them away.
24425: amən kɑ̀zwat hòrətə n'èməlu gòsput' gòsput' enò wr'ɛ̀me pu zem'ɛ̀tə vər'àl
People say there’s no God. [But] the Lord at one time walked on the earth.
24431: ɑ̀s vèk'e əmèn stògudìšna divindis'è bɑ̀bini səm čùvələ
I’m already almost a hundred years old – ninety. I’ve heard my ancestors
24435: kɛ̀g bìlu pu zem'ɛ̀ta gòsput' hòdel
[tell] how it was [that] the Lord walked on this earth,
24443: nə urɑ̀či̥t'ȅ kɛ̀k kɑ̀zəl də urɛ̀t na žèn:t'ȅ kɑ̀k kɑ̀zal da təkɛ̀t
and told the ploughmen how to plow, and the women how to weave.
24449: amà səgɑ̀ izmenì sə nəròdə ni puznɑ̀və gòspud'ə̟
But now people have changed, and they don’t recognize the Lord.
24455: tòj še zəwəlì pɑk n'èma də ustɑ̀ne tɛ̀j ama gɑ̀ mìne wr'ɛ̀me
He will make it rain again - it won’t stay like this. But when time passes –
24461: ama ɑ̀s ni ni gù znɑ̀m s'ɛ̀jə̟t li
I don’t [even] know if they’re sowing it [or not],
24464: mə tɛ̀j po s'èbe si vìdi mi se če sa s'ɛ̀li
though from what I can see it seems that they have sown [the seed].
24466: ɑ̀z s'àh ama s'à kvò š stàne
I sowed, but [who knows] now what will become [of it].
24470: mi n mamùl':t'ȅ mòž də sə dəržɛ̀t ma drùga gùnna sùša
Well, the corn can hold out, [because] in other years of drought
24474: ... they [will be able to] bring [it] in.
24477: znàči mlàdite ne ne znàjət gòspod segà ne xòd'at na cɤ̀rkva
So, the young people don’t know the Lord now, they don’t go to church.
24481: am kɑ̀zwat n'è e gòsput' sìn'a plòča
Well, they say it’s not God, [it’s a] [curved] blue slab.
24486: ne s'ɛ̀ ə kurnaz'àjti ne s'ɛ̀ kurnaz'àjti
Don’t puff yourselves up, don’t puff yourselves up.
24495: But [in the interim] the corn will wither, won’t it?
24504: ò bàbo i sià kvò sàkaš da ma pìtaš pàk
Ah, granny’s one. And now what do you want to ask me again?
24511: ud nɑ̀s pò dɛ̀rti n'èma ud nɑ̀s pò zapɑ̀nnali n'èma
There’s no one older than us, [no one] more on the decline than us,
24514: od nɑ̀s pò miz'èrno də žuv'ɛ̀jet n'èma
or who lives more miserably than us.
24520: idìna mi sìn gu ubìha kət edìn pɛ̀rvie b'ɛ̀še
One of my sons was killed, [that] was the oldest one,
24529: nìj ostɑ̀nahme v'èki ne nì z'èma gòsput dušɛ̀ta
We’re [the only ones] still here, the Lord hasn’t taken our souls [yet].
24533: There isn’t anyone to see us.
24543: də tùr'ət krɑ̀j də tùr'ət krɑ̀j n'èma də tùr'a krɑ̀j
[Yes,] to put an end [to us], put an end. [But he] won’t put an end [to it]
24546: də mə gl'èda gòsput’ kɛ̀k səm nakɑ̀zana
the Lord should see how much I’ve been punished –
24549: the one – He sees from [up] there.
24556: sigɑ̀ sàmo jnò sàmo jnò i hìč
Now [they] just [have] one, just one and nothing [else].
24565: ut nàšto sèlo əj tùk ednà kumšùja otìde nətàk kəm sòhia
One of our neighbors from our village has gone off to Sofia.
24567: ud d'è ste hòra sìčkitɛ̏ ud' enò s'èlo li ste
And where are all you people from? Are you [all] from the same village?
24571: ə nè nìe sme ot sòfia ama dnès dnèska sutrintà
Oh no, we’re from Sofia, but today - this morning
24578: b'àxme vəf kozìčino vəf erkèč b'àxme i dojdòxme pešà tùka
we were in Kozichino  – we were in Erkech – and we came here on foot.
24582: On foot? Ah, you poor things.
24586: [Yes,] on foot. Well, we made a bit of an excursion [of it].
24592: em pičè pičè am vìj pu kəkò hòjte
But it’s so hot, so hot!  Well, what did you come here for?
24597: tɛ̀j po hùbavo n'e st'è trɛ̀gnali h tòs p'èk
Didn’t you have some nice [reason] to set out [on a trip] in this heat?
24599: We had a nice [reason] to come!
24600: We had a nice [reason] to come.
24606: We’re looking for old-style talk, old stuff.
24612: stàrijə ezìk tɤ̀rsime da ni guvòrite pu pu gulìški
We’re looking for the old language, for you to speak to us in Golitsa speech.
24618: po erkèčanski li go vìkate kàg go vìkate po erkèčki
[Or] do you call it the Erkech speech? How do you say it in the Erkech manner?
24624: tìj v'èke sə izmòdia ud mèn'e baškɑ̀
24630: I’d spin, and [work] on the loom thus.
24654: people don’t speak the old language.
24660: tìj v'èke d'èto ìdiš bògə zabrɑ̀w'ət
Now wherever you go they’ve forgotten God.
24663: də im tr'àbva n'ɛ̀što nə bògə
24669: … [is] where they will [need to] turn, but …
24672: … [along the path] where you were walking?
24675: … they [think] they don’t need [God any more].
24683: They’ve all turned [the wrong way] now.
24689: əmə ut kədɛ̀ ste ìnače be bɤ̀lgari li ste
So other than that, where are you all from, huh? Are you Bulgarian?
24697: e kàžite kvò ìskate segà da vi prikàzvame
Tell me, what do you want us to talk to you about?
24703: t'à e ot amèrika ama ùči bɤ̀lgarski i go znàe mnògo dobrè
[This woman] is from America, but studies Bulgarian and knows it very well.
24708: əma t'à vɤ vòdi ili vìe ja vòdite nèja
Well, is she taking you around or are you taking her around?
24712: ami zàedno xòdim [laughter] segà kòj kogò
Well, we’re going together [laughter]. Who’s [taking] whom [doesn’t matter].
24714: kato ìdem kat ìdem f amèrika t'à še ni vòdi
When we go – when we go to America, she’ll take us around.
24718: i kvò ža pràite segà fìlm nɛ̀kaf
So what are you doing now? [Making] some sort of film?
24726: nè nè sàmo se interesùvame ot stàri ot stària rodòpski ə ezìk
No, no. We’re only interested in the old-time Rhodope language …
24728: kàk se govòri tùka u gelà
How you speak here in Gela!
24736: abe nìe da ti kàža bajɛ̀ gudìni živèeme f smòl'an
Ah, well, to tell you [the truth], we’ve lived many years in Smolyan,
24738: so we’ve messed up [our Gela speech] a bit.
24743: ut pedesè ut pedesè i òsma devèta gudìna sme f smòl'an
From ’58 or ’59 we’ve been in Smolyan.
24747: lɛ̀tnu vrɛ̀me sme v gelà zìmata sme f smòl'an
During the summer we’re in Gela, and in the winter we’re in Smolyan.
24750: tàm si ìmame kɤ̀šta decàta mì sa tàm i takà
We have a house there, my children are there, and that’s how it is.
24751: e kàžite tò ža kàžem tì pò znàeš àjde
So tell [us] what to tell you. You [tell them], you know more. Come on!
24752: Ah – what [do I have] to tell [them]?
24765: ni znàjet n'èto vərhɑ̀ni n'èto žètva n'èto hùrka
They don’t know about threshing, nor about reaping, nor about distaffs.
24769: Look at this guy, asking [all] these [questions]!
24770: They know, they know. They know everything.
24773: Well, so as to know more.
24777: They know all sorts [of stuff that] we don’t know.
24779: You know more [than I do], Tosho.
24784: d'èt harmɑ̀n:tȅ ne znàeli d d'èt sne žənèneli
... where the threshing fields are, they didn’t [seem to] know where we did the reaping,
24796: dèt sne vəršɛ̀li nìšto n znàjat ud nib'èto
where we did the threshing. Nothing! [They came] from the sky.
24800: ami è tvà kato ìma ofcà tùka e udòben slùčaj
Well, let’s say – since there are sheep here, it’s a good opportunity
24806: da ni kàžete ofcì kàk se glèdat
to tell us about how one looks after sheep.
24809: Tell them to make it start raining!
24813: əmhəm kàk se gl'ɔ̀dat nalì po
Uh huh. How one “looks after”, you know, in ...
24815: They’re not from the sky, these people.
24828: gl'ɔ̀dat sa sabìrat sa po mnògu ufcè
[One] looks after them, you gather together many sheep.
24833: čùkna: kəmbànite ìdeme v čèrkvə vrɤ̀nemè se ut tàm
The church bells ring, and we go to church. [When] we come back from there,
24838: stròexme jəjcàtə pà sme pà sme càl' pos pustìli
We painted eggs [for Easter], and we kept the entire [Lenten] fast.
24843: nèma ə čìstu rudòpsku li m guvòriš
Ah no, aren’t you going to speak pure Rhodope [speech] to them?
24850: hàjde nə tɤpənètu tùpa: č' ìim nə òrutu nə rekàtə
it's off to the drums, they’re drumming! And we’ll go to the horo at the river.
24854: tə òru tə òru təkà se e raptìlu ednò vrème
And dance, dance – that’s what people did in the old days.
24860: tə sme udìli də kòpəme də nəpràime pàte tàm də rəbòtime
And we went to dig, in order to make a road, to work there
24866: kəə rəzlòšku kəə gòdlesku pàte tə kòpəme čəkɤ̀l' tàm
on the road [going] towards Razlog and Godlevo. We dig gravel there,
24872: tə òdeme sus merudìjə s rəsòl kərtòfč'i kòpəme tàm càl' dè̝n
and we go with mint, sauerkraut and potatoes [for lunch]. We dig there all day,
24879: rəbòtame sè s pòsnu jàdene sètne vèče kət dòe pà velìjden
work all day [just] with Lenten food. And then when Easter comes,
24884: vèče pà se bujədìsa: červèni jàjca pà se ublàžime
everyone has been dyeing eggs red, and we break the fast.
24890: [laughter] tò čistu i às ne znàm ve [laughter]
[laughter] “Pure” – even I don’t know that any more! [laughter]
24955: lì t kàzvəm nì go sme umɛ̀sɤlɤ nàšijas ezìk ezgà
Like I’m telling you, we’ve mixed up our language now.
24960: ami kakvò zìmata gi hrànimɤ trì pati sùtrɤn òb'et i večèr'e
So – we feed them in the winter, three times [a day]: morning, noon and evening.
24966: dàvame hmi furàš tàm zòp mòže da e ečemìk də e čenìca
We give them forage, feed, maybe also barley, wheat.
24972: i pruletɤ̀ əma sɤ pàslɤ pu kɤ̀rɤ pu baìretu
And in the spring they were [taken out to] graze in the fields, in the hills,
24977: i sɤ sɤ zapludìlɤ i napròl'et pòčnat da sa da ràdat
and they’ve mated, and in the spring they started to bear–
24983: à da sa jɛ̀gn'at i ràždat ednò kòj ednò kòj dvè
Yes, to have lambs. They’d bear one – some would have one, some two.
24991: e tvà e pròle pròl'etèšnu àgɤncɤ ama e mɤ̀ničku de
and in the – A "spring lamb" (= one born in the spring), well it’s little, see?
24999: i drùgite sa màjkite sa pàk əv guràta baìrese pasɤ̀t
[So] the other mothers are out in the woods, they graze in the hills
25004: pək e tìja mɤ̀ničkite i gl'ɔ̀damɤ dètu sɤ sɤ ujɛ̀gnɤlɨ
but we look after these little ones that just got born,
25007: tɛ̀h glèdame sɤgà tò hòrata ìmat po mnògu ama
we look after [them]. People now have a lot of them, but
25012: nàs ni nèma nìe po màšku ufcè ìmame ednà kràva adnà òfcɤ
we’re not here. We have fewer sheep. We have one cow and one sheep.
25017: i ezgà katu dòjde noe uktòmvri nuèmvri dòjde ə adnà kulà
and now when October or November comes, they come with the car
25021: i àjde pà vəf smòl'an nɤ kàrat tàm da žuvèeme
and they take us off to Smolyan to live there,
25024: da smɤ pò blìsku du decàna
so we can be closer to the children.
25032: ìmamɤ sìn dɤšter'à čètɨrɨ vnùčeta ùčat slùžat
We have a son, a daughter, and four grandchildren. They’re in school, in the military –
25037: adnò ìmam otslùžilu drùgu zgà e vujnìk dòkturče
one has finished his military service, another’s a soldier, a [future] doctor.
25043: ednà ìmam ɨ fɤf ànglija zgà adnà vnùčka mi utìde f ànglija
I have one in England now, one of my granddaughters went off to England.
25047: enò vr'ɛ̀me prɑ̀vehme mol'èbie krɛ̀st'at sa
In the old days we used to do special prayers, people cross themselves …
25053: bòže mìla zəvəlì bòže mìla zəvəlì
... [and say] “Dear God, make it rain; dear God, make it rain.”
25057: pək sigɑ̀ n'èma də j š ìdət
But now it won’t be that way. They’ll go –
25059: Where are the others of your group?
25063: mi òn'a dèn ìmaše ednà ednì drùgi
Well, the other day there was another – There were some others.
25066: Yes, but now we’ve come [with] another [group].
25075: sigɑ̀ tr'àbva da sə mòl'at nə səv'èta
Now we have to “pray” at the [local village] municipal hall.
25082: na səv'èta d'èto ìma tɑ̀m pisɑ̀ri
At the municipal hall, in the place where they have scribes.
25087: tìj venčàwət də sə ž'èni čil'ɑ̀k
They do the ceremony when someone marries.
25089: tùj segà dèt gu prikàzvə zapìsuva li se
This – what she’s saying now, is it getting recorded?
25092: They do marriages, they do christenings –
25100: they do the funeral. There’s no priest.
25102: vìkaš na nègo i da se mòl'at ə
[So] you say that [people] also go to [it] to pray, right?

28185: izmìež vɤlnàtə ìdiš uvlàčiš jə upredèš jə vàpcəš jə
