28193: jà dàj s'à kato ja strižèš kɤdè ə vlàčiš kɤdè ja perèš
All right now. When you shear [the wool], where do you card it? Where do you wash it?
28196: mi mi nə derètu è nə rekàtə̥
Well, in the river. There, in the river!
28203: nə rekàtə e isperème issàhne ušt'àvim jə i pòsle jə udnesème
We wash it in the river, it dries, we tan it, and then we take it
28206: də də sə uvlàči i slèt kətu se uvlàči i
to – to be carded. And after it’s carded
28213: vèče smètəš zə štò ke jə slòžiš za kìtenìk le
you calculate how you’re going to put it [on the loom] – for a fleece rug,
28218: za prèstilki le zə čèrgi le kəkvòtu ti e nužnò təvà
for aprons, for rugs – whatever you need, that’s [what you make].
28221: dà e dobrè a s'àka vɤ̀lna li s ednàkvə li sa vɤ̀lnite
Yes. OK then. Are all [kinds of] wool the same?
28223: ili ìmaše ràzlika ot vɤ̀lna do vɤ̀lna
Or were there differences from [one kind of] wool and [another kind of] wool?
28230: mi vɤ̀lnə ìməše i mirinòsnə ìməše i krəstòskə ìməše
Well, there was Merino wool, there was crossbreed wool,
28233: pə i ud dɤ̀lgə si vɤ̀lnə
and [we made things] also from wool of long[-haired sheep],
28242: dà dà vìe ìmaxte òfci taka li
Yes, yes. So you kept sheep, right?
28250: mi mi i jàs sɤm udìlə s tèh
Well, I was the one to go out [to pasture] with them.
28256: i ìmah bràt predì mène sus nègu zàednu òdehme
And I have an older brother; he and I went out together [with the sheep].
28263: stò i dvàjse ufcì ìməhmè i i usemdesè kuzì
We had one hundred twenty sheep and eighty goats.
28273: And what did you make out of the goat hair?
28281: ɤ̀ àlištèta dà xɤ̀ i a àlištata kàk se rabòt'ɤt
Thick rugs, yes. Huh! And how did you make the thick rugs?
28285: mi i t'è nə nə dumàšen dəràk vlàčiš kòzinàtə
Well, you card the goat hair on – on a home carder,
28289: and then you spin it on the spinning wheel.
28295: i slet tuvà jə təčèš nə àlištè jə nəpràiš
And after that you weave it. You make it into the thick rug,
28299: i jə udnisèš nə tupàvicàtə i gu stùpə
and take it to the fulling mill, and it fulls it.
28302: i stàne càl' živòt s ednò àlištè də prekàrəš
And it becomes a thick rug that will last you your whole life.
28308: a də a na kakvò go tɤčèš
And what do you weave it on?
28326: tì tì čù čùvaš li si st stanɤ̀ čùvaš li go stanɤ̀
Have you – have you kept the loom? Do you [still] keep your loom?
28329: dà ìməm pə snài segà pə tè gu tè tɤkɤ̀t
Yes, I have it. And my daughters-in-law now use – and they now weave.
28335: jà sìčku znàet tìj mə kàk
Yes, they know everything. How [would] they [not]?
28343: And she gives it to the boy.
28345: Isn’t there kissing (ritual kissing of elder’s hands by the bride), or –
28347: And how do they do that?
28350: Well, I have heard [of the custom] but only heard of it.
28352: tr'àbva mi nèšto da mi kàže
[Someone] needs to tell me something [about it].
28355: [laughter] a ama kək jà lì ti kazvà vèče ne znàm
[laughter] But how can I? Haven’t I told you already? I don’t know
28360: Come on, come on, you’ve had enough.
28361: dobrè kato takòva kato s'à kato tàm
O.K., when this – now – when – well,
28365: na godèža li opredèl'at kogà če e svàdbata
is it at the engagement that they decide when the wedding will be?
28367: e pa na godèžo si opredèl'at
Yes, [it's] at the engagement [that] they determine that,
28369: i pòslem si pàk ìdat ednì u drùgi svatofštìnata
and then the future parents-in-law go back and forth to one another …
28372: da si opràvl'at àjde stìga vi
… to get things ready. OK, enough for you now.
28374: [to decide] when the wedding will be held.
28377: stìga vi vèče [laughter]  tì tì me iz izləgà
This is really enough already. [laughter] You – you, friend, misled me!
28382: All right, all right now. Pleasant journey!
28395: màž'eš' vrɤ̀zvəš' i mnògu e minàvəlu
You smear it [on], bind [it up], and it pretty much went away.
28400: [And this happened] to mine, to this –
28404: To her daughter, the older one.
28411: dəšterìčkətà mi nəpràvu kùcəš'è i kùcəš'e càl m'èsec
My little daughter was really limping. She was limping for a whole month,
28416: ni mòž'ehme də rəzber'èm kəkò je wòdeh pri l'èkər'ə
and we couldn’t find out what it was. I went to the doctor
28421: d'ètetu dùmə təkà š'e s ti ustàne krìvu
and he said the child will stay like that, lame.
28433: blàguvicə utìdəh pri n'èjə i t'à gu pubàrə e tùk f prègətìnkətə
(that is,) Blagovitsa – I went to her and she touched [her] here, on the crooked spot.
28439: pubàrə gu i dùmə nə m'ène əsib'è m'en mə zuvɤ̀t əsib'èjkə
She touched her and said to me, “Asibe,” (they call me Asibeyka –
28441: jà ti səm kàzələ əmə mòže də zəburìš
I told you that but maybe you forgot it)
28445: əsib'è kàzvə [sigh] nà ti màlku màs i v'èč'er' kàzvə
“Asibe,” she says [sigh], “here’s some lard. In the evening,” she says,
28449: š'ə gu rəstrìvəš i šə gu vɤ̀rzuvàš'
“you’ll rub it in and you’ll bind it up."
28458: ləjnà ut kràvətə nə ədnà bàl'evə kinìgə
28461: kət ìde də sə ser'è kràvətə i jà gi tùr'ə
When the cow goes to shit, I put it ...
28467: nə kinìgətə stòpl'ə gi màlku tùr'əm mu gu tàm
… on the paper, heat it up a bit, and put it on her
28473: i tòj l'ègne də spì v'èk'e zəburèvə sə č'i ìmə n'èštu
[= on her leg], and she goes to sleep and forgets there ever was something [wrong].
28483: mi kàk ə pres p'èt vèč'erə tuvà gu pràeh redòvnu
Really! I did that for five nights in a row,
28486: i d'ètenc'ètu sì mi uzdravè tàə mòmə
and my child got well. [Now she’s] this young woman.
28489: mòmə stànə kətu slɤ̀nce b'èše gìzdavə
She became a young woman, as [lovely] as the sun she was, a well-turned out ..
28493: ùbəvə mòmə əmi əku mi ustàneš'e krìvu
… beautiful girl. But if she’d stayed lame ...
28498: kəkvà kupn'à štèš'e ə mi bèš'e
... what a burden she would have been to me.
28501: Ah, [that would have been] very, very difficult.
28506: tə sì gu izl'ekùvəh jà si t'à mi putkàzə ž'enìčkətə stàrətə
But I healed her, I did it. This little old woman told me how,
28509: ə jà si gu pubàrəf jà si gu l'ekùvəf
and I touched her and I healed her.
28512: i si gu izl'ekùvəf i i seà š'ùker
I healed her and – and now all praise [to Allah].
28523: tìja  ne sɤ̀ možàli da ma vìdat òti mìslɤt če č sɤm
They apparently couldn’t see what [was with] me because they thought I was –
28533: ama še ta dṛžì gòspot vìž dokoto si ìmaž dnì
But the Lord will keep you going, you see, [for as many] days as you still have
28539: nì jàla pìla nì pikàla nì odìla po vɤ̀n
[even if] you haven’t eaten, or drunk, or pissed, or gone outside [for the other] ...
28544: i da ostànež da bɤ̀deš čovèk
... you’ll live on, and be a [real] human being.
28549: i kogà da se sɤžìvim na vadìci̥
And when I came back to life, on Epiphany –
28551: kogà da sɤ̥ sɤžìvim takà jà sɤm si bilà takà de
when I came back to life, I was apparently myself, more or less,
28555: ama ne sɤ̀m možàla da govòrim sɤs onìja kèle
but I couldn’t talk because of these rashes.
28560: i sɤ̀ga mène mi e kèlata tùk do tavà peknà malkò sḷ̀nčička
So now I have rashes all the way up to here. The sun came out a bit,
28566: zìmam jà ednò ogledàlce takà stròšeno̥ zèm če bèše takà u džàma
I take a bit of broken mirror, because it was there by the window,
28570: zìmam onovà ogledàlce takà i sreštu sḷ̀nce̥tu màlko zinà
I take this mirror [pointed] towards the sun like this, and I yawned a bit.
28577: kogà si vidè izìka a gṛkl'àna pokraj gṛkl'àna sàmo mèure
And when I saw [it] – My tongue! My throat! And next to my throat only blisters.
28581: ne mòe da pregḷ̀tnem ne mòe bɤ̀brem èj ulèze si
I couldn’t swallow, I couldn’t talk. And [this guy] comes in.
28587: jà mu dàvam ə onovà da glèda ama mu ne kàzvam
I give him this thing so he can look, but I don’t tell him
28589: kvò mi e ne mòe da kàžem i sɤ̀ga jà zinà
what’s the matter with me, I can’t speak. So now I yawned,
28593: i òn koto vidè òn kàe màlè kvò e tavà be
and when he saw he says, “Oh my! What is that?”
28597: jà si mìrno no jà bì mu kazàla kvò
I stayed quiet. [If I could have] I would have told him what it was.
28600: sɤ̀ga jà mɤ̀čim da mu kàžem da mi ku
But now I struggle to tell him that –
28605: da mi napràat čorbìca ot štàvl'ak ama onì ne mòe mɤ razbèrat
that they should make me some sorrel soup, but they can’t understand me.
28612: n'àmə n'àmə s'àə hòrə ni znàm kəkòt' ìskəd də
[No,] there isn’t. I don’t know. Let people have what they want.
28619: ku ìskə də ə kumənìskə əku ìskə dà ə rùsku
If they want the Communist [way], if they want, let it be the Russian.
28625: kukòt' ìskə də sàmu tr'àvə sə ràbut'i ni štɤ̀d də ràbut'ət
Whatever they want. All [we] need is work, but they don’t want to work.
28631: ut kəd'è kàž'te ut kəd'è še dòjd'e b'èz ràbutə
But tell [me] where [will money come] from without work?
28635: What can we – Isn’t that right?
28639: nè tè sàmo te slùšat t'èb'e s'egà
No, they’re just listening to you now …
28643: štòtu təkà se kàzva stàrite sɤ pò mɤ̀dri
… because, it’s said, old people are wiser,
28651: əhòw jà səm jàlə m'ètlin l'àp
28657: m'ètl'en m'i d'èt mitɤ̀t šə stɤ̀ržene ustɤ̀rgəni
[No, bread] from a broom. What you sweep with. We scrape [it], scrape [it] up.
28669: ... seeds [of the branches of a] broom. It’s called “syupyurge".
28675: tovà e tùrskə dùmə s'up'urgɛ̀ znàči metlɤ̀tə
That’s a Turkish word,” “syupyurge”. It means “broom”.
28679: à təkà i nəsɤ̀rgənə i màjkə utìde i kəl'èg
That’s right. So, [everything’s] scraped up, and mother went with my uncle,
28685: bòg də gu prost'ì utìəhə tə sm'èlihə e tùkə ìmə m'èlnicə
may he rest in peace, they went and ground it – there’s a mill here –
28695: um'èsiə l'àp l'àbə b'àše pròstu kvò də ti kàžə
and they made bread. It was just bread. But, what can I tell you?
28699: kət è unvà làjnu d'ètu e tàm nə təkɤ̀utu
It’s like that shit that [they have] over there at this –
28709: i əm òt' mi cɤ̀rn ud m'ètlə ut s'up'urg'ɛ̀ s'àme
Well, because it was dark – seeds from the broom, the “syupyurge” –
28714: kəkɤ̀v l'àp mə jəd'àhne təkòvu sme jàli
What sort of bread [is that?] But we ate it. That’s what we ate.
28722: du èj tùvə səm òd'lə bòsə nə učìlište nìšto mi n'è e
And I came barefoot all the way to here, to school. I had no problem with that.
28729: gà z gi gl'eəm t'àə krəkà bul'ɤ̀t bul'ɤ̀t bl'ɤ̀t
[But] when I look at my feet [now], they hurt, hurt – [how] they hurt!
28734: i t'àə nòkti bul'ɤ̀t gur'ɤ̀t ògən' ut udmrɤ̀znət'e
and the nails hurt, it’s like fire burning, from [having been] frozen.
28739: i du n'èskə səm živə du usems'è gudìni pək segà
But I’m alive today – eighty years [old]. But now it’s,
28747: vɤ̀h č'èdo vɤ̀h č'èdo də ne sɤ̀ pumɤ̀rdneš vɤ̀h č'èdo
“Oh child! Oh child, don’t move! Oh child!”
28752: tò ike dub'è li usvet'ènu tòj ne znàm kəkò bỳlu
And it’ll say “Is there enough light?” I don’t know what [other reason] there was,
28755: tòj ne znàm kəkò bìlo i pàk ne bỳvə
I don’t know. And still [the child] can’t manage anything.
28759: ut kəkò e tvà kàži segà ut kəkò e tvà tòo nəròt
Why is this? Tell me, now. Why are people like this?
28765: ud jàden'tu li mnòg jàd'en'e mnòg dròb'en'e jà
[Is it] from food? Too much food? Too many chunks of meat? As for me, I
28771: dròb'en'e pək n' jàm n'è jà nəpr'èš nəl' b'àh v bòl'nicətə
don’t eat meat – no, I don’t. A while ago I was in the hospital
28775: d'èt mi dədɤ̀t  mògə i təkà mə n'è n'è jà vìkəm
where they gave me [some]. I can [eat it], but – “No, no,” I said.
28779: du seà ne sɤ̀m jàlə dròbene še mə kàrət də jàm dròbene
“I haven’t eaten meat chunks till now. Why should they make me eat meat?”
28781: mə tì ednò vrème dròbene si ne id'àla
So you – in the old days you didn’t eat meat chunks.
28787: n'è əm ud d'è ənò vr'àme də jəd'àhme ud d'è də jəd'àhme
No! Where would we get it, back then? Where would we get [any] to eat?
28792: tòj n'àməše lùk tòj kàzvə dròbene kurmìt'ə
There weren’t [even] onions, not to say meat! [What] onions [there were]
28797: səkà žə gu učùkəne učùkəne i màjkə bòg də jə pròsti
got all pounded, pounded up like this, and mother, God rest her soul,
28805: bir'àše təkà təkɤ̀vu gròzd'e əmə gurìdə i pràeše uc'èt
would pick these grapes, but unripe, and would make vinegar
28809: and [we’d] scoop it up and eat – the skins too.
28815: ɤ̀ ud gurìdətə gribène uc'èt pək šurùpkite
Uh huh, of the unripe grapes. We’d take this vinegar, and the peels
28820: ut kurmìt'ə ščùkən e kurmìt lùk i greb'ène jədène
of onions, chopped onions, and we’d scoop it up and eat.
28824: slàtku jàdene ə s'à də idɤ̀t təkɤ̀vu
Sweet food [that was]! And [just] let [them] eat that now!
28833: nìe sni pò zdrài tr'àbvə də znàete èj tvà m'èz d'ed gu jd'ète
We are more healthy, you have to admit that. And that meat you eat
28840: i t'ɛ̀a imikàleni ràbuti càlə zìmə dumàti jədɤ̀t
and all these chemical things [they use]. [People] eat tomatoes all winter
28844: ud d'è tòu dumàt ba nəlì ut tòr i vòdə
and where do these tomatoes come from? From fertilizer and water!
28848: nɤ̀li n'è e ud zem'ɤ̀tə è tàm səm gi pus'àlə
They’re not from the earth, are they? But over there, where I planted mine,
28854: nìšt'u im ne sɤ̀m klàlə nìšt'u ne sàm vudà
I didn’t put anything on them, not anything. Just water.
28857: vudà ud dumàti hùbəi nìštu ne klàəh
[Just] water. [That gives] nice tomatoes. I didn’t put anything on them.
28865: əm zəštò zəštò š' ìdə də m'àtəm təkɤ̀vi tòrve t'àə utròvi
Why [not]?! Why would I go to throw such fertilizer, such poison on them?
28869: ama ne za iskùstvenijə ot ofcète ako zèmeš
Not that artificial stuff. If you [want] you could take [fertilizer] from sheep –
28874: à ud ufc'ìte n'à əmə ut kukòškite im go i klàah
I don’t have any from sheep, but I put down some from chickens.
28875: a e è pàk e tòr
Ah but [you see], that’s fertilizer too!
28882: kukòškite im klàəm nəkvàs'əm gu i im klàəm i drubnì
I put [stuff] from the chickens down, water it, put down lumps [of it].
28886: i kogàto go tovà kato go kopàeš li ili
And when you [do] that, do you dig, or –
28890: əm kətu nàprəə sərìjki i jà gu klàəm təkà də nək'ìsn'e
Well I make rows, and I put out [these lumps] like this so they’ll get soaked
28895: pək mnòg vr'àme də stujɤ̀t i tugà pu sərìte sìpvəm
when they sit there for a long time. And then I pour them over the rows
28898: i tvà e pək təkɤ̀v iskùstven nə dvòrə ne sɤ̀m klàlə
and that’s all. I’ve never put down anything artificial in my yard,
28901: zə ilàč təkà nəl' təkà e ni znàm kəkò
not even “medicinally”. And that’s how it is. I don’t know why –
28904: kəkò ne è nəròdə n' bỳvə n'è n' bỳvə
why it’s not – people aren’t right now. No, not right.
28913: ud jàden'tu li ut pìen'tu li ud nèràpten'tu li [laughter]
... from eating, from drinking, from idleness? [laughter]
28924: ìmə slùšəjte nà sigɛ̀ ni mògə vek'i n'àməm tàə sìlə əmə stìgə
Listen up now. I can’t [any] more, I haven’t much strength, but [I’ve] enough
28929: gòsput' du segà d'èt mi e dàəl tàa tvà səm m bləgudàrnə
to be grateful to the Lord for what he’s given me till now –
28936: də ìdə nə kɤ̀rə də z'èmə də kòpə bustàn'ə pul'èkə pul'èkə
that I can go to the field and manage to dig my melon patch. Little by little
28940: z gu iskupàh s mɤ̀ninkətə kupàčkə
I dug it out, with my tiny little shovel.
28948: dvà trì pɤ̀ti utìduh uhuhu bustàn' kòlku e
Two or three times I went, oho! [I dug] a melon patch as big [as I needed].
28954: təkà jà i ukul gərdìnətə ìməm si gul'àm dwòr če i nègə
And there it is. Around the garden I’ve got a big yard, and it’s [something]
28970: z gu pràəm  [unintelligible] nəpr'èš də ìd
I’ll work in it [unintelligible].   But to go out like before, to go out
28974: də ž'ènem də ìd də kòpə càl' d'èn' ni mògə
to reap and dig all day, I can’t do that now.
28975: è pa tò i ne tr'àbva
28983: n'àəm tàə tàə sìlə n'àəm mə stìgə tòlku
I haven’t that – I haven’t that strength. Enough already.
28987: əmə mlàd'te pək hìč ne bìwət li
But the young people, they’re just don’t make it.
28990: The young people don’t come [to see you]?
29018: i jà pokàzvam pokàzvam pokàzvam pokàzvam
And I gesture, gesture, gesture, gesture,
29021: ama jà ne mòe da kàam nìštò
29023: ustàta mi sa vèče otròven čovèk i tovà e  [cough]
My mouth is already [like that of a] poisoned person, and that’s all.
29026: setìa se onì nàj na nàj na sa se setìli
They sensed fina– fin– Finally they seemed to get it.
29029: tàa sàka kàe čorbà ot štàvl'ak i mi napràvea
“She’s asking for,” they said, “sorrel soup”, and they made me [some].
29031: i koto onàa čorbìca sàmo sɤm izèla takà
And when I ate only this soup –
29036: i sɤm a iskùsala čorbìca sàmo kìsala dvè kastrònčeta sɤm ispìla
I ate up all this sour soup, I drank up two small bowls of it –
29037: i tè tavà mi e i pòslem pàk àjde
that was all I [needed]. And then – “Come on,
29038: màlko na tavà àjde màlko ot onovà àjde màlko
have a little of this; come on, have a little of that. Have a little!”
29042: pa lè ne sì i jàla kojò edèš onò
But you know, when you haven’t eaten, everything you eat –
29054: sɤ počnà pa zàpek edìn mèsec pa zàpek stràšen
And constipation started up! A whole month, horrible constipation.
29061: No doubt because you hadn’t eaten.
29065: d ìdem gà da ìdem da ròdim detè pò dobrò
... go, and when I [try] to go, giving birth to a child is better
29070: otkòlko da sa nadùvam tḁ̀m i jà sa paralezìra vèče i nèš
than having to push like that. And I’d been paralyzed already.
29075: napràvix ìma dvàez dèna tàa mɤ̀kḁ ne mòe da òdim i
I went through that torment for twenty days. I can’t go, and
29077: ne mòe da òdim i kogà ìdem vèče prèmrem
can’t go, and when I do I almost faint.  and [it goes on] like that.
29079: i takà takà č ìdem pri dòktor
So on and on like that, and [I decide that] I’ll go to the doctor,
29085: pà u gṛdɤ̀ ma zakàra pa mòja sìn otidè pri dòktor tùka
so my son takes me to town,  I went to the doctor here,
29090: čàsnata poloklìnika i onà če ma preglèdat čɤ jà
to this private clinic, and she – they’ll examine me, because I –
29093: koto vèče se naduvà naduvà i kogà da se izòdim
since I’d already pushed so much and when I manage to go
29098: napràvo kàmik vèče premrè na stòla premrè
it’s just like a stone! I almost fainted [there] on the chair – fainted.
29103: i zè da m tè tùka koto izdɤ̀nem dḷbòko
And it started – here when I exhale a deep breath,
29105: tè ottùk i tùk ma dṛžì bodèš
the pains here and here are [like] needles.
29110: ako ìame č'e sme slagàle s òliò i napràeme
If we’d had it, we would have put it in. [No,] we made it with oil.
29114: a drùgi kvì bànici òšte ste pravìle
And what other kinds of banitsa did you used to make?
29118: drùgi kakvì bànici ste pravìle tàm sos zèle
What other kinds of banitsa did you make? The kind with cabbage,
29120: or with some other sort [of thing]?
29125: emi naprav'ɛ̀li sme s orɛ̀si so zàxar bɤklavà
Well, we used to make the kind with walnuts and sugar – [that’s] baklava.
29132: napràime pa srɛ̀žeme ja na parčènce i sɤs suròvo
We make it, then we cut it into small pieces and, before it’s baked,
29136: ta a polɛ̀eme s òliu z gorèštu òliu
we pour oil over it, hot oil.
29142: kàktu gu pulìvaš i sa nadùvaa parčèncə̥tə̥
And when you pour [the oil] over it, all the small pieces of it rise up [nice].
29146: ì pòsle tùremè ja da sa peč'è kat sa ispeč'è
After that we put it in the oven to bake. And when it’s done baking,
29150: ja pulɛ̀eme su siròp studèn siròp su zàxar
we pour syrup over it – a cold sugar syrup.
29152: i takà sa napìva i stàne bɤklavà
And it gets saturated [with syrup] and becomes baklava.
29157: a s tìkva pravìle le ste bànica s tìkva
And did you make pumpkin banitsa? [You know,] with pumpkins?
29160: s tìkva pa jà jàs fnògu sam pravìla s tìkva bànicḁ
Oh, pumpkins! Yes, I frequently made banitsa with pumpkins,
29163: dàže i s'à i pràvime pràvime
Even now we make that. We do.
29167: i tìkva pò ràno f stàro vrɛ̀me às ne pravìh
In the old days, though, I didn’t make banitsa with pumpkins.
29170: mòjta màjka a pràveše sos ə pɤ̀ržena tìkva bèz vòda
My mother made it [though]. She made it with fried pumpkins, and no water.
29175: ə dobrɛ̀ ama jà seà a pràva sà si sà a pràim drùgujàče
Fine, but now I make it – well, now, now we make it differently.
29179: sà pràime suròva tìkva ràstoča korìte ə
Now, we take the raw pumpkin – I roll out the pastry sheets, and then I
29183: tùra suròvɤ tìkva takà ɤràsa i olìvam òliu
put the raw pumpkin – I grate it, and then pour oil over [it all],
29189: i gu nàvia nàvià gu təkà na na rulò
and roll it. I roll it up into a long roll (strudel-like), like this.
29195: i vìa təkà f tepcìjata tùrem tùrem takà i se navìe i
And I roll it up and put it in the pan like this, and it curves
29198: i se napɤ̀ni tepcìjata pò ùbavo ut tìkvɤ
and fills the pan. [To think of] something nicer than –
29203: pò ùbavò e ut tìkvenìk vèk'e ne mòže sèm ùbuvu
It’s nicer. [Something better] than pumpkin pie isn’t possible! It’s completely wonderful.
29206: a pa ìnače ot stàro vrɛ̀me štu̥ sà napravɛ̀li napravɛ̀li sa
Otherwise, in the old days what they did – they made
29211: s pèčeni kòri tìkvenìk' i svàrena tìkva ma
pumpkin pie with pre-baked pastry sheets, and boiled pumpkin, and
29215: sedì zaplɛ̀skanu a takà se nadùl raš'č'urìl se e
it sat [there] all flat. That way, it puffed up, and rose [nicely].
29223: a kàži dèka bànsko jàdene ùbavo dèto pràvite tùka
So tell me [about] the nice dishes that you make here in Bansko.
29230: emi bàncko jàdenè am nàj ubàvotò e sùi č'ùšč'i sùš'eni
Ah, Bansko food! The best thing is the dry peppers. [They’re] dried,
29237: pa zìmno vrɛ̀me navàrimè ta tùrime kòkal ut slanìnata i kɤ̀rvavìcə
in winter we boil [them] up and add bones, pig fat and blood sausage.
29242: ta sè ta ùvri ùbaù ta tvà e bànsko
And it – it cooks up really nice, and that is a Bansko …
29247: And what other things did you make?
29250: mi drùgu sme pr pravìli fasùl sus ɤ č'ekàn
Well, [of] other [things], we made beans with “chekan”,
29259: emi kà də ti kàža cveklò
Hm, how can I tell you? It’s beets –
29263: što sè kàzva cveklò cveklò što pràvaa zaxartà
what’s called beets. Beets, that they make sugar ...
29265: ud nègo ta nìj gu pràvime na turšìja
... out of. Well, we make pickles out of it.
29270: ta tavà napràimè su̥s fasùle ìame i kapamì
So that’s [what] we do with beans. And stews.
29273: Have you heard of Bansko stew?
29276: bàncka kapamà ot tavà pò ùbuvu nèma
29284: … cabbage, and beets, and chunks of meat.
29289: ta d nè e fnògu č'ìsalu gu tùrime màlku da iš'č'ìsne
And for it not to be very sour, we put it to soak a bit
29291: da nè e fnògu č'ìsalu i tùrime vèč'e dròpka dròpka
to take the sourness away, and then we put in chunks of meat, "drobka" –
29295: I’ll use the old-time word for it –
29302: Meat chunks, blood sausage, a bone, lean meat –
29304: aku ìma i mèsu i mèsu tùrime
and if there’s [other] meat we put [that] meat in too
29309: òšč'e pò ubào e ta go zapečàtime
[to make it] even more tasty. And then we seal it up.
29312: What kind of pot do you put it in?
29318: ta tùri ə tùrime takà več'e tùra udòlu nàj naprɛ̀di
And then you put – we put – On the bottom first of all you put
29322: ud rasòlu pa pòsle kaverdì kaverdìsan urìs ìma
some sauerkraut. Then fri-  there’s rice [that’s been] fried up,
29327: sus enà glàva krumìt i urìs i màs
with a whole onion – rice, and lard.
29334: ta ta gu kavardìsam ta tùra nàpraa lòtka takà tèndžuràtḁ
And then I fry it, and I put – I make a space like this [in] the pan
29337: ta tùra urìz f stredàtḁ udgòre tùra slanìnata
and put the rice in the middle. Then on top [of that], I put the pig fat,
29340: kɤ̀rvavìcata mesòtu i pòsle udgòre rasòlu
the blood sausage, the meat – and finally on top, the sauerkraut.
29345: i vòd i tùrime i vòda
And water – we also add water.
29347: i vòda se tùra ma màlko ə ə ko tùram udgòre
You add water too, but just a little. Then on top I put
29353: dvòen' v'èsnik' ta go prìfpaa takà ud nètre tèndžuràta
a double layer of paper and it all gets stuffed inside the pan.
29357: ɛdnàš se plèskaše s testò ma bɛ̀še lòšu̥
At one time they used dough as a seal, but that was bad.
29359: [When] we seal the pan with dough, it …
29367: [Do you use] a pan, or a clay pot?
29373: prɤstɛ̀na tèndžura ta prìfpaa to vèč'e turìla sam
An earthenware pot. So, [it all] settles. I’ve already put in
29376: i vòda i sìčko i zabɛ̀la kòlkutu ìskam da tùra
water and everything, as much thickening as I need to put].
29380: pa vrì kat tùrime f pèčkata zadùš'enu da vrì
And then it cooks. We put it in the stove, layered well, to cook.
29385: ta vrì da ì zavrìm za trì č'àsa gutòva ɛ
And it boils – we boil it [all] for three hours, and it's ready.
29389: i sètne katò a izvàdime kugàtu ìskame vèč'e da a sipùvame
And then when we take it out, when we’re ready to serve it,
29394: ùveda mezètata što sàm turìla f stredàta fof čenìja
I bring in the appetizers that I’ve put in the middle of the plate.
29399: i tavà razbɤ̀rkam sas ednà golɛ̀ma lažìca dɤ̀rvena
And I stir [it up] with a big wooden spoon.
29403: razbɤ̀rkam orìzu da stàne na sɛ̀kade da se karaštìsḁ
I stir up the rice so that it is all mixed in throughout.
29408: i se sipùva f čenìi pò ùbavo ne mòže ot tavà
And you dish it into [people’s] plates. Nothing better than that!
29409: Isn’t that so! And what do you drink with it?
29421: tvà zìme pòvek'e če go če òt sèa lɛ̀te nèma
We’ll eat this [stew] more in the winter. In the summer we don’t have –
29458: əmə tòj b'àše hùbəu nìe f h nà pɤrvu əgà stànə
Well, it was fine, we – well, when it first came about –
29462: tvà vèk'e səà kumunìzmə li d'è də znàm kəkòt ìskə
now already it’s Communism or how should I know, whatever one wants
29467: də b'àše v'èke əm b'àše màlku mɤ̀kə dè òt' nəl'ì ə zèhə ni
to call it. Well, it was a little hard, because they took away –
29474: ìməhne vòluve ìməhne mùle mùletə vejàčkə əm kəkò də kàžə
we had oxen, we had mules, a winnower – what can I say, [they took]
29479: sìčku zimidèlci hòrə nəlì p'èt vòlə vnèsəhne vɤ̀tre
everything. [We’re] agricultural folk, right? We deposited five oxen into [the cooperative].
29488: kràvə ìməjne jùni ìməjne dvà dv'à mùletə ìməjne utɤ̀rnətə
We had a cow, we had a heifer, we had two, two mules. In the morning –
29494: ə ìməhme tòj b'àše kət ə təkɤ̀u gu kàzvəhne mɤ̀šku
We did. It was this, we called it – it was a male,
29497: b'àše ə nə dv'à gudìnki  jùni jùni
it was two years old. A bullock [yes, that’s what we called it], a bullock.
29504: jùni əhə d'àttu utirnɤ̀tə vìkə əmi s'à žèno kəkò də pràim
A bullock, yes. That morning Grandpa said, “So wife, what are we going to do?”
29509: dè də znàm duidòhə s kulàtə sičku nətvàrihə
What do I know?  They came with a cart and loaded everything onto it,
29512: they drove off the oxen, and when we –
29514: But you didn’t want [this to happen]?
29519: əm əmə òt' n'àmə də ìskəm kəd'èt wòrətə i nìe tàm
Well, why would I not want it? We [should go] where [other] people do.
29528: dòjdəhə večertɤ̀ kàzəhə bàj vɤ̀l'ču səkà i səkà ə dòjde idìn
They came in the evening and said “Uncle Vulcho, such and such.” And one came,
29535: idìn drùk è tòa nàš ìmə sìn gul'èmijə kumənìs
and then another, that one ours, his son a big Communist,
29540: əmə jà mu kàzvəm t'èbe əku tə b'àhə fàtili ə mur'ɤ̀t
and I say to him, “If they had taken you to torture you,
29545: če ti udir'àhə kužìčkətə utɤ̀rnətə večertɤ̀ pusr'àt nɤ̀ž
they would have skinned you – morning, evening, in the middle of the night.”
29548: dòjde vɤ̀lčo slùšəj kò šə kàžə še dòjde kumunìzmə
[So] he came [and said] “Listen, Vulcho, to what I say. Communism is coming.
29557: šə zəkàrət òlvetu tì ìməš mnòg òluve i ìd'e ìd'ə inò mòmče̝
They’ll drive off your oxen. You’ve got a lot of oxen. A fellow is coming,
29561: ìd'e ud vɤ̀lču.pòl də i prudəd'ène tòj vìkə à kòstə
[he’s] coming from Vulcho Pole, and we’ll sell them.” And he said, “Hah! Kosta  –
29565: kəd'è še vərìte i jà tàm ko š ìdə də prudàvəne
wherever you go, I [go] too. Why should I go off to sell [them]?
29570: t'è sàmu mòjte n'àmə də z'ème utrinɤ̀tə dòjdəhə ə vàj vàj
They won’t take only mine.” In the morning they came – ah, ah!
29577: če i nì dòjdəhme kətu innì mumàri inò vr'àme gà sə gləv'àhne
and we came too, like these matchmakers in the old days when we got engaged,
29579: èj səkà èj səkà èm dàdəhme gà gà stàne təkà
and this and that, and we gave [it over]. And when it happens like that,
29582: è gà vl'èzət hòrətə i jà še fl'àzə nəlì e təkà
when [other] people join, then I’ll join [too], right?
29588: fl'àzəjne s'etnətə ùtrinə zimàhə sìčku sià tòjə čuv'àk
So we joined, and the next morning they took everything.  Now this [my] man,
29593: tòj b'àše si rəbutlìf čuv'àk o òt' ìmə enì l'èli
he was a hard-working person, because there were “aunties”
29599: zə gl'èdəne d'àdu i bàbə b'àhə stàri tr'àvə sə ràbuti
that needed looking after, Grandpa and Grandma were old, one’s got to work.
29603: tòj vìkə s'à kəè kò də pràjə ìkəm nə znàm
He said, “Well what’ll I do?” I said, “I don’t know.
29610: nà vɤ̀ri gl'èdəj də vìdim kò pràət hòrətə utìde nədòlu
Go off and see what people are doing.” He went down the hill.
29614: gà utìde dòjde žèno zbèri mi l'àp kò vəzdìšəš b'è
He went, then came [and said] “Wife, gather me up [some] bread. Why sigh so?
29622: mə kàrat me d'èt' də vàdim kàmen'e nɤ̀j nəprèš 	də nəpràət ubòretu
They’re making me quarry some stone. First they’ll be building stables,
29630: tr'àbvət kàmene zberàh mu l'àb z'è kupàčə z'è mənèlətə utìdi
and they need stone.” So I got him the bread, he took a hoe, he took a lever, and he left.
29633: tùku hòrətə zəgrìzəhə nə tòu d'èn tə d'è utìde vɤ̀l'ču
Right off people started to bug me that day, “Where did Vulcho go?
29640: tàno tə tì zəštò pùskəš vɤ̀lču hòrətə gl'èdət də sə rəstùri səvà
Tana, why did you let Vulcho go off? People are hoping to see it all fall apart.”
29643: əm ə v'èke ìkəm [unintelligible] kəkò də v pràime nìe
But then I say [unintelligible]  “What are we going do with you?”
29650: tòj hòdi ràpti òrətə pučàkəə pučàkəhə  če nə s'ètn'e bil'à
He went to work, and the people kept waiting, and later it even turned out that
29656: i glànni b'àhə če tòj gà z'èhə pərì ə dàdəhə mu i žìtu̥
they were starving. So he – when they took the money, they gave him the grain.
29662: à t'è n'èmu dàdohə žìt pərì òti nàšijə bràt pək b'àše
They gave him grain and money because our brother was
29669: ə komtrol'ò təkɤ̀u əm brigədìr vəsìl d'è vàskətə
[someone] in control. Brigadier Vasil, you see – [our] Vaska.
29671: əmə nè če tòj b'àše brigədìr əmə ìmə trùdu.dèn
But not because he was a brigadier, rather he’d [done] a work day.
29673: [The one who] has worked, gets [the rewards].
29676: əmhə i dàdəhə mu i seà e təkà i tugàj
That’s right. They gave it to him, and now as well. Back then,
29681: ama i mnògu nə kàrəə də si krəstòsvət èj təkà nugìt'e
But they pushed us a lot, [and] they [just] cross their legs.
29693: kəkvò struvìhə kəkvò nòsihə ut tvà dəržàvətə rəzgràbəhə dəržàvətə
what they’ve built, what they’ve taken from the state. They robbed the state,
29694: də t'i kàžə rəzgràbəhə ə mə n'è e təkà nìj
let me tell you, they robbed it. It wasn’t like that [before]. We –
29700: inò vr'àme tòjtu žìt ku b'àše jèdru pò hùbəu tòjtu drèmnu
In the old days if one’s grain was big, it was nicer [than] another’s small [grain].
29705: əmə n'àmə də ìiš də z'èmiš ud nvà drèmnu əkù ti e
But you won’t go and take [grain] from that other. If yours is feeble
29712: še si vəršè̝me kòlkutu tòlkuvə dud'è stìgne dud'è sn'e
then we’ll thresh it. What there is, that’s it. So long as it lasts, so long as we –
29717: n'àmə še kupòvəne pək s'à n'àmə seà gràbite kòlkut mòšte
And if there’s none, then we’ll buy [it]. But not now. Now you grab what you can.
29725: rəzgràbəhə dər də də  bəlgàrijə nəlì mòž də sə̥ sɤ̀rdite əmə nà
They’ve robbed the –  Bulgaria. You can get angry but there it is.
29729: təkà si prikàzvəm nə sìčki təkà prikàzvəm či òt' n'àmə
I talk this way to everyone, I talk like this. Why is there nothing?
29736: òt təka	nəkà òt təkà òt dəržàvnutu e təkà
From this, from that, from this, because it’s state-owned.
29737: dəržàvətə sə e pək s'àkuj gl'èdə də z'ème
There’s a state, but everyone looks to get [what he can].
29741: è tùkə nəpràihə kɤ̀šti bèki n'e b'àhi i kàrali
Like here, they built these houses. It was as if they didn’t bring anything in.
29749: c'àlə nɤ̀š sùrnəhə t'àə žilizà i t'aə təkòvə cimènti bes pərì
They were hoisting this iron and cement all night long, without paying for it.
29752: ud ə təkɤ̀vutu ə ud nàšijə jəzuvìr
[It was all] from this – it was from our dam.
29758: d'èt ìkəne hùbəu hùbəu əku ràbutèše̝ še ìməše
what we called	 “good, fine” was if you worked, you’d receive.
29759: i kəkòt n'e ràptihə čàkaj segà də z'èmne bèki nìj n'e gl'èdəme
All that they didn’t work for: “Wait a bit, we’ll take it”, as if we didn’t see
29767: znàeš li kòlku ràbuta ìməm glèdaj  [unintelligible]
Do you know how much work I have? Look [unintelligible]
29771: dojdè ednà ženà od gṛdɤ̀ da bàam na ednò detènce
And this woman came from town for me to say charms over a small child.
29775: i jà kàžem na onàa nevèstica mlàda i onàa nevèstica mi kazà
And I speak to that young  bride, and that bride said to me –
29782: kàa idì pri dòktorete tèbe debèloto červò ti  kàa nèšto zarazèno
She said, “Go to the doctors. Your large intestine,” she said, “is infected somehow.”
29785: i sopštàvat tìja za sìn mi sìn mi vednàga dojdè
And they inform my son, my son comes immediately,
29787: ama jà ne sɤ̀m možàla nì da sɤm mòja sìn
but I couldn’t even, not even –  My son
29791: ma svìl takà mɤ̀či da ma ukàra u kolàta
bent me over, and had a hard time getting me into the car.
29795: bòže bòže kvò sa e mɤčìl s mène ma a nosìl
My God, my God, how he struggled with me, and [in the end] he carried me!
29798: ma a nosìl ta è krìvo.lèvo tàm iz onìja skàli
Somehow he carried me up all these stairs –
29801: ma nòsi do i onàa sɤ̀ga če ma preglèdva
carried me to – and that one now is going to examine me.
29831: takà e tè tokòfko i tùka ednà dṛ̀ška
a thing this big with a handle here,
29833: i onì ma sɤblìčɤt tàm ə jà ne mòžem nìšto
and they undress me there, I can’t do anything.
29837: i izmòlia sìn mi tàm i pomàga ednà nevèsta da ama
And they asked my son there [to help], and [another] girl helped, but –
29841: nə mòe də odvṛ̀žat jà sɤs sɤs nalì znàeš fùsta s
But they couldn’t untie  – I’ve got [this], you know, apron with –
29849: mòre nèmam pòjas amì sè jà pòjas ne mòe nòsim
Ah, I don’t have a belt! [Whatever] all else [I wear], I can’t wear a belt.
29853: i onàa nì tàa nì onàa è dòktoricata sìčki adrèsi ìəm
And [no one cared], not her, not her, nor that lady doctor. I have all the references
29858: i onàa ratìška ìəm kɤdè onà mɤ nakàra da se potpìsvam
and [I have] that piece of paper that she made me sign.
29863: Kədè ìmaxte nìvi tùkə nasèkəde glèdəm planinà
Where were there fields around here? Everywhere I look are mountains.
29872: kədè b'àhə nìvite əmi nəs'àkəd'e ìmə nìvi bə n'àməni nìi
Where were the fields? There’s fields everywhere! “We don’t have fields”!
29881: kəkò èj tàm ìmə inò ràmnu m'àstu cìmbel
29889: tòlkuə nìvə ìməne tàm udvɤ̀d'e ìməne c'àlə təkɤ̀və nìvə
we’ve got a field this big on the other side there. We’ve got a whole field like this
29894: tuk udgò uddòlu ìməne idìn blòk nìvə tùkə put s'èltu
here abo- below we have a section of field; here outside the village
29896: ìməne blòk nìvə kəd'è n'àmə ni zə nàštu sèlu
we have a section of field. Where are there “no fields”? For our village
29899: ìməne nìvi mnògu òt' kòj kàzvə če nìe n'àməne nìvi
we have lots of fields, so there. Who says we don’t have fields?
29902: takà mi izglèždə tuka tu katu planinà vi
It seemed to me like it was mountainous here.
29906: ə mòže də ə pləninɤ̀ əmə nè e təkà visòkə i tàm
Maybe it’s a mountain, but it’s not so high as [it is] there
29912: kət smòl'ən d'ètu e nàštə dəšterɤ̀ da n'àmə ništu
near Smolyan where our daughter lives, where there’s nothing [like fields].
29916: tùkə ìmə zèm'ə kɤ̀k nìe ìməme zèm'ə
Here there’s land. Oh, we’ve got land.
29921: o nà jɛ̀ gu km'ètə də kàže dəlì n'àməne zèm'ə nìe
There’s the mayor, [ask him] to tell you that we don’t have land.
29922: ə če nìe ìməme zèm'ə òt' n'àməne
We have land! How [can anyone say] we don’t?
29925: əməm a kakvò ja sèexte ednò vrème
And what did you plant in the old days?
29929: kəkò s'àene ednò vr'ème kəkòt ne sɤ̀ jəd'àše
What did we plant in the old days? If it wasn’t edible, we didn’t [plant it].
29937: i vəsùl i ləhùt i pčinìcə i càrivicə s'àihni i pəmùk i slənčugl'èt
Beans, chickpeas, wheat – we also planted corn, and cotton, and sunflowers –
29942: i susàn sìčku sìčku s'àehne sìčku stànvəše i pàk stànvə
and sesame. Everything! We planted everything, it all came up fine. It still does,
29950: e tàə gudìnə təkɤ̀və sùšə nəgòre kàzvət tìjə nàšie udgòri
but this year – such a drought. Up there they say – some of our folks from there
29956: b'àhə dušlɤ̀li̥ sigà tùkə nə svàdbə kàzvət kəde màlku.grədìšte
just now came here to a wedding, and they say [that up] by Malko Gradište
29961: gròzd'e ə bustàn n'àməlu hìč pək nìj sne blagudàrni
there are no grapes or melons at all. So we’re grateful.
29966: i gròzd'e imə i bustàn' ìməme èm ìč nè e l'ètnəlu
We’ve got both grapes and melons, even though it hasn’t rained at all.
29970: nàštə zèm'ə prez l'àtu̥tu təkà dvà trì pɤ̀t'ə də fàti dɤ̀š
[Here]  in our area in the summer,  we [just] get rain two or three times
29972: tò hi stìgə pòveče ne štè mə tàə zèm'ə n'à
and that’s enough. It doesn’t require more. But this region didn’t –
29975: There was nothing this summer, you see?
29981: tvà l'at n'àməše dɤ̀š tvà l'atu màj kətu vəl'àši i sigɛ̀
This summer there was no rain. This summer – [only a little] in May. But now –
29986: pò nəpr'àš bèše fànəlu mnògu dɤ̀š i pàk e nà e
[In] earlier [years] there’d been a lot of rain [by now]. Still, look there –
29990: grozd'ètu i tàm ìməne lòz'e gròzd'e gròzd'e v'èke sv'àt hùbəu
at the grapes. Over there we’ve a vineyard with grapes [and] the grapes are fine.
29994: i za živòtni kakvì glèdaxte nàj mnògo
And what animals did you raise mostly?
30001: nɤ̀j mnògu əm ufc'è̝ kuz'è̝ gl'èdəjne əm kun'è̝ ìməh
Mostly we raised sheep and goats, and I had horses.
30007: əm n'àməše zə jàdeni n'àməše zə kupùvəne čèdo kəkò də gl'èdəne
But we had nothing to eat and nothing to buy, child. What to raise?
30011: nìe kràvə ìməjne əmə kəd'è kuzì duv'àhne punèže dvənàese kuzì
We had a cow. What [can you do?] We milked goats – we had twelve goats
30016: i ofcì ìməjne məgàretə ìmejne nìe ìməhne i dv’à mul’etə
and sheep. And we had donkeys, and we had two mules.
30021: zəkàrəhə i nə fròntə v'èke n gì dukàrəhə ustànəhə si tàm
They took them off to the front, and didn't bring them back. They stayed there.
30041: žànem žɤ̀tva žànem na ràka sas sṛ̀p
we reap – we harvest reaping  by hand, with a sickle.
30049: à kàk sme vṛšèli nasrèt armàna izmetèm armàna
Ah, how we threshed! In the middle of the threshing floor. We sweep out the threshing floor,
30055: tùrim edìn strèžerᵊ i ə tùrnem snòpete i kàrame s magàreta
put a pole there, lay out the sheaves, and drive the donkeys:
30066: d'è d'è d'è d'è c'àl dèn d'àkame d'àkame dodè se stṛ̀ka slàmata
“Hey, hey, hey, hey!” All day we shout and shout until the straw is pulverized.
30073: izvàdim slàmata smetèm žitòtu ìmame takìva vejàčki ìmaxme
We take out the straw, sweep up the grain, we have these winnowers – we had [them]
30078: u zberèm go na kùp ut udvɛ̀em go s vejàčite i takà
– we gather it up in a pile and – and winnow it with the winnowers, and that’s it.
30081: ìmam dèca dvɛ̀ momìče i momčè ìmam
I have children. I have a girl and a boy.
30089: v ixtimàn živɛ̀e momčèto momìčeto si živɛ̀e tùk si vəv vṛšìloto
The boy lives in Ixtiman, and the girl lives here in Vŭrshilo.
30097: žènena ìma štè dvɛ̀ decà ednà še ednà štèrka ìma žènena
She has a married – [she has] two children, one – one married daughter,
30100: i ednò momčè ìma sɤ̀k še ìde vojnìk
and she has one boy, he’s about to go into the military.
30105: t'à rabòti v lùdnicata gòre gotvàčka e
She works in the mental home up there, she’s a cook.
30107: [How do you look after the grandchildren?]
30112: kàg gi glèdam càl dèn s nìx se raspràvam
How do I look after them? I fuss with them all day.
30115: glèdam gi kàrame se bìem se
I look after them, we argue, we fight.
30121: jà jà jà màjkata t'à si rabòti jà se pòveče kàrax
[No!] It’s me, me, me! The mother works, I’m mostly the one who fought
30125: s nìx pobìjvax gi čàt.pàt i lɛ̀toska bɛ̀a tùka i
with them. I struck them now and then. This summer they were here,
30128: i lɛ̀toska se poskàrvaxme sɤ̀ga si otìdoa
and we argued a bit this summer too. Now they’ve gone off.
30131: t'à si ìma i mənìnko detè momčèto i še ìde
She’s got a tiny child. Her boy is going
30135: vojnìk segànka ònija dèn mu praìxme ispràštane
into the military about now, the other day we had a sending-off celebration for him.
30141: à kogà se ožènixme li takà četìrese i šèsta godìna
When did we get married? In ‘46,
30145: četìrese i šèsta godìna pres mɛ̀sec januàri se ženì:me
in January of ‘46. We got married in the month of January.
30150: na dvàes sèdmi januàri se ženì:me  i dobrɛ̀ si živɛ̀exme
We got married on the twenty-seventh of January, and we lived well.
30155: sɤ̀ga počìna dɛ̀doto sɤ̀ga sam bez dɛ̀do počìna
Now Grandpa (= husband) died. Now I’m without Grandpa, he died.
30162: pòsle stanà tèkezesè gledàxme òfci dvàese godìni gledàxme òfci
And then came the collective farm. We raised sheep for twenty years, we raised sheep
30169: càl dvàese godìni gi pàso:me doì:me jàgneta gledà:me ranì:me gi
all– for 20 years we pastured them, we milked them, we looked after the lambs, fed them,
30175: dodè iskàraxme pèncijata kato iskàraxme pèncijata ta zaživɛ̀axme
until we earned our pensions, and when we got our pensions then we started to live –
30180: zemà ja dɛ̀doto trì godìni pučìna jà ostànah samìnka
Grandpa drew [his pension] three years and then died, and I was left alone.
30183: i sɤ̀ga samì se ne živɛ̀e tə̥ takà
And now you can’t live alone like that.
30185: Right, and when do [the grandchildren] come?
30189: lɛ̀tnoto vrème prez vakànciite na učìlišteto sɤ̀ga ne dovàždat
In the summer, during school vacation. Now they’re not coming.
30191: sɤ̀ga kòj še ta dìri vèče nèma
Who’s going to look for me – for you? Nobody any more.
30198: òo tòo fasùl se kàzva gradìnski fasùl
Ah! These beans are called “city beans”.
30205: mi rasàdim gu slòžim mu nìe mu vìkame rɛ̀jki po nàš
Well, we transplant them, and put them on [what] we call beanpoles in ou-
30213: nàšata stranà tùrim mu rɛ̀jkite napràime mu vàdite i pu go pulìvame
in our area. We put the beanpoles – we make irrigation channels for them, and water them.
30219: [When they are] green. Green, in the pods.
30225: ìma i uzrɛ̀l tè go tòja a zrɛ̀lija
There’s ripe [ones] too! They – those are some ripe ones.
30235: [With] the potatoes. We plant the pumpkins in [with] the potatoes.
30242: emi kòj sàdi càrevici nìe ne sàdim càrevici v nàšto vṛšìlo
Well, those who plant corn [do]. We don’t plant corn in our (= Gorno) Vŭrshilo,
30247: tùka mìnalite mìnalite godìni sàdexme dodè ne bɛ̀še stanàlo tèkezesè
[not] here.  In past – in past years we planted [it], up until the collective farm came in,
30252: sɤ̀ganka nèma ne sàdim càrevici vèče òti nèštat da stàjat
but not now. We don’t plan corn any more because it doesn’t want to grow [here].
30254: [What animals did you raise in the time of private ownership?]
30260: ami f čàsnoto sme gledàle volòve òfci kòzi svìne
Well, in the private [era] we looked after oxen, sheep, goats, pigs –
30262: te tovà sme gledàle f čàsnoto a pa sɤ̀ga f tèkezesèto
that’s what we had in the private [era]. Now in the [time of] the collective farm
30265: volòvete gi dàdoxme f tèkezesèto ofcìte dàdoxme tàm
we gave the oxen to the collective farm [and] we gave the sheep there [too].
30267: glèdaxme pà nə tèkezesèto i volòve sme gledàle
We still looked after them in the collective farm, and we looked after oxen.
30269: òfci dvàese godìni òfci gledà:me z dɛ̀doto i du
[And] sheep – we looked after sheep twenty years, Grandpa and I, until –
30274: i tàm glèdahme i domà si ìma:me si čùva:me òfci mnògo
We looked after them there, and we had some at home. We kept a lot of sheep.
30278: [What do you do with the milk?]
30285: mlɛ̀koto go sìra sɤs  vèče stàja pèt šèz godini go sìra
I make the milk into soft cheese. It’s been five or six years now that I’ve been doing this,
30290: i tàm ìma mɛ̀snostà cɛ̀reto ìma sofiànci vìlno mɛ̀stu
and there’s a place [called] Tsereto, there’s Sofia there – it’s a place for villas,
30295: i dovàždat i im prodàvam sìreneto xarèsvad go mnògo
and they come and I sell them the soft cheese. They like it a lot.
30300: onàa vèčer kadè večèra me digàa ta im davàx
The other evening at supper time they called me up [to come] and I sold [some] to them.
30308: kòl'edə vilègdèn s'ètne p'ètruvd'èn' i buguròdicə
Christmas, Easter, then St. Peter’s day, and then the feast of the Holy Virgin.
30311: kàk go praznùvaxte velìgden pò ràno
How did you celebrate Easter in the old days?
30317: əmə kɤ̀g də n tòj b'a nìj ìməjne zbòr nə velìgd'èn' gol'àm
Well, of course we did. It was – we had a big village gathering on Easter.
30321: kɤ̀k še gu gà dòjde velìgd'èn' sìčkutu še zgàdane še izmàəne
How shall I – when Easter comes we’ll fix everything, we’ll smear [the walls]
30326: še izlepìne nə velìk.četvɤ̀rtək še ubàgrime icàtə i velìgd'èn'
and plaster them. On Black Thursday we’ll dye eggs, and on Easter
30330: kətu nìkuj n'àmə də idè nì d'àte nì s'à bàgreni icà
nobody will eat [the eggs]. No, child, no! And now [come] the painted eggs.
30334: ò bàbo dàj mène tvà ò màjko dàj mene tva
“Oh, Granny, give me that! Oh, mother, give me that!
30340: jà da ìzedə àjde čùkət nàši dicà tuvà n'è
I want to eat it up!” [Everyone] is cracking the eggs, but not our kids.
30347: velìgd'èn kətu zəguv'àeme pɤ̀rvətə zəguv'àlkə b'àše še zəguv'àene misòtu̥
Easter is when we observe the first fast period. We would abstain from meat.
30354: m'èsu n'àmə də idène pɤ̀rvətə nd'àl'ə ə du ftòrətə ši idène
We wouldn’t eat any meat, not for the first week. And for the second we’ll eat
30359: icà sìren'e mlikò ə ftòrutu zəguv'àvəni du velìgd'èn' nìšto
eggs, cheese, milk. And in the second fast period of Easter, nothing.
30366: nìštu n'ètu mlikò n'ètu icè n'ètu m'èsu n'ètu rìbətə
Nothing. Neither milk, nor eggs, nor meat, nor – But [as for] fish,
30372: dvà pɤ̀ti jəd'àhi jàdəhne jəd'àhne i màjkit'e sə ni pìtəli
we would eat that twice, and our mothers would ask us
30375: təkà màjko zəšt'ò nə vrɤ̀bnəcə i nə
like this: “Mother’s children, why on Palm Sunday and on –"
30382: à təkà zəštòtu rìbətə nə gləvàtə imàlə krɤ̀s i təkà
Right. Because a fish has a cross on its head, and so –
30387: gòsput jə i u glɤvɤ̀tə [unintelligible] zərət tòu krɤ̀s
The Lord [unintelligible] to its head. And because of that cross
30391: dvà pɤ̀t'ɨ sə jàlə	i ə fs'àki pùs si e
[fish] is eaten twice.  And each fast is [its own] –
30396: pu n'àkəv den' imə təkɤ̀v də idə̀t zətùj se e jàlə
there’s a certain day when you eat a certain way. So that’s why [fish] was eaten.
30399: takà li go kàzvaxte ednò vrème blàgovec kàk se kàzvaše
Is that how you used to call it in the old days, Annunciation?
30404: dà da blàguvec blàguvec n'è n'è nìe ne gù kàzvəme blàguvec
Yes, Yes, Annunciation. Annunciation. No, no. We don’t call it Annunciation,
30407: nìe gu kàzvəjne sià gu kàzvəme blàguvec d'è də znàm
we used to call it –  [well,] now we call it Annunciation. How should I know
30410: kàk b'àše a jà gu zəbràih è kɤ̀kto i də è
what it was? I’ve forgotten. Well, whatever it is –
30412: d'è də znàm kàk b'àše tə səm pìtələ màjkə
how should I know how it was – I asked mother
30418: òt' pùs tə rìbə ni sɤ̀ jəd'è pək ə təkɤ̀vu pək jədèn'e
why, [if] fish isn’t supposed to be eaten during fast, [why] we still eat [it].
30420: òt' təkɤ̀vu čèdu òti rìbətə ìmə krɤ̀s
[And she said,] “Because of this, child, because the fish has a cross [on it].”
30423: kədè ja lov'àxa rìbata tùkə v
Where did they used to go fishing here, in the –
30426: əm tùkə əmə tòj s'à n'èmə v'èk'e sià d'è də znàm
Here, but now there aren’t any. How should I know
30429: kvò stànə s'àkutri rìbətə kət hòrətə
what happened? Everything has gone off, fish just like people.
30430: hòrətə ne bìvət i rìbətə ne bìvə
People aren’t right [any more] and fish aren’t right.
30436: inò vr'àme mòjə d'ad mòjə d'àd b'àše bələkčijə
In the old days my grandfather – my grandfather was a fisherman.
30441: nè mòjə mɤ̀š mòjə mɤ̀š si gl'èdəše ràptata
[But] not my husband. My husband looked after [his own] affairs.
30447: əmə nàs nèma də nə ìmə
30455: mòjtə turšìjkə pul'vìnətə ìmə sòl pul'vìnətə n'àmə pək n'aməm sòl
Half of my pickles are salted and the other half not, but I don’t have [any] salt.
30458: Wait a minute, let’s get some chairs.
30460: I have – I have [some things that need] washing.
30464: tò bèše pò hùbəvu vɤ̀tre f kmètsvoto da takòva
It would be nicer inside, in the mayor’s office, to go on talking.
30467: What do you have for washing?
30473: àa dèto tùka b'àxa sìčkite drèxi
Ah, all the clothes that were here?
30475: à t'è si gi z'èhə t'ànite
30481: a rèkox da ne sɤ̀ ti ostàili tìe drèxite rabòtnite
Ah, I was wondering whether they’d left you all these work clothes.
30488: e əm jà rəbòtnite dè t'ut'ùnckite si stuv'ɤ̀t əm kugàt dòjdət
Oh, those tobacco work [clothes]! They’re just sitting [there]. When they come
30493: še s gi uperɤ̀t ned'àl'ə še dòjdət še z gi uperɤ̀t
they’ll wash them. They’ll come on Sunday and they’ll wash them.
30495: jàs rèkux če ti še če tì še im gi perèš
I thought that you – that you’d be washing them for them.
30498: əm mòže də gi pèrə i jɛ̀ n'èskə ku n'è ùtre
Well maybe I will wash them. Today – if not, then tomorrow.
30502: nə sìčko na rəkà li perèš
By – do you do all the washing by hand?
30507: be segà nìkoj ne sɤ̀ mɤ̀či
Nobody goes to that trouble now.
30510: sigà hùbəvu hùbəvu pàk ne hər'èsvəti pàk pust'àvəte
Well, now it’s fine, fine. But you still don’t like it. You still curse
30515: the UDF [Union of Democratic Forces]. May it be cursed now, cursed!
30521: əm kəkò ne ər'èsvə čem ə wòt' tòlkus skəpotìjə stànə à
So what’s not to like? Why’s it’s gotten so expensive? Huh?
30525: Because we have [all these] debts to pay.
30529: wòt' ìməne bòrčuve kòj gi stòri tèə bòrčuve
Because we have debts! Well, who created all these debts?
30537: nìj stòrihne kòj gi stòri nəl'ì b'àhne
We created [them]. Who created them? Weren’t we …
30540: … part of this Bulgaria? We did it.
30546: We did it. Back then it was –
30551: wòt' t'àhnite zəplàti tòlkəvi gol'àm' a
So why are their salaries so high, huh?
30554: It used to be really inexpensive …
30560: še dòjde skɤ̀p cərvùl'ə šə dòjde èj tàm nì də ìdeme
It’s shoes that will get expensive! We [need] to go there ourselves …
30563: – because they take care of their own, …
30568: zə t'àhnite se bl'ɤ̀skət pək nìj ne mòžem tìj d'èt
… they work their asses off for their own, but we can’t. [We’re part of] those who
30571: ni mòət də kàžət nìj ni mòžem də kàžem zə tvà
have no say! We have no say. And why?
30577: zə tvà tìjə tòlku pərɤ̀ sə dàli nə učène
Because they spent so much money on [their] schooling.
30580: agà sə dàvəli nə učène gà
[It doesn’t matter] that they spent so much on education –
30582: [The old system] is not going to come back.
30583: gà sə dàvəli nə učène š ìdə tàm
So what they paid for schooling! I’ll go there, and [I’ll go]
30595: dàn dàn dàn dàn dàn dàn dàn dàn dàn dàn dàn
bam bam bam bam bam bam bam bam bam bam bam [just like]
30598: dànkət tàm na əf sòfijə àz də mògə də ìdə tàm
they go bam! there in Sofia. [Now] if I could go there
30604: zə dànkən še z'èmə ədnɤ̀ surovìcə še gi zàčukə i udzàt
for [some] banging, I’d take a stick and beat their behinds!
30607: tì də zlàtə vìkə də z'èmə ədnɤ̀ pùškə əm
You’re [like] Zlata, [she says she’ll] take a gun and –
30611: and who? Who will she shoot?
30618: əm ma wòt' nàšte sìnuve mà
What do you mean, our sons?!
30621: əm wòt' zlàti də stàne vujnɤ̀ də z'èmə ədnɤ̀ pùškə də pùkələ
Because there’ll be a war if Zlata [and her ilk] took up a gun to shoot.
30622: Hah, sure. There’ll be a war! …
30628: Won’t you be shooting at our sons …
30645: Let them [in Parliament be the ones to] get shot!
30654: òt'ɨ wòti tìje t'àhnite zəplàt' sə pu d'èset dvənàjse hìl'ədi
Them with their salaries of ten, twelve thousand each.
30656: tìjə s'à t'àh durd'è i zə
30662: durd'è sə izučìli znàeš li kòlku pərɨ̀ sə dàli
Do you know how much money they spent to get educated?
30665: Ah, so much for your money.
30670: vèče da ne gò obɤ̀rnaxte na vojnà bè
You two are on the verge of turning this into a war yourselves!
30683: t'à kətu zèmelə pùškə də təkɤ̀vu
It’s like she would take up a gun to do this and that.
30689: t'à ne hər'èsvələ s'èdes'ètu pə̥k səd'è ur'è nə čàsnu
And she says she doesn’t like the U.D.F., yet she’s always plowing private land.
30693: kòjtu ne hər'èsvə s'èdes'e hìč ne tr'àvə də ur'ɛ̀ nə čàsnu
If someone doesn’t like the U.D.F., there’s no way they should be plowing private land.
30696: òti še ə kò še jàm mà
Why should – So what am I going to eat? Huh?
30704: wòt' ur'èš nə čàsnu n'àmə də ur'èš nə čàsnu
... since you’re plowing private land. You shouldn’t be plowing private land.
30705: How am I going to eat?
30710: hèm na tr'àvə də jəd'ène də ur'ème
Well, we have to eat and plow both.
30713: d'è e tràkturə mà ìməme li tràktur mà
Where’s the tractor, hey? Do we have a tractor, I ask you?
30718: əm dà nəm'èrite ə b'èki nì sme im'àli
So find one [then]! As if we had one!
30726: kəkò šo t'èbe t'èbe t'èbe nìštu ne tr'àbuvə
So, you – you – you don’t need anything,
30734: And why do you [in particular] need it?
30737: wòti ìməm òšte d'àdu i bàbə sìne
Because I still have grandparents, my child,
30741: i decàtə sə vərt'ə̀t ukulu nàs [unintelligible]
30753: ə kəkò ès èšte də pìtəte kəkò še pìtət
And what else do you [have] to ask me? What are you going to ask?
30758: a tovà vɤ̀lnenija plàt dèto go istəkàvate kàg go kàzvate
This woolen fabric that you make by weaving, how do you call it?
30769: habɔ̀ habɔ̀ tə tèš tè ə š'ijət pəntəlòne drùguš' š'ìehə pəltà
... “habe”, “habe”. They sew trousers of it. Earlier on they used to sew coats,
30773: tè sà kupùət sìčkutu sàmu zə ədnì pəntəlòne
but now they buy all that. Only for some trousers.
30779: And how does that job get done?
30783: à nəvlàč'iš vɔ̀lnənə vəf tò segà ìmə tàm
Well, you card the wool in – they’ve got this [thing]
30787: f ùstoo tə jə vlàč'ət vɔ̀lnənə i z'ɔ̀meš
in Ustovo, and they card the wool [with it]. So you take it
30792: rəskɤ̀cəž gi təkà kɤ̀del'k'ite t'ènički i pr'əd'èš pred'èš
and tear it up [into] distaff-size pieces, thin. And you spin, spin –
30795: zə d'èn trì č'ètiri p'èt vretenà še nəpred'èš
in a day you’ll spin up three, four, five spindles’ worth.
30798: ɛ təvà dòlu kàk se kàzvə
And what is the thing down below called?
30810: And what do you put on it?
30814: nèjə kàk ja kàzvaš kato ja slòžiš na hùrkə
And what do you call that [stuff] you put on the distaff?
30818: kədèl'ə ne è li kədèl kədèl'ka
30822: če nè əm fùrkə jə kàzvəš vɔ̀lnə
Well, no. You call it the distaff. [For] wool –
30827: a vɤ̀lnata kakvò tr'àbvə da ja napràiš predi tovà kət
And for the wool, what do you have to do before that, when –
30831: Already from the time you finish shearing the sheep.
30836: isperèš' jə rəš'č'èš'eš' jə i jə nəvlàč'iš' nə fàbrikənə vlàč'ət
You wash it, comb it out, you card it – they card it at the factory –
30845: gà ispredèš pàk pupàriš pr'ɔ̀lutu usnuvèž gu stòriš
You spin it, and then you scald the yarn, then warp [the loom] and make
30848: kəkòt ti trɛ̀və zə kəkòtu gu mìsliš'
whatever you need, whatever you’re intending [to make] …
30856: ami vɤ̀lnata ìma li razlìčni imenà v zavìsimost ot tovà otkədè
So does wool have different names depending on where
30858: še jə ostrižèš znàči dalì še e ot nogàta na ofcàta
you shear it from? Like if it’s from the sheep’s leg?
30865: à rəzlìčno sàmu dènu e pò̝ kàlenkə nɛ̀kədɛ nàa
Oh! It’s different only where it’s more muddy. Those parts –
30870: mò də je ə izberèš pò zə f nɛ̀kvu pò̝ pròstu də pràiš
you can choose them for – to make something more simple.
30874: pəg dènu zə hùbəvu nɛ̀štu zə blùzi zə ednò drùgu
But for something nice – for blouses or for something else [like that]  –
30879: č'e pə gl'ɔ̀dəš pò hùbəfkənə izbìrəš'
you’ll look and find the nicer parts.
30886: ama n'àma drùgo ìme tovà da mu vìkate bəžɛ̀k tùkə na tàa
But isn’t there some other name that you call it, like “hip” for this here –
30890: bəžɛ̀ci ìnače ta agà e nɛ̀kvu kàl'enu də e kàl'enu
“Hips”, well that’s when it’s sort of muddy – a muddy [part]
30895: ud ufcɔ̀nə təgà mòe də je də ustàiš' nɛ̀kəde
of the sheep and you can leave it somewhere,
30899: màlku pò pəràtkəu pə əgà zə hàli̥šte gu iskàvəme prepisàci
for something less good. But when we weave rugs and aprons,
30902: sìčku nə ədnò mɛ̀stu rəš'č'èš'eš' i sə nəvlàč'i
everything in one place. You comb it and it gets carded,
30905: vìe mnògo li ofcì gl'ɔ̀dahte ednò vr
Did you raise a lot of sheep in the old [days]?
30910: ətkòle mnògu kuàt si bəh u nàs jɛ̀ səm čɛ̀k ud
Back then a lot, when I was back at home – I’m from all the way
30916: dòlnətə məhəlɔ̀ čɛ̀k dòlu səm etìm ìmə dvè trì kɔšti
down in the other district – way down there. There’s two or three houses
30919: dòlu jɛ səm ut tàm pək i nə sòə kràj səm
down there, and I’m from there. [I came] to this area when ...
30929: kakvì mahalì ìmaše vəf sèloto pòmniš li gi kàk se kàzvaha
What districts were there in the village? Do you recall how they used to be called?
30936: pòmn'əm ednɔ̀ nə esèjufce bùkuvu etùv mugìlicə
I remember one. There was Eseyuftse, [and] Bukovo, and here – Mogilitsa.
30939: əmhəm a gòrna mahalà n'àma li
Mmhm. And there’s no upper district?
30945: t'à t'à e kà a seà kàk ja kàat
And – and how – how do they call it now?
30946: They call it Elinden now too.
30950: pàk enèj pàk sètne pò̝ rànu
That then too. The same thing earlier.
30958: elìnden pàk bo go etùzi də оtkòlešnu həsànkòj
Elinden. And, this – here, what used to be Hasanköy
30967: And what are the ones further on?
30970: bùkuvi bùkuvu nəh tàm i jesèfce pək nə
Bukovo, Bukovo. And over there also Yeseftse and –
30973: pək ednò ìmə kòšnica po nə
And there was another one, Koshnitsa, more –
30977: ə kòšnicə ət ut tàm e məžɔ̀s
Oh yes, Koshnitsa! My husband’s from there.
30985: mè̟ne pɔ̀rvət mɔ̀ž mi puč'ìnə tùvə jɛ̀ səm se už'ènih i s
My first husband died here. I was – I got married, and
30989: i nə dvàese i p'èd gudìni mi beš'e məž'ɔ̀t i mi pučìnə
and at –my husband was twenty-five years old [when] he died,
30993: tə nə dvàese ustànəh duvìcə s ədnò dɛ̀te
and at the age of twenty I was left a widow with one child.
31000: hɔ̀ də ti kàžəm kàk səm mìnələ təgà vɔ̀trešni si bəhmə
Hah yes, let me tell you what I’ve been through. So we were there, insiders,
31004: ut kɔ̀šnicə təgà dòjde čulɛ̀k tòj beše nè žènen
and this man came from Koshnitsa. He was not married.
31007: ergènin bèše təgà pàk èšte dvè decà trì decà ìməme
He was a bachelor. So then two more children. We have three children.
31016: sìčkite mumìč'etə imɛ̀h mumč'è puč'ìnə ədnò e tvà i
All girls. I had one boy but he died, and there it is.
31020: trìte sə mo mumìč'etə i mnògu mi sə dubrì
So all three are girls. And they’re very good to me.
31024: mnògu me uvəž'ɛ̀vət jɛ̀ ti kàzvəm ìməm dvè unùč'etə
They respect me a lot, I can tell you. I have two grandchildren –
31030: p'ɛ̀t unùč'etə ìəm ədnò mumìč'enče č'ètiri mumč'ètə ədnònu zəvɤ̀rš'i
[ah no], I have five grandchildren. One girl and four boys. One graduated
31036: fsəs səjùzən indž'inèr drùgunu i tòj e sà še zəvɤ̀rš'i
in engineering, in the Soviet Union; the other is graduating now.
31039: May they live long and healthy!
31044: hà ž'èncku ìmə f smòl'ən i tò zəvɤ̀rš'ilu pək dimìtrigràt
Hah, [thanks]. There’s a girl in Smolyan, but she graduated in Dimitrovgrad,
31049: ləbəràntkə i drùite sə pàk f smil'ɛ̀n tìj sə nə ràbutə
she [works as a] lab assistant. And the others are in Smilyan, they are working there.
31054: màlkənə hudòžnə nɛ̀kvə sìčku mòže də pràvi
The youngest one is an artist of some sort. He can do anything!
31060: səz dɔ̀skite dè sə enəkòvə mnògu hùbəvi ràbuti
He does some really nice things with boards.
31063: The other one is in forestry.
31064: And what does he do [with] them?
31069: ad dɔ̀ski təkìi pràvi sìčku hùbəvu
From boards, he makes all sorts of nice things.
31076: preskràsə na udgòre ìkəm nə stàine burìkuvu enəkvò sìčkunu [unintelligible]
Pinewood decorations on the tops of rooms. All sorts of things like that. [unintelligible]
31082: hà mlògu mlògu e speciəlìs pu tvà
He’s a great specialist in these things.
31084: Some kind of construction worker then.
31088: nì d'ulgèrin enəkvò be hudòžnik e zə bə bə
No, he’s not in construction. He’s an artist! He –
31095: əhə zəvɤ̀rš'ilu i sìč'ku mòž'e sə enəkvò səz dɔ̀ski də pràvi
Yes. He graduated [in art], and can make anything from boards
31099: He’s got machines, and all that sort of stuff.
31123: ne mòžem sìrota d ìdem da i kàžem jà ma sèstro
I can’t go, poor me, and so I say to her, “Look here, sister!
31127: zaštò mi tegàva tì kazà takà tàa prìkaska kɤdè tavà
Why did you go and talk to me like this all these stories? What is this?
31129: tì si dòktor tì ne trèbva mène da ma uplàšìš
You’re a doctor! You’re not supposed to frighten me like this!”
31133: pl'às te tùka s onovà  àmà gà viknà na mène
Wham! with those [papers in my hand]. “But you!” she shouted at me
31137: àmà tì ne vìdiš če žḷ̀čkata gotòva da sa pùkne
“But you! You don’t see that your gall bladder is about to burst?
31139: če ta kàrame u bòlnica rèko nè ami kvò
We’ll take you to the hospital!” I said, “No!”  – “But why?”
31144: nèštem d ìdem potpìsvaj se potpìsvam se i z dvète rɤ̀ce
“I don’t want to go.” – “Sign this!” I sign with both hands
31148: i pèt parì ne dàvam vìe sàkate rèko da ma zakàrate
and I don’t give a damn. “You want,” I said “to take me off
31152: u bòlnica da ma rèžete da ma napràite na pɤstɤrmà
to the hospital to cut me up, to make pastrami out of me!”
31156: è onìja gà zèa da sa smèjat
And they all started to laugh.
31160: čèsno a sɤ̀ga na mèn me e tòo kɤdè kàe
Honestly! So now [I say] to that one that was talking to me,
31167: slùšaj ma dàko ìmam kàmɤn'e dàko jà revèm za aršìn'e
“Listen here! So what if I have stones? So what if I crying for stones?
31170: štò pràim kɤ̀šta i mi trèbvat aršìn'e
Well, I’m building a house and I need stones!
31172: dàko sa pùkne žḷ̀čkata jà ìmam pòlza od onìja kàmɤn'e [laughter]
So what if my gall bladder bursts? I have use for those stones! [laughter]
31177: da ja bàrem da a podigràam àmà àjde màne a
[I can] at least make fun of her. But let it go.
31182: sè ìmam jà sìčka pàstrim onovà àj kɤdè mi e snimàl
I still have everything, I’ve kept everything. And they took pictures of me
31186: e tùka rɤcète mi snimàa òrata sìčko mi kazàa
here, those people took pictures of my arms, and told me everything –
31190: če rɤcète mi sa bilè istṛ̀pnale nè e trebvàlo tìja ižèkcii
that my arms had gone numb and that those injections shouldn’t have been given,
31194: trebvàlo vednagà pèpi da a dòšɤl òn nè e nì dooždàl
that Pepi should have come immediately, and he never even came
31196: da ma vìdi nè e štrapnàl a jàla go
to see me, and he hasn’t put a foot [near us]. And there he is
31206: e tè u onàa kɤ̀šta pràvo tàm
just in that house right over there.
31217: əmi vìš segà əku še mu rèkə čòrbəžì l'udèsu sə glàdni
So look now. If I'll say to [the boss], "Hey boss, _these here_ people are hungry" ...
31271: kətu vərš'ɛ̀hmi znàč'i nə xərmàn znač'i m č'àkəmi murenìn utsvərš'èm
When we threshed at the threshing floor, we waited for the sea wind to finish [the job].
31276: znàč'i pòčvəmi udv'ɛ̀jəmi gu əmə murenìn č'àkəme̟ də dùhni
We start to winnow it, but we wait for the sea wind to start blowing
31281: də mòžim də udv'ɛ̀imi ə murenìn sìlnu dùhə znàč'i
so we could finish winnowing. The sea wind blows hard, you know,
31289: i udnàsə pl'àvətə nə tɛ̀j žìtu̥tu nə drùgətə strənà
and carries the chaff to this [side] and the grain on the other side.
31294: And that’s how we do it.
31295: [Каква работа имате като станете от сутринта?]
[How do you begin the work day?]
31299: sùtrin kət stànem bɛ̀rdzami tùj pràim unùj pràim
When we get up in the morning, we rush about, we do this, we do that,
31306: bɛ̀rdzəm də utìdim nə nìvətə c'àl dèn' kupàjə nàči
we hurry to go out to the field. All day long we dig,
31314: ilì pək də ž'ɛ̀nim nàči i s òbed dòdi ni sèdnem
or else we reap, and when noontime comes we sit down,
31322: nahrànim sə lègnem pučìnim màlku nàči̥ stàvəmi pɑ̀k pɑ̀k dòjdim
eat, lie down, rest a bit, then we get up again, come back again,
31326: pɑ̀k dòjdim əf.kɛ̀šti pàk ràbutim ne neumòrnu znàči sɨ znači n'àma
come back again to the house, work more – [It’s] unremitting, there’s no –
31376: ne ne mòžem də si səberèm sìlit'ȅ vèč'i̥ ut ràbutə
we can’t get our strength back any more from [all that] work.
31379: fl'àzəhmi u t'èkees'è za pò l'èsnu tò pò mɛ̀čnu izl'ɛ̀ze po t'èšku [laughter]
We joined the collective farm to make it easier, but it ended up more difficult. Much harder! [laughter]
31456: jɛ̀ če gà f kàzvəm pòvn'ə či màjkə stɤ̀rže stɤ̀rže stɤ̀rže
I’ll tell you: I remember that my mother scraped, scraped, scraped
31460: tàə s'up'urg'ɛ̀ issušìhə jə zberàhə ənɤ̀ turbìčkə
that broom [to get seeds] and when they dried, they gathered them into a bag
31464: i utìdəhə sm'èlihə i um'èsi màjkə l'àb də id'ème
and went off and ground them, and mother made bread for us to eat.
31488: enò vr'èm'ə kugàtu zəvɤ̀ršij učɨlɨ̀štetu pedes'ɤ̀t i trìtə
Back then, when I had finished school in ’fifty-three
31493: pedes'ɤ̀t  i četvɤ̀rtə gudɨ̀nə bème mnògu sirmàški
31500: pručùjme mnògu pərɨ̀ či sə dàvə u sìlu rìsen tɤ̀rnufsku
[When] we heard good money would be paid in the village of Resen near Tǔrnovo,
31507: trɤ̀gnajmi səz bəštà mɨ sɤs sestrà mɨ utɨ̀dəjme tàm
we set out [for there together] with my father and my sister. We went there
31513: də ràbutime òpšta ràbota u tèkezes'ɤ̀tu də berìm pəmùk
to do general labor work in the collective farm – to pick cotton,
31520: də berìm bàmjə da b'èlim kučèn'a na drùgijə d'ɤ̀n dujdì
to pick okra, to shuck corn, [etc.] The next day [there] came
31525: edɨ̀n čuv'èk rəzbràl če ìma ù:rə ut sìlu
a man [who] appeared to have heard there were people from the village
31530: generàl.nikulàevu plòwd'usku i dudì prɨ nàm
[named] General Nikolaevo, near Plovdiv. So he came to see us,
31537: pòčnə də mə rəspɨ̀tvə ut kəd'è sm'ɤ kəkvɨ̀ sm'ə
and began to interrogate me: where we’re from, what sort [of people] we are.
31542: nìe gu prièjme guštàvəjme gu čèrpijme gu səs tàm səs ɨ̀no
We received him, entertained him, treated him to wine
31549: kəkùtu ìməši mɨ̀nəxə dvà trɨ̀ d'ɤ̀nə pàk dojdı̀ də gl'ɤ̀də
such as we had. Two or three days went by [and then] he came again to see
31554: kəkvò pràime s'ɤ̀dnəjme nə sinìjətə tàm də jədìm nə màsətə
what we were doing. We sat down at the table to eat,
31558: i tòj vɨ̀kə slùšəjte kəkò žə vi kàža az mɨ̀slej
and he said, “Listen, I don’t know how to say this [but] I thought
31565: če vɨ̀e kətulɨ̀ci̥te ste slùšəl səm zə vàs če jədìte
that you Catholics were – I’ve heard about you, [I’ve heard] that you eat
31569: žɨ̀vi ù:rə zəštòtu ste jədèli tàm kuštanùgite
people alive, because [it’s known] you’ve been eating turtles there.”
31577: i nìa sə učùdijme kətu z'ɤ̀ də rəs rəskàzvə tɤ̀j zə nàm
And we were astounded when he just upped and said such things about us.
31583: učùdijme sə vɨ̀kəme kɤ̀k mòže də jədìm žɨ̀vi ùrə
We were amazed, and said, “How can [you think] that we eat people alive?
31588: e stàvə trɨ̀ če̥tɨ̀rɨ d'ɤ̀nə sɨ prɨ nàm zəbelèžvəš
It’s been three or four days that you’ve been with us, and you’ve seen
31593: kəkvò pràim kak ràbutime kàk sɤ punàs'əme səs ù:rɤtə
what we do, how we work, how we behave with folk.”
31597: i vɨ̀kə tìj kuètu sə prɨkàzvə znàči nè e ɨ̀stɨ̥nɤ
And he said, “[Yes,] what they say [about you], well, it isn’t true.”
31602: nə drùgijə d'ɤ̀n pàk dudì zəvàri nɨ nə blòkə tàm
The next day he came again, and found us out there in the field
31607: če berìm pəmùk az bèj nàj mɤ̀nenkətə nu berèj
where we were picking cotton. I was the smallest, but I [was the one who] picked
31613: nàj mnògu kilugràmɨ vɨ̀kə be tɨ̀ kəkvà si mɤ̀ničkə
the most kilos [of cotton]. He said, “Well, look at you! You’re as tiny
31616: kətu fəstɤ̀čə ə pək nàj mnògu kilugràmɨ berìš
as a peanut, and yet you pick the most kilos [of cotton].
31618: nə kòlku sɨ gudɨ̀nɨ àz zèj də mu kàzvəm če
How old are you?” And I upped and said to him that
31624: ùs'em d'əcà sme nə màjkə i nə tèjkə sɨruməšìjə nemutìjə
there were eight of us children, mother and father, very poor and with no property,
31630: dukàrə mə vr'èmetu čèk tùkə də dòdeme də ràbutime
and that times [like these] drove us to come all the way here to work.
31637: nəm'èrime ub'èžist'ə tùkənə dubrɨ̀ ù:ra ràbutime tùkə segà
We found a safe haven here, good people, and we work here now.
31642: mɨ̀slɨm zə nəpr'èt pàk də təkòs pàk da dòdime
We’re thinking that in the future we [might] come again this way
31645: əku mə izvìkət əmə əku mə ɤrìsət tòj vɨ̀kə
if they invite me, if they like me. And he said,

32164: stàrecə gu n'àma t'à zašto kàzvə stàrčesù

32182: stàrecə nèhin mɤ̀s e bìl ùnee stàrijə də rečème

32500: əmə ne b'àhə dušlìli b'àhə pòčnəli gà pudràstene də nə òt'
Well they didn't come – they started – when we grew [old enough] (because
32505: màjkit'e ne nɤ̀ pùskəhə əmə tàtkufci təkòvu še vɤ glubìne
our mothers didn't let us go), but our fathers knew [they'd hear] “We'll fine you”.
32509: təkà i təkɤ̀i zənəred'àvəhə màjkit'e n'àmə gi pùsnete əmə
So they gave the mothers an order: “You don't have let them go. But
32514: še və glubìne glòbə i ut'ỳvəhne tàm d'e ut'ùvəhne
we'll charge you a fine.” And [so] we went there. And we went
32519: du četvɤ̀rtu ə udel'ànie gòr'e.dòlu pìsvəm si č'ètəm si
up to the fourth grade. I can read and write, more or less.
32522: tì do četvɤ̀rtu otdelènie si ùčila
You were in school through the fourth grade.
32525: tùka ìmaše li učìlište v xùxla
Was there a school here in Huhla?
32526: Yes, there was, there was one, [but –]
32538: učìlištetu ə tàm če s'ètne nəpràihə tvà sià nəpràihə tvà
… the school. Over there. And later they built this one. They built this one [just] recently.
32541: tova nòvo tova e ot šejsèta godìna
This [one] is new, this is from 1960.
32546: tvà tvà e nòu tàə tùrskətə džəmìjə žəmijə e f nèjə
This is new. That Turkish mosque, the mosque, it's in it
32549: učàhne nìe tàm utìvəhne tə učàhne tàm duhòdəhə təkà učìteli
that we had school. We went there, studied there, and teachers would come.
32552: ìməše li si tùkə dàskal mèsten ili
Was there a teacher here, a local person, or –
32556: n'e n'e ud drùgəd'e duhòdəə gòn'iə sə tùkə
No, no, they came from somewhere else. There was hanky-panky here.
32563: ədìn b'àše dušɤ̀l če s ədnɤ̀ ə prijàtelkə če nìe ut'ỳvəne
One had come, and he [had] a girlfriend. So we went
32567: də sə učìne tè s prijàtelkətə vɤ̀tre nìe ut'ỳvəne kàzvəne
in to learn, and he was inside with his girlfriend. [So] we went to tell
32573: nə km'ètə dòjde km'ètə zəgòn' g'i nikulàj [unclear] nikulàj [unclear]
the mayor, and the mayor came and went for them. “Nikolay!” [unclear] “Nikolay!” [unclear]
32575: b'àgət tùkə nətàtək [laughter] èj təkà ednà ubɤ̀rkənə a
And they ran off, back [to where they'd come from]. [laughter] Oh, such a mess.
32581: i kət ne vɤ̀ pùskəxə na učìlište kvò pràexte
And when they didn't let you go to school what did you do?
32585: mi òt' kò də pràim še pred'ène be čèpkəne vɤ̀lnə še prid'ène
Well, what would we do?! We'd spin, we'd card wool, we'd spin,
32590: še iskàrəme pəmùk màjkit'e še nə nəkàrət də šìene
we'd produce the cotton. Our mothers would make us sew,
32592: dr'èhi də šìene kəkò pràite ìkə tò n'e kət sigɛ̀
sew clothes. “What do you do?” he says. It's not like now
32603: hɤ̀ nìj ne znàehme tvà ò gà n vretènu
Huh?! We knew none of that. Ah. When the spindle –
32616: kòlko gol'àmo tr'àbvaše da bɤ̀de vretèntu
How big did the spindle need to be?
32619: əmi tr'abə də nəpred'èš inò vr'et'ènu
Well, you had to spin a spindle-full.
32620: i kòlko na nègo da ìmə
And how much is there on [a spindle]?
32621: əm jà d'e də znàm kòlku kɤ̀k də ti kàžə
Well, how should I know how much? How can I tell you?
32626: tr'àvə də imə inò pàsmu dv'è pəsmà ìh ne rəzbìrəte vìe
You had to have one skein, two skeins. You don't understand.
32628: How many skeins on one spindle?
32635: dà ə mɤ t'ènku gà e tènenku mɤ̀ segà əku tvà ti
Yes, but little. When it's thin.  But now if you, this –
32637: əm sigà sìčku kùpi nà è gu kò še mu e
Now, go buy everything! Look at it, what's wrong with it?
32639: ə tugàj n'àməše jà p'èd dicà ə̀ c'àlə nɤ̀š ne sɤ̀m lègnuvələ
But back then, no such thing. Five kids, right? I never slept at night
32643: də gi òblekə i če təkàvə b'àh grižlìvə è
in order to keep them clothed, and I took such good care [of them] that
32650: učìtel'te ošte ne mòət də zəpòvnət təkɤ̀vi ud mòjte dicà
the teachers still can't recall anyone like my children.
32653: ə bàt tàn'uite  dicà gà dòjduhə učìlište kət t'àh n'àməše
Ah, brother Tanyo’s kids, when they came to school – there were never any like them.
32655: but [for that to happen], I never got a wink of sleep.
32704: də ràbuti də ìmə sàmo žyòt’ i zdràve də ìmə
And work. Just so people can be alive and healthy.
32707: də òdgledə d'àd bòl'ən bàbə bòlnə dv'ɛ̀ l'èli ìməh
to look after, a sick grandfather, a sick grandmother; I had two aunts.
32709: də ìdət tàm də pìjət kəf'è i càlə nɤ̀š tàm
where people go off to drink coffee, ad [sit] all night
32712: də gu nəpredène mɤ̀ninkə əku e vritènutu màlku
if we’d spun too little, if the spindle was small –
32714: màjkə də vìj sə kàrə tə òt mari̥ si gu ustàjlə
If mother saw it, she’d scold you: “Why did you leave off?
32715: c'àlə nɤ̀š kəkò si pràilə kətə ne gù si nəpr'èlə
What have you been doing all night if you didn’t finish the spinning?”
32725: When – when did you use to eat this dish?
32730: mi sɛ̀nga go edème i vèč'er i na òbet i sɛ̀nga
Oh, we eat it all the time! In the evening, at midday, any time.
32735: nè ә zìmә zìmәs lètes kogà
No, I mean, winter – in the winter, in the summer, or when?
32737: zìmata a ga se zakòla: prasètata
In the winter, when we slaughter the pigs.
32743: Well, [does that mean] before or after Christmas?
32745: Before Christmas, they slaughter [them] before Christmas.
32747: tò se pràvi i segà ku ìma prɛ̀snu da si kùpiš
It's done now too. If you can buy it fresh –
32748: i sà se pràvi i sàmu s mèsu
Now they do it too. It's only with meat ...
32754: nà ràskaži kogà ste klàli gùdetu kè gu rasfasòvate
Tell me [about it]. When did you slaughter the pig, how did you divide it up?
32764: They redden [it all] with the blowtorch.
32766: ot načàloto kažì i segà da
[Tell her] to say it now from the beginning.
32770: ràskaži go ot načàloto pɤ̀rvo rukate kolàč tàm m štò rabòtite
Tell it from the beginning – first, you call the butcher, then what do you do?
32774: à rùkame kolàč dòje kolàče zakòle gùdetu
We call the butcher, the butcher comes, and he kills the pig,
32812: and not to commit sin in any way.
32829: jà da mi kàžeš kə kàk mèsexte xl’aba vìe ednò vrème
Tell me how you used to make bread in the olden days.
32833: There weren’t [large outdoor] ovens, were there?
32834: mi nèma ìmaxme si domà fùrni
Well, no. We had ovens at home.
32838: domà domà si ìmaše fùrn’a no lòveše
At home. There was an oven at home, and it would take –
32842: po sèdem m òsem l’àba i opečèm si napàlim a
we [can] bake seven or eight loaves of bread at a time. We light it,
32845: sɤz dɤ̀rva i si a izmetèm natùr’ame si l’aba tamᵊ
the wood fire, sweep [the oven] out, then lay the bread there.
32848: vɤf nèa s lopàti opečè se izvàdim l’àba jadèm i tugà
[The bread gets put] into it with oven peels, it bakes, we take out the bread, eat [it], and then –
32850: tì tì si pə pə pèkla
And you – you [were the one who] baked [it]?
32853: pèkla sɤm takìva ràboti na lopàta s takòva səm
I baked it.  I [did] all these things, using the oven peel and such.
32855: e dobrè a kàk še go zamèsiš kə
O.K., but how do you make [the dough]?
32859: brašnòtu i i kvàsᵊ sə si ìmaše i zamèsa s kvasɤ̀
the flour, and – there was leavening – and I knead it with leavening,
32861: i tòj ftàsa i go razvalɤ̀ na ednà dɤskɤ̀
and it rises. And I separate it out into loaves,
32865: sè po edìn l’àpᵊ i go zanesèm ta go tùrnem
