one by one on a board. And we take it and put it
32866: into the oven, and there it is.
32871: e kàk poznàvaš kogà tr’àbva da go tùriš vɤf fùrnata
And how do you know when it’s time to put it into the oven?
32875: è mi poznàva sa tòj si ftàsa šùpne takà i
Oh, well, you know! It ferments, gets bubbles in it, like this. And
32879: kato vozidè i às si go tùrna vɤf fùrn’ata i takà
when it’s risen, I put it into the oven and that’s that.
32885: It’s been sitting in the kneading trough.
32888: kato go razvalɤ̀ pa na dɤskɤ̀ta voziòdi i takà
When I separate it out on the board, it has risen [nicely], and that’s all.
32893: And every woman makes her own –
32895: fs’àka ženà si mèseše domà l’àba
Every woman used to make her own bread at home.
32899: a pràexte li xl’àp bes kvàs n’àkəkəf
Did you make bread without any sort of starter?
32903: à nè tùrta sɤdè kogà sa pečè v onìja
Ah, no. Unleavened bread only when you bake it in those –
32905: f tìja takòva pr’àsno a ìnače
in this – [when it’s made] fresh. But otherwise –
32908: i n’àkɤde pàk u fùrnata li
Somewhere also in the outdoor oven?
32912: mi t’à mòže i vɤf fùrn’ata ama kato segà f pèčkite
Well, you can also bake it in the outdoor oven, but [usually], like now, in [indoor] ovens.
32915: Otherwise we would heat up the baking dish ...
32919: i vɤf pòdnicatà tùrnem l’àba i zaròvim go odgòre
... and put the bread into the baking dish, and cover it on top
32941: i go polìvame s vrɛ̀la vòda ìska da vrì f kazàne vòda
and we pour boiling water over it – the water needs to boil in the cauldron.
32947: polìvamè gu s vrɛ̀la vòda i pokrìvame z diplò da se zadùši̥
We pour boiling water over it, and cover it with a rug so it will stew a bit.
32952: trònka pokrìeme i stɤrgà več'e màže žèni i
We cover it for a bit, and then we start scraping it. Men and women
32958: stɤrgà: gùdetù da se oplɛ̀ši kòzinàtḁ uvedè se kòzinàtḁ
scrape the bristles off the piglet until it's “bald” and all the bristles are gone.
32961: After [the bristles are gone], then they scorch it with a machine –
32964: z bendžìn tu: takà gu pɤ̀rža: pɤ̀rža: rèda: ta stàne
a blowtorch. "Psss" – they scorch it up and down in rows, and it gets
32969: iscɤ̀rvi se stàne ùbu: ma se ukàdi i sètn'e
all nice and red, But it's also smoky [from the blowtorch]. So next
32973: so sapùn' s vòda se mìe stɤržè
you wash it with soap and water, and scrape [some more],
32979: ta stàne bɛ̀lu ta cәrvèna kòžata čùdna sɛ̀m ùbuu
until the skin gets all white and then red. Wonderful, totally beautiful!
32986: i se razrɛ̀žuva udrɛ̀že se udgòre tòkmu udòlu
And you slice it – the same distance from the top and from the bottom,
32990: to cut [into] the stomach, [to] what we call “smenka” (spleen)
32996: tovà gu vìkamè gu smɛ̀nka tovà što sè razrɛ̀žuva
We call it “smenka”  – that part that you cut out ...
33004: ut kurèmo i se podadà crevàta podadà
... of the stomach so that the intestines appear. They come –
33009: podadè se kulàk mastà pɤ̀rvu povedè bàbata
they come into view, first the leaf fat. The old woman pulls it out –
33011: e tì pòdnica ìmaš li si tùka
Do you have a baking dish – here?
33013: ìmaše ama sa trošì pòdnicata ta nèmam ni pòdnica
There used to be, but the baking dish broke. I don’t have [any] baking dish [now].
33015: You don’t keep it, you don’t –
33024: kɤdè si a slagàla tàja pòdnica
Where did you used to put that baking dish  …
33031: ami znàči nakladè se odžàkə tò si ìmaše odžàk
Well, so, you light [a fire] in the hearth. There was a hearth,
33033: tàm pret fùrn’atà tùka bèše i tùrnem go
there in front of the big oven, and we put it [the baking dish] in,
33037: pòdnicata sa napàli i grə svàlim pòdnicatà
the baking dish heats up, and – and then we take out the baking dish
33038: i tùrnem pogàčata i təvà a
and put in the quick bread, and that’s it.
33041: ama k znàči ə kɤ̀štite ne b’àxa kato tìja
Ah, so houses [back then] weren’t like these [now].
33045: ìmaše ìmaše ama segà a napràvixme sè
They did, they did. But now we’ve made ourselves all  –
33049: We’ve gotten to be somewhat modern [laughter]
33051: ama tàa kɤ̀šta vàšta e stàra ə i kòlko e stàra
But this house of yours is old. How old is it?
33055: ami pe pedesèta godìna e pràvena
33056: pedesè è znàči predì tovà vəf ə onìja stàrite
1950. Ah! Then before that, in those old ones –
33064: a tɤ̀zi nè e ìmalo odžàk takà li
But this one didn’t have a hearth, right?
33068: [laughter] Hey, hey, come on over, come on!
33075: a tì še ni kàžeš kakvì b’àa i kɤ̀štite ednò vrème
So you’ll tell us what houses were like in the old days [O.K.]?
33077: Well, the houses of olden days –
33083: starovrèmski kɤ̀šti sɤsᵊ po ednà takòva ə oddòle ili nàsipᵊ
Old-fashioned houses! Each had one of – well, earthen fortification underneath,
33087: i dvè stài odgòre i kɤ̀šta i sòba mu vìkaxme
and two rooms above. The house and what we called a “soba” –
33109: dvè stài a pɤk ìnače pòsle zèa gi pràvɤtᵊ
two rooms. Otherwise – later they started to make them
33114: pɤ nɤ dvà etàža ta odgòre dvè sòbi oddòle
with two stories:  two rooms above, and down below –
33115: pɤ nɤ dvà etàža ta odgòre dvè sòbi oddòle
with two stories:  two rooms above and down below –
33125: pɤ nɤ dvà etàža ta odgòre dvè sòbi oddòle
with two stories:  two rooms above and down below –
33130: And what was in the basements?
33135: i mòžeše a sa živèe i vɤf edìna bagàš si tùr’axme
Well, you could live [there], and in one of them we used to put luggage
33139: takà za takòva za xranɤ̀ dè
Like – well, for food, you know, ...
33143: a kakvà stòka ìmaxte vìe ednò vrème
What kinds of animals did you have in the old days?
33152: ofcète kàg gi pas’àxte i za kakvò gi go glèdaxte t’àx
... the sheep. How did you pasture them, and why did you raise them?
33157: i togàa kakvò se sèe po tovà vrème
Back then, what did you plant at that time [of the year]?
33163: əf əprìl' mɛ̀sec zəfàtə sə pusɛ̀e kərtòfite pò sètne pàk
In April you began to plant potatoes, and after that
33168: fəsùl' misìr' kəkòtu ìmə sə nəsɛ̀e gràh kəkvòtu
beans, corn, and whatever else you had to plant – peas, whatever.
33174: žìtutu tùkə ne sɛ̀eme tò dòlu
We didn't plant wheat here, that was down below …
33182: ə màlko màlko tùk tàm n počtì nèmə
A little, a little here and there. But hardly anything at all.
33186: pò rànu imɛ̀š'e gà behme nì pò drèbni
There used to be, when we were smaller (= held smaller land portions).
33191: mnògo rɔ̀š sɛ̀ehmə pu bərčìnetu tò segà se
We planted a lot of rye [then] in the hills. But now
33195: i zem'ɔ̀tə se zəràsne stànə tèkezesè i sìčku tè
the land is overgrown: the cooperative farm came, and everything –
33198: all the [fields] – the land became wooded Balkan [landscape].
33205: dɛ̀tu imɛ̀hme tərlì də ràdə žìtu tò sə zəràste
Where we once had “torli” (fields) that would bear grain – it all got overgrown.
33216: pò slàbite mestà tərlì hùbəite mestà grədìni
Fields were the less good places, and the nice ones were gardens.
33219: i kàk ə kàk se rabòti tərlàta kakvò tr'àva da napràiš
And how – how did you work this “torlata” (the field)? What did you have to do?
33232: àh nìvətə zəsɛ̀eš' i sɛ̀tne əgà uzrɛ̀e už'ɔ̀neš' jə səs sɔ̀rp təkà
Ah, the field. You plant it, and then when it's ripened, you reap it with a sickle.
33237: si jə už'ɔ̀neš' i jə vər vərhɔ̀t nə hərmàn
You reap it and then they thresh it in the threshing field,
33240: ž'ìtutu gu zberɔ̀t təkà f č'uvàl:e
and then gather the grain up into bags.
33245: a kà nə a kàg go vərxòt səs kakvò
And how do they thresh it? What [do they use]?
33251: səs mùl'e mùl'etə kòn'i təkà gi vər'tɔ̀t mùl'etənə
With a mule – mules or horses. The mules go around in a circle.
33255: ədìn č'ùl'ɛ̀k fsredè i gi s prɔ̀čkə gi kàrə
One person [stands] in the middle and drives them [forward] with a stick,
33259: i nèj si žìtutu pò rànu seà nè tò nèmə etùvə
and that's [how we got] grain earlier. Now they don't do that.
33261: Don't they winnow it after that?
33264: ne sè li vèe pòsle kəto
Don't they winnow it after they –
33267: če udv'ɔ̀d gu s lupàtə təkà gu v'ɔ̀t
They take it out with a shovel and winnow it.
33270: i dùje vɛ̀ter i pàdə ž'ìtu nə enèj
The wind blows, and the grain falls on the far [side] –
33272: i tvà go səbìrat i f xambàra
And all that gets gathered into the barn.
33279: Is that how you called it, "hambar"?
33284: i vəf vəf fs'àka kòšta li si imɛ̀še təkòvə
Was there one of these in every house?
33294: č'e vsɛ̀kə vrìt sìč'ku sɛ̀hə uvès rɔ̀š' sìč'ku pò rànu
Each one. All [of us], everybody planted oats and rye, earlier on.
33299: seà utkàktu e zə f tèkezesè č'etìrise gudìni məhnɔ̀hə
Now, after the cooperative farm [came] forty years ago, they stopped.
33302: tò tegaj segà nèmə segà kərtòfi sme sɛ̀li
And now, there's none [of that]. Now we've planted potatoes,
33305: ednò vrème kàk gi zov'àxte kartòfite
How did you call potatoes in the old days?
33314: əhɤ̀ a na domàtite kak vìkaxte
Aha. And how did you call tomatoes?
33331: zə fəsùl' enəkòf fəsùl'ef kuč'ɛ̀n gu zuvɛ̀hme
For beans. We called it a sort of “bean-beet.”
33336: š'ekèref kuč'ɛ̀n pò rànu ne sɛ̀hme sètne z'ɔ̀hme tegàj də sɛ̀eme
We didn't used to plant sugar beets. Then we bought [some] in order to plant them.
33343: tegàvə petmès ud nègə iskàrvəhme zàhərnu nəkvò beše
Then we made molasses from them; it was sugary, you know.
33344: a petmès kàk se prài petmès
Ah, molasses. How do you make molasses?
33347: č'e kuč'ɛ̀nən gu zə iskàrəš' ud nìvətə
You bring the beets in from the field,
33351: i ubɛ̀liš' gu hùbəvu i f ədìn kəzàn gu svərìš'
you peel them nicely, and and you boil them up in a cauldron.
33354: i tegà s prèsə gu se iscədì i tugàvə gu vər
Then it's strained through a press and then you –
33358: kətu gu izvər'ɔ̀t f ədnɔ̀ tòvə i stàne petmès
They turn it out into a pan and it becomes molasses.
33362: tò seà nə rɛ̀tki kɔ̀šti ìmə
[You find it] only in a very few houses now.
33367: sà èšte t'à kràvəsə mi pòjde nɛ̀gde
Anything else? This cow has gone off somewhere.
33377: ednò vrème ìmaxte li kràvi mnògo
In the old days did you have cows? Many, [that is]?
33379: ə nì pò rànu nəlì beme nè f tèkezesè imɛ̀hme əmi
Earlier on, because we weren't [yet] in the cooperative farm, we had, well,
33381: kàk po dvè trì kràvi si imɛ̀hme sìč'ku imòt' imɛ̀hme mnògu
we had two or three cows each. We had everything – we had a lot of property.
33384: tugà vlɛ̀ze sìč'kutu f tèkezesè z'ɔ̀hə mi gu
Then everything went into the cooperative farm. They took it [all] from me.
33390: ustànəhme nèj ku ràbutiš' š'e ti dədɔ̀t grədìnə ku nè
We were left like this. If you work [for them] they'll give you a garden, and if not
33394: nè nèməš'e nì lìč'nu pòlzvəne tugàvə nìš'tu
[then] not. There was no private use [of property] then, nothing.
33397: pɔ̀lnumàlu nɛ̀kvu a gà ràbutiš' dàvət ti gə
[Just] some poor thing they give you when you work.
33402: əm seà se zəvɤ̀rnə zem'ɔ̀sə əm seà ustərɛ̀hme nəkvi ràbuti
And now the land's been returned. But now we've grown old. And there it is.
33405: What did you feed the cows?
33413: sɛ̀nu ut càrevicətə tuvà misirlìg' gu zuvème misìrč'enu gi hrànehme
Hay from corn, [which] here we call “misirlik”. We gave them cornstalk feed.
33430: m'ètnət vəf fùrnənə ədìn č'ɛ̀z gòre.dòlu ispeč'è se i àjde
they throw it in the oven for about an hour, and it bakes, and there you are.
33431: əxə̀ a fùrnənə nèmə li žàr vɤ̀tre
Uh huh. But aren't there coals inside the outdoor oven?
33437: i pò màlku təgà sə hrànehə pòveč'e nemɛ̀š'e ɛ̀ce mnògu
They didn't get much to eat then. There wasn't a whole lot.
33439: zə zìmno vrème tr'àbva mnògo da səberèš
For the winter period, you have to gather a lot of –
33443: sɛ̀nu sɛ̀nu ìməme sà sɛ̀nu zəvɔ̀rnəhə si mi livàdite ìməme
Hay, hay. We've got hay now. They returned the meadows to me, we have [that].
33450: pə grədìnite mi nàmi flɛ̀ze regulàcijə tè gu zemàhə sìč'ku
[But] our gardens – this regulation came [into force] and they took it all,
33454: kɔ̀š'ti nəgrədìhə mnògu sme ə zlubèni nìe usòbenu
and built houses [there]. We're very embittered. Us especially –
33457: they took everything away from me.
33459: [But] now, didn't they give it back?
33464: e če f enèj regulàcijə gu ne vràštət dərž'ɛ̀vətə kəkò e seà
Well, [there's] this regulation. The state's not returning [our land] the way it is now.
33469: č'ɛ̀kəme nìštu ne stàvə kək jɛ̀ ti kàzvəm uzlubèni sme mnògu
We're waiting, but nothing is happening. As I said, we're very embittered.
33473: grədìni nèməme livàdi mlògu ìmə əmə grədìni nèməme
We don't have [our] gardens. There's a lot of meadow but we don't have gardens.
33479: ti kàzvəm i nəgrədìhə kɔ̀š'ti e təkvì təgà besràmnici
[Like] I told you, they then [went and] built houses and stuff. Shameless ones!
33482: də gi e nè sràm kədènu sə ugradìli bàre
They should be ashamed of themselves for building what they did. At the least
33484: kədènu e ustànəlu də si mi gu dədɔ̀t əmə i nègə
they could have given the remainder to me, but even that
33486: nè dàvət tè si gu s'ɔ̀t zgà dərž'ɛ̀vətə mi go e dàlə
they won't give me. They plant it now [and say] “The state gave it to me” !
33490: a kràvata sùtrin kakvò kət tr'àbva də napràiš kəto stàneš
With a cow – what do you have to do in the morning when you get up?
33494: kətu stànə mɛ̀tnə hi ednò edìn č'ul sɛ̀nu i
When I get up I throw it a horseblanket-ful of hay, and
33498: zbìrəh f ədnà kòfə brəšnò kəkòtu e kərtòfi nɛ̀kvu kənàtə ìmə
I used to put together flour, whatever, some potatoes, whatever there is, into a pail,
33501: əgà jə ìzdujəm še hi gu dàm
and I'll give that to it when I finish milking it.
33507: tr'àbva li da ja mìeš nèšto da ja čìstiš
Do you have to wash something first, to clean it off?
33512: a če navà nàj nəprèš ìdəm tə jə klàəm
That, yes; first of all [when] I go and get ready
33518: də jə dòjəm ìzmijəm hi vìmetu še stàn  nə əglɔ̀k
to milk [the cow], I wash its udder, I'll ge- a cloth
33522: i ìstučəm gu i pòčnəm də jə dòjəm klàəm si stòlč'ek
and wring it out, and start to milk it. I put down a little stool
33526: i si jə dòjəm s dvèse rɔ̀ki jɛ̀ səm sedɛ̀lə
and I milk it with both hands. I was [there],
33531: f tèkezesètu dəjɛ̀č'kə sèdem gudìni vəf ə dòlu etɤ̀s fèrmə
as a milkmaid in the cooperative farm, for seven years. In that farm down below,
33534: sedɛ̀h gà flɛ̀zəhme f tèkezesè pàk kò še pràiš
[that's where] I sat when we joined the cooperative farm. What [else] can you do?
33541: nè nàrəce nàrəce səm dujìlə kràvite
No, by hand. I milked [all] the cows by hand.
33543: pu dvàese kràvi nə ədnà dujɛ̀č'kə
Twenty cows for every one milkmaid.
33545: ofcète ofcète gi sme takòva zət nə ə
Sheep – we had sheep for – [we kept them] behind the –
33548: na sajɤ̀tə tàm sedɤ̀t tìa ne sedèa domà
They stayed there in the sheep pen, they didn’t stay in the house.
33554: nàšite òfce sə ne sɤ̀ sed’àli domà às d’àdo i tàte
Our sheep did not stay in the house. I – my father and grandfather,
33556: tìa sa gi gledàle na sajɤ̀tə ne sɤ̀ gi dɤržàle domà
they looked after them in the sheep pen, they didn’t keep them at home.
33560: pɤk às tùk otkàk sɤm došlà ne sɤ̀m ìmam ednɤ̀ ofcɤ̀
As for me, ever since I’ve come here I haven’t – I have one sheep
33562: i t’à ne sɤ̀m a vidvàla trì čètiri gòdin
and it – I haven’t seen it for three or four years.
33564: sè e pri bràta sedì tàm
All that time it’s been staying there with my brother.
33569: e dobrè za kakvò gi glèdaxte vìe ofcè zə
O.K., then. Why did you raise and look after sheep? For –
33571: Well for the wool, for the milk, …
33573: jà da mi kàžeš ml’àkoto kato
33577: kato go izdoìš kàg go prerabòtvate
Once you’ve milked [the animal], how do you process …
33583: mlekòto go izdoìm i precedìm go i m màlko tə gorèšto
we milk [the animal] and strain the milk, and when it’s cooled some,
33585: i go zèmem ta go potsìrim i stàne sìrene
we take it and put rennet in it, it becomes cheese,
33587: and we strain it in strainers, ...
33591: O.K., so you make white cheese –
33597: kvò stàva čàkaj da pòčvam narèd
What’s happening? Wait, let me begin [greeting each one] in turn.
33604: da da de mlàdenof se kàzvam
Yes, yes. My name is Mladenov.
33610: sednì màlko bàba še ti kàže
Just sit still, Granny will tell you [what’s going on].
33618: à postòj kàkto èto tòj vìe ste mladì a nìe mòem
Yes, you stand, like this one! You’re young, [laughter], we can ...
33621: … stay [where we are]. It’s gotten to be like that.
33623: So wait now. You say you strain it –
33627: mi prec kato go izdòat od ofcète precedì sa mlekòto
Well you – After they milk the sheep then you strain the milk.
33632: vɤf kakvò vɤf tèndžuri ili vɤfᵊ ə kɤzàn gul’àmᵊ katò e mnògo mlekòto
Into what? Into pans, or into a big cauldron if there’s a lot of milk.
33634: i se tùri sìrištè i potsìri sa i
And you add rennet, and it ferments, and –
33636: Where do you get the rennet from?
33640: mi kupùvaxmè pa n’àkoga i pràvea ut ə ègnetḁtḁ
Well, we used to buy it. At one point they would make it from lambs –
33644: kato zakòlet ègneta ìmaše sìrište i sčùkaa gò i
when they slaughter lambs there was rennet. They would pound it and
33647: tùrnat sòl razbɤ̀rkad go i go vɤf šišèto sa sìpe
add salt, then stir it and you pour it into a bottle
33649: sɤs vòda se napràvi i se od nègo se sìreše
and make it with water and – That’s what you made cheese from.
33651: n’àkoga d’àdo mòj sìreše sè sɤs ə takòvo sìrište
At one time my grandfather made cheese only with this sort of rennet.
33654: a pòsle evropèjsko zèa da ìmaše
And then [people] started doing it the European way, and there was –
33657: čàkaj čàkaj ne smè svɤ̀ršili po tovà sɤs sìrišteto
Wait, wait – we haven’t finished [talking] about this [kind of] rennet.
33659: Where do you put it after that?
33663: nè kat sìreneto kato s se fàne
No, I mean the cheese, once [the fermenting] starts up.
33665: sìreneto kat sa fàne sa razbɤ̀rka sɤs ednà takòva
When the cheese gets started, you stir it with a sort of …
33670: lopàtka i sa màlko sa utài pòsle go precedìm
… ladle, and it – it settles a bit and then you strain it into a –
33674: vɤf en takòva ednì ima si kalɤ̀pe takà se cedì
Into – there are these molds, and then it filters out, ...
33680: i sa narèže pa na felìi pòsle kato se iscedì sìpvat
... and then you cut it into slices. And after it’s strained they pour it [out],
33684: sa narèže i tùr’a se f kačètata sòli go
[then] you slice it and it put it in jugs, and salt it,
33689: a tovà dèto se iscèžda ot nègo
And the [liquid] that drains out of it?
33729: bàba si ìma da da razbìra tìa rabòti
there's old women who understand [how to do] these things –
33734: the old woman pulls out the leaf fat in the lard,
33738: ta izvàdi crevàta ta crevàta i mìeme
then brings out the intestines. And we wash the intestines
33744: z gorèšta vòda su sapùn' sus ucèt sus sìčku
with hot water, with soap, with vinegar, with everything [we have]
33752: da sà izmìeni ùbuù ta nafpàame vèč'e kɤ̀rvəvìci
so that they [get to] be really clean. And then we stuff blood sausages.
33757: odɛ̀lno zejrè si ìma za kɤ̀rvəvìcitè ә rìbicìte
There's separate sorts of stuffing for the blood sausages. The parts of meat
33762: za kɤ̀rvəvìci si ìma udɛ̀lnu bɛ̀liɤ dròp ә ә sɤrcètu
[that go into] blood sausages are separate – the lungs, then the heart,
33767: takvìa mèš'č'ini i krɤftà im za kɤ̀rvəvìci̥te̥
such bits of meat plus the blood – [it’s all] for the blood sausages.
33777: a pa pò ùbavìte krɛ̀šč'inì se nafpàva: bàbici stàrec kàzvame
But the nicer bits of meat are for “babitsi” (tripe), what we call “starets” –
33785: i šužùci tkà tavà napràime i pòsle slanìnatà se razrɛ̀žuva
and [for] sausages. So, that's what we make. And then the pig fat is cut up,
33792: i ja nasòluvàme f kàca ìmamè slanìnevi kàci golɛ̀mi
and we salt it in a barrel – we have big “pig fat barrels” [for this].
33799: ràskaži kàk go pràetè tvà slanìnata l
Tell [us] how you do this, [process] this pig fat.
33868: ìmam drùgu mumč’è tò už’ènenu ìma dv’ɛ̀ decà
I have another son, he’s married [and] has two children.
33874: i utìde w bez’erlìk’ u drùga dərdž’ɛ̀va ə č’e gu z’èha
And he went to Libya, to another country [where] they kidnapped him.
33877: i stuv’à ednà gudìna ə č’e gu z’èha bəndìt’tɛ̏
He was there a year. And [these] bandits kidnapped him.
33882: ə č’e stujà s’edemdes’è d’èn’ə ne gù znàemi
For seventy days we had no knowledge of him –
33888: žỳvu li e kəd’à e ə č’i̥ xòdime nə ednà wrɑ̀čkə
Was he alive? Where was he? So we went to a fortune-teller,
33892: ə č’e wrɑ̀čkətə kɑ̀zə nə snìmkə gl’èdə
and the fortune-teller said – she looked at a photo [of him] –
33895: i nìe ni gù znàeme gi bùlkata i tò dwɑ̀mətə otìdaha
We didn’t know [anything more] about him. He and his wife had both gone.
33900: i i š’es momč’èta ednò ot sòhia i č’ètir:tȅ ot wɑ̀rnə
[There were] altogether six boys, one from Sofia and the four from Varna
33903: i i bùlkata i nàj žinɑ̀ a č’e otìdaha tàm
plus the wife – and some other woman. So they went there,
33908: ə č’e t’è b’àha t’ehnìci tò arap’à tàm
33912: a če nalì i arap’àta mràz’at gi dàvat na t’àx parìt’ɛ̏
And the Arabs hate them, because they [foreigners] get paid [good] money.
33919: pak na un’às ne dàvat pak nàši̥t’ȅ kuìto ìdat ottùka
But the [locals] don’t get paid, as opposed to ours, who when they go there
33925: dàvat im parìt’ȅ a či nàšit’ȅ stojàə p’èt m’àse̥ca
get paid [good] money. And our folk stayed [only] five months
33933: i vèk’i nèma da da stojɛ̀t z’à si t’ɛ z’à si òtpuskata
and weren’t going to stay any longer. So they took leave [from work]
33939: če šə z duhɑ̀d’at tùka də dvanàisi čàsa pətùva sə oroplàn
to come here [to Varna]. It takes twelve hours by plane
33947: dù bezerlìk’ dvanàese čàsə pravì sm’ètka i si zi kət stujàa god’ìna
to Libya. Imagine, twelve hours! So when they had stayed for a year,
33952: i si z’èli bil’èt’t’ȅ še s duhɑ̀d’at za ed’ìn m’àsec
they’d bought the tickets and were about to come [home] for a month.
33955: i ban’d’ìt’i ìmalo dìvi xòra i gi z’èha i im kɑ̀zali
But there were these bandits. Wild people! And they kidnapped them. They told them
33964: t’ìj bilì ottàk vašìst’ɨ č’ètiristòtin dùši otsàm c’àl gràd bezerlìk
there were four hundred Fascists over there, the whole city of Tripoli,
33970: tì i pàk komunìst’i i nàšto momč’è tehnìk bùlkata əndž’ilèrka
but they were Communists. So our boy is a mechanic and his wife an engineer.
33977: i dàdəa im stud’èni kolɤ dv’à hòdiwa ot ə ə portakàlija
They had issued them driving school cars, two of them, from Portugal.
33981: z’èha dv’à kolì stud’èni i tàm tìa arap’à si ə očɛ̀t
So they took these two driving school cars out to give the Arabs driving lessons,
33987: pu ed’ìn i otòd’at nɑ̀štu mumč’è tehn’ìk pràat ym pɛ̀tištata
one on one. And they set off. Our boy the mechanic was building roads for them.
33990: ama tìe ne štɛ̀t komun’ìstetu un’às fašìst’i ottàm
But [some people] don’t like [us] Communists, those Fascists there,
33999: i nɑ̀št’ȅ mumč’èta šə ə z’èmat ə n’ègo d’èn kɑ̀rat kolìt’ȅ stud’èn:t’ɛ̏
and they thought to kidnap our boys that day. So they’re driving the school cars
34009: kɑ̀rat trìjset dùš’i arap’à to prɑ̀vi napr’ɛ̀d momč’èto kɑ̀ra kamiòne
and thirty Arabs were driving. Our boy was in front, driving a truck.
34015: i vèšti ednò i po edìn aràpin vəs t’ɑ̀x očɛ̀d gi
and [so was] another one; and in each car one of ours was teaching an Arab.
34018: i kat vər’àli i tòs ə kɑ̀zal če ə kòjtu e ut bez’erlìk
And as they went along, this [Arab] said, the one who is from Tripoli,
34025: če muamàr kɑ̀zal dn’ès n’èma da pùskat’e ban’d’ìt’t’ȅ na un’àz
that Gadafi had said that bandits weren’t going to be allowed today among
34031: na aràpi na fašìstit’ȅ i tì nàš’to mumčè utòd’a n’ègu d’èn
the Arabs, that is the Fascists. And so our boy went off that day,
34037: tò varì kɑ̀zva tùk še zabìš kòl’č’eto tùk še zabìš kòl’č’etu
and [as he went along] he told [his team] where to pound in the road marker posts.
34042: i vər’ɛ̀t otpodìr’e zabìrat arap’àta kòl’č’etata
[But] the Arabs went after them [in sabotage], and pulled out the posts.
34047: i tràktora orì pək pɛ̀t’a še im go pràvət
And the tractor was plowing [the ground] to make the road.
34052: i či muàr kɑ̀zal n’èma da pùskat’e ban’d’ìt’i n’ès tàm tìj pùsnaha
So Gadafi had said not to let the bandits out today there. But they did let them out,
34056: i vkèpaxa nɑ̀šte mumč’èta š’ès mumč’èta ednò ot sòhia
and [those bandits] grabbed our boys – six boys, one from Sofia
34062: i ednò ot vɑ̀rna i bùlkatȁ i v’èš ednà ženɑ̀ š’estìma dùši
one from Varna, the bride, and another woman. Six in all.
34068: vkèpaxa gi kat nì zakɑ̀raxa kɑ̀i tàm i ə izl’àzaha kɑ̀e
They took them. “And when they drove us there,” he said, “there emerged
34083: dìvi xòra savs’àm d’ìvu bizùmno i ə segɑ̀ spr’àha gi tàm
Wild men, completely wild! Senseless! And they kept them there.
34092: dvɑ̀ise d’èn’a kɑ̀e səs ə pɛ̀ster bòp ni hrɑ̀n’ət š č’urbɛ̀
“For twenty days,” he said, “they fed us only pinto bean soup.
34096: nie kɑ̀e vèk’i kɑ̀e hìč’ kɑ̀e ni znàeme kɑ̀e tɛ̀j  bleštùl’ki
We hadn’t the slightest idea [where we were], just flashing lights
34100: kɑ̀e na uč’ìt’ȅ ni i dòjde kɑ̀e edìn č’ov’èk poslàli si
in our eyes”, he said.  “And then,” he said, “this guy came, and they spread out
34108: s’àno na zem’ɛ̀ta s’àn:tȕ senòto kɑ̀e m’ètər i pol’vìna tàm u gorɛ̀tə
hay on the ground, about a meter and a half of hay there in the woods.
34113: poslàha ni kɑ̀e l’ègnali si to tòplu tàm b’ɛ̀ši̥
They spread it out for us,” he said; they lay down and it was warm.
34117: l’ègnali si na senòto i ətkrìt’i i n’àma nìštu̥
So they lay on the hay, out there in the open, and nothing to be done.
34121: edìn pàk ə go zèli ot portakɑ̀lia šees’ègodìš’en č’ov’èk
And they’d also taken [another person], from Portugal, a 60-year old guy.
34122: a dobrè a màslo pràexte li
Ah. So did you used to make butter?
34124: mi pràvexme če i go tàm za kato n’àkoga ə
We did make it. And it – when – at one point –
34130: otišèl àz rekɛ̀l še v donsɛ̀t fašìstit’e tòj vèk’e s t’ɑ̀h
He went and said the Fascists will bring you things (he was one of them) –
34133: sìpea go vɤf ə kàci tò si m napràveno takòva
They would pour it into barrels made like this.
34136: i ednò džurìlo i sa kàčim takà na ednà dɤskɤ̀
And there’s a mashing staff, and we climb up like this on a board,
34142: inò od’àlu i edìn briz’ènt da s pustèl’at əf takòsta
a blanket, and a [piece of] canvas, so they could spread it out there.
34146: i džùrkame tàm ta džùrkame ta izbìem màslo
and we pound and pound [until] we get butter.
34148: i sigà tɑ̀m nìe ne gì znàemi žỳvi li sa kakvì sa
So they’re there – and we here don’t know if they’re [even] alive, or how they are –
34151: a n’àmaše li ednò takòva visòko takòva kato
But wasn’t there this sort of tall –
34154: e ta tovà de takà tò zakàčeno
Yes, that’s it! It’s connected there –
34157: Churn, is that what it’s called?
34158: butàlka ama butàlkata na rɤ̀ka pa onovà bèše
A churn, yes. But a churn is for hand-made [butter]. This one was –
34162: pa na geràn bìexme go na bačìite kato e mnògo mlekòto
We would beat in a big churn in the dairy farm when there was a lot of milk.
34165: tò ne mòe po pèt šès v’àdra ml’àko mòže li
That’s not possible. Is it possible to [take] five or six buckets of milk –
34168: da go bìeš tì na rɤ̀ka tàm i da go sìriš
and to churn it by hand and get cheese from it?
34173: nì gì znàeme tɛ̀rsim pìtame ot sòhia čil’àk ìmalo
we don’t know. We look around and ask questions There was this man from Sofia –
34177: ed’ìn minìster ženà mu zapoznàhme se tàm i minìster ženà mu
his wife is a minister – we’d met him there. So [this guy] – his wife is a minister –
34179: i ə i tòj tàm i tòj č’ov’èk sàl ni kɑ̀zwa f sòhia
he is there. So this guy, in Sofia, said to us only that
34185: tìe gɨ z’èha ama tùriha gi učilìšte pək t’ìj na trevɛ̀ta
they’d taken them and put them in a school or out on the grass [or something].
34189: i nìj plàčem tùkana i [cough] ne gì znàeme v’èk’e
And we’re crying here, because [cough] we have no idea
34192: kakvì sa nìj žỳvi li sa n’èma pìsmu n’èma nìštu
how they are, or if they are alive: no letter, no nothing from them.
34198: i ə tùkanək ednà kadɛ̀nka ìmaši gledɑ̀čka i svàta
So there is this Turkish woman here, a fortune teller, my in-law,
34202: na mumč’èto mi d’àdo mu i tòd’a na gledɑ̀čkata
my boy’s [other] grandfather. So he went to the fortune teller
34207: t’à reklà nìj kaìl snim sàl da sme ž’ùvi
and she said – “We’d be content [to hear from them] only ’We’re alive’ ”, [we told her].
34209: ne ìm dàvat tàm ni pìsmo ni nìštu sàl da gi čùimi
“They don’t let them write letters or anything, we just want to hear
34213: ž’ỳvi li sa i tɛ̀z gledɑ̀čka kɑ̀zəla ž’ỳvi sa reklà
if they are alive.” And that fortune teller said, “They are alive,” she said.
34220: žu žə dəšter’à ti reklà inžilèrka z’èt’e ti t’ehn’ìk
“Your daughter is an engineer, your son-in-law a mechanic.
34227: s’edemdes’è d’èna reklɑ̀ ilì sedemdesè l’ m’às’ca reklà še gi derdž’ɛ̀t
They’ll keep them [captive] either seventy days or seventy months,
34230: ama ž’ỳvi sa reklɑ̀ i š ìdat m za roždènia d’èn
but they are alive,” she said. “And they will come back for her birthday,
34234: nabližàə še ìdat reklɑ̀ še dòjdat reklɑ̀ za ružd’ènija i d’èt’
which is coming up. They’ll come,” she said, “They’ll come for her birthday.”
34236: i še dòjdat za ružd’ènija i d’èn i tò tɛ̀j stàna
They’ll come for her birthday.” And in fact that happened.
34241: šèstija nə na s’èdmia oslobodìha gi oslobodìha gi togàs i ə
They liberated them on the sixth – on the seventh. They liberated them then. And
34247: i tɛ̀s ə aràpit’ȅ d’èto t’ì komunìsti d’et’ka mumč’èto ni
the Arabs that were Communists, [that is, on the side of] our boy,
34253: xòdili dvà pɛ̀ti da gi otn’èmat am ne mužìli da gi utɛ̀vnət
had gone twice to try to get them out but couldn’t free them.
34260: strɛ̀l’at kɑ̀e str’ɛ̀l’at on’às ingličàn:t’ɛ̏ i merikɑ̀ncit’ȅ gi podɛ̀ržat
There was shooting, he said. The others (Americans and English) were giving support.
34269: mɑ̀lko ama podɛ̀ržat gi s urɛ̀dia i s’ètn’e kat dohàd’a edìn rusnàk
Not much, but support with weapons. But then there came a Russian
34274: ot wɑ̀r ot ə rusìja i ednò mumč’è dvɑ̀ese i trì godìšno
from Var– from Russia: a young fellow twenty-three years old.
34281: i rusnɑ̀ka kɑ̀zal dud’è n’ gì nəm’ɛ̀rim  n’èmə də zəminùvəme
And the Russian said, “We’re not going to leave until we find them.”
34285: i ə tìj vər’àli vər’àli izl’àzli nə ednà pul’ànə glɑ̀nni
And our folk were wandering about, hungry, and came upon this field.
34289: id’ìn čil’àk gi vìd’el ama ut t’ɑ̀h ud un’às i rikɛ̀l
A man saw them, though he was one of those others, and he said
34294: às š ìdə də vi dunsɛ̀ mɑ̀lku l’àp əmə vujnìst’ȅ
“I’ll go off  and bring you back a little bread.” But the soldiers
34301: s’è gi tɛ̀rsili izl’àzli tàm žinà i mɛ̀š vìdehte li riklì
still sought them. They came out and said, “Did you see man and woman here?”
34306: tòj rikɛ̀l dòdəh vìkə tùkənək izl’àzəh rikɛ̀l še im tɛ̀rs’ə mɑ̀lku jàd
He said, “I got here, came out [and saw them], and was going to get them food”, he said.
34311: dòdəh vìkə t’è pɑ̀g gi strɑ̀h pɑ̀k sə ftìknəli u gurɛ̀tə
[But] when I came, they took fright and dashed into the woods again.”
34314: vər’àli vər’àli č’ètiri d’èn’ə vər’àli glɑ̀nni i izlɑ̀zət
And they walked on and on, four days, without food, and came upon
34320: ed’ìn hòdil zə rìba tòj rikɛ̀l mumč’ètu riklò də n zəved’èš
a fisherman, and he – this boy said to him, “Take us [to get food],”
34325: riklò glɑ̀nni sn’e i nìj snim rikɛ̀lə ərt’ìšti krìjət sə
he said, “we’re hungry." "And we’re actors,” said [the girl] (they were hiding).
34329: hùbəvu əmə tòj gi zəv’èl bùlkətə mu dàlə čəsòvnikə si
OK. Anyway, he took them. The wife had given him her watch.
34332: tòj gi puv’èl zəv’èl gi nə kulìbətə si i tò kɑ̀e
So he took them. He led them to his hut where, he said,
34338: ni jədɛ̀t l’àp n’èməd bràšnu əmi kɑ̀šə kərtòhenə rəzbɛ̀rkələ
they don’t eat bread. They had no flour, but [the woman] stirred up some potato mash
34343: i gi nəhrɑ̀nili i gi spɑ̀li tɑ̀m i trɛ̀gnəli də gi zəvəd’è
and they fed them and put them up overnight, and then left to take them
34346: kəm bezerlìk’ də kɑ̀že pɛ̀t’ə vər’àli vər’àli
to Tripoli, to show them the way. They walked, they walked –
34352: utòd’ət dv’à mumč’ètə ud ərɑ̀pit’ȅ bùlkətə v’èk ni mòž də vərì
and then two Arab boys came up. The wife wasn’t able to walk any more,
34357: pɑ̀nnəli ud glɑ̀t sedemdes’è d’èn’ə i č’e t’às mumč’ètə
they were fainting from hunger after 70 days. So these boys
34362: bìli s kulil’ètə z’èmət bùlkətə č’e vər’àli dràgu ni mòš
had bicycles. They took the wife, and because Drago couldn’t [walk either],
34367: č’e z’èli i n’ègu gi vòzili kudžà dvà trì kilum’ètrə gi vòzili
they took him too and drove them a long way, two or three kilometers,
34373: i gi zəv’èli u vujnìst’ȅ d’ètu vujnìci še gi vòd’ət və və vəz ərɑ̀pi̥tȅ
and took them to soldiers, soldiers who would then take them to the Arabs.
34376: i ni zəv’èdəə kɑ̀e tɑ̀m i vujnìst’ȅ kɑ̀e pu i səupštìə kɑ̀e
“And they took us there,” he said. “And the soldiers sent a message,” he said,
34380: dòjde kòlə ìnək tɛ̀rs’əd gi pək təkvìsə drùgi gi tɛ̀rs’ət
and a car came – they and several others had been looking for them.
34386: kəd gù vìd’ət kɑ̀e bɛ̀lgərin ubìvəd gu dòdəə kɑ̀e s kulìt’ȅ
“If they see [someone’s] Bulgarian, [bandits] will kill him,” he said. “Then they came with cars,
34390: z’èhə ni zəkɑ̀rəə ni kɑ̀e əm dɑ̀vət kɑ̀e dràgu
they took us and drove us and gave us [to eat],” said Drago.
34394: i jàden’e ìmət əm nə stòl səd’èvə əmə ɑ̀s kɑ̀e
“They had food there, but it was only canteen food, and I,” he said,
34398: dr’èh ne mògə də jàm i t’às rusnàkə i mumč’ètu
couldn’t eat [it].”  And [then] this Russian and another boy
34402: s vərtul’èt dušlì ud rusìjə i tìj ku n b’àha
came with a helicopter from Russia, and if it weren’t for them,
34408: ne mužàə ne mòž’eli də spəs’ɛ̀t mumč’ètətə nɑ̀št’ȅ rusnàkə gi spəsìl
they wouldn’t have been able to save our boys. The Russian saved them!
34414: i im z’èl ədr’èsə i šə duhɑ̀d’ə nə gòsti ud wɑ̀rnə
So they took his address [so that] he’ll come visit us in Varna.
34422: i ə i vərtul’ètət pùskə č’e si utòd’ət i hòp vərtul’ètə se zəpɑ̀lgə
Then the helicopter signalled that it was leaving, and without warning it took fire
34425: i izgur’àvət belòtit’ȅ i i mumč’ètu i m rusnàkə
and the pilots burned to death – both the [other] boy and the Russian.
34428: i nɑ̀s kɑ̀e pək ni pɑ̀z’ət ut ə drùgiətə
“But,” he said, "[the Russians] will still protect us from others [like this].
34430: huligɑ̀nt’ȅ kɑ̀e ìmə kət vìd’ət bɛ̀lgərin ubìvəd gu
There’s hooligans who will kill someone when they see he’s Bulgarian.
34431: Because,” he said, “that’s how they are.”
34432: i z’àha ni kolàta i gu ščùpiha kae v’èče tugɑ̀s t’ɑ̀h kolà xùbavit’ȅ̥
Then they took our cars and broke them,” he said, “these really nice cars.”
34450: Aren't there coals in the outdoor oven?
34454: ìmə ba tè gu o ometɤ̀t žərɔ̀n
There are, yes. [But] they [will have] swept out the coals.
34463: ìmə si i udèlnu səs rùo go nəkvàsət u
There's a special kind with cloth. They moisten it
34466: and sweep the ashes out [with it].
34474: mi kàk še go zamèsim še ogrèa vudɤ̀ta i še otsèa
Well, how do we make it?! I heat up [some] water, I sift out
34478: ami noštovì tòj si ftàsa v noštovìte pòsle vov
Yes, the kneading trough. It rises in the kneading trough, and then it –
34481: e tò e suruvàtka varì sa pa na izvàra
Oh, that’s whey. You boil it until it becomes curds.
34483: After that? Nothing! [laughter] After that they take it (= the bread) out.
34488: pòsle gu nəm'ɛ̀tət i č'ɛ̀kəd də sə ispeč'è
After that they throw it (= the bread) in and wait for it to bake.
34490: əmhəm i agà sə ispečè to mnògo xlèp kədè gu pàzexa
Mmhm. And when it's baked, that's a lot of bread! Where did they keep it?
34493: à ìmə si ud'ɛ̀lnu mɛ̀stu zə hlɛ̀bən
Ah. There's a separate place for the bread.
34497: əxə̀ udèlnu si m'àstu zə xlèbən i kədè e tò
Uh huh, a separate place for the bread. And where is that?
34500: kàk sə vìkə kàk sə vìkaše
What's it called? What did it used to be called?
34519: aha f klètən go pàzexte xl'àbən
Aha! You kept the bread in the pantry.
34525: əxə̀ i tàm ostàvaše mɛ̀k takà li
Umhm. And it stayed soft there, right?
34528: And there it didn't go moldy?
34530: It won't. It didn't go moldy.
34533: ə [cough]  tì si i oràl i kupàl nalì
[cough] You did plowing and digging, right?
34539: What – what did you plow with?
34547: uràlu səs dɤ̀rvenu i tugà pàlešnik mu uvr'ɔ̀t nə uràlunu
With a wooden plow. And they fix a plowshare into the plow,
34550: i urɔ̀t s vòlove səs mùl'etə
and they plow. With oxen, with mules.
34555: tùkə məšìni ne nemɛ̀še tò pɔ̀t nemɛ̀še nè mašìni də ìmə
There weren't any machines here. There wasn't [even] a road, much less machines.
34558: tè počtì si imɛ̀hə vòluve hòrətə
34565: à ta nèmaše m'àsto i za mašìnine
Ah! And so there was no place for machines either.
34569: ə č'e kədè še [laughter] tò məšìnə də vərì
And where would [they go]? [laughter] For machines [to be able] to move
34572: there need to be [good-sized] roads. Yes.
34574: a togàva səs kakvò se kàk se pridvìžvaxte
And back then, by what means – how did you move around?
34577: peš'ɛ̀ ottùv do plòvdif səm òdil peš’ɛ̀
On foot. I've been from here to Plovdiv on foot …
34584: də tuvàrime stòki nə məgəzinèrə tàm ot tàm gu kàrəhme
… to carry merchandise for the shopkeeper there. And we brought it back from there.
34585: nemɛ̀še tegà kàktu də hòd'ət i kulì tə tə to segà
Back then there wasn't [a way] to go with cars. But then
34589: stànə pɔ̀tes ut četìres i sèdmə gudìnə gu pòčnə tòu
there came a road. It was 'forty-seven when they began that [work],
34596: pò nəprèš' ut ut bàčkuu nəgòre tò beše tɛ̀sen pɔ̀te
Before that, from Bachkovo on up, the road was really narrow.
34604: vòl'cki kolì i nɛ̀kəde se fprɛ̀gə pu dvà pu dvà čiftə
and oxcarts, and sometimes they'd harness two, two pairs per [cart]
34610: nə nɛ̀kuj bəìr də hi də iskàrət kulànə vòlskə mùleštə li
to get the cart up some hill, whether it was an oxcart or a mule-cart.
34613: How many wheels did the carts have?
34619: səs kòlko kolelà b'àxa kulìte vòl'ɛ vòlskite i mùleštite
How many wheels did the carts have, the oxcarts and mule-carts?
34621: What do you mean, how many?
34625: kòlko kolel'èta ìmaxa imɛ̀xə kolìte dvè ili čètiri
How many wheels were there? On the carts? Two or four?
34626: pa pu ednà kulà imɛ̀hə hòrətə
Well, people [only] had one cart each.
34628: But these carts, how many wheels did they have?
34634: nəlì si vìdel tùkə e segà d'e sə
Haven't you seen any here? Here, where they're …
34640: sə kulì səs sɛ̀k kulelò əmə po səs ədnò mùle
… all with wheels. Each one has wheels! But only one mule each –
34642: though some of them have two.
34647: nəprèš n nemɛ̀še kulì tùkə pu s'èlusu segà imàt s sɛ̀ki
Earlier there weren't carts here in the village. Now they all have [them].
34652: mùl'i i kòl i kòlə si e kurdìsənə
Mules and carts, the carts all set up [and ready to go].
34655: a kogà bèše səbòra na repl'anà
And when was the [time of the traditional] village celebration of Replyana?
34659: sɤbòrɤt na repl'anà e na gerg'òvden əxə̀
The Replyana village celebration was on St. George's Day, yes.
34666: i si kòl'amo jàgɤnci i nòsimo u cṛ̀kvu jàgn'e
And we slaughter lambs, [but first] we take a lamb to the church,
34672: mùško jàgn'e koè ìma ròdzi zanesèmo ga cṛ̀kva tùka bèše
a male lamb that has horns [already]. We took it. There was a church here,
34676: onì g'u razvalìše tàm è tekvòj si ìmaše za jàgɤnci
[but] they tore it down. So that's how it used to be with the lambs.
34681: svèki si dṛžì jàgn'eto i pòp četì i na jàgn'eto na rògɤt
Each one held his lamb and the priest spoke, and on each lamb's horns
34687: there was a lighted candle. A candle was burning.
34692: əxə gorì i tekà zanesèmo jàgɤnciti dòm i tegàj zakòl'emo za večertà
Yes, burning. Then we took the lambs home and slaughtered them for the evening,
34695: za večertɤ̀ nә gerg'òvden bɤ̀š na šèsti šèsti bɤ̀š si e dɤ̀nɤt
for the evening of St. George's Day, the sixth [of May]. That's the exact day, the sixth.
34700: nə nә šèsti večertɤ̀ opečèmo jàgn'e edèmo i àjde na sèdmi
On the sixth in the evening we roast the lamb and eat it, and then on the seventh
34703: pòsle sɤbòr dòjdu ni drùgi drùgo jàgn'e drùgi kòl'amo jàgɤnci tegàj pòveče
is the celebration. People come over, we slaughter another lamb, lots more lambs.
34705: nò što ìma selà sìčki dòjdu ni na sɤbòr dòl'ni.lom od
And [people] from all the villages come to our celebration: from Dolni Lom,
34709: gòrni.lom tùka ot pṛtopòpinci ot blìskiti selà ni ìdvat
from Gorni Lom, from Protopopinsti – they come to us from all the nearby villages
34710: a kàk kakvì čàsti ìmə po ednò oràlo
And how – What parts are there on a plow?
34716: na zbòr mì pa ìdemo na n'ì n'ìm kadà e
for the celebration. And we go to them when it's time for theirs –
34722: dòln'i.lòm na tròica pètkovden u gòrn'i.lòm u čuprèn'u pa drùk
to Dolni Lom on Trinity, to Gorni Lom on Paraskeva, to Chuprenye on another [holiday].
34723: mì ìdemo pri n'i' a onì pri nàs
We go over to them, and they [come over] to us …
34734: axa axa è tekà smo odìli svè po zboròve
Aha, aha. Well, that’s how [it was]. We’d [always] be going to formal celebrations,
34737: and they would [always] come to us.
34740: a jàgneto u kvò go pečèš
And what did you use to roast the lamb in?
34748: pečèl' pèkli smo ga u tepsìje golemè ot lamarìnu nèmaše tɤvè
We would – we roasted it in a big pan of tin. There weren't the pans
34752: sɤ̀ga tavà è golemà pa ga prùžimo onò tepsìja ot lamarìna tepsìja
[they have] now, these big pans. So we stretch it out on a pan – a tin pan,
34757: pa svìena òbla ama pò golemà tepsìjata tùrimo gu u tepsìjutu
round, curved, a bigger pan. So we put it into the pan,
34761: pə nasìpemo vòdu tùrimo dṛ̀va i sə opečè pèčeno jàgn'e
pour water over it, put wood [on the fire], and it roasts: roast lamb –
34764: a nèma li takòvo zìdano vùrn'a nèma li m zìdano
But wasn't there this oven constructed outside, wasn't there some structure –
34767: a vùrn'a vùrn'a u pa tegàj u vùrn'utu ga tùrimo
Oh yes, [we light] the outdoor ovens, and then we put it into the oven
34775: pèčeno jàgne podròbicu si napràimo ot crèva dròp tùmbak
Roast lamb, [then] we make “podrobitsa”, with intestines, [diced] liver, tripe –
34779: ə ə napràimo podròbica lùk zelèni natùramo
34784: tòj štò strùkovete zelèni lùk pò ùbavo sәs zelèni
... those individual leeks. It's better with leeks.
34787: ìma na mestà ga pràe sɤs cṛvèni ama pò nè e ùbavo
In some places they make it with onions, but it's not as nice
34792: sɤs cṛvènijɤt lùk zelènijәt lùk i dušìčina zovèmo go dušìčina
with onions as it is with leeks and thyme. We call [that herb] thyme.
34794: Ah, it's around that time [of year] …
34799: dušìčina berè se tegàva mlàda za zbòra za gerg'òvden à
Thyme. You pick it then, young, in time for the St. George's day celebration. And –
34801: And what other [dishes do you put it] in?
34805: [What else] is it good to add wild thyme to?
34807: drùgo u kəkvò ja slàgaš dušìčinata
What else do you put wild thyme in …
34812: slàgam i u bòp tekà ama za u podròbicata
I also put it in beans, but [it's best] in “podrobitsa”.
34814: [That's] what we have [always] liked the best.
34819: i kàk ja poznàvaš kato vərvìš tùka iz baìrite
And how do you recognize it when you go out [to look for it] here in the hills?
34826: nò predstavl'àva màlko dòle do nìsko rastè ne rastè
Well, it looks like – it's little, low down. It doesn't grow ..
34865: nìsko rastè i i šùmicata mu òbla i poznàvamo g'u
It doesn't grow high. Its leaves are round and we recognize it.
34869: koè e dušìčina poznàvamo zbèremo dušìčina za zbòrɤt
We recognize which plant is thyme, and we gather it for the celebration.
34873: i pòsle si zakòl'amo jàgn'e pàk pṛ̀vi màj dòjde àjde
After that we slaughter a lamb, and then May Day comes. OK, [then],
34874: pà si zakòl'emo òvce si ìmašemo mlògo jàgɤnci
we'll slaughter again. We used to keep sheep [so we had] lots of lambs.
34875: no tegàj si za nàs a za zbòrɤt
But that was for us. As for the celebration –
34879: doòdәt li decàta segà za sɤbòra
Do [your] children come now for the celebration?
34883: doòdat mlògo abe doòdɤt ama pò se ìzmeni sɤ̀ga
Yes, often. Well – they come, but it's much more different now.
34887: nò mì kvò smo praìli no imà stàčka golemà za zbòrɤt
Ah, but [let me tell you] what we did! There was a big protest about the celebration.
34893: ot čuprèn'u dojdè edɤ̀n àngel bèše kmèt pa uvolnìše ni kmètɤt
This guy Angel came from Chuprenye, he was their mayor. And they fired our mayor,
34896: ne dàva da pràimo zbòr mì sàkamo da si ìma
and didn't allow us to put on our celebration. We wanted there to be
34900: zbòr repl'ànci praìli smo si zbòr i si obìčamo
a celebration. We of Replyana have [always] had our own celebration, and we like
34903: da si ni doòde čovèci da si ìdemo
to have people come to us, and for us to go to them,
34907: da se ne maìn'a tàa tradìcija dobrè ama onì dojdòše
[and we] don't [want] to abandon this tradition. OK. But these people came –
34910: i bèše ni è tùj gòre tàj kɤ̀šta sɤvètɤ onì dojdòše
and there was this house up there, our village council. So they came
34914: ot čuprèn'u sɤbràli se tekvìja kmetovè upràvnici da dòjdu
from Chuprenye, this group of mayors and bureaucrats got together to come
34919: da prepràe repl'enù da se odlòži zbòrɤt če mì nastojàvamo
and make Replyana different, to put off the celebration. We were insisting
34923: da si pràimo zbòr repl'enà a re a čuprènci
on having our celebration [here] in Replyana. But the Chuprenye people
34926: nèče da pràe zbòr onì pò ne obìču stòkutu
didn't want to put on a celebration. They don't like animals much,
34930: pò ne ubìču da čùvu òvce pò ne obìču gosjà
they don't like really like to keep sheep, and they don't like guests much.
34934: For them it's just the stomach …
34939: axà mì obìčamo živòtni da čùvamo òvce pa da ni doòde čovèci
Yes! But we love to tend animals, [especially] sheep, and to have people come over,
34942: pa da gim ìdemo obìčamo te tùj ràbutu običàli smo mlògo
and to go over to them. We like that sort of thing; we've [always] liked it.
34944: onì dojdòše tùj gòre mì po n'ì po n'ì òrl'ak
So these people came up there, and we went up after them, a [whole] flock [of us] –
34946: nò decà nò stàri nò mlàdi svìmo se pa pri n'ì
children, old people, young people, we swarmed up there around them
34948: pri sɤvètɤt onì se sɤbràli u sɤvètɤt
up by the council. They were gathered up at the council, and we –
34951: a mì sèdmi òsmi sèdmi òsmi sèdmi òsmi òkamo
we chanted “Seventh, eighth! Seventh, eighth! Seventh, eighth!”
34953: zbòrɤt da si pràimo da se ne odlàga
We wanted to put on our celebration, and not to abandon it, and [to do it]
34955: na sèdmi i na òsmi dvà dɤ̀na zbòr
on the seventh and the eighth, two days of celebration [in our traditional way].
34959: na šèsti se stègamo ta si večertù kòl'emo
On the sixth in the evening, we get ready, we slaughter [the animals],
34961: pa tegàj na sèdmi zbòr tùj òro ot svì selà naròt
and then on the seventh is the celebration: dancing and people from all villages around.
34963: pḷ̀no tùj sәs naròt pa tegàj àjde i na òsmi
It's packed with people here. And then we continue on the eighth –
34966: i na òsmi dvàta dɤ̀na mùzika i dvè nòč mùzika svìri
On the eighth [too]. Both days there's music, and both nights. Music playing
34968: dvà dɤ̀na pràimo zbòr a onì ne dàvu da pràimo zbòr
for two days. [That's how] we celebrate. But they didn't let us put on the celebration.
34969: mì sèdmi òsmi sèdmi òsmi svèki òka no pa àjde
So everybody's shouting, “Seventh, eighth! Seventh, eighth!” And then
34973: edɤ̀n i dzvònutu dṛ̀nnu čèkaj dzvònutu da l'òskamo
someone [came] and rang the church bells. So we thought, let's us ring the bells [too],
34979: da pìtamo gi štò su došlì tìja onì izlèzoše ot tàm
and ask these people why they have come. So they came out of there,
34981: ot ə sɤvètɤt mì po n'ì po n'ì po n'ì
out of the village council, and we went [swarming] after them,
34986: kòj sɤs dṛ̀vo kòj ovàk kìma kòj [laughter] da gi bìe
some with pieces of wood, some brandishing [them] like this, to beat them up,
34988: če sàkamo si zbòr ne ne ne sàkamo da si napùštimo zbòrɤt
because we wanted our celebration! We didn't want to give up our celebration.
34993: onì se sàl obràču sàl se obràču ot tàm odovàm
They just turned [away], they just turned this way and that,
34996: i i si otòše i ne dàdoše da pràimo zbòr
and went off without giving us permission to have our celebration.
34997: i kmètɤt ni tegàj ga uvolnìše uvolnìše ga štò òn sàka
And that's when they fired our mayor. They fired him because he wanted –
35000: mì naròdɤt sàka da prài zbòr i òn nastojàva
We the people wanted to have the celebration, and he stood firm [on that],
35003: da si pràimo zbòr onì ga tègaj uvolnìše ta turìše
that we should have the celebration. So they sacked him, and put in his place
35008: ednù ženù tekvàj s trèti klàs nìšto nè e bilà
this woman with a third-grade education, a real nobody.
35012: ama te tekà onà se nàvanu če pa drùk nèče se navàne
But she undertook it because nobody else wanted to do it.
35014: sàku da si pràimo zbòr nèče se navàne drùk
[Everyone here] wanted us to have the celebration, so nobody else would take on [the job].
35018: a tàj se nàvanu tà da mìne da mànu kmètɤt
But she took it on, to make things go their way, that the mayor would be fired.
35020: ta ga manùše kmètɤt uvolnìše ga
So they [the Chuprenye people] got rid of [our] mayor. They fired him,
35023: i tekà napraìmo mì manùmo zbòrɤt
and we had to do [it their way]: we abandoned the celebration.
35024: But there was a great deal of protest.
35028: è mnògo ti blagodarìm mnògo interèsni ràboti ni raskàza
Ah, we’re very grateful to you, you’ve told us many interesting things.
35032: If we’re alive and healthy – whatever we know …
35041: nìkoj ne mòže da kàže dèt ne gò znàe
Nobody can talk [about] things they don’t know.
35045: i kujòtu sme pàtili d’èt sə vìkə
… and what we’ve suffered through, as they say, …
35050: d’èt’ e preminàlu priz nàštu vrɛ̀me
35054: [That’s what] we [can] talk about. Unless, of course …
35059: xòdila li si n’àkɤde na drùgi mestà
Have you traveled around to any other places?
35062: ami ot prədì gudìni sme hòdili s’à dv’e trì gudìni
Well, a few years ago we went – it was two or three years [ago]
35065: when we got the little ones –
35074: v burgàs ž’itàruvu sme òd’eli s məž’ɤ̀ mi nə puč’ìfkə
[Then] my husband and I went on vacation to Burgas, to Zhitarovo,
35077: smòlenckijə kràj sme òd’eli tàm zlətugràt
[then] we went to the Smoljan region, to Zlatograd.
35084: tàmkə ìmme puznàti tàm hòrə nə svàd’b’i òd’ehme
There are people we know there, we were going to weddings.
35092: ə zə s’àvəne sə s’àvəm s’àvə sə izur’è sə nìvətə nəs’àvə sə
[For] sowing: we sow – You sow. [First] you plow up the field, [then] sow it [all].
35098: i tugàvə pàk sə puvlìč’ə i kotu stàn’e zə mʌ̀knət’e
And then you harrow it, and when it’s ready to harvest,
35106: tòə ž’èneš’e zə mumč’ɤ̀tu i dəšter’ɤ̀tə kət gi ž’èni
He was marrying off [both] his son and daughter, so [each time] when he married them
35108: tə òdihme dvà pɤ̀tə nə svàdbə
we went, [which means] two times to a wedding.
35110: ìnəč’e i nə gòsti sme si òdili
35119: tòj slùž’i tùk nə òrlinu d’èt je jəzuvìrə
He did his military service here in Orlino where there’s the dam,
35122: and [where there] was also a military air base, ...
35130: d’ènu̥ s’è mʌ̀kneme kujàtu je pò visòkə i səs kòsə jə kus’ə̟̀t
we harvest it like usual. We cut the taller [growth] with a scythe
35137: kujàtu je pò nìskə s rəc’è mʌ̀kni mʌ̀kni mɤ̀kni pràim ə̟
and the lower [growth] by hand. We harvest it [all], and put it
35144: nə kùpč’in’ki pòsl’e kləd’èm nə pò gul’àmi kòpi i tugà
into little piles. Later we put them into bigger stacks and then
35147: we thresh it again with horses,
35150: with a mule, or a donkey, or whatever is available.
35158: a n’è sɤgà z guv’ʌ̀də ne sɤ̀me ne sm’è vərš’ɛ̀li
Ah, no. We didn’t – we didn’t do threshing with cattle.
35160: nìe sme vərš’ɛ̀li s məgàre s mùl’e
We did our threshing with a donkey [or] with a mule,
35163: [or] with a horse. Not with cattle, no.
35164: [What was it you didn’t thresh with?]
35175: kətu jə udvìjem’ə vərìme si jə sìəm ə̟ səs rəš’ètu
After we winnowed them, we’d cook them. First we shake them through the sieve,
35178: pòsl’e si i tùrim vòdə f t’ènžurətə də ni vəzvərì
then we put them in water, in the pot, to boil [the first time],
35183: i tugàvə uplàvim s l’ʌ̀štətə i slàgəm’è jə də sə vərì
and then we rinse the lentils and put them to boil [the second time].
35188: nədrubìm i lùk kurmìt tùrim i òlivo i sə vərì vərì
We chop up onions and add them, also oil; and it boils and boils.
35190: č’i pòsle jə um’èsim pàk s màlku brəšnò
And then we thicken it with a little flour,
35198: bèše vujènen i tòj kətu vujnìk tùk iskàrə slùžbətə
He was in the military and did his military service here, ...
35202: i sə zəpuznàhə s mòjə i sə pubrətìhə
... [when] he got to know my [husband]. And they became sworn brothers –
35208: Ah, here [you have the custom of] blood brothers!
35212: i tò nə nàš’t’e svàdbi i n’è nə n’èguvite svàdbi
And he [comes] to our weddings, and we go to his weddings,
35216: i v’èč’e mlògu blìski i du d’èn’ dnèš’en sì sme təkà
and we [became] very close and to this very day we still are.
35219: jà jà da mi kàeš tovà tvà še bɤ̀e poslèdno
Come now and tell me about this last thing
35221: da zəpišem da mi kàžeš kogà kàk
so we can record it. Tell me how and when
35224: you become blood brothers – or blood sisters.
35229: uvəž’àvəš sə ubìč’əš sə ìməš sə s nèjə mnògu
You get to respect someone, like someone, get on well with her –
35232: You know, [it grows] out of friendship, ...
35236: blìsku prijàtelstvu i kàzvət pubrətèni sme
… close friendship, and they say “We’re sworn brothers”
35239: štòm sə mnògu ubìč’ət s nègu
since they love each other so much.
35242: dobrè pobratèn ə pràite li nèšto
O.K., sworn brothers – But do you do something,
35246: n’àkɤf običàj da ìmate da kàem
do you have some sort of custom, for instance, ...
35250: ... [to say] “From this day forth we are brothers” ?
35255: n’èmə ubič’ɛ̀j əmi tì kətu ž’èniš’ dərùvəš’ n’ègu
... there isn’t a [particular] custom. But it’s like a wedding, you give gifts to someone.
35270: tòj kətu už’èni n’èguvìte dərùvə t’èp
When he marries off his [children] he gifts you,
35275: kətu ìjš’ nə gòst’e zənàs’əš’ sì mu pu nɛ̀štu pudàrək
and when you go visiting [him] you bring him some sort of gift,
35278: tòj kətu dòjde i tòj pràzen ni ìdvə
and when he comes over, he doesn’t come empty-handed either.
35282: edìn nə drùk si sә̥ uvəž’àvəme i si pudnàs’əme kəkvò ìməm
We respect one another, and we bring each other what we have [to give].
35285: ut sìčku i əku ìskəš dr’èxi ìskəš nɛ̀štu pudàrəci ku ìskəš i
Anything – clothing if you want, some sort of gifts.
35290: ut.kɤ̀šti mu slòžiš nɛ̀štu zə jɛ̀dene udnisèš’
When he leaves your house you send food with him, and take some ...
35295: i tugàvə usulìm jə i [laughter]  jəd’ème nədrub’è [laughter]
and after that add salt, [laughter] and then eat it! With chunks of – [laughter]
35307: i nə təkà təvà vìkəme pubrət’àvəne
And that’s what we call sworn brotherhood.
35314: əmi pràvi se təkà vərìme si ml’àku̥tu pr’àsnu
Well, like this. We boil up fresh milk,
35317: ustàim gu màlku də puisc’ìne i pòsle gu putkvàsim
set it aside to cool a bit, and then add starter
35320: štòtu kətu ni tì e ròtᵊ fəf kətu ž’èniš’ dicà
Because – if he’s not related to you in – well, when you marry off your children
35325: səs màlku kìsəlu ml’əkò mu slòžim’e vəf ə rəzbìjeme gu
– a bit of yogurt. Then we put it in a – We beat it
35328: nəlì nə n’ègu dàr ni sɤ̀ pulàgə
you don’t gift someone [who’s not a blood relative], do you?
35333: i gu zəvìjeme vəf sədʌ̀t f kujètu gu kvàsim
and then wrap up the pot in which we will cause it to ferment.
35339: [Did you used to go out to do the harvesting?]
35344: əmi nə žʌ̀tvə òdin’e nìe segà se odùčihme ud žʌ̀tvə [laughter]
Well, we did go out to do harvesting, but now we’ve lost the habit of it! [laughter]
35346: [But in the old days did you go out?]
35351: ò ednò vr’ème òdehne i decà nòsehme nək nə l’ùl’k’e [laughter]
Oh [yes], we went in the old days, and carried children [with us], in cradles [laughter]
35355: nə gʌ̀rp i òdehme tə žʌ̀nehm’e zbìrəme snòp’ət’e
on our backs. And we would go, and do the reaping, and gather the sheaves.
35359: kəkvò də pràim i decà gl’ʌ̀dəme i s’àkəkvu sme pràili
What [else] could we do? We also had to take care of the kids. We did everything.
35366: nə velìgden sə hòdi f čʌ̀rkvə
You go to church on Easter [Sunday].
35373: ubikàl’ət ə kət’ ìdət tə ubikàl’ət čʌ̀rkvətə tàm ukulu ʌ
[People] circle around – when they go [there] they circle around the church –
35376: ə pə ìnəč’e kət sə mnògu ubìč’ət i təkvònət
But otherwise, when you love each other a lot and such –
35381: čʌ̀rkvətə sàmu ubikàl’ət tàm čùkət jəjcà
they only circle around the church. Then they crack eggs there:
35385: kət sə pubrət’èni idìn nə drùk sə dərùvəš’
When you’re sworn bothers, you give gifts to one another,
35388: i sə səbìrət kuìt sə utìšli f čʌ̀rkvə čùkət sə
[everyone] who’s gone to the church gets together and they crack
35391: i gu ìməš’ kətu svòj blìsək
and you hold [this person] as [someone very] close to you.
35395: tàm s əcàtə b’èl’əd gi ədʌ̀d gi [laughter] kəkvò də ti
eggs there, peel them, and eat them! [laughter] What can I –
35397: a mòže li decàta im da se žèn’ɤt slet tovà
And after this, can the children of  [two such people] marry?
35399: [Постите не продължават ли и на тоя ден?]
[Didn’t you keep on fasting on that day also?]
35406: əmì dutugàvə sə pòsti əmə tugà nə velìgden si jədʌ̀t v’èče
Well, you fast up till then, but on Easter you eat already.
35411: i m’ʌ̀su i jəcà i ml’əkò
35416: segà i bànici pràim’e jədʌ̀t sìčku
[Yes,] and now we make banitsa too. They eat everything [at that point].
35418: [На такива маси като тази ли ядяхте?]
[Did you eat at tables like these (you have now)?]
35423: əm tò pərəlìi ìməš’e drùgi pò n’ìski òbl’i
No, we had “paraliya” tables. They were different, round and lower down.
35426: i tàm si z nəs’àdəhme kətu pò màl’ki
We sat at those when we were smaller,
35430: nìe kətu̥ stànəhme v’èč’e ž’èneni nə màsi jəd’èm’ə
but when we grew up and married, we ate at [normal] tables.
35432: ə pək pò rànu nə pərəlìi əd’àhme i u bəštà mi
But earlier on we ate at the “paraliya” tables. At my father’s house
35436: bəhme mnògu xòrə tàm tàm ìməhə t’è s’èdem decà
there were a lot of us. They had seven children there,
35440: and all of us sat at the “paraliya” tables,
35444: nə stòl’četə kòj nə stòl’če kòj sə svìl nə kul’ànce
some on small chairs, some hunkered down on their knees,
35452: nə pərəl’ʌ̀tə i f ədnʌ̀ kùpə sme jàli vìkəme gu giv’èč
At the “paraliya” tables. And we ate out of the same bowl, we call it “gyuvech”.
35459: nəpɤ̀l’nim g’yv’èčən s kàš’e [laughter] səs l’èštə s fəsùl’ nədrubìm gu
We fill the “gyuvech” with gruel, [laughter] with lentils, with beans. We dip bread in it,
35460: and eat it. What [else] could we do? [laughter]
35472: ɛ̀ɛ vr’ème vərš’ìjehme pòveč’e vr’ème sə vərš’ìje kàrəme kòn’uven’e
[We needed] more time for threshing. When we thresh we drive the horses around,
35478: kàrəme d’ìgəm’e n’àkvi ìmə tə presìč’ət snòpi̥te
drive them, lift [up all the sheaves]. Some people would cut the sheaves ...
35485: səz bràdvə nə dnò dʌ̀rvu tə də sə pò kʌ̀si
... with an ax and a chopping block, to make them shorter,
35488: pò l’ʌ̀snu də sə vərš’ìje ə pək ìnəč’e kàktu si vərš’ìjeme
and easier to thresh. Otherwise, we would, while threshing
35494: drùgite ràbut’i tʌ̀j i rəštʌ̀t vəršìjeme
other things, also thresh the rye.
35496: [And how did you tie up the sheaves?]
35509: snòpine si ut snòpən ud ž’ʌ̀tvənə gi nəpràvime i tùrim gu
… the sheaves. We make them from a sheaf from the harvest, and put them
35515: nə zem’ʌ̀tə ž’ʌ̀neme ut ə rəkòl’kit’e i tùr’əme nə vʌ̀ženo
on the ground. We reap by handfuls and put them [in a bunch with] the cord
35518: stàne li pò gul’àmu vɤ̀ržeme pàk drùk si nəpràvim
and when [the bunch] gets bigger we tie [it off] and start another one,
35522: i təkà dukʌ̀t də si užʌ̀neme n’ìvətə
and so on until we have reaped [the whole] field.
35524: [And what did you do with the sheaves?]
35526: mi nəpràvim gi pàk də nə sʌ̀ mòkr’et
Well, we make them so that they don’t get wet,
35530: nə krɤ̀sci gi pràim àj tә̥kà tùk ədìn snòp
we make them in cruciform, like this. See, one sheaf here,
35532: tàm drùk tùj drùk i tùk odgòr’e drùk
another there, [yet] another here, and here up above another.
35535: təkà gi nəpràim pu šesnàese snòpə
We pile them like that [in bunches] of sixteen sheaves each.
35540: nə zem’àtə nə zem’àtə əmə pàk təkà tvà žìtutu
On the ground! On the ground, that’s where the grain is.
35544: ednò vərhu drùgu də sʌ̀ da ne sʌ̀ mòkri žìtu̥tu [laughter]
One on top of the other so that – so that the grain doesn’t get wet! [laughter]
35546: So tell me, tell me what –
35550: žìtutu kət sə nəmòkri i stànuvə s’ètn’e pò t’èklu pò t’èkl’enu
If the grain gets wet, then the [dough made from it] will get more – more soggy.
35554: gà gu nəlì segà bràšnu kətu z’ʌ̀meme tə gi um’èl’eme ž’ìtunu
When it – you know, when we take and grind the wheat [to make] flour,
35556: i nvà bràšnu stàn’e pò lòšu ne mòž’e də sə m’èli
the flour [from it] comes out worse. You can’t grind –
35558: də sə m’èsi xùbəvu də stàn’e xùbəf l’àp
that is, knead it properly, so as [to make it] become good bread.
35562: mi stànuvə č’il’ìk’ ədìn pʌ̀rs č’ilìk’ stànuvə [laughter]
Instead you get unbaked dough – a finger-length of unbaked dough! [laughter]
35564: That’s what we used to call it in the old days.
35566: [Как се преде и как се стриже овца?]
[How do you spin, and how do you shear sheep?]
35577: nə fùrkənə a pək zə strìž’en’e sp’ʌ̀vət ufc’èt’e
With a distaff. As for shearing, they hobble the sheep
35579: and then we begin to shear [them].
35584: də ne š’ɛ̀vət če ìnəč’e že gi pur’èž’em
So they don’t jerk about, otherwise you’ll cut them.
35589: kàktu si e l’ègnələ ufcʌ̀tə kàrəj kàrəj kàrəj s nòžicìne
Once the sheep is lying down then you go at it with the shears
35625: n’èmə də mu rəzreš’ìš’ də sə ž’èn’et
… would they be allowed to marry.
35632: nàšie tòj ut smòl’en ìskəš’è mi mòjtu tr’ɤ̀tutu
One of ours from Smoljan wanted [to marry] my third [daughter],
35638: à nàš’ijə vìkə n’è nè tòlku blìski sme prijàteli
But our [family head] said “No, no, our friendship is too close”, ...
35640: vìkə tvà n’èmə də stàne vìkə
... he said. “That can’t happen", he said.
35643: nì č’ìstu i pròstu sme vìkə bràt’ə s t’èp
“Simply and plainly, we are,” he said, “brothers with you.”
35645: [There] is already a blood relationship, yes.
35648: n’èmə si dàm dəšter’ɤ̀tə à mə š’ə mi jə dəd’èš
“I won’t give my daughter!”  – “Ah, [yes], you’ll give her to me!
35651: tә̥ š’ə mi jə dədèš’ e tvà e
You’ll give her to me, and that’s that.”
35654: People wanted [it to happen] a lot, but –
35658: po n’àkoi kràišta znàeš kàk stàvat pobràtimi
You know how they become blood brothers in some areas?
35678: ... and the other one will – he’ll –
35687: It happens that way here too.
35692: i mòjə svèkər təkà ə nəpràvil səs edìn tùkənə
My father-in-law did it that way with someone here …
35694: … when they were in the military.
35698: svekərɤ̀ mi tò təkà kàzvəš’e səs edìn ɤ̀ tùk
My father-in-law told me [that he’d done] that with someone here,
35702: nə mùt’etu tràmpuski z bubàjku mu
with the dad of Muteto Trampuski …
35707: i na mal’èn e tòs z bùbəl’a mu i nàš’ijə svèkər
… the grandfather of Malyen. And our father-in-law
35712: sɤ̀deš’e vìnəgi vìkə vàšte decà rəstɤ̀t
always laid down the law. He said: “Your children are growing up,
35717: i nə nə nə ònijə mòə vìkə pubràtim rəstɤ̀t d’əcà
and those –", he said, "My blood-brother’s children are growing up too.
35719: də ni sɤ̀ sə z’ɤ̀li vìkə
But they mustn’t marry,” he said.
35724: às iz gròbə š’ə və kɤ̀lnɤ əku sə z’ɤ̀mət
“I’ll curse you from my grave if they marry.
35728: nìj sme vìkə krɤ̀vni bràt’ə s krɤ̀f sə smɤ pubrətìli
We are,” he said, “blood brothers. We have sworn brotherhood by blood.”
35729: And that’s the way it is.
35734: i tè izràstuvət čuv’ɛ̀čni i mòjtə təjfɤ̀
And they grew up properly, that bunch of mine.
35739: i sì sə rəzbrà:me i s t’àh təkà sə dərùvəhme
And we came to an understanding, and exchanged gifts with them,
35744: kət puč’ìnə svekɤrɤ̀ mi ìdvəhà də gu vìd’et
and when my father-in-law died they came to see him, ...
35748: nìj òdihme də vìdim n’ègu nə pugrib’ènietu si òdihme
... and we went to see [the blood brother], and we went to the funeral [together].
35750: tvà ti unuvà ti uvəž’ɛ̀vət sə
[Blood brothers do] this and that [together]. They respect one another.
35754: Just as if relatives, exactly that.
35759: a a às sɤm po drùgi kràišta sɤm slùšal a dvàma
I’ve – I’ve heard in other areas that if two
35761: zastàvat i sɤs edìn pòjas gi u
come together [like this], they take a single belt and …
35766: ìmə gu i tvà kòj kàk ìskə
There’s that [custom] too, whoever wants to [do it] and however [he wants to].
35768: i gi opàšat i tè vèče tovà e
They put the belt around them and it’s a done thing.
35775: There is [that custom]. They respect one another.
35777: dobrè če se sètixme da pìtame
... it’s good that it occurred to us to ask [about this]!
35783: kòjtu sə nàč’i təkòvə tè sə pubrət’àvət n’è
So whoever does this, they are blood brothers. No, …
35787: ne mòdži də sə zìmət ne mògət də sə ž’èn’et pòveč’e
… they can’t get married any more [to anyone from the other’s family].
35789: da a ìmaše li takɤ̀f običàj ako ə ednà ženà
Yes. Well, and was there such a custom that if one woman
35792: ə kɤ̀rmi də ili zadòjva i drùgo detè
nursed, or gave first suck to another’s child –
35796: a tè tèzi dvè decà kakvì sa
So what relationship are these two children [to one another]?
35799: s’əstrì sə s’əs t’è sə kət s’əstrì
35809: ni mògət sə zɤ̀mɤt nɤ̀l’ s’à na d’èt’ ə [unintelligible]
They can’t marry. Wasn’t this the case with [unintelligible]?
35817: n’èguvətə dɤšter’ɤ̀ mòenə zifèjkə gu nəbizɛ̀vəš’e̥
35821: nəbizàvələ gu nə cvìk štòt nàštu d’ɛ̀te
She fed her with poor quality milk because our child
35825: was born two months early [so] she didn’t breast-feed her.
35831: udn’èli gu unuvà dɛ̀te də biz’ɛ̀e mòjtə dɤ̀šter’ə
So they took that child for my daughter to breast-feed.
35838: imɛ̀ saà dàr udn’èse də vìjš’ kəf ùbəf dàr udnèse nə
And then she brought a gift, you should see what a nice gift she brought to ...
35843: nə tvà nə zifèjkə òti bilà gu nəbizɛ̀vələ
... to Zifeyka, because [she]was [the one who]  had breast-fed the child –
35851: už’èni sə tvà mumìč’e i udnèse màjkətə udnèse dàr
And [when] the girl got married, her mother brought – she brought a gift
35855: nə mòjtə dɤ̀šter’ə də vìtte kɤ̀f ùbəv dàr
to my daughter, you should see what a lovely gift!
35862: tùka bi tr’àbalo da ne isɤ̀hvət
35866: tə kɤ̀rpə tə š’àpkə tə ənterìe nə z’èt’e
... and a headscarf, and a cap, and a coat for my son-in-law,
35868: òti e bilà nəbizàvələ nèjnətə dɤ̀šter’ə
[all] because she had breast-fed her daughter.
35874: nàštə sə rudì sidmàč’ence i ni mòdže də biz’èe
Ours was born a little preemie (at seven months), and couldn’t suckle.
35881: ùbuvù pə unuvà jèdrəčku d’ɛ̀t’e pə màjkətə n’ɛ̀štu n’èmələ ml’àku
O.K, and the other was a sturdy child but the mother didn’t have milk,
35884: i əkušèrkite gu pudnàs’ət i gu dàvət
so the midwives took the child and gave it ...
35894: i nəl’ s’à usp’àhə nəràstuhə si
And you see, they made it. They grew up [healthy],
35895: i sə uvəž’àvət kətu bràt i sestrà
and respect each other as brother and sister.
35900: i dərɤ̀ si mu dàde nə mòjtə dɤ̀šter’ə si̥ sə dərìhə
And she gave a gift to my daughter, and they gifted each other.
35903: səs takvònə i mòjtə dɤ̀šter’ə pàk kətu təkvònə
They did [all] this, and my daughter did the same
35907: and gifted that girl, and such.
35912: a vɤv goràta kakvò rabòtexte vìe tə
And what work did you do in the forest?
35915: sàmo mɤžète li nə xòdexa v  nə goràta na ràbota
Was it only the men who went to work up in the forest?
35921: ami məž’ète si rəbòtehə trùp’e si kàrəhə v ìndulə naprèš
Well, the men worked. Earlier on they carried [off] lumber to Yundula,
35936: i jɛ̀s pu zəles’àvəne sə òd’elə nɤ̀j mnògutu pu zəles’àvəne òdeh
I’ve [often] gone out doing such planting. I would go out for planting most of all.
35938: a pə zìmətə pa n’ɛ̀mə ràbutə zìmətə vɤ̀tre
But in the winter there wasn’t any work. In the winter [you stay] inside,
35945: dud’è puupr’əd’èš’ l’ənɤ̀ dud’è puutəč’èš’ dud’è si nəpràviš’ plàtnu
until you spin up all the flax, do all the weaving, make fabric
35949: nə decàtə pə gu b’ɛ̀liš’ nə rekàtə pa gu č’ùkəš s kòpəni
for the children, bleach it in the river, pound it with clubs,
35952: pə gu b’ɛ̀liš’ də stàne m’ɤ̀ku də sə iš’č’ìstə
and then bleach it till it’s soft, till it’s clean
35958: də sə təkòənə tugàv gu v’èč’ə isuš’ìš’ pà də də ubl’əč’èš’
and all that, then you dry it, so that – that you can dress …
35969: dumàšnu plàtnu lè s n’ègu sə zənimàvəme
Homemade fabric. You know?  That’s what we were busy with.
35977: znàči lenɤ̀ e stàval tùka ràždal se e
So flax grew here. It took root here.
35985: a segà vèče slàgate li nè
Do you still plant it? Or not?
35990: əmi sigà du sigà nəlì bəše drùgu vr’ɛ̀metu
Well now – up till now, you know, it was a different time.
35997: dəržàvnu i s’à uts’à nətàtək pə nèkə gu rəzrəbòt’et uttùk nətàtək
[Things were] state-owned. And now – from now on [someone should] develop it for the future.
36002: š’i pòčnət nɛ̀kuj pà də sejɤ̀t
Some people will [certainly] start to sow it again.
36003: dà a vɤ̀lnata kàk ja rabòtite vìe
Yes. And wool – how do you process that?
36010: Well, you know, you take it to the cauldron, to …
36016: nə kurìtutu tàmkənə nə piràlnətə i pupàriš’ jə
… to the trough there, to the washing place and you steam it.
36021: pu jnò rùnu ud inà ufcà
One fleece at a time, from a single sheep.
36023: Ah, and why do you steam it?
36027: idìn č’uvàl də vrì f kəzànə s’ərɤ̀tə də izlez’è
[We put] a sack [of wool] to boil in the cauldron to get rid of the “sera”
36034: məzninɤ̀tə də izləz’è serɤ̀tə nə vɤ̀lnətə pupàriš’ jə təkòənə
The grease. You steam the wool like that so the “sera”  (grease) will come out,
36039: sl’èt tvà jə fɤ̀rl’əš’ f stud’ènutu kurìtu pà
After that you throw it into the cold trough again …
36044: ... so it gets all washed through again.
36049: sl’ət tvà slàgəš’ pàg drùgu rùnu ud ufcɤ̀ f kəzànə
And after that you put another fleece from [another] sheep into the cauldron.
36056: mə ìməž d’èset mə ìməž dvàjsi runà vɤ̀lnə i sìč’ki
Whether ten or twenty fleeces of wool, they all
36060: idnìč’ku pu idnìč’ku š’ə gi prikàrəš’ v gur’ɤ̀štətə vòdə f kəzànə
get done one by one. You process them [all] in hot water,
36063: i sl’ət tvà v’èč’ə f stud’ènətə vòdə š’ə gi pir’èš’
and after that you wash them in cold water
36074: zə buedìsvənetu si zìmme bujɤ̀ ut cìgənkìte i limòntuzù si zìməme
For the dyeing you get dyes from gypsy women, and we [also] get lemon salt.
36077: pàk si slòž’iš’ kəzànə tùk nə dvòrə i si gi buedìsəš’
Again you set the cauldron up here in the yard, and you dye them.
36081: [You dye] the yarn [to be] whatever [color] you want.
36084: Ah, it’s the yarn that you dye.
36091: pr’èž’dətə buedìsvəme zel’ènə li s’ìnə li č’ərv’ènə li urànževà li
It’s the yarn we dye. Green, or blue, or red, or orange, whatever [you want].
36096: kvàtu ìskəš’ pr’èž’də slàgəš’ kəzànə buedìsvəš
Whatever [color] of yarn you want, you fix up the cauldron [again] and dye it.
36100: buedìsəš’ ednàtə màhneš’ jə buedìsəš’ drùgə pàk buedìsvəmè si
You dye one, take it out, dye the next, and [that’s how] we do the dyeing.
36103: And they used to dye with “kamenyok” (lichen), too.
36109: i kətu vəlì vrɛ̀metu pàk ìdim nəbirème kəmen’òk ut kàmənete
And when the weather is rainy we go out and gather “kamenyok” from rocks.
36116: ut kàmənite sɤ̀štu kətu sl’às təkòə
It’s the same as mallow [grass], [but taken] off of rocks.
36123: ìmə n’ɛ̀š’tu kətu kurìč’kə təkà vəs kàməkə
It’s sort of like a crust on top of the rock,
36127: Ah! That [thing you find] on rocks! So –
36132: a nə n’ègu kəmen’òk òti ut kàmək
[We call] it “kamenyok” because it comes from a rock (“kamŭk”).
36138: emi təkɤ̀f kətu sìf n’ɛ̀š’tu è kətu pəntəlònə
Well, sort of gray. Ah, here, like [your] trousers.
36142: màlku f sìvu təkɤ̀f e cvetɤ̀
A little grayish. That sort of color, gray.
36149: We pick the lichen. We pick it …
36156: izvərìme gu n’ègu vəf kəzànə izvərìme izvàdiš’ n’ègu màhniš’
… and boil it up in the cauldron. We boil it, take it out, get it out,
36160: slòž’iš’ pr’èž’dətə slòž’iš’ i kəmen’òkə vərhù òš
put in the yarn, and put the lichen [back in] on top of that …
36163: … and you keep it [there for a while] –
36173: ut jelhà pàk š’ə nəbir’èš’ kurà pàk səs jelhà kurà pà buedìsvəme
You pick bark off a fir tree. [Yes,] we also dye [things] with fir bark.
36184: ìmə tàm puslèstvutu mi e də ə ìmə
There’s [some] over there, my sense is that there is some,
36187: mə ne znàm kəd’è e vèč’e
but I don’t know where it is any more.
36189: So women did their own dyeing here.
36190: Oho, did they do the dyeing!
36193: ne ne dàvaxa na drùgi mestà da im se bojadìsva
They didn’t – they didn’t take it other places to have it dyed for them.
36195: No, there was no such thing then.
36199: na drùgi selà otnàs’at po bujadžìjnici
In other villages they take [things] out to the dye-works.
36203: n’ɛ̀məš’e tugàf nìkədè kədè  də buedìsvəš’ mɤ̀ i s’à si buedìsvəme
At that time there wasn’t anywhere to [take things] to dye. Even now we dye our own.
36206: i kugàt si ti dòjde i kugàt si ìməš’ vr’ɛ̀me
And when you feel like it, and when you have time,
36207: you’ll still do your own dyeing.
36213: kəd’è də ìdiš’ nə inò vrɛ̀me nɛ̀mə kəd’è n’èmə kəd’è də ìdiš’
Where are you going to go? In the old days there wasn’t anywhere to go.
36218: kòj də ti buedìsə i utkəd’è àš’kele minàvəhə təkà buedž’ìi
Who would dye for you, and where? Fortunately some dyers would pass by.
36224: cìgənki drùgi tr’èti tə nəzìmiš’ bujɤ̀ tə si buedìsvəš’
Gypsy women, other [groups], a third [group], you’d get dye [from them], you do the dyeing
36227: tə si nəpràiš’ nɛ̀š’tu də si ìma də se ubl’əč’èš’
and make something so you’ve got [clothes] to wear.
36235: dumàš’ni ɛ̀bi si pràvehme č’ɤ̀rnite vɤ̀lni si pà
We’d make “aba” (coarse homespun). Yes, [it’s] from the black wool
36240: pràvena əbɤ̀ dumàš’nə zə məž’ètu pəntəlòne
[that] coarse homespun is made, and [from that], trousers for the men.
36252: n’ɛ̀məš’e də kùpə ud məgəzìnə udd’è š’ə nəm’ɛ̀r’ə n’èmə utkəd’è
I wouldn’t buy [any] from the store. Where would I find it? Nowhere!
36257: č’i st’ɤ̀gəj sə pà pr’èdi nə rudànə tɤ̀nku pr’èdi
You’d get yourself in gear, spin it fine on the spinning wheel, spin it,
36262: l’ɛ̀ti pà pupàriš’ səs brəš’nò əbɤ̀tə də ni sɤ̀ kɤ̀sә̥
glue it – steam it again with flour so the homespun won’t tear.
36268: tvà nə sɛ̀ki r’ɤ̀t pu ednà stìskə brəš’nò urɤ̀ž’enu brəš’nò
On each layer [you put] a handful of flour – rye flour,
36272: ud rəštɤ̀ zəbɤ̀rkəš’ kətu pàrenìcə zəbɤ̀rkəš’ zəbɤ̀rkəš’
made from rye. You stir it up like porridge, you stir and stir,
36276: i gu sìpiš’ fəf vudɤ̀tə i nətupìš’ pr’èž’dite
and then pour it into the water. And [then] you put the yarn to soak…
36280: màlku də ftvərdì i slet tvà gu slàgəš’ n’ègu zə usnòvə
… so that it gets a little stiff. And then you put it on the warp
36284: ə drùgutu pək təč’èš’ zə vɤ̀tək
and the other [= non-stiffened yarn] you weave as the woof.
36292: pu č’itìrəsi pu pedes’è m’ètrə səm istkàvələ dumàšnə həbɤ̀ č’ɤ̀rnə
[In my time] I would weave forty or fifty meters of coarse black homespun at a time.
36302: [All] our men’s trousers [were] made out of it.
36303: Well, what [else] are you going to do?
36307: tugàf tràmpite sàmu tùk enì òrə ìməš’e ednòvrɛ̀meš’ni š’ivàč’i
At that time only the Tramp folk here – there were the old-fashioned "shivachi" (tailors) –
36314: əhə̀ terzìjətə tràmpuski tàm òdeə də gi š’ìjət
Right, the "terzija" Tramposki. People went there to have [trousers] sewn.
36318: à mɤ̀č’ehmè sə mlògu nə vrɛ̀metu mlògu
Ah, we suffered a lot in the old days. A lot.
36321: ama sìčko ste moglì da pràvite
But you were able to do everything [for yourselves].
36323: à mòdž’in i s’à mi s’à də mì sə uddədè
Yes, we can. And even now I – even now if the occasion came up,
36331: sìč’kite ùredi si sid’ɤ̀t sìč’ku sì ti s’ədì
All those instruments sit there, they’re all there for you,
36337: vrɛ̀metu kàrə kəkvò də pràviš’ də ti kàž’ə
The times push [you].  I tell you, what can you do?
36341: kàrə səmòtu vrɛ̀me si tə òdə
Time itself pushes you: it leads you [forward].
36348: dobrè abɤ̀tɤ ne e na val’àvica nə nòsix
So. And didn’t – didn’t you take the homespun to the “valyavitsa” (fuller)?
36360: tupàvicә̥ nà segà tàmkənà jə istùpvət i
Down to the "tupavitsa" (fuller). That’s where they also full
