36365: dumàš’ni turbì si təč’ème č’ɛ̀nti dumàš’ni vɤ̀l’neni pàk
homemade bags. We weave smaller homemade bags, also woolen.
36380: b’ɛ̀lu i č’ɤ̀rnu kvàt ti ujdìsə
Black and white, whichever suits you.
36383: And there were those colors too.
36394: i istəč’èš’ si əbìte b’àlətə č’ɤ̀rnətə turbìte
And you weave up black and white coarse homespun [for] bags,
36397: àjde i nə duspàt s kònə šə gi zəkàrəš’ tàm
and then it’s off to Dospat. You take them down there on horseback
36401: də gi istùpət də gi istùpət də gi is upràv’et
for them to full them, for them to –  do them up,
36404: i si gi zìməš’ pàk nəzàt’
and then you take them back again …
36411: They dry them up nicely so you can –
36417: ə č’i tugàf tùf dunesɤ̀t pà gi isp’ɤ̀niš sɤz bùkuvu dɤ̀rvu
And then you bring them here and stretch them out on oak beams.
36424: zəkòpč’iž’ gi nis teràsətə nədòl ili nis kɤ̀štətə kəd’è dòjde
You hang them up along the balcony or down the side of the house – wherever comes first …
36429: … and you stretch them out [with] weights –
36432: So the coarse homespun will stretch out ...
36437: s t’èž’es də mòdž’e də hlɤ̀tne əbɤ̀tə
With weights so the homespun will sag ...
36441: də stàne tɤ̀nkə də stàne isp’ɤ̀nətə
... and get thin, so it will stretch out
36446: də də mòdž’e də š’ìe š’ivàč’ə pò hùbəvu
so that the tailor can sew it better,
36447: tò də mu sə š’ìe ùbəve
so it can be sewn up nicely,
36453: inàče stàvə rɤ̀b’əstə stàvə nə gɤ̀nki
Otherwise it’ll be rough-edged, all wrinkled.
36457: a təkà plɤ̀tnu isp’ɤ̀nətə glàtič’kə stàne təkà
But this way it gets to be fully stretched out and smooth.
36464: eno vrɛ̀me n’èməš’e ytìi s kvò də se glàt’et
In the old days there weren’t irons or [anything] you could iron with.
36468: pəntəlònə dəlì e umàč’kət dəlì n’è š’ə nəgàdiš
Whether or not trousers got wrinkled, you’ll deal with it
36472: Hey you! That’s too much noise!
36481: ta də nìe be spr’àxme n’àkəde dokɤm ivànovden
We stopped somewhere around St. John’s day.
36485: àjde màlko da prodɤlžìm da də se potsètite də drùgite pàmetnici
Let’s continue a bit to [see if] you can recall other monuments ...
36490: e tovà pràznici à kakvì pò natàtɤk slèt ivànovden pràznici ìma
... I mean, holidays. Huh? What holidays come after that, after St. John’s day?
36493: Well, St. John’s day, Midwives day –
36496: è bàbinden tòj màj na vrèmeto ne stè go praznùvali tòj
Ah, you probably didn’t celebrate Midwives day in olden times. It ...
36506: nè tòj po modèren pràznik stàna da da a na làzar tùka
No, that’s become a modern holiday. Yes [it has]. But on Lazar – here –
36510: xòdexa li mu na vrèmeto momìčeta
Did [unmarried] girls go out on that occasion in the old days?
36520: kakvì mu ku koì momìčeta do kojà vɤ̀zras momìčeta
Which kind of girls? Which girls? Girls up to what age?
36524: ami učenìci dokɤd’à desetìna dvanàese godìni
Well, schoolgirls. Up to ten or twelve years old.
36527: amì razrɛ̀š' a na šès parčèta ednàš takà na puluvìnata i
Well, you cut [the pig] into six pieces, once like this in half, and
36531: takìva momìčeta sɤbìrat sə pèt momìčeta ednò za kumà
Such girls. Five girls get together and one [more] as “godmother”.
36536: sètne gu takà na trìš' na šès parčèta alì e golɛ̀mu prasètu
then [you cut] it like this into three – into six pieces if it's a big pig,
36542: f kàcatà se nasòli i več'e: takà ostàne f kàcatḁ
You salt it in the [brine] barrel, and it stays in the barrel
36547: ... they’d [go out] two by two and sing.
36552: pèa làzarɤ zèmat kòšnika sɤs ejcà kato ìdat
They sing Lazar-songs, they take a basket with eggs [in it] as they go along …
36557: da pèat dòdat u nàs pèatᵊ si ako ìməm icè
… singing. They come to our house, they sing. If I have an egg,
36563: koè mi e pò svòe še mu dàm pa i
Whoever is the closest [relation] to me, I’ll give her
36568: drùgo n’àšto grìvna bilò prɤ̀sten bilò
something else, maybe a bracelet, maybe a ring –
36574: ə kòj nè e sàmo icètu im tùrnə f kòšnika
For the ones who aren’t [close relations] I’ll just put an egg in the basket, ...
36579: tìa kəd gi sɤberɤ̀t si gi delɤ̀t pòsle
... and afterwards they’ll gather up [all the eggs] and divide them [among themselves].
36584: i kat na velìden tovà e na vrɤ̀bnica i
And on Easter – that was for Palm Sunday –
36592: na velìden  ˀotìvat na derèto nòsat buàlkata okɤ̀pat a
On Easter they go to the river, they take the laundry paddle and bathe it.
36600: alì e malènku ìnače trì mòže [laughter] i na se nasòluva
but if it's a small [one] then three will suffice. [laughter] And then you salt it.
36607: càla zìma ta proletà e izvàdime
all winter, and we take it out in the spring.
36609: … “godmother” of the “lazarki” (girls that sing in procession on St. Lazar’s day).
36612: na làzarkite ìdat na derèto dèk ne presɤ̀:va derèto
… with the “lazarki”. They go to the river, to a place where it never dries up,
36615: sà e f ìzbatə̥ f ìzbatà e sà ta e ednà e
Now it's in the cellar. It [stays] in the cellar now, until it's more or less
36618: okɤ̀pat buàlkat tàm dèt še bùame drèite è
they bathe the laundry paddle in the place where we launder the clothes –
36625: ispèčena isùšena sɛ̀m ùbo a prez zimàta du màrta
done and dried, really nice. So [it's there] all winter, until March.
36630: i f màrta daže na kràjɤ na màrt se izvàžda
And in March – at the end of March, in fact – you take it out
36633: si vìkame da ja fàne màrtenskìa vɛ̀ter
so it can, as we say, get a whiff of the March wind –
36640: ta [laughter] jà vìkam če uš ne mò vi kažùvam nìšču pa
Hah! [laughter] Here I thought I wasn't going to be able to tell you anything,
36644: na onovà dɤrvò mu kàzvame buxàlka i sa vrɤ̀štat
That piece of wood, we call it a laundry paddle – and [then] they come back.
36650: but I [managed to] tell you something after all.
36655: ìdat u kumàta u tèjnia dvòr tìa sčukàle bulgùr
They go to yard of the “godmother’s” house; they’ve already processed the bulgur.
36662: vìž kòlko interèsni ùbavi rabòti ni kažà
Just look at all these nice interesting things you told us!
36669: si i tùka si kòleme kòleme prasète nìe sè
it’s like that here. We slaughter – we slaughter all our [own] pigs.
36673: če a tàm varìm na svàdbata čùkat a zgòtvat a
… how we cook that for weddings – they process it and cook it up
36677: na màndža i na kàša mu vìka:me
as food, into what we used to call “kasha”.
36681: aa əm takòva bɛ̀š'e stàru vrɛ̀me i sà
Well yes! So – that's how it was in the old days. Now too,
36686: š ìem na kàša i še ni pokànɤtᵊ
And we go “for kasha”, and they’ll invite us, our parents, close [friends],
36691: jà sà ne kòla vèč'e ot sì sam uddɛ̀lnu ta decàta
I don't do it any more myself now because now I'm alone, but the children
36693: and we [will go with] our parents, close [friends], ...
36698: kòlaa tìa mi dàvaa jà nèam ama ga
do, and they give me [meat]. I don't have any [of my own]. But when
36703: bèše mažò mi žìf kòle:me i golɛ̀mi prasèta ta pu dvɛ̀
my husband was alive we'd slaughter big pigs, two at a time.
36705: dàvaj dàvaj t'à še si kàže
Go ahead, yes. She'll talk [easily] about that.
36712: i tavà ni e nàj temelìjata xranà slanìnata i mastà svìncka
And that is our most basic food: pig fat and lard – rendered pig fat.
36715: i še d ìdem tàm še gostùvame
... and we’ll go there, we’ll go visiting,
36717: That's the most nourishing food of all.
36721: še ni s polòžat si trapèza takà
and they’ll lay out for us a festive table, and such.
36724: mòe sìn tòo šo è dòlu
My son – the one that’s down [in the city] –
36725: tovà sè u kumàta stàva mm
And all that happens at the “godmother’s” house, yes?
36730: u kumàta tàa ka na baštàta
At the “godmother’s”, she – at the house of the “godmother’s” father.
36735: aga bɛše studènt ta ležà nɛ̀štu fnògu lòšu bɛ̀še bòlen fnògu
when he was a student, he was very sick with something. He was very ill.
36740: nɛ̀štu apandesìt naednàž go zabolɛ̀ ta stanà na peretonìt
Something like appendicitis. He fell ill all at once, and it went to peritonitis,
36745: ta se puknàl apandesìtu tə utvòrena rànata tə bɛ̀še takà
the appendix burst, [there was] this open wound, and such.
36748: a pa ìskḁše ìmaše da ùči òšč'e̥ ìskaše da ùči
But he wanted – his studies weren’t done, and he wanted to continue,
36751: pa e bòlen pa jà mu vìkam dž'òre bre dž'òre gu vìkame
But he was sick, and I said to him, “Dzhoro my boy,” – we called him Dzhoro –
36754: They set out the festive table, ...
36755: At the father of the godmother.
36760: nas’àdame ednì ottùk ednì ottùk nasìpat ni kàša
... we take our seats, some here, some there; they dish out kasha for us,
36763: ob’àdvame i zanesèm èjca tə tùrnem tàm
we eat a meal, we take eggs, and put them there
36766: on the table for the main Lazar-singer.
36771: dobrè tàzi godìna ednò momìče e kumà drùgata godìna
Fine. So this year one girl is “godmother”. [What about] the next year?
36781: takà a ako ìma mnògo gol’àma sùša ìmaše li
O.K. Now if there’s a very great drought, was there
36783: some sort of custom to – for [making it] rain?
36785: ami ìmaše obicàj če fàne d’àdo pòp pràvi molèbie
There was [such] a custom. “Grandpa” priest says [special] prayers –
36786: He goes out into the open field –
36789: nìvata i sə xòrata koìto vèče mògat da ìdat
– the [cultivated] fields – with people; those who can go,
36796: nemòj učì pa pò le è skàpu uč'èn'etu ut ә zdràvetu
"Don’t go on studying. Is studying really more valuable than health?
36805: nèka pòčini enà gudìna tòj rèče nè ne pučìvam
[You should] take a year to rest.” [But] he said, “No. I'm not going to rest.
36810: ta pa mi re rèkua takà sàmu ut svìncka màs
Instead, I've heard it said that all [I need] is some rendered pig fat
36813: da màža na felìa svìncka màs
to spread on slices [of bread]. Rendered pig fat (lard).”
36818: ta mu pràš'č'ajme f sòfia ùč'eš'e̥ pràš'č'ejmè mu
And so we sent him – to Sofia [where] he was studying – we sent him –
36826: bɛ̀jme zaklàli dvɛ̀ prasèta pa f kutìi mu pràš'č'ejme svìncka màs
we'd slaughtered two pigs, so we sent him containers of of lard
36832: ta tàm da si màže za zakùska i gà mu se priedè sè
so he could have it there for breakfast, and for whenever he felt like eating it.
36841: tə mu bɛ̀še vikàl dòktoro kàž'i vìka ut š'čò sè si upravìl
And the doctor kept asking him, “Tell [me],” he said, “What [made] you get well
36845: tòlkua bɤ̀rže tòj rèkal mi ut mi ut svìncka màs
so fast?” And he said. “Well, it was lard.
36848: mi tovà e vìka nàj sìlnata xranà
And that,” he said, “is the most powerful food of all.”
36855: Tell us how you used to celebrate Christmas.
36864: emì sà jàko ne jà sa praznuvàli [laughter]
Well, now, people didn't celebrate it a whole lot [laughter] –
36869: tàa vlàs amà pà de praznuvàlo sè e
this government [you know]. But still, it was celebrated.
36871: It was celebrated. [Of course] it was celebrated.
36876: rabòtte sì se e rabotìlu ama pà si sè e praznuvàlu
You go to work; people went to work, but they still celebrated.
36883: emì napràvea na kùpea maž'ètu mèsu naprài se zgòtvi se
So people made – men bought meat, we'd make – we'd cook
36888: jaxnìjə ә sùpa kapamà na pɤ̀rvu mɛ̀stu e kapamà
casseroles, or soup, or stew. At the top of the list was stew.
36894: na kòleda i na velìgden sɛ̀gda s'a napràve kapamà
At Christmas and at Easter people always make the stew.
36899: kapamà kat gu napràime i i drùgo vèč'e jaxnìja sùpa i
When we make the stew [there’s] also other [things] – casserole, soup, and
36905: i mezètta ut kapamàta i vìnu i rɤč'ìja è takà
and appetizers alongside the stew. And wine, and brandy, and all that.
36909: za tɤkàne i takìva ràboti dalì e tɤkàla i vɤ̀lnata
[Ask her] about weaving and such things – did she weave, [about] wool –
36914: tì razbòj ìmaš le tkàla lè si
Do you have a loom? Have you done any weaving?
36918: Yes, I have [one]. And yes, I used to weave.
36924: ràskaži za tvà kakvì čèrg'i č'ète tùka pu bàncko
Tell [me] about that. What kinds of rugs do you weave here in Bansko?
36928: emì vɤ̀rime i si kùpime vɤ̀na
Well, we go [to the store] and buy some wool –
36932: Shall I tell you about [weaving] tasseled blankets?
36937: resnàčị sam tkàla fnògu i č'èrž'i sam tkàla
I've woven a lot of tasseled blankets, and I've also woven rugs,
36941: i tìa dìpla šò e pòslano sìčku sam jà tkàla
and these mats that are spread out everywhere. I've woven everything.
36948: ә tùrime kùpime usnòva usnòva za č'èrg'ite kupùvame čelèta
So we put – we buy the warp, the warp for rugs. We buy skeins,
36953: cɤ̀rni čelèta o òsnuvà gu nàvià gu vdɛ̀nemè gu
black skeins. I make the warp, I wind it all around and thread it
36960: f nìš'tel'k'i v bɤ̀rdu òpna razbòe tùra
through the heddle onto the reed comb, stretch it out on the loom, and
36966: z prìvɤrzà gu lùpam lùpam i mɛ̀tam i sufàlč'ata tkàa
and tie it down tight. Then I bang, bang, throw the shuttle, and weave.
36973: nàtkaa mɛ̀ra kòlku ìskam da e dɤ̀lgu kòlku da e širòku
I finish weaving, I measure how long and how wide I want it to be, and
36978: tòlkuà gu nàsnuva i se tčè a pa resnàč'ite
I make the warp just that size. And you weave. As for the tasseled blankets,
36985: kùpme vɤ̀na isperèm a uvlàč'ime ja a predème
we buy the wool, we wash it, we card it – and [then] spin,
36991: tòpime mò mòtame ja na mutuvìlka da se ìspne
put it to soak, and wind it up on the yarn-crutch so it's stretched tight,
36996: tòpime mutuvìlkata da se ne nasùgruva ga svàl'ime pàsmutu
then we soak the entire winding frame so it won't tangle when we take off a tuft.
37002: i pòsle sùč'eme na rudàne usnuvème navìeme vdɛ̀neme
Then we twist it on the spinning wheel. We warp [it], wind [it], thread [it],
37008: tùrame na razbòe amà po rèsi̥te debèlutu vèč'e se fmɛ̀ta sus sufàl'č'a
and put [it] on the loom. For tassels – you weave the thicker [warp] with the shuttle,
37014: a pa rèsi presùkanu pò tànečku prèdenu ta e òdve
but [the wool] for the tassels is more thinly spun and twisted double,
37020: ta gò sme presukàle i nègu gu fmɛ̀tame takà na sufàl'kata
[that’s how] we’ve twisted it. Then we throw it with a shuttle
37025: na ednò lòš'č'e na ednà tɛ̀ga takà vàlesta tòledžèva mɛ̀tam
[that’s like] a little twig, a stick that's round, just like this. I throw –
37029: sus vàdička e tavà lòš'č'e ta mɛ̀tamè ta jà gu izvàždam
it's with a hook, that little stick  So we throw it, then pull it out, then
37033: tùa si mɛ̀tam izvàždam mɛ̀tam mɛ̀tam mɛ̀tam du kràj
throw it again, then pull it out, then throw, throw, throw – up to the end.
37039: ta vèče rèka takà pa prètka ta slòža rɤ̀bna
And finally I weave it through, put it [in place], cut it [to be a tassel]
37047: pòveda lòš'č'etu sètne pà takà i stàne resnàč'
and pull the small twig through. And it’s become a tasseled blanket!
37051: stàne na dìpla pòsle gu sŭšìeme na ә trì dìpla
[And when] it becomes mats, we then sew them together – out of three mats
37056: we put together a tasseled blanket. And that's how it happens.
37059: ә i takà gu pustìlate napràvu
And do you put it [in] that form onto a bed right off?
37063: štè gu rabòtite slèt tavà resnàče
What [sorts of things] do you do with the blanket after that?
37067: emi ne è nòsuvàme gu na valɛ̀vica da se svàle
No, it’s not [done yet]. We take it to the fulling mill to be fulled.
37070: Because straight off from the loom like that –
37075: emì ne stè le viždàli tùka v bàncku valɛ̀vica
Ah, haven’t you seen the fulling mill here in Bansko?
37080: nìe òdim da perèm na valɛ̀vica pu̥stèlite
We go [down] to the fulling mill to wash bedspreads [and such].
37083: ìma takà pu kràj ìmame rɛ̀ka ta ud rekàta
Down at the edge [of the village] we have a river and [that’s where] they’ve
37087: sa napraìli takà è kòlko tàa odajà
made a [place] about as big as this room here,
37095: ìnače ud razbòe takà pòsle da e [interference]
Otherwise, if you [take it straight] off the loom, then later it’s [interference]]
37101: i rèsite stàna: pò ùbavi i pò e tràjno agà se svàla:
and the tassels come out nicer – they last much longer when they’re fulled.
37107: sošìeni ta stàna: ùbavi sɛm izlɛ̀za: iz izbìea màx
[we’ve] sewn together. They get really nice, they come out looking like moss,
37111: ta tàm perème i tàm se vàla: resnačètu
That’s where we do our washing, and where they full the blankets
37119: zagràdeno takà sus tekvìja stojnàli dà sa takà ma màlko ispàč’eni
fenced off with these supports, that are – that stick out a bit.
37123: a kato ə ə se naredìte da žɤ̀nete kòj opredèl’a
So when you line up to do the reaping, who decides
37125: how broad [the swath of] field [each one will reap] is going to be?
37135: [For] each one as much as they can reap ...
37147: kòj e ə kòlkutu mòž’e nìvətə də sə ugudì mlògu š’iròkə
Each does what he can. A field can end up being very broad [though] –
37150: š’ə kàrəš’ i dvà r’ɤ̀də i trì r’ɤ̀də
you’ll do two rows, and [then] three rows,
37153: i š’ə jə kàrəš’ cɛ̀lətə nìvə
and [eventually] you’ll do the entire field.
37164: tòzi kòjto e nàj otkràja tòj e kàk mu vìkate na nègo
The one who’s at the very end, he’s – How do you call him?
37169: post nə po nə n’àkɤde i vìkat pòstadžìjkata
37172: t’à opredèl’a kòlko da bɤ̀de širòko
She decides how broad [the reaping swath] is going to be.
37176: nìj si kàrəhmè kòj kòlkutù si
[The way] we would do it, each one [did] as much as –
37179: čakɤ̀m li na čakɤ̀m li mu vìkate kat se nared’ɤ̀t
“Chakum”? Do you call [that section] when they line up, a “chakum”?
37191: enà pwòstə enà nìvə i hàjde
One “puosta”, one field, and off you go.
37199: i sɛ̀k ž’ətvàrin si ž’ɤ̀ne i si klàvə nə snòpuvə
And each reaper will do the reaping, and put [the cuttings] into sheaves.
37205: pràvi si vɤ̀ž’e snòp si pràvi i si gu vɤ̀rdž’e
He makes a cord [from the stalk], makes a sheaf, and ties it up.
37210: vɤ̀rže gu pà pràvi drùgu vɤ̀ž’e i
He ties it up, then makes another cord, and
37214: š’ə vɤ̀r’e də ž’ɤ̀ne tò n’èmə kòj tò tì si
goes back to reap. There’s nobody [else to do it], you’re the one.
37217: e nə t’èp si e nə gləvɤ̀tə š’ə bɤ̀rzəš’
[The responsibility] is on your shoulders. [So] you hurry …
37225: zəletì li dɤ̀š’ tr’àə də ə vɤ̀rzətù i də gu skləd’èš’
… [because] if it starts to rain your bundle has to be tied so you can pile it up
37231: ... so it doesn’t get rained on.
37236: [Otherwise] it’s a drenched mess, all over the place.
37242: tò dudè gu isuš’ìš’ i vàrdiš ə ne istrɤ̀siš’ pu zem’ɤ̀tə
Until you manage to dry it out, you make sure not to scatter it all over the ground.
37246: You’ve got to watch over it.
37249: i e tùka stàvaše i i pšenìcata
And did wheat used to grow here too?
37256: [People] used to plant only a very small amount of wheat.
37261: na nàj hùbavite nìvi dètu sə
37273: rɤ̀š i uvès sejàhə zə stòkətə
[People] used to plant rye and oats, for the livestock …
37276: i uvès sejàhə i ič’umèn’ nɛ̀štu gu ìməš’e̥
… and they used to plant oats, and there was a bit of barley as well …
37279: … and they put a little barley in [too].
37282: Barley and – and a little bit of wheat.
37288: znàči pòveče xl’àp ste pràvili ot
So mostly you made bread out of …
37300: aa a tovà misìr dèto mu vìkat vìe tùka
So, this thing they call corn, do you here –
37312: dàž’e i nə pu dvòrištətə slàgəhə
They even put [some] in the yard
37315: zə təkà zə zə z’əl’ènu də si svər’ɤ̀t
in order to boil some up while it’s still green …
37326: nɛ̀štu təkà mə tò təkà š’ si gu udmɤ̀knem
… we do get something, but we pull it out [while it’s still green].
37330: du s’à trì gudìni nè e stànəlu
For three years now nothing has grown fully.
37333: The calf will eat it all up.
37338: It doesn’t grow, doesn’t [get to be] grain.
37348: è n’àma mm kàk mnògo kràtko l’àtoto
It can’t! How [could it]? [It’s a] very short summer [here].
37354: nə visòku sme hil’àdə i dvèstə
37360: Our summer is very short now.
37363: It’s only in August that we have [unintelligible].
37366: sà kəkɤ̀ftu ni e fəsùl’e sigè
Look at the way the beans look now –
37371: ne cvetì òš’te ednò l’àtu də ìmə
they haven’t bloomed yet. If we had one [more] summer ...
37376: tugà š’ə stàne mə n’èmə s’à š’ə pòčne sn’əgɤ̀
... then they’d ripen. But we don’t. The snow will come [any day] now!
37384: nè sìgurno ìma sòrtove koìto sa pò
No! Surely there must be kinds [of plants] that are more –
37386: òšte màlku i š’ə nə zəp’əpelì
Before long we’ll be buried in ash (= snow)!
37390: Kinds [of plants] that [grow] in shorter time periods.
37395: idìn m’ɛ̀sic prɤ̀j mu sm’ɛ̀tkə idìn m’ɛ̀sic
One month. Just do the math, one month …
37397: Well, you know, spring comes late.
37402: ìməme d’ètu də ni pàlim wògən’ uf tùkə
... [is all] we have that we don’t [need to] light a fire here.
37407: And the whole rest [of the time] …
37410: And this is the month of August.
37414: sɤs jurgànə s ud’əlà sə zəvìvəš’
… you’re wrapped up in quilts and blankets …
37420: i ti jə stud’ènu də si spìš’
… and even still you’re too cold to sleep.
37430: è stud’ènu š’ pòč’n’e studɤ̀ è kəkvò š’ə č’ùvəš tì grədìnə
Ah, cold!  The cold [weather] will begin, and what’s the point of keeping a garden?
37437: No, there are some sorts of earlier [blooming plants] –
37443: tә̥kà mɤ̀kətə si ti ìde kəkvò si s’àlu kvò si ku kupàlu
It’s so painful to go [see] what you’ve planted and dug
37444: ə tàm n’èmə nìštu də stàne
[and know] that nothing’s going to come of it.
37450: a ìmaxte li vìe ednì pràznici po n’àkoi selà pə pàz’at
And did you have the kind of holidays [that] they observe in some villages,
37455: ne sè ràboti ə ə takàva žènska ràbota
[where] they refrain from doing so-called women’s work ...
37466: pàdat drèxite i da ne napàdat kɤ̀štite
… get into [your] clothing or take over the houses.
37468: [No,] we’ve never observed anything [of the sort].
37471: You don’t have such a holiday.
37480: n’è n’è tvà e tvà gerg’òvdèn’ də sə ni bàrə nì
No, no, we do [have that]. That’s St. George’s day, you mustn’t touch either ...
37492: ni iglà zə zmìi də ni sɤ̀ vìždət
… or a needle, so that no snakes will come into view …
37500: What sort of custom was there?
37503: pa jà si gu č’ùvəm i n’ègu
37508: znàči jà jà mi go poftorì da da go
So, well – please repeat this for me so,
37511: də zapìšem tovà na gerg’òvden kakvò ne sè bàra
so we can record  this. What is it you don’t touch on St. George’s day?
37516: iglà i kun’èc ni sɤ̀ bàrə də ni sɤ̀ vìždət zmìjɛ
You don’t touch either needle or thread so that you won’t see snakes.
37519: a nòž’icə ni sɤ̀ bàrə də ni sɤ̀
You don’t touch scissors so that there won’t –
37525: də ni vɤ̀lk vɤlk’ɤ̀ də ni fàštə ufc’ɛ̀t’e kətu pəsɤ̀t
So that wolves won’t catch the sheep while they are grazing.
37530: tr’àbvə də də ni ustàviš’ utvòr’əti nòž’icìte
37534: də sə zətvòr’əti i də gi ni bàrət
They have to stay closed and remain untouched.
37539: stàn kətu ìməme n’è təč’ème kətu ìməme rudàn də prid’èm
If we have a loom we don’t weave, and if we have a wheel for spinning
37548: l’ùl’ki sə pràvet l’ùl’ət sə pèjət
They make swings; they swing and sing.
37554: nèkvi bèz də pìpəš nə gerg’òvden’
Some people don’t touch [them] on St. George’s day.
37556: əmi nìe ne sì sm’e č’ùvəli
37566: jəcà ni tr’àvə də ni bàrəš’ stànuvəlò e nə nə stòkətə
You shouldn’t even touch eggs. [If you do] something will happen to the livestock,
37569: stànvəlu nɛ̀štu kətu jejcà pu pu ìmetu təkà
something like eggs [appearing] in – in their udders.
37576: pu ìmetu ni mòjž də bàrəž ni mòjž də duìš’
You can’t touch the udder, you can’t milk them [because]
37580: šè a bulì do drùgijə gerg’òvden’ tvà n’ɛ̀štu š’ə s’ədì
they’ll get sick and all these [ills] will stick around [until] next [year’s] St. George’s day.
37585: e tvà kòjtu gu č’ùvə pək kòjtu ni č’ùvə d’è də znàm
That’s for the ones who observe it. The ones who don’t – what do I know?!
37589: There were all sorts of [customs] everywhere –
37592: i čùvaà i ne čùvaà i
37599: ìmə mlògu d’ètu də sə uč’ùvənì si
There’s a lot of [people] who are involved in [these customs],
37615: jà da si spòmniš tì kəkvì b’àxa kɤ̀štite ednò vrème
Recall for me what houses were like in the old days.
37619: [They were] wooden. Well, my – our house …
37626: kə kakvà bè kakvò ìmaše f ednà kɤ̀šta
What was – what was it like inside a [typical] house?
37634: òho let’ì izgòre vəlì dəskìte kàp’ət vəz nàs
Oho! [when] it rains, the boards above drip on us!
37641: čɤtmɤ̀ dərvà bilà ə təkà mòjə bəštà [unintelligible]
The wooden roof beams that – my father [unintelligible] –
37649: istùk istùk drùgutu fsèč’enu gi zəkàč’ət
... from here to here, another one fitted in, [you know how] they hook [them in].
37653: a tùkənà je səs sə č’erv’ènə kàl’ ìməš’e
And over here, it was – there was red mud.
37684: [they] go out there. Grandpa priest says the prayers –
37685: I’m going to go outside, Granny.
37688: dobrè da ne da ne ìdeš na pɤ̀t’a odvɤ̀d
O.K., but don’t – don’t go out onto the street outside!
37690: i ìdat tàm četè d’àdo pòp pràvi molèbie vɤ̀rne sa
And they go there, Grandpa priest does the prayers, they come back –
37694: mòže i òšte v momènta da zavalì dòkato e
It might even start to rain just then while he’s …
37698: tàm na nìveto i mòlim sa za bòk
… still there in the fields. And we pray to God,
37701: [people] were doing – there were “vaydudulki” [performers in rain-making rituals] in the village –
37704: hà hàj tovà št’àx da pìtam za vàjdudùlkite
Ah! That! I was just going to ask about the “vaydudulki”.
37706: vàjdudùlki segà prìmerno tàa mi e sestrà
“Vaydudulki”, well – For instance one was my sister,
37709: ama i nàj màlkatḁ istɤrsàka mu kàzvame
but the youngest one. We call it “the baby of the family”.
37712: nàj napòsle kojà se e rodìla
The one that was born last.
37717: i ìmaše edìn ə bùren ta mu vìkaa tòstata tìkva
And there was this plant, they called it “fat pumpkin” –
37720: tò kato tìkva rastè obàče ne vrɤ̀zva ami takà si rastè
it grows like a pumpkin plant but it doesn’t give fruit, it just grows like that –
37723: i go naskùbem nègo i a natrùpame sɤs tòo bùren
and we pick it and pile this plant on her,
37725: i a vòdim is selòto i pèem
and lead her throughout the village and sing.
37731: [We lead] the "vaydudle" (rain-maiden) through the village, from house to house.
37762: po koè kàk pèete let’àla e
O.K., but how do you sing it?  [Something has] "taken flight”?
37764: let’àla e peperùda dàj bòže dɤ̀š
“The butterfly has taken flight / Give us, oh God, rain”.
37780: (pee) poletèla e peperùga dàj bòže dɤ̀š dàj bòže dɤ̀š
(sings)	“The butterfly has just flown off / Give us oh God rain / Give us oh God rain”
37784: (pee) izùlica vuzùlica vàjdudulè dàj bòže dɤ̀š dàj bòže dɤ̀š
(sings) “Izulitsa vuzulitsa, vaydudule / Give us oh God rain / Give us oh God rain”
37788: sèki iznòsi kotèla sɤz vòda i ja zalìva
And each one takes out a kettle of water and pours it over her (the rain-maiden).
37794: è ə s’àko momìče li mòže da bɤ̀de vàjdudùlka
And can any girl be the “vaydudulka”?
37797: sàmo koè sa e rodìlo nàj pòsle
Only the one that was born the most recently.
37803: There mustn’t be any one after her.
37805: ako ìma čètiri momìčenca f ednà kɤ̀šta poslèdnoto
[If there’s] four girls in one house [it has to be] the last one [born].
37807: The one that is the baby of the family.
37808: momìčeta momčèta koèto e vèče nàj pòsle
The one that’s the last [to be born, of all] the girls and boys,
37809: that’s the one that they make the “vaydudulka”.
37813: dà dà po n’àkoj selà fàštat cìganče da bɤ̀de
Yes, yes. In some villages they get a gypsy girl to be –
37820: pravìle sme go f čitàlišteto nìe tòo običàj predì segà nèma
Earlier on we did that custom in the reading  room, [but] now we don’t.
37826: So then this custom was found [here].
37829: štòto go n’àma f c’àla bɤlgàrija
Because it’s not [found] everywhere in Bulgaria –
37830: n’àkɤde go ìma n’àkɤde go n’àma
Some places have it, some don’t.
37856: tòu zənəjɛ̀t gu u̥prəžn’àvəm ut dècki gudìni ošte pres c’àlijə si živòt
I have been practicing this craft since childhood, [indeed] my whole life,
37880: drùgo nɛ̀kvu seà kənà də mə pìt kənà səm vi kàzva nɛ̀štu
Something else? What do [you want] to ask me? I'll tell you something.
37884: o òšte mnògo ìmaš da razkàzvaš za takòva za
Oh, there's still lots more [for] you to tell [us]. Like [for instance] about –
37951: dvàma dùši z ban’d’ì ban’d’ìt’i səs šmàjzere n’èma da mɛ̀r
two guys, bandits with sub-machine guns, [who said] we mustn’t move.
38123: č’e kà də ti ne kàže tò tuvà l’ɤ̀snu [laughter]
Well how can I not tell you this? [laughter]It’s easy!
38186: kumpɨ̀rjen kl’ɨ̀n ìmə si stərgəlcà tə gu nəstɤ̀rž’eme ub’è̝lime gu
For potato banitsa there are graters. We grate [the potatoes]. We peel them
38201: nəstɤ̀rž’eme gu i sugàni gləvìci mu nə stɤ̀rž’eme nis kumpɨ̀r’ən
and grate them. Then [we take] a few onions and grate them onto the potatoes,
38212: i ubɤ̀rkvəž gu i fəf təvɤ̀nə gu kləd’è̝š’ sə kòri mu stòrim’e
then you mix it up and put it in the pan with – we make pastry sheets,
38217: pu dv’è kòri ud visòke i ud nìsku i i kinà
two each above and below [the filling], and there it is.
38223: tò n’è kəsu es’à kòrine də i dunesɤ̀t nətwòč’eni
Not like the pastry sheets you get now at the store, already rolled out.
38230: enèj se s’èjət kərtòfine pu pu trì kumpɨ̀r’ə
Potatoes are sown in groups of three seed potatoes.
38236: səs vòl’ven’e gu stòr’ət brəlà i nìj min’ème pòslet
With the oxen, the others make ditches, and then we go by afterwards
38245: i zàruvì gu i hi i mìni gu wòprəš’i i nòlku ti e
You tamp [the earth] down good, then come by again to hoe it, and that’s enough.
38249: i vəzrìvə sə i prə brəlà s’ètn’e mu pràime
Then you dig around, and we make ditches [for planting] again.
38253: ədnɤ̀ž gu prəš’ìme kətu pɤ̀rvu i s’ètn’e pàk
We hoe it once like the first time, and then again,
38255: we hoe it again like this.
38258: za kvò glèdaxte kòtki ednò vrème f kɤ̀štite
Why did you keep cats in the house in the old days?
38263: zə mìški əmə nìe n’èməme mìškine
For mice, but we don’t have mice.
38398: màndžite dèto ste pràili ednò vrème stàri rodòpski màndži
the dishes that you made in the old days, old Rhodope dishes.
38408: hà stàrutu vàj kàk də ti kàž'əm stàrutə kəkò beš'e
Hah! The old times! How shall I tell you what it was [like] then?
38414: š'e svərìš' ədnà tèndž'erə fəsùl' š'e gu zəbɛ̀liš' i š'e
You'll cook up a panful of beans, you'll add [some] fat, and you'll
38420: v gəlɛ̀mi səhàni š'e sìpeš' i bànici š'e stòriš'
pour [it all] into big pots, you'll make “banitsa”–
38423: What [can] I tell you of this?
38428: a bànicata po avèlski kàk jə kàzvahte
Well, “banitsa” – how did you call it in the old-time language?
38436: i seà ne urətìsvəm kòtkə də mi fl’ɨ̀zə
And now I don’t [want to] deal with a cat in my house.
38444: [What kind of work did the  men do?]
38447: pək məž’ète fəf kɯ̀ržɯlɯ fəf plòdif
The men [would go] to Kurdzhali, to Plovdiv.
38458: xa nəkvò s pəstàl’i ɤdnì n’e pəstàl’i əmi č’el’ədìsvəhə
[They worked] with these bundles; [the problem was] not the bundles, but that they drove them crazy.
38474: nàšte mɤ̀ž’uve sə etàm ràbutili pək nij sme bilìli
Our husbands worked there, while we were [here]
38479: i ž’è̝ncki i mɤ̀ski i də ur’è̝mə i də sədɨ̀me
[doing] men’s and women’s [work]. We [would] do the plowing and planting,
38483: i mùl’etənə pàk də rəskàrvəme i dərvà də tvàrime
we would take the mules around and load up wood
38485: i də səč’è̝me i sìčku e bilò enèj
and chop it, and everything. That’s how it was.
38490: d’èt nìe sme ot tvà səkìvə ustànəli geter’ùne [laughter] kàk
And that’s how we’ve gotten this way – unable to get around. [laughter] What [can you do]?
38497: kàzvəm səkàt’i ustànəhme geter’ùne bez nògi i bez bez rɤ̀ki
I said we’re lame. We can’t get around. Without [use of] legs or arms.
38502: rəkìs’e ədnɤ̀tə es’à mùl’e nə ədnɤ̀tə mi skɤ̀sə ž’ìlis’è vrìt’
My arms [for instance]: the mule completely ruined the tendons on one arm.
38510: nugìs’e ut’ hòdeni i ut tvàren’e t’èšku zɤ̀ha də ne hòd’ət
And my legs have stopped functioning, from walking and carrying heavy loads:
38517: i ne dàət mi t’è də hòd’əm ni nəvɤ̀n vìkət s’èdi ejtùkə
they don’t even allow me to go outdoors. People say, “Just sit here!”
38521: tì si ishòdilə kinànu e tr’èvəlu [laughter]
You’ve already done all the walking you needed to!” [laughter]
38525: And then she stopped being able to get around.
38530: i stànəh tugàə get’ur’ùn esèj də gu s’èdəm
And I became unable to get around, and now I just sit here
38533: and get to eat for free [without working for it]! [laughter]
38540: enugà z’ɤ̀meme tə ìdeme tə gu nəmɤ̀kneme əšləmɤ̀ ejtùkə
Back then we’d get out and go pluck the tobacco seedlings here
38543: v grədɨ̀nətə i ut tùkə du i tùkə im’èš’e
in the garden. There were [tobacco plants all the way] from here to here.
38548: tə nəhàkəme užɛ̀ci i tugàə gu mʌ̀kneme i gu gu sədìme
We would make “hearths” (holes in the soil), then take them and plant them.
38556: tə č’è̝tiri d’è̝kərə vər kɤ̀štəsə ejt’ùvə sàden t’ytỳn
We had four decares planted with tobacco up above our house.
38563: i imèh i dɤ̀šterə i im’èh i ruždènik tugàə ustànəh i səmà
I had a daughter, I had a brother, and then I was all alone
38567: dur də z’iməm nev’èstə pàk nɤ̀j s’ètn’e səm rudɨ̀lə
until I could get a bride [for my son]. After all, that’s why I had [another] child,
38570: zə nev’èstə də zɨ̀məm tə zə bel’ɤ̀tə
so as to get a bride because of all the trouble
38577: tə tə nə mòi pl’èšti e bilòlu [laughter] tugà ìdə tə pìškəm
that was sitting on my shoulders [laughter]. I [would] go then to thread [tobacco].
38582: pìškəm dukəd’ènu mògə də sə òmur’ə ìdə sə nàjəm
I’d thread it as far as I could, until I got tired and went to eat my fill,
38589: pàk ìdəm pəč’è ne pəč’è š’e də pìškəš kinà še pràiš
and then back to thread again, heat or no heat. What can you do?
38592: t’è ne dàvət pərɨ̀ də nè ne nəpr’ègəš sə  [laughter]
They won’t pay you if you don’t harness yourself [to the work] [laughter].
38598: tə gu nə esòlku nədəl’è̝č’e nə nəpùskəme
and drop [the seed potatoes into the ditches] at this much of a distance [from one another].
38605: užɛ̀ci gu sèeme l’ɛ̀hi l’ɛ̀hine v grədɨ̀nənə hi nəsèeme
We make “hearths” (holes in the soil) and sow them in beds in the garden.
38611: tugàvə prumʌ̀kneme tə sədɨ̀me i i tugàvənəkən gi nwòsime fəf səndɤ̀ci
Then we pull them up and transplant them. We carry them in boxes –
38777: klìn š'ə ə zə rəzbìješ trì č'ètiri əjcà šə grìs màlku
For "klin" you beat three or four eggs, with a little semolina,
38783: urìs š'e svərìš' ədnò drùgu i š'e nəpràiž bànicɨ
you cook up rice, and other stuff, and you make banitsa –
38787: səs màslu tegàj gi pràehə i m'ɔ̀su
back then they made it with butter. And meat –
38792: še gu zdrub'ɔ̀t nəjɔ̀dru təkà nəjɔ̀dru gu sip'òt
they chop it up in large chunks, and pour it out in big ones like this.
38796: če gu presɛ̀vət s màlku vudìč'kə təkà š'e gu pritìkət
They run it through a sieve with a bit of water like this:  they push it through
38799: pu màlku š'e gu issìpət v gulɛ̀m səhàn
little by little. [Then] they pour it into a big pot.
38805: i š'ə svər'ɔ̀t kəč'əmàk š'ə gu izvàdət nə təkìvə tukmàci
And they make polenta, and take it out in big lumps.
38808: sɛ̀ki š'e ədè dùr sə nəjədè [laughter]
Everyone eats until they've eaten their fill! [laughter]
38812: tùk istàtək d’èt ìmə t’èlve tàm ìmə č’erv’ènə kàl’
From here over to where the wires are, there is red mud.
38816: meždu bilàtə màž’eš’ də n’èmə dùpki ə təkà
You plaster it on between the roof beams so there won’t be any holes – like that.
38818: So there won’t be a draft.
38823: màž’eš’ təkà də sɤ ž’ivɛ̀e sə prež’ivɛ̀və
You plaster it enough to be able to live properly.
38829: vrətàtə ə dɤ̀rvenə lù s dɤ̀ski ètu təkìvə dùpki ìmə
The door is made of wooden boards: you see what sort of holes there are.
38835: izvɤ̀tre ìmə dɤ̀rv’enə vərtil’ɛ̀š’kə si nəpràvilu də sə zətvòriš’ tvà i
Inside you’ve made a wooden knob to shut yourself in, and that’s all.
38842: ili nɛ̀kəf kòl uttùk əku ìmə n’ɛ̀kəf pò zdràf dir’èk’
Or some sort of stick over here, if you’re got some hardier pole
38845: tàm vrətàtə də zəpèniš’ tvà ə vrətà
to secure the door with, that’s the door.
38849: Things were primitive in the old days.
38850: a kòlko kɤ̀šti ìmaše f ednà kɤ̀šta
How many houses were there in one house?
38856: əmi tò tò bəjɛ̀ kɤ̀šti ìməhme təkvì dɤ̀rveni sìčku sìčku bèše̥
Well, there were a lot of houses. We had these wooden ones – it was all –
38858: What is the agricultural [work you do] here?
38859: In the fields – we [work] in the fields.
38864: [Out] on the field, [that’s what] we call agriculture.
38869: kəto rəbòtim nàči nəlì s kulà s vulòvi ur’èmi zem’ɤ̀tə
… when we work, it’s with oxcarts, you know, we plow the earth,
38874: sèjəmi pribìrəmi ž vəršèm žènim vəršèm i àjde nə vudenìcə̥ta [laughter]
we sow, gather, thresh, [then] we reap and thresh, then it’s off to the mill [laughter]
38889: čem sùtrin kətu stàneš nàj nəprèž žə si nəpràviš
So in the morning when you get up the first thing you’ll do [is]
39000: čem sùtrin kətu stàneš nàj nəprèž žə si nəpràviš
So in the morning when you get up the first thing you’ll do [is]
39004: šə s ušʌ̀təš fkɤ̀šti si nəpràiš zə jə jàdenetu̥
you’ll clean up around the house, and then you’ll make meals.
39070: f səndɤ̀ci gu utnes’è̝me rəsàdəme səs ədnì pə š’ilà dikilìč’e
carry them off in boxes and transplant them using awls, special awls
39076: sìčku i tugàə pàk agà gu uprəš’ìme gu dvàž gu prəš’ìme
[on] all [of them]. We hoe them – we hoe them two times
39086: č’e təgàvə zber’è̝mə pɤ̀rvə rɤ̀kə ftòrə rɤ̀kə tr’ɤ̀tə rɤ̀kə i č’etvɤ̀rtə rɤ̀kə
and then gather them in – the first group, the second, the third and the fourth.
39092: hə tugà gu ukus’ɛ̀əme pàk stàne fel’ìs
Then we mow it, and then you get offshoots.
39096: tə tə gu ne mòže izber’è̝hme tò sàə gudɨ̀nə kinà stànə
But we couldn’t gather anything of it in. And what happened this year?
39103: t’yt’ỳnə stanɤ̀ v’èke nà č’e sme dàvəli iz’èt’
The tobacco was [so bad] that [all the effort] we put into it was in vain.
39107: ut č’è̝tiri ut p’ɤ̀d dèkərə tə se tə səs wòsem istìfə sme
Out of four or five decares we got [only] eight rounds [of tobacco leaves].
39112: tə zə kinà si sme dàvəli iz’èt’ i n’èməme fəjdɤ̀ nìkəkvə
So why did we put in all this trouble and not get any benefit out of it?
39115: They gave us next to nothing for it.
39116: [През други години повече ли сте брали?]
[Did you get more in other years?]
39122: ə če kugà kugànu t’yt’ỳnən beše ejsòlkuf tə pànnə tə gu spìti
When the tobacco was this high, [hard rains] fell and ruined it.
39126: i tugàvə gu pàk uprəš’ìhme pribràhme gu pànnə
So then we hoed it over, started again, and [the rains] fell again,
39133: i drùguš pànnə i drùguš trɨ̀š i tugàə kinànu nəràste filìs
and  then again, and then a third time, and then the offshoots grew.
39141: tə pu pu utùs istìf’e pu trìjse istìf’e sme ìməli
[In the past] we’ve had "utus" (30) rounds, "trijset" (30) rounds [of tobacco] each,
39146: pu č’etìrese istìf’e sme pràvili pək pək sm’e stòrili wòs’em istìf’e
[in fact] we’ve made up to forty rounds each. But [this year] we managed [only] eight rounds.
39152: ejsòlkuf ə esòlkuvə sə istìfene kòlkusu ejsèvə rɤ̀ki wòs’em
[Just] this many. Just as many rounds as [the fingers on] these hands here: eight.
39153: [And in the old days, how many rounds did you do each?]
39156: pək ə pu pu kɯ̀rk istìfe
[when it should have been] "kŭrk" (40) rounds each.
39157: [What does a wooden plow look like?]
39164: mu klədɤ̀t pàl’ešnik nə jəgùptene iskuvàtu i uràlunu izd’èlənu esèj
They put a plowshare on it, forged by Gypsies, and the plow is shaped like this.
39170: tə vərv’ì  pr’əz zem’ʌ̀nə i gu nəvràtə gu nəvràtə gu
It goes through the earth, it turns it over, and turns it over [again].
39176: tò nè kənu nuvànəkən kənu tràkturən pu mnògu tò pu màl’ku
It’s not like this thing here, like a tractor [that does] a lot. [It just does] a little.
39180: že ur’è̝me ur’è̝me i pàk i ùtre še ur’è̝š’
We plow and plow and then tomorrow you plow [some more].
39184: š’e usùrneš’ vòl’ven’e  dvà vòlə i uràlunu fsredè vərvì
You squeeze the oxen [into the yoke] – two oxen, and the plow goes between them.
39185: nə uràlunu kinà i kinà ìmə
So what [exactly] is there on a plow?
39188: ìmə sìčku i wùš’i nə uràlunu ìmə i ž’è̝lezu ìmə i pàlešnik i
It’s got everything. There’s moldboards on the plow, and iron, and the plowshare, and –
39195: kɤ̀štənə iskupɤ̀t tem’è̝l’i i grəd’ɤ̀t je səs kàmen’e i gr’èdi
For a house, they dig out the foundation, then build it with stone and beams
39199: i dɤ̀ski nə nəd’èləni kùp’eni nem’è
and boards. There weren’t any that were already shaped, or bought.
39206: ud dəl’èč’e ut plənnɤ̀tə kòjtu si im’ɛ̀ dukàrvəš’e
Whoever had [anything] would bring it from afar, from the mountains.
39210: pək əku n’è̝ tugàvə səs d’èləni dɤ̀ski enìk’yvə
But if not, then [they worked] with some sort of shaped boards.
39212: nè ə nə nə nəkvò sme i sed’èli
Not in –   That’s how we lived.
39222: fəv bəžɛ̀ wògən’en n’è e im’èlu esəkìvə p’è̝čki d’èznə kinà
In the hearth! [That’s where] the fire was. There weren’t these stoves and what-all.
39226: nìe sme skòru vid’èli p’è̝čkise n’èkvə gudɨ̀nə
We’ve only recently seen such stoves, just a few years ago.
39228: vəf fəf wògən’en fəf bəžɛ̀ i s nə verùgə
[We did cooking] in the fire, in the hearth, [in pots hanging] on a chain,
39234: nə verùgə nə dɤ̀rvu klàdenə fəv bəžɤ̀nə tə i hàrkmə də vərìš’
on a chain [that was] put on a piece of wood in the hearth. You cook in a cauldron
39240: nə ub’è̝senu ud ž’el’ezà enəkvò verùgə gu zv’è̝me
hanging from this iron [thing] – we called it a chain.
39248: i prudəlž’àvəm də si gu rəbòt’e vɤ̀preki.če səm vɤ̀zrəsen
and I’m continuing to do this work even though I am on in years –
39257: So, and what do you want?
39262: še slòžiš vəf tòrbəta kvòtu tr’àbvə
You’ll put what you need into your bag, ...
39266: kətɤ̀kət kvòtu tr’àbvə i zəminàvəš nə ràbutə tàm kət ìdeš
... food that you need to take along, and you leave for work. And you go there ...
39274: p’èši tàm kət ìdeš sfàliš tòrbətə ukàč’iš jə nə nə òrexa
... on foot. When you get there you take off your bag and hang it on a walnut tree.
39441: Well, to talk a bit. We’re looking for –
39447: za sèloto za stàri običài za
[information] about the village, about old customs, about –
39452: əmɨ nìj jɛ̀ səm vɤ̀zrəsən čuvɛ̀k nə mòjtə məhəlà si
Well, we – I’m an old person. In my part of the village –
39458: ə nìe govòrixme sɤs sedènkof dèto pìsal istòria tùka
We spoke with Sedenkov, who’s said to have writen histories of the area
39460: i ni kàza če vìe takà nàj dobrè še ni kàete
and he told us that you would best be able to tell us [things] ...
39469: a jɛ̀ səm budəlɛ̀stə stànələ sìn jɛ̀ səm usəmdesè i trì gudìne
I’ve gotten all simple, child. I’m eighty-three years old.
39471: ami i nìe takìva xòra tɤ̀rsime da ni raskà
Well, that’s exactly the kind of people we’re looking for to [tell] us –
39475: So what should I tell you?
39479: ami kəkvòto znàeš tùka za sè
Well, whatever you know here about the vill–
39488: če be jɛ̀ nə znàjə nìštu sìn jɛ̀ nə znàjə
Well look, I don’t know anything, child. I don’t know about the old times
39497: stàrutù k səm zəburìlə pək ezgà mlədèžəs
I’ve forgotten about the old times. And [anyway] youth now –
39502: young people don’t believe [anything] about the old times. [laughter]
39520: tò hùbəvu vi vìkə bɛ̀ əmə jɛ̀ sem ednò zəburìlə
Well, he told you well. But I’ve forgotten stuff.
39522: drùgu kəkò də vɤ kàžə drùguš
What else can I tell you? Back then –
39807: Did you go out here around –
39809: rèko nè.znam kvò stànu pa g’u ne kazùjem
[and] said “I don’t know what happened.” But I didn’t tell her
39816: ə pres prəs kəčòrskən.igrèk gu vìkəme unvà derè čàkəj
Well, through what we call Kuchorskan Igrek. There’s a riverbed there –
39819: z glàdni du n’èmə du kəd’è čʌ̀kvəme̥ si pu edìn kumàt xl’àp
[You’d be] hungry like you can’t believe. We each tear off a piece of bread
39823: kət dòjdem vəf kir’èč’nicənə č’e gu nàtup’ə səz ə vòdə gu nàrusə
when we get to the limepit. I’ll dip it in water and sprinkle it
39827: səs sòl i dud’è sl’èzəm dòlu du r’àkəsə i nəjàlə səm se
with salt, and by the time we get down to the river I’ve had enough to eat.
39831: i nəbližɤ̀t li s’èlusu i pòčvəd də pujʌ̀t
And when they get near to the village they begin to sing.
39833: e i kətu vɤ sə vɤ̀rneme u ottàm
Yes, when we return from there
39840: i pòčvəm’e dvòjki še pujèm žətvàrski p’èsni vrɤ̀štəme se ot
we start to sing harvest songs in traditional pairs as we are returning from …
39847: nə sedemdesè i šèz gudìni pàk mɤ̀č’əm də ràbut’e zənəjɛ̀tə
I’m seventy-six, and still put in the effort to ply my trade
39853: də mògə də iskàruvəm pu n’àkəf l’èf zə stərinì
so as to earn a lev here and there for my old age.
39861: i təkà.če se nəlàgə də ràbute
39862: [What materials (= kinds of lumber) did you work with?]
39868: məter’àlə kòjtu se snəbd’àvəh b’èš’e nìe gu kàzvəme jèlə
The lumber I was [able to] get was – we call it fir,
39978: è tò̝jə ə ud mò̝jə bəštà nèguvijə bəštà imɛ̀šə tàm nàš kumšìjə
Well, the father of my father – there was this neighbor of ours there,
39981: dɤ vɤ kàžə imɛ̀šə grəmfò̝n žɤ vɤ pukàžə tugàvə
let me tell you. And he had a gramophone! I’ll show you. At that time
39989: təkòvə ədnò stàrček nàšijən bè̝še kəm usemdesè devedesè i dvɛ̀ gudᶤìšen
this old guy of ours was upwards of eighty– he was ninety-two. And
39996: tugàvə vìkə təkvò i grəmfò̝nən svᶤìr’e sèjneka i tò ut sò̝fijə svᶤìr’eše nvà
he spoke thus: “That gramophone plays like this, and it was playing from Sofia!”
40001: [laughter] ut sò̝fijə svᶤìr’e či vᶤìkə nə stàr:t’em nə bəštà m nèguvijən bəštà
[laughter] Playing from Sofia! And then the old man said to my father’s father,
40006: vᶤìkə žə dòjde vᶤìkə vrɛ̀m’ə ə tàm ə zgà dènu svᶤìr’ət
he said, “There will come a time,” he said, “when [the music] they play there,
40015: i pejɔ̀ tùv žə sə gl’ɔ̀dət sàmə čə žə sə vᶤìkə golò̝pəre
and sing, will be seen here. Except that,” he said, “[they] will be naked.
40020: kɤ̀su vᶤìkə žə nòs’ət i dò̝jdə tvà nɛ̀štu dò̝jde
They’ll wear short [skirts].” And this has come. It’s come.
40025: vᶤìkə etàm vᶤìkə svᶤìr’ət i p’ejɔ̀t i se vesel’ɔ̀t
And he said, “They sing and play and make merry and such over there,” he said.
40027: etùvə vᶤìkə že dòjde fsò etùv vìkə nà že gu gl’ɔ̀dəme
“And that will come here from Sofia,” he said. “Here, you’ll see. We’ll watch it
40029: pu svà pu televᶤìzijətə nəlì ezgà gu
on this – on the television.” And don’t [we have] it now?
40033: i pu vɛ̀snici i pu sᶤìčku [laughter]
And [that sort of thing now] in the newspapers and everywhere! [laughter]
40038: drùgu kəkvò dɤ vɤ kàžə sìn envà səm zəpòmnilə ut stàr:te
So what else shall I tell you, son? I remembered that one from the older people.
40042: ə pək ezgà e sᶤìčku mlədèšček čə̥ kəkvò də ìdiš də də təkòvə
But now everything’s in the style of the young. Why should one go about
40045: də vᶤìkəš tə də s səsɛ̀təš tə də kəkò kàk
and talk and work things out [to find out] what and why?
40051: èhehe kàži mɤ də vìge de kàži mi
Huh? Tell me so I can get it, O.K.? Tell me.
40056: kažì kàk ste živ’àli kòlko decà
Tell us how you used to live, how many children –
40063: kàk smə žɨvɛ̀le žɨvɛ̀lɨ smə urɛ̀xmə sɨ kupàehmè sɨ
How we used to live? We lived – we plowed, we dug –
40068: imò̝tə beše mnò̝go imòt nìe imɛ̀hmi i drùgi imɛ̀hə sìčkine imɛ̀hə
There was lots of property. We had property, others had, everyone had
40073: pu mlò̝gu imò̝t tugàvə sì gu urèm kupàemɤ̀ i ezgà
a lot of property. Back then we plowed it, dug it. And now
40080: zəfàtəmə ut ut ftò̝ri àvguz də kusìm də kusìm pu stàrutu
we start on the second of August to mow – to mow. According to the old way,
40083: pu stàrutu ilìndin gà gu zuvɤ̀t nəlì gu pìsvə ilìnden
on St. Elias’ day, when – it’s called. Don’t they write it [on the calendar] St. Elias’ day?
40088: nə nə kəlendàr’:te ezgà vəf tòj nə ftò̝ri àvgus
On – on the [church] calendars. That’s on the second of August now.
40092: tugàvə zəfàtəhme də də žɔ̀nem də è pu šukadàr
That’s when we started to – to reap, all the way over to there!
40098: tə prez zᶤìmətə du nò̝və gudᶤìna sklədɛ̀hme snò̝pɤne nə kupnì
And in the winter, up till New Year’s, we’d put up the sheaves, into piles.
40106: nə kupèn gu sklàdə sklàda sklàdə i budnɔ̀š fàneše snɛ̀k
I put – put it into a pile. And sometimes snow would start up.
40113: fàn’eše snɛ̀k tə hò̝dim tə č’ìstim unuvà ud dəl’ànə tə gu vərš’ɛ̀hmi
Snow would start up and we [would] go to clean that [place] with a net, and we’d thresh.
40118: i vò̝luve si imɛ̀hmi čis č’yv də si urèmə
and we had – a pair of oxen, so we [could] plow,
40122: i imɛ̀hmi si i ž’ìtu imɛ̀hme si sᶤìčku imɛ̀hmə dvà kò̝n’a
And we had grain, we had everything. We had two horses
40265: ə ìnəče pugòrckumu sə kàzvə smɤ̀rč sàmu təkɤ̀f məter’àl
or, as foresters say, spruce. Only that kind of lumber.
40269: i gu òdime pu guràtə i gu tɤ̀rsehme po kəmenìstu m’àstu
We went out to the woods and would seek it out in rocky places.
40273: trɤ̀sime à ə trɤ̀sime nə təkòvə m’àstu kəd’ètu ìmə kàməni
We’d seek it! Seek it in the kinds of places where there are rocks.
40275: vəf kàməni də rəstè tvà dɤ̀rvu
That tree [is best when] it grows among rocks,
40278: pun’èž’e kugàtu rəstè f kàməni dərvòtu e vɤ̀tre sìtno
because when it grows among rocks the wood inside is fine-grained,
40285: a sìtnutu dɤ̀rvu je zdràvu i tràjnu i ud n’èga rəbòtime sɤ̀duve
and fine-grained wood is strong and lasting, and [so] we make containers from it.
40288: təkɤ̀f məter’àl mnògu gudìni rabòtehme tɤ̀j.kətu tugàvə rəbòteme nə rəkà
We’ve been working this wood many years, because at that time we worked by hand.
40292: n’èməme məš’ìni rəbòt’eme nə rəkʌ̀ i tvà dɤ̀rvu
We didn’t have machines, and we worked that wood by hand.
40296: tvà dɤ̀rvu ne è tvɤ̀rdu kətu səlkɤ̀mə i dəbɤ̀
That wood isn’t hard the way acacia and oak [are],
40302: zətvà gu rəbòtexme nə rəkà i vopštè tugà n’èməhme nìkəkvi məšìni
[which is] why we worked it by hand. We had no machines at all then.
40307: sìčku si rəbòtehme nə rʌ̀kə a fpusl’ètstvie sl’ed mnògu gud’ìni
We worked everything by hand. Consequently when, after many years
40311: vèče nəlì izl’èzəhə məš’ìni jà si zemàx ednà plàničkə
machines became available, I got myself a planing machine,
40316: i nə n’èjə rəbòt’ɛ səlkɤ̀m dɤ̀p tɤ̀j.kətu t’è sə mnògu tvɤ̀rdu dɤ̀rvu
and I use it to work with acacia and oak since their wood is very hard
40320: nə rəkʌ̀ ne mòe se rəbòt’et a segà vèč’e rəbòt’et nə məš’ìnətə
and can’t be worked by hand. But now they can be worked with the machine,
40323: vɤ̀preki.če səm i vɤ̀zrəsen nu pàk prudəlžàvəm i si ràbut’ɛ
[so] despite the fact that I’m on in years, I still [can] continue to work.
40326: kugàtu ìməm ràbutə rəzbìrə se kugàtu n’àməm s’èdə [laughter] tvà e
When I have work of course. When I don’t I just sit around! [laughter] So there.
40341: Is there bread in the store?
40344: natàm navàm kòlko sàkamo da bùdu
here and there  [to measure] how long we want it to be,
40357: osòbeno malòvo nàj ne slùša nàj slùša malòto
This little one [by me], listens the least. The [other] little one listens the most.
40366: i kràvɤ dvɛ̀ trì i ò̝fcɨ mò̝jə bəštà imɛ̀ us’emdesè bràvə ò̝fcɨ
and two or three cows, and sheep. My father had eighty head of sheep.
40369: s enəkvò sə smə sìn zənimàvəlɨ
And that’s what we were occupied with, son!
40371: A lot. You had a lot.
40376: hɔ̀ sìčkite imɛ̀hə sìn če gu ràbutèhə pək ezgà utkət stànə sèjnekə
Ah, everybody did, son, and they worked it. But now, since it’s become like this –
40382: əzgà si dàduhə zəm’ɔ̀sə če kugà gl’ɔ̀də ajtùə mlədèš
Now they’ve returned the land [to its original owners], but when I look at these youth,
40388: How [do you mean], the bread is ready?
40395: jemi brəšnòtu si gu zèmim vèči nìj mòm si m’èsim
We [just] take some flour, and we’re able to knead [our own] bread,
40404: We would bake [all] our bread at home.
40413: i kɤ̀k sa pràiši l’àp idnò vrèmi fkɤ̀šti
Well, and how did you make bread at home in the old days?
40415: kàk sme rəbòtili ednò vrèmi nə pul’ètu
… how we used to work in the old days [out] in the field.
40420: mi jèməmi təkɤ̀vi kurìtə də ti kàžə
We have these kneading troughs. I [can] tell you.
40432: Like [those] outdoor bathtubs, like when [laughter] you take a bath. [laughter]
40441: nè vəf ə kòlko stài ìmaxte kòlko
No, [I meant] how many rooms did you have, how many –
40446: vɤf ə stàətə trì stàji i piš’tà fùrnətə si ni bè
In a room – three rooms. And the stove – we had a big oven.
40460: kəkvòtu vàs nᶤìkuj ne utìde də ràbuti sin i gurà stànə
like you, nobody is going to work, son! All has turned to forest!
40465: snovèmo na kòlci tòj klàšnite kòlci zabìeni
[When] we warp for homespun, we [wind thread along] stakes pounded in
40468: kòlko làkti da ni bùdu kojà naprèla pòveče
how many elbow-lengths. The one who has spun more,
40473: p’èd gudᶤìni stànə nəlì znàete vɔ̀rnə sə zəm’ɔ̀sə dàduhə jə
It’s been five years since the land was returned, you know? They gave it back!
40474: pòveče vḷ̀nu ìma napredè pòveče làkti
[the one who has] more wool will spin more elbow-lengths, ...
40481: kojà pò màlko no mètrove ga sɤ̀g zovù
... and the one who has less – well, now they call it meters,
40484: ma tegàj zovèšemo làkti na làk [laughter]
but back then we used to call it elbow-lengths, [measuring] by an elbow.
40487: se osnovè pa se tegàj navìe na krosnò
You warp it, and then you wind it onto the beam, ...
40496: tugà nìkuj nə hòdi də ràbutɨ nèməš kò̝n’ nèmə s kəkvò
And nobody goes out to work [it]. You don’t have a horse, there’s nothing [to work with].
40500: àjde ìməmə pu odnɔ̀ pu dvɛ̀ kràvɤcɤ jɛ̀ nèməm nìkəkvə kràva
Well, we have one or two cows each, [But] I don’t have any cows.
40505: tugàvə ìmat hòrəsə kràvcɨ žə si fpr’ɔ̀gne də s puurè
Back then people had little cows to harness up and start plowing –
40515: də s puurè če dè də gu znàem
to start plowing. But how can we understand [what’s happening]?
40520: mlədèšček ìmə tùkə tri čètiri pèt šɨz dùšɨ sid’ɔ̀t sid’ɔ̀t
Young folk here – three, four, five six of them – just sit. They just sit.
40525: kàžə m zgà ənəkvò be sìn pək drùguš beše nəkvò
Tell me this now, son, was it like that in the old days?
40527: jɛ̀ vɤ kàzvəm drùgučɛ̀šnutu beše enəkvò
I tell you, it was different in the old days!
40531: Were you [one of] a lot of children in the house?
40538: čètərə dicà behmə jɛ̀ beh nàj gulɛ̀mata i ud i truìcata beha bràk’a
There were four of us children. I was the oldest, and I had three brothers.
40543: tè izmrɛ̀hə bràk’ata tìjə ìmət nəslɛ̀dnɨcɨ zgà kɤ̀šti imɛ̀hmə
[All my] brothers died, they’ve got heirs now. [Since] we had [several] houses,
40545: pa àjde na razbòj pòsle uvedèmo u bṛ̀do
... and then onto the loom. Then we thread it into the "bŭrdo" (reed comb),
40549: a wooden reed comb. The reed combs were wooden.
40555: pu ədnò pu dvè krətò̝h sàdehmə kərtò̝f sàdehme pu mlògu
[they’ve got] one or two each. We used to plant potatoes, a lot of potatoes.
40559: tugàvə gu kàrəha è bəštà mɤ i nèguvijə bəštà səs kò̝n
They took them then – my father and his father, they’d [take] the horse
40565: že tuvàr’ət tə də ìdət nəh pulènu də gu smen’ɔ̀t səs càrevicə
and load [it up] and go [down] to the plains to trade it for corn.
40570: pò rànu ìməhme dòstə ràbutə ubàč’e segà s ednɤ̀ dùmə kàzənu
Earlier on we had a lot of work. However now – to say it with a single word –
40573: ràbutə n’èmə mnògu e slàba i pòsl’e nàš’ijə zənəjɛ̀t pòveč’etu ràbutə
there’s no work. Very little [anyway]. In our craft most of the work
40581: ìmə jèsenu vr’ème kugàtu tr’àvə zə zèl’e kàcə tr’àvə bɤ̀čvə zə vìnu
comes in the fall when people need crocks for cabbage or barrels for wine,
40583: So that’s how it was in the old days.
40591: [laughter] əma zgà dò̝de lòšku pìlence lò̝šku dò̝de nè e hùbəfku
[laughter] But now it’s gotten bad, dear one. It’s gotten bad, it’s not good.
40596: vərvì ud dèn’ nə dèn’ pəràtkə ràbutə
From day to day things get worse and worse.
40600: kəkvò že izlɛ̀ze ne znàjə zə mlədèšč’ekəs
What’s going to come of it I don’t know, [especially] for the youth.
40604: tr’àvə màlki bùrencetə zə rəkìjka bɤ̀kəl’č’eta za vòda i pòveč’etu
small kegs for brandy, small flasks for water [and so on]. So mostly
40613: i vìj ne znàete sìn utkəd’è də znàete
And you don’t know either, son. How should you know?
40616: rəbòteme jèsenu vrème prez l’àtutu mnògu slàbu a segà i prez esentɤ̀
we work in the autumn. There’s very little [work] in summer, but now in autumn
40622: n’àma ràbota zaštòto vèč’e izl’èzəhə nàj razlìčni ə plàsmàsuvi sɤ̀duve
there’s no work because now they’ve come out with all these plastic containers,
40630: če jɛ̀ f kàzəh če nèmə
And I told you [all] that there weren’t any [mushrooms up there]!
40632: i t’àh uputreb’àvət zə zə təkìvə ràbuti

No! Didn’t I tell you there aren’t any?

Well, I said we shouldn’t set out, but –

They want bread, they want it, they just – And I was talking with a woman [who]

His daughter – his daughter keeps a warehouse for the distribution of flour,

… with us was the furnace We called it the “klet”, ...

to one village for its bakery, tomorrow to another village

very pure,’ she said. ‘They’ve brought pure grain.’ And so now

his daughter runs the storehouse; [a truck] goes to Asenovgrad. ‘It’s already three days,’ she says

40834: məgàretu si ìmə səmàr’ i mùl’etu si ìməš’e səmàr’ pòvərž’e mùl’etu

40862: lòšku̥ e̥ sin vìkəm dənò sə pugud’ɔ̀t dənò stàne sìn ùbəvu

both for us and for the young people. So see, I’m waiting now for them to give me

my pension, to give me my pension, to give me two thousand, and from that
40878: žə kùp’ə dərvà šè s’èdemstò̝tən l’èvə sə stànəlɨ dərvàtə kubᶤìkə

40890: kòlku hìl’ədi žə dàm žə dàm hil’àdə əm tugàvə pə zə jɛ̀dini
how many thousands will I [have to] pay? I’ll pay a thousand just for food.
40895: tvà čùkəme drɛ̀ e təkòvə kugàtu də pɤrèm č’èrgite
This – We beat – Well, it’s when we wash rugs.
40901: əm žə gi prìpusk’ə ədnɔ̀š ut təkò nòču dušlᶤì sə
But I’ll let it go this time, because of that. Nocho! [These people] have come
40907: gɤ̀bɨ stànə kədètu vərv’ɔ̀ iznòs nɛ̀kəde

40911: kədè hòd’ehə nòče kədè hi nòsehə à
Where did they go, Nocho? Where did they take them? Huh?
40919: tugàvə hòd’ehə tə hi berɛ̀hə gɔ̀bɤte i hi suš’ɛ̀hə

40925: də mə pᶤìtət kəkvò i bəlò drùguš kəkvò i stànəlu əzgà

40931: a tùa sèj nərɛ̀duvàə nərɛ̀duvàə tè behə mnògu skɔ̀pi lənì

40937: m dìgnəhə stìgnəhə du du sidem.òsemstòtən l’èvə kilugràmə

40941: i jɛ̀ hmə kàzvəm jɛ̀ hmə kàzvəm vìkem
I’m telling them, I’m telling them, I say
40947: imɛ̀ imɛ̀ i gulɛ̀mki imɛ̀ i pò màšečki
There were – there were big ones and there were smaller ones.
40950: kəkvò be sìn drùguš kəkvò e zgà
how it was in the old days and how it is now.
40955: Yes, he told you. [They’re for] import (= export).
40960: tàa godìna nèma štòt fàna sùšata i gu udvèlu
There aren’t any this year because the drought came and [the wind] took them off.
40965: tà zgà hòd’əm pòvenke də putrɔ̀sə nəgòre
And now I’m going up there to look some more ...
40970: də vìdə əmə nèmə òd be sùš’e
... to see [if there are some]. But there aren’t any because of the drought!
40976: àku be l’etɛ̀lu nemɛ̀ privdìgəne əmə tò ne može i də letì
If it had rained [there’d have been so many] one couldn’t have carried them, but it couldn’t even rain.
40981: kugàtu ìmə dɔ̀š letè pək təkò̝və stànuvət
When there’s rain, then they come out [fine].
40984: əmə zgà nə sùš’ətə nə stànəhə sin
But now in the drought they didn’t make it, son.
40989: nè nìštu i tugàvə hi sušɛ̀ha ta bilè i gò̝tvihə ut tɛ̀h
No, nothing! Back then people dried them and even cooked with them,
40996: mèsət sy m’ɔ̀su i zətvàr’əhə fəv burkàne hi zətvàr’əhə

40999: gà isɔ̀hnehə hi zətvàr’əhə vəv burkàne i pučtì iznòs

41002: pučtì iznòs hi kàrəhə pučtì iznòs
Mostly they sent them as export, most for export.
41008: si ubràl ətàm čerɛ̀škite nè sɨ jɛ̀cə
Did you pick cherries over there? You didn’t [get very] much!
41017: kugàtu də pərèm č’èrgite tə gu tùrɨm i və kurìtu̥tu kupàtu kurᶤìtu
When [we go] to wash rugs, we put it in the trough, the dugout trough,
41018: i tugàvə gu čùkəme səs tvà
and then we beat them with it.
41022: nè e sìgur nè e mnògu tò ne mòže se pokàčiš
It’s not safe. There’s not many. You can’t climb up –
41025: d èeš gòre da i fàneš
[You can’t] get up there to reach them.
41031: They walk and sing [at the same time].
41035: kətu sə vɤ̀rneš dòjdeš ud ud unuvà p’àl si
When you come back from – from that, you’ve been singing,
41036: but when you get back you [still] have to
41039: d ìdeš  nə vòdə nə ul’èn’
go to fetch water at Olyen.

You’ll bring back water, and put the copper kettle on to boil.
41052: ə səs kutluvàr’k’ənə nə ràmutu nàiš kòlku vr’ème sə vərì
Do you know how long you had to walk with the kettle-yoke on your shoulder?
41059: če še fl’èzeš vʌ̀tr’e nàj nəprèž nəkləd’èš ògn’en še gu tùriš bəkɤ̀rən
[Back home] you ‘ll come inside, you’ll first of all light the fire and then put the kettle on

41066: segà decàta tìja decà nèka ti kažème
Kids today, these kids – let us tell [about our times].
41068: od dvanàese godìni sam počnàla xlèb da mèsa ednò vrème
I started making bread when I was twelve years old. [That was] the old days.
41072: ne è kat seà da ni donòsat xlèp mesùvahme si domàšen

41079: ìmame ednò stòlče nòšvi si ìmame takvìja drɤ̀veni tàm si sè stojàa

Ah. We have the outdoor oven, over there. See, there is what we have.
41100: Over there, in the outdoor oven.

take it out, and – my mother and father are reaping and plowing [out] there –
41113: we have sheep, we have goats,
41121: ìmahme volòve ìmahme kobìlə pa dzàran ìmam cadìlka
we had oxen, we had a mare. So early in the morning – I have a string-tie bag,
41125: zàdenàm lèbo pa im òdnesàm tàm na nìvətə
I [put] the bread [in it] and load it on my back, and carry it to them out in the fields.
41128: tì domà pečèš tì i rabòtiš

41139: a ami pèča ami cèl dèn i sos nìx i rabòta
Well, I bake but I also work all day with them
41143: sètne ne sàmo da pèča nè sàmo da sedìš

41147: ot kət sam proodìla ot kàk se znàm če sɤšestvùvam čovèk
From the moment I started to walk, from when I was conscious of myself as a person,
41150: pri baštà mi sè kozàrka i ofčàrka

41155: kòzi i òfce da pasèš i dèca da vàrdiš

No way!  Who dares have any more than two,
41169: once you’ve seen these hard times.
41179: kò̝pən se zəvè sìn [laughter] kò̝pən sə zuvè
It’s called a “kopan”, child. [laughter] It’s called a “kopan”.
41182: kɤdè xòdite da gi čèrgite da gi
Where do you go to – the rugs to –
41187: e tùvə ìməme si vudìcə tàm e blᶤìsku vudᶤìcata
Ah, we have a washing pool here. The washing pool is close by here.

41200: ud derètu ìməmè si i drùgətə sìn ni vudìcə duvèg’enkə

41205: duvèg’enkə ìməme vudìcə si tə ni e mnògu hùbəvə ni j vudìcəsə

41212: e tùkə dètu ìmə otvòd nə češmìcətə ədnə studènkə vudìcə

41220: i ədnɔ̀ gudᶤìnə ìmə pèt šèz gudìnɨ kàk stò̝rɨha etùkə pàmetnik
One year – it’s been five or six years since they built a monument there
41226: zə umrɛ̀lɨte dètu uttùkə imàlu prez vujnìte prez etɛ̀ə vujnì
for the dead, for those from here [who died] in the wars. In these wars
41229: prez è predì etɛ̀ə vujnì stàrɤte vujnì tugàvə dètu sə izbᶤìtɤ
in – ahh, way earlier, in those old wars, the wars where [people] were killed.
41231: … [that’s what we call a kneading trough.

which I myself fashioned, wooden centrifuges – we put the milk in the centrifuge

41277: ìmə si nə nìvətə spic’àlen ərmàn kədètu vərš’ìjeme tìjə snòpi səs mùl’etu

41280: i məgàretu kətu gi prenesème nə ərmànə jàs nàprəve kup’èn

and that’s how – that’s how we’ve winnowed it [all].
