41336: i dukàrvə gi f pòdnikən i lìst’enici̥ skəlàvəhme ut dəbìenu lìst’e
and brings them back to the cellar [where] we’ve piled up oak leaves
41341: nəkàstrenu nə lìsnici i hrànehme gi enèj i pəs’è n gi ufč’ɛ̀r’
[and other] leaf cuttings. We fed them that way, and the shepherd takes them to graze
41347: pu pu gòr’e lès uttùkə nəgòr’e sɛ̀kəd’e
up above Les, to all the places up in the hills around here.
41348: [And when do you milk the sheep?]
41354: əgà ut jègnetənə udmàhneme tugà dujìme ufc’èn’e tə i ml’èku
We milk them after we separate them from the lambs, and [get] milk –
41358: i i pr’èsnu i màslu ìmə sìčku ə zbìrəli sme
fresh [milk and yogurt] and butter – there’s everything [you need]; and we gathered
41362: məslà [unintelligible]  əmə pu mnògu òfc’e im’èhm’e
[sufficient] fat [unintelligible].  We had quite a lot of sheep.
41367: ne b’è pu altmɯ̀š dəvàr šejsè̝ ufcì i
It wasn’t [like now]. Each [of us] had "altmŭš" (60) [that is] "šejset" (60) head of sheep.
41374: i bubàjkunu si mi be ufčɛ̀r’ si im’è i i kulìbə si im’èhme
My father was a shepherd and had – we had our own [summer pasture] hut.
41380: i tə i sme n’è ejtùvə gl’ɤ̀dəli tò ejtùvə ne mòž’e fəf s’è̝lusu
We didn’t keep [the sheep] here: you can’t do it here in the village.
41385: èj dəl’è̝č’e nə kul’ìbə ədìn səhàt’ pʌ̀t’
[You have to go] far off in the summer pasture hut, an hour’s [walk] away.
41388: i tàm gi gl’èdəhme f kulìbənə
That’s where we kept them, in the summer hut.
41389: [And did you used to go to Komotini?
41395: ne sm’è hòdili nìe pu g’um’urž’ìne pɤ̀ nìe ne sm’ʌ̀ bəlì nìj
[No,] we didn’t go to Komotini. [No,] we weren’t
41398: nèkvi bugàti tə də ìdem nə gumurž’ìne [laughter]
rich [enough] to [be able] to go to Komotini. [laughter]
41402: èj tùkə kinàt si iskàrəhm’ə f kulìbənə i ku zəkòl’əš’
[We stayed] here and earned our keep from the hut. If you slaughter [your animals]
41405: ku prudəd’è̝š’ š’ə də ìməš pərì ku ne zəkòl’əš’ i ne prudàvəš’
and sell [the meat], you’ll have money. If you don’t slaughter and sell [your livestock]
41408: n’èmə də ìməš’ nì pərì kòjtu lu pàti  [laughter] i n’èmə nikinà
you won’t have money. Always suffering [laughter], without anything at all.
41411: ne smè hòdili pu g’um’urž’ìne də ràbutime nàšte hòd’ehə du
We didn’t go to Komotini to work. Our [men] would go to –
41413: du hàskuvu i du kɯ̀ržələ i i i du plòdif
to Haskovo, to Kurdzhali, and – and to Plovdiv.
41417: i t’è sə hòdil’i hòdum pu dvà dè̝n’ə də vərvìš’
They went there by foot. It took two days walking
41424: du plòdiv də pòjdeš’ dè̝ dè̝ e bilɤ̀lə kulà nè e im’è̝lu
to get to Plovdiv. Where were there any cars? There weren’t any!
41425: [What did the men do for a living?]
41430: nàšte mɤ̀ž’uve sə kəzəndìsvəli də nə hràn’et əm kàk tò nè s’èe
Our menfolk earned enough to keep us fed. Not like now, though,
41438: kəsu es’ɛ̀ də kàram’ə i ž’əvòt’ brəšnònu tɨ gu dukàrət sml’ètu
they way we enjoy life now. They bring flour to you already ground,
41443: vɤ̀lnənə tɨ dukàrət ispr’ɤ̀denə pr’ɤ̀lu tò se l’ɤ̀snu es’ɛ̀ ž’uvèi
they bring wool to you as already spun yarn. This kind of life is easy!
41447: əmə kàk sme nìe ž’ìli i tə tə səm ž’ìlə duksàn gudìni
But the way we lived – !  I’ve lived through "doksan" (90) years.
41460: My sister? My sister is dead.
41468: ìməm ɤd’ìn bràt èjtùkə ə blìze
I have one brother, he lives nearby.
41471: tò e nè e n’ɛ̀kəf stàr tò e nə həltmɯ̀š’ i
He’s not old at all, he’s around "altmŭš" (60).
41474: həltmɯ̀š’ jedì li e nə znàm kòlko
"Altmŭš-jedi" (67) maybe? I don’t know how old he is.
41477: əhə à po bɤ̀lgarski kàk e altmɤ̀š jedì ili šejsè i sèdem
Ah. How much is "altmŭš-jedi" (67) in Bulgarian? "Šejset i sedem" (67)?
41479: xɤ̀ xɤ̀ šejsè̝ i sè̝dem gudìni
Hah, hah! "Šejset i sedem" (67) years old.
41482: … [since you need] money [to go] to the store..
41485: A kneading trough. OK, and then?
41489: We knead the dough inside [the kneading trough].
41491: i kɤ̀k sə zamìsə tistòto vɤ̀tre
And how do you knead the dough inside it?
41497: zəm’ìsə sə səs vudìčka səs kvàs təkà ə učil’ùvəm gi
You mix it with a bit of water, and with yeast, then I divide it up
41500: zə də ne mòe də sə mòkr’et sìčki snòpi gi pràv’əm
so they won’t get wet. I make all of the sheaves
41502: nə kup’èn kugàtu zəvəlì də nə mòe də sə mòkr’et
into a pile so that when it starts to rain they won’t get wet.
41504: i kətu už’ɤ̀neme nəfs’àkəde sìčki nìvi i pòčvəme tugàvə də vərš’ìjeme
And after we’ve reaped everywhere, all the fields, the we start to thresh.
41507: vərš’ìjeme səs mùl’etu i məgàretu nə tòzi ərmàn kədètu sə kupnìte
We thresh with mules and donkeys, on that threshing-floor where the piles are.
41514: slet kəd gu uvərš’ìjeme iskàrəme slàmətə uddelìme jə ud ž’ìtutu
After we finish threshing, we pull out the straw, and separate it from the grain.
41519: vəzbərèm ž’ìtutu nə əd’ìn kùp i si ìəme spec’àlni lupàt’i dɤ̀rveni
We gather up the grain into a stack and – we have these special wooden shovels,
41522: kàzvəme mu lupàtə i pòčvəme də fɤ̀rl’əme vəv vɤ̀zduxə nəgòre
we call them “shovels”, and begin to throw [the grain] up in to the air,
41528: i v’àtərə udd’àl’ə pl’əvʌ̀tə i ž’ìtutu ustàvə č’ìstu i slet kətu
and the wind separates out the chaff, and the grain ends up clean. And after
41532: sìčku gu udvìjeme səbìrəme žìtutu f čuvàli pl’əvʌ̀tə səs slàmətə gi slàgəme
we winnow everything, we gather the grain up into sacks and put the chaff with the straw
41538: vəv vərvìl’niki t’ìjə vərvìl’niki gi tuvàrime nə mùl’etu pu ədìn vərvìl’nik òtstrənə
into net bags. We load these bags onto the mules, one on each side,
41543: i pràvu fəf pl’èvn’ətə zə prez zìmətə də mòe də ədɤ̀t
and straight into the barn, so that they’ll be able to eat during the winter,
41545: də ìmə kvò də gi rànime
so there will be something to feed them.
41549: kràvite i mùletə mùl’etu i məgàretu dubìtəkə guv’èdə guv’èdətə i mùl’etu
Cows, mules – the mule, the donkey – the livestock! Cattle, the cattle, the mule –
41550: [What time (of year) did you go out to do the mowing?]
41554: kugàtu l’uvàdite dòdət vr’ème də sə kus’èt utìvəm səs mùl’etu i məgàretu
When it comes time to mow the meadows, I go out with the mule and the donkey.
41563: zìməm kusʌ̀ta kuvəlàta brusʌ̀ i ut’ìvəm nə l’uvàdata i pòčvəm də kòs’e
I take a scythe, a small anvil and a whetstone, I go out to the meadow, and I start to mow,
41569: də ftàsə l’àba kɤ̀ktu i sigà ftàsuva kəto gu m’ès’ət
[for it] to ferment [and rise], like bread rises now after they knead it.
41578: tìj ìmət məjɤ̀ s’à gutòva pɤ̀k nìj si pruizvèždəjmi
Now they have ready-made yeast. But we used to make our own.
41583: i kɤ̀k se proizvèždə tàjə majà
And how do you make this yeast?
41588: amì təkà ut idnòtu du [laughter] ud idìnijə ud idìnijə l’àp du drùgijə
Well, like this: from one [laughter], from the one [loaf] of bread to the next.
41591: ne mòže se pokàčiž gòre be
41599: òti sèko sègane tò sə čùpi unuvà klònə
Because that branch breaks each time you reach up there.
41608: mlò̝gu sə kr’ɔ̀hki təj vìšnici tvà vìšni
They’re very delicate, these sour cherry trees. [Here,] these cherries:
41617: vìšnici tvà tò ìmə i dᶤìvɤ əmə dᶤìvətì sə i tè rudìlɨ
Cherry trees. There are ungrafted ones as well, and those have also borne fruit.
41620: The ungrafted ones are a little bitter.
41624: ò tì sə gurčìfki pə tɛ̀ə sə kìsəlki
Yes, those are a little bitter, but these are sour.
41625: Yes, they’re sour, [because they’re the] wild [type].
41639: tə hi jədɔ̀t tìj pil’cète krùški lənì behə rudᶤìli tə i
and these little birds eat [the cherries]. The pear trees bore fruit last year, and
41642: i t’àh krùški i krùški jədɛ̀hə i dènu pàščicənə
and those pears – they also ate the pears. [At the point] where the stem is,
41649: tə mu jə kəlvè kəlvè kəlvè i tugàvə pàdne krùškənə
[that’s where the bird] pecks and pecks and pecks at it. Then the pear falls,
41655: nə rʌ̀ka slèt kətu gu òkus’e səber’èm gu nə ərmàni issuš’ìme gu
by hand. After I finish mowing we gather [the hay] up onto threshing fields, and dry it,
41657: i dòle jə jədè tugàvə [laughter] tugàf hi jədɛ̀ə
[and when it’s] down, then it eats it. [laughter] That’s when they ate them.
41659: i slet tuvà nə kòpi gu səberèm i ottàm pàk vəv vərvìl’niki
and after that we gather it into stacks and from there again into bags.
41662: vəv vərvìl’niki i nə mùl’etu gu dukàrvəme pl’èvn’ətə zə dubìtəkə
Into bags, which we then drive in on the mules [to] the barn for the livestock –
41664: for the mule and the cattle.
41665: [What else did you do when you were young?]
41670: nə mlàdite gud’ìni də kàž’e jàz bèx mnògu gul’àm xurəž’ìj
In my youth, so to say, I was a great aficionado of the round dance.
41676: mnògu igràex xurò i sə səbìrəme ergènite fsìčki i mòmite
I danced the round dance a lot. We would get together, bachelors and maidens,
41681: tàm nə ednò spec’àlnu m’àstu kədèt mu kàzvəm’e igrìšte
at a special place that we called the dancing area.
41685: i s’àkə s’ed ned’èl’e se səbìrəme tàm i igràeme hòru
And we would gather there every Sunday and dance the round dance.
41693: iməš’e tugàvə muzikànte n’àkuj s cigùlkə svìl’exə svìr’exə n’àkuj
There were musicians then, some played the violin, and some
41701: gulɛ̀m zbò̝r stò̝rɨhə sìčkutu sə zbràhə tɛ̀hni rudìtəli i nàšɨ
They put on a big festival, they gathered everyone, their parents and ours.
41705: izlɛ̀zuhə rudnìni uttùkə ut širò̝kə.ləkə dèt si gu nìj znàeme
Relatives came out from here and from Shiroka Lŭka, the ones we know,
41709: širò̝kə.ləkə dɛ̀ uttùkə ut n sulištà drùgə məhəlìčkə ìmə
[from] Shiroka Lŭka and from here, from Sulishta, there’s another part of the village,
41712: tùkə imɛ̀ dvɛ̀ krùški tə hi duɛ̀duhə lənì
There were two pear trees here, and last year they ate up all [the fruit]!
41714: pràite li gi na burkàni ne
Do you put them up in jars? [Or] not?
41720: əmi žə gi tùr’ə nə burkàn žə hmə òčist’ə tvà upàškiti
Well, I’ll put them up in jars. I’ll take off the stems,
41724: səs zəhərč’ìcə i vudìcə i žə hi zàtvur’ə
I’ll cover them up with a bit of sugar and water
41725: i žə klòknət màlku i žə
and they’ll bubble for a while, and [then] I’ll –
41726: You don’t clean (= peel and seed) them?
41730: nè nè nè ne sɔ̀ čìskeni sìn nè nè ne sɔ̀
No, no, no. They’re not “cleaned”, child. No, no. They’re not.
41734: am tè sə tè sə nè prɤ̀skani nè nìštu [unintelligible] è go
They’re not sprayed, or anything [like that]. [unintelligible] Look at that!
41739: nè nè ə pučtì m burkànə hi tùr’əm tugà budnɔ̀š sə trɛ̀və
No, no. I put more [of them] in jars. Sometimes one – You have to
41747: də hmɤ učìstiš əku e slàtku də hmɤ učìstiš pɔ̀rs i tìn’ə
clean it, if it’s [for] preserves, to clean the dirt and mud off of them.
41754: i tugàə də stò stò stòriš siròpčekən i də hi tùrəš tugàvə
And then you make a little syrup, and put them in.
41763: klič’ònətə mu vìkəhme tàm ti e brəšnòt tàm ti e əmbàrə
We called it the “klichona”. That’s where the flour is, and the granary,
41770: d’èt si sm’èlilu ž’itòtu gu si dukàrəlu iz vud’enìcətə
where you’ve ground the grain. You’ve brought it from the mill,
41773: sm’èlilu gu si nəpràvilu gu si slòž’ilu gu si tàm
you’ve ground it, you’ve prepared it, you’ve put it away there,
41778: tì e gutòvu v’èč’e də m’ɛ̀siš i piš’tɤ̀ si e tàm
and now [everything] is ready for you to knead [bread]. And the stove is there,
41782: i trì stài imɛ̀hme dòlu trì imɛ̀hme gòre
and we had three rooms below and three above.
41788: əmə dɤ̀rveni dɤ̀rv’enu stud’ènu jɛ̀ se č’ùdim s’eà
But wooden! Wooden, and cold! I am amazed now,
41793: [how] all these beautiful houses [still] get cold.
41795: And what did you use for heating?
41801: əmì səz ž’àpkə p’èč’kə atùk tùkənà jə kumìnə
Well, a little oven here, and here a fireplace ...
41808: ... was lit and then a fire over there ...
41814: drùgu sèlce ìmə tə tùkə imɛ̀še n nə hòro tùkə igràha i
another small village, and it was here, and they danced the horo
41820: i tàm dènu onàja i pìsuvə kuì sa pučìnɤlɨ tàm nə č’ešmìcata
over there. And [the names] of [those] who died there, are written on the fountain.
41825: əmə zgà kadè ž ìdete də spᶤìte
But now where will you go to sleep?
41837: From one loaf of bread to the next.
41840: si ustàviš i drùgijə pɤ̀t gu m’èsiš
You put it aside, and then knead it [in] the next time [you make bread].
41842: You leave it like this in a little ball.
41850: a f kakvò go pràviš tovà tòpčence kədè gu slàgəš
And what do you make this little ball in? Where do you put it?
41853: əmi stàviš gu f inɤ̀ pənìčka
You leave it in a little dish.
41859: jednà turbìčka ušìem si turbìčka mənìnka
A little bag. We sew ourselves a tiny little bag
41865: təkà tə kòl’ku də zə jedìn l’àp tuvà zə inò misìlo
[that’s] just the size for one bread, for one batch.
41871: dvà trì l’àbə žə upičèš səs pòdn’icə gi pičèjmi
You [can] bake two or three loaves of bread [with it]. We’d bake them in a dish.
41920: ha ha ha ha dà sɛ̀t’uf sə sɛ̀t’uf sə sɛ̀t’uf sə sɛ̀t’uf
Hah, hah, hah, hah! Yes! I’ve got it. I’ve got it. I’ve got it. I’ve got it.
41926: tò e blìsku be uttùva žə fànte patèkata i nagòr təkà
That’s close to here, you know. You’ll take the path that goes up over there.
41928: Yes, we just came from there.
41930: We just came from there now. From there!
41931: Hah! Hah! You’ve come from there.
41934: ah ha ha ha nàči uttàm ste dušlì ud gelà
Ahh! Hah. So you’ve come from there, from Gela.
41940: əm pu gelà pìtahte li nɛ̀kva bàpka kvò s mène
And did you ask [questions of] some granny like me [somewhere] around Gela?
41949: pìta əm tà kəkvò v kàza ha
You asked.  Well, what did she tell you, huh?
41953: And [I bet] she too [talked about] the old days, [how it was] before.
41960: ednà legènda za kogà kurbàn se prài predì
A legend about when they used to make a sacrifice earlier on.
41966: It’s said that every year a deer used to come.
41969: tè stànvət hùbəvu əmə nèməm ne mì sə urəštìsvə
They come out nice. But I don’t have – I’m not up [for all that].
41972: Uh huh. And you have pears.
41973: Yes, there are two or three pear trees here.
41976: Two. They [both] had borne fruit, but –
41977: pràvime si ut ə n glìnə ə pòdn’icə i vɤ̀tre gi pičèm
We make [this] dish out of, uh, clay and bake the loaves inside it.
41983: vrɤ̀šnik ìməm stujɤ̀t òšti zə zət.kɤ̀šti səm gi ustàvilə
I have a cover [to that dish]. It’s still sitting in back of the house [where] I left it.
41988: Of course! I broke all of mine.
41995: n’è pòd’nicə ustàna v’èči n’è nìštu [laughter]
I don’t have a single dish left, nothing any more
41998: i ednà godìna ne gò ostàili da si počìne
And that one year they didn’t allow it to rest.
42004: gl’ɔ̀daj zgà ətùka zət tùrlata nìj ìməme pàk ə təkòvə ədìn
Look here. We have, here behind Turla another one like that.
42006: ə zət tùrlasa ìma tvà gu zuvèm tùrlata
Behind Turla there’s this – we call [that place] Turla, ...
42019: And where does that name come from?
42027: tùrlata istàtak ìma adnɔ̀ cèrkvɨca è napràvena cɤ̀rkvɨca ut starìnnu ò̝šte
Beyond Turla there’s a little church, a church built way back in olden times.
42033: ut starìnnu unàa cɤ̀rkvica napràv’ena enàa cɤ̀rkvɨca napràv’ena i etàm
It’s built in olden times, this little church. And at this little church
42039: trɛ̀va da kò̝l’et kurbàn’ aku nɤ kò̝l’et kurbàn’ pàda grò̝b
people have to make a sacrificial offering, and if they don’t then a grave opens up
42043: səs gàjdə svìrexa i n’è igràeme nə xurò vesel’àme sa dumɤ̀t
played the bagpipe. And we danced the round dance and had a great time at home.
42049: usòbenu kəgàtu pìnehme mnògu n’àštu veselì [laughter]
There was a lot to keep us happy, especially when we’d had a bit to drink! [laughter]
42050: [How do you make staves for barrels?]
42054: dəgìte nə bɤ̀čvətə gi pràv’əm po ednòvrèmešnu si òšte
I still make staves for barrels in the old-fashioned way.
42060: nə ògən gi nəvìvəm i im dàvəm fòr fòrmə nə dəgà
I bend them over the fire into the shape of a rainbow.
42063: i slet tu ku kətu gi nəvìjə fsìčkite dɤ̀ski zə bɤ̀čvətə
And after I bend all the boards for the barrel,
42075: slet tvà gi puč’ìstvəm č’ɤ̀rnutu d’ètu ògənə e gur’àl səs t’eslàta
after that I use an adze to clean off the blackened area where the fire has burned it.
42079: puizd’àluvam gi i slet tuvà vèč’e pòčvəm də gi prekàrvəm nə plàn’ətə
I cut them to shape and after that begin to put them through the planing machine.
42082: slet kətu gi prèkərə fsìčki nə plàn’ətə rəbòt’e gi nə čàp
After I run everything through the planing machine, I make them up on a model,
42086: tòə čàp ə gu izrəbòtvəm pu mòjə s isč’islènie
a model [according to] which I have worked out by my own calculation
42091: da ni kàžeš ednò vrème svàdbite kàk stanùvaxa nabɤ̀rže
Can you tell us – briefly – how weddings were done in the old days?
42098: svàdbite stanùvaxa togàva jà takà sme slagàli jà po zemjàta
They did weddings – back then we spread out on the ground,
42102: po ùlicìte takòva sme slagàli pešk’ìrčeta tkàeme ednò vrème
we spread out cloths along the streets, [cloths] that we wove in the old days
42107: ot stòkata takà ot ə vɤ̀lnička i si napràime a tòlkafki peškìrčeta
from the wool from our animals. So we made cloths of this size,
42112: i sobèremè si ot komšìite peškìrje sɤ̀štite òti ne mòžem
and we gather up the same kinds of cloths from the neighbors, since we wouldn’t
42116: da smògnem od nàšte peškìrje i si slàgame po ùlicìte trapèzite
