42842: [And how long is a cow’s pregnancy?]
42850: A cow carries [her calf] nine months.
42853: əmxəm i kàk gu vìkaš kə̥tu se rodì
Umhm. And how do you call it when [the cow] gives birth?
42858: utè̝l’uvə sə kràvənə i ràdə tè̝lence [laughter]
The cow calves, and a calf is born!
42859: dà pòsle kvò stàva na ednà godìna kàk mu kàzvate
Yes. So then what happens after a year [has passed]? How do you call it?
42865: Well, we – they call it a heifer.
42873: pòslet əgà e mʌ̀sku pàk vòl sə ə rudɨ̀l xə̀
Then if it’s a male, [you say] an ox has been born. Hah.
42876: əgà e ž’è̝ncku jinìcə vòl je pàk kugà stàn’e gul’èmu
If it’s a female, a heifer. [We call it] an ox when it gets big –
42877: gà [cough] dv’è gudìni tugàvə nə trì də urɤ̀t
when [cough] it’s two or three years old, when [it’s old enough] to plow.
42885: čilɛ̀ka hi i tòj uttàm əmə bɛ̀ha dušlì etùva da žyvɛ̀at
and her husband, also from there, but they had come here to live, [though]
42891: ne znàja kakvà kakɤ̀f srò̝t imɛ̀ha tugàva mumčèncetu
I don’t know what relation they had here. So [there’s] this young man –
42894: ìma tùka takòva dètu əa tuvà be dètu za za tò̝ka
and then there’s this thing here where – ah, where there’s – it’s for, for electricity.
42897: za tò̝ka dètu nəlì grad’ɔ̀t ednò visòku
For electricity, you know, where they build this tall –
42906: anəvà visò̝kunu dènu za tò̝kan i tò̝ sa gràbna i nò̝lkuva beše
That tall thing that’s for electricity. And he took hold of it. And he was this old –
42911: katu na petnàes šesnàes gudìni mumč’èncətu i tò fàna ta sa dràpna
a boy of maybe fifteen or sixteen years, and he went and pulled back,
42915: tà sa fàna i izgurɛ̀ cɛ̀lku i gu pùsnaha i pàdna
and then grabbed [it] and burnt all up. And they released him, and he fell.
42919: i pàdna mòmč’encètu dukàrahà gu etùka səs səs kulà gu dukàraha
The boy fell and they brought him here by – They brought him here by car.
42924: ur’ɛ̀hme səs vòl’ve sèj kinàtu sme to nè e səs s ejnəkvì
With the oxen we plowed like this – what we did was not like the way
42927: kəsu es’à urɤ̀t səs tràkturi i səs dìznə kinà əmi səs uràlu
they plow now, with tractors and who knows what, but with a wooden plow.
42932: i uràlə səm i i kupàlə səm i i səs vòlv’ene səm uràlə
I did the plowing and the digging, and I plowed with the oxen
42934: And it was you who did the spinning?
42941: jà tàa čèrga što tì a pokažà
Look at that rug that she showed you!
42947: tàa čèrga saà što à pokažàx
[About] that rug that I just showed you –
42950: if you knew what sort of –
42951: [Знаеш ли някоя друга жена в махалата която да поговорим?]
[Do you know of any other woman around the village we could talk to?]
42957: znàči sè tì fsè predèše na toà
You mean all that – you spun all that on this –
42964: I was going to marry [my] beloved
42968: na velìgden k’e se žèna prolettà
on Easter. I was going to get married in the spring,
42972: a tàa čèrga ìska da se istkàe i jàs tkàa
but this rug needed to be fully woven. So I’m weaving
42976: na tèmnoto večertà na ednà gàzena làmbička
in the dark of night, with just one gas lantern [to see by].
42982: drugàro mi sedì do mène da a ìstkaam ta da se ožènim
My fiancé is sitting by me [making sure] I finish weaving so we can get married
42985: òti nèmam čèrga pa a se òženàm
because I don’t [yet] have the rug [that I need] to get married.
42992: jà ama ne stignà vɤ̀lnata ne možè a stìgne
Ah, but there wasn’t enough wool. I couldn’t finish it,
42997: elì pa zìmašèa togàva pa narjàt mnògo vɤ̀lna
because they (the state) were taking for their quota a lot of wool.
43005: tàa mòjta màjka ošlà zainèla od ednì xòra
So my mother went off to some people to borrow
43008: tr’àvə də ftàsə təkà kətu ftàsə
It has to ferment like this, and when it ferments –
43014: i kətu gu ustàvim to s tòplə vudìčkə sə m’èsi
And [before] we leave it to sit, we [add] a little warm water and knead it
43019: vɤ̀lna sčepkàxme a nəprəìhme a rodìteli da vìdiš spokòjni
the wool. We carded it and made it up. Ah, such mellow parents.
43025: i e na ednò mùle prɤ̀f pàt mu tùrat samàr
And then they saddle a mule, the first time he’d carried a packsaddle.
43031: tùrat mu samàro zakàčat mu vɤ̀nata vjahnùam mùleto
They put on the packsaddle, load up the wool, and I ride the mule
43034: ot stàroto sèlo f sandànski samà
[all the way] from our old village site to Sandanski – alone!
43041: bès bèz da e kàrano mùl’eto
Without – without the mule having been ridden [before that].
43044: samà prɤ̀f pàt samàr mu slòžat i da go pùsnat tovà detè
Alone! The first time the mule is saddled! And to let this child
43049: da ìde na vlačàrka otìvam f sandànski izvlàčuvàm vɤ̀lnata
go [like that] to the carder. I go off to Sandanski, get the wool carded,
43054: kàčvam se ot trì časò na mùl’eto è slɤ̀ncetu takà
mount the mule again at three o’clock, the sun already [down to] here,
43056: kàčvam se stàroto sèlo takvìja smèli dèca sme bilì
and I ride all the way back to our old village. Such brave children we were!
43062: nèma i dnèska i na òhò nèma dnèska nèma noštèska
Day or night – oh ho! Doesn’t matter if it’s day or night.
43068: è tàm na balkàno kolìbata baštà mi me ostài tàm noštèska
My father would leave me there at night, way up in the mountain hut
43070: da sàm pri ofcìte da i pàza
to stay with the sheep and watch over them.
43075: s kvəsɤ̀ i ftàsə i pòsl’ə zìməš kòl’kutu ti tr’àbvə
with yeast, and it ferments. After that you take as much as you need,
43082: kətu mɤ̀š’ wòt’i məžɤ̀ mi e hòdil də mi kəzəndɨ̀svə
like a man, because my husband had gone off to earn a living for us,
43086: i də mə ràni siràk səm z’ə̟̀lə tə tvà e
and to feed me. I took [him on in marriage] as an orphan. That’s how it is.
43095: vè̝č’er pu ədnà kupàn’ə gul’èmə nə upštinɤ̀sə səm pè̝klə hl’èp
[Every] evening, I baked bread for the municipality, a large kneading trough [full].
43103: nem’èhme ni fùrnə ni nìkina ɤjtùvə im’ɛ̀ u mè̝ne ədnɤ̀ fìrnə
We didn’t have an outdoor oven or anything. There was one oven here near me,
43108: u ejt’ùvə càltu s’è̝lu [unintelligible] ʌd’ɨ̀n p’eš im’è tə
[the only one] in the the whole village [unintelligible] Just [the] one oven and
43116: tə pu p’ɤ̀t pʌ̀ti zə den’è ispìč’ehme ədnɤ̀nə ədnɤ̀nə kupàn’ə ispeč’è̝me
so we had to bake five times a day. We would bake from one kneading trough,
43124: i drùgə iskìsne i nə upštinɤ̀nə də i nòs’ət
with dough rising in another, and then take it to them at the municipality.
43134: jɛ̀ im səm p’èklə hl’èbən nem’èš’e fùrnə d’è e kəsu eseà
I did [all] the baking of bread for them. There wasn’t a large oven like there is now.
43143: tì n’əmòj gl’ɤ̀dəj s’à mnògu kɤ̀šti nìj behme nè esòlku
Don’t judge by how many houses there are now – we weren’t so many then.
43158: i upštinàtə be ejtùkə dè̝su et’ùvə minòvət ənɤ̀ d’è̝su ìmə
The municipal hall was here, here where people pass by, where there’s a –
43201: ejtùvə kətu məgəzìnč’e tə etàm beš’e tò dòlu nemè
this little store now, that’s where it was. There wasn’t anything there [then]
43203: nì behme màlku kɤ̀šti pək seà sə se isplòdili
there were very few houses of us, but now they've multiplied [many times over].
43210: vɤ̀rštəm sə nòs’əm ə č’e kvàs ta pàk drùgi zàmes’əm òti ne sʌ̀m
I would come back bringing starter, and mix up another batch because I couldn’t do
43214: zə ədìn p’è̝š’ i dvà pu p’èt p’è̝šti sme p’è̝kli nədòlu
just one or two. We did five bakings per day [for them] down there,
43217: nə d’ènu upštinɤ̀nə də ni nòs’ət ejtàm l’èbə
for them at the municipality to bring bread to [all of] us.
43221: nè ni e ud drùgəde fùrnənə es’à nemòj gl’èdəj
Our oven is not from another place, so don’t jump to conclusions
43224: gà ìmə fùrni ajtùkə ədnɤ̀ fùrnə im’èhme
when you see many ovens here. We had just that one,
43229: i tòə puìməš’e du trìjsi hl’èbə fùrnənə mùt’kə
and it would take up to thirty loaves. [It was] a small oven.
43238: əmhəm kòl’kunu je ugrəd’è̝nə bilà ev’è̝l ət kinànə səm nəšlɤ̀ ugrəd’è̝nu
Yes. The size it had been built earlier on. When I came upon it [it had already] been built.
43244: tò nem’è ejtùvən də grəd’èt ni budnòn nìk’əna
They weren’t going to build anything new [for so few people].
43246: tò es’à sə e nəs’è̝lilu mlògu pək
The area is much [more] settled now.
43253: i i nə č’ərkmɤ̀tə kləd’èš’ pàk kandž’èl’e gòre də svərìš’
And you put a hanging lamp up on the “churkma” in order to cook –
43261: ə f udž’àkə vɤ̀tre zəkàč’iš’ ìmə idnòvrɛ̀meš’en kəndžìl ž’il’ɛ̀zən
[Yes,] in the hearth. You’d hang this old-fashioned iron lamp –
43266: zəkàč’iš’ tàmkənə čərkmɤ̀tə kləd’èš’ burnìčkətə də ti svɛ̀ti
you’d hang [it] there [on] the “churkma” and light some kindling [in it]
43271: də vìdiš’ tvà tàm f tɤ̀vnutu n’èmə làmbə s kvò də sv’ɛ̀tiš’
so you could see there in the dark. There weren’t any [modern] lamps to light.
43275: sìč’ku stàrə ràbutə làmbə n’èmə drùgu n’èmə kləd’èš nə č’ərkmɤ̀tə
Everything [was] old-time. No lamps, no other [light source]. You put [up] the “churkma”
43282: də ti sv’ɛ̀tɨ vərìš’ pupàrətə bɤ̀rkəž z dɤ̀rvenətə lədžìcә̥
to give you light, you cook the porridge, you stir it with a wooden spoon.
43289: bɤ̀rkəž’ bɤ̀rkəš’ tàm čərkmɤ̀tə ti sv’ɛ̀ti udvɤ̀tre nə kòlə
You stir and stir and the “churkma” gives you [enough] light, from a post
43293: pə f kumìnə də dud’è sə svərì dud’è sə nəpràvi jɛ̀d’en’ètu
inside the fireplace to do the cooking and prepare food [to eat].
43296: ta nə koè kàzvate vìe čɤrkmɤ̀
And – what is this [thing] you call “churkma”?
43305: uvedèmo pa àjde če tɤčèmo a no napredèmo pàk stàrete ženè napredù
We thread it, and then we’ll weave. And then we spin again. The old women spin
43312: ot štìmɤt tòj štòto smo vadìle osnòvutu za osnòvu da vìemo
the woof thread. The thread that we got for the warp is [what] we wind
43313: na krosnòto a tòj pɤk stìm ga zovèmo sìtnoto
onto the beam, but “woof thread” is what we call the tiny stuff,
43321: onò pa za potkàvu za klàšn’ete da pretɤčèmo
what [we use] for the woof [for when] we weave the homespun.
43325: pa tegà àjde istɤčèmo ga ò iskàle smo klàšn’e
And then we weave it all up. Ah, now we’ve woven the homespun!
43330: à če nòsimo na val’àvicu u tṛgòvište ìmaše tùj ni sɤsèdno selò
And we’ll take it to the fuller: there was one in Tŭrgovište, the village next to us.
43333: na val’àvicu ta da ga vàl’u tàm klàšn’ete
[We take it] to the fuller to full the homespun for us there.
43337: ta gi vàl’u tùpu gi tùpan’e lùpan’e [laughter]
And they full it – they pound it. Pounding, banging! [laughter]
43343: pa pòsle gi učìnimo i àjde nòse na kròen’e šivàč koj jè
And then we dye it, and now they take it for sewing, [to the] tailor, you know?
43349: òn si pa skròi pantalòne drèju odàvna džemadàn’e kròešeu
He’s [the one who] makes pants, clothing. In the old days they made outer coats.
43357: ne čìne ga deràmčeta ò ženà pa si nòsi na ràbutu
He didn’t dye it. Vests. Ah, a woman wears those to work in,
43363: deràmče belò deràmče detè če ponesè pa da si zavìe detè
vests, white vests. A woman will carry her child [in it], wrap it up [in it],
43367: lùlila tùri pa tùri na lùlilata deràmčeto
put it on cradle supports, put the vest on the cradle supports.
43371: ta vàrdi detèto da ne dùva mu vètɤr
And that protects the child, so wind doesn’t blow on it, ...
43378: kədè e tùka tùka li f sèlo šivàčka ìmaše
Where’s he? Was there a tailor here in the village?
43380: ìmaše i u selò ama nosìli si u drùgo m
There was one in the village – but people took things to another –
43382: na drùgo mèsto ma ìmaše si u selò
to some other place. But there was one in the village.
43384: Was it Tŭrgovište [that they took things] to?
43392: è vìden nikòličov on opandžàci pɤk pràeše tɤčèmo i opandžàci
... um, Viden Nikolichov, he used to make hooded cloaks. We weave them too,
43397: ta kat ìdu ofčarè da si pɤk zagṛ̀nu opandžàk če vàli dɤ̀š
for shepherds when they go out, so they can cloak themselves up if it rains,
43401: pa studenò pa spù tàm na kolìbutu na tṛl’àkɤt ə
or is cold, because they sleep in the hut up in the sheep pen.
43405: pa opandžàci tɤčèšemo pa tìja s ofcète
And we would weave the hooded cloaks for the [ones who went] with the sheep,
43407: pa tìja gi čovèk šìeše vìden nikòličov ìmaše edɤ̀n stàr čovèk
and this old man, Viden Nikolichov. would sew them up.
43413: ò màjstor na opandžàci na deràmčeta [laughter]
He was a specialist in hooded cloaks and women’s vests. [laughter]
43420: svè od vḷ̀na vrèče àjde če tɤčèmo vrèče da zakàramo žìto
Everything from wool. Bags – let’s weave bags to carry the wheat,
43425: da zakàramo kukùrus na vodenìcutu i tòj smo tkàle vrèče
to carry corn to the mill, and such. [Yes,] we wove bags.
43431: vrèče vrèče sɤ̀ga zovù čuvalè tegàj ga vrèče zovèšemo
Bags, bags. Now they call them sacks, but back them we called them bags.
43436: a vɤ̀lnata ofcète go strìžat a prolettɤ̀ li lèto kogà
And [for] wool, when do they shear the sheep? Spring? Summer?
43440: proletɤ̀ kat mìne gerg’òvden kat se stòpli vèče
In the spring, right after St. George’s Day, when it's already warm [enough].
43444: Let’s be off to the sheep!
43447: ajde àjde da se da olɤ̀kne na ofcète če gim žèga
Let’s, let’s be off to the sheep, let’s lighten their load. Because they’re hot.
43451: ne mògu u žègutu ofcète s vḷ̀nutu
Sheep can’t take the heat when they [are still covered] in wool.
43495: i kɤ̀k se e pràvil harmàn idnò vrème
And how was the threshing field constructed in the old days?
43501: hərmàn’ə z’èmim tə puravnìm èj tùkə tvà ut tùkə nadòlu
[For] the threshing field, we take and level out [an area], about like from here on down.
43504: ə puravnìm gu i zèmim tə gu zalèim səs vudɤ̀ i
We level it out, and we take and we water it down, and
43507: i ìmə kul’endrò kujètu ut təkɤ̀vu ut kàmək ni znàjə
there’s a roller like this, made of stone – I don’t know
43514: dəlì sti vìždəli tuvà èj tòl’kəvi sə dlɤ̀gi èj takɤ̀vu dib’èlu
if you’ve [ever] seen one. They’re about so long, and so thick,
43519: i dvèti stərnì ž’ulezà sə pɤk nəpràveni təkà vəf kàməka
with iron on both sides and constructed like this: in the stone
43523: ə dv’è dərv’ètə sə fànət pɤk na tùkə
there’s two [pieces] of wood. You grasp them here
43526: tə sə vlɤ̀v’ət pɤk ə zə vulòviti li tàm tìj
and then harness it onto the oxen there, those –
43530: nelì sə mùət pək vulòviti ta tɤ̀j natàtəka
you know, those oxen that are bumbling about. And then [moving] onward
43535: d’è tə harmàn’ə tɤ̀j gu pribìvəmi səs ə tòjə kàmək
along the threshing field, we smooth it out with this stone,
43550: č’ərkmɤ̀ d’ètu slàgəme burnɤ̀tə ednò vrɛ̀me svetìlu
The “churkma” is where we put kindling in the old days, a light [source] …
43560: təkà zəkàč’enkə i dòlu è təkvà kətu reš’ètč’icə
[It was] hanging [from it], and underneath was a sort of little grate.
43563: kətu riš’ètkə nàč’i č’ərkmɤ̀ mu vìkəme
It’s like a small grate. We call it a “churkma”.
43567: i zəpàliš’ burnìč’kətə ti sv’ɛ̀ti ə tùk ti e kandžìlə
and you set fire to the kindling, and it gives you light. And here’s the hanging lamp ...
43570: slòžiš go sv’ɛ̀t’ə nə tàm nə jàdenetu dètu e
You put it where it will give you light while you’re eating.
43577: də sə vìždə kəkò də vərìš’ də gòtviš’
… so you can see what’s cooking so as to prepare meals.
43578: štòtu n’e jè kətu seà də ìmə tòk də ìmə svetìlu
Because it wasn’t like now, when you’ve got electricity and lights
43581: in the evening [when] you come home late from work.
43589: sklàlu si àrkumatə nə kəndž’ìlə a nìe si burnìč’kite si klàvəme č’ərkmɤ̀tə
You’ve put the cook pot under the hanging lamp, and we light kindling in the "churkma",
43592: i tàa sv’ɛ̀ti tì vərìš’ bɤ̀rkəš’ zə də svərìš’ jàd’ene də nəpràiš’
and it gives light, you cook, stir, finish cooking – you prepare the meals.
43594: znàči jèdeneto sèki dèn li go
So did you [prepare] meals every day?
43598: àmi tuvà si tì e redòvnu kàktu segɛ̀
Well, yes! That was your regular [job, just] like it is today.
43605: èdenèt trɛ̀və si gòtviš’ s’èki dèn’ tàm nə kòlə nə kəndž’èlə
You had to cook the meals every day, to [the light] of hanging lamp on a post.
43609: nə kɤ̀rə kətu id’ɛ̀hme pà də ž’ènem də təkvònəm
When we would go to the fields to do the reaping and do all that.
43612: àjde edìn kòl pà zəkuvàt tàm àjde isàn
And they pound a post [in the ground], come on folk –
43623: In the old days we’d do the cooking in those copper pots.
43636: decà glèdəm’i decàta pòsle šìl’encàtə pəsèm pɤk nalì
We look after children, then we take the yearlings to pasture, of course,
43639: [since] we have sheep. We produced [everything] ourselves.
43642: ml’àko n’àma udd’è də kùpim kəto sigà
There wasn’t anyplace to buy milk like now [when] we [have to] wait at the store.
43645: ə čàkəjmi nə məgazìnə də zèim
[Now] we wait [in line] at the store to get it.
43648: ə togàə ìməmi si v dvòrə
But back then, we’ve got it [right] in our own yard.
43655: kràvə žə ìjmi vulòvi kuètu ur’èm nìvəta
… we’d have cows, and oxen that we plow the fields with –
43714: s’èjm si žìto pruizv’èždəmi sə pruizvudìteli sme
We sow the wheat, we produce it all. We are producers!
43718: Have we gotten through [a whole] hour?
43720: àjde da sfɤ̀ršim səs tovà səs ə tàm səs nìvətə
Well, let’s finish up with this – with [what happens] there in the field.
43726: znači nè səs nìvətə də dovɤ̀ršim znàči kakvò žɤ̀ne sə
No, let’s finish up with the field. So, what do you reap?
43729: i slèt tùj kət sə ožɤ̀ne
And then afterwards, after you finish reaping,
43735: nə snòpi èj tòl’kəv’i èj tòl’kəv’i znàči kətu zbirèš
Into sheaves! They’re this big, this big, you know. And when you gather [them up]
43738: èj tòl’kəvu vəžè žə nəpràjš ud nìvətə i si nəpràjš
you’ll make a cord this size, you’ll make it [to tie up the wheat] from the field,
43743: ši zèmiš tò je tòl’kəu visòku dlɤ̀gu i təkà nəprìmer
you’ll take [the sheaf], it’s this high and this wide, so for instance
43747: kət gu vàždət dvèti sə krɤstòsət takà n’àkək
when you pull it out [and tie it], the two [together] form a cross, something like this,
43750: i slàgəž gu nə zem’ɤ̀tə nòsiš rəkòjkə ut tùk ut tùk
and you put it down on the ground, and you carry the small sheaves from here to there,
43754: dud’ètu zèmim karàre kòlku tr’àvə də je nə jedìn snòp
until we measure how much [we] need to [make] one sheaf.
43757: jedìn snòp p’èt ə snòpə sə zbìrət i sə sklədɤ̀t
One sheaf, five sheaves, you gather them up and arrange them
43763: də e tòl’kuvə i nə r’èd vèči inɤ̀ redìca gu nəredìm
so they’re like this, in order. We put them into a single row.
43764: tò bìvəlu gàtu se žèni də dòdət če də vìd’ət
It would happen when we were reaping that [outsiders] would come to see …
43767: … how the work [was going}. So now …
43771: ... [why do they want] you to tell them about it?
43775: čùnkim ne sɤ̀ òdili də vìd’ət
It’s as if they’d never gone to see [for themselves].
43777: nìj ìskəmi nìj ìskəmi i gòvorə da čùjm kàk ə
[What] we want [is] – we want to hear the local speech, how [you talk], ...
43780: s kakvì dùmi sa kàzvə ne sàmo də go vìdim
... how you express it in words, not just to see [things].
43790: nìj po knižàtə sme go glèdəli
43792: but [now we want] something else. So then, after that,
43793: kòlku vrèmi stoì na nə nìvətə tvà nèšto
how long does this thing stay [there] in the field?
43795: kòl’ku stoì kətu u užènim i pòčvəme də vəršèm
“How long does it stay?!” We [just] finish reaping and then start threshing.
43796: Where do you do the threshing?
43797: We do the threshing in the courtyard.
43800: In the courtyard, [that’s where] we do it.
43802: In the courtyard we clear out …
43808: ej təkàvə ploštàtkə takàa v dvòra ìməmi si dikàn’ə kujàtu
… a space like this, so – in the courtyard – [and then] we have a threshing board which –
43810: sià i n’èjə ni znàiti kvà i i kɤ̀k i e
Well now, you wouldn’t know about that, what it is or how it looks.
43816: krèmeni uddòlu nəbìti krèməni təkà i tò vəršè
[It’s got] flintstones embedded in it underneath. Flintstones, that’s what threshes.
43820: kɤ̀k sa nabìti nə kakvò t’à dikàn’ətə
How are they embedded, on what? This threshing board, …
43825: The threshing board is [made] from wood.
43830: A piece of wood about this size, …
43836: mòže bì i pò dlɤ̀gi i təkà
... or maybe even a bit longer, like this.
43837: i sə nəbìti səs inò inì krèməni pràvea gi
And then it’s got this, these flintstones pounded into it.	They were made by –
43842: tùrci̥t’e li bèši cìgəni li b’àhə ne znàm ne mòə vi kàžə
Turks was it? Gypsies was it? I don’t know, I can’t tell you.
43846: tìjə ni dokàrvəə tìjə takɤ̀u i sə nabìvaa fəf ə
[Whoever it was,] they would bring us these things, and they’d get pounded into
43849: the underside of the board we use for threshing.
43853: And then when it moves along, it cuts [the wheat].
43857: tàm zə pìtkə li žə e zə kvəsnìk li mu
whether it’ll be for a small round leavened bread, or for its yeasted piece –
43860: kvəsnìk mu vìkəjmi nìj è tòl’kəvi səs ə glìnə
we called it the “yeasted piece” [and kept it in a container] of clay about this size:
43864: təkà nəpràeno è təkɤ̀u tərkalò ot ə glìnə
[it was] made out of clay, round – like this.
43870: tùrim gu nə òg’enə də sə nəpịčè ə sə nətòpli
[Then] we put it on the stove to bake, to heat up.
43874: če vrɤ̀šnik ìmə udgòri pɤ̀k ə kàk sm’e sə mɤ̀čili bàbe
There’s a lid on top, you know. Ah, how we suffered, [us] old women!
43882: I can’t tell you [all of it].
43886: ne mòj ti iskazà də fànət kràjə
I can’t tell you [in a way] that you would understand it all.
43892: tvà e kolendrò mu vìkəmi nìj
this [thing that] we call a roller.
43895: əxə i naprɤ̀skəti go z vodà
Aha. [And then] you spray water [on] it?
43901: nəprɤ̀skəmi gu s vodɤ̀ či səs slàmə ud gòri i ubikàl’əmi
We spray water on it, and then put straw on top, and then circle around
43905: səs vulòviti fpr’ègnət vulòviti i ubikàl’ət təkà de ə
with the oxen. They harness up the oxen, and circle around so that –
43910: əxə mì trevà ne ponìkvələ li pòsle pàk kəto gu takòvə
Ah. But didn’t grass grow up again later on, when [you did] this to it?
43913: It won’t grow up again! No way.
43916: zəštòtu nìj kətu gu nəpràvim tvà pɤ̀rvo
Because when we do this thing up – So, first.
43917: tvà pɤ̀rvətə godìnə də ti kàžə ftòrətə gudìnə
Well, that’s the first year, to tell [the truth]. In the second year,
43919: t’à punìkni trivɤ̀ punìkni mə ni mòj də punìkni
grass does come up. It does, but it doesn’t grow up
43923: gul’àmə trivɤ̀ təkà lòšə stràšnə i z’èmim s mutìkiti
[to be] such tall grass, not so bad and awful [that we can’t] take the hoes
43927: i gu ut’èsəmi gu tì mutìkə nəlì si čùvəl [laughter]
and cut it back. You’ve heard of hoes, haven’t you? [laughter]
43930: ku ne sì ja vìždəl [laughter]  ut’èsəmi gu isfɤ̀rl’əmi
[Even] if you haven’t seen one. [laughter]  So we cut it back and throw
43933: nə utpàdəci̥ti d’ètu trivɤ̀tə i pàk təkà ftòri pɤ̀t pàk
the cut grass onto the trash pile, and then again a second time –
43936: e na drùgətə gudìnə də kàžə d’è i pàk gu nəprɤ̀skəm’e
I mean, the following year. And then we sprinkle it again
43940: pàk gu zərìjem səs slàmə udgòri pɤk ə utpàdəci slàmə
and cover it again with straw on top, those waste bits of straw.
43943: i pàk səs vulòvit’i s kul’endròtu ubikàl’əmi ubikàl’əmi ubikàl’əmi
Then once more with the oxen and the roller, we circle, circle, circle
43949: dud’è vìdim či sɤ̀ i ul’ègnəlo v’èči təkà sə je pribìlu zim’ɤ̀tə
until we see that it’s all packed in [smoothly], that the earth is trampled down.
43951: i kəto dòjdi vr’ème àjde də ìdət ut kɤ̀rə
And when the time comes, here they come from the field.
43956: prinàs’ət snòpiti d’ètu sme gu užènəli dukàrəmi tùkə
They take the sheaves that we’ve reaped, bring them in here,
43964: nəpràim kupì he kòlku slìvətə visòki
and make piles as tall as [that] plum tree [over there].
43968: uhù či kòj kɤ̀k gi pràjti tìjə
Oho! So who – how do you make these –
43971: kɤ̀k sə je pràelo tùj nèšto
how was such a thing made?
43974: mi tè sə šəròki tè ut unuvà duvàrči
Well, they’re broad, [extending] from that little wall [up to here]
43976: kvò ə ti kàžə du du tùkənə e šəròki
What can I tell you?  As broad as to here.
43979: a pɤ̀k gi pràim visòki fɤ̀rl’ət səs vìlətə
And then we make them tall. They toss [the hay] up with a pitchfork.
43983: edìn gi nər’èždə drùk fɤ̀rl’ə ut kulàta
One puts them in order, the other tosses [them up] from the cart,
43986: i pòsl’e pàk kutu dukàrət ə pàk təkà
and then when they drive in [the next load], they do [the same] again.
43989: amà n’àkoj ìma se e pukačìl gòre li
But [surely] there’s someone [who must] have climbed up there?
43993: n’àkuj i gòri ne mòj bez čuvèk’
[Of course] there’s someone up top! You can’t [do it] without a person [up there].
44000: tòj tr’àə də grəd’ì duvàri nəprìmer kɤ̀k sə grad’ɤ̀t i
He has to build [it]. Like they build walls, for instance –
44003: this is built up the same way.
44007: And the pile of straw, and –
44008: i žìtutu kəto sə dukàrə snòpite
And of wheat, after they bring the sheaves in.
44013: či žìtutu dè nəprìm’er kət sə dukàrə tò ožènəto na nìvətə
Of course the wheat! For instance, when they bring in what’s been reaped in the field,
44016: nə nìvətə vìj i sɤ̀rpuvi ni znàjti kvò i
out in the fields [with sickles]. You [probably] don’t know what sickles are.
44019: Ah? Do you know [what they are]?
44028: A picture. I saw [one] in a picture
44033: rèkex əkù ne sì vid’àlə tı dàm srɤ̀b də vìdiš
I was about to say that if you haven’t seen one, I’ll give you a sickle to see.
44039: mòž də ne è vìždələ ne znàm ne smè guvòrili
Maybe she hasn’t seen one. I don’t know, we haven’t talked [about that].
44043: She said that she’s seen one.
44045: Well, I’ve seen [one] in a picture.
44058: So wait then, and I’ll show you.
44069: amì pəlamàrkə̥tə̥ mi n’àmə t’à i
Well, I don’t have my swaphook [right here], it’s – uh –
44075: It’s up there. I need to ...
44080: nə pò nə visòk stòl də sə kačɤ̀ də
... [stand on] a taller chair so that I can climb up [there].
44085: è zɤ̀pčetàtə è jà	žèniš è s tvà pribìrəš’
See, [it’s got] little teeth. See now? You reap with this, gather it in
44091: pələmàrkətə nə rɤkɤ̀ta fàštəš strəntɤ̀ r’èžiš
[with] the swaphook on your hand, grab the stubble, and cut [it],
44094: ostàv’əš nə inò m’àsto tàm inɤ̀ rəkòjkə nəpràjš
leave [it] in a certain place there, make one small sheaf [of it].
44097: i kəto žèn’im i sləd mèn slàgəm si gi ej tùkə
And when we reap, [they come] after me, and I place them all like this:
44099: idnɤ̀ tàm drùgə i təkà nə r’èt
one here, another there, and so on in order.
44103: màjkata beše etùva n dàduha da gu vìd’ət pak edìn čuvɛ̀k
His mother was here [but] they didn’t allow her to see him. However one man
44108: ut nàštə imɛ̀še imɛ̀ edìn čuvɛ̀k ud nàšɤte ta utìd tə gu vìd’e
of our [people], there was this one man of ours [who] went and saw him, [and he was]
44113: sìčku izgurèlku̥ izgurèlu̥ šù tàm žə ìmə aku nə sɔ̀ zaklàlɨ
all burned up – completely burnt! That’s what’ll happen if they haven’t done the sacrifice,
44117: aku sa nè zaklàlɤ tàm kurbànček i òfcɤ že z’ɔ̀me
if they haven’t made a small sacrifice there. It’ll take a sheep,
44120: i kràvɤ ža z’ɔ̀me čulɛ̀k etàm že pàda nə nàt sè
it’ll take a cow, [otherwise] a man will fall there above the village,
44122: zàt tùrlasa vìš etàm kadè visò̝ko zdì unuvà
beyond Turla. You see where that high [place] is over there?
44127: səgà sa kàzva tùrlata gà vɤ rɤkò na tùrlata ta istàtačko envà
Now it’s called Turla. When I said to you “in Turla”, [I meant] that [place] on the other side.
44134: ač’ìk enəkvò̝ gò̝lu gò̝lu tarlì lyvàdɨ i cɤ̀rkvicana je tàm
[It’s] open and rather bare. Bare – fields, meadows, and the little church is there.
44138: i ezgà pustàv’enu atàm unuvà nɛ̀štu i zgà hò̝d’at tàm
And now there’s this other thing [that’s been] put there, and people go there now.
44144: pò̝p ìma ta vaspejè envà kurbànčekən nəlɛ̀gat raznesɔ̀t
There’s a priest, he sings [over] the small sacrifice, they prostrate themselves, share out [the meat],
44150: jadɔ̀t pijɔ̀t i i i enèj šù že z’ɔ̀m čulɛ̀k aku nèma
eat, drink, and such. A person can be completely abducted if that’s not [done].
44157: ta mumč’èncetu beše izgurɛ̀lku gùrelč’ica ne muž’ɛ̀hme d ìdem plàkahme tùka
And that young boy was burnt up, burnt little thing. We couldn’t go. We cried here
44162: nè vìd’enku sìj màjkata si gu i baštàta sì gu utkàraha
[for him] unseen. And his mother and father took him off home,
44165: tàm nadòlu nàa ut kutrò beše sèlu tùka
back down there, [I don’t] know what village they were from.
44167: kàk da vɨ kàža ne mòga da vɨ gu kàža
How can I tell you? I can’t tell that to you.
44181: ta nakìva ràbuti sìn ta zatvà sakìva d’èsu ìma paraklìsč’eta
Such things, son. And that’s why [we have] these things, where these little chapels are.
44183: zatvà hòd’ət ta sàmu uttùka sàmu uttùka na drùgise nè
That’s why people go [there]. But only here, only here. Not to other ones.
44184: na drùgise nè nè sàmu atàm
Not to other ones, no. Only there.
44185: ami znàeš li zə zaštò se kàzva tùrlata tàm gòre
But do you know why [that place] up there is called Turla?
44194: zə səbòrə n’àkuj gi kòl’ət ə bəškà pək nìj kut si ìməmi
Well, at village celebrations some slaughter their own way but when we have [it],
44205: zemim tə si zəkòlim jègne li žə i əkòt sme si zəklàli
we take and slaughter a lamb, or whatever we’ve slaughtered;
44217: kukòški žə zəkòlim ə s nəlì svìnsku bəškà šә̥ sə zgòtvi
then we’ll [also] slaughter hens. For instance, pork is prepared
44221: pìleškutu bəškà šә̥ sə zgòtvi pu dv’è màndži s’è si pràim
its own way, and so is chicken. We all make two [meat] dishes each.
44223: And that’s how you did it.
44228: i təkà smi pràvili i sèa kvòtu i nə jèsen
And that’s how we did it. And now in the autumn
44232: kvòtu ìmə təkɤ̀u sə xə prài jɛ̀ turšijki inò drùgu
we make whatever there is, either pickled or some other thing.
44236: i stanà dv’è trì gudìni pək znàči nìj mnògu sùšə tùkə
It’s been two or three years now, you see, we’ve had a serious drought here.
44250: əm da mi kàžeš kàk mèsexte xl’àp ednò vrème
So tell me how you kneaded ( = made)  bread in the old days, ...
44254: znàjš kəkvò je ìməše inì cìgən’i im vìkəmi lìnguri
You know what? There were these gypsies: we call them “wooden-spoon [makers]".
44260: i t’è kəto z’èmət ə jèsenno vrèm’i kəto dòd’i
And when they take – when it gets to be autumn,
44263: i kəto z’èmət i po inɤ̀ m’èčkə i še gi ràn’ət
and they take one bear each, they’ll feed them
44266: i gi gl’èdət iz balkànə nə dòlu i tàm gi udgl’èduvət
and look after them [on their way] down from the mountains. They raise them there,
44271: i gi nəùčuvət də igràat i kəto trɤ̀gnət pu s’ilàtə
and teach them to dance. And when they come through the villages,
44279: ta s’àku s’èlu utvòri vratàtə i cigùl’kətə svìri i [laughter] i p’èji
each village opens up its doors, and they play the violin, [laughter] and sing,
44286: i i m’èčkətə vɤ̀rdzənə tùkə za krɤ̀stə duvid’è ə òpreš kɤ̀šti
and they bring the bear, tied here around the waist, in front of [peoples’] houses.
44293: kəto pòčnet də zəsvìri i t’à kəto zərečè è təkà krəkàtə pr’èdniti
And when they begin to play [music], [the bear] takes its front legs like this
44297: də gi dìgn’e pràvə sə ispràv’ə
and lifts them up: he stands straight upright
44302: du kutu čuv’èk mòje takà də stàn’i
just like a man! It’s able to stand up that way.
44307: ispràv’ə sə i pròsto t’èpə də igràj i tòj svìri
It stands up, and stamps like it’s dancing, and [all this time the guy] is playing music –
44309: the bear trainer is playing music.
44315: tòj nə cigùl’kə zème si cìgənski kiminčètə im vìkəmi nìj
He’s playing violin – the gypsy kind. We call them “kemanche’s”
44318: mòže i də gi znàiti vìj
44321: dà kato nə takòva kato nàšti tìja instrumènti
Yes, it’s something like [one of] our instruments.
44323: A little like a gŭdŭlka [Bulgarian folk fiddle]
44337: səs takɤ̀vo s takɤ̀vi s takɤ̀vo gi vòdija tìjə m’èčki
So they would lead these bears around with this – with these [sorts of things],
44343: i à bàbo dàj rɤ̀ka də ti celùvə rəkɤ̀
... and [they’d say] “Hey, granny! Give me your hand, so [the bear] will kiss your hand!
44347: dàvəj rɤ̀kə də cəlùvə š ti s fàni rəkɤ̀tə
Give your hand here to be kissed!” And he’ll grab your hand [and say],
44353: You have to say what it is –
44358: kvò žə i pudar’àvəš na m’èčkətə fàn’i rəc’èt’e i takà
what you’re going to give the bear. And he takes you by the hands and such.
44361: ma às ma n’è e straš’ štòtu
Well as for me, I wasn’t afraid, because
44364: not everybody gives their hand [to him].
44368: i à kvò žə obeštàjə kvò ìməm fkɤ̀šti kvò ə
And so what shall I promise? Something I have in the house, whatever.
44373: tìjə kut sə trɤ̀gnəli tìjə n’àmaa nìštu mečkàrit’e
When they set out, these bearkeepers didn’t have anything at all,
44377: b’èl lùk kartòfi takɤ̀vi ràbuti pudarìm im dad’èm
just onions, potatoes, things like that.  [So] we make gifts to them, we give
44380: da ìmət za zimɤ̀tə i tìi
[them something] so that they too will have [provisions] for the winter.
44385: After all, that’s why they drive them [= the bears] around –
44392: xèm də ni pup’èjət də ni puigràat [laughter] m’èčkiti
not just to sing for us and have the bears dance for us, [laughter]
44396: xèm də si puzbìrət zə zimɤ̀tə takɤ̀vo napràvea
but also to gather some provisions for the winter. That’s what they would do.
44400: Well, that’s [our] life. Anything else you want?
44403: [cough] à t’è kɤ̀k sə gi fàštəli tìjə mèčki
[cough] Well, how did they get hold of these bears?
44405: They’re said to have taken them [when they were] tiny.
44415: ukùčeni òšti gi fàštali i gi udgl’èdvəli tèj mečkàri
These bearkeepers – they’d even take them as newborns, and then raise them up.
44421: i t’èj kutò ə sə v’èči zimàl’i n’àkoə gud’ìna
Some years, since they were taking them anyway,
44425: t’ì si zìmət i mɤ̀ški i žènski znàči i si gi udvɤ̀ždət
they’d take [both] a male and a female and then, you know, breed them.
44428: amà nàj nəprèš sə gi zìməli i kòjto
But primarily they would take them [from their mothers]; whoever
44433: ni jè mòžəl pɤ̀k tɤ̀j də si pruizved’è ud gorɤ̀tə
wasn’t able to “produce” [= breed] one, [would get them] from the woods.
44436: òd’ət iz gorɤ̀tə nəmìrət si ukùčeni takɤ̀vi mənìn’ki
They would go about the mountain forest, find these tiny newborns,
44439: i si fàtət ut tàm i si gi odglèduəš
and capture them from there. And then you raise them up.
44445: i jà pugl’edn’ète mi dumàtite veči̥ kvò ostànaa
Just look at my tomatoes, what they’ve already become:
44451: isɤ̀jnaa i àz gi zər’àzəx i kukòškite i pùštəm
they’re [completely] withered. So I abandoned them and let the hens at them,
44455: i t’e idɤ̀t ut kràjə [laughter] kvò də gi pràiš
and they graze [there] at the end. [laughter] What can you do [with] them?
44458: mlògu mlògu sùšə stənà dv’è trì gudìni v’èči
It’s been a really bad drought, two or three years already;
44465: əmə i dnèskə iskl’učìtel’nu tàə gudìnə dètu jə prekàrah
but today, especially this year that I’ve lived through –
44467: [It has been] a terrible, terrible drought.
44476: a predì ìmalo li e v sèlo sèlo sèloto vudà mnogo
Earlier on was there much water in the village?
44486: nìe zèjmi tùka e rezervoàra du nàs udgòri
We got [it from] – there’s a reservoir here near us, up above.
44492: à nè li gu zabel’àzə tuvà e rezervuàra è tùka du nàs
Didn’t you notice it? That’s the reservoir, right over here – near us.
44495: i də pruòdim pàk dvà č’àsə pʌ̀t’
and to get through another two hours’ travel on the road.
44499: i pàk də si zìməme ubràtnu tòrbənə bɤ̀klən i d’ètenu
and then to take up the return trip with the bag, the waterflask, and the child,
44501: də səbìrəme snòpene də gi pràvim nə krɤ̀sci
... gather up the sheaves and put them into cruciforms,
44505: dušlòlu v’èč’e nəkrivìlu sə ə tr’àvə
[till] it’s come to be all “tilted”  (dusk). [But we still]  have to …
44508: i kò š’e ràbutiš’ š’e ràbutiš’ dòde li slɤ̀nceno təkà vìkəm
And what will you do? You’ll work until the sun gets to be – as I say –
44513: nìj ut tùka z’èmami vodɤ̀ i prɤ̀snətə i čàk u udvɤ̀dnətə majalɤ̀
We get water from here. Water is distributed, even [as far as] the other neighborhood.
44519: i i i d’ètenu e f rəkète f rəkìse i kətu ìdeš tàm
… [to go] with a kid in your arms. And when you get there
44523: pràj mu sm’ètkətə kòlku e dəl’èč’e
Just imagine how far that was …
44528: ə idìn innɤ̀ vudɤ̀ pək ìəmi tùka priz vrɤ̀ju pək čak uttàtəkə
But we have another water source here across the summit, over there on the other side,
44531: i bɤ̀kəl zə zə vudà dvà č’àsə pɤ̀t’
and a flask of water, it was a two hour trip.
44535: tò i mnògu dəl’èč nə unàzi vudɤ̀ pək də vər’ɤ̀ tàm
It’s very far, to walk [all the way] to that water.
44541: p’èš’i du səftɤ̀šte tòrbənə nə rəmòt nə ràmutu
on foot for Sǔftǔshte with our bags on our shoulders
44548: ne mužàa də ja fànət sìčkətə tə bəjà zəkɤ̀cvəmi zə vudɤ̀
They couldn’t pipe it all in, so we have a lot of trouble [to get] water.
44553: When we set out – set out from here ...
44555: [So, well - where did you go for water?]
44558: dà dà ti kàž’ə ìstinətə səgà jà t’èbe
I’m telling you the truth, really!
44562: can scoop up [spoonfuls for themselves] from the “gyuvech” pot.
44566: č’e ž’e slòž’iš’ kàš’ənə də jə strɤ̀siš’ č’e sìč’ki nəòkulu
You’ll put the gruel in it, pour it in so that everyone all around
44571: ə č’e tugà že tùriš’ pərəl’ʌ̀nə č’e ž’ə slòž’iš’ g’yv’èč’ən
and then you’ll set up the “paraliya” tables and put out the “gyuvech”.
44576: b’àgəš’ də dujìš’ kràvənə sə vɤ̀rniš’ pàk nə svìnenu
You run off to milk the cow, you come back [to tend] the pigs,
44580: kuètu e pò l’èsnu n’ègu žə žə vɤ̀ršiš’ tàm izlìzəš’ zìməš bəkɤ̀rč’enu
Whatever is easier, that’s what you’ll do. Then you go out, you take the smaller pot.
44581: ama zaštò zaštò se kàzva takà
But why? Why is it called that?
44583: əm kàk da vɤ kàža à č’ɛ̀kaj da vɤ kàža
Well how can I tell you? Ah, wait! I’ll tell  you –
44588: jɛ̀ gu ìmam atùka na adnɔ̀ knìga vɤsòku vrɤ̀x
I have it here in a book, way high up on top.
44590: i etàm ìmalu drùguš ə takòva č’ɛ̀kaj da v kàža
It’s there, [or] it was earlier on, something like that. Wait, I’ll show you –
44591: adnɔ̀ knìga da gu vɨ da vɨ̀ gu kàža
[There’s] a book that I [want] to show you.
44595: pesnupìsec ìmame nìe tùka vaf mahalɔ̀sa ža vì gu kàža
We have someone here in the village quarter who writes down songs, I’ll show it to you –
44598: esvà càlasa knìga etùva càlasa knìga č’ɛ̀kaj žə vɨ kàža
[His] whole book is here, the whole book. Wait, I’ll show you.
44599: žə vɨ kàža žə vɨ kàža dè je unuvà nɛ̀štu
I’ll show you, I’ll show you where that thing is.
44605: vìž bàbəcḁsa kakvò ìma tò na sìčki razdàl enòa čulɛ̀k
Look at this little granny, what she’s got. This guy distributed [it] to everyone,
44607: esakìva knìgi ezgà žə v kàža kakvò i imàlu
books like this. And now I’ll show you what it’s said to have been there.
44611: strelì strelì ìmalu i kakvì ràbutɨ ètu nəblìže
Arrows. There were said to have been arrows and such things. Here, [look] closer.
44613: ètu gu zgà ètu gu zgà na vərhɤ̀ kakvò e ìmalu
Here it is! Here it is, up on the summit, what there was said to have been.
44614: Here it is, here it is!
44617: prez tùrsko vrɛ̀m’a èto gu əm dè da gu znàja
During the Turkish times, there it is. Well, how should I know
44622: kakvò je strelì pək esvà mahalìcasa nàša è uttùka utsrɛ̀štu
why the arrows? And here’s our little village quarter across from [it].
44630: s’èlutu e bìlu zəs’èlenu gudìnite ne znàm predi ednò izvèsno vr’ème
The village was founded – I don’t know what years. A certain time ago.
44635: stàrite kàzvət če sə ut ənədull’ìjə dušl’ìli trìmə dùši vəv vərbìnə
The old folk say that three people came to Vŭrbina from Anatolia
44639: i sə zəs’èlili sèlutu i uttàm sə konstantìrə kutrɤ̀ gudìnə
and that they founded the village. That’s established. But what year
44643: i kugà e ne ne mògə ti kàže sletvà e vərv’àlu tuvà
and when, I cannot tell you. Things went on after that,
44648: purèdni gudìni i prudəlžɛ̀vəlu utnòvu gu rəzbìrəme nìj
the succeeding years, and it continued on. This is what we know from recently.
44654: ə càrevicətə ə s’èeme prul’ètešnu vrème kugàtu jə ur’ème s vulòvete
We sow corn in the spring, when we plow with the oxen,
44659: i jə s’ɛ̀eme pu nèjə sɛ̀eme i kučɛ̀ni kərtòfi fəsùl’
and we sow it [then]. Next to it we sow beets, potatoes, beans,
44666: kəkvòtu ubrəzùvəme s’èlsku stupànstvu rəštɤ̀ gu sèeme nə pòdziməšnu vr’ème
[according to] the way we organize our village economy. We sow rye in the autumn:
44670: kàktu nàštu edìn mɛ̀sec du gerg’òvden’ i i i gu prudəlžɛ̀və
in our region [that’s] one month before St. George’s Day. And - and we carry on
44673: e tàə ràbutə s envà sme zənimàvəli nìe i pòsl’et
with this work. That’s what we occupied ourselves with. After that
44680: vərš’è̝me urème i vərš’ème gu ca tuvà rəštɤ̀ gu vərš’e̝me səs katɯ̀r’e
we thresh, and plow, and thresh –  We thresh the rye with hinnies,
44685: kàktu pu.stàrumu təkà vər’èše slàmətə ispòlzvəme pàk jədɤ̀t dubɨ̀təkə
that's how it went in the old times. We use the straw to feed the livestock
44688: i nèe si ispòlzvəme sɤ̀štu kusìme pràime dubɨ̀təkə si
[and] we use it as well. We also do the mowing, and make [food for] the livestock
44692: ut sɤ̀štu̥tu ut sɤ̀štətə priròdə ut nàštə si
from the same – from the very natural [resources] of our own [area].
44695: ud vɤ̀nkə ne nè ni flìzəše sàmu sə xrànime se
Nothing comes in from outside. We feed ourselves
44698: ut səmòtu s’èlu tuvà beše stàrətə priròdə drùgo nè
from within our village. This was the old nature. No other [way].
44704: urème səs vulòvete zə càrevicətə pràim jə nə brəzdɤ̀
We plow with oxen. For corn, we make a furrow
44713: kà e s càrəvìčen vəzvərìme vadɔ̀ta i naškvᵊì si imème
If it’s corn [bread] we boil up water, and we had [this] kneading trough,
44719: naškvᵊɨ̀ g zav’eme sᵊɨ̀pem ats’ème brašnòto
we called it a kneading trough. We pour – we sift the flour.
44730: sìtɔ ats’ème brašnòto vazvr’ènata vòda sᵊìpeme gà a càrevìčevo
A sieve. We sift out the flour, we pour boiled water – [when it’s for] corn [meal, that is].
44736: vazvrènata vòda sᵊìpeme papàrime go azàm pàk slàgame at rɔ̀š rɔ̀ž’onko
We pour the boiled water over it and steam it. And then we add rye [flour, and]
44743: am’èsime go agà go vaskᵚɨ̀sne takà go klad’ème f tavɔ̀ta as pònicɔ
knead it up. When it’s fermented then we put it in a pan with a “ponitsa” (a lid).
44785: i gu sìpvəme s zərnàtə i klàvəme pur’èdnu i pu n’èjə
and fill it up. We put the grains into it in order, [first the corn] and after that
44788: klàvəme i i zə tìkvi i sìpvəme udgòr’e tòr
we put [seeds] for the pumpkins. Then we put fertilizer down
44792: i gu zəràv’əme i pòsle tvà kətu gu zəròvime iznìkne
and tamp it down good. And after we tamp it down it sprouts.
44796: prəšìme gu pàk pòsled gu prəšìme i ftòri pɤ̀t
[Then] we hoe it again, and then later hoe it a second time.
44797: i təkà gu pràime nàštu si
And that’s how we do it in our manner.
44803: žɨtutu gu pòčvəm təkà pus’èeme gu izlezè tə gu tə ftàsə
The grain starts out like this: we sow it, it comes up, it ripens,
44807: tə gu žèneme slet tvà gu sklədème nə kòpi i gu č’ùkəme
then we reap it. After that we put it in stacks and pound it
44810: i pòsled gu vərš’ème i rəštɤ̀ iskàrvəme i gu slàmətə ispòlzvəme
and then we thresh it. We do up the rye also, and we make use of the straw
44811: zə dubɨ̀təkə rəštɤ̀ gu kàrəme tə i xrànime
for the cattle; we get in the rye and feed [them],
44814: pà gu m’èl’eme tə stàne brəšnò zə furàš i zə nègu
then we grind it and it becomes flour for fodder for them.
44816: i dàže gu jəd'ɛ̀hə i hòrətə
And people would even eat it too.
44817: [How do you make the threshing floor?]
44821: xər xərmànə e stòr’en ut zem’ɤ̀tə kàktu nə l’uvà
The – the threshing floor is made of earth like in a meadow [that is, like]
44827: nə pul’ɛ̀nətə n’è s kàmen’i əmi pul’ɛ̀nə i gu umet’ème mètneme rəštɤ̀
in an open field, an open field without stones. We sweep it, put down the rye,
44830: vərš’ème gu sletvà skàrəme slàmətə i gu i gu smɨ̀təne
thresh it, then take away the straw and –  sweep it
44834: i gu vɛ̀eme i gu zbìrəme vəf čuvàlite po po nàšenski
and winnow it, and gather it up in sacks in – in our own manner.
44838: səs kətɰ̀re i səs kòne gu vərš’ème dàž’e ìməš’e xòrə
We threshed with hinnies and horses. There were even people
44841: tə gu vəršɛ̀ə i səs səs vulòve dètu n’èmə kətɰ̀r
who threshed with oxen. Where there were no hinnies,
44845: i vulòve sə vɤ̀rhəli d’ètu e pò b’èden səs məgàre gu vəršè
oxen did the threshing. Those who were poorer threshed with donkeys.
44848: pò bàvnu stànvə pò l’èku e pò bàvnu vərš’è
That goes more slowly. [The weight] is not as heavy and the threshing goes more slowly.
44849: [Did the men travel somewhere to work?]
44852: ottùkə sə xòdili zə g’um’uržìne i sə kàrəli dɤ̀ski ut plənnɤ̀tə
They would go from here to Komotini, they would take boards from the mountains
44855: dètu č’ɛ̀muvi dɤ̀ski sə kàrəli du g’um’urž’ìne i səs t’ɛ̀h
they’d take pine boards to Komotini, and for that
44858: sə zìməli kirìjə ut tàm sə pàk tvàrili nəh tùkə
would charge portage. They’d load up there again for here
44862: pàk sə ubràtnutu vrʌ̀štəli kirìjə i sə ž’uv’ɛ̀li səs tvà
on the way back, charging portage as well, and they made a living with that,
44865: s tòu vìt kirəž’ilɤ̀g gu kàzvəme nìe pu.stàrumu
with that kind [of work]. We called it “carting trade” in the old manner.
44866: So what would they carry to there?
44869: dɤ̀ski a nəsàm sə vòzili pàk drùk məteriàl
Boards. And then they would bring other things back this direction.
44886: a nèma po vàšta stràna nèma takvᵊì ràbatᵊi
Aren’t there things like this in your part of the world?
44889: And there didn’t used to be [either]?
44891: There used to be, but it’s …
44898: minàva minàva tò [unintelligible] tò segà hùvu fɤ̀rd’e
It’s gone, gone [unintelligible]. But now there’s a lot of good [things].
44901: i pòsle noškvìte s kakvò gi ostɤ̀rgvaš
So after [you’re done], what do you scrape out the kneading trough with?
44908: We scrape it out with a knife.
44912: We put it (the scrapings) out for the animals.
44919: agà go istɔ̀rgame astàvime birìs kvàsɤ kvàsɤ da vaskᵊɨ̀snəvə
When we scrape it out, we leave a little bit of the starter there, to ferment
44928: pàk s’è drùgiet l’èp s’ètniet l’èp astàvime kvàskɤ naškvᵊìte istɔ̀rguvame
[for] the next bread. We leave [behind] some starter when we scrape the trough.
44932: amᵊìjeme gᵚɨ pàk ùtre gà peč’ème pàg ga am’èsime
[Then] we wash it. The next day we bake, and then we knead again.
44935: i pòsle kàk pečèš kàk pàliš pe peštà u pèš
So then, how do you do the baking? How do your fire up the oven?
44938: tò n’è f p’èčka tò f pònica
It doesn’t [go] in the oven, but [rather] in a “ponitsa” (the dish with a lid).
44942: tò na agnìš’e tò n’è əf sòba
[We put] it on the hearth, not in the oven.
44949: po s pònica na agn’ète badž’elɔ̀kč’e si ìmame
In the “ponitsa”, on the fire. We have a small hearth,
44955: klad’ème pònicətə pahlùpme f tavɔ̀ l’èbat’e i azàm go s’ètne
and put the “ponitsa” [there]. We cover the bread in a pan, and then later
44959: gà go ispeč’ème rɛ̀ž’eme ga da ga id’ème
after we bake it, we slice it and eat it.
44962: It’s a big loaf of bread.
44966: Not like what one buys [at the store] now.
44971: And what sorts of banitsa did you used to make?
44976: We made [different kinds of] banitsa. We roll out the pastry, and –
44980: What do you do with the pastry? Roll it out?
44985: l’èštətə s’èjət nə pàk sɤ̀štu kàktu kàəh nə pròl’etnu vrème
They sow lentils like I told you, in the spring.
44990: k’ɛ̀sta m’èsime gà am’èsime ga am’èsime ga azàm mu go
We knead the dough. When we knead it – we knead it and then –
44997: azàm go na sin’ɔ̀nɔ i z’èmeme si tač’ìlka ga zvème
then we [put] it on the table and take a – we call it a rolling pin.
45003: č’òpka tač’ìlkɤ sùč’eme kòrᵊi arìsč’e klad’ème sᵊɨ̀renke klad’ème
[Like] a stick, a rolling pin. We roll out the pastry, add some rice, some cheese –
45011: sakvᵊìn pràim bànice segà drùgak ama na pò naprèš štèm do et’èj
We made these kinds of banitsa. Now it’s different, but back then we’d [eat] that.
45013: i kakvì bànici ìmaše vìe kàk i vìkaxte bànica li
And what kinds of banitsa were there? How did you say it?  “Banitsa”?
45033: ta tòj z’èlnikət peč’ème al’è s nèkvi žàl’kᵊi kaprìvi kàk gi zav’ème
We baked “zelnik” only with these – nettles. Nettles, how did we call them?
45040: i hi ber’ème na ə na amᵊìjeme gɤ nadrabìme gɤ
We pick them, then wash them and chop them,
45044: azàm mu slò klad’ème arìšk’e klad’ème mu kòrᵊi mu isùč’eme
and then add some rice, and put them into the pastry sheets, roll it out,
45053: à ot testò kakvò pràvexte drùgo osvèn bànici
What else besides banitsa did you make from the pastry dough?
45061: atèj ad brɑ̀šno isùč’eme kòrᵊi am’èsime ga isùč’eme kòrᵊi
We make pastry sheets from the flour: we knead it up and roll out pastry.
45062: ot testò drùgo kakvò pràvexte osvèn bànici
[But] what else besides banitsa did you make from the pastry dough?
45068: č’e l’è f kɑ̀šnica demèk at t’ɛ̀sta zabɔ̀rkaš
Well, there’s “kashnitsa” [you make] from the dough [that] you mix up.
45073: i tò i tò s kòrᵊi
That’s – that’s also with pastry sheets.
45075: i kàk stà i tò s kòri
And how – [Ah,] and that’s also with pastry sheets.
45078: What about “trahana” (pastry of dried yeast mixed with milk)?
45082: s trì kòrᵊi tràanata a m’èsime s kvàsa i s ml’èkɔ
“Trahana” with three sheets of pastry. We knead it with yeast, and milk.
45085: [cough] azàm ga azàm vaskᵚɨ̀sne sedì p’èt d’èna azàm je nakɔ̀came
[cough] Then it ferments. It sits five days and then we cut it up
45094: na kalàčkav’e na sakvɤ̀n kalàčkave azàm isɔ̀ne azàm esèⁱj reč’ème
into small pieces – small pieces like this; then it dries, and then we go and
45098: azàm em e m’èleme f rašnìcɤ
then we grind it, with the millstone.
45104: a nèšto na tùrma na tùrma nèšto
And [did you prepare] anything by means of smoking?
45113: Couscous: how did you make that?
45117: i je sèjət kàktu i rəštɤ̀ i sə kupàe i sə sèe
They sow them at the same time as rye: you dig, then you sow.
45121: puslè tvà t’à sə pl’əvɨ̀ i se mʌ̀kne t’à sə nè žène
After that you weed them and then pick them: you don’t reap them.
45127: t’à sə mʌ̀kne i sə sklàə nə kòpički i sl’ətvà sə č’ùkə
You pick them and put them in piles and then pound them
45133: kuskùs’ete l’e varìme ga na parlìva vòda vazvrìena vòda
Couscous, is it? We boil that up with hot water in boiling water.
45145: nᵊì kupùvame nɤ pràvime kuskùzɤ ne znàme kàk da
We buy it. We don’t make couscous, we don’t know how to,
45148: kàk sa pràvi i n’è sme pràv’alɤ
how to make it. And we have [never] made it.
45156: ifkɔ̀ i ifkɔ̀ta kùp’etə̥ i t’è kùp’et
"Ifka” – that’s also for purchase. That gets bought also.
45164: i t’à kùpeta tò ifkɔ̀ varìmen si agà tr’èva issùč’eme kòrᵊi
And that gets bought. We’d boil “ifka”, and if necessary roll out pastry sheets.
45169: azàm af parlìva vòda m’ɛ̀tneme atl’èmen mu vadɔ̀ta azàm klad’èmen agùrt’e
Then we put it in hot water. Then we’d pour out the water, then add yogurt
45174: zab’èlime ga s màsla tazì ifkà
and thicken it with butter. That’s “ifka”.
45179: i stàvə nə l’èštə i ustànvə tvà zrənòtu sə ispòlzvə nalì
and they become lentils – the remaining [pounded] grain which we can use.
45180: [Житото по какво се различава от ръжта?]
45185: žɨ̀tutu e pò jèdro a pšenìcətə e pò drèbnə
“Rye” is larger and wheat is smaller.
45188: a i drùgu d’ètu ərpɤ̀ gu nìe zəvème
And there’s another kind – we call it “arpa” [barley] –
45191: zə kətɰ̀rite s’ɛ̀jət t’à e pò drèbnə
that they sow for the hinnies; it is even smaller still.
45197: eč’emìkə ərpɤ̀tə st ərpɤ̀tə stànvə pò bɤ̀rzu ut ud rəštɤ̀
Barley – “arpa” – comes about more quickly than rye.
45199: t’à e pò bɤ̀rzu zrèe i zə dubɨ̀təkə ə ispòlzvəme nìe
It is – it ripens more quickly. We make use of it for the livestock:
45204: zə kətɰ̀rite zə xrànene nè jə m’èl’əd zə xrənɤ̀ zə xòrətə
we feed the hinnies with it. They don’t grind it for human food,
45208: ə zə pɤ̀k rəštɤ̀ gu mèl’eme zə xòrətə zə jèden’e gu mèl’eme
whereas we do grind rye for humans: we grind it for [our] food.
45212: tàm nəgrɛ̀fki pràət ud n’ègə ud ərpɤ̀tə kugàtu ist’ìne čuvɛ̀k tə nə
And they make heating packs from it, from barley. When someone gets a cold
45217: pràət nəgrɛ̀fki nə dubɨ̀tək nezəvìsimu nə dubɨ̀tək sme pràili
they make heating packs, [also] for the livestock. Even for animals we made
45221: təkìvə nəgrɛ̀fki ərpɤ̀ nəpàriš’ i nə gərbɤ̀ mu klədèš’
such heating packs. You steam up the barley and put it on [someone’s] back,
45224: kugàtu ist’ìni i dète i sɤ̀štu e nə dète mu klàəme
also if a child takes cold. For a child we put it
45227: nə gərdìte i nə dubɨ̀tək dàže ispòlzəme ərpɤ̀tə i nvà e ərpɤ̀tə
on his chest. We use barley for the livestock as well. And that’s barley.
45232: ufcìte ìəme ednɤ̀ dèjnos zəpludɛ̀əhne hi pòdziməšnu vrème i sletvà
We have one [main] activity with sheep: we breed them in autumn. Then
45237: təkòvə prul’ètešnu vrème kətu dòjde pɤ̀rvi màjsku vrème sə ràždət jàgəncite
in the spring, when the first days of May come, the lambs are born.
45240: sàmu edìn pɤ̀t sə f nàštu ràdəhə jàəncite
Lambs are born only once [a year] in our region.
45242: i sə i tugàvə i gl’èdəne jàgəncite
And then – it’s looking after the lambs.
45248: ami [cough] da mi raskàžeš segà ednò vrème kàk kàk žènexte
Now, can you tell me how you used to do the reaping in the old days?
45252: How did you reap? How did you reap? With – ?
45262: ... what’s been sown in the fields.
45274: as kalmùje as kalùje ìmame fàtame ž’ìtoto adr’ɛ̀ž’eme go
Sickles. We have sickles. We grasp the grain and cut it.
45276: fàtame adr’ɛ̀ž’eme go pràime go na snòpɤ
We grasp it, and cut it, and make sheaves of it.
45280: tavà dèto go fàtaš s ednàta rɔ̀ka kàk sa vìka
How do you call the amount that you grasp in one hand?
45292: rakùl’k’e sa namɔ̀k nakòt narɛ̀ž naž’ɔ̀nɤlɤ klàdəm
A handful is what you pull, snip, cut –  We take and put what we’ve reaped,
45298: dvàš trìš p’èt rɔ̀kᵚɨ stòr’əm go snòpɤ sv’ɔ̀ž’eme go snòpɤ
in two, three, five handfuls  – we make a sheaf [of it], and tie up the sheaf.
45300: What do you tie it with?
45302: pàk si e sɤs ə sàzɤ
With a stalk of the same [thing].
45307: pàk si e s tò at ə tazì ž’ìto sv’ɔ̀ž’eme go
With the same thing. We tie it with [a piece of] the same grain.
45311: stòrime go na at ə dvà bel’ùka sv’ɔ̀ž’eme go
We make two large piles of it, and tie them up.
45313: We tie them up and make sheaves out of them.
45316: tɤ̀j tə i kàk se narèždate vɤv nìvata
Right. And how do you arrange yourselves in the field?
45320: pɤ̀rvija dèto žɔ̀ne kàk se zvè
How do you call the one that reaps at the head of the line?
45330: pàk kalmùje dalì sa ž’ɔ̀ne nìvata
Well, also with a sickle! We’re [talking about] reaping in the field, right?
45334: We gather it up [using] only a sickle.
45337: But the first one who [goes to] reap?
45340: That person, how do you call him?
45344: tò s tò s tirpàna tò ne bᵊìva tò s klà
You can’t do it with a scythe. Only with a –
45347: The scythe [is for when] we mow in the meadows.
45357: narèždat se pèt šèz žòni pɤ̀rvi ftòri trèti četvɤrti pèti
Five or six women arrange themselves in a row: first, second, third, fourth, fifth.
45360: č’e tò n’èma takvᵊì n’èmame ràbati
There isn’t anything like that. We don’t have [such] things.
45361: You don’t – you don’t say [such things].
45371: əmhm i pòsle kato go ožɔ̀neš snòpete tàm gi ostàv’ate
Uh huh. And when you finish reaping, do you leave the sheaves there?
45378: sklad’ème ga tukurdž’ùm na tukurdž’ùmi go sklad’ème kogàta se spànne
We put them in cruciform – in cruciform. And when it all settles down,
45381: then we carry them to the threshing floor.
45383: Right. And how do you prepare the threshing floor?
45390: da ga varš’ɔ̀me zav’ɔ̀ž’eme dv’è mùl’eta tràptiti trùptiti a ta drebn’ɔ̀t slàmɤtɤ
For threshing we tie up two mules, and hippety hoppity, they cut up the straw.
45395: What do they use to cut up the straw?
45403: tò i tò im’ɛ̀ i drùgi ràbatᵊɨ as vòlave i z d’uv’ène
There were also these other things: [they used] oxen and threshing boards.
45407: drabɛ̀han go d’uv’ène až’ìt ìma d’uv’ène
They’d chop it fine [with] threshing boards, whoever had threshing boards.
45410: And how did one prepare the threshing floor?
45420: č’e etèj nakal’v’èš ka e rɔ̀š nakal’v’èš e rašnɔ̀n i armànat zam’ètet
Well, you cut it up, if it’s rye; you cut up the rye. They sweep off the area,
45426: i ž’ìtətə pàdne əv zem’ɔ̀na slàmata gu padber’èš as savurgɔ̀
and the grain falls on the earth. You sweep up the straw with a besom,
45431: azàm ž’ìtətə pàk s as m’ètla at adv’èeme go fnes’ème go
and then the grain with a broom. We winnow it, and carry it inside.
45437: vidɛ̀hte lì gu svà gu e svà gu e imàlu
Did you [both] see it? This [thing], this [thing] was there
45438: during the Turkish times! In Turla.
45440: esvà kakvò sa kàzva tò sa kàzva strelì li kakvò i
And this, how do you call it, arrows? Or whatever.
45444: i è svà vidɛ̀hte lì gu zgà kakvò i bɨlò
… and this. Did you see it now what it used to be [like]?
45453: takà i [laughter] è tùka adìn čuvɛ̀k dètu i snìmal etùka
So, there. [laughter] And here’s a man who took pictures here,
45455: What is there underneath, on the threshing floor?
45474: ma tò tò se akrɔ̀t’eva tò se akrɔ̀t’eva
Well, the ground gets all broken up and tramped down!
45479: elè met’ème ga s m’ètlᵚɨ s m’ètla go l’è met’è̟m
And we sweep it with brooms. We sweep it only with brooms.
45485: etùka pìsvalu takìva tùka s tɛ̀a sa edìnas sa gu ubᶤìli
and such things are written about them –   They killed one of them
45491: pa drùgia si bìl fànat f plèn asòja ugradìl etùva
and the other was taken into captivity.  And this [is the one who] built this,
45495: sòo paraklìsč’ek esòja èj gu tùva zgà č’ešmìcasa
this chapel. This one. Here it is now, this little fountain
45498: dèsu ə tùka napràv’enka na mahalɔ̀ta tùka tuvà stàrutu
that was built in the village quarter here, the old one.
45500: tovà tàa češmà tùka li e
And this fountain, is it here?
45503: It’s here, it’s here. The fountain is just over there,
45509: jɛ̀ tɛ̀j ja etùka asvà a čətàlištè̝tu etùka ìma
Yes, it’s here, and this is the reading room, and here are
45514: ufč’ɛ̀re tùva sme nìe na ràbuta e tɛ̀a sa bəlì fruntuvàcɨ
shepherds, and here we are at work. And these are said to be soldiers at the front,
45516: Some people even sweep it [that way] now.
45521: We sweep the edges as well.
45522: i pòsle žìtoto kakvò go pràvite
And after that, what do you do with the grain?
45528: We would grind it [and then] eat it.
45537: kɤdè go nòsexte fkɤ̀šti f kakò
Where did you take it in the house? In what?
45542: f sakùl’:e f sakùl’:e nòsime go dvà trì p’èt sakùl’a
In sacks, in sacks. We carried it in two, three, five sacks.
45546: And we –  we spread it out inside.
45549: azàm na vadenìcata go m’èl’eme da id’ème
And then to the mill. We grind it [so as] to eat [it].
45558: kanà da pràim tò ne imè sakvòne sakvɔ̀n ballɔ̀kᵊi atvɛ̀ana atsɛ̀ana
What [else] could we do? There wasn’t such plenty that’s winnowed and sifted.
45561: kvòto ìš’eš takvòn ìma bràšno segà napr’èš ne im’è
Now you can get whatever kind of flour you want. You didn’t have that before.
45569: tòo tòdor žìvkof da žìvɨ ìš’e mlògo
May this [guy] Todor Zhivkov go on living a long time yet!
45575: He put [things] in order. He put the [whole] world in order.
45579: dètu ìmat značkì na fr takìva sa bɨlì èto gɨ
the ones that have medals from the –  That’s what they were, here they are.
45586: ìm ma è tùva sɤm jɛ̀ etùka na kràjč’eka
I’m here. Way over – here I am, over here at the end.
45595: nìj smə tùka bəlìli nə ràbuta te tùka pàk ufčɛ̀ri ìma
We were at work here! And here’s more shepherds,
45598: i etùka è tùka dètu igràjat na dvò̝ra dètu č’ušmìcata
and here – Ah, here is where they’re dancing in the yard by the fountain.
45603: è tùkə zbòrə dètu sa igràlɨ è tùka sekàčɤ nɛ̀kvi rabòtnɨcɨ
And here’s the festival where they danced. And here are woodcutters, some workers.
45607: è tùka mahalìcata è tùka č’əšmìcata dètu sa pudàl’ɤ tuvà
And here’s the little village quarter, and here’s the fountain where they provided
45612: sìčkutu tùka dètu ìmat umrɛ̀l’ta sa pràvɤl’ɤ vəncì
everything, [those who] have [relatives among] the dead, and made wreaths.
45618: d’èset l’èvə limunàdətə dv’estə gràmə dvà l’èvə
Ten levs! Two hundred grams of lemonade, two levs.
45628: pèt limunàdi d’èset l’èvə ədìn lìtər mlɛ̀ku čètiri lèvə
Five lemonades, ten levs. A liter of milk, four levs.
45633: ədìn kilgràm furàš p’èt l’èvə i tò gu àjde tè čɛ̀sni̥ci̥te kàrət
One kilogram of fodder, five levs and it – Well, private owners bring it.
45640: əmə n’àkuj dukàrvət hùbəf n’àkuj dukàrvət kràvi̥te̥ se rəzbàl’ət umìrət
Some bring good [stuff] but some bring – Cows get sick and die,
45644: də dukàrəš ədìn l’ɛ̀kər tùkə sme nə kilum’ètri
and it’s hard] to bring a doctor here, we’re [several] kilometers away.
45650: kad’è pò naprèt fəv vɤrbìnə zootehnìkə dukuà də ìdiš
Where should you go first? There’s a vet in Vŭrbina. By the time you go
45654: də gu z’èmeš də gu dukàrəš tò nə bendzìn dədèš
and get him and bring him back, you’ve paid out on gas
45659: stò i pedesè dvèstə l’èvə tò əku ti e prijɛ̀tel šuf’òrə
a hundred-fifty to two hundred levs. And that’s if the driver is a friend,
45662: əku ti e blìzək ìnəče p’ètstutin l’èvə tr’àvə mu dədèš
if he’s [someone] close to you. Otherwise you’ll have to pay five hundred levs!
45666: a drùgata dèto e s nèja pò mlàda li e
And so – the other one with her. Is she younger?
45672: prez l’ètutu sàmu duìne i ufcète i kàrəme i nə pàše
During the summer we only milk the sheep and take them to pasture;
45674: màndri pràine e təkà beše̥ stàrətə dèjnos
we process dairy products. And that’s what our activity was like in the old times.
45680: strìgən’ètu e striž’ɛ̀hme si nìe i strìžene gi vɤ̀lnətə si
For shearing: we did the shearing. As for the wool we sheared,
45685: nè jə vlàčime dàže ne nòsine nə dəràk səs stəruvrèmski deràci
we didn’t card it, nor did we take it to carders. We used the old-time carders
45694: i vlàčine i predɤ̀t je i pràime drèhi ut t’èh
to card it and [the women] spin it and we make clothes from it.
45696: è segà sme pàk dubrè nə vrèmetu stàrite hòrə nàšte
Well, we’re fine now. In the old days older people, our folk,
45701: sə hòdili də tvàr’ət ève ut slavèino dʌ̀ski də kàrət è nadòlu
went to load lumber from Slaveino and to carry it [all the way] down [here] …
45709: š’ìeme pu.stàrumu pətùri əbì pràine d’ètu š’ìene
We sew baggy trousers in the old fashion, and we make thick homespun for sewing
45710: dà əmə tì pòmniš li mə às də t gu kàžə jɛ
Yes, but do you [really] remember? Let me tell you
45712: kàk je òti jɛ̀ səm kàrəl dɤ̀ski
what it was like, since I [myself] transported lumber.
45713: à i tì mòe si kàrəl
Well, you might have done it too.
45716: vɤ̀l’neni pəltà ut samì si gu pràime nìe sìčku
wool coats from [it]. We make everything ourselves,
45718: à jɛ̀ šə t kàžə kàk e idɛ̀hme zə edìn dèn
Well, I did, and I’ll tell you how. We’d go and in a single day
45724: dukàrəhme dɤ̀skite ut sləvèinu zə dvà dèn’ə vəf kìril i benkòvski
we’d bring lumber from Slavieno. Two days to Kiril and Benkovsky,
45726: ut stànuvi si gi tkàeme n’è
we do all the weaving ourselves, on the [old] looms.
45731: utkàrəme i sə vɤ̀rneme ubàč’e zìməhme pètstòtin kilà càrvicə
there and back. And – mark this – we’d take five hundred kilos of corn
45733: sìčkutu sə pràeše nə mèsnə plòč’e
Everything was done on local grounds.
45736: [Имаше ли някъкъв обичай преди да започне да се строи къщата?]
[Did you practice some sort of custom before starting to build a house?]
45742: predì də pòčneš kɤ̀štə də grədìš še pràiš ubičèj
Before you start to build a house, you’ll perform [this] custom:
45746: ɤ̀ v gudìnətə kətu nəpràiš š’ès s’èdem kùrsə prez l’ɛ̀tunu i
Hah! So if you make six or seven runs in the summer,
45750: i càlənə gudìnə si pučìvəš ə sià kòlku tr’àbvə də rəbòtiš
then you can take it easy the whole year. But now, how much do you have to work
45755: še zəkòl’iš’ ednò š’ìle nə ednɤ̀tə kèš’e i tvà e stàr ubičèj
you’ll slaughter a yearling lamb on a corner. That’s the old custom.
45760: i pòčvəž də grədìš màsturit’e̥ š’e gi hràniš tàm še purəznesèš
And then you start building. You feed the builders and distribute
45765: màlku po kumšìete i tvà e stàr ubič’èj pu kɤ̀štə grədèn’e
[meat from the sacrifice] among the neighbors. That’s an old custom for building a house.
45775: i pòčvə gradèn’eto gradèn’etu̥ sə grədèš’e nè səs vàr
Then the construction begins. The house was built not with lime
45782: a səs sòpstvenə pɤ̀rs d’ètu gu vɨ̀kəme kàl i səs sɤ̀štijə kàl
but with local earth, or as we call it, mud – with that very mud
45785: də z’ɤ̀meš pètstotin kilà càrevicə kòlku vrème tr’àbvə də rəbòtiš à
to get five hundred kilos of corn? How much time do you have to put in? Huh?
45791: Those days – it’s in the past.
45794: cənìte še mi nəpràiš sm’ètkə kàk sə
And the prices – do the math on that too!
45796: dà de tàm kirəžilɤ̀k se prài
Well, but people are still working in transport.
45797: əmi tòj kirəžilɤ̀k əmə ti kàzvəm kətu nəpràiš
Transport, yes, but let me tell you: [back then] if you make
45802: p’èt š’es kùrsə du benkòfski i ubràtnu i gudìnənə iskàrvəš
five or six runs to Benkovsky and back, that gets you through the year.
45805: ə vɤ̀r nàpraj segà trìes kùrsə də vìdim kòlku še iskàrəš
Now just go and make thirty runs and see how much you’ll make!
45806: I don’t know how much you’d get.
45810: əmi ne mòž’e štòtu zəfč’èrə šə hòde f mədàn
Well you can’t! See – the day before yesterday I was about to go to Madan.
45817: zəmàh ədnà sùpičkə tə imɛ̀še urìzeni zərnà mòž’eše də sə prebrujʌ̀t
I bought one small soup, with [so few] kernels of rice in it that you could count them,
45820: i dv’è̝ č’ùški è tòlku bɛ̀hə gulɛ̀mi i f n’ègə də imə
and two [stuffed] peppers – this big – and in them [barely]
45822: dvàes gràmə urìs dvàese i čètiri l’èvə səs trì filìjki hlɛ̀p
twenty grams of rice. And that was twenty-four levs, with three slices of bread!
45828: bèz drùgu nìštu à vərì žìvi də ìdim kàk še živèeš
And nothing else! So just go try and live [like that], to see how you’ll manage!
45835: a pù nəpr’èt əgà nəblìž’ehme ùstuvu tə hl’ɛ̀bə mirìše̥še̥
Earlier, it used to be that we’d get near Ustovo and you’d smell the bread
45838: i segà tòo ə kòjtu i ɤ pu vudɤ̀tə
And now the one who’s [responsible] for the water
45841: ot əgà se pudədèš òšte ut pòdvis
from there (Ustovo) as soon as you reach Podvis.
45846: s’àkə sùtrin gi utvàr’ə v’èčir gi zətvàr’ə
opens [the taps] every morning and closes them in the evening.
45852: à i l’èštə mu tùreše stò gràmə zejtìn
Right. And lentils [to which they’d] add a hundred grams of oil,
45855: i sə nəjədèš əgà dòjdeš ejtùvə i vèč’erə ne jədèm
and you’d eat so well that when you get home we don’t need any dinner.
45858: a sià ìiš f ùstuvu kvò še zɤ̀meš də jədèš
But now when you go to Ustovo what are you going to get to eat?
45861: tè s’à sə pʌ̀tnici kət sə udbìjət f ùstuvu
Travelers now [who] stop off in Ustovo
45862: də z’ɤ̀mət də jədɤ̀t də vìdim kvò še jədɤ̀t
to get something to eat, let’s [just] see what they’ll eat!
45865: tvà i tvà imə ràzlikətə ut nəpr’èž du segà
And there it is, that’s the difference between then and now.
45872: štòtu im’ɛ̀še p’èč’enu nə fs’èki č’òp egà zèmeš jɛ̀renu
There used to be roast on every branch. You’d take a kid
45878: tə gu zəkòliš prudədèš kužʌ̀nə i mesònu ustàvə bes pərì
and slaughter it and sell the hide, and the meat ends up free.
45880: a sà zə də zèmeš ednò jàre tr’àbvə də zìməš
But now to buy to buy a kid you need to get
45883: That’s the way it is now.
45887: i kòlku p’ènsijə zìməš tr’àvə dv’è p’ènsii də dəd’èš zə ədnò jɛ̀re
And how much pension do you get? You need to pay two [full] pensions to get one kid.
45888: pəg zə hlɛ̀b də ne guvòrim
Not to speak of bread even.
45890: zə hl’àp n’àmə li də dədèš
Don’t you need to pay for bread?
45893: e sedemdesè l’èvə m’ʌ̀su̥ kòlku m’ʌ̀su si zimàl tì zə ədnɤ̀ gudìnə
Seventy lev [a kilo] for meat. How much meat have you bought in a year?
45899: ne mòžeš ə pò nəpr’èt etùvə kòlehme sɛ̀kə s’èdmicə kràvə
You can’t. And before? Each week we used to slaughter a cow – [sometimes]
45901: dv’è i pu trì sme klàli i vərvɛ̀še štòtu bɛ̀ jèftinu
we slaughtered two or three. And it worked fine! Things were inexpensive.
45906: dvà l’èvə m’ʌ̀su ə s’à sə zəkòli sɛ̀ku gl’ʌ̀də
Meat at two levs [a kilo]. But now if someone slaughters, everyone [just] watches.
45912: kakvò e tovà vèče čeverm’ʌ̀ sìgurnu kàk se prài
… most likely, what it is to roast on a spit. How did you do it?
45918: dàž’e i də gu vìdim n’àma də gu puznàeme
Even if I saw one I wouldn’t recognize it!
45920: [laughter] a kàk se prài š tovà čevermèto
[laughter] And how do you do this roasting on a spit?
45922: tò mnògu l’ʌ̀snu sə prài əmə n’èmə ut kəkvò də sə nəprài
It’s very easy to do, but there’s nothing to do it with!
45927: i səs kakvò se pàli tovà nèšto s kvò s opàli
And what do you make the fire with? What do you make it with?
45930: è dərvàtə vìš kədè sə sàmu č’everm’ètu
With wood! See, over there. You only [need] the spit,
45932: də i kòl’etu sə gutòvi zə č’everm’ètu
and the posts are ready for the spit.
45935: tùri sə nə ədìn prɤ̀t i sə vərtì
And then you put it on a stick and it turns.
45942: stàvə i t’èle i òfcə i kòzə sìčku stàvə
[It also] works [with] a calf, or a sheep, or a goat. It’ll work [with] everything.
45944: sàmu gul’àmu živòtnu ne mòž də stàne
It’s only a big animal [that it] won’t work [with].
45945: You can’t do it [with] a cow.
45947: dò pedesè šejsè kilugràmə štòm e mesòtu stàvə
Up to fifty or sixty kilograms, given that it’s meat, is OK.
45950: uttàm nəgòre ne mòže tèšku e zə vərtène
Any more than that isn’t possible. It’s [too] heavy to turn.

46661: nə kədè gu dəržìš kòj kinà kədènu ìmə n’àkəf kujədžɛ̀k

46666: ìməme si gòr’e ə təkà kətu l’yvàtki ìməš’e kəš’li

46667: i tovà dèto mèsiš f nègo kàk se kàzvə

46670: kopàn’a tò ot kakvò e napràveno
A trough – and what is it made from?
46674: əh znàči ne è bil tugàva lèg živòta à
Life wasn’t easy then, was it?
46682: ìdeme səs məž’ète ž’èni i striž’ème ədìnən dərdž’ì drùgən striž’è
So we go [together], men and women, and shear [them]. One holds, the other shears –
46686: əmi tò živòt’ət kugà kàktu ìmə nɤ̀j je nè sə

46690: Well [of course] we hobble the sheep!
46694: a bè piš’ìn š’e jə pustriž’è kur’èmə

46697: ta kogà ti se strùva kogà bèše pò l’ʌ̀ko segà ili togàva
So how does it seem to you? What was easier, then or now?
46704: fàtəme im fàtəme im jʌ ə ustriž’ème kur’èmət i pòsle im fàtəme
We catch them – we catch them and shear the stomach. And then we grab them by
46707: amì i tugàvə bè təgàvə nugàvə be nəgà hùbavu

46714: č’ètirite nò̝gi i gi vɤ̀rdzuame s ədnɤ̀ vərzùl’k’ə i i

46717: təkà e kugà kəkònu dòjde nəkà e təkà e

a general celebration, with everyone (men and women) together. And that’s how it was.

46772: vudɤ̀tə ispòlzvəhə i pràihnə gul’èm ədrəl’ès tàm

46773: “Adreles” [is what] we call it (St. George’s Day).
46774: [And how did they put on weddings?]
46777: svàdbite gi pràime səs adnò vrème səs mùl’etə ìdiš nə svàdbə
We make wedding with – in the old days it was on mules. You travel to the wedding,

46787: trì č’ètɨri dùši nə kətɰ̀re pàk se kàč’ət

46798: nə kətɰ̀rete xòrətə jɛ̀hət nə mùl’etə nə məgàretə kòj kvòtu mòže
on hinnies, people rode on mules, or on donkeys, whatever anyone had –
46801: i dàž’e i peš’è vərv’ɛ̀hə unvà e

46816: kòj d’èset l’èvə kòj dvà l’èvə nə decà nə stàri

46821: kòjtu isfɤ̀rne rùbətə udvʌ̀tre unuvà e kupòvən’ètu

46825: m drùgu lùk s’àvəme c’ìkvi s’àvəme sìčku s’àvəme
Hm, what else? [Ah] we plant onions, we plant pumpkins – we plant everything!
46826: [А има едно нещо, което прилича малко на фасул]
[And there’s also this thing that’s a little like beans –?]
46828: What [would that be]? It would have to be beans.
46837: səbòrə nə nə l’ùtə kogà bèše na vrèmeto

46842: ... of November, I think it was – I don’t know.
46851: i kàk kàk se praznùvə tovà ka kàk stàvaše səbòrə

46860: po pòčne de da znàame če a zbòra mèsime si omèsime lèp
It starts when – we know there will be a celebration, and we knead up bread,
46865: ə zakòl’ame si ako ìmame nèšto pò golèmo alì àgɤnce

46866: mòž də e vəsùl’ kvò drùgu

46874: i i gi zakòl’eme i gòskite ìdat zborjànete se gòtvime

46884: dòjdɤt zborjàne srèštame gi narèdile ne sa takà	 golèma takòo
the visitors come and we greet them. There’s been set up for us a big –
46890: l’è l’ʌ̀štətə jə s’àvəme s’à fəf màrt f əpr’ìl i kətu stàne

46898: umʌ̀kneme e wòd’ìme tə ə mʌ̀kneme i jə kləd’èm nə ustròzi

So they come from other villages? [If you say] “celebration guests”, that means
46901: tè sə od drùgo m’àsto ìdvat
that they are coming from other places.
46903: uttùkə slàgəme i uttàm slàgəme i stàne nə kòpə gu vìkəme
We put some here, we put some there, so it becomes what we call a pile.

[So how do you call that plant?]
46912: ... [or] if they are relatives by marriage.
46917: əmi tò l’ʌ̀štətə sə s’àvə pròleteš’nu vr’ème i sàmu sə mʌ̀kni
So these – lentils get planted in the spring, and are just harvested,
46919: a vìe xòdite li na tèxnite səbòri

46924: i pòsle se vərš’ìje əmə vəsùl’əd gu gu ku kupàjeme

46932: sìjemè gu ìdem iskupàemè gu jèsencku vr’ème gu mʌ̀kneme
We plant them, go out and hoe them, and then harvest them in the autumn,
46935: uč’ùkəme gu ə l’ʌ̀štətə tr’àə də jə vərš’ìjeme pò trùdnu e l’ʌ̀štətə

46939: emi jà sɤm od lexčèvo pa màk’a mi e od vlədimìrovu
You see, I’m from Lehchevo, but my mother is from Vladimirovo.
46945: jà ìdvam od vlədimìrovu pa onì pa dovàždat u lexčèvo
I go from Vladimirovo [to theirs] and they come from Lehchevo [to ours].
46947: pa ìma nelì po drùgite selà òdime na drùgi pa tè tekà
And the same thing with other villages: we go to them and they [come here].

46954: nalì sèki ròd da si znàe kòj mu e svetèca
such that each family group knew which was its [own] saint,
46959: i da sa sabìra nè cèloto sèlo a sàmo edìn golèm ròt
and that the gathering would be not the entire village but just one large extended family –
46963: i kàk na kakvò m’àsto se pràveše tovà
And how – what sort of area was that celebration held in?

Whoever decides he’s going to do it, [that one] decides where it will be,

How can I tell you? It’s, well, you say there will be [something],
46975: də sə zbèrɤt si ròdovete le svòjte decà si zbèreš
that relatives will come together, that you’ll gather together your children,
46979: si napràiš pa gòsk’e sè si e ednò če a zbòr
you put it together, guests come, and it’s just like a village celebration anyway.
46985: [laughter] a kogà kogà zapòčnaxa tùka xòrata da si slà ə
[laughter] And when – when did people here begin to – uh –
46988: ìma li loz’à da slàgat ə ə xòrata lòzeta ìmat li tùka
Do people plant grapevines here? Do they have vineyards here?
46993: There used to be a lot of vineyards!
46996: mnògo ìmaše sèki si ìmaše lozjà i pres predì da pòčnət
A lot of them. Everyone had a vineyard here before they began
47000: tovà pò ə ə golèmite ə ro dèkare zemjà
[to put together] those big chunks of land (= collective farms).
47003: ìmaa si po mà pò màlko dè ama si ìmaa òrata
People had them. On less space, but people had [their own],
47007: pu mà i pòslem stanàa mnògo lozjà ama seà dalì ìma lozjà

47012: nìe za tovà zn znàeš če rètko pìtame zə
You know, [it’s surprising] that we rarely ask about this.
47014: kàk se tovà kàk se glèda na ednò lòze
How is that done? How do you cultivate a vineyard?
47015: What do you need to do for it?
47022: emi ə lòzjeto trèbva go kòpaš da go vrɤ̀zvɤš
Well, for a vineyard you have to hoe it, and tie it up,
47024: dɤ gu prɤ̀skɤš sɤs sìn kàmik še
and spray it with copper sulfite, and –
47029: You spray it, you tie it [to supports] –
47031: koè e nàj trùdno ot sìčko

47036: abe trùdno šò trèva mnògo kòpan’e i vrɤ̀zvan’e	 i ə ə filìzene
Well, what’s hard is that it requires a lot of hoeing and tying, and pruning –
47038: And what do you do with the shoots [you’ve] pruned?
47042: ami tìja li filìzite pròlet prə kə frɤ̀ frɤ̀gɤme nìe
Well, these shoots – in the springtime, we – we toss them out.
47049: sàmo tovà si ostàime na kolcìte si tùrame kòlci še òdim vṛ̀žeme

47052: m tovà lozàta i onà si gròzg’e i tè tekà

47060: a a decàta ìskaxa li ə da pìjat tovà predì da

47066: kàk mu vi kàk mu vìkaxa na tovà nə
47077: nèkoj se ubìe nèšto kogà nèšto se slùči sɤs nèkogo
… someone hurts themselves, when something happens to someone,
47080: kàk si fàštate svetèc i kvò pràvite za ček
how you grab a saint, and what you do to –
47083: kogà nèkoj se ubìe nèšto kogà

47084: The day! The day! The day!
47086: [Yes,] tell about the grabbing of the day.
47088: àbe i na dène i a i drùgu a
Well, about the day. And the other, and –
47103: ehehe nəkìvə ràbuti sìn sìčku nənòvu
Eh, son. Such things. Everything [to be started] anew.
47105: Should I take a photo of her?
