And that’s what’s coming for me now.
47121: enəkvò žə dò̝jde sìn enəkvò [laughter] dvà mètrə
That’s what’s coming son, that. [laughter] Six feet.
47125: ezgà nòč’e nɛ̀kvu štɛ̀lu də ìmə pàk pu zəm’ɔ̀sə
Now Noche, weren’t they about to do something about the land once again?

Well, whatever there is [to come]. Do you have any sort of documentation?
47135: əm tò žə zbərèm že sə zbìrət òtə nəlì tè hi
Well, we’ll get [them]. They’ll be collected. Because haven’t they –
47139: zə p’èk’ gudìn ni sɤ nè trɔ̀sɨlɨ

47154: dè si kusìm lyvàdɨse i kərtò̝fček i ud grədìna kvòtu ìməš

47167: əmi l’èš’tə tekà e sɤ̀štu jà š’ə ti rəspràəm kàk səm wòdilə

47172: də wòrəm l’ʌ̀štə səgà zəbràli smə tùkə məgàretu i
to plow lentils. So now. We got the donkey moving and –
47177: i i tvà i kràvətə i kàrəm decàtə də mi wòd’ət

47182: s ugləftʌ̀ gi vìkəm də mi wòd’ət  i jà wòrəm pòs’l’e
I tell them lead [the animal] by the bridle. And then I plow after that,
47191: è is pləninàtə əgà zèt s nàč’u də ti rəspràvəm nàč’u
up in the mountains. When my son-in-law Nacho – let me tell you, when Nacho and I
47193: žə ìštət nə nègu pərì də plàtəmə

47199: pàri də plàtəmə ut sigà pərì vìkət nòčo bəjɛ̀ žə i skɔ̀pu

47223: ìməm dvɛ̀ kukòški i ədìn pətèl’ nə nègu si e nvà
I have two hens and one rooster. He’s got [all] that,
47224: tò žə gu plàtə əm kəkvò
[and] he’ll pay for it. What else?
47229: [laughter] kò̝jtu gu pò̝lzuvə tò̝ žə gu plàta
[laughter] The one who uses it is the one who’ll pay for it.
47231: m tə nəkìvə ràbuti sìn enəkìvə
Ah such things, son, such things.

47249: i hi uprustɛ̀ə kàktu si beše nərɛ̀dbətə

47254: izlɛ̀zuə p’èttu gudᶤìnɤ zgà žə dàvəme

47258: Well! You’ve done well asking me things!
47262: də stə zdràvɤ i žìvɤ sìn
May you live in health, boys!
47266: čàkaj ednà snìmka da ti napràvime
Wait, we want to take a picture of you.
47269: I want to take a picture of you.
47272: e segà də mə stòrite jɛ̀ səm nè zə snìmkə sìn jɛ̀ səm

Oh, so I’m pretty, am I? Ah, if only it were the truth!

47302: ami n’àma da se kurdìsvaš xùbava si takà xùbava si

Well sure, I’m pretty! For eighty-two [that is]. Eighty-two.
47306: You’re doing well [for your years], you’re doing well.

No, I say (= want) to be standing.

47337: up’ʌ̀vəme tòə mòmčencenu op’ʌ̀vəme i	prez edìn mòs də mìn’e məgàrenu
pull up the reins – [there’s] this boy – we pull tight as the donkey’s crossing the bridge,
47346: i tò pàdnə pud mòstə uddòlu èh bòž’e kəkvò stànə
and the boy fell off the bridge. Oh Lord, what [a thing to] happen!
47349: [Just as] we’re going off to plow.

47361: tuvà i stàna i utʌ̀rnəə pàk də si prudəlž’ɛ̀vəme də urèm

47367: ut’ìdəme də ur’ème kràvətə ni st’èlnə pòčnə də vəlì
We go off to plow. The cow is pregnant, it starts to precipitate (“vali”),
47369: [all this when] we are plowing the lentils.

And it began [laughter] – it began to precipitate (“leti”), and I –
47391: i nìe təkòvu nìe təkòvu ìkəm əmi segà vìkəm nàsko kəkvò
And so we – we – I said “Well now,” I said “Nasko, what,”
47395: vìkəm šə pràim segà ìkəm zì dɤ̀š’ i dəšter’ʌ̀ mə beš’e
I said, “are we going to do now?” I said. [There was] this rain, and my daughter [there] too.
47402: slàgəm jednì č’uvàl’ nə gərbʌ̀ privɤ̀rzvəm nə kràvətə vòdim si
I throw a bag onto my back, tie up the cow and lead it along.
47410: è pɤ̀tištə t’àsni duv’èdəh sì jə stujɛ̀me tùkə uràli uràlutu stujà
Ah, the narrow paths! I led it [back] and we stayed here, the plow sat [unused]
47418: bl’ìzu dvàese d’ènə puluvìlu sə kòlko go sme puuràli
for nearly twenty days. Only half of what we’d needed to plow was done,
47424: drùgunu nè e uràtu gà utìdəm’e utàm s’ètn’e pàk
the other half was unplowed. When we managed to get back there,
47429: kràvətə mi sə pə ut’èllə pàk z dv’è məgàrtɤ ut’ìdəme də ur’èm
my cow had calved, so we went off to plow with two donkeys.
47436: səs ə ìməhm’e ìməh təkwòvə nə bràtə ž’enà zəv’èdəh i
We had – I had – my brother’s wife had [one], so I took them out
47443: pàk s t’àhnutu məgàr’e i smo i s mòtu də wòd’im də ur’èm
again, their donkey and mine, to go out to plow.
47465: zə čə čʌ̀stunu ml’àku du ìməhme kràvi dujɛ̀hme gi dujɛ̀hme kràvine
For yogurt you – we had cows, we milked them. [First] we milked the cows.
47469: š’e gi svər’ìme š’e gu ustàim də sə ist’ìn’e màlku
[Then] we boil [the milk] and leave it to cool a bit.
47474: š’e bàrəme s prɤ̀stə kɤ̀k se istìnəlu li e ne lì e
We’ll touch a finger to it to see if it’s [sufficiently] cooled or not.
47479: pərl’ìvu ku gu slòžiš to e stàne pəràti̥ku n’èmə
If you put [the starter] in when it’s [too] hot, it won’t be good, it won’t –
47486: səsìčə sə i putkvàsiž gu š’e z’èmeš’ fəv burìlutu də sìpež
It curdles. You put the starter in. [Then] you take it and pour it into the churn
47490: də gu bʌ̀rkəš maslò š’e iskàrvəš təkà
to mix it up, and get some butter [out of it].
47491: [What kind of animals do you have?]
47499: gov’ʌ̀da ìmame vòluve gi kàzvame xɤ̀
We have cattle. Oxen, we call them. Yes.
47507: We had both cows and oxen.
47511: And how did you call them [all]?
47523: ù š’ɤ̀təne buklùkə də iznìsəš ləjnàtə sìč’kunu də č’ìstiš’ ubòrə
Oh! Clearing up the garbage – you have to carry out the shit, to clean the stable,
47528: də gu kàrəš səs ə ə̥dnì səndɤ̀ci məgàre səm tuvàrilə də kàrəm
to take it off  with – I loaded up boxes on the donkey to take
47533: g’ubr’ʌ̀ nə nìvətə əm təkà beše decà kət ìdə də ž’ʌ̀nem’e
manure out to the fields. That’s how it was. [And] children – when I go [with others] to reap,
47545: nə n’ìvətə də də im pust’èlim àl’ištetu də i gi zəvìjeme
to the fields and spread out a rug for them and wrap them up,
47549: i tò šə me čùvə jà š’e žʌ̀nə nə m’èseči̥nkə
and he’ll watch my back ( = the kids)  [while] I reap in the moonlight.
47555: təkvò səm kàrələ i pàk š’ ìdeš’ sutrintʌ̀ də də vərš’ìješ’
That was my lot. And you’ll go [out] in the morning to thresh
47560: kugàtu skləd’èš’ užʌ̀než gu š’e gu kləd’èš’ d ìdeš’ pàg də vərš’ìješ’
after it’s piled. You reap [the grain], you pile it up, and go again to thresh it.
47566: šə nəl’ìvəš’ ərmànə š’e nòs’im nə rəmòtu vòdə də gu nəlìjeme
You water down the threshing floor: we carry water on our shoulders to pour out.
47572: i i tugà š’e nəs’àdəme ə nìe si pràime vəž’ètə nàč’i
And then we sit down [to tie sheaves]. We make our own cords, you know.
47574: utmɤ̀kneme ut tuvà pò dɤ̀lgu ut tuvà dè e tùkə
We pull out the longer ones of this, of what’s here, ...
47581: i šə gu vɤ̀rž’eš’ vəž’ètu i slàgəž gu i tùr’əš
... and you twist it into a cord. You put it (the stalks) [together],
47590: ami kàk se e zasè̝lilo nalì ti kàzvam takà
How was it settled? Well, let me tell you. [It was] like this.
47595: tùka tetev’èncite sa sa zas’è̝lile zərəd dobìtakḁ da im e širòko
People from Teteven settled here because of their livestock – to have enough space
47599: da pasɛ̀t i si sə podṛžèli i v gradɛ̀ kɤ̀štite
for them to graze. And they also kept houses in town.
47601: tovà tùka si rabòtat a po gradɛ̀ si podṛ̀žat kɤ̀štite
So - they work here [in the field], and keep houses in the town,
47604: du učìlišteto̥ ud učìlišteto tàm sa sa zas’è̝lile pa brusn’ène
up to the school. [The area] beyond the school was settled by people from Brusen.
47609: ut sredɛ̀ta na vasìl’ovo tàm pa brusn’ène udd’è̝ sa došlè
From the center of Vasilyovo onwards, it’s Brusen people – where they came from
47613: pàk ud brùsen pò nagòre pa šòpeto̥ šòpeto pa tàm
[is] Brusen. Then further up are the “Shope” people. The Shope people are there.
47620: pà šòpe sa izb’àgale ot šoplùka ta sa došl’è̝ tàm
The Shope people escaped from the Shope region and came there.
47625: ta sa zas’è̝lia pa t’èa ot tàm pò nagòre pak gṛ̀cite
Then they settled there. And further on up are Greeks,
47629: pa gṛ̀cko pl’ème ìma i i takòva klisùrsko pl’ème
a Greek tribe. And then there’s also a tribe from the Klisura region.
47633: s’è̝ takà sa izb’àgale koto e bilò puštin’àk tùkəna
All [of them] fled [from somewhere], and since it was empty here,
47636: i sa zas’è̝lile i si zastànale tùka i takà si ostanà
they came, and stayed here, and that’s how it happened.
47641: i se zas’è̝li selòto si stanɛ̀ gɤ̀sto v’è̝ke kòlko kɤ̀šti
The village got settled. And [the population] got to be dense. How many houses –
47643: ne gì znàm kòlko sa segàkana i nì sa interesùvam
I don’t know how many there are now. I’m neither interested in [that fact]
47644: nì gi znàja kòlko sa ama səm gi zapòmnila trìese kɤ̀šti
nor do I know [it], but I remember it being thirty “kushti” (houses).
47648: [How did you observe the holidays in olden times?]
47653: ama n’àkogi takà prekàrvame pràznicite̥ dòdeše velìgden
In the old days this is how we observed the holidays. When Easter came,
47657: trì d’èna si go pràzvame i si òde:me ta si sa sabìra:me
we celebrated it for three days. And we we’d go and gather together
47659: sas ribàrčanete da sme pòveče če beme màlko
with people from Ribarche for there to be more us, since we were few.
47664: i si vìka:me gajdàre cigulàre d’è̝ mùzika ud n’àkade dòde
And we’d engage bagpipe players and violinists, wherever musicians came from,
47666: ta ni svìri ta si pràzvame po trì d’è̝n’a
and they played for us, and we celebrated three days.
47668: nalì trì d’èn’a si òde:me i si svìrea i si go pràzvame
For three days we’d go out, musicians played, and we celebrated.
47670: dòdeše pòsle pa svetì.dùx pa na svetì.dùx še ìdem
Then would come the day of the Holy Ghost, and on that day too we go –
47673: pà pràznici n’àkade sa sabèrem pà spàsovd’en i takà s’è
[as] on holidays, we gather somewhere – and then the day of Ascension, and so on.
47677: na n’àkakvi obròci se sabìra:me ta si igràe:me
We’d gather together at certain ritual spots outside the village, and dance.
47679: i s’è takà ni svìrea gajdàre d’è svìrki d’è gajdanìci
And the bagpipe players would play for us, either with whistles or bagpipe chanters,
47682: è takìva svìrki pà s na tramp’è sme igràle
such types of reed whistles – and we even danced to trumpets!
47684: i na tramp’ènce i na tramp’è sme igràle
Little trumpets - we also danced to trumpets.
47686: pri vàs čùval li si tàja dùma
Have you heard this word around here?
47688: i segà ako ìma kàmən’e nèšto prɤ̀s slet tvà
So now if there are stones, and some dirt [comes in], after that,
47690: čìsti li se po drùk nàčin n’àkəf prìmerno kət zərnòtu
do you clean it some other way? For instance the grains.
47693: zərnòto go zbìrate pòsle na kùp nalì
You gather the grains up afterwards into a pile, right?
47696: vìkaxte li mu sòr ednò vrème ili kàk dùma ìmaše li zə
Did you call that “sor” in the old days? Something else? Was there a word for [it]?
47698: nə kùp nə kùp se səbìrə
In a pile. It’s gathered into a pile.
47711: dà i d’ètu ìmə sùšk’e əf rəš’ètutu gu zəvɤ̀rtə təkà
As for the husks, you twirl the grate around like this.
47716: ženìte gu vərtɤ̀t i sùšk’etu ustàvə vdìgə sə gòre
The women twirl it around and the husks stay behind. [All that] rises up.
47721: izlàzə ud žitòtu i se dìgə gòre
It gets separated from the wheat and rises up.
47725: tɛ̀ gu pribìrət s rəcète i gu fʌ̀rlət
They gather it up in their hands and throw it off [to the side],
47728: and that’s how it gets purified.
47731: à na tovà rešèto ìməše li mu speciàlnə dùmə
Ah. So then this grate: Was there a particular word
47732: da se kàzvə tò rešèto ot kakvò e napràveno
you used for it? What is it made from?
47736: ut kòže səs ə otdòlu nàči
47741: dùpki kòlkutu cigàrətə dol də fl’ène
Holes, the size of a cigarette, [for things] to go [through].
47745: əhà ot tàm mòže da pàdnat kàmene e nə
Aha. So that stones could go through there, and –
47747: No, that’s where the grain goes through –
47749: à žìtoto si minàva odòlu pàda
Ah! [It’s] the grain [that] passes through and falls –
47752: dà ž’ìtutu minàvə uddòlu i tvà d’ètu č’èkləsə sùšk’e ustàva
Yes, the grain falls through, and what’s left is the awns and husks.
47754: ahà i tò se obìra s rəkà
Aha, and then you gather that up in your hands …
47758: … and throw it off to the side. Right.
47760: mòž’e i nə livàdə də sə vərš’è d’ètu e ràvnu
You can also thresh in the meadow. Where it’s flat, [that is].
47762: ama pàk tr’àbva da ìma kàmene otdòlu
But still you’d have to have stones underneath, [wouldn’t you]?
47764: But how do you do it [then]?
47768: mòž də nèmə kəto e sùvu təkà pò trùdnu sə smìtə ž’itòtu
You can do it without, if it’s dry. But it is harder to sweep [up] the grains.
47775: ne sɤ̀ li učìstvəše trevàta predi
But didn’t the grass get cleaned [out] beforehand?
47777: Well, like it is down there, you see …
47784: e tàm mòe də də vərhʌ̀t i vɤ̀rli sə puubrìšəd gu
That’s where they could thresh. And they did. They clear it off
47787: səs turpànə màlku də nèmə jʌ̀dru i i vərhʌ̀t
a bit with a “turpan” (scythe) so there’s nothing big [in the way], and – they thresh.
47794: turpànə dètu kusì tre senòtu kus’ìlu
A “turpan”, [the thing] that you mow hay with. A mower.
47805: dà ə nìvətə sə žʌ̀ne səs sɤ̀rp tàə nìvə rəštɤ̀
Yes. But in the fields we reap with a sickle. Fields with rye.
47808: sɤ̀rp nəlì gu znàete təkòvə ednò zəkrəglènu
You know what a sickle is, right? This thing that’s round.
47811: ot prèdnətə stranà dèto dèto e ustrìloto
On the front part where the blade is –
47813: tovà ə glàtko li e ili
Is that [part] smooth, or is it –
47816: əmi àz gu ìməm mòə ti gu kàž’e sərpɤ̀t
Well, I have one. I can show it to you. My sickle.
47818: Is it smooth, or is it this [other way]?
47825: [It’s] jagged [in the area] that does the cutting.
47828: It’s got these teeth, and that’s what does the cutting.
47831: na l’àvata rɤ̀ka nad’àvahte li nèšto
Did you put something onto your left hand?
47834: nə l’ɛ̀vətə rɤ̀kə ìmə pələmàrkə kàzvəhə
On the left hand there’s what they used to call a swaphook.
47847: səbìrə pòveče slàmə štòt t’à e səs kùkə e tùkə s ròk
It gathers more straw because it’s hooked here, like a horn.
47858: Have you ever seen one? No?
47862: dɤ̀rvenà e bùčne čètirite prɤ̀stə ìmə tùkə ròk tugàvə
It’s wooden. You push your four fingers in, and there’s the horn here.
47864: sl’ət prɤ̀stite ìmə ròk e təkɤ̀f
After the fingers there’s a horn. See, like this, ...
47868: dètu səbìrə slàmətə zəgreb’è təkà i uddòlu ž’ɤ̀ne sɤ̀rpə
.. where it gathers up the straw. You grab it thus, and the sickle reaps from below.
47871: oddòlu ə go sečè ili go
From below. Does it slash [the grain] or –
47878: rèže gu tò e òstru nəzɤ̀benku rèže təkà nèkulku pɤ̀te
It cuts it. It’s sharp, jagged. And it cuts like this. Several times,
47881: rəkòjki gu kàzvət tùr’ə gu nə snòpə drùk ìmə pàk
[in] handfuls, they call them. I put [the straw] in sheaves. There’s another [person]
47885: ta gu səbìrə gu vɤ̀rzvə təkà nə snòpje i zəminàvə zə hərmànə
who gathers it and ties it, like this, into sheaves. Then off to the threshing floor.
47888: əmhəm əmhəm tɤ̀j i pòsle kato go zanesète vəf plèvnikə
Uh huh. Uh huh. So, O.K. Then after you take it to the hayloft
47891: tàm na otdèlno m’àsto f čuvàli go pàzite
you keep it in a separate place there, in bags.
47895: You pile it up in a pile [there].
47899: trùpə sə nə kùp i pòsle sə zèmə f kòšə zə
You pile it up in a pile, and later you take it in a basket for –
47900: zə kràvətə zə mùletu zə zə dubìtəkə
the cow, the mule – for the livestock.
47901: The straw is for the livestock.
47909: zərnòtu ud’ɛ̀lnu f č’uvàlete f həmbàre ud’èlnu
The grain [is kept] separately, in bags. Separately, in the barn.
47911: So, and [then] where did you used to grind it?
47916: əmi ìmə vudenìci̥ ìmə vəf l’èskə vudenìci̥ kədètu ìmə hòrə pu rekʌ̀tə
But, there are mills! There are mills at Leska, where there are people by the river.
47922: sə nəpràili vudenìci zəkàrvə sə tàm i sə mèl’e
They built mills [there]. They take [the grain] there, and it gets ground.
47927: əmhəm əmhəm a vəfkɤ̀šti ìmaxte li si vodenìci təkìva
Mmhm, mhmh. And did you have any sort of mills in the house
47930: da sə mèli də mèl’ət ženìte na rəkà
that you could grind with – for women to grind by hand?
47933: ìmə d’ètu càrevicə mèl’ət ə nəč’ùpvə gu zərnòtu nə
There’s one that they grind corn with. It chops up the kernels into  –
47934: Well, how can I tell you?
47936: Say the word the way you call it.
47943: nə s’ìtno gu nəmèl’e i gu vər’ʌ̀t səs màlku bòp
It’s ground up very tiny, and then they cook it with a little bit of beans, ...
47951: čorbɤ̀ ste mu vìkali n’àmaše li tàja màndža speciàlno ìme
You called it soup. Didn’t that dish have some particular name?
47955: n’àkakvo ìme nèjno si sàmo čurbɤ̀ kətu kàžət tovà
Some name that was its alone? When they say “soup” that means –
47961: Uh huh – that’s what it’s called.
47964: Uh huh. [So then.] How did people used to plow?
47969: səs vòluve pò ràno orɛ̀hə dvà vòlə sə fprɛ̀gət
Earlier, they plowed with oxen. They harness two oxen
47972: səs dərvò tùkə zəkòpčeni i s uràlutu ədìn gi kàrə
with [a piece of wood] connected here, and a plow. One person drives it –
47975: dà ə adìn otprède ili odzàde
Yes. Uh [this] one – is he in front or behind?
47977: nè sàmu udzàde dèt dəržì uràlutu
No, only behind, where he holds the plow.
47979: a segà vòluve nèmə segà səs mùl’etə urɤ̀t
But there’s no oxen now. [People] plow with a mule now.
47982: a segà tàm dèto sa zakòpčeni vòluvete tovà kàk mu kàzvaxte
Now, this thing where the oxen are attached, how did you call that?
47991: Is that how you used to call it?
47995: zəbràil gu səm màmə mu stàrə èj umòt’ umòt’ i oràlu
I’ve forgotten it, devil take it! Yes, the yoke. The yoke and the plow
47996: è vìš tì kàg gu znàeš [laughter]
Look at you, how do you know that?! [laughter]
47999: na mèn tùj mi e ràbotata [laughter]
Well, that happens to be my [line of] work! [laughter]
48005: zəbràil gu səm tuvà udàvnə ràbutə bè
I forgot it. That’s stuff from a long time ago, you know?
48007: tuvà tùj mi e ràbota znàči oddòlu dobrè koè se kàzva
Well, that’s my work. So, O.K., that’s below. Which part do you call
48011: the yoke – the upper piece of wood or the lower one?
48064: [Where did young people used to gather earlier on?]
48068: nìe pò ràno kato momì ergène takà sḁ si opredelìle̝ sedɛ̀nk’i
Back then [when] we were maidens and bachelors they had work bees.
48072: səs ràbota sme prèle̝ ìdvat mumčèata nìj kàzvame ergènite̝ ìdvat
with work! We'd spin. Then come the boys – we called them “bachelors”.
48076: kòjta ergènin si ìma prijàtelka sèdne si do nèja
If one of the bachelors has a girlfriend, he sits down next to her,
48080: ìma tò nalì e od dvè dərvèta
And [it’s made from] two [pieces of] wood, right?
48082: ud ednò dərvò ednò odgòre dərvò tɤ̀j li
From one [piece of] wood. One [piece of] wood on top, is that it?
48085: ednò odgòre ednò odgòre dərvò ə lɛ̀gə nə vrətʌ̀
One on top. One [piece of] wood on top, and it lies on the neck
48087: nə edìnijə vòl i nə drùgijə e təkà ednò dərvò lèku
of both one ox and the other, like this – one light piece of wood
48091: nə vrətʌ̀ i tùkə ìmə prubìtu dùpki spùsnəti ž’eglì
on [their] necks. And there’s holes bored here, and large pins dropped [into them].
48096: lègne i f pulɤ̀ta prikàzvat si t’à si predè tòj
puts his head in her lap and they chat. She keeps on spinning, while he,
48100: ž’eglìte ə slàz’ət təkʌ̀ ə tùk ədnò i tùkə drùgu
The pins come down like this. Here’s one, and here’s the other.
48103: tòj akò se e poizmòril màlko na ràbota mòže i da zàspi
if he’s gotten tired out from his own work, can even fall asleep
48108: tɛ̀sni i tùkə sə vʌ̀rzvə səs vrəfč’ìčkə vrɤ̀fkə
[They fit] tight. And here’s [where] you bind it up with a tie. A rope.
48116: ne è za čùdo i stuìm dukadɛ̀ idinàez dvanàes čəsɤ̀
That wouldn’t be a surprise! So we stay there until eleven or twelve o’clock,
48118: è gu s’à kɤ̀k e tùkə ìmə tovà ednòto kɤ̀k se kàzva
O.K. now, we’ve got it. There’s this thing here, how do you call it?
48122: pribìrame sɤ kojàto momà si ìma prijàtel tòj si ja ispràšta
and then go home. If a girl has a boyfriend, he accompanies her.
48125: puprikàzvə si tàm nə ùlicətə i sə pribìrət
They chat [for a while] there on the street, and then they go home.
48132: te tì sɤ pravìle̝ gulɛ̀mi svàdbi f sɤ̀bota pregòtvɤd zə svàdbətə
Well, they put on big weddings. On Saturday they prepare for the wedding,
48138: ə tvà nədòlu d’ètu spùsnətu sə kàzvə ž’eglì
And this that’s hanging down below, that’s called the pins.
48142: f nedɛ̀l’a svàdbətə f pondɛ̀lnik pràvat prik’àš na bùlkata
on Sunday the wedding, and on Monday they prepare the bride’s dowry.
48147: One “pin”, is that how you call it?
48153: tɤ̀j i pòsle oddòlu kàk se svɤ̀rzvət
O.K. And then, how is it tied down below?
48163: pò debèl də nè go skʌ̀cə sə stɛ̀gə
Thicker, so it won’t break. You fasten it
48165: and [then]  it (the ox’s head) won’t slide out.
48173: Another of the same, and then [another of] the same.
48177: dà i nətàtək vɤ̀rzənu tugàvə uràlutu zə
Yes. And in back, it’s tied like this to the plow for –

48283: tɤ̀j tovà sa ùši dobrè tìja ùši
OK, these are the moldboards. Fine. [But] these moldboards,

But now it’s – now it’s freedom. Yes, it’s freedom now, but

48340: ne sɤ̀m go čùval tovà be
48343: ə e e segà segà rəspràjət tàə sùtrin

I take them along. We had an old lame man – I take them

48443: š’e gi tùriš fəf fəf tupìlutu də gi kvàsiš’
then you’ll put them in а soaking place to soak them.
48447: š’e dòjdež də gi m’èniš š’e gu stòriš’
[Then] you’ll come to swingle them. You’ll put [the result]
48452: nə təkìvə dɤ̀lgi š’e gi pràjə š’e gu nəvìvəme nə fùrki

We called them “kochani.” People don’t call them “kochani” any more
48475: but back then we called them “kochani”.

home, into the house area, [where] we pour it out [into containers] in the barn. Then –

I was born in the year eighteen ninety-eight

48815: i t’à e rudènə fəf sled dv’à gudìni slet tvà
and she was born in – two years later. And after that
48818: ìməh pò màlək nàj màl’kijə ni bràt gòru

God has given! There are [trees] in the forest as far as the eye can see.

48859: sòpi sòpi sòpi mə təkìvə dərvètə dà

They didn’t – They treated the ones from Italy really badly.

So the railway line came from Momchilgrad to Podkovo. And [the workers]

48888: e ut tùə ud nàštu sèlu imɛ̀šen turduvàci rəbòtiə pu lìnijətə
there were also conscript laborers from our village working on the line.

[laughter] That’s what I’m telling you about. I was afraid!

Well, the Germans were saying “Hey, five more days,” they said,

48906: pəg bràt rəzbìš li dòjdəh si às tùkə pùsnəə nə màlku
a brother, you know. And I’d come here – they’d let us out a bit,
48911: nə pučìfkə ednà sèdmicə da si nəpràime ə dòjdeh si nə pučìfkə
[given us] a week of leave to sort things out. And I came here on leave
48915: às mu vìkəm nə m bràt mi slùšaj be mnògu ùbəvi pərì
and I said to my brother, “Listen here, there’s really good money
48919: dàvət germàncite ùbəvə rənà dàvət vìkəm vàr tì nə bràt mi
to be had from the Germans, and good food. Go for it!” I said to my brother.
48924: e ne jàs strà mə ə vìkə še sə pòčnət vujnà
“Ah, I’m afraid,” he said. “They’ll start a war
48927: and they’ll kill us as well.”
48931: š’e gu pr’ed’èm tə pràvime pròsturi gu kàzvəhme
spin it, and make [of it] what we used to call hemp rugs.
48937: xɤ̀ i č’ùvàli pəg drə drùgutu gu č’ùkəhme
Yes, and bags. And the – We pounded the rest of it,
48942: pàk i gu pràvehme zə č’ùvàl’i i pràvim ut t’ìjə pròsturi
and made it into bags. We make hemp rugs from it.
48946: pɤ̀l’nehme gi slàmə vɤ̀tre tə pràvime d’ïš’èci
We would fill the insides with straw and make mattresses.
48955: mʌ̀kne se i se kvàsi fəf ə tup’ìlutu sed’ì ədnɤ̀ s’èdmicə
You harvest it and soak it in the soaking place; it sits there a week.
48960: i si od’iš də gu izmìjež’ də isɤ̀hn’e i m’èneme go pàk
Then you go to wash it, and [when] it dries we swingle it again.
48965: nə ìməme si̥ n’àvgə nə m’elicə nìe ɤ̀ dɤ̀rvu
We have – sometimes we use [what’s called] a swingle. It’s, uh, wood
48973: utstrən’ì ìmə ž’èl’ezu fkòpč’enu təkà mi ə tùkə drɤ̀škətə dərž’ìš’
There's an iron piece attached at the side and you hold on to a handle.
48980: də ne sɤ̀ spl’èskvət tɤ̀j i ottùkə tovà nàči tovà
So they don’t flatten out. Right. And this [thing] here –
48981: kàk se kàza èj tovà dərvò tùka
how did you call this [piece of] wood here?
48984: əmi cɛ̀lutu sə nərìčə uràlu bè
Well, the whole thing is called a plow!
48986: c’àloto si e oràlo i tovà i tovà pàk
The whole thing is a plow – this, and this too.
48990: sə vìka oràlo a tovà tùka dèto go dəržɤ̀t udzàde
It’s [all] called the plow. And this thing where they hold it from behind?
48997: ne sè seštaš ne sè sèštaš drɤ̀škə təkà
You don’t remember. Ah, you don’t remember. A handle. O.K. then.
48998: drùgo ìma li dubrè tùka tovà tò ne sɤ̀ li
Well now,  is there something else? Ah, here. This thing. Aren’t these –
49001: kàk e zafànato za za uràlutu
How is this connected to – to the plow?
49003: əmi tùkə e fkupànu səz gulɛ̀mə dùpkə i tvà ə
Well, there’s a big hole dug into it here, and this, uh –
49005: it’s pushed in there – the handle.
49009: ili pək cɛ̀lutu nèkugàš izràstvə təkà nə səmòtu dərvò si
Or sometimes the whole thing had just grown like that. The same piece of wood.
49015: And the three of them all grown together.
49017: nè trìte nè e tvà è tvà e ud’èlnu
No, not all three of them. This [here], this is separate.
49023: udèlnu tùkə si e zəfànətu səs ə ə dùpkə nədòlu
It’s fastened separately here with – there’s a hole underneath –
49027: i tùka si ìmə čuvìja dɤ̀rvena
And here there’s a wooden peg. Right?
49031: ahà znàči tovà e pàk čuvìja
Aha. So that’s a peg too.
49036: a tùka drɤ̀škətə kàk se zafàšta za oràloto
And the handle here – how is it fastened to the plow?
49039: ə drʌ̀škətə sə nəmìrə cɛ̀lutu izràslu təkà
The handle – the whole thing is grown together like this.
49044: This thing is here like this ...
49046: ... and this is together with this.
49057: drùgoto c’àloto oràlo drɤ̀škətə i tovà tùka dòlu
The rest, the whole plow – the handle, and this here below.
49060: tovà tùka dòlu n’àmaše li si odèlno ìme kàk se kàzva
And this thing below, wasn’t there a separate name for it? How do you call it?
49062: uràlu sə vìkə a tovà tùka vuìšte uvìšte
It’s called a plow. And this here? “vuishte”? “uvishte”? (pole)
49066: əmi čɛ̀kəj kətu flèneme vɤ̀tre še zəpìtəm unèjə
Wait a bit, let’s go inside and I’ll ask some people
49070: kəkvò ìme mòe də mu kàžem
... [to see] what name I can put to it.
49076: dobrè tùka kato orèš ako e pò vlàžno se zbìra prɤ̀st nalì
O.K. then. So if it is more moist when you plow, the earth will clump up, right?
49082: da nətrùpvə sə nətrùpvə sə màlku i kətu ìde
Yes, it piles up. It piles up a bit, and when you get
49086: nə kràjə də ubrɤ̀štə gu drùsne màlku ta se
to the end and make the turn, you shake it a bit so that –
49088: And wasn’t there some sort of ...
49096: a volòvete s kvò gi pətkàrvat
And what do they drive the oxen on with?
49108: kopràl’a da mu vìkat ili nè n’àma si takòva
[Is there a chance] that they call it “kopralya”? Or not? There’s no such –
49111: takòva si ìme si n’àma həm
[It appears] there’s no such name. Hm.
49115: Well, you told me so many things!
49117: ìnače n’àmaše oddè da gi takòva tovà
49125: n’àmaše se zapìše tovà kàk se takòva kàk sa zbìra
It wouldn’t have gotten recorded. This is how – how it’s collected,
49133: t’a sə hàrkumətə nəpɤ̀lni òpeni i še nətòč’im òšt
The cauldron’s gotten full. Take a sip, and we’ll pour out some more.
49136: əmì səs rəš’ètu ednì drɤ̀ški təkìvə
Well, with grates. These [things with] handles.
49143: And what did you [use] to reap with?
49148: səs kakvò žɤ̀nehte tvà dèto žɤ̀nete s nègo
What did you reap with? That thing that you use to reap with,
49159: səs srɤ̀p i pəlamàrkə žə tùriš nə tàjə rɤ̀ka
[You reap] with a sickle, and you put a swaphook on this hand.
49171: So, you shove [your arm] into it.
49173: žə si utrèžiš rəkɤ̀tə [laughter] tvà e dɤ̀rvenu
… you’ll cut your hand! [laughter] It’s this wooden thing
49176: d’ètu gu nəmùšiš tùkə nə tìjə prɤ̀sčetə
that you shove [your arm] into like this, into these little fingers,
49179: i s tuvà səs sɤ̀rpɤ pribi
and with this and the sickle, you –
49185: pribirèš udrèžiš gu pribirèš udrèžiš gu
you gather, you cut [the wheat], you gather it, you cut it.
49189: dàvajte po ednà motìka po edìn srɤ̀p i po ednà palamàrka
… [just] give them each a hoe and a sickle and a swaphook,
49192: so they can see how it’s done.
49197: n’àməmi pələmàrki vèči izgùbijmi gi nìj sɤ̀rpuviti
We don’t have any swaphooks any more, and we lost the sickles.
49203: All of mine are still here.
49213: du n’àvgə žə mi gi tùr’ət
…  until some [future] time when they’ll put them [in my coffin] with me.
49217: čètiri pəlamàrki i čètiri sɤ̀rpə əko ìməte dàvəjte i də
Well, if you have them, [just] give us four swaphooks and four sickles, and –
49220: Oh, we’ll find [some], to be sure!
49227: Back in the old days  [we had] these carriages –
49230: mi n’àmə kvò də sə žèni sià
Well, there’s nothing to reap now [anyway].
49238: za vəršìdbətə ə rəskažì kàk vəršèexte
[Yes,] the threshing. Tell [us] how you used to do the threshing.
49244: segà tr’àbva də utìdem də izur’èm nìe žinìte
We women need to go off now to plow.
49248: vəršìdbətə mɤžèti kutu žènim mɤžèti gi vɤ̀rdzuət
[Ah,] the threshing. [Well,] the men, after we reap, the men tie it all up
49249: na snòpi mu vìkəmi təkà na
in sheaves, that’s what we call them, about …
49256: tòl’kuva təkàva dib’èlo takà snòpi mu vìkəmi nìe
… this size, this thick. We call them sheaves.
49261: [aside] That must be the former Party secretary.
49266: segà kək se kəto ìdət znàči na nìvətə
So now, how did – that is, when you go to the field, ...
49273: kàk trɤ̀gvət də də žɤ̀nət kàk sə narèždət
... when you set out to – to do the reaping, how did people arrange themselves?
49276: Into lanes (specific sections of the field).
49279: My mind’s gone off wandering somewhere [laughter]
49290: nə rəkòjki mɤžèti go vɤ̀rdzuvət pràət vəžètə ut àsəl’
… in handfuls, and the men bind it up. They make a cord from the very –
49294: òdil sam tàmone dàvam mu za ə takòvo jɛ̀den:e
I went down there, I give it food.
49295: He gives it this and that, and –
49305: And what do you put it in?
49307: What do you put the grain in?
49312: žìtut f kapàn’ḁ vəf takòvə jɛ̀sla ìma napràvena čumènt tàm go slòžiš
The grain [goes] in a trough, in a manger made of cement. You put it there.
49319: ami kədè se dəržì bikàn dènu sa sidì vɤ̀tre
But where do you keep the bull when it’s inside?
49327: tò e jɛ̀slʌ tò ustrənì dès duvàrčeta jɛ̀slʌ nəpràvenə za takòva tàm
That’s a manger. It’s by these small walls, a manger made for such.
49332: tàm mu slòžuvame za za ràne za rànete
That’s where we put his food.
49333: [Tell me now where you keep the hens.]
49337: kukòškite si edɛ̀lnu be kukòškite e tùka da kàeme tò si napràvena
The hens are separate, you know! The hens are in what we call – it’s made –
49342: ìma takòvo əm napràeno ìma kət kùrnik tɤ̀j e napràvenə kakòškite
There’s this thing that’s made – it’s like a coop, made [for] the hens.
49346: pɤk dubᵊìtaka tàmone kat tàmo oddòlunu dàm dàm sa kàžuva
But the livestock are over there, separate. In the barn. It’s called a barn.
49347: [What kinds of livestock did you have?]
49351: We had different sorts of livestock: cows, sheep, goats –
49352: [А как се казва на малкото на кравата ако е мъшко?]
[How do you call the young of a cow if it’s a male?]
49357: [If it’s] a male, then a baby ox.
49369: pòsle trèbva da or’è orè vɤ vɤf na takòvata s orà oràn:e
Then it has to plow. To plow, to go and – you know, do the plowing.
49373: We harness them with a yoke.
49381: s ədnò dɔ̀rvo takòvo bandrùk i gu klad’èš i z’ɔ̀l vòla
With a piece of wood, a yoke. You put it on and the ox takes off.
49383: And let’s go! off to the plow!
49384: [What different parts are there on a plow?]
49389: ìma n’èma ùša ušà ìma na ràlata takìva dèd da ras
There is – there isn’t – there are moldboards on the plow, to –
49394: da rastvàra da razdɛ̀l’a zèm’ata ušà drùgo kvò
to cut apart, to cut the earth apart. Moldboards. What else?
49395: [Where do you store the grain after you reap it?]
49400: a nòsime go pòsle žìtətə agà z go priberème sɤ sɤs kalmu
We carry it off – the grain, after we gather it with a  –
49404: sɤs sɤ̀rp sɤ̀rpue kalmùje gi kàžuvame nìe ožɔ̀neme go i nə
With a sickle, sickles, [but] we call it a “kalmuya”. We reap it all,
49407: a takòvo svɔ̀rzvame go i àjde pòsle nòsime go na armànete
and then tie it up. And then we’re off to – we take it to the threshing floor.
49414: i vòloveto az d’uèn’ az d’uèn’ i d’uèn’a e tàm
And the oxen. With a threshing board. A threshing board there
49419: sɤs krèmekᵊi naonòden da s da rɛ̀že zərnòto žìtoto
with flintstones, set up so as – to cut up the grain – the wheat.
49423: žìtətə sapo sàpoveto da rɛ̀že dè i go varšòme tɤ̀j
To cut up the grain –  the stalks, you know? And we thresh it.
49426: i pòsle i s katᵊìre go varšòme ə səs magàreta s katᵊìre takà
Then we thresh it, with hinnies, with donkeys, with hinnies, you know?
49427: [Did the women make “klin” in the old days?]
49434: i klìna klìn dè ama na klìna demèk kòrᵊi sùčat ženᵊìte
“Klin”, yes, “klin”. Well, for “klin” the women roll out pastry sheets,
49439: i àjde nə nə takòvata slòžuvat mu bulgùr ali arìs
and then, well, they put such stuff in it – bulghur, rice,
49460: [Can you recognize the types of mushrooms?]
49464: ami paznàvam tò iz izlìzat at at zem’ɔ̀ta tàm
I recognize them. They sprout out of the ground,
49468: gɔ̀bički ùbvi zə jèdene jadème gi nìe pɤk ìma pàk
little mushrooms that are good to eat. We eat them. And there are also some
49471: pa darv’ètata izlìzat i tàm i gɔ̀bi izlìzat ama bɛ̀lᵊì
that grow on trees. The ones that grow there are white.
49476: ìmə na červ’ènᵊì červ’ènᵊì mu takòvoto vɔ̀tre
And there’s also red ones: they are red underneath.
49477: [А кой ви ловеше мишки в къщите?]
[Who used to catch mice for you inside the house?]
49480: kò kòtetata kapàn ìmame i kapàn na napràveno na kapàn
Cats. We have traps, traps that are made
49485: takòvata at ə dɔ̀ska i ə takòva na dùpkɤ na dùpkɤ napràe
so that – There’s a board, so that the board has a hole [made] in it,
49489: i kato ga slòžəš vɔ̀tre lɛ̀p màlku zakàčiš i tòj se màje
and you put a little bread in it and hook it on, and the prey gets tricked:
49493: tàmo vlìza i pɔ̀hɤla i sa fàštat mᵊìškite
the rat goes in there, and [that’s how] mice get caught.
49498: gul’ɛ̀mi sòpi kuìtu id idvàm gi dìgahə i
Big cudgels, [so big] that they could hardly lift them.
49499: [Ходехте ли в гората да берете нещо?]
[Did you gather things in the forest?]
49502: səbìrəme kɤ̀k ne səbìrəme səbìrəme lɛ̀šniki l’àtnu vr’ɛ̀me
Ah we do! How could we not gather [anything]? We gather hazelnuts in the summer
49504: and dry them for the winter.
49508: uttùkə sə vərì uttàm tàm tò i strɤ̀mnu təkànə tò
[It’s best] if you go this way. That way is steep. So this [way] you go
49513: vdèsnu fl’àvu utìvəš ìmə utrìenə utɤ̀pčenə ut hòrətə
you go right, left – [the road is] smoothed out, beaten down by the people
49519: t’àsnə t’àsnə kulà ne mòž’e də mìne
[It’s] narrow, narrow. A car can’t get through.
49526: tugàa kətu uvərš’ème snòpetu tə gu zberèm vèč’er gu zbìrəme
When we gather the sheaves up to thresh, we gather it in the evening
49528: səz greblà gu tìkəme gu tu nə sòr gu pràime
with rakes and push it together. We make it [all] into a pile.
49531: pràime gu nə sòr izmìtəd gu ž’ènte nəòkulu
We make it into a pile. The women sweep all around it,
49536: zərnòtu se strùpvə sič i č’àkame vɛ̀ter segà də dùhne də
and the grain is all piled up, and we wait for the wind to blow.
49539: fɤ̀rgəme səs nihnitìrje hmi kàzvəhme ednì təkìvə
[Then] we throw it up with these things we call “nihnitiri” (large pitchforks),
49544: səs č’ètiri p’èd zɤ̀bə č’èrpvəme i fɤ̀rl’ime v vɤ̀zduət
with four or five prongs. We rake it and throw it into the air.
49548: slàmətə jə zìmə vɛ̀terə ž’ìtutu pàdə tùkə nə drùgətə stɤ̀rnə
The wind takes the straw, and the grain falls here on the other side.
49551: i udmìtət ž’ènite s metlɤ̀tə udmìtət i gu tìkəme təkà nə
The women sweep it up with a broom – they sweep it up and we pile it like this in –
49554: we “dermonize” it, [run it] through a “dermon” (big sieve)!
49558: tò e udvɛ̀enu tuvà vèč’e tvà e ud’ɛ̀ennu ž’ìtutu
It’s been winnowed already! The grain is winnowed.
49561: dà predì tuvà se i gu v’ɛ̀eme
Yes, before that it’s – we winnow it.
49573: i n’è iməme [unintelligible] st’àgəni səs nèjə
49576: jɛ̀ səm m’ʌ̀nələ jɛ̀ segà səm səs puv’àsmutu segà
I was swingling [just] now, and I have a whole distaff-ful of it now.
49586: m’ènicə sə kàzvə m’ènicə m’èneme nə n’ègə tràkaš tràkaš
It’s called a swingle. A swingle. And we swingle with it. You beat and beat,
49591: iskàrvaž gi puvesmàtə pàk š’e gu tùriš’ nə ədnʌ̀ dʌ̀skə
and you make them into a distaff-ful [of hemp]. Then you put it again on a board
49596: də gu č’ùkəš də mu izl’èze puzderɤ̀ də stàne č’ìstu
to pound it, so as to get the swingling-tow to come out clean.
49600: ò ìməme rìzi pràvim ut təkìvə tkàeme rìzi
Oh, we [even] have shirts from this [substance]. We weave it [for] shirts.
49616: jòrš’uveto pa trɛ̀va trɛ̀va trɛ̀va trɛ̀va pasɤ̀t t’è
Hedgehogs? Grass, grass, grass, grass – that's what they eat!
49675: kəkò èj tàm ìmə inò ràmnu m’àstu cìmbel
What [do you mean]?! See, over there, there’s a level area, Tsimbel,
49744: bès də gi bɛ̀lim pə pòsle bèrem kočànite̝
without husking them, and then we gather the “kochani” (corncobs).
49773: ud žìtu̥tu̥ si d’ètu i gu vɤ̀rdzuvət nə snòpi
from the wheat itself, and [use] it to bind up the sheaves.
49776: gi zbìrət pràət gi takà nə krəscì nə gul’èmi
They gather them up, and make them into big cruciforms, like this.
49783: sètni gà dòe vr’èmi za vəršìdbətə pràm ərmàne təkà èj tòl’kəvo
Then when it comes time for the threshing, we make threshing fields like this,
49789: kòl’kutu è tvà i dukàrvət snòp’it’i i z dikàni
as big as this here. And they bring in the sheaves, with the threshing boards
49792: i s vulòvi i sə vəršè ubikàl’ə sə i sə sm’èli
and with oxen, and you thresh: [the oxen] circle round, and then you grind it.
49795: Then in the evening, you winnow it –
49797: It gets ground.  We had machines [for that].
49808: za kvò raspìtvat t’è sigà šə gu vìd’ət kvò je mà
Why are they asking questions? Now they’ll just see what it is!
49822: drùgu kanà da t kàžɤm n’e kanàta me papᵊìtate ažoto znàm
What else can I tell you? Ask me whatever, just so long as I know it.
49828: We used to dress in “shalwars” (loose Turkish trousers).
49842: Foreign headscarves. The headscarf is foreign.
49852: Nothing after that. [Just] these kinds of dresses.
49859: à i ròkl’e i i f’èredž’e d’ul’b’èn’e zəkəč’ul’me tò a bilò napr’èš
Dresses, and the outer garment. We put on headscarves. Earlier on there were
49865: səz d’ulbène drùgɤkvᵊi abanìef g zavàhme abanìef zavàhme
– different headscarves – foreign, we called them. We called them “foreign”.
49869: ma tò segà l’è na tò s’eà ne trèva
But now, well, now it’s not required [any more].
49879: And what did you put on your ears?
49886: nə ušìtə u ùšnikɤ zlàtnɤ zlàtnɤ pɔ̀rsten’e pɤk drùgu nɤ̀ im’è
On the ears – earrings of gold, and gold rings. But there wasn’t anything else.
49888: And that’s what you used to put on –
49893: ami kàži za medžète segà kàži kàk ste pràvili medžè
So tell us about work bees now. How did you set up work bees?
49903: We go to carry in the straw.
49910: azàm flez’ème wònkiš’ì da id’ème klìnɤ ispeč’ɔ̀t č’orbɤ svar’ɔ̀
Then ten of us come in to eat. They bake banitsa, they cook soup –
49949: s kakvò go vèete kàk se vìkə tovà
What do you winnow it with? What do you call that thing
49951: dèto gi m dèto se dìgə
49954: Way long ago, in the old days …
49955: [Yes,] what was it like in the old days?
49958: … the really old people [used] a two-pronged pitchfork
49961: Oh, in the old days it was …
49964: They toss it up into the wind, ...
49980: i òpki ìmə i lupàti ìmə
There are [the old] pitchforks, there are shovels,

52245: praìme godèš slet tovà na pazàro i pràvo
we concluded the engagement. After that, to the market, and then straight
52252: štòto sa tè na na drùgətə na gəzɤ̀ na zem’àta
Because they’re on the other – on the rump of the world.
52256: àjde àjde sàa ženà ud amèrika èj
So now, so. This woman is from America. Well, how about that!
52258: čàk ut amèrika e dušlà də se interesùvə tùkə ot
She’s come all the way from America to find out
52260: ot vàšto selò kàk se govòri
about your village, about how you talk.
52266: ùbəu amèrikə čùvəli go səmè rəspràjət rəzbìrəš li
America’s nice. We’ve heard about that. People talk, you know,
52274: bugàtə dəržàvə ə bilò i v’àrnu e tvà n’ɛ̀štu znàči dà
It’s supposedly a rich country, and that’s a true fact. Yes,
52278: priznàvət sìčki či i bugàta ednò vrème rəzbìš li prez
everyone admits that it’s rich. Earlier on, you know, during
52282: è tuvà fəšìskə germànijə kugàtu hòdime də də sə bìeme
this – fascist Germany, when we went off to do battle
52285: səs nègu às hòdih dàže səm i rənèn ut ut
with them, I went. I was even wounded by – by
52290: germàncite dà tugàvə rəzbìš li əmèrikə bləgudərènie nə əmèrikə i
the Germans. Yes [indeed]. And, then, you know, America. Thanks to America, and –
52295: i rusìjə t’è pumògnəə ìnək germànijə kəkò štè də nə stòri nàmi
and to Russia too, they helped [us]. Otherwise what Germany would have made of us,
52300: tì kòlko kòlko si godìšen tà na vojnà si hòdil
How old are you? You’ve gone to war, so –
52312: dà əf ungàrijə òdime bìjme se tàm səs germàncite
Yes, we went to Hungary. We fought the Germans there.
52316: obàče əm bləgudərènie nə əmèrikə t’àa səmolèti kətu izlìzəhə gòre
But, well, thanks to America –  These planes that flew overhead,
52321: ednì səš čèrni krilè drùgi səz bèli i pudred’èni təkà rəzbìəš li
some with black wings and others with white wings; [they were] arranged, you see,
52325: pu d’èset o utìvəu də bumbədìrət bùdəpèštə
in rows of ten – Ohhh! They were on their way to bomb Budapest.
52333: sutrintà kòj kolè prasèto kòj na prɤ̀vio dèn’
In the morning someone slaughters a pig. Some on the first day,
52338: kòj na ftòrio dèn’ postà si pòstat togàj pòstejme
some on the second day. And they do the fast – back then we fasted
52348: càla pòs mrɤ̀sno ne edèjme na božìk k’i se omrɤ̀sim
the entire fast period: we didn’t eat any fat. On Christmas we’ll break the fast.
52355: k’i čèkame da dòim ot crɤ̀kva i što ìma fkàštə
We’ll wait till we get back from church, and then [using] whatever’s in the house,
52358: bləgudərènie če pumògnaə ànglijə i əmèrikə i rusìjə
Thanks to the help from England and America – and from Russia too –
52361: ìnək germànijə štèn də nə glɤ̀tne kətu [laughter]
If not, then Germany would have swallowed us up. [laughter]
52363: Like a wolf [swallowing up] a lamb.
52367: ohò n’èmaše də sə vàrneme adìn žìf
No sir, not a one of us would have come back alive!
52374: jà dvàese hìljədi žèrtvə dàdəme nìe bɤ̀lgərìte ə rusìjə dvàeset mil’ònə
Yes, we Bulgarians [alone] suffered 20,000 casualties, and Russia – 20 million!
52379: vìš kəkò n’ɛ̀štu e zə kəkò se izbìhə t’à hòrə
What a thing this is. And why did these people kill each other?
52382: n’àmə zəštò nìe pàk pàk bləgudərènie əmèrikə dərdžì svetàd
No reason. We – well, thanks to America for keeping the world [together].
52385: be èj tò dəržì svetàt tò ko e nè
Yes indeed, it’s keeping the world [at peace]. If not [for them],
52388: pàk še sa is i i izbìjət e vìš kəkò pràjət
they’d start the killing again. Just look what they’re doing
52393: ošte ne mòe da se uredàt
They still can’t put things in order.
52399: istrè zə kəkò nì nì zə kəkò nè ja
And why? For nothing! Nothing at all! So you see?
52403: i pìtam milicionèra da mi kàže kɤdè e
So I asked the policeman to tell me where it was,
52408: stoì tòo rèjs štòto če da putùe za ràzgrad
[where] stood the bus that would be going to Razgrad.
52414: òn mi kazà kudè e onò tàm ne è bilò
He told me where it was [though] what [I needed] wasn’t there.
52416: a jà se tegàj ukačì gdèto òn kazà
But I got on [the bus] where he told me to.
52423: jà se ukačì i kat sèdo onò se ùkači edna kondùktorka žènska
I got on, and when I sat down this female ticket-taker got on.
52437: i vednɤ̀ga na mène dojdè pṛ̀va
And she came straight off to me first of all ...
52444: i mi ednɤ̀k nàdupči bilètɤ ne mè pità
... and immediately punched my ticket. She didn’t ask me
52447: za gdè si nì pa četè u tòa
“Where are you going?” nor did she look at this …
52450: u bilètɤ da vìdi kɤ̀v je
… ticket to see what kind it was.
52458: i nelì dɤšterà mi pìše pismò i jà po pismòto putuvà
You see, my daughter wrote me a letter, and I traveled according to the letter
52460: onà mi pìše kudè kakvò če vìdim če mìnem
She wrote me [about] where [we’d travel], what I’d see on the way.
52466: dobrè ama jà do nègde vṛvè vṛvè i svè tekà razgledžuvà i
Fine, but I went along to a certain point, looking out at everything,
52470: i po pismòto opazì če ne otòdim kudè sɤm pošlà
and realized from the letter that I’m not going to the place I had set out for.
52472: k’e napràime jàdene mrɤ̀sno nèšto i k’e àjde prasèto k’e se zakòli
we’ll make a dish with fat in it. Then it’s time to slaughter a pig.
52474: i togàj k’i se omrɤ̀sim du togàj što ìma bòp takvìa rabòti
And then we’ll break the fast. Before that [you eat] whatever there is, beans and such –
52478: tovà se edè mrɤ̀sene nèmaše kat saà vi za vilìgden k’i zapòstim
that’s what you eat. No eating whatever, [as they do] now. We fast for Easter.
52482: càla pòs pòstexme vilìgden’ kat k’i dòi i ot cɤ̀rkva
We would keep the entire fast. On Easter [Sunday] when we come back from church,
52485: i k’i ni dài màjka ni po ednò ejcè
mother will give each of us an egg.
52488: k’i ìem na cɤ̀rkva gl’àame da izl’èzem ot cɤ̀rkvata
We’ll go to church, and look [forward] to leaving church,
52492: i da go skàpim da àpnim i k’e dòim dòma
so we can crack it, and eat it. [Then] we come home,
52500: zbṛkàla sɤm tòj jà si miruvà nìšto ne kazà
I’d gotten confused. He [confused me]. I stayed quiet, and didn’t say anything.
52505: rèko sɤ̀k kudè sprè rèjsɤt če da
I said [to myself that] when the bus stops, I’ll …
52508: [Surely] it will stop at some point.
52511: a pò tòpličko da ti slòžim
Can I warm up your cup?
52516: màjka k’e ni ispɤ̀rži ìjn’ tigàjn’ jàjca [laughter] štò e ostanàlo
[and] mother will fry us a pan of eggs [laughter] – and what’s left [of]
52522: vṛvè vṛvè i onò edɤ̀n brèk kakò na nàs
[So] I kept on going, and then there was a cliff like we [have]
52527: mrɤ̀fki svìncki k’e rùčame i xàjde na vilìgdeno
pork meat chunks. We’ll have dinner, and then it’s – “Let’s go to the Easter [celebration].”
52530: ovdèg dòle popòva.padìna edɤ̀n brèk i tùk tàm se vìdi
here down at Popova Padina. A cliff, and here and there you could see
52537: tekà keremìtke stṛčù onò i kako u gòru kato ulèzo
these tiles peeking up. It was like I went into the woods,
52541: òro džumbìš pràat prɤ̀vio dèn’ ftòrio dèn’ trètio
[There’s] dancing and a party; they do this on the first day, the second day, the third –
52544: sè si izlèvaa na a segà nèma takìva rabòti
everybody came out. But now they don’t do such things [any more].
52548: nì vilìgden’ se znàe kogà e nì bužìk kòj kogà nàe
People don’t even know when Easter is, or Christmas. Whenever anyone finds [something],
52550: togàa edè i mrɤ̀fki i jàjca i sìčko togàj biše
he eats it right then – meat and eggs and everything. But back then it was –
52553: buguròičina pòs k’e dòe pà takà petròvata pòs càla pòs pòstejme
The fast of the Holy Virgin is coming, and then St. Peter’s – we did the entire fast.
52558: càla pòs na petròvden’ k’i sprɤ̀žim ùrda nèšto štu ìma togàj
The entire fast. For St. Peter’s day, we’ll fry curds or whatever there is, and then
52563: k’e se umrɤ̀sim càlata petròvata pos bogoròičnata k’i dòi
we’ll break the fast [after] the entire St. Peter’s fast. Then comes the Holy Virgin fast,
52566: pà takà sàa štò sàa ni znàim nìšto
and the same again. [But] what now? Now we don’t know anything.
52568: narèt je sìčko kòj kogà nàe
Anything goes. People [eat] whatever they find [whenever they want].
52570: mlàdite ne znàjat vìe mòže da pàzite
The young people don’t know. [But] you [all] can keep [the fasts].
52575: nèkoj òšte pàzet nèkade ama rètko tì ako pàziš drùgio ne pàzi
Some people still keep [the fasts], but rarely. If you keep one, another won’t keep it,
52579: i takà a togàj semèjno sìčko se pòsti sìčkoto semèjstvo
and so on. But back then [it was a] family [affair]. All fasts kept, [by] the entire family.
52583: togàva na pòkladi večèrame bànici mèso se e zgotvìlo
Then on Shrovetide we have supper [together] – banitsa, meat was prepared.
52584: što sè e štò ostàne na prasèto li e
Any leftovers went to the animals, either the pig
52585: from there over here – [to] the wedding.
52589: koj òdeše de ja tèra momàta
Who went to seek the girl?
52593: emi jà mòa čovèk odì drùgi nèkoj [laughter] nìa si odìme stàrite
Well, then – my husband went, some others [laughter]. We went, us old ones!
52600: ama kàk im vikaxa na tìja ne pràštaxa li speciàlni xòra
But how did you call them? Didn’t they send [some] particular people?
52603: spiciàlni òra kòj mi nìa si òdime i
What particular people? We [аre the ones who] go, and
52608: na kokòški li e izmìem panìci̥te togàj nèmaše pràx s pèpel
or the chickens. Then we wash the pans, with ash – there was no detergent powder then.
52611: pòstim na boži na vilìgden’ jà na božìk ìnače nèma
And we fast, at Chr-, at Easter– no, at Christmas. And otherwise nothing.
52617: bòp papùda sùšini slìvi zàxar nèma kìseli ne kìseli dròbi jàdi
[Just] beans, “papuda”, dried plums. No sugar. Sour or not, crumble [it] and eat!
52618: Do you know what “papuda” (mung beans) is?
52626: nèkoj komšìa nèkoj pò blìsok zakàrame
we take [along] some neighbor, someone closer [to us].
52628: stròjnici nèšto da im vìkat ilì
Something – do they call them “stroynitsi” (matchmakers), or –
52631: mi sròjnici de sròjnici na tava se vìka sròjnici
Well, they do say “sroynitsi” for that, “sroynitsi".
52635: [Those are the ones] that will go and mix the ashes.
52641: tàm k’i si znàat k’i sa sròjnici
So that people there will know that these are  “sroynitsi”,
52645: they poke around in the burnt logs with tongs.
52647: Who? Who mixes up the ashes?
52649: mi tòa štò e ošèl da pròsi momàta
Well, the one who went to ask for the girl.
52650: axà i po tovà se razbìra če
Aha, and that’s how they know that –
52652: That a seeker has gone there.
52658: tavà e bìlo svàdbite krɤstènkite po dòma sìčko nèma restorànte
That’s how it was for weddings, christenings – [always] at home. No restaurants,
52662: nèma takvìa rabòti tàpanèto si pràat tùka bednotìa drɤ̀veni lažìci
none of these things; they [just] played drums. It was poor here – wooden spoons,
52665: i džilèzni kakvì ìma na sofràta
iron [spoons], whatever there was at the low common table, [to eat what was]
52667: in the [single] pan they put [there]. No [modern] tables.
52669: sà restorànto ako nè e ne mòže
But now, if it’s not [in] a restaurant, you can’t [do it].
52672: babo jà ìskaraj mu dàj mu da si svàri ednò ot
Granny, go get some for him so he can cook one of –
52673: There isn’t [any] here, I don’t have [any].
52687: əm mòr o dèt gu tèrat po gradištàta kupùvad gu papùda
Well, it’s what people search out in the cities. They buy these mung beans …
52690: papùda s pràs mnògo e ùbaf
Mung beans with leeks – [that] is very nice.
52693: a tvà kato kato b’àl bòp nèšto li
Ah, is it something like white beans?
52696: nè nè ne dàže i dùmata ne sɤ̀m čùval
No. No, no, I’ve never even heard the word.
52699: togàj beše takòva pò ùbuu pò ùbuu beše togàj
Back then it was nicer that way. It was nicer back then.
52701: Uh huh. [So] when did the wedding begin?
52706: What did they do on Thursday?
52709: četvɤ̀rtok vèjkata k’e pràat ferùglicata pràat
On Thursday they’ll make the [ritual] bough, they make the wedding flag, and
52714: kànat kumò priz din’ò kànat selòto i pòčvat
they invite the godfather. During they day they invite the village, and they begin
52718: svàdbata àjde sa sàbota dòat tapanàreto večertà òro
the wedding – let’s go! On Saturday the drummers come and in the evening, a dance.
52723: nedèl’ata òat za momàta dokàrvat venčàvat a
On Sunday they go [to get] the girl, they bring her, marry her formally
52725: na cɤ̀rkvata òdat togàj dukàrvat si momàta dòma
in the church. Then they go – they bring the girl home,
52726: i na drùgio dèn pàk svàdba f ponedèlnik
and on the next day it’s still the wedding. On Monday,
52728: togà i e na momàta svàdbata f ponedèlniko
that’s the wedding for the girl – on Monday.
52736: nègde u ednu padìnu a onò kondùktorɤt i šofjòrɤt
somewhere into a pit. And [when we stopped] the driver and conductor
52742: jednɤ̀k slèzoše i otòše u ednà magà  tekvàj pìvnica
both got off and went into – into this sort of bar.
52746: a onò mòs ìma tekà i onì prèz mòstɤ minàše̥
There was a bridge there, and they crossed the bridge …
52752: ta otòše u pìvnicutu jà pogledà tekà kò da pràim sɤ̀ga
… and went into the bar. I looked around [and thought], “What shall I do now?”
52756: onò edɤ̀n stàrc tekà sèdɤl na ednù pèjčicu ta sedì
Then [I spied] an old man [who’d] sat down on a bench. He’s sitting there,
52761: i jà slèzo sɤz bagàžɤt i otò pri stàreca pa rekò
so I got off with my luggage and went over to the old man and said,
52763: drugàrju jà mi kažì tì kàk se kàzva tovà selò tùka
“Comrade, [can] you tell me please what is the name of this village here?”
52768: tvà gu ìma tùka f makedònija sàmo tùka gòre.dòlu
You find it here in Macedonia, more or less just around here.
52770: rèče è jà te poznàvam po prìkaskata tì si severjànka
He said, “Ah, I can tell from your speech that you are a northerner.”
52774: tùka ìmat sèjan tie nagòre kəm tìa kəm latìnkevo tà
These people have planted it, higher up near those – near Latinkevo, and –
52776: əxə a pòkladito kakvò e pòkladi
Aha. So – Shrovetide. What is Shrovetide?
52779: pòkladi zapòstuvame za bož za božìk tòe dèn’ ùslet saà se vèk’e
Shrovetide – we start the fast for Chr- for Christmas. From that day on, you’ve already
52782: dnèska zapòstuva se za božìk kòlko vrème sa pòsti
started to fast for Christmas, [for] how [ever] much time the fast is.
52787: tàa vèčer k’e napràim bànica isprɤ̀žim petèl li k’e zakòl’at
That night we make banitsa, we fry up [meat] – people slaughter a rooster
52789: rekò abe severnjàčka sɤm severnjàčka ama
I said, “Well [yes], I’m a northerner. A northerner, but ...
52790: nèšto da ìma mèso da se zapòstuva pòkladi
or something so as to have meat, so as to start the fast, the Shrovetide observance.
52791: i k’i zapòstim na božìk togàj gi fàtim za vilìgden’
And we’ll start the fast. At Christmas we start it then. And at Easter,
52792: pà pòkladi po zapòstuvame ednà nedèl’a pòstim ut sìrenetu̥
there’s Shrovetide again, and we start the fast. One week we have “white cheese fast” –
52793: tovà ut ə sìrene jadèm bèz mrɤ̀fki sìrna nedèl’a go vìkame
we eat white cheese, without any meat. We call that “cheese week”.
52794: drùgata nedèl’a drùgata vìki zapòstuvà se ut sìčku
The next week – the next one already, we begin to fast, abstaining from everything.
52795: i na vilìgden’ prɤ̀ži jàjca jàdi togàj [laughter]
And [then] on Easter, it’s	"Fry up those eggs! Eat then!" [laughter]
52796: Given that there were [any] eggs, [that is].
52798: a u pètəko kvò pràexa f četvɤ̀rtəka vìkaš
And what did they do on Friday? On Thursday, you say –
52799: And the mummers? When did they do [that]?
52803: decàta òdat ə k’i napràat takvì tojàgi dɤ̀lgi
The children go out, and they’ll make these long clubs;
52804: utprèt s takòvo pɤ̀čišta pràea i k’i dòjdat k’i pèat
they made them with this big ring on top. And they’ll come and sing
52805: k’i igràat k’i mu fɤ̀rliš inì vàgle ena glamn’à ògin’ i
and dance, and you’ll throw them some embers, a burnt log [from] the fire. And
52806: da takòva ina màl’ka misìrka k’i kɤ̀cat k’i čìnat
they’ll shuck and grate a small ear of corn and such.
52807: štu ìma k’i gu daròvaš k’i stàni̥ k si izlèze
You’ll give them whatever you have, and they’ll get up and leave, [and]
52808: po nìx drùga grùpa dòjat i na sutrintà stančinàre pràat sɤ
another group will come after them. And in the morning the mummers dress up
52809: i sèkakvi takòva igràat pròsat sàa ni pròsat da ti go kàža
in all sorts of ways, and dance, and beg. [But] now they don’t beg, to tell you the truth.
52810: kat otò u kubràt tàm i lènče mi gòtvi
When I went there to Kubrat, Lenche was cooking [something] for me.
52811: nalì sɤm došlà na gòsje dobrè ama ìmaše tàm ednà bàba marìja
I was there as a guest, you know. Fine, but there was this – Granny Maria.
52812: bàba marìja t’à pak ìskaše da mi e sestrà na mène
Granny Maria. And she wanted to be [as if] my sister,
52813: če imàla tekvùj sestrù kako mène pa počìnala
since apparently she had a sister similar to me, who had died.
52815: i kat me vidè onà se ùlovi za mène i tekà me dṛžì
And when she saw me she latched onto me and sticks to me.
52827: f pètoko vìki pràat tokòvo zbìrat ə mèso kol’àt
On Friday, they’re already – whatever. They gather [things], slaughter [animals] for meat,
52828: stègat se tavà onovà takvìa rabòti f pètoko f sàbota vike
prepare this and that – such things on Friday. On Saturday already,
52831: f sàbote kakvò stàva tòčno ot sabàle kvò pràət
What happens exactly on Saturday? From morning [on], what do they do?
52836: In the morning they begin by washing out the cauldrons.
52843: mite ndej čùka malko tùka da mòem da napràim tovà pòsle ši
Mite, stop beating [on that thing] there [for] a bit, so we can do this. Later you’ll –
52845: kazàn’e mìjat lažìci zbìrat po selòto
They wash the cauldrons, they gather spoons [from] around the village,
52849: they gather up low tables [to make] a large common table. On Saturday,
52851: tovà se rabòti da e gotòvo za ùtre
that’s what you do, so that it’s ready for tomorrow.
52853: dà i na drùgija den kədè se səbìraa
Yes, and on the next day, where did they gather,
52855: and what exactly did they do?
52863: e to za pròsene nè ma stančinàri ne stànvat li tùka
Well, [I’m not asking] about begging. But don’t the mummers do something here?
52868: pràat stančinàre ma tàm na ploštàdo k’i igràat k’i visèl’at
They do! The mummers here on the square, they’ll dance and make merry,
52870: pu pàk’o k’i òdat drùgio ploštàdo i àjde
and then they’ll go down the road to another square and – Let’s go!
52873: a ednò vrème koì stàvaxa stančinàre
In the old days who could become a mummer?
52880: mladèžeto mladèži i stàri se pràeja sas stənčinàrto s zvònci sas kòži
The youth! Young people, and old too were mummers, with bells, with skins –
52881: i decàta ili nè sàmo mladèži
Children too, or not? Only youths?
52883: ama kažì mi kàk se kàzva tovà selò

54359: ama ə po kràj i go zalòžime kotèla u edìn kàmik tùrame

54419: I said you should rest a little.
54422: You should rest a bit! [Take] the opportunity.
54425: dà dà dà dà tò hèrg’un počìvəm

54430: Now there’s no work [to be done].

When you come back [from the field], you have to take care of the cow,

you have to give the calf [something] to eat, you have to muck out the stable,
54446: tr’àvə də zgòtviš zə jàdene d ìiš hl’ab də zèmeš
you have to cook meals, to go and get bread,
54450: d ìi əku n’eməš hl’àp še ispeč’èš
to go – if there isn’t bread, you’ll bake [it].
54453: tvà ni e f kàštata tvà e

54458: ni mòež də s’ènneš də uper’èš

54460: è tò mnògu ràbutə ìmə nə žènckutu
Ah! There’s lots of work for a woman.

In the outdoor oven. What? You don’t know?
54477: dà bè tò i nì kupùvəme sigà
Well, yes, and we buy it too now.

54485: s’àvi kurità nuškuvì nìe gi zvème

they cut out the [shape] of the “opinki”, and we made “opinki”, and
54502: s čeràpe nèma ə ə takòvo
54514: štòto zavìvame i navùšta dèt mu vìkame takòvo koto parcàle
because we wrap up – what we call leg wrappings, like rags
54517: da navìeme ta da ni nè e ama pà se izmòkrime
that we wrap on so we don’t get – but we still get wet
54520: i kot si dòjdeme i dodè da sə sɤbùəme

54532: mu vìkame na ednì znàm če mu vìkat papadùrki ednì tekìva širòčki

54561: rìbena čorbà š si napràvə òšte drugi den

54567: kəto zavrì vodàta izmìeš ùbavo rìbata i kəto zavrì vodàta

54572: You can also do it with –
54573: Do you clean the fish first?
54578: takà nàšto òden’e e bilò na živòd bèše

54579: ahà a za za kòleda kəkvò pràvexte za kòleda kàk praznùvaxte

54580: i i za za kòleda takà
54592: What you – however you call it.
54593: kòleda i na u božìč kàzvat tè
54596: è ə ə ko ko kòleda zakòl’ame prasèto zbìrame sɤ
Well, at Christmas we slaughter a pig, we gather together –
54600: à kɤ kɤkvò jadèxte sa sa sàmo prasè ili

54601: Well no, [not just] the pig. No.
54604: go gòtvime si mesòto si gòtvime na gòzba sɤs

54606: nè nè tovà za drùgite dnì a kogà kòl’ate prasèto
No, no, that’s for other days. When you slaughter a pig,
54612: izbèrɤd dobrò mescè upṛ̀žɤt elì opekɤ̀t
you choose the good parts, you fry them or roast them …
54617: sɤs kìselo zèle ili turšìjka nàj naprède
… with sauerkraut, or pickles [as the] first course ...
54621: da pìjɤt rakìjata i slet tovà ìdva mesòto
... when people drink rakia, and after that comes the meat,
54624: a na tòo na kol’àča oddèliš ut mesòto
and you put some parts of the meat aside [to give] to the butcher –
54625: e nèka t’à da go kàzva
54632: e ə ònea kol’àča ko o čùš a pa ako si e
Well if the butcher is someone from outside, if he is –
54638: koto mòjɤ bɤštà si i kòl’aše i si gi pràeše takà
My father slaughtered them himself, and did them up that way.
54641: narèžɤt mesòto tə ə ə tovà e takà op opečème go
People cut up the meat, and then – then they roast it
54645: na obèt sɤ zbèrɤt adɤ̀t ta ədɤ̀t pòsle si gu tur
for the meal, everyone gets together to eat, and then
54647: they put the rest into small barrels.
54650: è še a iščìstiš še a nare
Well, of course you clean it, and then –
54653: zavisì kvà rìba ìma ko e sìtna
it depends what sort of fish it is. If it's little ...
54658: i lùk čùščici nətùraš i č čùbricә̥ n
... you add onion and peppers, and summer savory, [though]
54661: nə rìbata sə tùra u čorbàta čùbrica sàmo
for fish soup you only [need to] add summer savory.
54665: əmhəm a a ot pìle ako pràiš če ja zastròjvəš li čorbàta
Uh huh. But if you make chicken soup, do you put in thickening?
54672: mesòto i go pə posòlime ə ə sɤs sɤlɤmùr ta
The meat. We salt it, using brine, so ...
54677: ... so that it won’t go off.
54683: koto napràiš tàm si mòe da tùraš i orìs u čorbàta
... when you make that [kind of] soup, you can also add rice,
54684: o onò nè e koto prèsnoto ama si e mesò
It’s not as if it were fresh, but still it’s meat
54690: mòže elì fidè elì kakvì drùgi ràboti i kəto səs ə
or noodles, or some other things. And when
54693: [You keep it] in the cellar. In the cold [of the] cellar.
54698: às sɤm čùval če stàrite xòra kato se zakòli prasèto
I’ve heard that older people can – When a pig is slaughtered –
54702: ə svàri sìčko da a gotòvo še zastràaš tùriš stròšiš jàjcata odèlno
it’s all cooked, when it’s ready, you thicken it. You break eggs separately,
54705: tàm ne znàm vɤ̀tre vɤf nègo kakvò ìma ama mòat da poznàjət
I don’t know what there is inside but they can predict [from it]
54707: kvà še bɤ̀de zìmata ìma li takòva nèšto
what the winter will be like. Is there something like that [around here]?
54710: ɤ̀ tvà e tvà e bàbata dèk mu vìkat tùmbakɤ
Oh, that’s – that’s “baba” (sausage), what they call tripe.
54715: čer červàta da napḷ̀nime sɤs mesò ə segà mèj à
When we fill intestines with meat. Now they use skin pouches
54719: tegìva sme gi re go rèžeme na sìtno na mrɤ̀fčici
but back then we cut [meat] up very small, into tiny chunks –
54721: na mrɤ̀fčici i napḷ̀nime bàbata sɤs màlko lùkčec
into chunks, and we fill the sausages with it, and some bits of onion
54724: čùšcici narèžime i mesòto i a napḷ̀nime i i sɤšìjeme
and bits of pepper, we cut up the meat, and fill them, and sew it up,
54730: i koto jɤ vàrime màl tɤ tɤkà da ne è
and when we boil it a bit [we need to take care] that it’s not –
54733: da sa spùka e nə sè glèdat da ɤ takà
that it doesn’t break. You have to keep watching it.
54734: razbìvaž gi sìpvaš po màlko vodìčka də sə da stàne
beat them, pour in a little liquid [from the soup] so it gets ...
54741: kòlko corbàta a tòpla i də sɤ ne presečè e takà

54745: əmxəm a bòba kàg gu̥ go obìčaxte pòveče
Uh huh. As for beans, how did you prefer them?
54747: takà zelèn li go edèxte na šušùlki ili ilì kato uzrèe
Did you eat them “green”, with the pods still on, or [wait] till they ripen?
54749: You mean when do we pick them?
54753: e pa də u də uzrìe go bèreme
Well, uh – we pick them when they’re ripe.
54756: ako a mu vìkame pešàk nìe go skubème
If it's the kind we call “peshak” (white beans), we pull them off [ripe].
54760: òn òn uzrìe od edìn pɤ̀t sìčkia ako ɤ lozàr
They – they all ripen at the same time. 	If it’s vine beans,
54766: i jə dṛžìme na navisòko natùrame ta prez zìmata se exè
And then we keep it – we put it up high so that during the winter – Ah!
54768: da mìne kòleda pa predì zàgovenki de də si trèbva
After Christmas and before the Lenten fast begins, that’s when you need
54775: so that you can do the fast before Easter.
54779: And how did you celebrate Easter?
54783: a velìgden sɤs červènite be [laughter] jàjca
Oh, Easter! With eggs [dyed] red, you know! [laughter]
54785: a kə kakvò pràvite sɤs jajcàta
And what did you do with the eggs?
54787: Well, we crack them [against] each other’s.
54791: dà i ə kòlko jajcà pràvi fs’àko detè
Yes? And how many eggs did each child make?
54794: pa onò nə tegìva zbìrɤt šò nalì pres postìte sa ne jadè
Well, back then they collect them up. You know that during fasting no one eats eggs,
54800: onì sɤ zbèrɤt tùmba mnògo jàjca
so they pile up. Piles of them, a lot of eggs.
54804: i gi bojadìšat i kòlko dùši sa na tòlko mestà
And they dye them, and [depending on] however many people there are in however many places,
54807: šə gi rəzdèlat sèki da si znàe kòlko ejcà ša adè
they’ll divide them up so each one will know how many eggs he gets to eat.

54813: u segà ìma boì ama tegìva sme go varìle ə trevojàci
Well - now there are dyes, but back then we boiled up herbs.
54817: čer ot červènijə lùk ə šùmata
The outer peel of onions [for instance],
54820: makes a brown [dye] for an egg.
54825: a bèreme takòvo i s ə goràta mlèčnica dèt mu vìkat
And we gather – out in the woods we get what they call milkweed,
54829: e i unà onà pa tovà stàva takòo koto zelèno nèkakvo
and that becomes a sort of green color [for dyeing].
54834: a risùvaxte li gi sɤs sɤs vòsɤk ili
And did you make designs [on the eggs], with wax, or –
54838: risùvame gi [laughter] sɤs sveštìci pa kvò stàne takòvo
We made designs on them [laughter] with candles, but 	what it became –
54845: òn sə dèka o tùraš u ə po càrevica tovà
they – you plant them [together] with corn, and that’s
54849: òn sa kàči po drɤ̀vo eli takòvo bèreme sàmo čùškite
[how] they climb. Up a tree or something similar. We pick only the pods,
54853: when they ripen, [only] the ones that are ripe.
54855: əmhə a tòo zrèlijə kɤdè dèk dèto go vìkaš pešàk
Uh huh. And those ripe ones, the ones you call “peshak”,
54856: pòsle nèšto prài li se tàm vèe
do you do something with them there afterwards? Do you winnow [them}?
54859: pòslem go tùrame ta sɤ napečè i s ednò dṛ̀vu
Afterwards we put them out in the sun and then [beat them] with a piece of wood –
54864: [thump thump] bùame bùme ako a mnògo [thump] čùkame odgòre nəšìbame
[thump thump] bang, bang – if there’s a lot [thump] we pound them on top, thrash them,
54867: òn sə i òn go prevèeme na vètera i tè tekà
and they – and then we winnow them in the wind, and that’s it.
54870: à nàči trèva da čàkaš vètɤr da dùxne
Ah, so you have to wait for the wind to blow!
54873: àko [unintelligible] nalì vèter da ìma pa znàš sme iskarvàle
If [unintelligible] there was a wind. But you know, we were getting
54876: po mnògo pà ìde na na gerèna è tàm sɤs kòlata
a lot of them. And we take them down to the marshland in a cart
54877: i tàm ìma vèter štò ùlicata pò nèma vèter
because there’s wind there. Where there are streets, there isn’t enough wind
54879: a tàm ìma vèter i go odvèeme
but there’s wind there, so [that’s where] we winnow them.
54882: əmhə tò kàk se vèe zìmaš ot ut u tenekìi
Uh huh. And how do you winnow? Do you take these large tin boxes and –
54887: ko ə tenekìjata kòfi takòvo grebèš i sìpvaš
Tin boxes, buckets, and such. You dig through and pour it out [and the wind takes the chaff].̀
54890: [You have] to put something below it [to catch the beans in],
54892: štòto bòba bòba tvà pò tèško a tovà drùgoto
because the beans – the beans are heavier. But as for the other –
54893: kàk mu se vìka dèto e
54905: gà fkìsne ə l’àbət dur ne fkìsne vòdə
When the bread [dough] ferments – [you wait] until the water ferments enough –
54908: də fkìsne àsəl kutu məjà kàktu e
Until it ferments enough to be just like yeast.
54912: ə tugàvə f sòbətə li e fùrnə li še go mùšneš
And then you shove it either into the stove, or the outdoor oven,
54917: We were very good [at this], but –
54919: ama vìe po edìn hl’ab sàmo li pečàxte

54923: pu id’ìn l’àp ednà tavà gul’àma
One loaf [of bread] at a time, in a very big pan.
54927: But a big one, you say.
54929: A big pan – one this big.
54932: nə slet trì d’èn’a pàk izpečèš
And three days later you bake again!
54933: One pan [was enough] for two days. [laughter]
54938: ə s’à s’à s’à mnògu l’àsnu vàr si kùpi l’àp i gutòvu
Now – now it’s very easy: go and buy bread ready-made!
54940: jòk pràime ìč segà ìč jòk pràime
We don’t make anything now. We don’t make anything at all.
54941: pə si kupùvəme segà əmə ku ìməš pərì
We buy it now. If you have the money that is.
54942: If you don’t have money, you [wait and] see [what to do].
54943: If there’s no [money] you’ll make [your own].
54946: abe skɤ̀p ne skɤ̀p kənà gà ìmə l’àp
Well – expensive or not, what [can you do?] When there’s bread [you buy it],
54948: pàk də sə prudàli i da pràime
but if they’ve sold out, then we make it.
54952: zə l’àp vìkə še ìmə pərì bàbətə pək pək drùguto
As Granny says, there’ll be money for bread. As for other things –
54961: drɛhàtə zàkərpi gu i vɤ̀ri si gl’àdəj ràbutətə
Mend the clothes, and go off and tend to your work.
54966: əmə s ə l’àbət ni sà zəkàrpuvə kurèmət t’ kəzùje
But you can’t mend bread. Your stomach tells you –
54973: ne fàtə svàne ne fàtə səs svàne gà si glàden
Onions aren’t enough – onions aren’t enough when you’re hungry.
54979: And meat roasted on a spit? Did you do that?
54980: čeverm’à ut kənà də pràime kòjtu ìmə òfce prài čeverm’à

54982: [And] in the old days didn’t you have [any]?
54986: a nè ne sme nè im’àli nìkogaš òfce
Oh no, we didn’t. We’ve never had sheep.
54988: i kòze nèame i òfce pu ednà kràvə i tvà e
We don’t have goats or sheep. Just one cow [per household] and that’s it.
54993: pu ednò t’èle si zəkòl’uvame è tuvà ni e rənàtə nàmi
One calf each. We slaughter [it], and that’s our food.
54996: i kvò go pràixte tèleto agà go zakòl’əte

55000: t’èletu nədrubìme gu f kəzànə kəvərmà gu nəpràime

55002: We cut it up into small pieces, …
55007: č’e svərìme gu tugàvəkə č’e gu istrɤ̀sime f təvìt’i i
… cook it up like this and shake it out into pans and
55010: ə burkàne gu nəsìpvəme i c’àlətə zìmə tuvà gòtvime
then pour it into jars. Then all winter long we cook with it.
55012: And when there were no jars?
55015: agà n’èməše v burkàne p’ìti pàk

55018: Lard slabs, and then [we’d] make casseroles [with that], ...
55024: è təkà nə ednà pìtə gu
Then [you make] it into a lard slab.
55028: ednà p’ìtə be əf təvàtə gu sìpi evè se zəvɤ̀je tugàvəkən
A lard slab, you know. You pour it into the pan and cover it like this,
55030: and it keeps for a long time.
55032: [You wait for it] to cool down and settle ...
55035: [Yes,] to settle until the tallow congeals.
55038: ... [and to become] an entire lard slab, you see
55041: An entire slab. Slabs [was how] we made them.
55043: i slòžiš gu f n’àkvə kòšnicə tugàvə i
And you put it in some sort of basket and then …
55046: nàj mnògu ədìn dvà mɛ̀səcə i rəzvəlì sə
… [it lasts] one or two months at the most, and then goes off.
55050: jə əmə burkànete sed’àt mnògu burkànete mnògu
But it stays longer in jars. Jars [last] a long time.
55053: [The contents of] jars don’t go off.
55055: A jar will keep [its contents] an entire year.
55056: a s kòžata kakvò se prài

55060: kòžətə mòže də gu z pustəkìi də gu slòžiš
You can put the hide down [on the floor] for rugs
55064: də l’ègneš də spìš gà derìjətə bè
and lie down to sleep on it when –  The hide, you know …
55065: The hide, you know. The skin.
55070: əm mòžeš də gu ustrìžeš džuràpe də si nəpràiš
You can shear [the sheep] and make socks,
55075: It’s used for everything. It’s used for everything.
55078: jà da raskàžeš za tìja žènskite ràboti
So tell [us] about these types of “women’s work”.
55082: ud òfcata vɤ̀lnata kət se zème kəkvò sə prài
About sheep [and] how you get the wool. What do you do?
55083: But [tell it], in [the] order [you do it].
55085: č’e zèmeš ə še ustrìžeš ufcàtə še gu izmìeš
You take the sheep and shear it, and you wash –
55088: ə z vòdə be še gu izmìeš də iščìstiš vàlnətə
Well, with water of course! You wash it to clean the wool, ...
55095: So that what should come out?
55099: šùštetu šùštetu ə də pàdne bè də isper’èš
The dirt. [You want] the dirt to come out! You wash [it]
55101: to make it get nice, [to make it] white.
55103: For the dirt to come out.
55106: dà tugàvə še zèmeš əd na dəràk də gu izvlàčiš gà gu izvlàčiš
Yes. And then you take a carder to card it, and after you card it
55110: še gu isprè ispred’èš ut tùkə še gu pirpred’èš še gu təkà
you spin it like this, and then you twist the strands like this.
55112: kàk se predè kàk se predè
How do you spin? How do you spin?
55119: We spin with a distaff and a spindle. That’s right.
55120: A distaff, a distaff. A distaff!

55124: perprìdəš tugàvə pək še go plit’èš džuràpe svà nvà
You twist the strands, and then you knit it into socks, this or that –
55125: whatever you want, that’s what you’ll do.

And have you worked on the loom?
55131: tàm kàk se takòva kàk se rabòteše
So that – how did that work?
55137: stàn imə stàn ìmə səkɤ̀n stàn tùrenu gr’èben ìmə
The loom has – The loom has – it’s set up – there’s a reed comb, and
55142: n’ìti ìmə àbe mnògu ràbuti bè mnògu mnògu
there’s a heddle. Oh, there’s lots of things. Lots, lots.
55143: And then he meets a carriage with earthenware pots.
55153: [laughter] ìmə mnògu stànve a tvà də tkàeme nìe čàrgi si tkàeme sìčku
[laughter] There’s a lot of looms. We weave rugs, we weave everything.
55167: There are these oxen pulling it –
55173: kojà e kojà e pò gol’àmata
55174: kàži tì kujà e pò kujà e pò gul’àmə
You tell [us]: which one is older. Which one is older?
55178: Well, how should I know? As if –
55182: vìdi vìdi pò stàrə pək səm pò mɤ̀škətə
See? I’m the older one but I’m smaller.
55186: tàə pò màlkə pək vìš pò stàrə
She’s smaller, but you see, she’s older.
55193: kàktu umìrət’ i decàta i tɤ̀r ràždət sɤ už’uèj i umìrə
whose children die. She has one, it lives a while and then dies,
55200: tòru trètu vèči tùj èči kət sɤ rud’ì da k prìmer
and then a second and third, the same. So when for instance,
55206: ftòru li trètu li i wìkɤm’e dàj dɤ i xvɤ̀rlim nɤ ùlicə̥tȁ
the second or third is born, we say “Let’s throw it out on the street,
55214: nɤ krɤstupɤ̀t’a kòjtu nəmèri nəm’ɛ̀ri nɤ n’ɛgu kɤsm’èt’ vèči nɤ n’ègu j
at the crossroads, and whoever finds it has fortune, and it’s with them
55221: and we bind it up all around with the tie.
55225: a pòsle vṛvcàta se tekà gòre se nanìže vṛvcàta
And then the lace gets threaded, up above
55228: so that it’s bound tight to your leg ...
55233: a a drùgo kvò nòsexa ženìte enò vrème
What else did women wear in the old days?
55234: What kind of clothes did they wear?
55236: o sìne kvò smo nosìli nìštu nìštu nèmaše
Oh, my son, what did we wear?  We didn’t have anything at all.
55238: ž’ètvəta à ž’ètvəta e pràjm’e ubič’èj žètva
Ah the harvest. We do the harvest. That’s a custom, the harvest.
55242: Well, you put the shift on underneath, [don’t you?]
55249: m’i kət sə zəž’èn’i à s’igà ž’ètva vèči̥
And when we go out to start reaping, that’s the harvest.
55264: em’i s’igà ž’ètvəta p’ɛ̀jm’i inò vr’èm’i zəž’ènvəm’i kətu zɤž’ènvəm’i
Well now. For the harvest, we would sing in the old days. We begin reaping,
55272: kətu udr’èž’im tɤ̀j pɯ̀rvətu strɤ̀kč’ɤnc’i ž’ètvəta ut zə ž’ìtutu
we cut off the first small stalk of harvest – that is, of the wheat,
55273: nò nò košùl’a pràimo ot pṛ̀teno platnò tekà e bilò
Well, well, we make the shift from hemp fabric. That’s how it was.
55278: ut ə i ut utrɤ̀gvɤm’i uddòlu kòren’ә̟ istɤ̀rgvəm gu
and we pull it out from below – pull it out [by] the root,
55280: u selàta tekà bèše košùl’e od gṛ̀snice
In the villages it was like that. [We made] shifts from hemp.
55285: i slàgəme gu tùkə nə gɤrbɯ̀ si i ìkəm’e krɤ̀š’č’ec
and put it here on our backs. We call [it] a cruciform (little cross).
55290: krɤ̀z də bul’ì nàs də n’ bul’ì
“May the cross hurt, so that we won’t hurt!"
55295: kàzwəm’i tùkə nə krɤ̀š’č’ecə nàč’i d’èt pràim žìtu krɤ̀š’č’ec
That’s our saying about the little cross, why we make wheat into a little cross,
55297: platnò istə̥čèmo tòpi se tòpi se pa se trè
