We weave the fabric, [then] it soaks. It soaks and then gets rubbed –
55302: krɤ̀x də bul’ì nàs də n’i bul’ì slàgəmi gu tùkə
so that the cross will do the hurting and not us. We put it there,
55308: i c’àl’ d’èn’ i dɤrdžìm t’à ə
and we carry it [that] way all day long, ...
55314: dùmamo mu trè se na tṛ̀licu̥ tàm
We say it [that way]. It gets rubbed with the hemp-beater there.
55318: še ž’uv’ɛ̀i ut’ùəmi nəpràim slàgɤmi nɤ krɤstupɤ̀t’ə i
that the child will live." We do this – we put the child at the crossroads, and
55324: màjkata sa skrìva i sigà vèči n’àkuj kətu kòjtu minàə iz ùlicta
the mother hides. And now when someone comes along the street
55327: tṛ̀lica tè tekvòj napràeno dvè dɤ̀ske tè tekà ta usrèd
A hemp-beater. It’s this [thing] made [of] two boards like this, so that in the middle ...
55335: kɤt i nɤm’ɛ̀ri z’èmə i tùj d’it’è z’èmɤ i i ut’ùət ukɤšti
and they find the child, they take it and go home [with it].
55339: da ìma màlko megdàn i drùgo ednò sɤz dṛ̀šku
... there will be a little space. And there’s another piece with a handle,
55341: sigà sigà sigà ši i na t ši i krɯ̀štɤmi
And now – now, now, it’s time – we’ll christen it.
55345: and you pound it and pound it ... [laughter]
55347: nɤ trì jim’enà slàgɤmi tùj d’it’èto ə žə v guràta
We’ll give this child three names. [One] will be from nature (“the forest”),
55358: i nə žil’àzoto i na krɤ̀snictȁ kòjtu i nam’ɛ̀rilə vèči̥
one from man-made life (“the iron”), and one from the godmother who found the child.
55363: də da opàdne pazdèrɤt i tegàj kat opàdne pazdèrɤt
So that all the combings fall out. And then when the combings fall out,
55370: trì jmenà i ə kətu sa vɤ̀rnim tàm wìkə inàtə ìkə
Three names. And when we return, the one [who found it] says,
55379: n’èskə n’id’ɛ̀l’ə jà id’e id’ɛ̀ti j krɤštàvəjti tùj d’èt’i d’èt’i
“Today is Sunday. Let’s go. Go [now] and christen this child." The child –
55384: d’èt’i mu kàzvəli tùj d’èt’i id’ɛ̀te nɤ čèrkwəta i krɤ̀štajte štòt tò
they just called it “the child”. Go to the church and christen it, because it’s been
55389: čitìrijz dèna n’e sì j čùlu ìmitu i ut’ùɤt nɤ č’èrkvəta
forty days and the child hasn’t heard its name yet. So they go to the church,
55397: tòj ənɤ̀s d’ètu ud z’im’àtḁ d’ètu ud ž’ìtutu utrɤ̀gnatu̥
... that thing that was pulled out of the earth, pulled out from the wheat.
55398: i krɤ̀štat vrɤ̀štat sa i sigà krɤ̀snictȁ d’èt b’èb’i d’èt i nəm’ɛ̀ri
christen it, and return. And now the godmother who found the baby –
55403: žinàta spìra sa vɤ̀nka bùlkata udvɤ̀tr’ɛ i nə prəgɤ̀
this woman is at the threshold, outside; while the “bride” (the real mother) is inside.
55409: i ž’ènim ž’ènim kòlku səm bilà àz əmi mumìč’ita nə nìvəta sp’ìm
And we reap and reap. How old was I [then]? We girls [would] sleep in the fields,
55412: tàm sp’ìm z bəštàta mi ə mòjə č’ìču mi
sleep there with my father and my uncle
55418: tàm drùget’ȅ pu dvənàs’i p’ətnàs’i d’ènə nə kɯ̀rɤ sp’ìm
and others. We [would] sleep out there in the field twelve to fifteen days
55422: so as to reap. We have a lot of food, ...
55425: ... [to be able to stay in the] fields.
55432: ž’èn’im bɤ̀rdz’im xòrətə dukət sə vɤ̀rnət ut n’ìva s’èlu də dòət
We hurry to do our reaping by the time people who’d gone to the village get back.
55439: nɤ vrɤtàta xem nɤ prəgɤ̀ slàgɤmi inò s’ìto sìt dɤrmòn’ d’èt sìtu
And right at the doorstep, on the threshold, we place a large sieve, a “darmon”,
55445: nɤlì znàjš i tɤrkàl’əmi t’à ìkɤ tɤ̀s ə d’èt i nɤm’ɛ̀ri žinàta
you know? And we roll the child around in it and she says – the woman who found it
55452: vìkɤ tì mi dàdi ə jɤvrèn’č’e às ti dàɤm xristijànči tɤrkàl’emi i
says, “You gave me a little Jew and I now give you a little Christian.” We roll it
55457: pu sìtutu i žinàta bu màjkɤtɤ i z’èmɤ pàk i dàvɤ
around in the sieve and the woman – the mother – takes it and then gives
55467: sutr’intà kàzwəm’ pu id’ìn č’ɤkɤ̀m iskàrvəm’i n’ìj ž’èn’im č’etirìma č’uwèkə p’èt’
In the morning we say, “Let’s do one reaping track each.” So we reap, four or five people.
55473: ama ràwnu t’è ptič’èncə t’è və kət zəsvìr’əl’i bə v’ès’elu
It’s flat, and the [morning] birds started to chirp, and it’s joyful.
55476: i ž’èn’im tàm dùkət pòsl’e kət sə ə puž’èn’im
So we reap there until we’re finished.
55490: For the other holidays they celebrate – we get together –
55497: gerg’òwd’en’ pò rànu pràeme gerg’òwden nə šèstij tòj nə šèstij
St. George’s day. Earlier we observed St. George’s day on the sixth. It’s on the sixth ...
55506: a pɤk ə nɤ n’id’ɛ̀l’e də kla nəprìmer ftòrnik e gerg’òwdèn’
So on Sunday if we – for instance, [if] St. George’s Day is on a Tuesday,
55511: n’id’ɛ̀l’eta si pràewme zbòr zbòr sə vìkə pə̀k s’gà
we’d observe the village celebration –that’s what it’s called – on Sunday. But now, [with]
55515: èm gerg’òwdèn’ èm zbòrɤ nɤjnò a gu pràviš inò àgn’i
both St. Georges’ day and the village celebration at once, you’d [roast just] one lamb
55519: dèt wìkɤt s idìn kuršùn dvà zàjəka
[and kill], as they say, two birds with one stone! [laughter]
55522: du petròvden tr’àvə də dožènim du dvənàjst’i
We have to have finished reaping by St. Peter’s day, the twelfth.
55527: [laughter] səs inò àgni sigà nə gerg’òwdèn’
[laughter] A single lamb now on St. George’s day.
55528: ... comb it and then you spin it, and –
55531: emi mòjta màjka inò vr’ɛ̀mi stàwələ hɤ
So in the old days my mother would get up – Huh.
55535: a ka u koè vrème se sàdi tòj ə gṛ̀sti̥te̥
How – What time of year do you plant this hemp?
55540: pròletno vrème se posèje i te kɤ̀mjesen se obère
You sow it in the spring, and you harvest it when it gets towards autumn.
55549: jùl’ij tr’àə də duž’èn’im a kòjt ìmə mnògu n’ìv’i prudɤlz’àvə
Of July. [That’s when] we have to finish reaping. Those who have lots of fields continue on,
55557: a št’èli ə ut’ùət mɤl’čàna vudà mu kàzwat ut’ùət dunàs’ət
They’d be off [to get] what you call “silent water”: they go [at night] and bring back
55561: əmə nìj pò n’àməm’i duž’ènvəm’i pòčvəm’i s’ètn’e snòp’it’e də izvòzuvəm’i
But we don’t have so many, so we finish reaping and begin to carry off the sheaves
55564: kat uzrèju ìma ednè dùmamo im ednè bèlke i ednè cṛ̀nke̥
When it get ripe, there’s these – we call one “white hemp” and one “black hemp”.
55575: s kərùc’i kol’ì ə nòs’iš snòp’i pràjm’i klɤnn’ì sə kàzwə gùl’èmi trùpəm’i
in carriages, carts. We carry the sheaves and make what’s called heaps. We pile them up big.
55582: pr’àsnə vudà ut ču̥šmàta um’ès’et p’ìt’i xl’àp
fresh water from the well. They knead up loaves of bread –
55587: u cṛ̀nk’ete ìma sème za ta da se sèje za na gòdinu
The black hemp has seeds that [we keep] so as to sow for the next year.
55589: i m mòjta màjka sùtrin kətu stànim ə tò inò vr’ɛ̀mi
And my mother – in the morning when we get up, back in the old days –
55594: s’ètn’e vɤrš’èm bə kəkò e̥ b’ìlu tò ubìstwu gul’àmu iz’èt
And then we thresh. Ah, what hard work that was, killing [work].
55601: tɤ̀j gu kuprìwa nəbìrɤt kòlkut čuv’èkɤ sni nəprìm’er’ d’èsit’ ču
for every one of us [in the house] they’d pick a nettle stalk, for instance if we’re ten –
55606: kɤkvò kvò e tovà čakɤ̀m čakɤ̀m dètu vìkəš
So what’s this thing you call “reaping track”?
55611: kòsur’i kòsər’u [laughter] i ə kòlkut čuwèkɤ nəprìmer’ nìj si b’àwmi čèt’ir’i
[like] blackbirds!  [laughter] Anyway, however many people. For instance there were four of us
55616: n’ì si bèremo odèlno a bèlk’ete odèlno i kat se
We harvest those separately, and the white hemp separately. And when –
55623: i d’v’è šès šès strɤ̀ka kuprìva utkɤ̀svə màjka nər’è nər’ɛ̀ždə je
and [then] two [more, that’s] six. So my mother would cut six stalks of nettles, and arrange them
55635: emi ɛ̀ nəpr’ìm’er è tòlkus pòčwəm’i utùkə è č’ètr’i čuwèkə
Well, uh, for instance, four people or so start out from here, and this much [space]
55637: nə p’ištà nə p’i̥štà d’ètu p’i̥č’èm xl’àp nə fùrnata
on the stove – on the stove where we bake bread, on the large oven.
55639: ə upr’id’ɛ̀l’əm’i si i ž’èn’im sə kàzwə č’ekɤ̀m
[is what] we set out for them to do, and we reap [that much]. That’s called  a reaping track.
55641: However much each one can reap.
55645: dà əmə às kət pòčnə ž’ènə ž’ènə du tàm st’ìgə
Yes! I start out. I reap and reap and get up to this point, [and then]
55651: i natòpi se ta sedì dvè nèdel’e pràimo topìla
And then it soaks and it sits for two weeks. We create a place for it to soak,
55653: t’à drùgəta pòčwə utàm nətàtək č’ètr’i čuwèkə p’èt’ kòlku̥tu sni
the next one starts from there and goes on. Four or five, however many there are of us,
55658: i u topìloto i tegàj se ispère izvàdi onò omeknùlo
[it sits] in the soaking place, then it gets washed and taken out [when] it’s all soft.
55666: upr’id’ɛ̀l’əmi si idìn č’ə də iskàrəm’i nəpr’ìm’er’ kət pòčn’im n’àkuj s’i ỳkə
we decide that we’ll finish one [track].  So for instance we begin and someone says,
55673: à glànn’i sni də id’èm n’è č’ekɤ̀mə tr’àbə sə iskàrə dukràj
“Ah, we’re hungry! Let’s [stop and] eat.” “Ah, no. The track has to be finished to the end.”
55676: kàktu j n’ìvəta kòlkut i n’ìvəta də s’i iskàrə dukràj
However big the field is, it’s got to be [reaped] through to the end.
55680: kət iskàrəm’i s’àdəm’i tugàskə də id’èm a pək n’àkuj s’i wỳkəm’i
When we finish it, then we can sit down to eat. But someone [among us] will then say,
55686: kət sə zəòbləč’i vr’ɛ̀mitu̥ àjd’i stàvɤjt’i stàvɤjt’i də vɤ̀rzvəm’i
if the weather turns cloudy, “Come on, get up – let’s tie up [the sheaves]
55693: č’i mnògu rəkòe ìməm’i š’e dòd’i n’àkuj v’etrùškə də prɤ̀sn’i rɤkòet’ȅ
because we have many handfuls and some wind will come and scatter the handfuls,
55700: tr’àə də gi izwɤ̀rdzwəm’ә̟ s’ètn’e mɤ̀kn’eš snòpui pràim’i krɤ̀š’č’et sə kàzvət
so we have to tie them up.” So you drag the sheaves, and we make cruciforms, as they say.
55704: pu tr’inàjs’i snòpə nə krɤ̀š’č’ec pràjm’ә̟ slàgəm’i təkà təkà
We make cruciforms of thirteen sheaves each, and lay them out like this, and this,
55709: i təkà č’ètr’i snòpa i udgòr’ə nà kət sə dvənàjs’i gòr’ə
and this. Four sheaves, and on top – when there are twelve,
55714: tr’inàstijə snòp slàgəm’i krɤ̀š’č’ec èj n’èska èd’i kòlku krɤ̀scə
then we put on the thirteenth, and that’s a cruciform. “Here’s how many cruciforms –
55719: ə krɤ̀š’č’ecə nɤpràjəm’i puž’ènəl’i sn’i mnògu sn’i ž’ènəl’i n’èskə [laughter]
cruciforms we made today. We reaped – we reaped a lot today!” [laughter]
55723: What a lot of banging about that was!
55724: a pòsle sɤs dikàn’ata kogà a
And then with the threshing board, when –
55726: What did you do the reaping with?
55733: sɤs sɤ̀rpui s pələmàrki sɤ̀rp pələmàrka è tɤ̀j slàgəm’i tùkə pələmàrka
With sickles and swaphooks! The sickle, the swaphook. We put the swaphook here.
55736: n’i znàjš li tò n’àəm ìməm pələmàrka ìməm às s’ìčku
You don’t know? I don’t have [them here], but I have a swaphook, I have it all.
55738: t’à ìma i sɤ̀rp ìma i palamàrka
She has both sickle and swaphook.
55742: We do the reaping [with] sickles and swaphooks, and the men tie off [the sheaves].
55746: We give [them] the handfuls and they pile and pile [them up], ...
55763: The wheat as we reap it …
55767: How large does it need to be?
55773: xranàta xranàta ə nəpr’ìm’er’ ž’ì po ž’ìtu kà kàk də t’i kàž’ә̟
Food, food! For instances, it’s wheat, it’s – how can I tell you?
55778: tò e è tòlkus kət i ž’èn’iš ž’èn’iš slàgəm’i tɤ̀j n’àkolko pɤ̀t’a
It’s the amount that you reap and we put down several times
55779: nə inò m’àstu rəkòe sə kàzwə
in one place, those are called “rŭkoye” (handfuls).
55786: i t’ìe rɤkòe kətu gi z’èmim wèč’i vɤ̀rzvəm’i gi
And these handfuls – when we take them, then we tie them off
55790: i pràjmi tɤkò ə bə tòlk gul’àm s’i
and make [of them these piles] that are so big –
55795: snòp’i ìmə gəgəv’èli sə sə kàzvə
Sheaves have these – you call them “gŭgŭveli” (twisting crooks) ...
55800: A twisting crook that they tie with …
55806: … and then move it like this.
55815: tò e də mòž’i də sə svɤ̀rž’i
55818: də sə svɤ̀rzu̥wə də nəpràet ba
…[use it] to bind [them] up and to make –
55822: tò inò vrɛ̀m’i gəgəvèl’i pələmàrki sɤ̀rpui
In the old days [they had] twisting crooks,, swaphooks, sickles –
55824: inò vr’ɛ̀mi n’àmə təkòs n’èštu s’igà n’àmə
[That was] the old days. None [now]. There’s no such thing like that now.
55830: s’à gòš’u nàšət id’ìn d’èn’ pìtə bàbo kəkò j tùj n’èštu
So now our Gosho one day asks, “Granny, what is this thing?”
55835: əmə mə às i wìkə kɤkò i zə kəkvà
And I said, “What do you mean?” What kind of …
55838: dùma mə pìtə kò kàə tùj sià d’èt i kàzvəš
… word is he asking me about, I wonder. And he said “This thing you said now.”
55843: emi vìkəm i vìj n’i st’è č’ùəli ba d’ecà
“Ah,” I said. “You haven’t heard of that. Ah, children!
55847: v’ìj mlədèž’it’ȅ s’igà sè ùč’it’e n’i st’è č’ùəli wìkə
You young people now learn everything, but [this] you haven’t heard,” I said.
55850: èj tʌ̀s dùmə kəkvà b’èši n’i znàm
But [in fact] I don’t know what word it was that this was all about.
55855: e b’è hùbuu kəkò də t’i kàjə zə ž’ètvəta
So, OK. What can I tell you then about the harvest?
55861: s’è pòsl’ə kət nəpràjm’i n’àmə ə vɤrš’ɛ̀čki kət s’igà də vɤrš’ɛ̀jət
All of what we did next – there were no threshers like they thresh with now.
55868: inò vr’èm’i məš’ìni vɤrš’ɛ̀čki b’èši̥ č’àsni nàj gul’ɛ̀m’ bugətàš’t’ȅ si gi kupùvəə
Back then threshing machines were privately [owned. Only] the richest people bought
55872: məš’ìni čàk s’igà kumbàjnəta puž’è z’èm’im
[such] machines; now it’s harvesters. [But back then] we [next] take
55874: [what we’ve reaped] and begin [threshing] on the threshing floor.
55877: [First] we scrape out (= smooth) a large threshing area.
55892: mi tòj ìməš’i məš’i tòj məšì
Well, he had a mach– he had –
55900: ustɤ̀rgvəm’i ərmànɤ pul’ỳwəm’i gu wə də sɤ nɤbìj ùbuu
We scrape off the threshing floor, we water it down so that it’s trampled down nice,
55903: də n’i təkòə i tàm kət nəst’il’èm s’igà snòp’it’ȅ tùj ž’ìtutu
so that it doesn’t, you know, when we spread the sheaves out, the wheat.
55905: kɤt isɤ̀ne i se òtre i si stàne platnò
When it dries, it gets scraped down, and [then] it becomes fabric.
55912: i səz dikàn’a è inò vr’èm’i digàn’a
and [then begin] with a threshing board. Ah, in the old days, [we had a] threshing board!
55915: onò nè e zgòdno za nosèn’e ama se nosìlo  [laughter]
It’s not [very] comfortable to wear, but we wore it [all the same]. [laughter]
55919: a sɤs ə č’əkmàci odòlu tì nàje tàm tàm ìməš dikàn’a ìməš
With flintstones below. You, Naye, over there, you have a threshing board, don’t you?
55926: i kət pr’ègn’im vulòv’it’ȅ gi kun’è l’i vulòwi i kəkòt ìməm’i
And we harness up the oxen, horses, oxen, whatever we have,
55927: əməm znači oddòle košùl’a a od
Uh huh. So then, underneath there is the shift.
55934: i n’ìj d’ә̟càta s’àdəm’i nə d’ikàn’ata i t’è vɤrɤ̀t vɤrš’ɛ̀jm’i
and we kids sit on the threshing board and they go along and we thresh.
55941: ubikàl’em’i ubikàl’em’i dukət sə pànn’i ž’ìttu kətu pàdn’i ž’ìttu zɤ̀rnutu
We go around and around until the wheat falls out. And when the kernel of wheat falls out,
55942: And what did one wear on top [of that]?
55944: i odgòre pràimo klàšn’e i ne smò umejàli
Well, for on top we make homespun [fabric]. We didn’t know how –
55952: səz v’ìl’i v’ìl’i è tɤ̀j istrɤ̀s’əm’i istrɤ̀sk n’in’tìr’i n’in’tìr’ sə kàzvə n’in’t’ìr’
we take pitchforks and toss it about. Big wooden pitchforks, they’re called “nintir”.
55956: istɤ̀rs’əm’i èj tɤ̀j èj tɤ̀j kət z’èim è tɤ̀j istɤ̀rs’əm’i istɤ̀rs’əm’i
We toss it about like this and this, we take it up and toss and toss
55958: imàlo e òvce po dva.trìeset òvce e imàlo
There used to be sheep, each [one] had up to twenty or thirty sheep,
55963: ne smò umejàli da si ispletèmo vḷnèlu
[but] we didn’t know how to knit sweaters.
55966: nè.znam kvì smo bilì tò  glùpavi čovèci
I don’t know what sort of silly folk [we were, but] ...
55969: ne smò se setìli da si ispletèmo čeràpe smo plèli i klàšn’e
... we didn’t figure out how to knit them. We did knit socks, and homespun.
55972: klàšn’e pàk tekà se napredè osnòva potkàva se napredè
For homespun – you spin it like this, you set up the warp and woof, and you spin it
55976: so the wheat will fall out, and then we do the “removing”.
55981: m’ɛ̀s’im n’àkolko pɤ̀t’e i tɤ̀j ubikàl’em’i ubikàl’em’i m’ɛ̀si̥
We remove it several times, and then go around and around [again] and remove it,
55987: pàk mu vɤr’ìt kumbàj tùj d’ikàn’eta pàk minàvə
and they walk on it, and then the – the threshing board passes by again –
55990: i pràimo tkan’è se nòsi na val’àvicu
and turn it into woven cloth. And then you take it to the fulling mill.
55994: nər’ɛ̀ždə nə ker’em’ìd’it’ȅ udgòr’e tɤ̀j i sutrintà ut’ùwa də gl’èdə
She’d arrange them on the tiles on top [of the oven], and in the morning she’d go to look.
55999: vulòvit’ȅ kun’è l’i kəkòt ìməš dubìtɤk minàət
The oxen, the horses, whatever sort of livestock you have – they pass by.
56002: nə gerg’òwdèn’ də gl’èdə kujà kuprìva e uv’àxnala
On [the morning] of St. George’s day [she’d] look to see which nettle stalk had wilted.
56004: And whichever one had wilted, that meant that ...
56011: bul’edùwə d’et’ètu il’ n’ɛ̀štu š’e e tɤ̀j
... [someone’s] child would be ailing, or that something else would come about.
56017: kət sə swɤ̀rš’i i kətu pàdn’i ž’ìttu utn’èəm’i slàməta wèč’i
When it’s done and when the wheat has fallen out, we take the straw away,
56024: mə m’ɛ̀s’eše xl’èp pɯ̀stri pìt’i sɤs ə è kùkata ufčàrskəta kùka
So she’d make bread – round breads decorated	with – well, a hook, a shepherd’s hook,
56025: nɤ ə krɤ̀snictȁ pàk t’ì mi dàd’e evrèn’č’e às ti dàɤm xristijànče̟
it back to the godmother, and again: “You gave me a Jew, I give you a Christian”.
56027: kətu utn’èim’i slàməta na id’ìn kùp kùp nəstrən’ì
And we take the straw off into a big pile on the side
56036: You take it off with the big wooden pitchforks?
56038: uscète nə pìtkit’ȅ pràjət slàgət i tòpč’ənca ufcè
or sheep, on the breads. They make sheep out of little balls of dough and put them there.
56040: Do you use the big wooden pitchforks to take the straw off with?
56045: s n’in’t’ìrit’ȅ udn’èməm’i i kɤt ustàni wèči sàmu zɤ̀rnutu
We take it off with the big wooden pitchforks. And when only the wheat is left,
56049: kətu i sm’it’èm’i nə id’ìn kùp inò vr’èm’i n’àməš’i n’ìštu
when we sweep it into a large pile – In the old days there wasn’t anything to –
56054: mi pràim nə v’ɛ̀jm’i nə dɤrmòn’ nə dɤrmòn’ sə kàzwə
We then – we winnow it with the large sieve. It’s called a “darmon”.
56060: i gol’àmu e tɤ̀j e tɤ̀j nə trì kòlə i [unintelligible] i s’ɛ̀im’i
It’s big, like this, set up on three stakes [unintelligible] and we sift –
56064: s’ɛ̀jm’i ž’ìttu a pə kət ìmə v’àtɤr səs lupàtt’ȅ
we sift the wheat. And when there’s wind we [use] shovels
56071: kət vɤ̀rl’im’e etɤ̀j sr’eštu v’àtɤrɤ tò sə udd’ɛ̀l’ə slàməta b’àgə
to throw it up into the wind, and it separates. The straw falls off
56077: nəstrɤnì fɤrč’ì ž’ìttu tɤ̀j bə kəkò j bìlu bə kre’št’ìt
to the side, the wheat flies about. So it was like – everyone is shouting,
56081: n’ìj n’i mòž’im d’ecà n’i mòž’im də vɤ̀rl’em’e tɤ̀j
“We can’t –[you] kids – we can’t – we can’t throw [the wheat] [with you in the way]!”
56087: kəkò kàrət nə sa ama tɤ̀j b’ɛ̀š’i inò vr’ɛ̀m’i i t’è pòsl’e wèč’i ̀
That’s how they scolded us. But that’s how it was back then. And later,
56090: na trì pɤ̀t’ɤ nɤ trètij pɤ̀t’ i nə dà t’ì mi dàd’i
Three times in all. And the third time, it’s “You gave it to me,”
56096: kət i sm’it’èm’i də ispruv’ɛ̀jm’i pr’ib’ìrəm’i u hɤmbàr’e i slàgəm’i tàm èč’i
when we sweep it up and winnow it, we gather it into the barn, and put it there ...
56101: kàzɤ biz ìme̟ às ti dàam sɤs ìmi tudòrkɤ nɤprìmer
she says, “with no name; I give it to you with the name Tudorka.” For instance.
56108: kàktu gu kàktu žinàta ìmetu i tudòrka li p’ènkə li ivànkə li
Some name like a woman has – Tudorka, or Penka, or Ivanka – something like that.
56112: tudòrka i t’à màjkətə i z’ìmə vèči i s’àdəmi u kɤ̀š
Say it’s Tudorka. So the mother takes it, and we all sit down in the house.
56116: u vèči slàgəmi sufràta krɤ̀snictȁ ja dar’àva ə
We’ve already set the table. The godmother gifts the mother,
56122: màjkata dar’àva krɤ̀snicəta t’à vìka ma às cigà ə i nam’ɛ̀rix
the mother gifts the godmother. She says, “Now I’ve found it,
56134: d’àutu stànəl i i təkìə gerg’òwdèn’ xu
It appears Grandpa’s gotten up! So such things on St. George’s Day, dances –
56138: But [how about] when they slaughter the lamb?
56141: za àgn’itu i kòl’əvmi vɤfkɤ̀šti n’è e tɤ̀j sə vìkəli
We would slaughter the lamb at home. Not like [those] who call [someone else to do it].
56154: vɤfkɤ̀šti nə inò kur’ìtu slàgəvmi kòl’im àgn’itu i na samàta krɤ̀f
[We do it] at home. We’d put the lamb in a trough and slaughter it, and from the blood –
56163: čàkəj čàkəj čàkəj tòj š’ə si sèdn’i
[No,] wait a minute. He’ll [find a place] to sit.
56164: e èto ìma ìma òšte m’àsto
No, here! there’s more room here. Indeed [there is].
56170: tùk tùka elà è tùka sednì è tùka
Here, here! Come and sit over here!
56186: But you could fall [from that seat].
56192: òpa à š’ə dàm drùgu stòlč’i š’ə dàm
There you go! Now I’ll get another stool, let me get –
56200: əm a d’et’ètu əma n’àməm nìštu š’ə mu s ràzgele
this child, but I don’t have anything. I’ll – well, fortunately,”
56203: kàzvə ìmam inà pərà š’ə mu dàm enà parà pɤk drùk pɤ̀t’
she says, “I have some money. I’ll give it some money and then next time
56208: š’e mu nakùp’ə drèxi de i obl’àka t’à i d’it’ètu də ubličè
I’ll buy it some clothes to dress it.” And she dresses the child,
56210: dr’èxi mu kupùva pərì š’ə mu dàm i sigà v’èči š’ə snì
she buys it clothes. “I’ll give it money, and henceforth we’ll be
56212: inò c’àlu ròt ròt kət màjkə nàči màjka sə kàzvə v’èči
a family, I’ll be as a mother.” She’s now called a mother
56215: tɤ̀j nə d’it’ètu d’èt i nam’ìr’a i tàm ə ə gòsti dər’àvam
to this child that she found. So now – “I gift the guests,”
56220: pòčnuvəmi də id’èm àd’i sigà zə d’ət’ètu zə zdràv’i i t’à vìka
we start to eat. “Here’s to the child for its health,” she says,
56223: àjdi də si ut’ùəm či mnògu ustàna [cough]
“We’ll be off because I’ve already stayed a long time.” [cough]
56224: They don’t know [where] I [am – I need to be going].
56230: [cough] mnògu s’əd’àx àd’i vèč’i č’e duwìždən’i vìj š’ə ìdvət’i nìj š’ə ìdvəm’
[cough]	“We’ve sat here a lot, so goodbye now, you’re off and so are we.
56236: wèč’e̟ kɤtu krɤ̀ sè jnò i sɤ̀štu nàše d’ət’è vèč’e̟
After all, it’s as if it’s our child now.
56241: mòja dɤšter’ə̀ wìkɤ tɤ̀ž žinà i i e tɤ̀j xvɤ̀rl’en’i̥ nə b’èb’i
She’s now my daughter,” says this woman. And that’s the throwing of the baby,
56244: i nə tùj ə zə ubičàj zìami pàk pu stò l’èa zìami
the custom that we once again got a hundred levs for presenting –
56245: that they award us a hundred levs for! [laughter]
56251: ama tovà za da da bɤ̀de detètu žìvo li da da da
But [the purpose of] that is that the child should stay alive, that – that ...
56263: dà də n’i umìrɤt d’əcàta na trèttu vèč’i
Yes, that her children shouldn’t die. And [it’s] after the third one –
56267: inò dv’è trì vèč’i sè i umìrɤt d’əcàta i t’è vèč’i rešàvət
one, two three children die [in a row] – that they decide
56268: ìma si podi selò pa i u drùgi selà val’àvica
There’s one down below the village, and other villages [also have] fulling mills.
56273: i tàm kat se zanesè se mɤ̀n’e na val’àvica
And when you take it there, you beat it at the fulling mill.
56277: i pràe za za mužjèti pràe a el elbrevenèci
And [from it] you make clothing for men – "elbrevenetsi",
56280: and on top a white vest.
56285: a za pò mlàditi mùžje go učìne ta pràe drèxi
And for the younger men, they dye [the fabric] and make clothes [of it].
56286: a kvò e tòj ə elbrevenèci
56292: i dòle tèsno tè kakò ə kakò
... and tight down below like, like –
56300: I know, I know, I’ve seen [them].
56301: So you know what that is then.
56302: i tùka odgòre kvò če navìje na nogàta
And here, on top [of that], what do you wind around the leg?
56306: What gets wound around the leg?
56309: navìva navìva navòšta mu mì dùmamo
You put on – you put on “wrappings”, [that’s what] we call it.
56315: navòšta e otgòre sɤs ə povòrke pà ga ovṛ̀že dotùj
The wrappings go on top, and the ties bind them up [tightly], up to here.
56321: a ženàta otprèd kvò slàga tùka
And what [about women]? What does a woman wear here in front?
56323: a ženàta u suknò pràe ot klàšn’ete suknò
Well, the woman [puts on] a tunic. We make [them] out of homespun cloth –
56331: košùl’ete tekvèj pṛ̀tene pa sɤs rukavè dotùj
The shifts are made of this thin (= two-ply) cloth with sleeves to here,
56334: i ozgòr suknò i tòj ama nìkoj nè e umejàl
and on top, the tunic, and that’s it.  But nobody knew how
56339: da si ispletè sɤ̀k kvè vanèle pletù ot ə vḷ̀nu
to knit for themselves. Now they knit all sorts of pullovers from wool,
56346: mì ùmemo da si pletèmo ama nìkoj se nè e sečàl
We know how to knit, but nobody ever figured it out.
56348: [So] nobody wore [anything other than rough fabric clothing].
56357: i gerg’òwdèn’ kətu upič’è zəkàrəmi àgn’itu
And on St. George’s day, after it’s roasted, we bring in the lamb ...
56362: ... and [some] of the blood  into the house, ...
56367: i na samàta st’enà pràimi è tɤ̀j krɤ̀s
... and we make a cross right on the wall, right here.
56371: krɤ̀s i màlki d’ecà kət ìmət z’èmət ut krɤftà
A cross. And if people have small children, they take some of the blood
56375: slàgət nə č’èlutu im də stàvəli č’erv’èni
and put it on their foreheads, so they’ll be red.
56382: dà kət nə krɤ̀w i č’erv’èni d’ecàta napɤ̀streni
Yes. The children are decorated in red, from the blood.
56387: i pòsl’e gu up’ič’èmi àgn’itu up’ič’èm ama inò inò wr’èmi
And then we roast [things]. We roast the lamb. But in the old days –
56389: s’eà gerg’òwdèn’ pràjmi sɤz zbòr n’i mòeš
Now we observe St. George’s day together with the village celebration. You can’t
56394: n’èto da gu prèkə pɤk inò vr’èmi kət sɤ sɤbir’ɛ̀mi
do it now [separately]. But in the old days when we’d get together,
56398: č’èt’ri p’èt’ kɯ̀št’i e nəprìmer’ è tèj k də pust’il’èm
it’d be four or five houses [of us]. For instance if it’s these [houses], we’d spread out
56405: nə n’àkuj ràvn mi ràv’in dvòr rugòski də pust’il’èm tè misàl’e
reed mats on some flat place, a flat yard – we spread out cloths
56410: nə nərid’ìmi t’ìe àgn’ita pr’àsnu s’ìr’en’e kòjtu ìmə uscè
and arrange [on them] the lambs, fresh cheese – those who have sheep
56414: də i xvɤ̀rl’ә̟t nə krɤstupɤ̀t’ə kòjtu i nəm’ɛ̀ri nə n’ègu kɤsmèt’
to throw one out at the crossroads, and whoever finds it has fortune
56420: v’èč’i nɤ nègu š’ə i ərìžet ar xərìzvət à kət sə vɤ̀rnət
and will give gifts on its behalf, will gift [the mother] when they return
56423: ut ə čèrkvəta pr’ekàrvət ə prez rìza tɤ̀s u žinà
from the church. They’ll pull it through the shift: this woman – [the one]
56428: dunàs’ə jnà rìza d’èt i namìrə pr’ekàrvət i du trì pɤ̀t’ə
who found it – brings a shift, and they pull it through the shift three times.
56437: du trì pɤ̀t’i i prikàrvət də e ž’ìvu i zdràu v’èč’i
Three times they pull it through, so it will be healthy and live,
56439: dɤ n’i sè rəzbul’àwə i tɤ̀j
so that it won’t fall ill. That’s why.
56443: ako e geòrgi kàg gu krɤštàvət gàna tɤ̀j li
So if [the finder] is Georgi, how do they christen the child? Gana, right?
56448: e na mumìče  əku è mumičinci gu krɤštɤd girgànə
Well, for a girl – if it’s a girl, they christen it Gergana,
56452: i kàktu gu tò nə trì iminà sə krɤštàət
since they christen it with three names.
56457: If the first [one to find it is] a man.
56459: dà dà pək às kətu hvɤ̀rl’ə kətu pɤ̀rvi pɤ̀t
Yes. Yes, when I “threw” the baby – the first time
56463: kəd dàəmi tùj tòz ubičɛ̀j àz b’àw
that we performed this custom, I was the one –
56468: às ut’ùvam səs ə stòmnite zə vudà i ut’ìvəm vìždəm ednò d’it’è
I’m going along with water jugs to the well. I go along and I see a child
56472: à vìkəm kakò i tùj dit’è kòj i fɤ̀rlil tùkə bè
and I say, “What is this? A child? Who threw it here?
56476: bòže kùčettȁ kàk ne sɤ̀ i rəskɤ̀səli tò kùklə əmə t’è b’èb’i
My God, how is it that the dogs haven’t torn it apart?” It was a doll, but [acting as] a baby.
56479: vɤ̀ bòže vìkəm tùj b’èb’i kə kòj hwɤ̀rl’i tùkə kò
“God almighty,” I said, “it’s a baby! Who threw it here? Who?”
56482: i màjkətə iskàčə t’à sə skrìwə
And the mother jumps out – she’d been hiding.
56489: à àjd’e nə t’èb’i kəsm’èt’ zimì i zimì às i zèw
“Well, fortune to you – take it, take it!” So I took it.
56495: zèw b’èb’itu à sigà ši ìd’im ukɤ̀šti ut’ìdim u nàx
I took the baby, and now we’re going home. We go to [them]
56497: u t’àx uš ut’ùəm tàm nə sc’ènətə tò əmə ut’ùəm u t’àx
– as if to them, this is on the stage you see – so I go to them
56499: i kàzvəm tàm v’èči i pək də bùl’ətə vìkə
and I speak to them, and the older sister [in the performance] says,
56504: è tò n’èskə ùbəwo nid’ɛ̀l’ə ìmə pòp čerkwətə utòrenə
“Well good. Today is Sunday, there’s a priest and the church is open.
56509: jà vìe id’èt’i krɤ̀štəjt’i tò tùj d’it’è čitirìjsi d’ènə nəbližàə
You go ahead and christen this child. It’s been nearly forty days,
56512: pək ni sì j čùlu ìmito àjd’e ut’ùəmi krɤštàəmi vrɤ̀štəmi sə pàk
and it hasn’t heard its name yet.” So we go and christen it. Then we return,
56517: i tàm v’èči dər’àvəni pris sìtutu sə tərkàl’ə tàm na trì pɤ̀t’e
and there’s gifting, rolling the child three times in the sieve –
56523: əmi pràili sn’e às si pràjew i dubrìnə jè tɤ̀s ivànuvətə
Well, that’s how we performed it. I did it, and Ivan’s Dobrina,
56525: i čàkəj kujà ženà tòs ubičàj gu dàvəmi b’èb’itu
and I don’t recall what other woman. This is the custom we performed – about the baby.
56532: bɛ̀:me̝ čètiri mumìčetə ednò mumčè tò mɤ̀ninku i iskàreme̝ tovà
There were four of us girls and one boy – he was small. So we got through that –
56536: ožèni sɤ dvɛ̀ sestrì ìməm pò gulèmi i sə užènii
Marriages – I have two sisters older [than me], they both got married.
56544: àjde sə užèni i àze i uprài:me ràbuttə pribrà se bɤštɤ̀ ni
And I got married too. And we took care of things. Our father came back
56550: od vojnɤ̀ta nàj pudìre tòj s bɛ̀ə gu fanàle̝ ròp
from the war finally. He had been taken prisoner.
56554: podìre dudè i tòj i nìštu ne rasprɤ̀sname̝
Finally he came. We didn’t [have to] disperse anything [of our property],
56559: əmə gulɛ̀m zòr vidò:me òd dvanàesta gudìnə do usemnàestə
but we saw very hard times between 1912 and 1918.
56566: orà kopàče̝ žetvàre̝ tɤkàče̝ da predèš da šìe̝š tuvà a
I did plowing, [we worked as] diggers, harvesters, weavers – you spin, you sew - like that.
56572: kupà:me žɤ̀ne:me kòse:me sɤbìra:me sɛ̀no zə stòkә̥tә̥
We went out digging, harvesting, mowing, we gathered hay – for the animals.
56573: [What kind of work did you have in the morning?]
56576: sùtrin sùtrin utìəme nə ràbutə du̥dè e vrɛ̀me utìvəme
In the morning – in the morning we go out to work.  We go at a time
56581: pu lɤdɤvìna da žɤ̀nem də žɤ̀nem durdè sə nəpečè žìtoto
[so as] to do reaping when it’s cool – to reap up till the grain gets [too] hot.
56587: da go izvɤ̀ržem da go sɤbère̝m na petìne̝ pòsle na krəscì
We [go to] tie it off, and gather it into groups of five sheaves, and then into cruciforms
56590: i ostàvə də sə prekàrva pòsle za kupnìte̝
and then it remains to transport it afterwards to [where] the bundles are.
56594: ìmašemo lòzje tùj gòre pa ga oràmo sɤz dèdo vàn’o
We had a vineyard up the hill here, and we plowed it with Grandpa Vanyo
56596: no baštà ti znàe dèdo vàn’o a pà edɤn pùt jà
(your father knew Grandpa Vanyo),  and once I –
56600: bèmo gòre kòpašemo li kvò li a nò se pòkaza oddòle
We were up there digging, or something, and from down below there appeared
56603: nèkvo nò ìmaše ukràse kvò li nè jà dùmaše
something, it had [some sort of] decoration. What sort of thing is this, I thought,
56606: tòj madžìe kàe nò bilò nišàn na parì imàlo
is this some sort of magic? But it turned out to be a sign of hidden money
56608: u tòj mèsto a nò si ìskopa sìne bàbo
in that place, and so he dug it out and – Ah, child, dear one,
56612: sèdni sèn’k’u čà tàm tùj če se tèp ti stàne lòše
sit [in the] shade! [If you stay] over there, you’ll get sick.
56614: He wants to pour water on his [head].
56629: màni go žèga mu ìska da se takòva
Let him be in the heat – he wants to do it that way.
56633: nò nèk se izmìje no no tòj də jà sednì na sḷncèto
Let him wash [his head], but he should – [And you,] sit in the sun [if you want],
56636: no tì si sèdɤl če ti stàne lòšo na glàvu
but you’ve sat [in a place] that will give you a headache!
56654: No, it won’t. My head is strong.
56657: My head will hold its own.
56661: a tì bàbo uznì sèn’ku pa sèdni na sèn’k’ə
Well then, you, dear one, come into the shade! Sit in the shade,
56665: No I won’t, granny. I’m fine.
56669: pa tì kvò pomìsli če e tì dùmaše če če madžìja takà li
So what did you think this was? You thought [it was] magic, right?
56674: e pa kòj če go napràj tòj
And who performs this [sort of thing]?
56680: [cough] no tekà odàvna bèše madžìje e decàta bèu kazùjem g’im za
[cough] But there was magic a long time ago. The children were –  I tell them –
56681: What happened [with that riddle]? Who was it that was working?
56686: ò znàe gim dùpe kòj kvì su nèma se sètu
Oh, they haven’t got a clue who it was. They won’t figure it out
56687: even [when they go] to the other world!
56689: ta da vìdim znàči kvò e kogà e nišàn kvò e
So let’s see then what [it’s about]. What is it when it’s a sign of treasure,
56690: kogà e madžìja kvò e tovà e li što sa dvè razlìčni
and what is it when it’s magic? Why are the two different [from one another]?
56694: Ah, when is it a sign of treasure?
56703: odàvna bàbičke pa bàju pa plàšu naròd
A long time ago old women would cast spells and frighten people.
56708: bàbičke splàšu mladìčite pa zbèru edno drùgo
Old women would frighten young people, they’d collect this and that
56713: pa ìdu na čovèka na vràtḁ pa pràju màgije
and go to someone’s door and cast spells.
56723: uvìvaju kadà kṛpl’àk kadà cvèk’e tùru kadà svèče tùra
They’d wind rugs [on the door], or  leave a flower, or leave candles.
56728: nalì znaèš i tòj kàe pràeno madžìje na èdi si na kogà
You know, don’t you, that means magic spells are cast on somebody or another.
56730: tòj e bilò odàvna a ìnače svàdbata
[But] that was long ago. Now about weddings –
56732: Children’s hair would be shorn [in an effort to bewitch them].
56733: n è na mòja sìn n è
Well, [in the case of] my son –
56734: a decà če strìžu e štò
Ah, they would shear children’s hair? But why?
56737: bòže no mòjə sìn je napràeno mu detìnstvo
Well, my God, it was done to my son when he was a little child.
56742: dojdè tùja a nò mu kosìcata  tùj na tèmeto ostrìženo
He came up and [I saw] that his hair was shorn, here around the crown of his head.
56745: è tòlko parčènce ostrìženo mu ot kosùtu i ga izèdou
Here, just a part of his hair shorn away. They ( = magic forces) did him in,
56749: na drùgo devòjče tàj štò gi praìla šturotìe
and also the other girl. That one who was doing stupid things to them –
56751: [Spells] were cast on [all] three of them!
56755: na edìnijə za bòlest na edìnijə za pijànstvo
One was bewitched into illness, another into drunkenness,
56757: and the other one into dying.
56772: pr’àsnu s’ìr’en’e pràj slàgəmi p’ìt’it’ȅ mu ba i màlkit’i d’ecà
make fresh cheese. We put out the round breads, and the little children,
56774: sɤs inà koprìva i sɤs vudà
[each] with a nettle stalk, and with water –
56785: də prɤ̀skəmi prɤ̀skəd gi rɤ̀s’ət rɤ̀s’əd gi
... and we sprinkle. [The children] sprinkle them, they shower them [with the wet nettles].
56788: i kətu pòp kətu i pòp sè jnò i sɤ̀št pòp
Like the priest. Like the priest, exactly like the priest.
56792: tɤ̀j rɤ̀s’əwmi i id’èm pièm i vìkət v’èsela ràbuta
So we’d sprinkle [people], and we eat, and drink, and shout – merriment!
56797: s’igà g’urg’òwdèn’ n’i mòm dɤ rəzbìr’èm tɤmàn s’èdn’i
We can’t understand [how people observe] St. George’s day now. You sit down,
56804: čə̀tə sə s’àvə ubiknuv’ènu màrt m’èsec màrt m’èsec sə s’àvə
[Len]tils are usually sown in March. They are sown in March.
56809: sìčko təkà i nə pò strɤ̀mni mistà izdɤ̀rž’ə nə pò tɤ̀n’ki
They survive even in the steeper regions, and in thinner soil.
56814: nə hərmàn kət ut’ìdeme nìe še gu pràime še d’àləme səs mut’ìki
When we go to the threshing floor we make it – hoe it down – with hoes,
56817: s’ètn’e pɤ̀k kɤt sɤ vɤ̀rnɤɤ ut kɤzàrmata
Later when [his draft group] returned from the army,
56825: vànaa pulùčɤd zɤplàta mà tɤ̀z v’èč’er spìɤm nɤ.inò pɤrìt’ȅ
they got their pay and right off that night: “Let’s drink up all this money!”
56831: da vi kazùjem òn men čèsto tìk’e me zastùpi
Let me tell you, he often surprises me and insists on talking to me.
56846: drùgɤ v’èč’er mà spìɤm nɤ dvà pɤt’ɤ
And the second night: “Let’s drink [it up again]. Two times [in a row]."
56854: nə nàj ràvnətə pul’ànə še izber’ème še d’àləme səs mut’ìki
We choose the most level field, and then hoe it down with hoes.
56863: i ut kup’ènə hvɤ̀rl’ət ta tə gu nəsəd’ʌ̀t nəsəd’ʌ̀d gu
Then they toss them off the pile and arrange them. They arrange them,
56867: i tugàvə d’àutu fl’ez’è səs mùl’etətə i bùlkətə ž’ə vdìgə
and then Grandpa comes in with the mules and the bride lifts [the sheaves]
56872: n’è nə dib’èlə pòčvə i əku n’èmə səs kəkvò nəl’ì
They don’t [need] thick soil. And if you don’t have anything else,
56874: səs vìlətə ut kràjə snòpit’i sìč’kit’e še gi rəstrɤ̀svə
with a pitchfork, at the edge of threshing floor, and shakes out all the sheaves
56877: də mòž’ də sə ukàp’e ž’ìtutu də mòž’ də pòsl’e
so that the grain can drop out, and so that later
56882: səs səz zgriblò šə sə zətərlì gu vìkəm’e də sə zəròvi l’èštətə
you take a rake and harrow it, as we say, to dig in the lentils
56885: də sə udd’elì slàmətə i tugàvə sə vìješ’e nə v’àtər
the straw will get separated off. And then it got winnowed in the wind.
56888: n’ɛ̀məš’e tugàa ətəkìvə məš’ìni kàktu sigà
Back then there weren’t the kind of machines they have now.
56893: sl’et tvà məš’ìnite dòdəhə əmə kət stànəme t’èkees’è v’èč’e
The machines came later, when we became [part of] cooperative farms.
56901: gòst’i glàdn’i də sə xràniš tɤmàn stàa àjd’e pɤk tugàwə s’àkuj
[there’s] hungry guests to feed, then they get right up and leave. But back then, everyone –
56902: nìj tùkə d’ètu e drəgust’ìnuvi è tàm dafìnkini d’èt sɤ
[Say] we’re here where the Dragostin family is, or there where the Dafinkin family is,
56911: è tòj dvòr ràvin z’il’ènə muràva kət napust’el’èm’e rugòskit’i da nəs’àdəmi
where there’s a large yard, a green meadow [where] we lay out reed mats and sit,
56918: č’èt’iri p’èt s’əmèjstva jàd’en’i pìen’i vìkə vèselsku s’igà g’erg’òwden’
four or five families. Eating, drinking – merriment! But St. George’s day now?
56922: ja nèmam kadà da vrèvim òn me tìk’e zastùpi
I don’t have time to talk. But he keeps on insisting
56927: ta da vrèvimo da mi kazùje ednù stàru kn’ìgu
that we talk and starts telling me [something] from an old book [of his]
56930: òn kn’ìgutu nèma da dadè a tekvìja ràboti e pisuvàlo
(he won’t give [me] the book) – such things are written down [there].
56936: rèkuw à t’à tɤ̀s ràptɤ n’àɤ a stàni sìn’ tɤ̀j
So I said, “This sort of thing can’t go on, son.”
56944: ùš ə ìskɤm mu də m’ dɤd’è tò du v’eč’ɤrtɤ̀ mi ìš’ti pàk
It’s as if I’m asking him to give me [money] and by evening he wants it back from me!
56952: za tìja u granìtovo štò bilò tùrsko u granìtovo
[He wrote] about these – [It was] in Granitovo, that used to be Turkish. In Granitovo –
56956: u kalùger dètu go zovèšeu pò ràno
In Kaluger, as they used to call it?
56970: kvò če pràju vṛtèli praìli kutàli se ne mòže
What could they do? They messed about, did this and that, hid a bit, but to no avail.
56973: kvò če napràju ugotvìli kako sɤ̀k štò vrèvimo
what were they going to do? They prepared – like we’ve just been talking about –
56977: i priglàd’i sə vərhù səs n’àštu dɤ̀skə li kəkvò li
and smooth out the surface above with something, a board or similar,
56980: də sə prip’ìt’i i pòsl’e izn’ìkn’e l’èštətə hùbəvə stàne
to make [the soil] more compact. Then the lentils sprout, all looks good,
56984: i pu l’àtutu v’èč’e cəft’ì i zəvɤ̀rzuvə uzr’èe li l’èštətə
and in the summer they bloom, and the fruit starts to form. If the lentils are ripe
56986: pu p’ètruden tàm kəm àvgus m’èsec v’èč’e sə mʌ̀kni
by St. Peter’s day, towards August, they are harvested.
56990: nə rəkʌ̀ mʌ̀knehme mʌ̀kneš i slàgəš təkà nə klàdnič’kə jə slàgəš
We used to harvest them by hand. You pull them out and put them on a small pile.
56993: kət puisʌ̀hn’e i t’à sɤ̀štu sə vərš’èje ku n
When they dry, then we thresh them [like grains]. If not,
56996: i nə v’àtərə jə udv’àvəme v’èč’e də jə izdùhə
and [then] winnow them in the wind, once it blows.
57002: əmi rɤ̀š’ sə s’àvə jèseno vr’èm’e rəštɤ̀ i vəf pu gèrg’uvdèn
Well, rye is sown in the autumn. By the time of St. George’s day
57007: č’ɛ̀kət hòrətə berik’èta kləsʌ̀ də sə jəvì
people expect the resulting crop: that the spikes appear.
57015: kɤ̀ sme živɛ̀le siromašìjka beše golotìa beše pris marabètu
How did we live? There was poverty, there was hunger. It was wartime.
57018: baštà mi beše vɤ̀zrasen màjka mi be pò mlàda t’à
My father was an old man; my mother was younger. She –
57023: došlà pò mlàda za nègo naràždaa dačurlìga šès dvuìca bràk’e
she came young to him [as a bride]. They bore six children. Two brothers.
57027: živɛ̀eme si dubrɛ̀ sirumašìa ama golotìa ama beme dobrɛ̀
We lived well. Poor and ill-clothed [though we were],  we were fine.
57028: màjka mi beše vràčkə̥ ut selàta dovàždaa òra tə gi cɛ̀ree
My mother was a seer. People came from [other] villages for her to heal them.
57036: dòeše vèčer ednà vèčer si dodòjme ot kɤ̀rɤ̥ sednàjme
Evening came – one evening we got back from the fields and sat down [to eat],
57041: i tìa do dodè edìn stàrec i dovèdi dvɛ̀ decà dvɛ̀ momčènca
and there came an old man, leading two children, two boys –
57045: ednò pò golɛ̀mo i ednò pò màlko̥ i sednàa
one older and one younger.  And they sat down.
57047: i màjka mi be si došlà ot kɤ̀rɤ i tò sa mrɤk’ìn’a
My mother had just come from the field, and dusk was falling,
57051: i t’à vìka na stàreca dɛ̀do štò si dovè: tɛ̀a dečìca
and she said to the old man, “Grandpa, what did you bring these kids for?”
57056: tòj vìka tè dovè: sɤn gi dàj t’à glèaše na bɛ̀jek
And he said, “Well, I brought them. Have a look.” And she looked at the mark.
57060: otkɤ̀sneše ednò končènce drɛ̀ška dèto spì
She snipped off a thread from [the child’s] clothing [at a point] where he slept [on it],
57065: i tùrne f ədnɤ̀ čàša vudɤ̀ i gl’èda po tàa stàru tә̥kòvu
and dropped it into a glass of water and looked at it in the “old manner”.
57067: abe dɛ̀do dàj dàj rèče da ti poglèdna tòj dàde
“Well, Grandpa, give over,” she said, “so I can look at you [too]. And he gave –
57072: dàde ednò končè ud nèja i t’à gu spuštì dvà pɤti̥
he gave over a thread from his [clothing] and she dunked it twice,
57077: trì pɤti f čàšə̥tə i vìka prez mlàdi godìni si bì: pastìr
three times in the glass, and said, “In your early years you were a herdsman,
57081: dèca ìmaše prìkaska i n’ù če vi g’u kàžem
Children – there was this tale, and I’m going to tell it to you.
57083: rèkuw tɤ̀s ràptɤ n’àɤ stàni še tɤ užènim
I said, “This sort of thing can’t go on. We’re going to marry you off.”
57089: nɤm’èriw bràtɤ sɨ d’èt ə na vetirnàrnie nɤ bɤštà mu
So I [went and] found my brother (= cousin), the one whose father is a veterinarian,
57094: tò šə sə zɤvɤ̀rni tùka pɤk ìnɤč’ә̟
then he’ll come back here [and settle down]. Otherwise –”
57099: mɤ dònke zɤ̀mɤš si òšti inɤ̀ b’elɤ̀ nɤ glɤvɤ̀tɤ
“But Donka,” [he said], “you’re taking yet another burden on your shoulders.”
57105: bàče b’elɤ̀ ni b’elɤ̀ šə vìdim sètn’e t’àw li šə màwnɤ
“Brother,” I said, “burden or no, I’ve got to see it through. Either I send them
57111: u grɤdɤ̀ dvàməta pàk dɤ si  ìmɤt sim’èstu às li še sə màjnɤ
off to the city as a pair so that they’ll [settle down and] start a family, or I’ll disappear myself
57117: še gi ustàjɤ u dumà šə tɤ̀rsim idìn kulàj dàvɤj
and leave them [to stay] in this house. We’ll find a way. So let’s get on with it.”
57125: sètn’ә̟ bàču kɤžì de dè dɤ idìm pɤk ìmɤ dv’è mumìč’ә̟ncɤ
Then – “Brother, tell me where we should go [in search of a bride]. There’s [these] two girls
57135: ut s’èlu štòt smi kràjnu b’èdni kràjnu kràjnu kɤ̀štɤ ìmɤmi vɤv v’ètuu
from [our] village, because we are really, really poor. We’ve got a house in Vetovo
57139: a nòsexte li go àgneto kato go opečete nòsexte li go
And did you take the lamb – when you roast the lamb did you take it
57141: drùgu n’àɤmi nìštu kràjnu b’èdni e či nə kujà kɤ̀štɤ dɤ ìdɤ
but nothing else – nothing. [We’re] really poor." So which house shall I go to [in search of]
57152: zɤ snɤxɤ̀ d’èt n’àɤ stàni tɤkòs ùbu əmɤ tɤ̀z bùlkə
a daughter-in-law? It’s not going to happen like that. So O.K. But [there’s] this young woman
57157: nè pr’edvərìtelnu gu nòsim predvərìtelnu pr’ed’ì
No. We take it earlier on. Earlier on, before –
57166: prəz inɤ̀ kɤ̀štɤ smi na n’èe kumšìe sme pustujànnu sm’ә̟ tìj
one house over that we’re neighbors with, that I see all the time; they’re always
57171: u dumà i às u t’àw vrɤ̀štɤm sɤ id’ìn ə vèč’ә̟r
at my house and I at theirs. So one evening I’m on my way back
57177: pr’ed’ì dɤ zɤ dɤ gu zɤkòlim
57179: kəd gu zəkòlim əmə s’igà gu kòl’im òšt’e sɤ̀buta àgn’itu pɤk
When we slaughter it. But now we slaughter it already on Saturday.
57184: … the priest sings a blessing on it.
57187: inò vr’ɛ̀mi nòs’im gu nə cɤ̀rkvəta
... back then we carried it to the church ...
57195: də mu č’i̥tè tàm pòpɤ dɤ gu up’ɛ̀j
... for the priest to read over it, to sing a blessing over it.
57199: s’àkuj kɤt i slòži è tùkə inà čèr ə pr’estìlka kət slòži
Each one – when they put it here, when [the butcher] puts an apron
57202: amì nalì e pisàl za tìja ràboti
Well, didn’t he write about these things [we’ve been discussing]?
57206: nə vrɤtɤ̀ si dɤ slòži tò àgn’i dɤ m’ètn’i è tɤ̀j
onto his neck, [ready] to put the lamb there [for the slaughter], then
57209: nə gɤrbɤ̀ si nɤ cɤ̀rkvəta gi nòsewmi tugàva kət sə vɤ̀rn’i
[he hoists it] onto his back and we’d take them to church. And then when it comes back,
57213: də gu č’i̥t’è pòpɤ tàm kət sə vɤ̀rn’im zəkàl’ɤmi i
[he took it] for the priest to read the blessing – then when we get back we slaughter it
57219: či tugàskə pič’èm ə n’àməmi zòr də bɤ̀rzəmi də i
and then roast it. There’s no need to hurry to –
57224: a na àgneto slàgaxte li mu nèšto na vrətɤ̀ venčètə n’èšto
Did you put something around the lamb’s neck? Wreaths or something?
57281: ud n’ìwɤtɤ nòs’ɤ s’ drèxi̥t’ȅ tɤ̀j nɤ rɤkɤ̀tɤ bùlkɤtɤ s’èd
from the fields, I’m carrying clothes over my arm, and this young woman is sitting
57289: nɤ t’àwnɤtɤ wràtničkɤ rèkuw kìno mɤ wòt’ sidìš tùkɤ mɤ n’ètkini
at their doorstep. “Kina,” I said, “why are you sitting here? Hasn’t the Netkin [family]
57295: zɤmìnɤɤ  nɤ mòminɤ b’el’ànkɤ pɤk tò tɤ̀j zɤplàka i kàzɤ
all gone off to the maidens’ work bee?” And she burst into tears and said,
57302: è bùl’u dònke kòjt n’àɤ màjka n’àɤ dɤ ìdi nìjd’e štò
“Ah, Auntie Donka! The one who has no mother isn’t going anywhere.” “Why?” [I said].
57308: bùl’ɤ ut’ìdi nɤ kùrsuje às n’àɤm màjka ku ìmɤw màjka
“[My] older sister went off to study, but I don’t have a mother. If I had a mother,
57314: šə ustàni dɤ gl’èdɤ nɤ bràta dit’ètu pɤk às št’àw dɤ ìdɤ
she’d stay here to watch [our] brother’s child  and I would have gone.
57320: əmɤ sigà kɤt n’àɤm màjkɤ ustàivə m’ène dɤ ispràštɤm tàtka
But as it is, since I’m without a mother, they left me here to get father
57327: ofčàr si pàsɤl òfce sɤs òšte dvuìca tòj vìka
a shepherd. You pastured sheep along with two others.” He said,
57333: o̥fčàr bèx vɛ̀rno e pàsox emi katu pàsi tɛ̀a òfce
“That’s right, I was a shepherd. I pastured [them].” “Well, when you pastured these sheep
57337: sɤs tòo sɤs tɛ̀a dvuìcata kvò sa nagovaràxte koto fanàxte
with these guys, these two, what did you scheme to do when you stole
57343: dvà pràza i gi za zavèdoxte kɤm vàzi i gi zatvòrixte
two rams and took them off on your own and shut them up
57349: f ednɤ̀ mazɤ̀ da:bòkḁ i tìa blɛ̀at i tì kɤ̀ kazà
way down in the cellar, and they were bleating. And what did you say?
57355: dàjte də i odrɛ̀žem ezìciti da na blɛ̀:t štòto
‘Let’s cut their tongues out’ [you said] ‘so they won’t bleat, because [otherwise]
57359: še ni čùat komšìiti̥ vɛ̀rno vɛ̀rno ə napràvimè go tovà
the neighbors will hear us’’’  “That’s right,” [he said]. “That’s right, we did that.”
57363: èj koto skočìa onɛ̀a decà koto zakàčia da go šìbat
And then these kids jumped up and started to punch him,
57369: na ràbutɤ dɤ mu j zgòtv’enu də gu pusr’èštɤm kɤt kài
off to work, to cook for him, to look after him. So when she said
57372: kòjtu n’àɤ màjkɤ n’àɤ dɤ ìdi nìjde tɤ̀j mi dužəl’à rèkuw
“the one with no mother isn’t going anywhere,” I felt really sorry [for her] and thought,
57374: bòže tùj dɤ gu jìskɤ dɤ̀l’ šә̟ dɤ̀l’ šә̟ stàni ràptɤ
“Goodness, if I ask for her [as my son’s bride], will that come to pass?
57383: às šə si isɤbɤ̀ prìkɤskɤtɤ pɤk mòže i dukàrɤm pɤk m’ušt’erìi
[Even if] I squander my negotiating ability, still I could bring other ‘customers’
57388: dɤ kàɤt dònkɤ šɤ ìd zɤ snɤɤ̀ či nìj li
who’d say ‘If Donka can ask for her as a daughter-in-law, then what about us?
57393: n’àɤ dɤ ìjme tàm i kàzɤw na bàča tùj n’èštu pɤk
Why can’t we also go there?’ ”. So I told my brother about this, and what do you know?!
57402: bɤštà i nɤ bùlkata i mòjt’ә̟ bràt’a l’àtnu wrèmi sɤbìrɤt bylỳc’t’ȅ
The girl’s father and my brothers [work together] in the summer herding animals.
57407: (When there’s a lot of sheep, we call it a “herd”.)
57413: i ə sɤbìrɤd gi u kɤ̀ro nɤ n’ìvata tàm spɤ̀t
So they herd them up at the pasture in the field – they sleep there,
57422: tàm dujɤ̀t s mɤgàr:tȁ nòsɤt ml’àku̥tȕ tɤkòstu s’è sɤ nɤjnò
they milk them there and bring the milk back on donkeyback – they do everything together.
57428: ùbuu sɤ upuznàti̥ bàče š šɤ̀ nɤpràim in id idìn rìsk pɤk
Great – so they’re acquainted. “Brother,” I said, “let’s take the risk,
57436: kòtu̥ stàni vèke ut’ìduwmi ɤmɤ i cànkɤ̥tɤ pruòdijmi
since it’s come this far.” So we went, and took [my son] Tsanko along
57440: sɤz žinìjlit’ȅ àje i tì s t’àw nɤjnò dɤ č’ùiš tì bùlkɤtɤ
with the matchmakers. “You come along with them too, to hear what the girl
57446: kò š’ɤ kàžə š’ɤ tɤ ìšti l’ n’àɤ l’ tɤ ìšti
is going to say, whether she’ll want [to marry] you or not.”
57448: è tɤj ut’ìdi tòj sɤs nèjɤ nɤjnò sɤs t’àw nɤjnò bàče rekɤ̀l
So O.K. He went together with her – I mean with them. And my brother said,
57453: bà dìmo tì n’ì pìtɤš pɤk nìj zɤ kò dòduwmi
[to the girl’s father] “So Dimo, you’re not even asking why we came!”
57455: ɤ č šə kàžeš ama nìj dòduwmi zɤ bùlkɤ bà
[and Dimu responded] “Well, you need to say ‘We came for a bride –
57461: tùj màlku̥tu štò ne g dɤd’èš nɤ sɤ̥srɤ̀tɤ inɤ̀ bùlkɤ bɤ̀
why not give this young girl here to my sister as a bride?
57467: jèm zɤ dɤšter’ɤ̀ dɤ je jèm tɤkò bɤ ilìjo ustɤ̀j gu bɤ
Then she’ll be both a daughter to you and a bride to us.’ ”. “Ah Iliya, leave her!
57473: tò d’èti βèšti̥ kò təkò pɤk ə tòj rikɤ̀l bàču mu kàzɤl
She’s still a child. Why now?” So then my brother said to him,
57479: či tò tè tɤ n sì li t’ì tì
“It’s not you, is it – you aren’t the one [who]
57483: dɤ kàžiš tə t’à šə kài kɤlìnke kɤžì mɤ
needs to say it. She’s the one to speak. So then, Kalinka, tell me now:
57487: šɤ gu zɤ̀mniš li cànku il’ n’è šɤ gu zɤ̀mnɤ
will you take Tsanko [as a bridegroom] or not?” “I’ll take him.
57497: àjd’a tò t’ičә̥ɤškɤ̀tɤ bàču dàj inò kilò rɤkìjɤ mɤ dàduw
So then my brother came up running and said, “Give [us] a kilo of rakia!” I gave [them]
57501: inò kilò rɤkìjɤ bùlkɤtɤ kàj ž dòdi prigòtv’əj sə prigòtv’əj sə
a kilo of rakia. “The bride,” he said, “will come. Get ready! Get ready,
57502: i t’à mu vìka dɛ̀do šɤ tɤ nakàži priròdata
and she said, “Grandpa, nature will punish you!
57509: nèma nakàži tèp mi še nakàži nɛ̀ko eli unùci ili prɛ̀unùci
It won’t punish you [yourself] but another. Either your grandchildren or great-grandchildren
57517: da glèdat živa də glèə žìva žàba i t’è koto skočìa
will stare at a live – a live frog.” And when they jumped up –
57520: koto zakàčia da go šìbat po glavɤ̀ po rɤcɛ̀
when they jumped up to punch him on the head and arms –
57522: When the spikes form into ears, [that’s] the crop.
57527: hɤ̀ jəvì sə berek’ètə i sə ràdvət č’e ìmə klàs nə gèrg’uvden
Hah. When the crop appears, all rejoice that there are spikes on St. George’s day.
57533: tvà e trəd’ìcijə də ut’ìdət stupànite də si ubikul’ʌ̀t n’ìvite
That’s the tradition – for the owners to go about the fields
57538: də vìd’ət dəlì sə iskləsìli i rəštɤ̀ stàvəše jèdrə è čuv’èš’ki bòj
to see if the spikes have come out. Rye would grow strong, the height of a man –
57541: jèdru i pòsle sə žʌ̀ne žʌ̀ne sə kəm jùli v’èč’e pu sr’edʌ̀tə
strong. And then it’s reaped. It gets reaped in July, around the middle [of July].
57544: tugàvə sə žʌ̀ne užʌ̀və sə i nə snòpi sə zəvʌ̀rzvə
It gets reaped then. You reap it, and tie it off in sheaves.
57546: snòpite sə kòlkutu mòž’i də gu prifàn’eš’ də mòž də sə nòs’ət
Sheaves are as large as you can grasp, that can be carried.
57548: nəlì nəpràvi sə nə kòš’uv’e kət puisʌ̀hn’e pòsl’e nəpràjət kup’èn’ məž’èt’e
They make it into cruciform when it dries, and then men make it into a pile.
57559: məž’èt’e gu pràjət gul’àm kup’èn’ də fàštə gòre.dòlu
The men make it into a big pile, comprising more or less
57562: kəm stò i dvàisi stò i pedes’ʌ̀ snòpə fàštə
up to a hundred and twenty to a hundred and fifty sheaves.
57566: i sl’ʌ̀t kəto v’èč’e je isɤ̀hnəlu hùbəvu tvà stàvə kəm àvgus m’èsec
After it’s dried nicely – this happens around August –
57569: i sə nəpràvi hərmàn nə nàj ràvnutu m’àstu iskupàvə sə
they make a threshing floor in the most level place. They dig it out,
57572: nəlìvə sə səs vudà də mòž’e pòčvətə də ul’ègne
pour water over it so that the soil can settle,
57575: i sə nəsàždət snòpiti i pòčvəm’e v’èč’e də putp’ìrəme hərmànə
and place the sheaves on it. Then we begin to prop up the threshing floor
57578: də n’e izb’àgət kət mùl’etətə gu tɤ̀pč’ət sìlnu
so [the grain] doesn’t fall off [the sides] when the mules trample it heavily.
57581: səz vìlit’e putp’ìrəme v’èč’e hà uddòlu hà uddòlu də ne sʌ̀ putp’ìt’i
We prop it up with pitchforks from below – right, from below, so it doesn’t settle,
57584: snòpit’e də ne sʌ̀ putp’ìt’ət i kət stàn’e v’èč’i slàmətə
so the sheaves don’t settle. And when it become straw,
57600: If the lamb is a male.
57607: nɤ rogòvit’i slàgət sv’ešt’ìčki pàl’ət sv’ešt’ìčki
They put small candles on its horns. They light little candles.
57614: nə rogàta ɤ pàl’ət sv’išt’ìčki i tugàskə gu kòl’u
On the horns, they light little candles. And then they slaughter it
57618: ukɤ̀št’i gu vrɤ̀štɤt pàk ut cɤ̀rkvəta i gu kòl’im tugàskə pičèmi
at home. They bring it back from the church and we slaughter it, and then roast it.
57622: utstrən’àvəme jə pàk səs vìlit’e jə pretrɤ̀skuvəme utstrən’àvə sə
we move it to the side – we toss it about, again with pitchforks, and push it
57626: nə əd’ìn kùp i ž’ìtutu nəsr’əd’è hərmànə sə səber’è nə kùp
into one pile. And the grain in the middle of the threshing floor is gathered into a pile,
57629: i č’ɛ̀kəm’e veterʌ̀ dùhne li veterʌ̀ udv’àvəme gu̥
and we wait for the wind. When the wind starts to blow, we winnow it.
57634: udv’àvəme gu ž’ìtutu v’èč’e rəštʌ̀ je izl’èznələ isš’uš’ɛ̀vəme i m’èl’əm’e
We winnow the grain: rye that’s already emerged [from winnowing], dry it, and grind it
57638: v’èč’e nə fud’enìcətə ìməhm’e pròsti fudenìci̥ səs kàmək sə vərt’ì
at the mill. We had simple mills [here]: a stone that revolves
57641: vudɤ̀tə gu kàrə v’àtərni n’èməš’e tùkə s vudʌ̀
[and is] driven by water. We didn’t have [the kind] with wind. Here it was with water.
57649: ugotvìli jèden’e pìen’e i turcìtȉ če dòjdu na zgòvor
they prepared food and drink, since the Turks were coming for the agreement.
57655: došlì turcìtȉ na zgòvor dogdè onì jèli i pìli turcìtȉ u sòbu
The Turks came [to conclude] the agreement. And while the Turks ate and drank inside,
57659: onì si nàdvor sìčko prigotvìli da izbègaju i kato
outside they ( = her people) were preparing everything so as to escape. And when –
57669: napìli se turcìtȉ kàču nevèstutu i màjka baštà u karùcutu
The Turks, [by now quite] drunk, hoisted the bride and her parents into the carriage.
57673: dogdè onì tùj da se opet a drùgi ostàli
And by the time they got –   The others stayed
57678: ta obnodèli kɤ̀štutu səs tekvòj i zapalìli
and messed around with the house, and then set it on fire.
57683: dogdè onì da se opòvnu ednò izgorèlo ednò utèklo
By the time they came to their senses, some were burnt and some escaped.
57691: minùli kùla tàm prez grànicu i utèkli
They’d gotten past Kula, and escaped across the border there.
57693: i dvɛ̀te nemì ne mòe prikàzvat tòj se fanà za glavɤ̀ta
both of them mute, they couldn’t talk – he grabbed his head
57698: ta ìmeto ta tòj sìčku mi kazùje ànta i kn’ìgu
That name, well it’s Anta [who] tells me all this. A book –
57700: i vìka vɛ̀rno dɛ̀do pòmoš ne mòe ti dàm nìšto ut bòga
and said, “That’s right.” “Grandpa, I can’t help you. I can’t give you anything from God.”
57707: tìa sə gledàle gledàle sa i netì tovà mòe prodùma
They looked and looked [at him], and neither could the one speak
57710: kn’ige e napisàl ne znàm kvò kadà če dòjdeš
books, he’s written books, [but] I don’t know what [about]. “When will you come,”
57712: netì onovà i tòj si gi zavède tovà beše
nor the other. So he took them away, and that was the end.
57720: [How did you work in the old days?]
57723: bùlkɤ šə dod’ tɤ̀z vèčer i ut’ìduwa è tùkɤ dun’èsuɤ bùlkɤtɤ
the bride will come this evening.” So they came and brought the bride,
57724: kàk sme rabotìli poràsvame po golɛ̀ški trɤgnàme da ràbotim po kɤ̀rɤ
How did we work? We grew up ill-clothed. We went off to work in the fields.
57729: i ut tàm im’ɤmi bùlkɤ d’è sètn’e gu užèniwmi ul’azə u zɤvòdɤ
and from then we’ve got a bride! We married him off, he went to work in the factory
57734: t’à u kɤncilàrijətȁ ràpt’eše i ràwutta mi punɤpr’èdnə
and she worked in an office, [which meant] things started going really well for me.
57739: kɤt n’àmə urìs znàjɤt n’àmɤ urìs šɤ kùpɤt
They [in her office] know when there won’t be rice, so they buy it [for me];
57745: kɤt n’àɤ wòl’uw znàjɤt či dvèčərə š sɤ vɤ̀rnɤt tùkɤ nɤ jàdini
they know when there won’t be oil, so when they come in the evening for supper
57750: šɤ kùpɤt šɤ duncɤ̀t às ud m’èn’e pàtki̥t’ȅ dɤ pusrèšnɤ t
they’ll have bought some and brought it. My side [of the bargain] is to look after the geese,
57754: uc’ète dɤ pusrèšnɤ dɤ gi skàrɤm i kɤt ìmɤt b’èbi
bring in the sheep and take them out. And when they have a baby,
57758: nɤ.l’c’è sɤm vèk’e àz dɤ gu gl’èdɤm
well, here I am ready and waiting to look after it [for them].
57761: i tɤ̀j sètn’e bùlkɤtɤ rud’ì i gu tùrivɤ dònkɤ
So eventually the bride then did have a child, and they named it Donka.
57767: i du dn’èz dn’èšen jèpten’ mi j snɤxɤ̀ ɤmɤ ìmɤm jɤ
And to this day she’s my daughter-in-law, I have her
57773: ama dɤržìm dvà vòla i i dvɛ̀ kràvi i čètiri bìvale
But we had two oxen, and – and two cows, and four water buffalo.
57775: zɤ mòjtɤ nɤ cànku ni gù kàzvɤm kòlkut mi j mɤ̀kɤtɤ
for my very own. I never tell Tsanko how many troubles I have,
57778: nɤ nèjɤ si iskàzvɤm mɤ̀kɤtɤ i tɤ̀j
she’s the one I tell my troubles to. So there it is.
57781: i trì čètiri kòn’a ìmame edin kòn’ ždrebèc [cough] gulɛ̀m
And three or four horses. One of the horses we had [was] a big [cough] stallion,
57787: pḁ às mnògo se raspràvaj sɤs nègu nòsej se na kon’ète
and I had a lot to do with him. I spent time with the horses,
57792: pasɛ̀h gi glèdajme gi [cough] na pojànata ni e tàm dèto
I pastured them. We looked after them [cough]. [It was] to our meadow, where
57795: igràa orò àz žɤ gu zàveda na vòda go zàveda
they danced the round-dance, [that] I took him to water him. I took him
57799: na vòda [cough] a pa tòj potskàča pràvo nagòre sa plàši od mùzikata
to water him [cough], but he jumped straight up in the air – he was frightened by the music.
57804: From Dryanovets – the village of Dryanovets.
57807: sigà sɤm nɤ dividisè i dv’è
57813: da si žìva i zdràva kàk si prekàrala dètstvutu
Long life and health[ to you]! How did you spend your childhood?
57816: mòjtu d’ètstvu ni b’èši mnògu v’ès’ɤlu nu nɤ̀l’ kɤt sɤm zdràva
My childhood was not very happy. But at least I had my health,
57821: kɤt ìmɤm bɤštà aku nìmɤm màjkɤ š’ɤ ìmɤm bɤštà
I had a father. If I had no mother [at least] I had a father.
57824: aku nìmɤm bɤštà š’ ìmɤm bràte sè sɤ mɤ zɤštitàvɤli
And when I didn’t have a father I had brothers. They were always protecting me.
57826: tugà pɤk s’igà bɤ̀rzəmi zə zbòrɤ
[That was] then. But now we all hurry to the village celebration …
57835: em’i inò vr’èmi kàk də t’i kàɤ xùbuu b’èše
Well, in the old days – how can I tell you? It was nice.
57839: na pòpə ostàv’axte li mu ut
Did you leave the priest some of –
57843: na pòpə ostàv'axte li mu ot pèčenoto
Did you leave the priest some of the roast?
57855: jà sam si vɤrzàla sindžìrɤ səm gu zàvela na rɤkɤ̀tɤ si̥
I had tied my hand to the chain I was leading him by
57861: da ne opùšta kòn’a i tìja mi vìkat òrɤtɤ ut stɤrnɤ̀
so the horse wouldn’t get loose. And these folk called out to me from the side,
57864: ma marìjo ma puštì tòo kòn ma puštì tòo kòn
“Hey Maria, let go of that horse! Hey! Let go of the horse!”
57868: às vìkam kà še go pùšta tòj mi e stegnà: rɤkɤ̀tḁ
I said, “How can I let him go? He’s fastened tight to my hand!”
57873: pristɤ̀pi edìn čovèk tàm lèko lèko go fanà otkopčà mi rɤkɤ̀ta
A man came up and carefully caught him, and undid my hand
57878: puštì kòn’a tòj pobɛ̀gna otidè si baštà mi izlɛ̀zi [cough]
and let the horse go. It ran off, it got away. My father came out, [cough]
57882: tòj mu raspràva kəkvò sam napràila tòj vìka bè màma mu
and he (this man) told him what I had done. He said, “Well damn it all!
57886: abè puštì go koto skàča kòn’a puštì go še ta prebìe
Let the horse go if it jumps! Let it go! It’ll batter you –
57889: še ta povlečè da ta prebìe da ma prebìe ko štè
it’ll drag you along and batter you up.” “Ah, let it batter me, what of it!”
57890: àjde trɤgnàjme po kɤ̀rɤ ràbutim [cough] dòəme si vèčer
So we went off to the fields to work [cough], we come home in the evening,
57897: màjka mi prigòtvila jàden’e nalè abe nie  de kato decà slòbodno
mother had made me something to eat. Well, we were kids! Free and light.
57902: sàkame da igràeme še izlɛ̀eme i da poigràeme
We wanted to play. “We’re going out to play!”
57906: t’à ni vìka jàlate si počìvajte zaràn pà ši ìdite
She said to us, “Come in and rest, tomorrow you’ll go out again [to work].”
57919: žɤ̀nim kupàame mamùle bèrim bòp sìčko kvòto ìma
We did reaping, we hoed the corn, we picked beans. Everything there was,
57924: kòjtu ìmə wòfce hòdeš’è nə màndrə nəlì utìdət nə màndrə nàj nəpr’èt
Whoever has sheep would go to the dairy farm. When they go [there] they first
57928: nə zdòj də si rəspredel’ɤ̀t ut kòlku òfce kəkvò mòže də pulùči
deal with the milking, so as to figure out who gets how much milk from how many sheep.
57931: i kət sə ə upredel’ìlo vìkəhə gu v’edrà kòlku v’edrà
Аnd when they’ve determined – they called [the amount] a “pail” – how many “pails”
57935: mòže də z’ème nəprìm’er n’àkuj ìmə p’ʌ̟̀t n’àkuj d’ès’ət
each can get; for instance some have five, and some have ten –
57939: i kət ìde si zɤ̀me d’èsettu v’edrà də kàžeme
and when you go to get [your] ten pails, let’s say,
57943: izbɤ̀rkət si gu pàk tàm vəv burìlu sə bɤ̀rkə
they churn it for you right there. It gets churned in a churn,
57948: i sə iskàruvə màslutu ə uš’m’èrət ə si gu utsìpuvət ud’èlnu
and butter comes out, as well as “ushmer”, which they pour out separately.
57951: tòj je ud nàj hùbəvutu pr’àsnu ml’àku uš’m’èr’
The ushmer (mixed soft cheese, flour, milk) you get from fresh milk is best of all.
57954: dàž’e i nə decàtə pràvehə pìl’etə də sə ràdvət ud uš’m’èr’
They even made "chickens" out of ushmer to please the children.
57960: upredel’ɤ̀d gu kətu pìl’ence i vɤ̀gəlč’e mu slòž’ət zə uč’ìnku [laughter]
They shape it [in the form] of a chick, and put charcoal bits for little eyes, [laughter]
57964: i decàtə sə ràdvəhə či ud màndrə pìl’e sə dun’èli [laughter]
and children were happy that they brought them chickens from the dairy farm! [laughter]
57965: [What did you do before the Lenten fasts?]
57968: kugàtu sə zəguv’àvə zə velìgden nə pùs gu vìkəme zàguv’èznite
When we would prepare for Easter, for [what] we call the fast, [for] Shrovetide,
57976: i tugàvə ni vɤ̀rzuvəhə həlvɤ̀ i jàjcə svər’èni vɤ̀ržət n’ì nə məzònə
at that time they would tie up halva and boiled eggs for us – they tie it onto the ring
57980: d’èt sə bilì l’ùl’kite nə decàtə nə təvànə nə bàdəmətə
where the children’s cradles were attached. On the ceiling, on a plastered [beam]
57985: ìmə məzòn ž’èl’eznu vɤ̀ržəd gu tàm i zəl’ùškət nì gu
there’s an iron ring, and they tie it there, and cause it to swing for us.
57989: i nìe decàtə sə ràdvəme č’e š’e se làckəme gu vìkəm’e
And we kids were happy because we could, as we called it, jump up for it.
57993: làckəm’è se kòjtu fàne jəc’ètu zə n’ègu e həlvʌ̀tə
We [all] jumped for it, and the halva went to whoever caught the egg.
58001: visì nə kəndàp nə kəndàb gu vʌ̀ržət i n’è sə ràdvəm’e
It hangs on a string of hemp. They tie into onto the hemp string and we take delight
58003: č’e sə zəvərt’àlu unuvà i decàtə də gu fànət
in how that thing spins around [and in the fact that] children can grasp for it,
58006: də mu sə pàdne jəjc’è də əd’è i həlvɤ̀
[each one trying to] win the egg so he can eat the halva.
58009: pò vɤ̀zrəsnite č’ɛ̀kət nəlì mlàdit’e də dòdət də sə pruštàvət
The older adults wait for the younger ones to come to ask forgiveness [since]
58015: tu̥và e d’èn’ zə pruštàvəne zə c’àlə gud’ìnə nòs’ət həlvʌ̀ i rəkìjə
this is the day of forgiving for the entire year. [The younger ones] bring halva and brandy
58024: dud’è ìməše bɑ̀ba ìməše sičko mɑ̀ndžə nəgòtvi nəjədèm sɛ sədìm
So long as granny was alive we had it all. She made food, we ate our fill, we’d sit –
58028: n’àkuj pɛ̀t sə skɑ̀rəme n’àkuj pɛ̀t sə sm’ɛ̀jme
sometimes we argued, sometimes we laughed …
58033: … [but] things went on fine. Now I’m alone.
58040: f sɛ̀butə gi ber’àhme ama kət ìməše bɑ̀bə i s’ɛ̀ehme mamùli
We picked it on Saturday. Well, when granny was alive we also planted corn.
58048: sigà nè məmùli s’ɛ̀ja nè lòze kupàja səmìčək nìčtu nèmə
Now I neither plant corn, nor dig the vineyard. I’m alone. There’s nothing.
58050: prɛ̀snə sə sìčku nèmə nìkuj tùkə
Everything’s scattered [to the winds]. There’s nobody here.
58059: mnògu tèškə ràbuta sɑ̀m də ustɑ̀ne čuvèk də žuv’ɛ̀e səs mnògu hòrə
It’s very hard to be alone. [It’s fine if] a person lives with many other people,
58061: ə də ustàne nə stàri gudìni səmìčək ə
but to be alone in later life –
58073: kàktu vìždəte səmìčək slɑ̀gəm səmìčək dìgəm ku nəm’ɛ̀r’ə jàm
As you see, I’m alone. I set the table alone, I clear it alone, if I find something I eat it,
58077: ku ne nəm’ɛ̀r’ə glɑ̀den l’àgəm glɑ̀den stɑ̀vəm i tɛ̀j
if I don’t find [anything] I go to bed hungry, get up hungry – and there it is.
58082: kalùger nalì kalùger mu e stàroto ìme
Kaluger! Wasn’t Kaluger its former name?
58094: e tekà e kalùger sɤ̀k i otišlì tùrci da sàkaju devòk’u
That’s right, it’s Kaluger now. So these Turks went off to ask a girl’s hand [in marriage].
58096: dobrè ama baštàta ne dàva da ìde za tùrčina
Fine, but her father wasn’t going to let [that happen] – that she could marry a Turk.
58101: da ti ga četìm mòre àj manì mi se òdglav
[he says] “so I can read them to you?” “Get out,” [I answer], “leave me alone.
58107: How many children did I have?
58115: ìməwh dèved decà ubàč’ə sìčkit’ɛ̋ purɑ̀snəə i sə ižžèniə
I had nine children. But then they all grew up, and went off to get married,
58121: i ɑ̀s ustɑ̀nəh səmìčək i bɑ̀bətə umr’à i sinɛ̀ mɑ̀l’kijə
and I was left alone. Then granny (= wife) died, and the younger son
58124: kòjtu t’ɛ̀j də mə glèdə i tòj umr’à
who was going to look after me  – he died too.
58128: i i ɑ̀s seɑ̀ tɛ̀j vərt’ɛ̀ sɛ sàm
And now here I am, carrying on alone.
58134: bəštɑ̀ mi umr’àl f tùrskətə vujnɛ̀
My father – they say he died in the Balkan wars,
58138: and I was left an orphan,
58146: a m ud mɑ̀lək sə fɑ̀nəh nə ràbutə ràbutih pràvih strùvəh purɑ̀snəh
so I had to start work very young. I worked, made [things], did [things], grew up –
58151: užènijmi sə səzdàdəhme mnògu hòrə živ’àhme dò segà
[Then] we got married, made a big family, and lived together – until now.
58152: [Didn’t you say you  had a brother?]
58159: tòj kəkvò də kɑ̀žə zə nègu tòj ə b’ɛ̀še pò gul’ɑ̀m
He – what can I say about him? He was older [than me]
58162: but he was – he was lame.
58168: əmə kol m’ène sə nìi gu glèdəhme kàktu glèdəhme decàtə
He [stayed] by me. We looked after him. Just as we looked after [all] the children,
58173: i n’ègu tɛ̀j gl’èdəhmi dù gd’è pučìne
that’s how we look after him too. All up until he died.
58181: səs svìn’i mɑ̀lku mɑ̀lku svini vɛ̀dehme səs t’ɑ̀h sə zənimɑ̀vəše tòj
[Yes,] with the pigs a bit. We were breeding pigs a bit, and that was his job.
58185: əmə ɑ̀z gu glèdəh kɤktu glèdəwh decàtə i nègu tɛ̀j glèdəh
But I looked after him. Just as I looked after [all] the children, so too with him –
58193: What [do you have] that you could read to me?”
58197: punɤčàlo àz b’àx nɤ čètri bràte idnɤ̀ sistrɤ̀
Basically I was a [single] sister to four brothers.
58200: nògu sɤ bòr’lɤ màjkɤ zɤ mumìči čàk p’ètɤtɤ sɤm às vèk’i
My mother really fought [to have] a girl. I was the fifth child already,
58206: i uvɤžàwɤ mɤ obàče tɤ̀j sa pulùči či mòjtɤ màjkɤ umr’à
and she had high regard for me. But it so happened that my mother died
58213: tòčnu nɤ g’urg’òwd’en b’èšə̥ bilà brèminnɤ às ni gù znàjew tùj n’èštu
on St. George’s Day, the very day. She’d been pregnant, but I didn’t know that.
58219: i t’à m kàzwɤ dònke zimì bràtči̥tu̥ si id’ì nɤ l’ùl’kata
And she said to me, “Donka, take your small brother and go to the swing.”
58225: pɤk vìždɤm jɤ t’à sɤ krivì tù nɤ jurgàntȅ sɤ putpìrɤ
But I saw that she was bent over, leaning now on the bedquilts,
58230: nɤ dulàpu tɤ̀j nɤ òdɤro tù tɤkò ɤmɤ ni sɤ̀m rɤzbìrɤlɤ
now on the cupboard, now on the bed, and such. But I had not understood
58235: če e br’èmennɤ i zɤrɤt tùj mɤ j pràt’ilɤ dɤ igràjɤ
that she was pregnant, and that’s why they sent me off to play
58239: tɤ̀j də i àz zimàw d’it’ètu utìduw do nɤ l’ùl’kata
like that. So I took the child and went to the swing.
58246: i č’ùwɤm l’ùl’kata d’ètu u t’àw xòra bùl’a bòjka sɤ kàza
The people whose swing it was – Auntie Boyka was her name –
58256: vìknə bùlkə ivànke bùl’ə stòjkə ìmɤ mumìči̥ kətu kàə
called out, “Auntie Ivanka! Auntie Stoyka has a girl!” And when she said
58261: bùljə stòjkə ìmɤ mumìči às zimàw d’it’ètu uluìw gu zɤ rɤkɤ̀tɤ
“Auntie Stoyka has a girl”, I took the child, I grabbed it by the hand –
58267: tò bèš’ č’ètr’i gudìni màlku ud mèn’e àz b’àw na wòs’ɤm gudìni
it was four years younger than me (I was eight years old) -
58272: i utìduw si̥ u dmà vìždɤm tàt’ɤ plàč’e č’ùwim mumìč’i
аnd I went home. I saw Dad crying. I’d heard there was a girl,
58276: mɤ ni vìždəm b’èb’i i uluvìw tàt’ɤ tɤ̀j zɤ kul’àntȕ
but I didn’t see a baby. And I grabbed Dad by the knee.
58282: We finished [what we set out to do].
58286: svṛšìme ràbutu màlko nu svṛšìmo nèka nèkakvu
We finished a bit of it. We finished something [anyway].
58304: Look what this girl here wrote out!
58313: momèvo m zàpisa štòto mòže da pìše ako ne mòžeše da pìše
This girl has recorded [things] because she can write. If she couldn’t have written –
58320: à dà ama nò čùje tèje dùme i pisùje
Yes, but it’s because she [can] hear [and understand] the words that she writes them!
58323: ko ne sɤ̀m oratìla kvò če pìše
If I hadn’t been talking what could she write?
58328: nìšto à slùšaj ženà ne znàm ne znàm ž
Nothing. Listen, now. Your wife – I don’t know, I don’t know [whether]
58345: i tòj plàč’e i às ə vɤz n’ègu dùmɤm tàt’e ɤm
He was crying and I was with him. I said, “Dad, but
58349: d’è im b’è b’è b’èb’itu bà d’è j b’èb’itu
where is the ba- ba- the baby? Where is the baby?”
58351: pɤk tòj ìkə èj tàm i u tòs mum’ènt mòjtɤ màjkɤ
And he said “It’s over there.” And at that moment my mother –
58358: t’à sɤ jɤ l’ɤkùvɤlɤ izgl’èždɤ vànɤ tɤ̀j dɤ r’ìtɤ
she’d been taking medicines, it seemed – started to kick,
58365: dɤ tɤkòžd’ɤ p’ànɤ pu ustàtɤ i i àz zɤplàkuw i izl’àzuw
to thrash about and foam at the mouth, and I burst into tears and went out.
58369: ubàd’uwa sɤ nɤ l’èkɤr ud grɤdɤ̀ jìd’i l’èkɤr
They called for a doctor and a doctor came from town –
58372: ɤmɤ s kɤkò j duš’ɤ̀l n’i znàm i l’èkɤrɤ kàza
I don’t know with what [conveyance] he came – and the doctor said,
58378: v’èdnàga kàrɤjte u grɤdɤ̀ i sɤz dv’è kɤrùci nɤ̀tə nɤ č’ìč’uwi
“Get her to town immediately!” So [we took] two carriages, one from оne uncle
58383: inɤ̀tɤ nɤ svàka i nìj upr’àgvɤmi vulòwi tugìs i zɤkàrɤ jə
and one from another. We harnessed the oxen and started off with her.
58389: i t’à pu pɤ̀tištɤ kàzala nɤ tàt’ɤ gèrge ìskɤm vudɤ̀
And along the way she said to Dad, “Georgi, I want water.”
58392: tòj rikɤ̀l či nìj ni zimàxmi i màjkɤ tàm izdɤ̀xvɤ
He said that we hadn’t brought any, and mother gave up the ghost right there.
58397: i vɤ̀rnɤ jɤ nɤdzàt’ i nɤ sɤmìjɤ dèn’ nɤ gerg’òwden’ bèš’e tùj
He brought her back on the very day that was St. George’s Day.
58402: òrɤtɤ sɤ ràdvɤt nɤ àganca nɤ tùj unùj pɤ̀k nɤ nàs zl’è
People were celebrating, [roasting] lambs, this and and that, but for us bad [times]
58409: dòdi i prebràwme sɤ bràtt’ȅ fsìčkit’ȅ kɤt zɤròviwmi màjkə prɤbràwmi sɤ
had come. And all the brothers came together when we buried mother.
58415: i vɤ̀rnɤm sɤ n’àmɤ kàk dɤ nɤpràjmi č’ùdim sɤ udd’è dɤ jɤ svɤ̀rdz’im
We came back (what else could we do?) and we wondered – how will we manage?
58425: n’àmɤ kòj dɤ m’ès’i̥ n’àmɤ kòj dɤ p’irè n’àmɤ kòj dɤ šetɤ
There’s nobody to make bread, nobody to do the washing, nobody to do housework.
58430: puč’ùdi sɤ tàt’i puč’ùdi sɤ kàza nɤ bàč’a nɤ nàj gul’ɛ̀mije
Dad puzzled about it, and then said to my brother, to the oldest one –
58434: tòj b’èše s’id’imnàjsi usimnàjsi gudìš’in tàt’i m kàza
he was seventeen or eighteen – Dad said to him,
58438: dàj dɤ tɤ už’ènim t’èb’e dɤ zɤ̀mnimi inò mumìči
“Let’s marry you off! Let’s get [ourselves] a girl.
58440: sàmu dɤ p’ir’è t’èz d’ecà i dɤ im gòtvi sàmu ukɤ̀šti
She only [needs] to do the washing for these kids and to cook for them in the house.
58448: pɤk tɤ̀kɤn prèžba drùgtȕ š’ɤ dàvɤmi nɤ xòrɤtɤ srištu pɤrì
Weaving, spinning, all the other [tasks] – we’ll hire people to do those.”
58451: bàču̥ sɤ ubɤ̀rnɤ či mu kàzɤ tàt’e àš š’ɤ t’ dàm
My brother turned to him and said, “Dad – I’m going to give you
58453: drùgij akɤ̀l pɤ̀k tì si trìjsi i šèz gudìš’in
different advice. You’re thirty-six years old.”
58463: t’ì b’èž ž’inà ni mòž’iš dɤ skàrɤš tòz živòt
“You can’t make it through [the rest] of your life without a woman.
58466: i tr’àva tì də sə užèniš štòt àz aku sɤ ožènɤ
You’re the one that needs to marry, because if I get married [first]
58467: tì n’e mòež dɤ gu iskàrə tòjtə ž’inà š’ɤ zɤvàri mòjta
you won’t be able to handle it. Your wife will encounter mine [already here]:
58470: mòjtɤ sɤ č’i̥t’è svikɤ̀rvɤ v’èke pə tòjtɤ ž’inà šɤ bɤ̀di snɤxɤ̀
Mine will consider herself the mother-in-law and yours will be the daughter-in-law,
58481: i šɤ stàvɤ kɤwgɤ̀ miždu nàs pò dubr’è t’ì sɤ užənì
and this will give rise to quarrels between us. Much better you get married
58485: pò nɤprèt’ às pò nɤpud’èr’e s’è š’ɤ nɤm’èrim inɤ̀ n’àkɤkvɤ
first, and I after that. Somehow we’ll find one [for you].”
58489: i òd’ɤ tàt’e srùvɤ pràj nɤmèri inɤ̀ žinìčkɤ ud dubròškɤtɤ mɤɤlɤ̀
So Dad went off, looked about, found a woman from the Dobroshkata neighborhood,
58501: When did the wedding begin, from morning [on]?
58507: sùtrin ràno li u kòj dèn u kòj dɤ̀n pòčva
In the morning early? On what day? What day did it begin?
58509: è pa u nedèl’u pòčvaše ama
Well, it began on Sunday, but –
58514: u nedèl’u ot sùbotu ot pètɤk pòčne vèči i
On Sunday, well on Saturday, well actually on Friday. And –
58518: u nedèl’u tàm na cṛ̀kvu se ìde venčàvka i takà
On Sunday they go to church for the [church] ceremony, and that’s that.
58520: What do they do on Friday?
58526: e pa u pètɤk nalì pòčnu da zbìraju màse tovà onovà
Well, on Friday they start to gather together tables, this and that.
58534: e pa se mèseše se lèp se mèsi pa se kòl’u òvce
Of course there was baking: they made bread, they slaughtered sheep
58537: za jèden’e pa dà spràvl’aju se dà
for the meal. Yes, they manage [somehow]. Yes.
58540: i nèkakɤf speciàlen lèp li se mèseše
Did they make any special sort of bread?
58542: e pa kò što se jedè kvò speciàlen
Just the kind you eat. What do you mean, “special”?
58544: nè e takɤ̀f za za pra kato za pràznik
Nothing like the sort – like on a holiday?
58552: dun’èse əmə nìj smi pèt’ pɤk inìčku d’èt ɤ màjkɤ gu ustàj
and brought [her here]. There’s five of us kids, and the tiny one that mother had left –
58558: tò n’ikàk ni zɤsùkɤ ud màjkɤ zimà go innà nàštɤ rudnìnɤ
it had never suckled from its mother. One of our relatives had taken it
58562: n’ègu dèn’ kɤt zèvɤt dɤ jɤ kɤt jɤ kàrɤwɤ u bòlnictȁ
