the same day when they took [mother] to drive her to the hospital,
58567: dàduɤ màlku òwču ml’àku i d’èt’tȕ t’à tàm gu dɤ gu
they provided a bit of sheep’s milk. And the child – she was there to look –
58571: gl’e dɤ gu glèdɤ u t’àw dukɤt sɤ zɤvɤ̀rni tàt’i
to look after it at their place until Dad came back.
58577: i sètn’e i tùj d’èt’i mɤn’ènku i nìj p’èt’ drùgi pò gul’èmi
So then there was this tiny child and the five of us other bigger ones,
58581: n’àmɤ nɤkɤd’è nɤmèr’ tàt’i inɤ̀ ženà dod’ t’à dòd’i z dv’è
nowhere to go. So Dad found a woman, she came with two [kids],
58585: [That means] there got to be seven of you.
58594: i jnò mɤ̀n’enku òs’ɤm ubàč’ɤ nìj gulèmtȅ pàk pò sɤ rɤzbìrɤwmi
And one [more] little one [made] eight. And although we older ones got on better,
58600: ɤmɤ pò mlàdtȅ n’è sluč’ì sɤ nèintȕ mumìč’i mnòu kìs’ɤlu
not so the younger ones. It turned out that her girl was very ill-tempered.
58605: nàšij edìnɤ č’i̥tvɤ̀rtijɤ ni bràt i trètijɤ tòj
And one of ours, the fourth [oldest] brother – [No,] he [was] the third [oldest] –
58608: i tòj tɤkɤ̀w kìsɤl tè sɤ bìewɤ mnògu
he was similarly ill-tempered.  And the two of them fought a lot.
58614: i trùdnu ž’uwòt nɤpràiwmi trùdnu ž’uwòt ubàč’ɤ t’à pàk izl’èzi geròj
We had a hard life. It was a hard life, but that one ended up a hero:
58617: mnògo dubrà màjkɤ b’èši i sigà kɤt plàčɤ kɤt kàža màmo
she was a very good mother. And even now, when I cry, when I say “Mom!”,
58625: s’àkɤš sè nɤ n’èjɤ vìkɤm sigà kàk sɤm l’ègnɤlɤ às si l’àgɤm
she’s the one I call out to. Now when I’m in bed, when I lie down to sleep,
58628: sɤnùwɤm s’è n’èjɤ mòjtɤ màjkɤ nè jə vìždɤm nìkɤde
she’s the one I dream of. I don’t see my own mother anywhere [any more].
58633: nàj golèmijɤ òd’ɤ sɤs màstur:tȅ dɤ ràbuti dɤ pràj kɤ̀šti̥ d’ulgèrin b’èš’i̥
The oldest was apprenticed to work as a mason, to build houses.
58646: da ti vi da vìdim ženùtu ču vi kàem da te popàri
but if I see your wife, I’ll tell her to blanch you!
58655: dà zaštò tùja bràdu i onà bradàta da ti e cṛnà
Why this beard here? At least if that beard were black ...
58667: govorì za tovà kakvò te pìta nè mu govorì na čovèka
Talk about the things he’s asking you! Don’t tell the man
58672: i ìma kafènce da ti sìpem li
There’s more coffee, may I pour you some?
58678: ne sì li faštàla dèn na
Didn’t you grab the day for…
58688: vɤž a a lovìli sme ngi dèn elì na gèrg’ovden
You see,  we “caught” a saint’s day for them – either St. George’s day,
58693: elì na ə spàsovden elì na svetì ilìja elì na drùgi dène
or the Savior’s day, or St. Elias’s day, or some other days,
58697: So what does it matter that it’s reddish?
58699: e pa ne tì e ùbava
Well, it doesn’t look nice on you.
58702: e pa odèka te znàm zaštò
Well, how should I know why not?
58707: ùzni pa ju takòva sɤz bojù
You should go and – you know, with dye.
58710: Look how much she’s writing down!
58712: da ne sɤ̀m ženà ta sɤz bojù à
Well, I’m not a woman, to go off messing with [hair] dye and such
58718: e žène gi bojadìsuju vìš kosàta ti čèrna
Women do dye their hair. See, your hair is black!
58730: à ednì mùžje mustàci si bri onòdu
Ah, but some men – their mustaches – They do something –
58731: ama mùžje mùžje ne gì bujadìsat
But men – men don’t dye [their hair].
58733: The ones – the ones among us that are old.
58736: e pa stàrite ridžì mu mustàci i onì ùznu bojù i
OK, the old ones. If one [such] has a reddish mustaches, they take dye and –
58747: Koleda – do you have such a holiday?
58766: na božìč pràimo takà mužjète dṛvà sečù kodžà
For Christmas we do the following. The men cut a great deal of wood
58773: ìdat na dṛvnìk nalì dokàraju se dṛvà mlògo
They go to the chopping block. They’ve brought in a lot of wood.
58777: e pa dṛvà dlɤ̀ga è iz gorùtu gòre s volòve dokàraju
Well, wood! Long pieces, from the forest up there. They bring them in using oxen.
58790: e nò bìl takà si kož kɤ̀f si edèm edèmo lèp
It was like – The kind we eat, the [same] bread we eat
58791: is the kind that we make for weddings.
58807: Or [ones] from here, around the neighborhood.
58811: ut po məlàta tìja se kàzuju standženìi
[Guests] from around the neighborhood – they’re called the Standzhens.
58813: ama kàg gi kànexte na svàdba
And how did you invite them to the wedding?
58819: e pa na svàdba momčè ùzne o kaničè s rakìju
Well [to invite people] to a wedding, a boy takes a flask of brandy,
58826: i tupàn lùpa lùpa barjàk nakìten i ulàzu u komšìjutu
and with decorated flag and banging of the drum they go in to a neighbor’s yard.
58831: komšìjata gi posrètne i uvedè gi vɤ̀tre podadè im
The neighbor receives them, brings them inside and serves them
58836: čàšku rakìju ili kavènce ispijù àjde če otìdu
a glass of brandy or cup of coffee. They drink it up and leave,
58839: pa u drugòtoga tàm kànu tekà sa
and on to the next [neighbor], and there they invite [him] the same way.
58841: kàzvat li mu nèšto kakvò kàzvat
Do they say something to him? What do they say?
58844: è kvò kàzvat e pa nìšto ne ka òn gi kàni momčèta
What do they say? Nothing much. He invites them: "Hey, boys –
58850: zapovèajte na svàdbu i onì odgovàraju dobrè če dòjdemo
Come to the wedding!” And they answer “OK, we’ll come”.
58855: i dòjdu omèsu pogàču omèsu bànicu šìše rakìju i àjde
So they come. They bake quickbread, banitsa, a bottle of brandy – and we’re off!
58856: And we’re off to the wedding.
58863: i s nevèstata gi dàri namètne rìzu na gṛbìnu i onì tùru
And the bride gifts them. She puts a shirt on [each one’s] back, and they put it
58867: na gṛbìnu edù i pijù [laughter] kvò kazùjem ovakà
on their backs. They eat, and drink [laughter]. Whatever I say, that’s how it is.
58873: najedù se dòjde vrème da se izlàzi nevèsta da se venčàva
They eat their fill; [then] it’s time for the bride to leave for the [church] ceremony.
58879: svìrk’e svìru naròt tàm i u cṛ̀kvu se ulèzne pòp venčàva
Flutes play, [many] people there. They enter the church, the priest marries [them],
58882: izlèzne se iz cṛ̀kvu òro i i takà
she comes out of the church, there’s dancing – and that’s it.
58887: ɤhɤ̀ i pòsle is cɤ̀rkvu kato izlèznat kɤdè otìvat
Uh huh. And after they leave the church, where do they go?
58892: nə pò vʌ̀zrəsnit’e i fàštə rəkɤ̀tə celùvə pruštàvəj kəkvòtu sm’e zgreš’ìli
to the older ones. They kiss their hands, [saying] “Forgive us whatever we have sinned.”
58895: i stàrijə ti kàž’e pròstu də ti je
And the old one says to you, “You are forgiven.”
58903: ətə sə ə pràvilə pu təkʌ̀f nàčin če eli gi zəgud’àvəxə
[Wed]dings were done in such a way that they either betrothed [the pair],
58906: eli nəpràvu bùlkətə jə vòd’exə tòčnu f svàdbenijə d’èn
or they brought the bride straight [to her new home] on the very wedding day,
58910: i sìčki sə ràdvət če si zìmət mumà zə fkʌ̀šti
and everyone rejoiced that a maiden was being taken into the house.
58911: [So how exactly did they put on weddings?]
58916: nàj nəpr’èt utìdət tə z’ʌ̀mət kumʌ̀ səs mùzikətə səs ə
First they go to get the godfather, with music and with –
58919: sìč’kit’e svədbàri ut’ìvət də z’èmət kumʌ̀ i utàm ut’ìvət u bùlkətə
all the wedding guests go to get the godfather, and from there they go to the bride’s,
58923: də jə z’ʌ̀mət səs c’àlətə svàdbə v’ɛ̀č’e bùlkətə č’ɛ̀kə
to get her, along with all the wedding party. The bride is waiting
58930: də i slòžət vàlu kumàtə š’e slòž’i neprem’ènu vàlutu
for them to put her veil on. Without fail, the godmother will put [on her] a veil
58936: səz zel’èni drɤ̀š’č’ìci ut sl’ìvə ut ə n’èštu kuètu e ruždelìvu
adorned with green stems of plum, or of something fruit-bearing,
58938: zə də bɤ̀de i bùlkətə ruždelìvə
so that the bride also will be fertile.
58940: So she’ll give birth more often.
58941: [And how do they prepare the newlyweds?]
58947: l’èznət kumɤ̀t s’àdə ə də sə puč’èrpi səs məž’èt’e sìč’ki s’àdət
They come in, the godfather sits down, all the men sit there and toast each other.
58951: ə ž’en’ìt’e l’ubopìtsvət də vìd’əd bùlkətə kàk š’e i stuì vàlutu
while the women are curious to see the bride, and how the veil looks on her,
58954: e kumàtə kàk š’e jə nəprài kàk um’èe nəpràv’ət jə bùlkətə
whether the godmother has done it as she should. They prepare the bride
58962: i hi pùsne perd’èncetu utpr’ètkə vàlutu perd’è gu vìkəhme
and let fall the “curtain” in front of her. We called the veil a “curtain”,
58969: n’è e vàlu kəktu s’egà perd’ètu hi e pùsnətu pred lìcetu
not a veil, like now. [So] the curtain is dropped in front of her face
58972: i šte jə utkrìjət v’èč’e kugàtu də jə venc’ɛ̀və pòpət
and she’ll be uncovered only when the priest "crowns" her –
58976: e pa is cṛkvu ka izlèzne i prìmer otìva si pòsle
Well, when she comes out of the church, for instance, after that she goes
58979: takà i tàm kakvò se prài kàk ja posrèštat
Right, and what do they do there? How do they greet her (the bride) ?
58984: e pa tàm a posrèšta svekṛ̀vata nalì ti kazà odèva
Well, the mother-in-law greets her. I told you [that] before, didn’t I?
58993: posrèšta dvè stòvni vi dadè nèvu na nevèstutu
She greets her with two jugs. She gives [them] to her – to the bride,
58998: i vi slòži pṛ̀sti tùka ko jà što sɤm turìla
and puts her fingers here like I [just] put mine [here],
59002: i uvedè vɤ̀tre i pòsle ju pràti dòle na klàdenɤc
and leads her inside. After that she sends her down to the well
59005: na vòdu də donesè vòdu nevèsta
to [get] water, for the bride to bring water [from the well].
59007: What does she carry it in?
59009: And the flutes are playing – tralala tralala ...
59018: naròt se zbìra napùni se stàe èden’e pìen’e kòj dokude òče
... people gather, the rooms fill up. There’s eating and drinking as long as anyone wants,
59021: i kòj pàdne kòj [laughter] se napìje i takà
until anyone falls down [laughter] or gets drunk. And that’s all.
59025: I can’t tell you any more [than that].
59035: ama tì zaštò se ne obrìčiš
59039: Well, your wife – I’m going to –
59041: I don’t have – I don’t have the money.
59047: tugàvə sə venč’ɛ̀vəhə pòpə š’e e utkrìje ə pìtə jə
back then they got married in church with crowns. The priest lifts the veil and asks her
59050: ubìč’əš’ li gu tì mumč’ètu i mumč’ètu š’e pìtət
“Do you love this young man?” And the young man will be asked
59055: ubìč’əš’ li jə tàjə mumà də sə venč’ɛ̀ete səs n’èe
“Do you love this young woman? Do you wish to be joined with her in marriage?”
59058: i kàzvət č’e se ubìčət i pòsl’e gi vòd’ət nə
And they say that they love one another. After that they lead them to [the spot]
59063: pr’et š’ɛ̀renijə kàmək vəf čɤ̀rkvətə s’àkə čɤ̀rkvə ìmə š’ɛ̀ren kàmək
in front of the multicolored stone in the church – each church has a colored stone –
59067: pret š’ɛ̀renijə kàmək gi venč’ɛ̀vət tàm v’èč’e kumʌ̀ him dərž’ì sv’èš’t’i
and "crown" them in marriage before the multicolored stone. The godfather holds candles
59071: nə rəmenàtə də im sv’èt’i i t’è pòpə im č’et’è
at their shoulders to illuminate them, and the priest reads to them [about]
59078: kàk tr’àvə də ž’iv’èjəd də sə pugàdət rəzùmnu də rəzmìsl’uvət sìčkutu
how they must live, [that] they should behave reasonably and ponder everything,
59081: n’è də bɤ̀rzət i də uvəž’ɛ̀vət rudìtelite nàj vàžnu
not to hurry, and that the most important is to respect their parents.
59083: kòlko pràznici ìma mòo go narečèš nàj màlko na trì pràznici
however many there are. You have to pick at least three holidays [for candidates].
59087: i l’ùdete i zə i tekà ngi lòvime ə ìma st stolèta
And people – [the way] we “catch” for them is – there are these stools
59089: s trì kràka ako ste stàri
with three legs; if you’re old [enough] …
59091: “You’ve got no money, you’ve got no money!”  You’ve got money,
59095: no kàeš tovà e mòda kà si tekà
you’re just saying it’s the fashion to be like this.
59098: i mlàdite takà me arèsvat pòveče
The young ones like me better like this.
59100: e pa nalì si se oženìl
59103: arèkše li te onà takà pa jà če te n
Does she like you that way? Well, I’ll [do] you –
59107: jà da e takà jà ču ga nòčem popàrim
If I were [in her place] I’d come in the night [with boiling water] and blanch him!
59111: sɤs vrèla vodà ču ga popàrim ma takà nèma ga tṛpìm
I’d blanch him up with boiling water. I wouldn’t stand for him this way.
59117: i tì takà ako vìdiš priàtelɤ si takà
And you too. If you see your boyfriend like this,
59122: zèmi ta ga nèče li se brìči s vòdu lùp
if he doesn’t want to shave, just pour [hot] water on him!
59125: Take him and blanch him good!
59136: i kogàto se kogàto se rodì detè kakvò se pràvi
And when – and when a child is born, what do you do?
59140: At the time of birth. That is –
59144: kvò se prài ròdi se detèto pa ga povìju
What do they do?  The child is born, then they wrap it up,
59149: pa lègne màk’a mu na krèvet i n’èga ga tùru
and its mother lies down on the bed and they put it
59156: na krevàta i go ràni dòi ga ako ìma mlèko
on the bed and she feeds it. She nurses it. If she has milk
59160: če ga dòi ako nèma zabṛ̀kaju od brašɤ̀nce màlko
she’ll nurse it, if not they mix up a little from flour
59167: dodèka kùpu tekòva mlèčno bràšno i takà i ga rànu
until they [manage to] buy powdered milk, and that’s it. They feed it.
59174: mòre svè razbìraš ta me zamlàtuješ
Of course you follow it all, you’re just pestering me!
59178: i [laughter] i gi dokàraju tùka u dvòrɤt i na kòledu sečù dṛvà
And [laughter] and they bring [the wood] into the yard here and cut it up for Christmas.
59179: What do they cut [the wood pieces] on?
59183: na trùp ednò dṛ̀vo takà debelò i sɤs sek’ìra
On [some] tree-trunk. A piece of wood this thick – you [cut it] with a “sekira” (ax),
59186: bràdva li se òka sek’ìra li nìe sek’ìra
or a “bradva” (ax), as they say. We call it “sekira”,
59200: i sečù dṛvà nasečù pùno a ženète mèsu omèsu pogàču
They cut the wood – a lot of it. And the women do baking. They make “pogacha” –
59206: kolačè kolačèta omèsu za decà koledarì ìma pa doòdu
Buns – they make little buns for the children. There are carolers, who come by –
59215: s kvasɤ̀c se omèsi kolačèta pa drùgo drùgo pogačè sa tùri
You put leavening into the buns, but for a small “pogacha” it’s different. You put –
59220: pàj pogàča pa u n’èga se tùri parà
again for the “pogacha” – in those, you put in pieces of money.
59224: dvàese stotìnk’i li su dèset li se tùru tàm
They put in [a coin] of twenty stotinki, or ten, or whatever.
59233: à decà vìe ni obṛkàste ne znàm
Huh? Kids, you confused us. I don’t know …
59239: i se mèsi mèsi tùri se paràta i se mèsi mèsi
And you knead it. You put in money and knead it, knead it,
59247: ako ste vidèle na tìja st obṛ̀neme stolèto i krakàta
… if you’ve seen them – we turn the stool over [so that] the legs –
59250: umèsi se ùbavo i pòsle se pogàčata tùri da uzbùne
knead it up to be nice, and then put the “pogacha” aside to puff up.
59251: trìte kràka sa nagòre i tùrame tùrat sveštìci
all three legs are pointed upwards, and we put – they put little candles [on each leg]
59253: i gi zapàlime i detèto kojò fàne tavà na tòo
and light them. And whichever candle the child grabs for, that’s the one
59255: i go narečème dnèska gèrg’ovden zaràn
that we name as his saint’s day.	 Today St. George’s day, tomorrow –
59263: i ka uzbùne podìgne i se tùri ta se pečè
And when it puffs up, and rises, you put it in to bake.
59269: u crèpn’utu u crèpn’u dà i se ispečè pogàčata
In a baking dish. Yes, in a baking dish. And the “pogacha” bakes up.
59273: i nà i zel’ànik se omèsi kolačèta takà se omèsu
And you make banitsa with greens, and they make up little buns,
59277: pa se takà prekṛ̀stu i takvàja dečìca
and they make the sign of the cross over them and then children –
59281: the boys, but not the girls, come.
59288: nàjutro dòjdu im se dadè po ednò kolačènce i onì pojù kolèdo kolèdo
They come in the morning. They’re given a bun each and they sing “Koledu, Koledu”.
59290: kàk im kazùju na na tìja na na
How do they call them, these –
59297: dà koledarì na momčètata tàmo momìčeta pa làzarica ka dòjde
Yes, koledari. That’s the boys. And the girls are “Lazar-singers”. When they come …
59306: a odgòre na lèbɤ kakvò pràexte na lèbɤ
But on the tops of the bread: what did you do on the bread,
59309: [and] on – on the buns, on the buns?
59313: na kolàčɤ tùramo takà rečèmo pa tṛlù
On the bun, we put – I guess you call it – “tŭrlu” (sheep-pen [object form]).
59328: à ta natùramo takà po ednò takòva ot testòto
And we put one of these on each bun, it’s made out of dough.
59340: tòpčeta tòpčeta dà àjde kràvu ka onòdemo nalì muzè tavà vìmeto
Little balls, little balls, Yes. So the cow when we, you know, milk this – the udder.
59343: e pa na kolačètata natùramo takà i ga
Well, on the buns! We put [them] on there and –
59345: ì takà i na tòo dèn mu pràvime pìtka nèšto i
And on that day we make him a round bread, or something, and –
59346: a kogà se ə lòvi takà svetèc kogà detèto
When do you do this “catching of the saint”? When a child
59348: nèšto e bilò bòlno li ə
59349: ako mu nè e dobrè detèto
If things aren’t going well for the child,
59352: ili sè takà e slàbičko nèšto
or if it’s doing poorly, if something is [not right]
59354: ne tè i trèbva tovà takà pràat
and you can’t [do] what’s needed, that’s what they do.
59367: Do you do it this way?
59383: əmhəm tovà odgòre ozgòre na lèbɤt
Um hm. So this [goes] on top, on top of the bread.
59385: Uh huh. And they feed it. And so.
59388: i ga rànu i porastè detè i stàne mùš
And they feed it, and the child grows, and it becomes a man.
59392: Either a girl or a man.
59397: znàči ako se rodì žènsko dète mùš vìkate
So that means that if a female child is born you call it a man.
59401: ako se rodì žènsko detè vìkate devòk’a se rodì
If a female child is born you say that a girl is born.
59403: e pa devòk’a razbìra se momìče
Well yes, a girl of course. A girl.
59405: And if it’s a – a little boy?
59409: ama na momčèto se pò ràduju
But people are happier when a boy [is born].
59412: è tè takà ràduju se pò na momčèto
Well that’s how it is. People are happier [when it’s] a boy.
59421: a onò devòjčeto pò slùša i màk’utu i baštùtu
A girl obeys her father and mother more.
59428: a tò kato izlìza detèto kato izlìza nalì ìma a vrɤ̀f takàva
So then – when the child comes out, when it emerges, isn’t there sort of a cord?
59432: They cut it, and that’s all.
59439: They bandage it up a bit and that’s the end.
59441: i kràj a pòsle kakvò izlìza zàedno sɤz detèto
And that’s the end. But after that, what comes out together with the child?
59442: kàk mu se vìka na tovà dèto ìzliza s
How do you call that? The child comes out with –
59446: plodnìca li bèše takòva nèkakvo bèše
Afterbirth, was it? Something like that.
59452: plodnìcata izlèze i se isčìsti i
The afterbirth comes out, and it’s cleaned off and –
59453: It’s cleaned off, and you’re done.
59461: tɤ̀j i nèšto slàgaha li m i f kakvò go zavìvaxte detèto
So. And did they put something on [the child]? What did you wrap up the child in?
59466: They wrap it up in diapers.
59469: Well yes. [Like I told you] before.
59475: tùka se povìje u pèlenk’e ottùka ottùka tàm takà ga povìju
So they wrap him up in diapers from here to here, they wrap it
59478: i ga slòžu na krevàta i màk’ata do n’èga lègne
and put it on the bed, and the mother lies next to it.
59487: na lèbɤt i kojà e mesìl’a e mesìl’a sa onà mèsi samò
On the bread. And whichever woman is the head kneader, only she kneads
59493: a drugìte pa naòkolo i sìčko na krùgɤt krùg
[these breads], and the others all stand around. It all goes on the [one] breadboard.
59501: tì vidè tàm sàmo tovà e màlko i natùra svè na n’èga
You saw one there, except it was small. So she puts everything on it.
59506: postèl’e se nàzeme slàma ozgòre se tùri čèrga
They spread straw on the floor, and put a rug on top of it [and everyone] –
59514: i kòlko dùši su tè nasèdaju takà stàrci svèkɤr svekɤ̀rva
however many people there are – sit there. Elders, father-in-law, mother-in-law,
59523: momčè tìja onìja i nasèdaju i kojà e mesìl’ata mesìs the h
son, and so on – they sit there. And the one who’s the head kneader – she made
59526: i takà i pòsle kato poràsne sɤs kakvò go oblìčaxa
That’s that. And later, when it grows, how did they dress it –
59528: kato zème da da da xòdi vèče
when it starts to walk already?
59533: e pa sɤz drèšk’e ako e momìče èj takà
Well, with children’s clothes! If it’s a girl, then like this,
59535: and if it’s a boy, like that.
59539: In the fashion of old-time dress?
59541: po stàrata nosìja sɤs kakvò gi oblìčaxa
According to [the fashion of] old-time clothing, how did they dress them?
59546: e pa tùka ednò vrème kogà tì si bilà detè
Well, like here in the old days, when you were a child.
59547: e pa ka sam jà bilà takà e a pa pòsle
Well, when I was a child, it was just the way it was, otherwise
59549: before my time I don’t know!
59555: e pa i rìza nò nè e golò
Well yes, a shirt, but not just that (= not otherwise naked)!
59561: pantalònče te pantalòni mu obùju rìzu mu oblečù
Pants – they’d dress him in trousers, in a shirt.
59568: ako e studèno pulòverče mu oblečù čoràpci mu obùju
If it’s cold they’d put a little sweater on him, and socks.
59572: àjde ìdi si gràj na pṛzàl’k’u
"Go on, run off and play, sliding down the hill!"
59575: And there’s a lot of sliding places here, [right?]
59579: ot tùka sɤs šajnì ta dòle pràvo u klàdenɤc se pùštaju decà
Kids would swoop on sleds all the way down to the well,
59583: ama onà si stròšu i nòs
but they would also [fall and] break their noses.
59587: natùra u krùgɤt i nesè i slòži na postèl’utu
[the breads] – puts it all on the breadboard, carries it in, and lays it on the cloth.
59589: i ùznu kandìlo kandìlo znàeš li ga kandìlo
And they take a “kandilo” (candle-dish).  Kandilo – do you know what a kandilo is?
59592: No? Well it’s this – an earthenware thing.
59599: pòpɤt ne sì li vidèl pòp sɤs kvò onòde
Haven’t you seen the priest when he does his thing with it?
59600: [I don’t get] what a kandilo is.
59603: pa ne užmìkuj takà e kandìlnica
Well, don’t get in a bother. It’s a “kandilnitsa” (small candle-dish).
59613: ama zeml’àno e pa e napràeno takà ìma dṛ̀ščica
Well, it’s earthenware, and it’s made like – it’s got a handle,
59623: pa decàta ka pàdnu sčùpnu nòsɤt onò kṛ̀v potečè
Well, the kids! When they fall and break their noses, blood would flow.
59625: But they get up and ride [the sleds down] again!
59630: pàj se vòzi a stàrata nosìja kakvà bešè tùka žènskata u sèlo
They ride again. So, what was women’s old-time dress like here in the village?

59928: because nobody pays anything for the wool.

59999: mòži u gradɛ̀ də gu j n’èmalu tùj n’ɛ̀štu

60052: You can’t manage without a “chift”, because –

60334: tùj u rebràta a onò a onò pozapṛlò màlko
here in the ribs. But this – this [new fabric] blocked it a bit
60337: pa ta pod mìškutu ta rèko no vòlɤt me obòde
in the armpit. So I said, “Well, the ox gored me.”
60340: baštà mi ùze vìlu želèznu pa idè pa si volà bì
And my father took an iron pitchfork and beat the ox.
60344: bì bì svè ga skḷ̀če ama ga nè je čuvàl mlògo
He beat it [so bad] that he nearly pulverized it.  But he didn’t keep it long
60345: prodàde ga no rèče da te ubìe no decà pràčam
[after that]; he sold it. “By God,” he said, “I’ve got children!”
60347: And that’s it. That’s how we do it.
60348: a pa ednò vrème kàk ə kàk bèše kɤ̀k ə
What was it like in the olden days?  How did you, um,
60351: strìžeš ə ovcàta i kəkvò pràviš səs vɤ̀lnata
shear a sheep, and what did you do with the wool?
60358: i jə̟ pàrim i pràimi čeìs às kò ti kàəm kətù
We scald it, and make it up into dowry [items]. What can I tell you?
60365: nəpràim zàsefki tr’àə də ìmə jurgàn’ tàm pu dèsi̥t jurgàn’ə tɤ̀j jà
[When] you make a betrothal you have to have quilts, about ten quilts layered in a pile,
60371: i pumiždù pu inɤ̀ vlɤ̀zgəncə slàgəmi tɤ̀j i tì kət ìdiš
and then between each [quilt and the next] one we put a pillow, so when you go [to the new place]
60373: ìmam i dvàma bràk’a no r’èče da vi ubìe
– I have two brothers – and he said, “If [it’s going] to kill you [kids],
60374: za kvò mi e mèn vòl da mi utrèpe detè
why do I need an ox that’s going to kill my child?"
60376: pa ga òn prodàde ama ga dòsta bì
So he sold it, but he beat it a lot [first].
60377: pa tegàj nèma dòktor tùj a màti mi prespàmo
And then there’s no doctor here. So mother and I slept through the night,
60380: pa jutròto ràno no u dòlni.lòm fèršil onà me zavède tàm
and early the next morning she took me to the paramedic in Dolni Lom.
60382: ta me prèmi prèvṛza me tàm səz bìnt dòktor
The doctor there cleaned [the wound] and tied a bandage on it,
60384: ta mi mìnu nè e me vodìla vèče
and I got over it. She didn’t take me [there] again.
60386: ama patìli smo mučìli smo se sɤ̀ga decà živèju
But we suffered, we had a hard time. Children nowadays live [much better].
60390: òn nè e li kròtək vòlət
60392: a bè òn nè e bòl nìkada òn bìl kròtɤk
Well, yes, he’d never gored anyone before, he was [generally] mild-tempered.
60395: pər’ìt’ȅ ne st’ìgət zə l’àbə ni st’ìgət zə mlògu rɑ̀pti
Money doesn’t cover bread, it doesn’t cover lots of things;
60399: and there will be [many more things] that it won’t cover.
60404: za mlògu ràpti zə pìen’i n’èma st’ìgət za drèhi za ubùhk’i
Many more things. It won’t cover drinking, or clothes, or shoes –
60407: vərxu pòdə n’àmə da štò də sə slòži
There won’t be anything to put on the “pod” (shelf area in village house).
60413: pòd n’èmə ìmə tòj še e nə gərbɛ̀  t’
There won’t be any “pod” (shelf) – the shelf will be on your back!
60424: pòt še e nə gərbɛ̀ t pək tugàs təč’ɛ̀hme dìgəhme h pòdə
Your “pod” will be on your back. But back then we’d weave, and put [it] in the “pod”.
60432: vɛ̀lnə mlògu təč’èm pr’id’èm i tə kupùəhm’e pəmùk’ təč’ɛ̀hm’e si rìzɨ
Lots of wool! We weave, and spin, and we’d buy cotton and weave ourselves shirts.
60437: pamùč’eni rìzɨ səgà kupùvəme plàtnu i təč’èm ə šìjimi si rìza
Cotton shirts. Now we buy the fabric and weave – sew ourselves shirts.
60440: hɑjà ut kùp’eno plàtnu pək tugàs gu təč’ɛ̀hme tùj plàtno
Yes, from purchased fabric. But back then we wove the fabric,
60445: i si šìjm’i rìzɨ nə d’əcàtə nə məž’è nə sìnkit’ɛ̏
and we sewed shirts for the children, for the men, for everyone.
60457: stənɛ̀ šə təč’èš əko istəč’èš’ nà sìč’kutu tùj səgà hùstə
You weave [on] the loom, and when you weave a full piece, you see – now here’s a skirt.
60460: [But] back then we called it “vrahan” (red-checked woolen skirt).
60465: ut vɛ̀lnə gu prid’èm i gu bujd’ìsvam’e i gu tač’èm
We spin [the thread] from wool, and [then] we dye it, and [then] we weave it.
60469: i ne sɛ̀ izrabòt’və skòru kəd’à š’a spìš
And it doesn’t get accomplished quickly. When will you [have time to] sleep?
60476: za skòro kòj ti kàza a napràvo tà
Whoever told you [it would be done] quickly? Truly, it’s …
60485: tò nìštu àtli ni sɤ̀ iskɤ̀swə amə gul’àmə gul’àmə əməlògijә̟ e bilò
there’s no way these bed coverings will get worn out. But it was a big, big job.
60491: l’àbə š’e gu m’ɛ̀sim š’e gu pič’èm š’e jed’èm
You’ll knead the bread, you’ll bake it, you’ll eat [it] –
60495: But the bread we ate [tasted] sweet.
60498: sridžèš jə tɤ̀s ufcɤ̀ vərìš udɤ̀ i zəlìvəš ut’ɤ̀vəš
You shear this sheep, you boil water and pour it [into pots], you go
60503: nə ču̥šmɤ̀tə də jə pirèš sə wrɤ̀štəš pək jə č’èpkəš
to the well to wash the wool, then you go back, then you card it –
60506: you dry it and then you card it.
60517: You card it with your hand!
60518: slàdək l’àp jed’ɛ̀hm’e nìj si pruizv’ed’èm žìtutu vìkəm’ə hrənɛ̀tə čìstə
We ate sweet bread. We produce our own wheat, and [can] call our food pure.
60521: i utìvəš pək ìməše dəràci ìmə dəràci
Or you go and – there used to be carders, there are carders –
60524: sigà u àjdemìr ìmə zɤ̀mət ti nə inò k’ilò idìn i pidis’è
there’s one in Aydemir now, they charge one lev fifty per kilo
60526: də ti e də ti e wlàči sə kàzvə
to do this for you, as they say, to comb it.
60531: a tì səs rəkɤ̀tə si e pàriš si e pir’èš
But if you do it by hand, you scald it, wash it,
60535: i e č’èpkəš i ut’ùvəš də e izwlàčiš i s’ètne prid’èš pək
and card it, and go to comb it out. Then you spin it –
60537: na fùrkə slàgəmi tɤ̀j na fùrkətə
on a distaff. We put it like this on the distaff.
60539: Here, [this is where] we put the distaff.
60542: And how do you do [the spinning]?
60546: prɤ̀st’:i tìj nàšti prɤ̀sti znàjət vèk’i də pridɤ̀t
... [with your] fingers. These fingers of ours know how to do spinning already.
60550: znàjət də pridɤ̀t nàšt’e prɤ̀sti a če tì
[Yes,] our fingers know how to spin. And if you –
60551: And have you done [a lot of] spinning?
60553: pràef be kɤ̀k də n sɤ̀m pràila
I did, of course. How could I not have done [spinning] ...
60559: sàmu bùlkata dàvə nə sv’èkaru nə sikùrvata
[But] only the bride gives gifts to her father-in-law and mother-in-law
60562: na zɤ̀lvata bùlkata ud bùlkata sa dàwa
and to her sister-in-law. The bride – it’s from the bride that [gifts] are given,
60566: na krɤ̀sni̥cə̥ta na krɤ̀snicə dàwət èm jèm bùlkata dàwə jèm zèt’o
to the godmother – [well,] they [both] gift the godmother. The bride gives and [so does] the groom,
60571: nə nə krɤ̀snicə̥tȁ ama nə svədbàr:t’ȅ drùgit’ȅ sə strənìčni
to the godmother. But the other wedding guests are outsiders.
60572: čim às səm užèn’ələ dicà kət vìkət
... since I’ve married off children, as they say.
60575: də ti kàžə dvənàjs kilà vɤ̀lnə səm gùdilə
Let me tell you, I put twelve kilos of wool [into the dowry]
60578: nə inɤ̀tə unùkə i nə drùgətə dvənàjs kilà
of one granddaughter, and twelve kilos [into that] of the other.
60582: s’àkoj si ko kòlku̥tu̥ xòrə sə si kànili tòlkuz gi
Each –  As many people as they have invited, that’s how much –
60588: prɤ̀j sm’ètkə kilìm də im pràә̟ zə
Do the math – I [had] to make them kilims [to cover all] ...
60592: ... the floors in [apartments] in the apartment complexes.
60599: tòlkuz gi takòzwəš gi kal gi kəlèsvəš tòlkuz gi ə dàwəš dàr
that’s how much you do. You give as many gifts as the guests you invite.
60602: pɤk ə bùlkata dàwa vèči dərì krɤ̀snik krɤ̀snica sv’èkɤr
So the bride gives – she’s already gifted her godfather, godmother, father-in-law,
60605: sikɤ̀rva tàm nə zèt’u bəštàtə màjkata ša darìš
mother-in-law – And then you’ll give gifts to the groom’s father and mother,
60609: tòj kət ìmə bràt’e ìma sèstri nèguit’ȅ blìski
his brothers and sisters, if he has [any].  His close [friends] –
60612: tàm vèke kət sà razber’ɤ̟̀t sa rəzberɤ̀t
Already they are deciding, they decide
60615: kəkò kəkò še dər’èt kòj kàk i tàm več’ si̥ prikàzwət
what – what [gifts] will be given and by whom – already they’re discussing all this.
60618: Anyway, that’s how it used to be in the old days.
60619: a kòlko vrème meždu svàdbata i
So what was the interval between the wedding – [I mean]
60620: meždu godèža i svàdbata kòlko vrème minàva
between the engagement and the wedding? How much time went by?
60624: zəvìsi̥ kàk se rəzberɤ̀t kàktu̥ se rəzberɤ̀t àko də rišɤ̟̀t
It depends what they agreed on – whatever they agreed [to do]. If they decided
60626: dvè sèdmici àko də àko àko də rišɤ̟̀t še e trì sèdmici
it would be two weeks, if – if they decided it would be three weeks,
60628: te inɤ̀ inɤ̀tə sèdmicə pràjət zàsefki̥ zàsefki na jergèn’u
then [during] one of these weeks they do the betrothal ritual. The one for the groom
60633: u pèto u p’ètok še nəpràət zàsefki̥t’ȅ sə nə jergèn’u
[is] on – They do the betrothal rituals for the groom on Friday.
60638: às è às n’è às ə gu nəpràəm gu nòs’ә̟
Yes, I [did]. Well I didn’t make everything [myself]. I took it –
60641: there was this factory, you know –
60645: u grədɤ̀ dàəmi purɤ̀čkə əmə plàštəm gu
in town. We give them an order, and pay for it ...
60650: t’è kət mi gu prərəbòt’ət amə i sn’e təkàli u s’èlu
... after they make it up for me. But [yes], we did our own weaving in the village.
60653: àu čem sə zbìrəmi pràjim inò ə mu kàzvəme n’ègu wr’ème
Oh my, [what we did!] We’d get together and make a – we call it at that time
60659: s trɤ̀stuwt’ȅ udbìrəš utpud’ère drùgə u stənɤ̀ təčèš
[weaving] with reeds. You pick [reeds left behind] after others, and weave on the loom.
60662: s’à kò znàet tès mlàtt’ȅ nìštu ne znàet n’àmə stàn n’àmə nìštu
What do these young people know now? They know nothing! No looms, no nothing.
60666: səgà is sklàduətɛ̏ kad’ɛ̀ jɛ nòsət kad’ɛ̀ ɛ bɛ̀rkət prep pəpəràtija
Now they take it through [various] warehouses, where they mix it with – with chemicals
60675: tàm ja rɛ̀s’et ot žiwòtni də ni dəd’è
and they spray it so it won’t let animals (= insects) [come near] –
60681: [cough] gəgrìci li kəkòtu i rɛ̀s’et žitàta s’è sɤs utròwə i tɤ̀j
[cough] weevils or whatever, and they spray the wheat. With all this poisonous stuff.
60683: ne znàm s kəkò gi rɛ̀s’ət əmà
I don’t know what they spray it with but –
60687: l’àba hìč’ nè e dubɛ̀r səgɑ̀ pri tùj pulužèn’e
Bread is no good at all now under such circumstances.
60689: ne znàm s kəkò gi rɛ̀s’ət əmà às kəto b’àx detè ìməše ə
I don’t know what they spray it with but when I was a child, there were
60691: ama tegàj štò tekà od mùe li se zàvardi
[I don’t know] what happened this time, maybe he tried to ward off flies?
60692: òn me nè e bòl da rečèš
You [couldn’t really] say that he [actually] gored me, …
60693: da ne sɤ̀ bilì ot tìja
Maybe it was some of these …
60698: štṛk štṛklìci li kvì sa tìe mùi ə tìja mùje
… gad- gadflies? What kind of flies are those? These flies [that] –
60703: e nò od mùjete hà no tèj tèj
Well yes, it was flies, right. Those – the ones
60705: that sting oxen and make them run about, that ...
60707: štò àpu pa tegàj òn me nè e
... that bite them. And so he didn’t –
60708: nè e me bòl sàl si tekà kìmnu i jà òp
he didn’t really gore me. He just gave a shake and there I was,
60709: ta na rodzìte mu kvò stànu štò stànu štò me
up on his horns. What happened, how it happened, how I – ?
60710: òstai me prenèse me vodà golemà bèše onà se čùdeše
He left me [there], he took me across; there was a lot of water. And she wondered,
60713: tàj drugàrkata mi àna se zovè onà se čùdeše kvò
this friend of mine – her name is Anna – she wondered how
60716: če mìnemo vodùtu če valèlo dɤ̀š pa vodàta golemà
we were going to cross the water, because it had rained and the water was high.
60718: a òn me prenèse prez vodùtu i me òstai
So he carried me through the water and left me [there].
60719: nè e me bòl nè e me nìšto kako čovèk
He didn’t gore me, he didn’t [do] anything. Like a person [would],
60721: gràbnu i me òstai ama ama kakò me zamašìl
he [just] picked me up and dropped me. But while he was waving me about
60724: òn si me pod mìškutu utrepàl pod ednùtu ta
he struck me under one of my arms.  And so –
60726: i drùgo kvò čùvašete nàj mnògo
[What] other [animals did you have]? What did you used to tend the most?
60765: zàsefki zàsefkit’ȅ b’ù̟əwə tɤ̀j pu̥kànvə n’àkuj drùgu mumìči
The betrothal – the betrothal rituals went like this: they invite some other girl,
60769: ìma sviràč svir’ə̟t igrajə̟t na ergèn’u
there are musicians [who] play, they dance – for the groom.
60773: kət minà kət utìvət òšte kət sə pòčvət zàsefkit’ȅ zɤ̀mɤt ə
When they – when they go, already at the beginning of the betrothal ritual they take –
60776: kət ìdat u jergèn’u utàd’ət na mumàta slòžili swərìli
After they go to the groom they go to the bride. [There’s been a lot of] cooking
60782: ut ə ušàf ut kumpòt ut sùh sùhi suh imìš
of ritual food from dried fruit and compote, dry –  dried fruit mixture,
60783: bòp ušà ə ut suh imìš kumpòt i z’èli i ti slàgət
beans, dried fruit mixture, compote, cabbage. And they put it out for you,
60788: i ub’ukàl’ət səs bos’ìl’ək i slàgət s’àkoi si zɤ̀mɤ
and decorate [it all] with basil. They put it out and everyone takes some.
60790: tàm zàsefki̥t’ȅ kuìtu ut’ùət u zèt’u si zɤ̀mət tàm
[That’s] the betrothal there. Those who go to the groom’s take
60793: ut suwrɤ̀tə ut màsata i pòsle mitɤ̀t səz busìlek
from the low table – from the table. Afterwards they sweep up, using basil leaves.
60797: sètn’ə sə wrɤ̀štət i swiràči swìr’ə̟t sə utàd’ət èči c’àla
Then they go back, and the musicians play, they go on – it all [goes on]
60801: du kɤ̀sno tàm swìr’ə̟t igràət u jergèn’o gu brɤ̀snət ìma
until really late there. They play and dance at the groom’s, and they shave him. There are
60804: otàd’ət da go brɤ̀snət tàm prijàt’el’:t’ȅ ut nèguit’ȅ kəd gu brɤ̀snət
friends of his [who] go there to shave him.  While they shave him,
60808: svi ə sviràči̥ ìma də ti svìr’ə̟t kət tə ubrɤ̀snət
there are musicians to to play for you while they shave you.
60810: tì si zgudenìk i šə ti svìr’ə̟t ìma sviràči̥ šə ti svìr’ə̟t
You’re the engaged one, and they’ll play for you: the musicians will play for you.
60812: ama tvà na svàdbata ili na zàsefkite
But is that for the wedding or for the betrothal?
60813: tùj nə zàsefki̥t’ȅ dèt tə brɤ̀snət tì ə u četvɤ̀rtək tə brɤ̀snət
This is at the betrothal, where they shave you. You – they shave you on Thursday.
60816: u p’ètək u p’ètək u rànu i večertɤ̀ zàsefki̥t’ȅ tùj tugàə
On Friday – on Friday early and in the evening the betrothal. That’s – [it’s] then
60818: tuj sə šə gu brɤ̀snət sètn’e pɤ̀k u nid’èl’e u sɤ̀buta
that they’ll shave him. And then on Sunday, [I mean] on Saturday –
60821: u sɤ̀buta sə pə b’ùwa na mumàta zàsefki̥t’ȅ kət lèziš na mumàta
on Saturday there’s the betrothal at the bride’s, when you go into the bride’s house
60825: mumàta kakòt ìma tàm dàr:tu kəkòtu e šìla kòtu e plèli
[to see] the gifts the bride has [made], what she has sewn, what she has knitted.
60834: tàm čəršèvi kuvertùri šìti pl’èteni kwòt ìmə slòženu enɤ̀ vɤ̀rva
Sheets, bedding, [all sorts of handwork] sewn and knitted, [all] displayed on a line
60840: i àku̥ s aku̥ sə nəlòži i dvè vɤ̀rvi šə slòžəd
And if – if they need to, they put up two lines [to display it].
60844: zəvìsi kəkvòtu ìmə dàritu tàm kəkvòtu si e šèla slòženu tɤj
It depends what sorts of gifts there are there. Whatever she has sewn [is] displayed there.
60849: i prem’àtwəš prem’àtət prem’àtvəd gu i katu dòdət zàs’əfkitȅ
You toss it [up on the line], they toss it [there], and when the betrothal [time] comes,
60853: utòr:nu e tàm u nèja stàja sìčki̥t’ȅ xòra utàd’ət tàm
her room is opened up, and everybody goes there.
60859: ìmə svir’àči igràjə̟t pèjə̟t wlìzət ukɤ̀šti də gl’èdət
There’s live music, dancing, singing, They go into the house to see
60863: kəkò ìmə jurgàn:t’ȅ ìmə ràkli idnò vr’ème ni bèše kat segà
what  [there is]. There are quilts, there are chests, [and all]. Back then it wasn’t like now,
60867: garderòpi ama ràkla sɤndɤ̀k tɤ̀j kàktu̥ e
[when you have] wardrobes. [You had] rather a chest, something like a trunk.
60869: tàm i dàže ìməmi tàm àz ìməm tàm enɤ̀ edìn sɤndɤ̀k
We even have some over there. I have a trunk like that over there.
60875: gòre bil’à i màmin:tȅ sɤd’ɤ̀t màmin:tȁ bàbin:tȁ sɤd’ɤ̀t si
Mother’s are upstairs. Mother’s, and grandmother’s, are stored up there,
60879: sè gi drɤ̀šɤt prəbìrəm tɤ̀j prədin’à
they always pull [stuff out], and I rearrange it – all the spinning,
60882: inò drùgu sə prəbìrə i zàsefkit’ȅ tɤ̀j
various sorts things get put back there. And that’s the betrothal.
60889: imàla màti dèvet sìna i ednù dɤ̀šteru màjka imàla dèvet sìna
A mother had nine sons and one daughter. A mother had nine sons ...
60896: i ednà dɤšterà bàbo sne i i  izlèznete
... and one daughter. Ah, you young ones – come out [of the sun and over]
60900: na sènk’u mamo da vi ne stàne lòše
into the shade, my dears, so you don’t get ill [from the heat].
60904: às səm dobrè seà še si polèem glavàta i səm dobrè
I’m OK, I’ll just pour a bit of water over my head, and I’ll be fine.
60907: a i nàj mladìjɤt sìn g’u oženìl dɤšterùtu
And her youngest son saw the daughter married off,
60911: past nine villages [and] into the tenth.
60917: i se naùči cṛnà čùma izmorìla devetè sìna
And the black plague learned [of them] and killed off [all] nine sons.
60925: òn pomognùl ta se oženìla dalèk i
He [had] helped [his sister, and] she married [and moved] far away, and –
60931: i matertàta g’u svè kle ga e klèla
and her mother cursed– cursed him constantly.
60934: i došlà cṛnà čùma izmorìla devetè sìna
And the black plague came and killed the nine sons.
60940: a sestrùtu g’u zovàli petkàno onà prez devetè sèla
And they called the sister Petkana, the one [who’d gone] beyond the nine villages
60944: u desètoto i matertàta čùmata izmorìla svìte
into the tenth. And the mother, the plague [having] killed all [of them]
60948: zakopàla devetè gròba ama a dɤšteràta si oženìla
dug [all] nine graves. But the daughter had married [far off]
60952: ama ne doòdi a matertàta si tekà sedèla u sòbutu
so she didn’t come. Thus the mother sat [alone] in her room,
60960: uràsla sòbata sɤs pelìnove sɤs ə burjan’àci i svè klèla tòga làzara
a room [now] overgrown with wormwood and weeds, and kept cursing that Lazar,
60961: štò g’u oženìla dɤšterùtu prez dèvet sèla u desèto
who had seen her daughter married past nine villages to the tenth.
60968: òn edɤn pùt sèdne i se molìl na bòga bòže mìli gòspodi
[As for him] one day he started to pray to God: “Dear God, oh Lord,
60982: na ɤ bɤ̀klicu da ìdem da dovedèm sestrù petkànu na mojù màjku
into a wine jug, so I can go and bring my sister Petkana home to my mother.”
60984: i otìšɤl prez devetè sèla u desètoto i tàmo otìšɤl
And he set off through the nine villages and into the tenth. He went there
60989: uzèl ɤ onà praìla dobredòšlo s n’èga i reklà
and started to –  and she made him welcome and said,
60995: bràtko làzare làzare štò ti rukà na plèsɤn merìše
"Oh Lazar brother of mine, oh Lazar, why does your hand reek of mold?"
61001: a òn izlèzɤl iz gròbɤt bòg ga prestorìl smɤrdèla mu rukà
He’d come out of the grave [of course], God had transformed him, his hand was stinking
61003: na plèsɤn lì e mṛtvɤ̀c a òn òn tegàj g’u kazàl
of mold (he was dead, after all). So he said to her,
61010: sèstro petkàno petkàno mì smo devetè dùše bràk’a
"Petkana Petkana, sister of mine, we were nine brothers,
61014: dèvet smo kɤ̀šti napravìli a na mèn se pàde
and the nine of us built nine houses. And [the job that] fell to me
61018: zeml’ùtu da isvṛ̀l’im zatòj mi rukà na plèsɤn merìše
was to dig out the earth. This is why my hand smells of mold."
61023: òn mrtvɤ̀c stìgli do gròbištata a ottàm kat vɤrvèli
He’s dead, [after all]. They got to the graveyard. On their way there –
61028: òn g’u na kon’àtogo kačìl a ptìčkete pèle
he’d hoisted her up onto his horse – the little birds had been singing:
61035: gdè se e čùlo vidèlo mṛtɤ̀f žìv da òdi
"Where has it ever been seen or heard that a dead man goes about alive?"
61038: onà òdi òdi pa rečè bràtko làzare be la làzare
So they went and went, and she said, "Oh Lazar, Lazar, brother of mine,
61042: štò ptìčkete tekà pèju žìf mṛ̀tɤv da òdi
why do the little birds sing thus: “a dead man goes about alive’?"
61045: a onà na òn g’u rekɤ̀l sèstro petkàno petkàno svèkakvi ptìčki
And he, well, he’d said to her, "Petkana, Petkana, sister of mine, all kinds of birds
61050: razlìčni glasovè znàju i onà se pà ubedìla detèto
have different voices.” And she was reassured. After all, the child
61052: ìde pri màter stìgli do gròbištata òn g’u rekɤ̀l
was going [home] to her mother. They got to the graveyard, [and] he said to her,
61058: sèstro petkàno nà ti mòjɤt pṛ̀sten turì ga na
"Lo sister Petkana, take this my ring, and put it on –
61074: nɤ rùku si kat otìdeš pri màjku pokažì g’u mòjɤt pṛ̀sten
on your finger, and when you see our mother, show this ring of mine to her.
61083: jà če da dòjdem ama da vṛ̀žem kon’àtoga da pasè
I will come along, but [first] I must hobble the horse and put him to pasture,
61084: tìe mušìci dètu prez noštә̀ dèto svèt’ət kàk im vìkate vìe
these little insects that glimmer in the night. How do you call those?
61091: i če da dòjdem po tèbe dòm si da pri sestrùtu̥
then I’ll come after you, home to be – home with my sister".
61092: nè pres noštə̀ kət stàne tɤ̀mno
No, at night, when it gets dark.
61095: otìšɤl i ulèzɤl si u gròbɤt i bɤ̀klicu tàm na kvò prestorìl
He left, and went into his grave, and the wine jug became what it was before.
61098: ulèzne si u gròbɤt a onà išlà išlà i stìgla
He entered his grave, and she went on and on, and arrived
61104: do kɤ̀štata na matertùtu poglèdne dvòri u pelìn uràsli
to her mother’s house. She looked: the yard all overgrown with wormwood!
61109: onà počukàla na vratàta [cough] i pità on əm ə onà
So she knocked on the door [cough] and asked – he, that is she,
61121: … and fly away, then glimmer again.
61126: à e kədè segà ìma svetùl’ki
Ah. And where are there fireflies now?
61130: am nà n’èm ne sɛ̀m vìd’ela
Well – there aren’t –  I haven’t seen [any].
61133: nàj napr’èt ə da kàža li nàj napr’èt ə kugàto beme
Shall I talk first of all, first of all, [about] when we were
61138: mumìčeta òšte štòto às ne b'èx žè̝nena kugàto za vojnɛ̀ta
still young girls – because I wasn’t married yet when the war –
61141: è kogàto stanɛ̀ vojnɛ̀ta tò beše dvanàeseta godìna
When the war – when the war began. That was in [19]12.
61145: bìa sa bɤ̀lgarete i sṛ̀bete i gṛ̀cite bìa tùrcite
The Bulgarians and the Serbs and the Greeks fought – they defeated the Turks.
61149: na tùrskata grànica tàm gi bìa è tə sə vudì vojnɛ̀ta
On the Turkish border, that’s where they beat them. Eh – that was the war.
61152: ne vodì sa mlògo i t’è v’èki koto sa ne znàm
It didn’t last long. And they, since they are – I don’t know.
61155: tò ìmaše p’èsen ta ja pejàa zərət vojnɛ̀ta
[But] there was [this] song that they were singing. [It was] because of the war.
61157: štòto ama ne pòmna kà beše tàm ə načàlnik im
I don’t remember who their commander was,
61159: the one who said to them [in the song]
61163: stàejte bràt’a stàejte i utkrìvəjte ògan
“Stand up, brothers, stand up, and open fire!
61167: ako ə bòk r’èkɤl skòro òdrin še prezè̝mem
If God has ordained it, we shall soon take Edirne,
61176: We shall take him to Sofia,
61179: [and] we will make coffee for him.”
61184: tovà beše ɛ̀ pesentɛ̀ bàa ispèl’e zərət vojnɛ̀ta
That was the song – [the one] they’d sung because of the war.
61187: i pòsle pɤk ə ɛ̀ nal’ì sa bìa pɤk
And then – didn’t they fight again?
61189: da ti kàža za s ə kà sme poprekarvàli
Shall I tell you about how we carried on,
61191: or – or about the other war?
61196: e ə pə nìe bème togìva ne b’ème gol’èmi
Well, at that time we weren’t – we weren’t grown [yet].
61200: ìma:me bràt tòj se kàzvaše gàčo tòj zagìna v dòbrudža
We had a brother, his name was Gacho. He perished in Dobruja,
61203: reklà matertàta vṛnì se vṛnì cṛnà čùmo
Her mother spoke: “Go back, black plague, go back [whence you came]!
61208: dèvet si mi sìna umorìla dɤšterù si nègde ostaìla
You’ve killed my nine sons, and you’ve left my daughter behind somewhere,
61211: a sɤ̀ga ìdeš i mèn da me umòriš onà počukàla
and now you come to kill me as well?" She knocked [again]
61215: i reklà màjko màjko jà sɤm tvòjta dɤšterà petkàna
and said, "Mother, mother, it is I! Your daughter, Petkana!"
61218: onà otvorìla vratàta pa g’u gà g’u pitàla
And so she opened the door and when she asked her,
61222: kòj te ə dɤ̀šte dovède a màjko mìla màjko
"Who brought you here, daughter of mine?" "Ah mother, dear mother,
61225: bràt mi làzar me do na kon’à dovède pa otidè
[it was] my brother Lazar who – he brought me on a horse and then went off
61228: da si vṛ̀že tè ti màjko pṛ̀stenɤt na bràtatoga
to hobble [the horse]. Here, mother, take the ring of my brother.
61229: otidè da si vṛ̀že kon’àtoga u gròbištata i če da dòjde
He has just gone to the cemetery to hobble the horse, and then he’ll come.”
61233: òn ìč i nè e došɤ̀l onà rovàla matertàta i dɤšteràta
But he never did come, never. And the mother wept, and the daughter
61238: tegàj ostàla pri n’ù a onìja òn se skutàl
stayed with her henceforth. As for that other one – well, he hid.
61243: ošɤ̀l si u gròbištata mrɤ mr̀tɤv lì ti kazùem
He went off into the cemetery, a dead man. I told you, didn’t I,
61245: what those little birds were singing?
61251: tovà ga davàu na večerìnku jà sɤm išlà na tùj vèčer
That’s what they performed at the dinner feast. I went [there] that evening.
61277: tòj smo čuvàli magàreta pò nèmaše nèkvo
… that’s what we kept. There weren’t so many donkeys at that time.
61281: sɤ̀ga magàreta zapatìmo sɤ̀ga čùvamo magàreta
Now, we’ve bred [some] donkeys and so now we keep donkeys.
61284: ot kvò stànu stopànstvo svèki magàre [laughter]
Since the state-owned farms came about, everybody [has] donkeys. [laughter]
61286: kràve tekà nèkoj kràve nèkoj volòve čùvaše òvce
And cows. Some people kept cows, some kept oxen, some kept sheep.
61288: pa si tàm è dèda mi səs ofcète tàm
So there was my grandfather with the sheep, [up] there
61290: na košàrata si na livàdutu tṛl’àk pa si ìdemo pri n’ì
at his summer pasture, at the pen in the meadow. And we’d go up to them,
61296: vɤv vojnɛ̀ta kogàto sa bìa pək ə da gònat ə sɤvèckija sajùs
in the war when they were fighting to drive out the Soviet Union.
61298: ne sì vìdelə štòtu dètu rɛ̀sə  i  gi istròv’ehə
You haven’t seen them because they spray [where they were] and they poisoned them.
61305: nəli gonìa e təvà germàncite bàa i bɤ̀lgarite
Weren’t they chasing – those Germans were – and the Bulgarians,
61315: n’èe pək tùj tò ə təkwòs kumɑ̀r’i inò
Well, and there’s also this thing [called] mosquitoes.
61316: [What did you do when you were girls?]
61319: seà za momìčeata li za momìčeata nìe beme momìčeta
[Ah, should I talk] about young girls now? Ah, girls. We were girls
61322: i se zbìra:me na sed’ànka tò sa sa zbìrame na sed’ànka
and we’d get together for a work bee. We’d get together at the work bee,
61327: zbìrame se momčè̝ta momìčeta sedìm ə ràbotim si
boys and girls would get together, we sit and do our work.
61334: momìčeata momčè̝ata sedɛ̀t pàk stànat kato zasvìrat saz gàjda
The girls and the boys sit, and then they get up when the bagpipe starts playing.
61341: svìr’a saz gàjda stàneme igrèem i se razvalì sed’ànkata
The bagpipe plays, we get up and we dance. And then the work bee breaks up,
61345: d’èt tə u uhɑ̀p’e stà č’èš’iž gu stàni inɛ̀ bùcə izl’ɛ̀z’e kumɑ̀r’i
Where they bite you it gets – you scratch it and then a lump comes. Mosquitoes.
61349: i tè si stàne sèki ta si ìde u t’àx dorì i
they all get up and everyone goes home. Even if
61354: da sedìm sedìm pà kato ogladnè̝em taka bè ni aràktera
we sit and sit – when we get hungry, that was how we were.
61359: è ta mòjta màjka ta zèmem ə t’è ogladn’èli stànem
And my mother – and then we start – Everyone [at the work bee] is hungry. We get up,
61364: vàrim kəčəmàk tè mu vìkaa mamal’ìga germàn  tavà
and make polenta. They called it “mamaliga”, the Germ-
61373: [Не бяха ли Румънците дето му викат мамалига?]
[I thought it was Romanians who called it mamaliga?]
61380: i sìpem ml’àku s’ìrene če ìmame dobìtak daržìme gl’èdame dobìtak
We pour milk and white cheese [on polenta]. We’ve got livestock, we raise livestock –
61382: sp’ɛ̀hmi nə n’ìvətə v’èč’er kətu̥ sì l’èg’n’em udòlu pust’èl’em
We used to sleep in the fields. In the evening we lie down and spread out below [us]
61385: najad’è̝m sa stànat ta si ìdat è pa koto dòdeše kòl’eda
We eat our fill, [then] they get up and go home. And when Christmas came,
61392: m’èsvame pa krəvàje m’èsvat krəvàj l’àp t’àsto zamèsile
we make “kravay” (ring-shaped buns). They kneaded bread dough
61394: m’èsim krəvài i go nòsat na baštàta i na màjkata
and we make “kravay” and they take it to [their] mothers and fathers.
61399: kòjto vèke kakvòto dadè̝ màjka mi baštà mi
Whatever anyone [makes] they give to [their] mother and father.
61400: And you had a hand loom?
61403: à hə am kə̀k am kòlku
Yes, of course, and so much –
61405: So you used to weave a lot?
61409: dà am kòlkə č’èrgi səm istəkàlə təkìvə
Ah, [I can’t count] how many rugs I’ve woven, these ...
61417: ed’ìn kòzənik i udgòr’e səs kòz’ənik pràwim təč’èm gi ut kòzitɛ̏
a goat-hair rug, and above [us] a goat-hair rug. We make them, weave them from goats.
61423: kòzina prid’èm’e i təč’èm kòzənik i tə nə tèpəwcətə ìməwme
We spin the goat-hair and weave the rug, and then to the fulling mill. We used to have
61427: təpəwdž’ɛ̀ri nə s’àko s’èlo ìmə wɑ̀l’əd gi kòz’ənik
fullers, there’s one in each village. They full the goat-hair rugs [for us].
61432: i tìj kətu mrɛ̀kne v’èč’er də zapɑ̀lim wògən’ə tìj katu brɛ̀nnət
And when it gets dark in the evening and we light a fire, they (= insects) start buzzing
61436: c’àl ròj ni mo ni mòži m m mɑ̀hɑm’i təkòəme
Whole swarms, you – you can’t – We wave and such
61440: səs n’àkuj hrɑ̀stɨ ut n’àkuj utč’ùpim šùmkə
with some boughs [that] we cut off of some shrub.
61446: ami tò zaspìm kət sì mɑ̀hɑme zaspìm i tìj kət nì nəp’ìt’et
We fall asleep after waving [branches]. We fall asleep and they make honeycombs of us!
61451: strinɛ̀ta stànem hìč ne vìždəm’e č’èš’im sa
We get up in the morning, we don’t see anything at all, but oh, how we scratch!
61454: tùj hìč n’e vìždəm’e tuj č’èl:tu ti ə tùj bùcə bùcə
We don’t see anything here. [And] here on your forehead are lumps, lumps,
61464: səm dràla nòsila parcàli sam zɤ̀mala uttàm sam gi dràla
... I tore up and got rags that I took from here and there, I tore them up
61466: a či pək kətu plɛ̀vne pɑ̀ri sə mìjme səs udɛ̀
and when they fire up and start burning, we wash [them] with water.
61468: səm gi tɤkàla kvò də ti kàža
and wove them [into rugs]. What can I say?
61473: s udɛ̀ sa mìjme e kumɑ̀r:tȅ ni iz’àdat kət spìm nə n’ìvətə
We wash with water. Those mosquitoes, they eat us up when we sleep in the fields.
61474: jà pək səgà kòj spì nə n’ìvətə
Ah – but now who sleeps in the fields?
61480: səgà mrɛ̀kni v’èč’er səbl’ekɛ̀t sə gòl’i pə nòšnici
Now when it gets dark in the evening, people undress naked, [just] nightclothes.
61484: l’ègni nə pùf tə h kr’ewɑ̀tə
You lie down on [something] soft, in a bed.
61488: namàži se də ne gò hàpət komàrite
You smear on [something] so the mosquitoes won’t bite –
61490: əmì rəskəžì mi kàk e səs səs stənɤ̀
So tell me what it’s like with the loom.
61493: ja d’è j tòj kumàr’ d’è j tugàs nə nə bùctȅ lež’ì
And what are these mosquitoes [compared] to those then? You lie on those lumps
61499: tàm nə n’ìvətə nə bùctȅ l’ežì lì  t kɑ̀zvəm
out there in the field, you lie on those lumps, like I told you,
61504: kòz’enikə i s kòz’ənikə pukrìt ša wɑ̀di l’àp
[on] the goat-hair rug, and covered with a goat-hair rug, all to earn some bread.
61506: štotu səm čùvələ no n ne sɤ̀m vìždələ ne ne znàm
Because I’ve heard about them but I’ve never seen one [and so] I don’t know
61512: ku n’i l’iž’ì nə bùctȅ tàm l’àp n’èma
And if you don’t lie on those lumps, there’s no bread [for you]!
61514: … parts [of it] are, [or] how it all works.
61518: tò sə prài səz dv’è dərv’ètə da kàžem
It works with these two [pieces of] wood, let’s call them.
61523: ə kàk se z tì znàči ə kòz’inicit’è nə tepəvəčàrite gi dàvaxti̥
So how – these goat-rugs, you gave them to the fullers, [right]?
61524: tɤ̀j kɤ̀ktu i stənɤ̀ sigà ìmə təkòs kɤ̀k mu kàzvəə tè
Like a loom is now, there’s this – how did they call it?
61529: zèw də zəbràəm i às vèk’e kròsnu mu kàzvəme
I’ve started to forget. [Ah, yes,] we call it a beam.
61531: jà sə nìj si gi istəč’èm pr’id’èm kòzintȁ istəč’èm gu
Yes, we weave them, we spin the goat hair and weave [the rug],
61538: i dàvəme gu nə təpəwdž’ɛ̀r’ə uwɑ̀l’ə gu stàwɑ hùbɑwu hùbɑwu ə kòzənik
and we give it to the fuller. He fulls it and it comes out nice, a nice goat-hair rug.
61542: ə vɤ̀n tuj dètu šə gu təč’èm tùj kròsnu kupùvəm’ì kòi pr’èžbata
… at the outer edge that we weave [onto]. [For] this beam, one of us buys the yarn.
61544: i ìməmi č’i̥krɤ̀ci t’ès č’i̥krɤ̀ci gi ə nəvìv’əme nə məsùri
And we have [these] spinning wheels, we wind [the yarn] onto spools.
61551: s’ètne pək zəkàčəmi inì klèčki də kàim tàm inɤ̀ klèčkə
And then we suspend some sticks, let’s say [there’s] one stick here,
61556: še im dadà sas krəvài na màjkatə i na baštàtə
They give it along with the “kravay”, to their mother and their father.
61558: è še dòde vasìl i ga dòde koto dòde vasìl
Then comes St Basil’s day, and when that comes – when St. Basil’s day comes
61561: ìmaše əm è decà òdat ta suruvàkat
there was [the custom] that children go out as “survakar” (New Year’s well-wisher).
61565: a pa nìe momìčeta sə zbìra:me pɤk ta pejè̝m pṛ̀stenete
And we girls would get together and sing [songs of enchantment] over our rings.
61568: tùka vaf rekɛ̀ta sme sa zè̝le ta gi pejè̝m
We came to “sing” over the rings here at the river, [which]
61571: i tò ə l’è̝t ɛ̀ zbràli sa sa momìčeta i momčè̝ta
is [at this point] ice. So the boys and girls got together,
61576: i nìe z’è̝mat belò kotl’è i sipàle vɛ̀tre vòda
and we – they take a tin-plated kettle [that] they’ve poured water into,
61580: i tùrnat na ledɛ̀ put kutl’èto ə uv’ès put kutl’èto
and put it on the ice, and under the kettle – there’s oats under the kettle.
61585: i nal’ì ìmame s’è̝ pṛ̀stenčeta pu rac’è̝te pṛ̀stene
And, you know, we all have little rings on our hands. Rings.
61591: ɛ̀ s’è̝ki si spùsti pṛ̀sten’e vɛ̀tre vav vodɛ̀ta i pejè̝m gi
So each one drops her rings into the water, and we sing over them.
61596: ta ispejè̝m pesentɛ̀ i prib’è̝rat tovà sproti vasìl
We finish the songs and they take – on the night before St. Basil’s Day –
61599: i prib’è̝rat kutl’èto na vasìl zarantɛ̀ še si dòdem
they take the kettle. [So,] early in the morning on St. Basils’ day we'll come
61600: pà ràno da pejè̝m dòdem ta pejè̝m tùka na rekɛ̀ta
early again to sing. We come to sing here at the river
61603: i vàdat ə pṛ̀stenete i da gi narìčat pṛ̀stenete
and take out the rings to identify the rings [so as to learn]
61607: kumù kakvò še sa pàdne na ednì sa pàdne zdràv zdràva godìnčica
what fortune will come to whoever [owns each ring]. Some will have a healthy year,
61668: səšìvəme gu h č’ètiri plàta nìj a tòl’kis plàtove təč’èm
We sew it in four separate pieces. We weave it in pieces this wide, [and] ...
61674: drùgi pàdne sa prevìt krəvàj gòs t’e čàka è tovà
others will have – if it’s bent like a “kravay” [it means] guests are coming.
61678: gòs a gòs t’e čàka godežàre čàkat è ftòrija pàk
That is, guests, and maybe even matchmakers, are coming. Another [fortune]
61681: ə bèše ìmaše kupɛ̀ s’àno na pɛ̀t’a kòjto mìne
was – there was a haystack by the road and someone goes by [and]
61683: oskùbne si t’à pàk drùgata pàk a i pà gu narìčat
pulls some out [to read her fortune]. And another and another. And again they tell fortunes
61687: pàk unuvà vèk’ ne pòmna kàg gu narìčaa pùsto
from that one, but I don’t remember anymore how they interpreted that one. Damn it,
61690: zabràila sam kàg gu narìčaa zabràvila sam go ne pòmna
I’ve forgotten how they used to interpret that one. I’ve forgotten it, I don’t remember.
61691: ne mòa ti gu kàža unuvà kàg gu narìčaa
I’m not able to tell you how they interpreted that one.
61695: je vìš pà gi poftòrim [unintelligible] gi pàk poftòrim
You see, we repeat them, [unintelligible], and repeat them again.
61699: takà posr’èštame vasìl à še dòde pa ivànovd’è̝n’ momčè̝ata
That’s how we observed St. Basil’s day. And then will come St John’s day. The boys
61704: kòito sa tùka momčè̝ata jèzdat kun’è̝te̥ prepùskad gi na ivànovd’è̝n’
who are here ride horseback. They run them at a gallop on St. John’s day.
61710: è̝zdat kun’è̝ i prepùskad gi še dòde zàgovenki da zagov’è̝em vè̝če
They ride horse at full gallop. Then comes Shrovetide, and we start to fast.
61711: tàm inɤ̀ si pràiš sm’ètkə kòlku m’ètrə mòž də ti j
one there – you figure out how many meters [of rug] you can –
61714: də ti tr’àvə t’èbe zə inɤ̀ stàjə i gu snuv’èm mu kàzvəmi
that you’d need for one room. And then we warp [the loom], as we say.
61717: pa za velìkija pòs napràim si bànici zb’è̝rem sa
for the “great fast” (Lent). We make banitsa and get together.
61722: usnuv’èm tùj n’èštu kəd gu usnuv’èm s’ètn’e gùždəmi glàvi
We warp this thing. After we warp it, then we put the skeins on.
61726: ə pu dv’è kɤ̀šti sa zb’è̝rem na ednò m’àsto da si zagov’è̝em
Every two houses get together in one place to observe the fast [together].
61731: kupìle sa ednì kùpat alvɛ̀ ud b’àlata alvɛ̀ ɛ̀ napràim bànici
They bought – some buy white halva. So we make [different kinds of] banitsa.
61734: či tɤ̀s gləvɤ̀ inòtu̥ tɤ̀j drùgutu nədòlu inòt nagòr’e
You’ve got one skein [here], and then another – one below and one on top.
61740: i tès trɤ̀stuw’e tɤ̀j stàwət jà tùkətɤ̀jk’i i ud n’ègu gu udbìrəmi
And these reeds  – they go here, see, and that’s how you keep [the two skeins] apart.
61745: i s’ètn’e t’ès trɤ̀stuje gu uprəwl’àət nədòlo
And then, these reeds direct it from below.
61750: nagòtvili sme si sìčko i okàčim pa s’ìrene bùca sìrene gol’àmə
We’ve cooked up everything. And we hang up a big lump of white cheese –
61751: i drùgə žinà pɤ̀k nəvìvəm’e drùgətə è tàm às tùkətɤ̀jk’i
And [with] another woman we turn [the beam]. The other one is over there and
61754: às səs inì urtincà gu nəvìvəmi nə tùj kròsnu
I am here with these spindles, and we roll it up [the fabric] onto this beam,
61758: vṛ̀zem ja sas kun’è̝c i ja okàčim na gredìte
we tie it on a string and hang it on the beams.
61762: i tò ìdi ìdi sìčkutu du tùkə i tugàz gu gùždəmi
and we keep on going until it’s all [rolled up], up to here. Then we put it
61769: i jɛ spùstim takà nìsko i otkɤ̀ sa najadè̝m s’è̝ki da tìča
Then we let it down low, and after we’ve had our fill of eating, everyone runs
61771: nə tòs stàn tòs stàn tɤ̀j si je te tòlkus tɤ̀j jə šəròk
on this loom. The loom itself is like this, this wide.
61778: tùkə ìmə inò krɤ̀stu̥ inò kurì ə təkòs a s’à
Here there’s a cross, a – this –  uh,  [wait] now
61782: i da làpa hàp l’ùškat e takà nasàm natàta nasàm natàta
to take a bit of it. Jump! They make it swing from here to there, here to there,
61784: dukɤ̀t gu kàžə pàk tùkə nə krɤ̀stu t’i dètu i kròsnutu
until I can say it. There are these cross-like handles on the beam ...
61788: ud n’ègu gu uprəwl’àəš nə tɤ̀s strənɤ̀ ìmə inì klèčki
... and that’s how you make it go. And over on the side there are some sticks.
61792: l’ùškat i s’èki ìde làpva [laughter] abè takàva be mi
they make it swing, and everyone runs to take a bite. [laughter] Well, such things –
61796: tès klèčki upənɤ̀vət kət gu prətəč’èš tùj n’èštu pòčvəš drùgu
These sticks keep up the tension. When you finish weaving one thing you start another.
61798: i či ìmə i čumbàr’ mu kàzvəmi čumbàr’ i tɤ̀j gu slàgəš
And there’s a “chumbar” (temple), as we call it. You put it there
61807: tavà ə nàvika sìčkite tɛ̀j pràvea i gu l’ùškat i
That’s our custom.   Everyone did this, they made it sway
61809: upənùvəš tuj nèštu aku nè e upɤ̀nətu tò šə sə izbir’è
and stretch this thing [you’re weaving]. If it’s not kept stretched out it will shrink.
61815: a pək kət gu upən’èš i tò stàwə tɤ̀j kək ìkət
And when you stretch it out then it gets, as they say,
61817: e pa nìe sm’à adì ednì pàdnat otk’ɛ̀snat
and we [all] laughed. Some would fall down, would [manage] to cut [a piece] off,
61819: kəto upɤ̀nətu i pràu amə kòlku č’èrgi
stretched out straight. Oh – [who knows] how many rugs [I’ve woven],
61823: drùgi ne mòe otk’ɛ̀snat džumbìš pràvejme i tàa ə bùca
others wouldn’t be able to cut it off. We made [it into] a great party. And that lump –
61825: i kòj še gi iznòsi də n’aə kò də ti kàžə
or who will use them up?  What can I tell you?
61831: še ja ustàvat v’è̝ke t’èa ìmaa koto za c’àr li ìmaa
they’ll leave it there. They had (= used) it as a sort of medicine.
61834: gùdim nə leglòto mi i nòvi i xùbavi i lòšəvi i s’àkəkvi
We put – [there’s] all sorts of them on my bed – new ones, nice ones, lousy ones.
61835: i tɤ̀j živèjmi nìj nə sèlu
And that’s how we used to live in the village.
61844: ostàvea kogà imam ìmame dobìtak ta n’àko mladìšte da prudrìšte
They left it [for] when – We have livestock, and when some young person has diarrhea,
61847: rəgòski prədì nìj štòtu smi blìzu du bàltә̥tә̥ tùkə ìməme pəpùr’
Earlier we [had] straw mats because we’re close to the swamp. We have bulrushes here,
61854: nògu rəgòski òrtə žuvèli inò wrème əma nə rəgòskətə
[and so] lots of straw mats. That’s how people lived in the old days, with straw mats.
61855: da skɤ̀same ut ə sìreneto da gu zavìjeme ta da
we cut off a piece of that cheese and bind it on him in order to –
61857: a pək nìj sigànkə rəgòski n’àmə əmà i nìj putkuàəme stàit’ȅ
But now there aren’t any straw mats. Now we put floorboards in the rooms.
61862: nə starì gudìni in’ète bil’à gi nəpràime tàm u pi̥šnìk’u
Even in old age we do them up new, [like] the oven room up there.
61866: ə səs ə gìps gi nəpràime znàiš kò i stud’ènu
We do them up – uh, with plaster. You know how cold it gets!
61869: nə krəkàtə pək d’èt sə sigà kɤ̀ktu sə nə dɤ̀ski
On your feet. So now there are these boards.
61874: pək n’ègu wrèmi màžewmi zim’ә̟̀tə i zəmàzvəš udgòre
But back then we put clay on the ground. And you plaster it on higher up [too], ...
61879: ... let’s say, [to make it] white – the walls [get to be] white.
61883: tùkə dolu səz žèltu jə zəmàzvəš i pu̥stìləš
And here below you plaster it with [something] yellow.  And then you lay out
61886: tès rəgòski i səs tès rəgòski̥ tɤ̀j sme žuv’èli
these straw mats. And that’s how we lived, with these straw mats.
61889: i bàltətə ni tùkə štòt blìzu nìj ìməme pəpùr’ mu sə
Because we’re close to the swamp here, we have bulrushes, as …
61894: i tòs pəpùr’ pàk si ìməši stàn də gu təč’èš
And [for] these bulrushes, there was a loom [out there] so you could weave [them].
61900: ut stàr’:tȅ tùj n’èštu gu pràeə pək às sià ìməm inɤ̀ rəgòskə
They did this in the old [days]. And [even] now I have a straw mat –
61904: gòr’e inɤ̀ ìməm pò t’àsnə tùj ustànəwə tìj drùite gi ishàjkwəmi nìj
one upstairs [and] a narrower one here. They are what’s left, we’re getting rid of the others.
61907: əmə i nìj pu̥tkuàəmi dè trìte ni stài gòre putkuàni
But we’re nailing down floorboards in the three rooms upstairs, those all have boards.
61912: dòlu sàmu nəpràime səz gìps i s’à pu̥stìlaš čèrgite də kàž’em
Downstairs we only put plaster, and then you lay out the rugs, on – you know –
61915: pu pu dɤ̀skit’ȅ č’i tɤ̀j bèši inò wrèmi tɤ̀j tɤ̀j sne živèli
on the boards. And that’s how it was in the olden days, that’s how we lived.
61918: amə nìj kət prəd nàs stàr:tȅ sə žuvèli kət kàzwət
Like the older [generations] before us had lived, as they say.
61922: tòj mòju sv’èkər sè kàzvəšə̥ a vìj s’à ni ər’èsvəti
My father-in-law always said, “You don’t like [anything] now.”
61925: inò wrèmi màmə kàj kət svərì inɤ̀ t’èndžerə bòp
In the old days, Mom says, when she made a pan of beans,
61932: i t’à bəkɤ̀renə tèndžərə c’àlə nd’èl’ə edèm kàzwə nègu bòp
one of those big copper pans, we would eat that for an entire week, these beans.
61935: i tòj nè upràžen n’è nìštu pək s’à sə izn’èžiwme i nìj
And they weren’t fried or anything. But now even we have gotten soft.
61938: əmə mlàttȅ s’a pək òšte pò iznèžini i tɤ̀j təkòs b’èš’i
But the young people now are even more spoiled. So – that’s how it was.
61944: da mu sə spr’è̝ tavà d’è̝to go gòni po vɛ̀nka mladìšteto
to stop whatever it is that drives the young person outside [to the outhouse].
61949: takà go prekàrvame za velìgd’en’ pa pràve:me pa jèjca pà krəvàje m’èsvaa
That’s how we observed [Lent]. For Easter, we’d make eggs, and they make “kravay” again.
61954: dòde petəròvd’èn’ nìe ìmame tùka kṛ̀s na svet’ì p’èt’er
Then comes St. Peter’s day. We have here a cross [dedicated to] St. Peter.
61957: še zakòlim àgne še dòde pòpa še svetì vòda za
We’ll slaughter a lamb. The priest will come and consecrate the water for –
61963: b’àl kot’èl sv’etì vòda čet’è̝ tàm i s’èki i še tṛ̀gnem
[It’s in a] tin-plated kettle. He blesses the water, reads [a prayer there, and then we all go off.
61964: bàbo eminè jà da mi kàžeš kato pòčneš i ostrižèš vɤ̀lnata
Granny Emine – tell me now, when you begin to shear the wool [from the sheep]
61966: kàk ja rabòtiš dokato stìgneš də da ja tɤčèš
how do you process it until you get to the point where you can weave it?
61969: ə kato isčet’è̝ s’èki otìva pri pòpa tòj go pṛ̀ska
After the prayer, everyone goes up to the priest and he sprinkles them
61976: kato ostrigà ufcè̝te tùriš’ mìješ’ jɤ su vudàtә isɤ̀wne
After I shear the sheep you put it in water, and wash it, [then] it dries,
61981: i e tәkà kàktu ә rәbòtim nìe č’eš’à ja tәkà
and then what we do is I comb it like this,
61988: sas kìtkata napràil kìtka ud zdràvec i bosìl’ek kṛstàd bosìl’ek
with a bouquet. He’s made a bouquet of wild geranium and basil, shaped in a cross.
61990: and then it’s time [to go] to the carding.
61995: To the carder, to the carder!
61998: To [where] the carder is, and you card it.
62000: i tùri gu tùk čùkne go takà ta go pṛ̀sne
He puts it there, taps it so that it sprinkles.
62002: kədè ìma dəràk tùka u sèlu
Where is there a carder? Here in the village?
62008: i si ispùstiš parìte i mu celùvaš rɛ̀ka i si zamìne
You give him some money and kiss his hand, and he goes off.
62018: There’s [one] in Yakoruda, and [one] in Velingrad.
62020: taka pràvejme na svetì ilìja pà sɤ̀štoto beše
And that’s what we did. For St. Elias day it was the same thing all over again.
62025: i gu pràvea nә nìška ali pa i
And they would make it into threads, or [also]
62030: And that’s how it was in the old days.
62031: Into big hanks [of wool] – they’re this big.
62033: [Did you have a lot of corn here?]
62036: i si go kàč’aš’ i si go prid’èš’
And you put that [onto the distaff] and you spin it.
62038: nalì n’èma n’èma kakvò da da dadɛ̀t òrata
Well, you know, people don’t have enough to give [for the government’s quota].
62043: əmi tṛgnàle baa da z’è̝mat na drùgite kukurùza
They went to get corn from others [for that].
62048: nìe si tùk sme si imàle ama po gradìšətə ne sɛ̀ imàle
We here had [enough] but in the cities they didn’t.
62052: ami tṛgnɛ̀a koto komìsija da z’è̝mat da ni z’è̝mat càrevicata
And the [state] committee set out to take [quotas], to take our corn.
62054: nìe sèeme tùka ìmame nìva gol’àma ìmame kukurùs mnògu
We plant it here, we have a big field, [so] we have a lot of corn,
62057: tà koto nam’èrat i ti ostàvat màlko i
so that when they [come to] find [the quota] they leave you a bit and
62061: ti gi onovà go z’è̝mat da go odnesɛ̀t da go predadɛ̀t
they take it from you, so as to carry it off to give it
62063: pa na tìja koìto n’èmat da im go dadɛ̀t
to those who don’t have enough to give them (the commission) [as quota],
62067: pa t’è da ne gladùvat z’è̝mat ni càrevicata
so they won’t go hungry. They take our corn,
62072: ta sme go krìle i nosìle po gɤstàcite da da si krìem càrevicətə̥
so we hid it and took it into the bushes so as to keep the corn for ourselves.
62075: You spin it on the spindle.
62078: čàkaj segà glèdaš na vretènoto kàg go
Wait a minute, see here. [Is this what you do] with the spindle when –
62080: Ah, that’s it! That’s how you spin.
62082: ә tò nìsku e tәkà i rič’èš’ tәkà i tәkà i stàvә
This part is below, and you do like this and this, and that’s how it happens.
62086: mi è tәkà gu rәstàniš kato pòčne nә vәrtènotò gu vìješ’
So you stretch it out like this and when it begins to go on the spindle, you twirl it.
62091: i kato go izvìješ’ nәtòč’iž gu na motovìl’č’eta i go isper’èšᵊ
And when you’re done then you wind it onto the yarn-crutches, and you wash it
62094: tùriš usnuvèšᵊ i nәr’èiš nә nèko vìkamè go e takìva dɤ̀rva dɤ̀rveni
and put it to warp it, and arrange it on these, what we call these wooden –
62103: i go navìješᵊ i go tùriš’ i go tač’èš’
And you wind it up and put it on, and weave.
62104: Wait – but [what about] the dyeing? Who –
62106: ami ìma i bujәdìsvane pa i nèma bojadìsvane
Well, there’s dyeing, and then there isn’t dyeing.
62115: č’ɤ̀rno i bɛ̀lo pa ìma i p š’àreni
Black, and white, and there’s also multicolored.
62116: O.K. And who dyes them for you?
62121: ednò vrème a pa pò ràno è  ot po
But in the old days? Earlier? From way, way back?
62123: i sè ot tàm li ste xòdili tùka vàšte stàrite
And did you always go there, your ancestors here?
62128: n’àma tàm tàm vrɤvɛ̀a sìčko ž’ìvo tàm vrɤvì
No. [We went] there. Everyone, but everyone went there.
62133: tàm n’èma tùk n’èmәš’e bojadž’ìjnici sàmo vèlingràtᵊ ali pàzardž’ìk
There aren’t, and weren’t, any dyers here. Only [in] Velingrad or Pazardzhik.
62138: i tavà e i pòčnež dә gu tәč’èš’ dә gu š’әrìš’ᵊ
And that’s [that part]. You begin to weave it, to make it into patterns.
62140: e kažì mi seà kato tɤčèš za rìza kato tɤčèž za
So tell me now how you weave [fabric] for a shirt, [and how] you weave for –
62143: No shirts. We don’t weave shirts.
62146: sàmo za prestèlki sàmo za pokrìfki tavà za pres zә tәkòvә
We only [weave fabric] for aprons, only for coverings, and such.
62151: aha e tovà sa vɤ̀lneni takà li
Aha. And those are woolen, right?
62154: [Did you weave] anything out of cotton?
62159: We buy that sort of thing – shirts, fabric.
62160: a ednò vrème pàk takà li e bilò
And was it like that in the old days?
62162: takà si e bìlo kàkto si
That’s how it was. Like it was …
62167: ot stàro na na esɛ̀ takà si e bìlo
... from the old [times] up till now. That’s just how it was.
62169: We buy those sorts of shirts.
62171: takà e dobrè a šàrkite kòj ti kàzva kàg da gi tùriš
O.K. then. [When you weave], who tells you how to arrange the patterns?
62174: bojadžìja bojadžìja fànem sà ut š’àrkitè i
The dyer, the dyer. We look at the patterns and
62178: t’à si gl’èdə ud drùgətà i si gu vèzə tàm po tàmcək
one [of us] looks at [what] another one [does], and arranges [the threads] that way.
62182: She looks at the yarn and –
62185: pr’èždətə kəkvàt si tùrišᵊ  ə kət
At the yarn the way you put it on [the loom].
62195: kəkvàtu ujdìsuvə nə təvàkə i si gu š’ərìš’
... so as to fit the pattern, and then you follow it.
62196: znàči tì si rešàvaš tòj ti
So you decide for yourself. He – do you –
62201: [So then] he’ll dye it for you,
62203: ama tì kàg da tùriš kojà šàrka kɤdè da bɤ̀de
but you [decide] how to place it, which pattern goes where.
62208: vìkamè go ìmə i č’erv’èno ìmə i zel’èno
We call it [like this]: here’s the red, here’s the green,
62211: ɛ̀to gi è tùka ìma è təkìva sìni
And over here, here’s the blue ones.
62215: aha tovà vèče ot tèbe zavìsi
So it all depends on you.
62225: tàm po razbòja kakvì čàsti ìma
… on the loom there, what kinds of parts does it have?
62226: Well, wooden ones. That’s what kind.
62232: ednò krosnò ednò otprèt ednò odzàt
[There’s] a beam. One in the front, and one in the back.
62234: ednò krosnò ednò uttùk tə uttùk
A beam – one over here, and one over here.
62236: i nə stredàtə d’ètu go vd’èneš nìš’elki
In the middle where you thread the heddle.
62238: In the middle – that’s how you thread it.
62247: təkà dèto fàtəš nəbɤ̀rdilà se kàzuvə
Here where you grab it, it’s called battens.
62257: This, that, you assemble it, and –
62259: And inside the battens, what’s in there?
62266: əm kət ustrižèm ufcèt’ȅ z’èmem ə upɑ̀rim vɛ̀lnətə isč’èpkəme jə
After we shear the sheep, we take and scald the wool. We card it,
62270: wlɑ̀čim jə prid’èm jə kitɛ̀ gu prid’èm f trì kɑ̀tə
comb it, spin it. We spin it for tassels in three layers,
62275: če gu pr’asùkvəmi če xòdim də bir’èm lìs
and we twist them together. [Then] we go gather [some] leaves
62277: vìe kàe tòj te pìta za vɤ̀tre kàk e s nìš’elkite
You’re saying [something else]; he’s asking you what’s inside, about the heddle.
62282: e dà vìka vɤ̀tre šo ìmə f nəbɤ̀rdilàta
Yes, he says, “What’s inside, in the battens?”
62284: i sɑ̀čkə či gu bujəd’ìsvəme vɑ̀pcwəme gu də stàvə č’è̟rən
and we dye them [with] “sacha” (ferrous sulfate). We dye it [until] it turns black.
62285: a onòva je e onòva e
And that one is, that one is –
62288: kəd gù vɑ̀pcəme či gu nəwìəme nə mutuvìl’čitu̥
After we dye it, we wind it onto the yarn-crutch.
62294: The comb, the heddle, and you hook everything up.
62296: And who makes the loom for you?
62300: tò mnògu pɛ̀ti tr’àbvə də sə nəwìvə nəwìvəne rəzvìvəne
You have to wind it many times. Winding, unwinding,
62301: tò si ìmə tùkə nàšte òra si̥
62308: dukət stàne pròstu də stàne hùbəwu pràwu slòžim gu nə stanɛ̀

62309: tùkə s’àkuj š’e tì go naprài

The men do it, women can’t.
62331: tùrim gu nə stanɛ̀ pòčwəme də təč’èm təč’èm
We put it on the loom and begin to weave. We weave,
62334: kupùvəmè gi kupùvəme i nìh kòjtu màjstur nəpràje

[alternating] warp and woof, and line up the tassels. When we’ve lined it up,

62349: kòjtu e màjstur tòj si nəprài
The one who’s a craftsman makes one for himself.
62355: i sàmo vɤ̀lna li rabòtixte vìe
So did you all only work with wool?
62356: kət sɛ̀ uprust’ì kitɛ̀ tugɑ̀s jə ispir’èm upir’èm jə
When [each] tassel gets all smooth, then we wash it – we wash it well,
62359: Well, we work with woolen things on the loom.
