62367: i kət jɛ̀ upir’èm ə tugɑ̀s vèči jə dìgəm’ə zə huròtu
and after we wash it, [we put it away] and then take it out for the round dance.
62369: All that’s pretty much gone by the wayside.
62371: tə tò tùk gul’ɛ̀mi vɤ̀lni n’àmaš’e əmi
There never was a lot of wool here.
62372: nɛ̀kuj ìmə tri č’ètiri p’ètᵊ nɛ̀kuj ìmə sèdem òsem
Some have three, four, or five [sheep], some have seven or eight.
62385: səs nèjə hòd’im nə huròtu hòd’im nə vəl’ɛ̀nki hòd’im nə səd’ɛ̀nki
We [wear] it [when] we go dancing, when we go to fulling bees or to work bees.
62386: tə də e imàlu f gulɛ̀mi vɤ̀lni əmi tò zbìrə
… to have produced a lot of wools. So you have to collect it
62388: zə ədnɤ̀ gudìnə əlì zə dvè tugà gu nàtč’i
over a year, or two. And then – weave it all!
62478: sidì vəf  štàgə əf štàgə i
It stays in a crate. In a crate and –
62566: bàba mi i onà pri n’èga si mu svàri
grandma [and I]. She would cook food for him up there –
62567: beans, potatoes, soup – whatever there was. [laughter]
62569: svàri mu nò bàba i jà si ìdem
Granny’d cook it up for him. And [sometimes] I went
62572: ta gim zanesèm lèp ò onì vèseli bàba mi dèda mi
and took them bread, and oh, they [were] happy, Granny and Granddad,
62575: ìdu če gim nòsim lèp nòsim gim jèden’e [laughter]
they come [to meet me] because I bring them bread, bring them food. [laughter]
62578: a vèseli ràduju mi se ràdos ò dè si prespì
They were overjoyed [to see] me – such joy! “Sleep over [here with us],
62580: pa jùtre če si ìdeš ò bàbo no mèn mi kazàli
and go back in the morning!” “Oh Granny,” [I’d say] “but they told me
62581: da se vṛ̀nem ə ò àjde àjde jùtre če si ìdeš
to come back.” [And they’d say], “Ah, come on. You [can] go in the morning,
62584: nèmaš mlògo ràbotu jà si prespìm pri n’ì ostànem pri n’ì
you don’t have much work.” So I would sleep over with them, I’d stay with them
62676: kəd gì səjdin’ìm č’ètiri plàtə kəd gì uwɑ̀l’əš  stàni ubiknuv’ènnu kòzənik
when we join the four pieces, when you full them, it becomes normal – a goat-hair rug,
62681: pust’ìləme gu hùbɑwu hùbɑwu stɑ̀wə pustìləme gu spìm nə n’ègu
[the kind] we spread [on the floor]. It turns out really nice. We spread it out, sleep on it,
62684: səd’ìm nə n’ègu n’èməše pl’ùš’eni ràbuti tugàs
sit on it – there weren’t any of these plushy things back then.
62687: à kəd’à hìč kòj t’à b’èše stàra ràbutə tugàs
Nothing like that. Things were old-time back then.
62863: nìj kətu b’ɛ̀hm’e d’əcà də zəpòvn’ə pri màjkin’i det stàrə ràbotə
When we were children, I remember [things] with my mother’s people. Old things.
62866: i s’ètn’e i nìj gàt pòčnəhmi tùj i nìj gu prəkɑ̀rəhmi
But later when we began [living like] this, then we too went over,
62870: i nìj gu vɛ̀rš’ehmi səgà v’èč’e nə nàštȅ gudìn’i nàštȅ d’əcà
we did it too. Now in our [advanced] years, [we see that] our children ...
62876: preobɛ̀rna se i nè e sɛ̀štoto
It’s all changed. It’s not the same [any more].
62878: jà n’ì e s mlògu sə ubɛ̀rna sigɑ̀ pək hèpt’en èč’ə hèpt’en’
Right, it’s not. It’s changed a lot. Now totally already. Totally.
62888: nàšte unùki kət stìgnəhə èpt’en èč’ə stànə səhsɛ̀m drùgu
By the time it got to our granddaughters, totally. Things became altogether different.
62890: səvs’ɛ̀m bè səvs’ɛ̀m drùgu e sigà
Altogether indeed. It’s altogether different now.
62894: am znàči zə tepavič’àrə tòj n’àkvə məšìnə ìmə da
So about the fuller. He has some sort of machine, right?
62900: tèpawcɛ mu dùməm’e tòj səgɑ̀ ìmə tàm ə wudɛ̀
“Tepavsta”, [that’s] what we call it.  He – well, there’s – there’s water there.
62905: wudɛ̀ ìmə i kɑ̀rə tùj às mlòk kətu d’v’ɛ̀
es – well – I’ve [been] many – there’s two –
62910: təkòs krusnà lì vɑ ennì krusnà gul’ɛ̀mi i tìj krusnà
like, beams. You know, right? These large beams. And these beams –
62916: kətu pùsn’i tu̥ n’ègu plàt plàt d’èt š’ə go š’ìjmi nə mɛ̀ž’itɛ̏ jəmurlùk
when he puts that fabric there, the fabric that we’ll sew raincloaks for the men out of –
62922: d’èt š’e šìjmi nə mɛ̀ž’it’ɛ̏ plɑ̀t za gɑ̀št’i
fabric that we’ll sew for the men [also] trousers –
62928: kətu gù pùst’i hɛ̀tr’e tìj pòčnət də də gu bìət tìə
When he puts it inside, they (= the beams) start to beat it, they –
62933: tù tùpə tùpə tùpə tùpə i gu rəs tùpəd gu i gu rəzbìvət
Bang, bang, bang, bang, [and] they – they pound it and break it down
62937: i stɑ̀wə plɑ̀t d’ib’èl’ i šìe š’ɛ̀jek mu vìkəm’e
and it becomes a thick fabric, and we call it – homespun.
62943: š’ɛ̀jek i š’ìjm’e nə mɛ̀š:tɛ̏ gɑ̀št’i i š’ìim nə jele
Homespun. And we sew trousers for the men, and we sew – sew for –
62949: ə təkòs abɛ̀ abɛ̀ abɛ̀ gòrnə dr’èha abɛ̀ mu vìkəhm’e
well, [it’s] this “aba”. “Aba, aba” a felt cloak. We call it “aba”.
62957: səz dɛ̀l’g’i rəkàvi abɛ̀ n’i jè kət pɑ̀ltu s’ètn’e izl’ɛ̀z’e mòdətə paltà
It has long sleeves, the “aba’. It’s not like a coat. Coats became the fashion later.
62959: pək nìj mu š vìkəhm’e tugàs i vìnəgi t’ɛ̀j b’ɛ̀še abɛ̀
But back then we called it [that], and it’s always been [for us], the “aba”.
62964: a nə dòlu nə kòlko bɛ̀ dɛ̀lgo
And how long was it? How [far] down [did it go]?
62967: kət pàlto tò du təd’às tɤ̀j
Like a coat, about down to here.
62970: do tùkə du màlko tɛ̀j ut krɛ̀stə màlku
To here, to here. A little here, a little below the waist.
62974: ja ja no, ə a tɛ̀j ə tòlkus du kɛ̀lkite tɛ̀j
Well, yes, uh – ah there! Just that much. To the thighs – there.
63385: f čèstinatḁ sa dəru̥vètu i darùvat si màjkata nèjnata ròda
on the “honor” are the gifts. Her mother gives gifts to her kin.
63388: i na drùgio dèn’ punedèlniko tàa svekɤ̀rvata štò e utùka
And on the next day, on Monday, the mother-in-law – the one from here,
63391: u mom momčètu ponedèlniko si darùva nègovata ròda ama
at the boy’s house [that is] – gives gifts to his relatives on Monday. But
63652: òn’i tùrat togàj màsata tàm sofrà li šo k’è da e
then they set some table there, maybe a low one, whatever there is,
63653: i vìkat darùvat si na tàa ròda
and they invite people, and give gifts to those relatives.
63657: kòj što ìma nèkoj krɤ̀pče nèkoj  kušùl’a nèkoj što nàjdat [laughter]
Each [gives] what he’s got – one [gives] a towel, one [gives] a shirt, one whatever he finds. [laughter]
63662: a kòj koj b’àxa nàj glàvnite na svàdbata
And who – who were the major [participants] in the wedding?
63664: mi nàj glàvnite sa kumò màjkata tàtkoto
Well, the major ones are the “kum” (godfather), the mother, the father,
63667: the best man – these are the major ones.
63669: ama vìe kùm ne vìkaxte edno vrème
But you didn’t use to say “kum” in the old days, [did you?]
63670: àmi kàk nè togàj òšte pò vìkaa
What do you mean we didn’t? Back then they said it even more.
63678: kalitàta kalimàna tìa s’i takà s si vìkaše
The “kalita”, the “kaliman”, back then that’s what they called ...
63956: i sàa se takà vìka i sàa si tùka vìkame
And that’s what they’re called now too. Now also we say here
63960: ne štòt na men mi go izm’ataš
No, [I’m asking] because [it seemed] you were twisting [the words] on me.
63963: I want to learn the old [words].
63964: mi taka si bèše kumò se vìka kùm si
Well, that’s how it was. You call the godfather the “kum”
63969: za da gu znàat či e kum drù da gu znàt òrata
so that people will know that he is the godfather. So that people will know.
63971: a nìe si gu znàem i kalitàta kalimàna
But we know them as “kalita” and “kaliman”.
63972: Aha. So that’s why it’s that way.
64219: pa si spìm no onì znàu nàšte če səm pri n’ì
and sleep there. After all, my folks knew I was with them,
64222: ne sɤ̀m nègde zaletèla àjde pàk utròto pòsle
that I hadn’t flown off somewhere. And so in the morning [I went back]. Later,
64227: kat izlèzne dòjde džùrdžovden onì gi iskàru iz livàdete
when St. George’s Day came, they take [sheep] from the meadows,
64232: zavàrde blàguvesti vàrde livàdete za sèno
to keep – [from] Annunciation [onwards] to keep the meadows free for hay.
64238: àjde kudè nèma livàde pokràj glàmete ednì napraìli tṛl’àci
But in stony spots where there are no meadows, some have made sheep pens,
64241: ednì pa napraìli gòre po kràištata na nə livàdete
[while] others have made [them] up at the edges of – of the meadows.
64246: izlèznemo od blàgovesti tàm nò jàganci se izjagnìle òvce
We go there at Annunciation, to the lambs – the sheep having given birth –
64248: jàganci òvce tàm gi pasù àjde bàba i dèda
up [to] where they’re pasturing the sheep and lambs. And Grandma and Grandpa
64250: pàk tàm na košàrutu jà bàba mi
are up there again the summer pen. And I – Granny said to me,
64257: ò ednò jàgn’e se bòlno nèkvo mukàvičavo bolù ga nòge
“Oh, [there’s] a sick lamb, [it’s] bad off somehow. Its legs aren’t right.
64260: da dòjdeš da ga napòimo səs orlòvi nòkti
You should come up and [help] us feed it with ‘eagle’s talons’.”
64262: “Eagle’s talons” – that’s some kind of herb.
64270: [laughter] àjde bàba svarìla orlòvi nòkti jà ìdem onà dṛžì jàgn’eto
So Grandma boiled up the “eagle’s talons”. I go [over] and she holds the lamb
64274: jà sipùjem ta ga napòimo tovà ozdravèe jàgn’eto
[while] I pour, and we feed it to it. And the lamb gets better.
64281: àjde sɤ̀ga da gi popasèmo da i pùštimo màlko jàgancitȉ
And now it’s time to take them to pasture, to let the little lambs out a bit.
64287: pùštimo gi jàgancitȉ jàganci ulòve bṛ̀ze kòj na gdè vìdi
We release the little lambs. The lambs catch [the wind] and rush off, each on its own.
64291: i jà jà po n’ì bṛ̀zim bṛ̀zim bṛ̀zim ta gi svì
And I – I’m running after them, running, running, till I’ve surrounded [them],
64295: pribrà gi jàganciti a dèda mi se javìl
and gathered up the lambs. Then Grandpa came up –
64300: sɤs ovcète oddalèko i me vidèl če bṛ̀zim rèče
he’d been off with the sheep and seen me running. And he said,
64306: jà ka te vidò če bṛ̀ziš po jàgancitȉ od ràdoz bi lìtnul
“When I saw you running after the little lambs, I could have leapt with joy.
64310: stàr səm ama mìlo me če tṛ̀čaš po jàgancite
I [may be] old, but it’s sweet for me [to see] you running after the lambs.
64311: jàganciti bṛ̀ze tì bṛ̀ziš po n’ì
The lambs run off, and you run after them.”
64314: mìlo me kat te vidò če bṛ̀ziš po jàganciti [laughter] a dojdè
“I [was so] happy when I saw you running after these lambs.” And he came
64315: pa ə mi se ràduje tàm če sɤm bṛzìla po jàgancite
and was so happy that I had been running after the lambs.
64320: otišlà sɤm pri n’ì rèko dèdo no jà sɤm došlà
So I went over to them and said, “Grandpa, I’ve [actually] come
64323: da gi lekùjemo bàba lì mi kazà da dòjdem da dòjdem
to help treat them. [Didn’t you know that] Grandma told me to come – to come
64325: da napòimo jàganciti jàgneto če e mlògo k’òpavo bòlno
so we could feed the lambs, [especially] the lamb that’s sickly and lame?”
64328: no dobrè dàko si došlà nè e me jèt
“Whatever – you’ve come, and I’m not angry
64331: če si došlà rèče ako si tè tekvòj
that you’ve come”, he said. “I don’t mind at all”. And that’s how it was.
64404: už’ènix sə nə trìjes i p’èd gudìni i p’e ə d dà
I got married at thirty-five, at five – [ah], yes, [it was in]
64411: e ednò vrème gà se gàlehme nìe sas mòjas čulɛ̀k
Well, back in the old days when my man and I were courting,
64417: drùguš gà ž’ɔ̀n’ehmɤ tugàva sarpɔ̀n zɔ̀meš i palamàrčicana
In the old days when we’d [go out to] reap, you take a sickle and a little swaphook.
64425: è òdə n’èkuj pɤ̀t nə pulè̟tu tə berɤ̀ čùšk’ɨ kupàjə pipè̟r’ət
Well, sometimes I go to the field to pick peppers, and to dig in the pepper patch.
64444: nəlɨ sɨgà si prɨkàzvəm’e səs nàšte ə s nàšijə sɨ̀n
Recently we were talking among ourselves, and my son [said],
64449: vkɤ̀šti si kə v dvòrət ìməme bàmn’ə b’erɤ̀ jə sùtrɨn
At home in the yard we have okra, and I pick those
64452: fs’èkə sùtrin fs’èkə sùtrɨn jə berɤ̀ i pòčvəm pàk itnòvu
each morning. Every morning I pick some, and then I start again
64455: də šɤ̀təm i sɤ̀štutu s’èejme tɨ̀kvɨ pu pulè̟tu

64460: mɨ ràbutə mnògu snòštɨ xudɨ̀xmi də berè̟m pipè̟r wòlele umurɨ̀x sə

64468: vɨ̀kəm be kɤ̀k təkà žə sə umorɨ̀ž be nìj inò vr’ème vɨ̀kəm
I say, “But how can you get tired [from that]?” In the old days, I say,
64471: səs ə bəštà tɨ i tòj u sòfijə rəbòt’eše̥ rəbòt’eše tàmkə
your father and I – [that was when] he was working there
64475: u sòfijə às vɨ̀kəm səmɨ̀čkə səs ə vulòvet’e še ìdə də uprè̟gnə
in Sofia – I [did it] all alone. I’d go harness the oxen
64481: də uberɤ̀ càrvicə də sià nəlɨ̀ mumè̟ntə zə càrəvicətə
to bring in the corn, because now, you know, is the right time to bring in the corn,
64485: i sàm səmɨ̀čkə žə si tvàrə kulàtə i že jə dukàrəm
and all by myself I would load up the wagon and drive it back
64490: priz bəìrə kɤ̀ktu j ə dɤ̀lək vè̟ke̝ bəìrət i žə sə vɤ̀rnə
through the hill, going lengthwise [not across] the hillside. Then I’d come back,
64493: i pàk šə ìdə i skàrvəjmi pu ə četirìjse kilà càrvicə
and go out again and bring in forty kilos of corn each time.
64496: samɨ̀čkə vɨ̀kə də gu berɤ̀ pək ə bəštà mi bèše čubàn
Each time, he says I should do it by myself.  [After all,] my father was a shepherd.
64521: pu nàštə sɨ nɨ̀vɨ čàsni ìməjme i bustàn càrevicə ìməjmi
We had our own private fields, a melon garden, and we had corn,
64522: mnògu dè̟kərɨ i mnògu trùdnu ja prɨbɨ̀rəjmi sɤ̀štutu i nè̟jə
a hectare or so –  and a hard time bringing it in, it as well,
64523: štòt bèše mnògu mnògu i tugàvə i dicàtə mi b’èjə màlkɨ
because there was a lot of it. A lot. At that time my children were small
64524: às səs ednɤ̀ zɤ̀lvə òdej sàmu pu kɤ̀rɤt
and I had to go out to the fields with only my sister-in-law [to help].
64525: i dè̟v’ət dè̟kərə càrevicə ìməjm’ə i bustàn ìməjme
We had 9/10 of a hectare of corn, and we had the melon gardens.
64526: ə tɨ̀kvɨ sme s’èjəlɨ ə pəmùk sme s’èjəlɨ vasùl
We planted pumpkins, we planted cotton, and beans.
64527: mnògu b’èjme s’è pu pulè̝tu na mlàdi gudɨ̀nɨ
We were always out there in the field. In our younger years [that is].
64547: a s kakvò si svètexte bàbo eminè ednò vrème vɤfkɤ̀šti
What did you use to light up the house in the old days, Granny Emine?
64560: We would light a fire in the fireplace.
64567: The hearth here – here in the house.
64571: And to – we light the fire.
64572: So that it lights [things up] again.

And when gas lamps came around, each of us bought a couple of them.
64586: pә pә s làmbite dujdè pә tòko hà pa tòko fәnà:me
So then along with the lamps, electricity came in and we got electricity.
64589: That’s how we first started [doing that].
64595: tòj beše š’ɛ̀fer àz beh š’ɛ̀ferka kugàtu pòčnahme da sa l’ùbim
he was in a wedding party, and so was I, when we began to fall in love.
64600: i zagàlihmɨ̀ sa gàlihmɨ̀ sa trì gudìni tòj utìdi vujnìk
We began courting, and we courted for three years. He went off to do his military service,
64607: rasɔ̀rdi mì sa srèštam jɛ̀ ednà ùtrɤna sɤs mòmɤ sɤs kumpànija
and got angry at me. I meet one morning with a girl, with a group –
64614: jɛ̀ sam tɔ̀rnala sas takvò nastrojɛ̀nie di gi sr’ɔ̀šna i ma por’ùka
I’d set out with such anticipation to meet them. And he called me,
64620: àjde vìka nax nàs če dušɔ̀l svàtəd g’òrgi i jɛ̀ si vìkam
“Come to our [place], our [ritual] kin Georgi has come. And I say,
64621: znàči pòmnite kogà e došɤ̀l tòko
So you remember when electricity came.
64629: How should we have remembered which year?!
64635: How can it be that you don’t remember?
64639: znàči na na ogìna si svètixte vìe
So then, you all got your light from – from the fire.
64645: a ne pràvexte li od bòr takìva
And didn’t you make some sort of [something]  from pine trees,
64647: kàk im vìkate vìe da pàlite od bòr eni ə ə
what did you call it, [something] to light a fire from pine –
64662: vɔ̀r si vìkam tì jɛ̀ d ìda da sa st’ɔ̀gna u nàs
“You go ahead,” I say, “I’ll go and get dressed up here,
64664: i tugàva ža dòjda tugàva tɔ̀rnah uttàm am vìka
and then I’ll come”. So I set out from there. “But,” he said,
64668: u nàs ìma mòmi i junàcɤ ta gl’ɔ̀daj vìka
“there’s [many] girls and ‘heroes’ (= boys) at our place. Make sure,” he said,
64672: kàk ža vlɛ̀zeš òti svàta mi g’òrgi gu nìkuj nè e vìg’el
“that you enter [properly, as did Georgi], because nobody saw my ritual kin Georgi
64688: i nìkoj ma ne vìg’e hùbavu ama gà vlɛ̀zuh kàk da flɛ̀za
and nobody saw me. Fine, but when I went to go in, how can I go in?
64692: tò trì gudìnɨ sɤ sme nè vìdvɤlɤ mèn me hèm sràm hèm stràh
We hadn’t seen each other for three years. I was both ashamed and frightened.
64696: tugàva utìduh u s’èstra mu i tà mɤ fɤvèdɤ
So I went to his sister’s, and she took me in.
64700: kàk se sme zdravòvɤlɤ nemòj pìta utèkuha m učìte ut sràm
Don’t ask me how we greeted each other.  My eyes were swollen up from shame.
64704: Is it kindling that you call it?
64709: Did they use it for light?
64711: e kàk se svèteše sɤs nèja
So how did you get light from it?
64717: n’èmә n’èmә nә ugìnә nәàkәme drɤvà i
No, no. We piled wood on the fire and …
64722: … and you light it with the kindling and …
64730: We lay – we lay a fire in the hearth …
64735: Whoever has something to do today …
64744: … and we’d light it with the kindling …
64746: i kòjtu kvò si ìskә prài
64748: … and we’d get warm and have light.
64751: dobrè ako tr’àbva da večèr’ate na tàja svetlinà li
O.K. And if you need to have supper in this light?
64753: Well, [we’d do it] in this light.
64756: e a s kakvò se zavìvaxte slàgaxte oddòlu pràpak’
And what bedcovers did you have? Underneath you put woven ferns,
64764: mi udgòr’ lè si vnesèš zәvivàlә haš’ì
Well, for on top didn’t you bring [with you] some bedcovers, rugs?
64773: She takes [them] with her [from her parents’ home].
64775: They would bring a hundred each!
64778: dɤ̀lgu vr’ɛ̀me pu stò pәrč’ètә udnisɛ̀a ednò vrɛ̀me
[This went on] a long time! They’d bring a hundred covers each in the old days.
64781: è nә vnùkә stò i usemd’esè udnèse
[Someone] took her grandchild a hundred and eighty!
64784: e če kòlko vrème gi e pràvila t’à
And how much time did it take her to make them all?
64787: tò i e rùb’nu tò i e rùb’enu
That was her dowry, that was her dowry.
64790: ednò pu ednò màjkә i turɛ̀lә
One piece at a time, her mother put them aside …
64791: kuè mòže màjka i turɛ̀lә i
Her mother put aside whatever she could for her ...
64805: … let this woman [go] and see it.
64810: No, no. She bought [some of it] too.
64811: s’à še go vìdime s’à še go vìdime
Soon we’ll go see it, soon we’ll go see it.
64812: Also from the store, also from the store.
64815: è ìdi i kàž’i vàso ìdi i kàž’i dà vìdi
Hey, go and show her, Vasa. Go show her, let her see it.
64823: ne sè smɛ̀eš ìdi i kàž’i
Don’t laugh, go and show her!
64826: What are you laughing for? Go on!
64827: èto še dòjdem nìe še dàže i ednà i snìmka še napràim
We’ll come [too], and we’ll even take a photograph.
64834: Let them see what they’re like.
64839: i vìš’te drèite tàm kәkvì sә tugàә
Look at the clothing there, [and see] what they were like then.
64846: a dobrè a n’àkoja momà kato ne mòže da si napràvi
O.K., and if some girl isn’t able to make herself …
64861: All of them made their own.
64902: gà e dušɔ̀l i jɛ̀ tugàva uttàm nadòlu vəz adnì šᶤìpki
when he came. And I – from there downhill into some rose-hip bushes,
64904: pud adnᶤì lyvàdɤ vəz adnɔ̀ der’ɔ̀ pu terlìcɤ utìduh i skrìh se
around some meadows, into a riverbed, [all] in my socks:  I went and hid,
64908: i kòlko bàbici ìma ta pò bɔ̀rže predɔ̀t ud mèn
Ah! There are so many grannies that spin faster than I do
64912: jɛ̀ z’ɛ̀h da ne mòga da prèda
[that] I started to be unable to spin!
64913: [What do you use to reap with?]
64915: az žɔ̀na sas sɔ̀rp ama gà nèmam palamàrka
I [normally] reap with a sickle, but when I don’t have a swaphook,
64917: ta ne mòga i sas sɔ̀rp da žɔ̀na mɔ̀kna gu
then I can’t reap even with the sickle, [so] I [just] pull it out.
64918: [Срещаш ли се често със своите приятели?]
64923: nì sa čɔ̀stu sr’ɔ̀štame sas drùškise səz bàbicìse gà kurdìsame
We frequently meet with friends, with [other] grannies. When we arrange
64927: ne duhòd’a nàum da sa razg’alìm
It doesn’t occur to us to go our separate ways.
64936: gà letì dɔ̀š ta stànvat hùbavɤ gɔ̀bɤ ta berèm ama sàa gudᶤìna
When it rains, nice mushrooms come out, and we gather [them]. But this year
64942: a sùš’ɛ nìštu ne nakùsihme nìkakva gɔ̀ba nemɛ̀še sàa gudᶤìna
there’s a drought and we haven’t tasted anything. No mushrooms at all this year.
64948: muhabèk’ nə pɔ̀k’an ta pu trì sahàta sadìm
conversational get-togethers on the main road, we sit there for around three hours.
64962: əmi pu kɤ̀rəd žɤ̀n’eme kòlku žɤ̀nem žɤ̀dnɨ glànnɨ
In the fields we reap what we reap – hungry and thirsty
64967: d’èk dukətu svɤ̀ršim nɨ̀vəta də gu səberè̟me rəkòjkite də vɤ̀ržem snòpete
by the time we finish the field, gather in the handfuls, to tie them into sheaves,
64972: də gi nəstrùpəme nə sindžɨ̀r tuvà se pràeše mnògu e lòšu bèše kàto
to arrange them in a proper line – that’s what we did. It was very bad when –
64975: pə mɨ zəpòčnəə pə də mi zɨ̀mət i narè̝t nə unuvà vrème
when they started to take part of it from me for duty taxes at that time
64979: nər’àt n’àmə nìj sɨ mòeme nə nɨ̀vɨte kətu
[when] we didn’t have [anything] for duty. We used to be able to work our fields,
64983: nè̝mə kòj də də rabòtɨ drùgi čùždi òrə mi rəbòtət nɨ̀vite
but [when] there’s no one [else] to work, others, outsiders, came to work my fields,
64986: nè̝məh si nè̝məm zɤ̀rnu də dàvəm pàk kò də nəpràim
and I didn’t have any grain to give [them]. So what could I do?
64992: ama dùpkete kvò se zovèšeu u glàmu
How did they call the holes in the stony hill?
65003: jà za dùpkete se ne mòk sètim jovàn znàe
I can’t recall [anything] about the holes. But Ivan knows.
65006: [One of them is called] Stanishin hole.
65010: à ə əm hàk e sigɛ̀ če slət tvà mi b’è̝še mɤ̀čno
Well [that’s what we] deserve now. After that, I had a hard time.
65019: b’ė̀me ìkə nà svà f t’èkezes’è̝ fl’azəhme
We were – he said, in – we joined this cooperative farm,
65023: [and we thought] we were going to die of hunger.
65032: hùbuu əmà tò i ne bìlu lòš’u zə b’èhmi kɤ̀k zə ràptim
Fine. But it wasn’t [so] bad, we were – how [were we going] to work?
65037: svɨ̀knəhmi nə tvà si izlɨ̀zəme nə grùpə ràptim’e
[Well,] we got used to it. We [would] go out in groups to work;
65042: p’ejət òrətə svìrət ə če izl’àzəə məšɨ̀n’
people would sing, play music, and then these machines appeared.
65047: s’èət mə tütünə təkà sə rəsàdə
They’d plant the tobacco, and then [we’d] transplant the seedlings.
65051: əm mlògu bè̝še prekàrəhme bəjà gudɨ̀nɨ sə səs tvà
It was a lot of work, [and] we had many years like that.
65059: n’è nɨ̀kuj ne nɤ̀ trɤ̀seš’e zə dànuk ut t’eə s  t’èkəzəsè̝t
Nobody from the cooperative farm ever came to ask us [to pay] tax –
65064: mòži vɨ̀kə č’e màlku mi plàtət əmə pàk b’è̝hme duòl’ni
You can say they didn’t pay me much but still we were content
65067: nə tvà nìe nəl’ dèl’ču təkà bèše sɨ̀ne
with that, weren’t we Delcho? That’s how it was, right, son?
65073: hə i dàvəme vek’e tòj zɨ̀mət t’èkezesè̝tu tìj ə ni dàvət
Hah. So we give, the cooperative farm takes, [and] they give us [back].
65076: ama jà nè.znam ednà stanìšina ednà a u
Well, I don’t know. One [might be] Stanishin hole, another –
65081: ednà odovàm ednà ottàm mèča dùpka nèkakvo ìmaše iz ovàm
There’s one here, another there, and there was some sort of Bear’s hole here.
65087: ovàj golèmata dùpka kvò se zovèše što od ovùj strànu
How did they call this big hole, the one on this side?
65089: e pa stanìšina dùpka tàj ne è li
Well, isn’t that the one that’s Stanishin hole?
65092: tè tàm tè tùj sɤ̀k u tàm
65107: vìj ednò vrème kakɤ̀v dubìtək se glèdaše tùkə vəv vàšto sèlo
In the old days what kinds of animals did you raise here in your village?
65110: vòluve kràvi səs tèlencètə pu dvè kràvi s dvè kràvi səm imàlə
Oxen, cows with their calves. Two cows per [household]. I had two cows
65111: dvòrə i dvà vòlə məgàre sìčku ìməše
[in] the yard, and two oxen. [Also] donkeys. There was everything.
65117: nìe č b’è̝hme ə əf ədnɤ̀ kɤ̀štə trɨ̀ brà trɨ̀mə bràtə
We – we were all in the same house, three brothers,
65119: tùkə d’èt səm sə ɨž’è̝n’ilə jà trɨ̀mə bràtə f ədnɤ̀ si kɤ̀štə
here in the house I married into. Yes, three brothers in one house.
65126: nəpràihme nə edɨ̀nə bràt tàm dòlu dònətə mahlɤ̀ ədnɤ̀ kɤ̀šticə
[And] we built a little house for one brother in the lower quarter down there,
65131: stòrime tòj fəkìrə umr’è̝ i žinɤ̀tə mu i tòj
we did that. And then, poor guy, his wife died, so he –
65136: i ednɤ̀ dɤ̀šterìcə imə i tàm ž’ènetə f drùk sè̝lu
He has a little daughter, she’s married off in another village,
65142: nə krɨ̀vu.pòl’e i sigɛ̀ kɤ̀štətə s’ stvì  n’àmə hòrə f nè̝hi
in Krivo Pole. So now the house is sitting empty, nobody lives in it,.
65147: i nìe tùkə əv bàt’ə blagodərì nə svà t’èke nə tvà t’è̝kezesè
and we’re here, in my brother’s [house]. Thanks to the – to this cooperative farm,
65153: ràptehme mlògu mlàdi b’èhme mòž’ehme də ràptim iskàrəhme sɨ pərɨ̀
we worked a lot. We were young, we could work [hard]. We earned a wage
65158: nə dəšterɤ̀tə stòrime blòk uf hàskuu ut trùt
and built my daughter an apartment (in a complex) in Haskovo from that work.
65163: tütün s’èime mlògu tvà e svà segɛ̀ sme s’è̝li
We grow a lot of tobacco, we’ve just planted some now.
65167: dv’è gudɨ̀nɨ stànə dəšterɤ̀tə jə səkrətɨ̀hə ud ràptətə səkrətɨ̀hə jə
[But] two years ago my daughter was laid off from her job, they laid her off.
65173: če b’èš’e glàven sčetuudɨ̀tel sr’àdnu brəzuvàne zəvɤ̀rši če
She was the chief accountant; she’d finished secondary school and
65177: i dv’e gudɨ̀nɨ sč’etuudɨ̀tel sl’èdvə tə če jə səkrətɨ̀hə
studied accounting for two years. And then they laid her off.
65183: sigɛ̀ e biz ràptə i siɛ̀ kukò də pràime nìe
Now she’s out of a job, and what are we going to do now?
65189: ž’ə ìmə dicà t’è sə už’è̝nihə əmə s’è pàk bàbə əgà e
She’s got kids. They’re married, but still, when you’re a grandmother
65196: ìskət nəl’ɨ̀ gà dòjdət pàk tr’àvə də dəd’è̝š n’è̝štu
they want [things] when they come, and you have to give them something.
65197: n ne tr’àbvə təkà də e pək i sigɛ̀
It shouldn’t be like that, yet now it’s –
65201: kùpi mi bàbo vɨ̀kət kùpi mi d’àdo
“Buy me this, Granny,” they say. “Buy me [that], Grandpa.”
65205: ò i bàbo oh vɨ̀kə t’kiə ràpti [laughter]
“Oh, Granny, oh!” they say, and things like that. [laughter]
65209: sè utišlò du drùgijə d’àt sigè
And now [one of the kids] went to the other grandfather, and [once again]:
65210: kùpi mi bàbo kùpi mi d’àdo
“Buy me this, Granny! Buy me [that], Grandpa!”
65214: pək bàbə n’àmə utkəd’è də kùpi̥
But Granny doesn’t have any [money] to buy [anything] with.
65218: kupùvə pəmùk dàvəme ràbuti sàmu i sàmu də sè umirɨ̀
I bought cotton and such things to give them, just to cool things down.
65221: trìjset kilugràmə rɤ̀š mi dudàdi n’àmə nè̝mə utkədè də gu zè̝mə

65224: às glànnə žɤ̀nnə əmə kvòtu ìmə nərèd ni dàvəə nə unìjə gudɨ̀nɨ
I was hungry and thirsty, but in those years they required us to give as duty.
65257: dèto dèda g’òrg’a se bèše zavṛ̀l
That’s where Grandpa Georgi had wriggled [down into] –
65260: à gòre bèše pàvlova pàvlova zakàpina
65271: dèda g’òrg’a nadzṛtàl bèše sɤs ovcè pa mu pàdla kàpata
Grandpa Georgi was peering down [it]. He’d been with sheep and his cap fell off.
65274: pàdla mu kàpata òn ulèzne za kàputu
His cap fell off, [so] he went into [the hole] for his cap,
65278: pa ne mòže da izlèzne pa si sedèl tàm
and [then] couldn’t get out. So he just stayed there.
65281: pa ga onì tražìše jutròto če go nèma
And they sent a search party in the morning when he didn’t show up.
65283: imàlə səm prez živòtə sme i
65288: ... and a horse, and a mule.
65289: i kòn’ ìməme i sìčku ìməme
We also have a horse. We have everything.
65294: dvè mùl’tə səm prikàrlə dvè məgàrtə i idìn kon’
I looked after two donkeys and one horse.
65299: tugàə što sì iskàrəme zə nàs si j tugàj ìməše i dɤ̀žduve
Back then whatever we produced was ours. Back then there were [strong] rains,
65306: tìi nìvi št’u gì glèjš i nəgòre i nədòlu ògərdi ìmə
[there were] these fields that you see – up there, down there, with fences –
65313: We brought in good crops, my son.
65315: ami a s’à štò a s’à nik’ɤ̀t tə edìn nə drùk
But now, what is there? Now they don’t want it. One against the other!
65319: kòlku ə tùkə màl màlenku sèltu tə tòlku e i devolòsənu
This little village here is just as cursed as it is small.
65325: kràmuli kàrət sə nìtu tràktur pùštət də surɤ̀t də sèet
Quarrels! They fight! They won’t let a single tractor in to plow, or to sow,
65329: də ìmə ədnà kukòščinkə kət sme k’i si zèmə budnà kukòhčinkə
to have [even] a puny little hen. As we [are now], if you [can] buy some little hen –
65333: ìmə žìtu k’i si nəhràniš kukòškitə nèmə
There’s grain, you can feed the hens. But there aren’t any [hens]!
65337: fčèrə səm ut kətùnci səm kùpɨlə i pu dva lèvə
Yesterday I was – in Katuntsi I paid two levs each …
65342: It’s gotten to be two levs?!
65352: à dèset icà zèh kò nàjdi smètkə kòlku pərì sə
And I bought ten eggs. Do the math, how much is that?!
65361: tòj bèše u bunàrɤt odnèlo dà
It was by the well that it [his cap] slipped off.
65364: ò tòj e gòre gòre è na ravnìšte
Oh, it’s way, way up there. Up on Ravnishte.
65367: Where the well used to be a long time ago.
65369: gòre kvò se zovèše te tòj gòre u gorèlino nè nè
What was that called up there, Gorelino? No, no –
65374: màle mìto gòre tàm tàm tàm tàm u nàštu glàmu tòj
Ah, Mita – Up there. There – there, the one in our stony hill.
65393: bàbə n’àma pək nə kədè nəp nə pèncijkə e nɤ̀z ženà
Granny doesn’t have anywhere to go, that woman’s on a pension.
65403: dà mə zəpɨ̀š’e b’àhə n’ dàli p’èncijkətə
So let them record me! They had given [me] the pension …
65406: tvà si e tkà kò də nè e nèštu s krɨ̀vu
[Ah, OK,] it’s like that. There’s nothing wrong [with it].
65410: ut trùt znàči tytỳn sə ə iskàrvəlu èj sòe tytỳn’
… from my work, it was earned from the tobacco. From this tobacco,
65412: sə e iskàrvəlu nə nə hil’àdə i hil’adə i
came earnings. There were a thousand – a thousand and
65417: stò i pedesè kilugràmə i hil’àdə i čètɨrɨstòtɨn kilugràmə
a hundred fifty kilograms, and fourteen hundred kilograms
65421: zə p’è̝ncijə də sə uveličɨ̀ du hil’àdə i òsəmstòtin
to get a better pension, up to one thousand eight hundred
65425: i pidesè kilugràmə tvà e tytỳn’ pu dv’è hìl’ədi i dv’estə
and fifty kilograms. For tobacco, that’s two thousand two hundred
65432: a katu trɤ̀gnəxme ut sòfija b’àxa pu lèf i šijsè ejcàta
But when we left Sofia, eggs were one lev sixty each.
65437: i pu səndèndski tàm pu rəzlično [unintelligible]
Also in Sandanski, it’s different there [unintelligible]
65439: i tùk bèše təkà nəprèš pu lèf i usimdisè əmə ut
It was like that here earlier, one lev eighty. But at
65446: dàže ud juguslàvijə b’àhə dukàrəli pu lèf i dèset əh f kətùnci
They even brought [eggs] in from Yugoslavia, at one lev ten, to Katuntsi.
65453: s’à ne sɤ̀m nəkùsilə jàjce nit ni pòmn’əm utkugà
I haven’t tasted an egg in I don’t know when!
65457: a jàs e tùkə ut kòl’u bəjà pɤ̀ti səm [unintelligible] –
And from Kolyo so many times I [unintelligible] –
65458: ne pòmn’əm utkugà ne sɤ̀m jàla jàjca
I don’t remember the last time I ate eggs.
65460: dvà lèvə li ti gi fàštə tòj dvà lèvə
He wants two levs each for them! Two levs!
65462: ne mòžeš da si glèdəš kukòški
65464: m ne mòə ìməh kukòški əmə iz’èdi gì n’àštu i kràj
I can’t. I had [some] hens, but something ate them up and that’s the end.
65468: In the space of two evenings [I lost them all].
65472: ne mòže də gi zəfàtiš segà pàk
You can’t get any again now?
65475: ne mògə ni mògə s’à pidesè levə i šijsè lèvə ednà kukòškə
I can’t. I can’t. One hen now costs fifty or sixty levs.
65479: That much! Tsk tsk. That much. [It’s gotten] expensive.
65486: sərɤ̀ka i pedesè̝ znàči sərɤ̀ci̥ pu trɨ̀ m’ètrə dl’ègi
poles, and fifty [more] poles, each of them three meters long.
65490: əmə z d’àttu nɨ̀ž’ehme i nɤ̀šte əmə i sigɛ̀

66919: ə nə dvàtə d’èn’ə š ìeme u t’èvnu še ž’ɤ̀neme
And on two of those days, we’ll go out in the dark to reap.
66922: She was really wasted and faded.”
66927: t’à s’à sə upràvi kàzvə əmi
“Oh, now she’s better,” she said. But –
66930: kòlko gud’ìni d’eved’esè i trì gud’ìni e tàə bàbə
How old is that old lady? Ninety-three?
66936: d’evedes’è i trì gudìni əmə ìnəč’è e mnògu ùmnə
66947: nìšto ne sò e izumìlə gləvòtə si e sɤ̀štətà
No problem with her mind. Her head is the same,
66954: sɤ̀štijə əkòl si ì e prikàzvə si
[She’s got] the same mind, she talks [fine].
66956: dàž’e pò pòvni i ud m’ène
She even remembers more than I do.
66968: kòj ə gl’èdə kòj jə gl’edə kàko l’ènko pə t’à kàzvə
“Who’s looking after her, sister Lenko?” And she says,
66973: t’è i putsigur’ènə n’èi jàdene kàzvə suc’àl’ni grìž’i mi kàk
“They – her food is insured,” she says. “Welfare.” “But how is that?”
66978: kət vəz mòjtu vr’ème š’ ìim š’ ž’ɤ̀nim du səbàjl’e dukəd’ɛ̀
... how in my time we’d go and we’d reap until daylight, until …
66984: guvedàr pò kɤ̀sničku təkà kəde d’èset čəsò
… the cowherd [comes], a bit late, so up to around ten o’clock.
66988: i s sa pribər’èm pə kət sə premenìm dumà
And we’ll come home, and after we dress up, at home,
66992: fkɤ̀šti nìštu ni bàrəme sàmu šə izmet’èm š’e isč’ìstimè i
we don’t touch anything in the house. We’ll only sweep and clean, and
66994: tvà š’e nəpràim i š’ə iz pràim si ùbəvi jàden’ètə

67006: We used to have it really well,
67008: seà tùkə nə tuvà s’èlu ìč nè e ùbəvu
[but] now in this village here it’s not nice at all.
67009: a kakvì bànici kàk se prài bànica
And what sort of banitsa? How do you make banitsa?
67011: à kàk se prài mi mi bànicə š’ə tùriš sìrence
Hah! How do you make it? Well, for banitsa you’ll [first] put in cheese, ...

67017: Well, yes, I wove. How [could I not]?
67032: nə stan kàk golèm li e kažì kàk e stanɤ̀ kakvì sə čàsti
On a loom. How – is it big? Tell me what the loom is like? What are its parts?
67045: ... and the foot pedals. And you weave!
67047: əmi kažì mi nè če ne sɤ̀m vìždələ
Well, but tell me [how], since I’ve never seen.
67054: əmə ne mì e klàden stanò lanì də b’èše dušlà
Well, my loom isn’t set up. If you’d come last year, [when]
67059: the loom was ready [to go], I could have gone in [the house] …
67064: So tell me. (answer shows confusion of “tell” and “show” in dialect meanings)
67066: seà ne mì e nə s kurdìsən stənò
But my loom isn’t set up now.
67070: š’ə gu kòrdisàm əmə pò nətàtək
I’ll be setting it up later.
67075: e segà kàt priberèm š’e gu kòrdisə i stanò
Now when we finish the picking, I’ll set up the loom,
67079: i š’e tɤ̀kə š’ im š’e nəvlàč’im vɤ̀lnətə
and I’ll weave. We’ll go and we’ll card the wool.
67082: š’e jə ispredòt i tàm si ispredòt
They’ll spin it. They do the spinning there.
67085: jà tùk si a pred’èf sè nèə gudìni əmə vèk’e
I used to spin it all here in years past but now
67091: še à pr’ed’èm tàm nə dəràcite̥
... we’ll spin it on the carders.
67096: And then we’ll bring it here ...
67100: š’e ja ìstəkàm də sə nàjde tkànu [laughter]
... and weave it up, so as to have fabric. [laughter]
67109: We washed it in the spring, and –
67112: òb’asni i kàk se čèpka i kàk sa
Explain to her how you card, and how –
67115: kàk sa predè tàm kàk vrɤ̀zvəš kədèl’kətə
how you spin, how you tie [the wool] onto the distaff –
67126: icà kvàsenu ml’eč’icè š’e i màlku sòdič’kə š’e spùsneš’
... and then eggs, yogurt, and you’ll add a little soda ...
67137: And [there’s] already a bit of oil there –
67143: [laughter] šərlàn i š’ə spùsnem š’ə gu nərɤ̀sim listòtu
[laughter] [Yes,] oil. And we’ll put – we’ll sprinkle it [over] the leaves,
67149: š’ə ja nəvìjm š’ə ja nəredìm f tepc’ɤ̀tə pudmàž’em šərlànče pòveč’ke
we’ll roll it up and arrange it in the pan, baste more oil on it –
67157: pudmàž’em ì š’e se ispeč’è udgòr šə jə umàž’iš’ màlku vudìč’kə
We’ll baste it and it’ll bake. You baste it on top with a little water [mixed]
67169: əmi ut p’èncijàtə p’èt stutìni i spìrət
“Well, from her pension. They take out five hundred, and
67171: give [the remaining] four hundred to her,” she says.
67176: à pèt stutìni spìrət č’ètiri stutìni i dàvət nə nèi si
So they take out five hundred and give four hundred to her.
67179: jà dùm è əmə izl’èlu ùbəvu vr’ème dùməm
“Well,” I say, “Haven’t we come upon nice times?” I say.
67182: štòm təkà i jàz dùməm s’à š’e jàm š’e pìjə
"Since it’s like that, I too,” I say, “will eat and drink,
67183: stànə li stàrə dùməm i jà š’ ìdə zə suc’àl’ni grìž’i
[and] when I get old,” I say, “I’ll go on welfare too.
67188: n’èmə də ìməm kòštə č’ètiristòtin l’èvə š’e dàam zə kvərtìrə
I won’t have a house [but if] I pay four hundred levs for housing, and ...
67192: p’èt stutìni də mə ràn’ət i š’e ž’ìv’ə
… five hundred for them to feed me, then I’ll live …
67198: tàmkənə məjtàp ja fàtəm fàtəm ja nə məjtàp l’ènka
… there!” I’ll make fun of her – I’ll make fun of Lenka!
67202: òti jə sə dàli nə suc’àl’ni griži wòt ne sì i gòtv’ət t’è
Why did they put her on welfare? Why don’t they cook for her?
67206: əmə tòj bɤ̀lgərɨ̀nə izl’àl sɨ̀len nədvɨ̀l tùrcite tùrckite pehlivàni
So he, the Bulgarian, came out strong and defeated the Turks – the Turkish wrestlers.
67209: šte stàne kato ednò vrème nàči pàk da təkɤ̀t xòrata da
It’ll be like the old days, people will start to weave again, to …
67215: kòj še təč’è nìj šə umrə̀ nìj zə umr’è̝me
Who’s going to weave? We’re going to – We’ll die.
67217: da hòd’ət po ìzvorite za vodà
… to go again to the springs for water.
67221: There isn’t anyone left to weave.
67222: There isn’t anyone left to weave.
67225: tìj ni znàjət mlàtte də təčɤ̀t jà
These young people don’t know how to weave.
67228: tàm i e pò ubàvu kàzvə ràn’ət i sə upràvilə kàzvə
“She’s better off there,” she says. “They feed [them] and she got better,” she says.
67232: upràvilà sə i seà šə si òtkə
“She got better, and she could [just] leave.”
67234: òt tè sə si s’è skrɤ̀ndzi n’èmə nìštu də i dədɤ̀t
Because they are all misers and they aren’t going to give anything [for her].
67238: wòt n’èmə də i gòtv’ət sìnuvèt’u vìd’uvàt č’e ž’ènitè mi
Because they won’t cook for her! Her sons see that their wives –
67243: t’è zə t’èh ne mòž də si nəgud’òt zə məž’ètu
they can’t even look after their husbands,
67247: tə š’e uddel’òt č’inìi i zə stàrətə nəlì
much less put aside some plates [of food] for the old woman!
67252: pə sàə i e ùbəvu kàzvə
And now she says she’s fine.
67260: tìjə gu nəmràzili reklìli kɤ̀k tɤ̀j li ne
They took a hatred to him and said, “How could this [happen]?
67265: tr’àvə də mu si udməstɨ̀me kɤ̀štə̥tə m bɨ̀lə tàm nəkrəj s’è̝lu
We have to have our revenge on him.” His house was at the end of the village.
67270: ìməl n’àkəvi dicà mòmč’eto sə bɨ̀lu už’è̝nilu sə
He had some kids (the boy had gotten married),
67276: i t’è̝ gu nɨpànnuvət tùrcit’e n’ègə n’àməlu
and the Turks attacked [the house], but he wasn’t there.
67278: They set fire to his house.
67280: zəpàlili mu kɤ̀štətə i pək tòj kəd’èt e bɨ̀l n’àkəde
They set fire to his house, and he, since he’d been elsewhere
67285: e bɨ̀l izl’àl n’àməlu gə gàt sə vɤ̀rnel
(he’d gone out, he wasn’t there), when he came back [and saw]
67291: kɤ̀štətə mu izgur’àlə  tòj tugàvə sə jədòsəl i stànəl voevòdə təkɤ̀vu
his house all burnt down, he got angry and became this rebel leader –
67299: n’è həjdùtɨn səberàl č’ètə tùkə ùž
[No,] not an outlaw. He gathered this band of warriors here, supposedly,
67303: s revərvòl tùkə mùglə də kàžem
with guns there in, let’s say, Mugla.
67311: mlòg gudɨ̀nɨ živ’àl tə č’e ùž č’e umr’àl č’àk kəd’e
He lived a long time, and supposedly he died as far away as –
67314: kò gu sə premàzali ə təkà də umr’àl kə f smòl’ənsko
they trampled him – in short, he died in the Smolyan area.
67316: lènče kàk sə kàzvə tvà be kàk bə ràkjuvu li
What’s the name [of the place], Lenche? Was it Raykovo?
67330: a tò kràl’u vùjvòda šte e uttùkə nəgà v’è̟ke nəlì ti kàəm
Yes, Kralyo the rebel leader, that’ll be it. And from here. Didn’t I tell you?
67333: tùrcite kəd gu nəpànnəli təkà i tòj v’è̝ki tùkə səz žinɤ̀tə mu
When the Turks attacked him, he was still here with his wife.
67336: ike kɤ̀štətə mu izgur’àlə tòj sə màhnəl uttùkə
[But] when his house burned down, he got out of here,
67337: i sə səberàl s ednɤ̀ č’ètə i tvà zə tvà
and got together with a band. And that’s why
67339: they gave this name [to the village].
67345: Kralyo the name of that leader.
67347: That I know (for sure) [from] my grandfather.
67355: səs šərlànč’e š’ə jə pulùpiš da odm’èkne i də vìš
with oil, and cover it so it gets soft. And then just see
67358: Mmm! And how long does it bake?
67364: On a fairly strong flame, you know?
67369: kət pucərven’èe izgòr’ kurìč’kətə du dòlu š’e ubɤ̀rneš tvà
When the crust on top browns through, you turn it over.
67374: i pə ədnò vr’ème bè dòjdi ž’ɤ̀tvə mòjtə màjkə eš’t səbìrəhme
And in the old days, oh! When it came to harvest, my mother would gather up
67381: ərgàte ìməhme bəjà ž’ɤ̀tvi t’èški ž’ɤ̀tvi wòti bràtetu ufč’èr’ə
workers. We had a lot to harvest, difficult harvests because our brother shepherds ...
67385: turòt nìvite stàvə mnògu ž’ità t’à kət ìde də ž’ɤ̀ne
... had fertilized the fields, and there was a lot of grain. And when she went to reap,
67388: i sɤ̀rpə truš’èš’e pu dvà sɤ̀rpə struš’ɛ̀vəš’e nə nìvətə
her sickle would break. She’d break two sickles per harvest on the field –
67397: mnògu i təkɤ̀j kətu zəž’òneme t’à kətu pusəber’è màlku ərgàt’e
A lot. So when we’d start the harvest, and when she’d gathered a few workers,
67401: svər’àvə bòp svər’ènə vəsùl’ ispeč’è ədnò jàgn’e
she’d cook up boiled beans and she’d roast a lamb.
67404: bòp bòp š’e ispeč’è bòp š’e svərì
And beans – she’d bake beans, [that is] she’d boil beans.
67408: əmi təkì ràbuti kət nəpràvi enì ùbəvi jàdenètə bànicə š’e nəprai
Such things. When she made these nice dishes, like [when] she’ll make banitsa,
67410: t’à càlə nòš’ n’èmə də zəspì š’a gòtvi
she wouldn’t sleep all night. She’d [just] cook.
67415: i kət udnes’èm s kòš’uve nə ərgàt’etu
And when we carry it in baskets out to the workers, v...
67418: i tə tìə tɤ̀rčeə u nàs də ədɤ̀t i də pìjət
... they’d run up to us to eat and drink.
67423: š’e zətrìjmi misìr mòmč’etàtə sìč’ki u.dumà frèt še dòət
We’d shell the corn. All the boys, everyone in the house, they’d all come
67428: š’e č’ùkət š’e trìjət nàšə màjkə še mi nəprài bànici
to break and shell it. And our mother would make them banitsa
67435: kumpìr’ š’e mi svərì nìe ùbəvi kumpìre imàhme frèt tɤ̀rčəə
She’d cook them potatoes. We had nice potatoes. They’d all rush
67439: u nàs də ràbut’òt tə ədnò vr’ème b’èš’e èm lòš’u èm i ùbəvu
to work for us. Back then it was both bad and good.
67442: Well, all times are like that!
67444: Both the bad and the good.
67446: èm lòš’u èm ùbəvu ùbəvu b’èš’e
Both bad and good. It was good [for us],
67449: nìe si b’èhme mlògu vəzmòžni fəf nàštu s’èlu
we were very well off in our village.
67454: mlògu vəzmòžni wòt təkà nəlì turò kàrə də ìməš’
Very well off, because, as they say, fertilize so as to have.
67456: [That is,] if you put down manure, you’ll have [what you need].
67461: wòti turìhme gi nìvič’kìte i ìməhme sìč’ku
Because we fertilized our fields, and so we had everything.
67464: sìč’ku si imàhme ə kòj ne gì tur’èš’e
We had everything. But he who didn’t fertilize ...
67471: dà vrème da se gòtvi ami mnògo ùbəvu tùkə
Yes, [you need] time to keep it up. [Ah,] it’s really beautiful here.
67473: ùbəvu mnògu e ùbəvu tùk də ìmə vòdə znàš’
It is nice, very nice. If there were water here, you know,
67475: what a rich area this would be!
67483: zət kɤ̀štətə ìmə ednà grədìnkə ednà gudìnə pùsnəə vòdə
In back of the house there’s a garden. One year they brought in water
67493: t’à ne mòž də ə priber’èš
67496: tə bòp li si ne nə nəkòcəh də si nàprəə burkàne
What I didn’t manage! I chopped beans to make preserves,
67499: tə dumàti li nè tə pip’èrki li misìrč’e stànə mi
and tomatoes, and peppers; and the corn came in fine. Everything!
67501: sìčku sòlč’inkə grədìnkə əmə t’à ni b’èš’e kət kràvə
A garden this big – well, it was like a cow to us.
67506: pə seà sùš’ə pàk pàk berek’èt’ pà màlku ìmahme
But now there’s a drought. Even still we had a few crops in.
67510: pà imàhme ne sm’è bez ìč’
We had a bit, so we’re not totally without.
67511: Let’s hope all will be O.K.
67515: pà ìš’əlà dugudìnə bàr də ìmə dɤ̀š’
If Allah wills it, next year at least to have rain.
67517: sàə gudìnə vèk’i kəkò b’èš’e b’èš’e
This year is done already. What’s done is done.
67525: nə rudànč’e seà nə rudàn v’èjk’e
[I use] a spinning wheel now. A spinning wheel already!
67528: òb’əsni i òb’əsni i kàk ti e bilò
Explain it to her. Explain to her how it used to be for you,
67531: i stàroto i nòvoto sìčkoto i òb’asni
both the old and the new. Explain everything to her!
67537: nə seà pò nəpr’èš nə vərt’ènu nə kul’èntu ž’ùr
Not now, but earlier – the spindle on your knee, whirr!
67541: And I’ll make the thread [that way].
67546: š’e gu nàvərt’ə vert’ènutu i š’e a nàpraa
I’ll twirl the spindle, and I’ll make it [like that].
67550: ə pə seà nə rudànč’etu vɤ̀rti i pùskəj
But now [I put it] on the spinning wheel. It goes round and gives out [thread]
67557: i sə nəprìdət məkərìč’ki nəprìdət se məkərìč’kit’e i š’e gi ugòneš’ li
... and it spins onto spools. It spins onto spools, and you’ll twist it
67562: ud ədìn kàt li kàktu ku təč’èš kilìm ud ədìn kàt
as needed, as a single thread if you’re weaving a flat-weave rug, ...
67566: ku təč’èš ə š’əltè ud dvà kàtə
... [or] as a double thread if you’re weaving a quilt.
67569: šə gu uluvìš še gu umàəš’
You’ll wind it up and beat it, ...
67574: i šə gu vàpcəš vèk’e kəkò ìskəš əku e b’èlu
... and then you’ll dye it, whatever [color] you want, if it’s white –
67576: And do you do the dyeing?
67582: ku ìskəž də dòjdeš dumà də vìdiš kəkì təkàni ràbuti ìməm
If you want, come to the house to see what things I’ve woven.
67592: ìməm i tkànu bəjà tkànu nə mumàtə ìməme
I have lots of woven things, we have things woven as girls.
67597: jə jə jə jə a boì otkədè gi zèmaš
Yes, yes, yes, yes. But where do you get your dyes from?
67602: a takà li a ednò vrème pràvat ot trevà li
Is that right? And in the old days did they make them from herbs?
67608: We used to buy them from the store.
67616: e s’à bujədìsuvàme nèjde ud òrei
But now we sometimes make dyes from walnuts.
67620: ud òrei bujədìsvəme ut kàmen bujədìsuvàme
We make dyes from walnuts, we make dyes from stones –
67626: ut kàmen nədɤ̀rpuvàme kàmenìč’evu i si gu izvàrim izvàrimè i
We pick lichens off of stones, and boil them up. We boil [them], and
67632: s’ètn’e putàp’əme pr’èlutu pə də vìdiš kəkòf krəsìf cv’èt stàvə
then we soak the yarn [in it] and you should see what a pretty color it gives!
67653: ud òreòvu təkà bujədìsu̥vàme pə ìnəč’è si kupòvəme bujà
… from walnuts. We’d make those dyes. Otherwise we buy colors
67657: from the store, and we buy them from gypsy women.
67661: And do you have a lot of sheep?
67664: seà ìməm bəjà si ufč’ìci dvàese òfci ìməm
Now I have quite a few little sheep. I’ve got twenty sheep.
67670: əmə n’èəme s’ènutu ni e màlko furàš’ əm i kupòvəmè gu
But we don’t have – we’ve [only] got a little hay, and we have to buy fodder.
67680: i n’èmə mòž’em də gi pr’ekàrəme
… and [still] we’re not going to be able to get [them] through [the winter].
67686: tə dùməme š’ə gi rəsfɤ̀rlim ufcètu še gi màhneme
So we’re thinking of giving the sheep away – we’ll get rid of them.
67688: c a ednò vrème pòveče òfce ìma li
Tsk. And in the old days were there more sheep?
67693: ednò vr’ème imàš’e pòveč’e sek t’èkeskite kəd b’èə
Back then there were more. Now the cooperative farm people came,
67698: ə pə ədnò vr’ème si imàhme dàž’e pò màlku
But in the old days we had even fewer.
67700: s’à tìjə təkà puzəsəbràhme gi əmə n’èmə gi kàrəme
Now we’ve gathered up these few but we can’t keep them.
67710: nə sò nəìməme də mi pràvi ìzmet mə də tɤ̀rčəm pu t’eh
We can’t take on all the trouble to run after them.
67712: c è dà a kogà se strìže òfce po kogà
Tsk. Yes. So when do you shear sheep? When –
67717: əmi fəf pròl’et se srìž’i kəm pɤ̀rvi màj
Well, in the spring. We shear [them] around May 1st.
67722: ut pɤ̀rvi màj s’ètne sə srìž’ət ufc’ètu kəm pɤ̀rvi màj
The sheep are shorn from May 1st on, [starting] around May 1st.
67724: When we begin to do the churning, at that point.
67734: You knock it down, and tie its legs.
67739: Two [that is,] four legs, like this –
67747: č’ètirite nògi təkà še gi vərz’èš
You tie up all four legs like this …
67756: i jə kùtniš’ i t’à še sidì mirnu
And you throw it down and it’ll sit there quietly.
67758: i tì səs no s məkàze
And you [do it] with – with shears.
67767: [Of course] it will, since it’s tied down!
67777: kò š’ə prài vɤ̀rzənkà e i təkà sidì srìž’iš’ jə
What’s it going to do [indeed]! So now, tied up, it sits there, you shear it,
67779: and then we wash the wool.
67784: tə n’èməše vòdə òdilì sme v bəlkàn’ə
There wasn’t water [here so] we went up into the mountain woods
67794: tàmkə sme bilì seà sàa pròl’et è nəkàč’ime kəzàn’ə kupàn’ə
We were up there now, this spring. We loaded up a cauldron and a trough –
67798: i sìčku nəkàč’ihme vəlnɤ̀tə s č’uvàlč’etàtə tə tàm
we loaded up everything, the wool in bags, and then
67801: v bəlkàn’ə isprà jə dòjdəə i dəšterìte səs m’ène
I washed it up there in the mountain woods. My daughters came with me
67809: pumògnəà mi ispràhme jə pučìnəhme tàm pujàdəhme nə stud’ènə s’ènkə
and helped me. We washed it, and rested and had lunch in the cool shade.
67817: i si dòjdəhme tùvənə isuš’ìhme jə seà t’ut’ùnč’etu pribràhme
And we came back here and dried it out, and now we’ve picked the tobacco
67822: seà še a təkòvəme seà še jə pòč’epkàm əf č’èpkətə cɤ̀rnətə dàže
and now we’ll deal with it, I’ll card it with the carder. The black [first]
67824: and [there’s] still a bit more white [to do].
67825: And how do you do the carding?
67828: Well, you stretch it out like this.
67835: č’e kuèt ne mòž’e i nə dəràci̥ti̥
And what you can’t [manage like that], you [do with] the carders.
67840: I have these carders [that I use] sitting down.
67846: I sit down, and stretch it, stretch it out – and they card it.
67854: And it comes out [laughter] – the wool.
67856: tì ottùka li si ot òreše
Are you from here, from Oreshe?
67858: I’m from Oreshe. Where [else would] I be from?
67861: e tùkə stàr čuvèk e tòo mòž də ti kàže mnògu ràbuti
This here is an old man, he can tell you lots of things.
67870: tə prekàrəme sì ž’ivòt’ə gò sme prekàrəli hm kòlku gudìni səm vèke
We’ve lived out our lives, we’ve lived them. So many years I’ve already –
67873: e tòs stàr čuvèk sìčku ispìtəl
This is an old man, he’s experienced everything …
67876: This life we have here – there’s …
67885: pudòben živòt’ nèmə ədnì š’e stànət
.. nothing to compare with [how bad] it [is]. Some will become …
67888: You shouldn’t talk about anything [to these people].
67892: mil’onèri pə ednì š’e umìrət òdgladi
… millionaires and others will die of hunger.
67895: nèmə də guvòriš əmə segà še kàžə zə hùbəvu
He won’t talk [badly]; he’ll talk about good [things] now.
67899: us’ètəš li ràbutə̥tə̥ ədnì sə mil’unèri pə ednì š’e umìrət òdgladi
You get the picture? Some are millionaires and others will die of hunger.
67908: petnàesti nàbur sedemdesè i òsem godìni
67911: sedemdes’è i wòsem gudìni [laughter] à təkà
67916: tì kato kato mlàt kakvò rabòteše
What [sort] of work did you do [in your] youth?
67924: bəštà mi gu ne pòmn’ə kəkòf čuvèk e bìl tòj utiš’ɤ̀l
I don’t remember what sort of man my father was. He went off
67930: màšku dètence siràč’e t’è sə utiš’lì i mnògu r’ètku sə vər
A little child, an orphan. They left, and it was rare that they returned.
67937: n’è gi istrèpəə sìckit’e i nàš bubà kəd’è gu sə utr’èpəli
They killed them all, including our dad. Where they killed them [I don’t know].
67941: t’è se ne vərnə  jà g ne pòmn’ə kəkòf čuvèk e bìl nədòlu
They didn’t come back.  I don’t remember what kind of man he was down there.
67946: i jà b ə ustànəhme vèke təkà siràč’etə ə pə
And I – so we were left as orphans.
67952: b’èvme pet šès decà hùbəvu əmə jà ustànə v’èk’e təkà na
There were five or six of us kids. Fine, that’s how I was left.
67955: u wòdeh s’è pu ràbutə pu gàteri nəgòre nədòlu s’ètne
I was always moving, [looking] for work, in sawmills here and there. And then
67960: pu zàpəs òdihme nagòr nədòlu ama pòmn’ə kəkòf ž’ivòt’ imàše nəpr’èt
we went to the [military] reserves. I remember what life was like before.
67965: pə i seà pòvnim kəkòf ž’ivòt’a ə pə dnò vr’èm’ə
And I remember now too what life is like. And also back then –
67972: e tvà kvòtu gu kàzvə isùs hristòs vəv bìblijàtə trìte slɤ̀ncə
Now there’s this thing that Jesus Christ said in the Bible [about] the three suns –
67975: [unintelligible] tòj si e bìl nàj pràf čuv’èkə
[unintelligible] He was the closest [of all] to the truth.
67978: nə bìblijàtə trìte slɤ̀ncə kəkvò e pìsəl tòj nə zem’òtə
What he wrote in the Bible about the three suns: this one to the earth,
67979: tòj pàdnə nə zem’òtə dè tòj pàdnə nə zem’òtə
this [other] one fell down to the earth, and this one fell down to the earth.
67986: š’e pàdne čeverè červènətə zvezdà nə neb’ètu i še utròvi mur’ètu
A – a red star will fall into the heavens and it will poison the sea.
67990: kujè e mur’ètu n’è sme nəròdə naš’ š’e utròvi
What is the sea? It is we, the people. We will be poisoned.
67996: š’e vi t’èrət kàa gòrnətə rìzə gòrnətə rìzə jə dàjte
You’ll be asked, he says, for your upper garment. Give [over] your upper garment,
68001: wòd gòrnətə rìzə zem’òtə nəli zèa zem’àtə kumunìzmə de
because the upper garment is the earth. Didn’t communism take the earth [from us]?
68007: še vi tèrəd dòlnətə rìzə dòlnətə rìzə ku jà dədète
You’ll be asked for your lower garment. And if you give over your lower garment,
68011: kàzvə həlèl isùs hristòs tòj bìl vəskrèsnət ut dž’ihnèmə e bilò
it says, all be forgiven. Jesus Christ was resurrected from Jehennem, that’s how it was.
68013: še vi tèrət kàzvə gòrnətə rìzə kàzvə gòrnətə
You’ll be asked, he says, for your upper garment. The upper –
68019: əku jə dəd’ète kàzvə gòrnətə rìzə vèčnijə wògən š’e vɤ v ugurì
If you give the upper garment over, he says, the eternal fire will burn you up.
68027: ve vèčnijə wògən šə vɤ̀ gurì vèčnijə wògən dž’əhn’èmə
You’ll burn in the eternal fire. The eternal fire, Jehennem.
68038: i tvà demèk əku kàž’eš’ nèmə gòsput’ n’è əku kàž’em n’èmə əlàh
And that means if you say, “There is no Lord” – No, if we say, “There is no Allah,”
68041: vəv dž’əhn’èmə sme ə tè samu zbɤ̀rkəə ədnò
we are in Jehennem. They did one very wrong-sighted thing
68045: č’e zətvòriə č’èrkvite zətvòriə i dž’əmìjti
[in that] they closed the churches, they closed down the mosques.
68049: tàm zbɤ̀rkəhə tàm zbɤ̀rkəhə də ti kàžə əč’ìk às [laughter]
They did badly there, they did badly there, I tell you openly!
68053: kàži segà tì si vinòven jà səm vinòven nəlì pu iskàzuvàn’etu̥
Tell me now, are you at fault, am I at fault – in the way we talk [to each other]?
68057: a ovoštàrstvo rabòtil li si ovòški
And did you work at fruit-growing? In orchards?
68072: kòlkut smi ìməli pràexme mərməlàt sl’ìvi pistìl
... to the extent that we had [fruit]. We made marmalade, plums, fruit leather –
68078: pestìlə tòj ot kvò se prài
[Ah,] fruit leather. What do you make that from?
68086: ə pistìlə z’èmə sə t’è ìməše idnì təvì gulèmi təvì bəkɤ̀reni
[For] fruit leather you take – these - there were these pans, big copper pans [that hold]
68090: pu trìstə trìstə i pidisè kilugràmə səbìrət pək ìmə i pò gul’èmi
three hundred or three-hundred fifty kilos each. And there’s even bigger ones,
68094: əmə sr’èdnu t’ès kuìt gi ìməši pu s’èlu
but [we use] an average one, like those they had around the village.
68101: ə z’èmət sa slìviti nəsìpvət sә̥ təvɤ̀tə sə nəpɤ̀lvə sə iskəvər’àvə
So you take the plums and pour them out, filling up the kettle, and cook them.
68105: prài sə c’àlu ugnìšti zə təvɤ̀tə t’à sə slàgə təvɤ̀tə udgòri
You prepare the entire hearth for the kettle, and put the pan on top
68111: nə ugnìštu i vèči nasìpvət slìvite zəpàlət ògən’ə
of the hearth, and then pour in the plums, and light the fire.
68115: i tàm zət ìmə zəstruèni kəm nə stànčef.xàn i xòd’ət tàm
There are some [facilities] built over towards Stanchov Han, and people go there.
68121: tò eptèm bəjà cèntər tò krəj n’ègu ìmə tàm mnògu silà nəgòri
It’s quite a large center, there’s lots of villages in the area higher up …
68129: krə̀j stànčif.xàn n’àkulku ukulu čàs i pulvìnə dvà čàsa
… near Stanchov Han. [So] for a few – about an hour and a half or two hours –
68133: putklàvə sə slàp ògən slìviti sə pupàrvət
you set the fire low, and the plums steam,
68139: i pòčvət da pùštət i t’è sòk sòkə sə kàzvə vəràk
and begin to release juice. They – the juice is called “varak” (juice concentrate).
68145: n’èštu kətu sigàšniti siròpi kuìt sà ìma ud vìšni ut slìvi
Something like the syrups there are now from [sour] cherries and plums.
68148: That sort of thing – a concentrate.
68155: mnògu slàtku i dicàtə nàj ubìčəhmi tùj kət stàni vəràkə
It’s very sweet, and we kids liked it most of all when the concentrate was ready,
68159: səs kipčètə ši ìdət ši gr’èbnət ši nəl’èjət tàm
and they would go to scoop it out with ladles and pour it
68164: vəf n’àkui kànči təkòvə i nìi pìem i sə ràdvəmi
into some sort of mug. Then we drink it and are very happy.
68169: kətu v’èči z’èm’i òšt’e pòviči də stàni vəràkə
And when there gets to be more concentrate,
68174: tә̥kà də sə sl’ègnət slìviti pòčvə sə bɤ̀rkə
such that the plums settle, you start to stir it.
68179: bɤ̀rkə sə rəzbɤ̀rkvə stàvə nə kàšə
You stir and stir it all until it becomes a mush.
68183: kət stàni slìviti kət stànət nə kàšə sìčkiti ìmə idnì spec’àlnu n’èštu
When the plums get – when all of them get to be mush, there’s a special thing:
68188: kətu təgàr mu kàzvət pək ə dərmòn mu kàzvət
they call it a “tagar” (sieve), or they call it “darmon” (big sieve),
68195: The bottom of it is copper, with little holes.
68201: They pour this mush from the –
68206: tuvà ut ə təvɤ̀tə sìpvət vəf təgàrə
Um – they pour it from the pan into the sieve, [which is placed]
68211: nəd idnò bùri precèždə sə tə də pàdnət kustìlkiti̥
over a barrel. It strains through and  so that the pits fall out.
68216: kət pàdnət kustìlkiti sa vrɤ̀štə ubràtnu pàk vəf təvɤ̀tə
After the pits fall out, you return it back to the pan,
68221: i sa vrì v’èči dukətu ə dukòlkutu ìskəž də gu zgəstìš
and it boils until it’s as thick as you want it to be.
68226: pək ə pistìlə pistìlə sə pràjət pustàfki nə məgàrətə i dɤ̀ski
Now for fruit leather, for fruit leather you make racks – boards on a sawhorse,
68235: nə xərmànə nəred’èni məgàreətə i dɤ̀skiti i pistìlə
boards on sawhorses arranged on the threshing floor, and the fruit leather –
68239: ə kətu stàni nə kàšə də gu pricid’ɤ̀t ni gò vrɤ̀štət
after it turns to mush and they strain it, they don’t put it back
68243: də gu vər’ɤ̀t v’èči emi nəlìvət nə dɤ̀ski̥ti̥
to boil any more, but rather pour it out onto the boards.
68251: dn’èskə nəl’èjət idìn r’èt sìčki̥ti dɤ̀ski də kàem dvàes trìis dɤ̀ski ìməš
Today they pour out one row on all the boards, let’s say you have twenty or thirty boards.
68255: kòlku dɤ̀ski si slòžil nəpràiš sm’ètkə də gu zəl’èiš
[So depending on] how many boards you’ve laid out, you calculate [how much] to pour.
68260: zəlìvəš idìn r’èt i gu ustàjət də sɤ̀xni priz din’ɤ̀
You pour out one row, and they leave it to dry during the day.
68265: cèlijə d’èn sɤ̀xni tùj ubiknuv’ènu stàvə sùtrin c’èlijə d’èn sɤ̀xni
it dries throughout the whole day. This usually happens in the morning. It dries all day.
68269: nə drùgijə d’èn sutrintɤ̀ sə̀štə ràbutə pulìvəš ftòri pɤ̀t
Next morning the same thing: you pour a second time,
68275: tr’èti plàs i kòlku̥tu ìskəž də gu nəpràiš dib’èlu nəlìvəš
a third layer, [and so on]: you pour as many [times] as you want to get it [as] thick [as you want].
68279: i tò isɤ̀xni na kràjə gu ustàv’ə də si isɤ̀xni
And it dries. At the end you leave it to dry.
68282: kət isɤ̀xni udl’èp’əd gu ut əmə xùbəvu tr’àbvə də isɤ̀xni
When it’s dry, they scrape it off, but it has to be really nice and dry.
68286: udl’èp’əd gu ud dəskɤ̀tə səs nužòviti lupàti si spic’àlni ìmə
They scrape it off of the board with knives – there are special paddles [for this].
68290: udlip’ɤ̀d gu i gu nəvìvə nə nə kəlbò
They scrape it off and roll it up into – into a ball.
68294: Like when they roll up [that] plastic [sheeting].
68300: navy nəvìje gu tò stàvə dòlu gòri èj tòlkus širòku
You roll it up and it gets to be more or less this wide.
68304: i nəvìvəd gu nə tòpkə i gu slàgət
And they roll it up in a ball and put it away.
68307: tòj sə zəxəròsvə i sə zəčerv’àvə i
It crystallizes and turns red and –
68309: na slɤ̀nce pàk li go ostàv’at
Do they leave it in the sun again?
68313: n’è v’èči sùxu pumištènie tr’àbvə də è i də e pruvetlìvu
No, now it has to be in a dry place and to be well ventilated.
68314: i tɤ̀j si sidì mòž də sidì i p’èd gudìni
And it stays like that. It can stay even for five years.
68317: tòj sə zəčerv’àvə udgòri sə zəhəròsvə
It gets red on top, and crystallizes,
68320: kugàt ìskəš tugàvə ši gu prudàvəš
and you sell it when you [decide you] want to.
68327: jà hìč ni sɤ̀ umur’àvəh əm sigɛ̀ ne mòə
I never used to get tired but now I can’t –
68332: sigɛ̀ ne mì sə č’ùje gləvʌ̀tə mɨ huč’ì
Now I have a hard time hearing. There’s humming in my head,
68337: šɨ̀p f krʌ̀stə tù a tekḁ̀
a bone spur in my spine, here.
68340: Lots [of things] have started to hurt.
68343: ami tò mnògo se e rabòtilo zatùj
Well, because of working so much, that’s why.
68347: d’è də znàm nə mlàdus bòl’es ne znàeh
How should I know? In my youth I never knew [a day] of illness.
68350: sɨ̀čku ràbut’ɤh i bòl’es ne znàeh
I did everything, and never knew [a day] of illness.
68354: dòktoret ìmaše li dòktore f sè
Were there doctors? Were there doctors in the village?
68356: ìməše i dòkture əmə jà ètu i sigɛ̀
There were doctors but even now I [don’t go]
68360: nə dòktur n’è sɤ̀m utišlà nè ə
to a doctor and I never went [to one], no.
68364: kakvì jàdeneta gòtvexte ednò vrème da mi kàžeš
Tell me what sort of dishes you used to cook in the old days.
68369: ɛ̀ əmi s’àkəkvi domàt’ fasùl’ dumàt’ɨ è sigɛ̀ glèj
Oh, all sorts [of things]. Tomatoes, beans, tomatoes. Look, now,
68376: gòtvim tvà sigà pup’èr’ žə up’eč’è̝m č’ə gu nədrubì
now we’re cooking. We’ll roast the peppers, then chop them up,
68380: č’ə gu vərì č’ə i dumàt’ə č’ə burkàn’ə pʌ̀l’nim
then cook them and [some] tomatoes and then put it up in jars.
68387: am f kvò gi pɤ̀lnaxte l’ùtenica pràexte li
So what did you [put] the filling in, then? Did you make “lyutenitsa” (salsa)?
68399: ìmahne kərəmànk’i̥ kət nəc’ɛ̀pim t’à kərəmànk’i kəd gi issuš’ɨ̀m
We used to have “karamanki”. When we cut them, and dry them,
68401: tì štòm si rabòtila vs’àkva ràbota znàči i i vɤ̀lna si rabòtila
Since you’ve done all sorts of work, I guess you’ve worked with wool too.
68405: ohò vɤ̀lna č’èrgi trì etɤ̀rvi i màmə rèč’ə tuvà ìməše daràcɨ̥
Oho! Wool, rugs – Three sisters-in-law! And Mom said there were carding machines.
68407: n’èmə vr’è̝me jà tòlko pərì ne dàvəm
“[But] there’s no time [to go there, and] I won’t pay that much.
68411: i zə jə uč’èpkəme tàə vʌ̀lnə krìv dəràk reče
So we’ll card this wool [ourselves, with a] slanted carder,” she said.
68417: jà fəf hàskuu nə pəzàr’ə zə z’èmə adìn dəràk i etəkà vlàč’uf
“I’ll buy a carder at the market in Haskovo.” And that’s how I carded.
68426: tùrim ənɤ̀ pʌ̀nca tùri svàri sùpə jèš
we put them in a bowl. Put it on, cook it up, and [you’ve got] soup. Eat!
68428: kvò e tovà karamànka kɤ̀k sa prài
What’s this “karamanka”? How do you make it?
68430: The “karamanki”. We have them here but –
68436: əm kərəmànkətə jà kàk sə zəla jà nə zem’ʌ̀tə
Well, a “karamanka”. Look how it’s – [look] here at the ground, ...
68445: kət jàbəlkə jàbəlkətə e ìnək pək kərəmànkətə e zəùš’enə
It’s like an apple [but] an apple is different. A “karamanka” is ear-shaped.
68449: təkà zəùš’enə kəd’èt è t’a è du bùr’et
It’s ear-like, where [you have] – that one over by the barrel,
68453: kəd’è ìmə nòu pànnəti òšte n’è e [unintelligible] ftàsənite̥̥
where a lot have fallen. It’s still not [unintelligible]. The [others] are ripe.
68455: A pear? Is it a pear?
68464: And what [dishes] did you prepare from “karamanki”?
68473: enɤ̀ t’èndžərə issušìm gi dibid’ùs sə sùhi
… a pot. We set them to dry until they are totally dry.
68475: How? All in one piece as they are?
68478: sià žə gi nəc’ɛ̀pim kəd gi nəc’ɛ̀pim i gi prost’ʌ̀
Now we’ll cut them up. After we cut them up I spread them out
68482: nətàtək sušɨ̀m təkà i t’àh issušìm gi isʌ̀hnət dibid’ùs
over there and dry them. We dry them out until they are totally dry.
68488: n’è slɤ̀ncetu̥ issušàvə gi i kəd gi issuš’ì
No. The sun dries them out. And when they’re dry,
68491: žə gi nəpʌ̀l’niš kòš li žə è kòt žə è i zìm’e
you’ll fill a basket or something with them and in the winter –
68497: nè nè tvà kat vèče kat e isɤ̀xnal
No, no. The [fruit] after it’s dried.
68499: jà səm čùl če gu vìkat ošàf
I’ve heard that they call it "oshaf".
68503: kət isʌ̀hneši pàk kətu ušàv žə gu svərìš
When it dries, then when it’s "ushaf" you’ll cook it.
68507: əhə̀ žə gu svərɨ̀š i slɨ̀vi slìvi d’èt ìməme təkà ədnò vr’ème
Yes. You’ll cook it, with plums. The plums we have. Like in the old days.
68510: i prez zìmata sàmo tovà li jad’àxte
And during the winter did you eat only that?
68516: à əm fəsul’ i bəlgùr’ urɨ̀s prài kàš’i kartòfi patləž’ɛ̀n’e sɨ̀čku
Ah [no]. Beans, bulghur, rice. [We] make kasha. Potatoes, eggplant, everything.
68519: kogà var’àxte takìva pò speciàlni màndži ìmaxte li za n’àkoi pràznici
When did you cook these special dishes? Did you have [them] on holidays?
68522: ɛ̀m əmi gà ìmə pràznik pò hùbəvə žə è səs màs
Well, when there’s a holiday, [yes.]. It’ll be nicer [to eat things] with fat;
68524: it’ll be [nicer to eat things] with – with meat chunks.
68525: [laughter] And if there’s no meat chunks?
68527: Does the village have a [particular] celebration?
68530: Well in the village – hens. Hens.
68542: krìv dəràk uddòlu drʌ̀škə i uddòl drʌ̀škə i se stʌ̀rže
A slanted carder has a handle below, [another] handle below, and you scrape [with it].
68548: i n’èskə jà zə ìzlač’ə adìn ədìn kilugràm ùtre jètərvətə zə izlàč’i
And today I’ll card one – one kilo, and tomorrow my sister-in-law will card,
68552: drùg d’è̝n’ drùgətə nìj b’è̝hme tri jètərvi i i zə gu
the next day the other one – there were three of us sisters-in-law. And [then] we’ll –
68557: zə gu ispr’əd’è̝me i pàk s’è̝tnijə d’è̝n’ pàk vlàč’im pàk pr’edè̝m
we’ll spin it, and then the following day we’ll card some more and spin some more.
68560: tɤ̀j znàči vɤ̀lnata kato ja ustrižète tì si strìgala òfci
OK. So [to get] the wool when you shear – you’ve sheared sheep, [right]?
68563: n sàm tvà ne sɤ̀m srìgələ òfce
No, I haven’t. I haven’t sheared sheep.
68567: tɤ̀j kato e e ostrìgana vɤ̀lnata zèmeš inò
So, after it’s shorn, you take one –
68568: and what do you do next?
68574: kəto usriž’èš òf vəlnɤ̀tə də zəvərìš kəzàn’e è kət segà udà
After you shear the – the wool, you boil [it in] a kettle and when the water –
68577: i fəf gul’èmi kurità i jə pupàrim kət jə pupàrim
And we scald it in these big troughs. After we scald it,
68583: zə jə isper’èm č’ɨ̀stə udʌ̀ əku n’èməš’ tùkə nə r’àkə̥tə̥
we’ll wash it with clean water – if there’s none here, then in the river.
68588: isper’èm tàə vʌ̀lnə i s’è̝tn’e č’èpkəj i s’è̝tn’e vlàči
We wash the wool, then we pick it over by hand, and then we card it.
68590: tɤ̀j kàk se čèpkə nə nə nə
Yes. And how do you pick it over it, by, by, by –
68593: təkà č’èpkəj tàə vɤ̀lnə zə ə rəsč’èpkə zə a rəsč’èp
Like this. Pick the wool over, you’ll pick it over, you’ll –
68603: oh vr’etèn:tu i pr’èšleni i zə pred’è̝š
... [you’ll take] the spindle and the weight on it, and you’ll spin.
68608: siɛ̀ t’ahnətə dəšter’à nɨ̀t e pr’èlə
Their daughter now has never done any spinning.
68614: kɤ̀k də gi nəùčiš tìjə sə tìjə sə ùčət
How are you going to teach them? These –They learn –
68615: mlàtte si sə ùčət l’i tìjə ni znàjət
Young people learn on their own, and then they don’t know [anything]!
68619: siɛ̀ nìtu i mòjtə snəhà jà n’àməm dəšter’ɤ̀ ìməm snəhà
Now, even my daughter-in-law (I don’t have a daughter, I have a daughter-in-law),
68621: nɨ̀tu i t’à znàe nɨ̀t də pridè nɨ̀t də təč’è
even she doesn’t know – neither how to spin nor how to weave –
68631: drùkte mlàtte izòpštu nìe ni mòžem vè̝ke nìj sme
… all the other young people. We can’t [do it] any more, we’re –
68636: gudɨ̀ni jà səm nə sedemdesè i ednɤ̀
68639: t’à nə usemdesè i dv’è gudìni òšte rəbòti ràbuti
She’s eighty-two, and she still does [serious] work …
68641: d’ètu sìgurnu v grədɤ̀ nə usemdesè i dv’è
… whereas city people at the age of eighty-two surely …
68644: si stujɤ̀t i i si četɤ̀t
68649: ədnò vr’è̝me əgà òšte gà b’è̝hme màl’k’i òšte gà stàneš
Back then when, when we were still little, already when you reach
68653: nə nə četirinàjse gudɨ̀nɨ ud màlkə zəfàtəš də pred’è̝š
the age of fourteen –  You start spinning [very] young:
68656: ud d’è̝set gudɨ̀ni pòčvəš də pred’è̝š vɨ̀kə də sə ùčiš
you begin to spin at the age of ten, [your mother] says you [must] learn
68660: də pred’è̝š i màjkətə ɨ̀kə ùč sɨ əgà sə už’è̝niš
to spin. [In fact] your mother says “Learn [so that] when you marry
68664: svikɤ̀rvətə də tə ni bəht’è pu rək’ìti
your mother-in-law won’t club you on the hands!”
68668: də znàeš sɨ̀čku də pràiš i də gòtviš
[You need] to know how to do everything: to cook…
68675: i də pr’əd’è̝š i də təč’è̝š’ i hl’àb də peč’è̝š’ i
… and spin, and weave, and bake bread, and
68676: sɨ̀čku də gu də znàiš də pràiš
to [do] everything. You’ve got to know how to do everything.
68679: təkà sə ž’è̝nehə hòrətə enò vr’è̝mi
That’s how people entered into marriage back then.
68683: ž’è̝n’ət sə nəuč’èni pək segɛ̀ [laughter] segɛ̀ [laughter]
They marry already having learned. But now?? [laughter] Now? [laughter]
68686: Now [a few] coffees and they’re married!
68688: They know how to go out for coffee ...
68697: sig’è təkà i kədè še mi ìde də mi rəbòt’
That’s how it is now. And where are they going to go work?
68700: də nɨ̀vətə də i dədɤ̀t i də ìde də rəbòt nɨ̀vətə
In the fields? They’ll give her work to do out in the fields?
68708: də si ubrəzòvət ədnɨ̀ kuperàcii i də məšìnte
So let them set up some cooperative farms and let the machines …
68716: trìjs i p’ètə gu četvɤ̀rtə gudìnə sə už’ènix trìjset pètə gudìnə
68723: mlàditi səs stàriti sə smèjət màj [laughter]
The young people laugh at the old people ... [laughter]
68730: tùriš si gi vəf turbìcana tùriš si hl’àpč’e za òb’et
You put them into a little bag, you put in a bit of bread for lunch,
68733: kɤ̀k se predè səs kakvò se predè
How do you spin? What do you use to spin with?
68738: vɤ̀lnətə f rəkʌ̀tə dəržìš i təkà i zə vrʌ̀tkəš i
You hold the wool in your hand like this, and you’ll rotate [the spindle] and –
68742: n’àmaxte li nèšto da slàgate vɤ̀lnata tàm da ja vrɤ̀zvate
Didn’t you have something to put the wool on, to tie it
68745: n’àmə t’à sə vʌ̀rzvə d’èt sa mùcə
No [not at all]. You tie it down [in the spot] where [you] spin-twist it –
68748: pək tàə d’èt sə zə č’èrgi t’à e təkà dib’èlə
The [wool] that is [intended] for rugs is [spun] thick, like this.
68750: aha a tàa dèt sə mùca kakvò
Aha. And the part that you “spin-twist,” what –
68753: tàə d’è̝t sa mùcə t’à ə nə hùrkə vʌ̀rzənə
The part you spin-twist, that’s tied to the distaff.
68756: hùrkə vərzàlkə s ìmə zə jə vərzè̝š i
There’s this ribbon, and you’ll bind it to the distaff and –
68759: You pull. What do you pull from the wool?
68761: zə mùcəš i zə vrʌ̀tkəš zə mùcəš i zə vrʌ̀tkəš i
You’ll spin-twist it and rotate [the spindle], spin-twist it, and rotate it –
68764: ɤ nè ja znàeh tàa dùma zamùcam
68766: That’s how I used to spin-twist.
68770: mɤk izmɤ̀kvə tr’àbvə də e tovà
(to self) It’s probably from izmɤ̀kvə (“pull out”).
68773: i kakvò se izmùcva uttàm ut tvà ut ut
And what gets spin-twisted from this, from, from –
68779: rudìx pɤ̀rvətə dəšter’ɛ̀ ftòrətə rudìh č  č’etrìstə gudìnə
I gave birth to my first daughter. I gave birth to the second one in ‘40.
68783: dv’ɛ̀ dəšterì ìməm ž’èn’eni sə i dv’ɛ̀te ut s’èlu si vòd’ət mumč’ètə
I have two daughters. They are married, both of them to boys from the village [here].
68785: ustànələ səm duvìcə nə trìjsi i p’èd gudìni
I was widowed at the age of thirty-five.
68791: i hòdilə səm pu bəjìrə kupàlə ž’ɔ̀nələ vɔ̀rhlə dərvà kàrələ
And [then] I went about the hills [working]. I dug, I reaped, I threshed, I carried wood.
68794: č’ùzdim səm hòdilə də vɔ̀rš’əm də hmi kàrəm dərvà də hmi kàrəm s’ɛ̀nu
I went [to work] for others – to thresh, to carry wood for them, to bring in hay for them,
68798: də hmi kàrəm tòrət i s č’ùzdə ràptə səm minɔ̀lə du segà
to cart around fertilizer for them – and I’ve done work for others till now,
68800: du s’ɛ̀ə gudìni segà səm nə sedemdesè i č’ètiri gudìni i
up to the current years. Now I am seventy-four, and
68805: i hòd’ə r’edòvnu hòd’ə səs ədnò mùl’ənce mùt’i̥ku im’ɛ̀h
I go out regularly. I go out with – I had [this] sweet little mule.
68809: səs n’ègə sìč’kəd’e ùlum vərš’ɛ̀h sìč’kəd’e hòd’əh
I used to thresh everywhere with him, my son. I went everywhere,
68813: sìč’ki mə rùkəhə əmə zə gin’l’ùk’ zə ž’ivòt’
everyone offered me [work], but paid by the day, to survive.
68814: [Защо ходеше да работиш на чужди хора?]
[Why did you have to work for others?]
68820: ìštəm də mi plət’ɔ̀t n’ɛ̀kuj l’èf  č’ɛ̀kə də mi dədɔ̀ n’ɛ̀kuj l’ɛ̀f
I want them to pay me a lev or two, I’m waiting for them to give me a lev or two.
68825: budnò mi dəd’ɛ̀š’e trì svìtkə slàmə zə mùl’etu i trì zə m’ène
Someone would give me three bunches of straw for the mule and three for me.
68827: mu səm càl’ d’èn’ vɔ̀rhlə ədìn tvàr slàmə səm hòdilə [laughter]
I threshed for him all day long [but] I’d gone [for only] one load of straw. [laughter]
68832: mùl’etu mi zɔ̀hə t’èkezes’è i jɛ̀ hòdih nə trùduv d’èn’
They took my mule for the collective farm. And I went to work
68839: n’ɛ̀kəv d’èn’ i rəzbul’àh sə ut sərc’è visòku krɤ̀vnu sərc’è skleròzə
one day, and I fell ill with heart disease: high blood pressure, arteriosclerosis.
68842: e segà səm esèj puč’ìvəm əmə ni mògə nìštu də ràbut’əm
And now I’m like that. I’m resting [from the farm] but I can’t do any [of my own] work.
68846: dəšter’ète mi ràbut’ət tìjə mə gl’ɔ̀dət pumàgət mi
My daughters work. They look after me, they help me.
68849: zɔ̀t’uvete mi sə hùbəvi i tìjə dukàrvət mi dərvà c’ɛ̀pət mì gi
My sons-in-law are good, they bring me wood and split it for me,
68853: gòtv’ət mi zə zimɔ̀tə kutròtu ə pò trùdnu
and prepare me for the winter [by doing the things] that are more difficult.
68859: i ednò šišè səz barkanìca i s’ìr’ɤnce nɛ̀štu takà i ìd’em ž’ɔ̀nem
and a bottle of buttermilk and some white cheese, and we go. [Then] we reap.
68872: ta gu už’ɔ̀nem vrɤ̀zvami gu na snòpɨ i gu kàrat sas mùl’eta
When we finish reaping [the grain], we tie it into sheaves, and they take them with mules,
68875: i gu napràv’at kòš’uve kòš’uve nəpràv’enu hùbavu i kòšuv’ène tugàva i
and make them into cruciforms, nicely made cruciforms, and [we take] these cruciforms –
68878: gà isɔ̀hne žìtunu hùbavu i slàmana i nasàdat tugàva na harmàn
When the grain has dried nicely, and the straw, they put them on the threshing floor,
68882: harmàn snòpenu na harmàn fpr’ègat mùl’etana i pòčvat
the sheaves on the threshing floor. They harness up the mules and start up.
68884: sas ednà k s edìn kamš’ìk’ bahtɔ̀t mùl’etana i ti varhɔ̀t varhɔ̀t varhɔ̀t
They beat the mules with a – with a whip, and they thresh, thresh, thresh
68888: dùkat stàne ž’ìtutu pàdne s’ìč’ku i pòčvat tugàva da izvàdat
until it’s done, [until] the wheat falls all out. And then they begin to pull it out
68891: səs vìli izvàd’at slàmata izmetɤ̀t hùbavu harmàna
with pitchforks. They pull out the straw, they sweep the threshing floor out nicely,
68894: i pòčvat da vejɛ̀d ž’ìtutu i udvejɛ̀d gu hùbavu i pòčvat tugàva
and they begin to winnow the wheat. And they winnow it nicely, and then begin
68897: də gu kàrat də gu nasìpvat səs krìni vəf č’uvàle
to take it off to pour it into bags with a half-bushel measure.
68898: [How do you make banitsa in the Rhodope manner?]
68902: nàj naprèš prìnesa tavɔ̀na tə č’e ja nàmaža sas màslu tə č’e
First of all I bring out the pan, and then I grease it with butter. And
68909: tugàva tùr’a kragɔ̀n i z’ɔ̀ma tuč’ìl’kana tə f ednà kùpa ràzbərkam
then I get out the breadboard and take the rolling pin. I mix it in a bowl.
68915: ta stò̝r’a tɛ̀stu tə gu ràstuč’a tɤ̀nič’ku na l’ìstu i
Then I make the dough, and I roll it out into thin sheets.
68920: tugàva tùr’a adnònu l’ìste i svàr’a r’esìl’ka r’esìl’ka urìs
Then I put one sheet [into the pan]. I boil up stuffing – stuffing with rice.
68924: tə č’e mu č’ùkna jajč’òca kòl’kunu sa pò mlòčku
Then I’ll break eggs into it –– the more [I put in],
68928: i pò hùbavč’èk je č’ùkna mu jajč’òca a č’e nàras’em resìl’kana
the nicer it is.  I break eggs into it, and spread the stuffing in the pan.
68930: i ràstuč’am i drùgu l’ìste i gu tùr’a vərhù
[Then] I roll out another sheet [of pastry] and put it on top,
68932: i gu tùr’a də sə peč’è na sòbana
and put it [all] to bake in the oven.
68941: m’ehuvè e pràehə mlògu ut òfcet ud òfč’etu m’əhuvè pràehə
They made many [containers of] skins. From sheep, they made bags of sheepskin,
68945: əmi kato e n’àmalo tenekìi sìreneto v kvò sa go dəržàli
But when they didn’t have tin cans? What did they keep cheese in?
68951: i kəd gu nəl’ɛ̀jət ə nàeš čud’èsnu sɨ̀ren’e stànvəše
and when they poured [milk into it], you should see what wonderful cheese emerged.
68954: tùr’ət mu i màlku svər’ʌ̀t ut kràvətə ml’àku kət stàne
They put a bit in – they boil some cow’s milk and when it gets
68958: pò təkɤ̀vu izvàd’ət ud m’àhə i ut tvà nətrun’ʌ̀t
to be more [like cheese], they remove it from the skin and grate off [some].
68960: tùri i ut tvà gàt tùriš stànvə
Put some of this [with other ingredients, and] when you do, it becomes [a dish].
68963: ami če tò ne n’àma li kɤ̀k səs kòsmite
But– but won’t there – What [do you do] with the hairs [from the animal skin]?
68975: tì ne mì dorazkàza za kòleda tàm minàvaxa li
You didn’t finish telling me about Christmas. Did they come by –
68978: na kòleda minàvaxa li koledàri takìva
At Christmas, did carolers and such come by?
68981: dà dà dà minàvaxa kuledàri dà i nòvәtә gudìnә
