I managed one or two tracks till evening, and took turns
73778: səs nə tè̟tkə mi nə lè̟l’ə mi mumčè̟tu̥ sme u ednɤ̀ gudɨ̀nə
with my aunt’s son, the boy who’s the same age as me.
73779: i tòj iskàrə dvà trɨ̀ òtkusə àz dvà trɨ̀ òtkusə
He finished two or three tracks, and I did two or three tracks.
73781: ònzi d’àt ti nikòlə gu nè̟mə čàk večertɤ̀ si dudè̟
And still no trace of that Grandpa Nikola of yours. He came only in the evening.
73782: i tɨ̀ čàkəj že dòe də kusɨ̀
You wait for him to come to mow [but probably in vain].
73786: kəkvò teglɨ̀lu səm iskàrələ às ud mɤ̀nenka i dù segà
What hardships I’ve been through, since I was small, and even to now.
73789: dù segà kàk me e zəbul’àlə tɤ̀j še me dubulèj
Even to now. That which has made me ill till now is going to finish me off.
73792: kàk se kàk se mèsi znàči tàm go brašnòto go dəržìte
How do you – how do you make bread? So you keep the flour
73796: vəv hambàr’a tɤ̀j li vəv g’ò  g’òz
in the barn, right, in the – in the compartment?
73800: səndɤ̀ci si ìməme spec’àlnu zə tvà
We have special chests for that.
73806: zɨ̀mət màjkite ìməhmi kurità gul’èmi utcèim gi srùnkə ìməše
[Our] mothers took – we had big troughs, we sift things – there was a sieve ...
73810: ... and then we knead the bread …
73815: What do you knead it with?
73828: A bread-trough, we call it a bread-trough.
73830: dɤ̀rven kurɨ̀tu nìj mu vìkəhme nuškvɨ̀
A wooden trough, we used to call it a bread-trough,
73833: əm hàs kurɨ̀tu e i dɤ̀rvenu
but basically it’s a trough, made of wood …
73837: ... and we put water in it.
73840: točno kàktu mu vìkəhte təkà tr’àbvə
Exactly the way you used to call it is what [we] need.
73842: hà vudà tùrime sòl tùrime i gəč’ìm
O.K. We put in water, we put in salt, and we crush it.
73848: dəkɤ̀t də sə uznuìš ùbəvə zə gəč’ɨ̀š
You crush it up real good till you get sweaty ...
73852: zə stàne l’àbə səkà də sə dɨ̀gə dà təkà
... so it becomes bread like this. So it rises. Yes – like this!
73857: jà gə dòdəh mlàdə bùlkə i č’ìč’u p’ètər dòjde
When I came [here] as a young bride, and Uncle Peter came [and said]
73862: à sigɛ̀ də ɨ̀dim dòrə mòže li l’àp də m’ès
“O.K., let’s see if Dora can make bread.”
73865: i jà m’ès’ə tùkə um’ès’ə z bràšnu n’è s udà
So I knead it here, knead it up good with flour, not with water.
73867: vm’àstu də tùr’əš udà pək tɨ̀ bràšnu tùr’əš m’ès’ə
Instead of putting water in, you put flour. So I knead
73875: i vè̝k’e tàə znòj t’è̝knə  asəkà izm’èsih gu ta up’èkəhme
and this sweat began to flow, and so I finished kneading it and we baked it.
73878: hùbəv l’àp stànə mnògu hùbəv l’àp
It was nice bread, really nice bread.
73885: ud znojtà mə mnòk səm gu izgəč’ìlə
… from the sweat! But [because] I crushed it up really good!
73890: ùbəvu səm gu izm’èsilə mlada bulka
I kneaded it up really good, young bride [that I was].
73893: I kneaded that bread really well.
73900: gredɨ̀te nə kɤ̀štətə gà prukàp’ət tugàvə bɨ̀l izm’èsen hl’àbə [laughter]
When the house beams start dripping, that means the bread is all kneaded! [laughter]
73903: gredɨ̀te nə kɤ̀štətə gà prukàp’ət tugàj i bɨ̀l izm’èsen hl’àbə
When the beams of the house start dripping, that means that bread is all kneaded –
73905: that’s what the old people said.
73908: and we crush hard when we knead [laughter].
73915: s’è̝tne iməhme hùrni pɤ̀k dè̝s’ət pitnàjset hl’àbə fàtəha
And then we had big outside ovens, they used to hold ten or fifteen loaves.
73918: hùo tovà sìčkutu si gu umèsila sìčkutu za edìn hl’àp li e
Wow. So you kneaded all that, all of that, for [just] one loaf of bread?
73925: da govòrite edìn sled drùk štòto tùka sìčku se zapìsva
… to speak one at a time? Because everything gets recorded
73926: all at once and afterwards I …
73929: i às pòsle ne mògə də
… and afterwards I won’t be able to …
73932: əm zəpɨ̀svə jà vìj ni zə rəzbràhte li
Well, he’s recording. I – you all –  Didn’t you understand?
73934: I see it, this thing is going around. [laughter]
73937: n’àmə da mòga pòsle da go sval’ɤ̀ štòt kəd guvòrət
… later I won’t be able to transcribe it because when people talk
73940: sìčkiti i n’àmə də mògə də rəzbìrəm
all at once I won’t be able to understand.
73946: a siɛ̀ ɨ̀kəm če ni zəpɨ̀svəš zətvà sə jùrnəhme utədnɤ̀š
Now I get it, you’re recording us, and we all rushed in at once.
73947: a ne [laughter] sè še ìma m’àstu za sìčkite [laughter]
Ah, no worry! [laughter] There’ll be room for all [of you]! [laughter]
73955: pək jà jà rəzbràh č’ə zəpɨ̀svə èjke
But I knew all along that it was recording …
73960: əm če tò n’àmə nìštu tàjnu f tvà səs
But there’s nothing secret about this, with –
73963: nəlì ti vi kàzəh če šə və zəpìsvəm
Don’t [you recall] I told you I would be recording you?
73966: də sə č’ùi də sə č’ùi pre̝t
So it’ll be heard, it’ll be heard, by –
73971: nìj rəspràjəme kò sme pr’əkàrəli ənnò vr’è̝me tvà e
We’re talking about how we used to do things in the old days, that’s all.
73974: əmhəm i kakvò znàči kətu sə sə nəsədɤ̀t snòpite
Right. And what does it mean to “lay down” the sheaves?
73976: Do you cut them, or not?
73983: dikàn’ətə s t’è̝ə krè̝mene udòlu i t’à vərɨ̀ ubikàl’ə càl’ d’è̝n’
… there’s the threshing board, with these flints below. It goes around, all day long …
73988: dukɤ̀tu də stàne slàmə tvà žɨ̀tu
73992: čə k səber’è̝me nə kùp gul’àm č’e vejàlkə ìmə
And we gather it up into a big pile, and there’s a winnower.
73996: əm n’è̝mə kɤ̀k də g udvè̝em nə veterɤ̀ ni mòže
Well then, there’s no way to winnow it. You can’t do it [only in] the wind.
74002: kɤ̀k də uvè̝m žɨ̀tut zərnòtu pək nìe ìməme vejàlkə
How [else] to winnow the grain, each kernel? So we have a winnower.
74006: təkà vərtɨ̀me i tvà žɨ̀tu s’ t’ič’è žɨ̀tut bəškà
We rotate like this and the grain falls out. Grain separates out,
74008: slàmətə bəškà klàs d’è̝t e ustànəlu tòj bəškà s’ t’ič’è̝
straw separates out, and the ears that are left, that separates out; it all falls out.
74013: i s’ pòsle òšte enɤ̀s sàm zərnòt privèeme i gu sɨ̀pvəme tugàvə
and then once more, we winnow just the kernels, and then pour them –
74019: f həmbàr’e ìməjme g’òzve təkà gul’èmi nəpràeni fkɤ̀šti
In the barn. We had big compartments for that, made at home.
74031: nəpràenu è təkà gul’àmu izgrəd’ènu č’ètiri
It’s made – this big, built [with] four …
74035: səz dɤ̀sk’i pregrəd’ènu pregràdi nəpràenu təka z dɤ̀ski
Fenced off with boards, you fence off [a place], like this, with boards …
74041: č’è̝tiri li sə p’è̝d g’òzə təkà təkà mu kàzvəme nìj g’òz həmbàr
… four or five compartment, that’s how we call it – a compartment [in the] barn.
74044: i pregrəd’ènu i tàm sɨ̀pvəš tvà s tùr’əš drùgutu žitò
And it’s fenced off. You pour [the grain] in there, [in] separate [areas].
74049: ečemɨ̀kə ud’èlnu kəzəldžɤ̀tə ud’èlnu nəlì nə sòrtuve nəlì zitàtə
The barley by itself, the red wheat by itself – into the different types of grain.
74053: i udèlnu slàgəš i s’è znàeš gà m’è̝liš
And you put [them] separately so you always know [what is what] when you grind.
74055: svàliš pàk m’è̝liš tàm uttàm ut əmbàrə tàm ut təkɤ̀utu
You take it and grind it, [take it] from the barn, to this –
74060: i m’èliš nə m’èlnicə i tvà ti e žitòt zə prehrànə
and you grind it at the mill. And that’s your grain for food.
74062: zə hl’àb bèš’e tvà tvà iskàrəš nə m’èlnicə
What you got down at the mill was for bread.
74071: i ž’èn’tȅ m’ès’ət fkɤ̀šti i nè
... and the women knead [bread] back home, and not –
74073: We [are the ones who] used to knead [the bread].
74078: [With] flour [that you get] when you go to the mill.
74081: dà nə ədnò zə gu m’è̝tnəš pitnàese hl’àbə
Yes. You can toss in fifteen loaves of bread at once.
74084: n’è te udel’è̝ni pu dvà kilugràmə li sə pudèleni təkà
No, they’re divided up – two kilos or so each. That’s how they’re divided.
74086: [unintelligible]  pu dvà hl’àbə pò gul’èmi hl’àbuve
[unintelligible]  Two loaves at a time, [but] bigger loaves.
74089: Whatever size we want, that’s how we divide it up.
74134: n’è̝məše m’àrkə tugàvə nə nàšijə l’àp
There wasn’t a standard measure for our bread back then.
74136: It didn’t get weighed [the way it is] now.
74148: fùrnətə upeč’è sə tòu l’àp iskàrəž gu pitnàes duši̥ pu ədɨ̀n l’àp
... into the big oven, it bakes, you take it out. One loaf each for fifteen people.
74151: kət s’è̝nnem zə ədìn dèn gu izjəd’è̝m
When we sit down [to eat] we’ll finish it off in a single day.
74156: nì b’è̝me mlògu stò i dvàjse d’èkərə ìməhme nɨ̀vɨ
We were many. We had 120 decares of land
74158: əmə p’etnàjse dùši̥ f ədnɤ̀ kɤ̀štə
and fifteen people in one house.
74169: i kakvò i pòsle kɤ̀k f fùrnata kvò ima po fùrnata
And what happens next? What about the outdoor oven, how is that set up?
74174: [For the] outdoor oven, we heat it [with a] wood [fire].
74182: i um’ət’è̝me ìməhm’ə pòm’et ut pərcàl’e nəpràen vɤ̀rdzən nə ənə̀
And we sweep out – we had this pole with rags tied onto, onto …
74187: … onto a piece of wood [making] a mop.
74189: nəkvàsiž gu nəkvàsiž gu vudà màlku
You moisten it, moisten it with a bit of water.
74199: grəbùčkə təkà nəpràenə d’è̝t də stɤ̀rže žərtɤ̀
… scraper made like this, that you [use to] scrape the coals.
74202: s’è̝tne pòm’etə pək ə pepelɤ̀ um’et’è̝
After that I sweep out the ash, sweep it out …
74206: hùbəvu i m’àtəme l’àbə upečè̝ sə
… nice and good and we put in the bread and it bakes.
74209: And then we take it out.
74213: i kɤ̀k gu razbìrate hlàbə kugà e šùpnəl tɤ̀j
And how do you know when the bread – when it’s risen?
74215: But how could we not know?
74219: tòj pučerven’è̝e fùrnətə kàk n’àmə ìmə s kəpàk fùrnətə
It browns [in] the oven! What else? The oven’s got a lid.
74226: utòrɨm kəpàkə vɨ̀dɨme əkù s puč’erven’àl l’àbə
We take off the lid and we look. If the bread is browned  –
74229: ku e mlògu puč’erven’àl svàl’əme žarɤ̀ kəpàkə sɨ̀čku dòlu i
if it’s very brown we take out the coals, the lid, everything and –
74237: a tùkə vəv stàlevo mi kàzaxa če tàm pečàli
But here – in Stalevo they told me that there they used to bake
74238: i bèz takòva i bèz fùrni
without this, without this outdoor oven.
74240: What do you mean, “without an oven”?! In a pan, maybe?
74245: [Yes, you] can do it in a pan.
74248: tr’àvə f p’è̝čkətə də sə gu p’èkəli
It must be in the stove that they would have baked it.
74250: There used to be [these] baking slabs.
74252: Not [any more], but there used to be.
74256: takòu sàčve nəl’ì pràehme ut prɤ̀s
Didn’t we used to make such baking plates out of clay?
74260: č’e e zə k nədùpiš nə ògən’ə də ugurɨ̀ də ugurɨ̀
And when you put it on the burner upside down to heat it white hot,
74263: i təgàə zə ubɤ̀rneš zə tùriš l’àbə i zə sə̥ upeč’è̝
and then you turn it over and put the bread on it to bake.
74268: zə puhlùpiš i vrɤ̀šnik udgòr ìməhme ugurɨ̀š i vrɤ̀šnikə
You cover it. We had a lid for on top. You heat the lid
74269: səz dɤ̀rvə puhlùpiš i təkà f təvɨ̀
on the wood flame, and cover [the bread]. That’s for pans.
74270: f təvɨ̀ sm’e p’èkəli əmə f sàčve ne sm’è p’èkəli
We’ve baked [bread] in pans, but we haven’t baked [it] on baking slabs.
74274: à jà p’è̝kəh càrč’evu bràšnu təkà bəkl’enɨ̀ci ìkəhme
And I used to bake with corn flour. We used to call that “bŭklenik” (cornbread).
74289: sàmu càrəvičnu bràšnu stàvə mnògu blàk
[With] only corn flour it comes out very sweet.
74294: mlògu je hùbəv l’àbə ut càrəvcə
Bread from corn [flour] is really nice.
74297: And we used to bake that in these ...
74303: èj tòlək èj kət təvà prɤ̀st’enu sɤ̀tč’e
... in something this size, like this little earthenware dish here.
74306: əhə zahl’ùpvaxte li go s nèšto ili nè
Uh huh. And did you cover it with something, or not?
74309: We cover it with – there’s a lid ….
74313: … made out of iron. [They covered things] with a lid [unintelligible].
74317: i tòj sə ugur’àvə nə ògən’ə
And it heats up on the burner …
74320: ut t’èšku ž’èlezu si ìmə drɤ̀škə
Of cast iron, with a handle.
74325: And that’s how we used to bake.
74464: nə əskèr’ə tugàf bəlgàrijə i tùrcijà sə bìli ədnò
as a soldier. At that time Bulgaria and Turkey were still the same [country].
74468: č’e ud nàšto sèlu č’etirèese dùši utìdua utiš’lì sə
And forty people went off from our village. They left –
74473: jà gi ne pòmn’a gà sə ušlì jà bef dètence dè
I don’t remember. When they left, I was a small child, you know?
74729: nòsehme pəmùkə gà gu ber’è̝me də gu issušɨ̀m i də gu vnes’è̝m
and we’d take it [there]. When we gather it up to dry it, and to take it
75000: kɤt sə užèn’əh dòjdah tùka sikɤ̀rvə mi b’èše mnògu rəbòtnə
When I married, I came here. My mother-in-law was a hard worker.
75021: jenò vrème̝ čorbədžìiti sə n’àməli mnòu gol’ɛ̀mi kɤ̀šti̥
In the old days the rich people didn’t have very big houses,
75025: ama nəlì čurbədžìja ə ličɤ̀t mu dicàtə ut nàšti dicà
and their children were different from our children, you know.
75030: t’àn’te dicà sə ubl’àkəni ə pək nìi cərùlkiti i tò
Their children were [better] dressed. But us – our shoes; well –
75035: e n’è təkìvi cərùlki̥ əmi ut svìncki nəpràeni i təkà si ə b’à:mi
they weren’t like their shoes, but rather made of pigskin. That’s how we were.
75039: i nə làzərcə tɤ̀j sme òd’əli səs cərùlkiti smi ubùti
And we even went out that way on Lazar’s Sunday, with those shoes.
75043: sùtrin kət stànə t’à nəpràilə bàncətə up’èkələ gə dàže
When I got up in the morning she had made banitsa, and had even baked it already
75048: i təkà si n’àma:me nìštu pə čurbədžìiti t’è i sìčku iskupùvaa
So in fact we didn’t have anything. But the rich people, they bought up everything.
75050: i e jàlə m’ène ma je sràm če də pus’ègnə
and had eaten. I was ashamed [even] to reach out
75060: i kwòt ni dɤ̀t ə na bəštìte ni tvà i t’ut’ùnə usòbennu
All we had was what they gave to our fathers. And tobacco especially –
75061: də z’èməm də jàm vìkəm às ležà pə t’à gə nəpràilə
and take [something] to eat. I said: “[Here I was] lying [in bed] while she made it
75065: pɤ̀ gu iskupùvət i nàšte t’ut’ùni mògu jèftinu minàvəə ə pək
They bought that up. Our tobacco sold for very little, but
75068: i gə up’èkələ mə pà stàvəm də jàm vìkəm
and baked it, and then I [just] get up to eat it." [That’s what] I said.
75075: t’à:nite t’ut’ùni tì znàči vìnəgi pò skɤ̀pu čurbədžìjskija t’ut’ùn minàvə pò skɤ̀pu
their tobacco was always more costly; the rich peoples’ tobacco sold for more.
75076: d’è də znàjə slùšəhmi sə štòd b’àw səmà li
[But] what do I know? We got on, because I’d been alone, you know –
75079: n’è kətu f t’èkezesètu ə minàvə tàm kumìsijətə
Not like in the collective farm, where there was a committee [regulating things].
75083: merəklìjə b’àhə mnògu zə m’èn’ə às mnògu p’èeh
They were very solicitous for me. I sang a lot,
75086: mnògu sa ràdvəə t’èe tòj utìdi vujnìk às trì gudìni
and they were very happy. [My husband] was in the military, and for three years
75088: səm živ’àlə pri t’àh nìkuj nìštu ni mì i rikɤ̀l
I lived with them, and nobody said a word to me.
75089: i tàm ìməše pàk ràzlika əmə s’è pàk pò màlku
There was a difference there too, but it was less.
75093: rəzbìrəhmi sə əmi svèkɤr i sikɤ̀rvə t’èe n’àmə nə drùk
We understood one another. Well, my parents-in-law had nobody else
75098: nə kògə às krəj t’àh s’ènne se ubrəzùvə t’èkezesètu
to [talk] to. I was [the only one] near them. Then the collective farms were set up,
75104: əmi inò vrèmi nìj t’ut’ùn’a ud màrtə òšti pòčvəmi
For tobacco, in the old days, we’d begin already in March
75106: trɤ̀gnəhme nə ràbutə səs tùkə p’èt šes kumšìjki səs t’àh hòd’ə
and we went to work there with five or six neighbors. I went with them.
75109: də si pràim lixìti əmə n’àməše tugàə utròvi də gu prɤ̀skɤmi
to prepare the beds, but there wasn’t any insecticide then to spray on them.
75112: nəpràeni sə lixìti ni i səs kurìšnici̥ gu prɤ̀ska:mi ə
Once our beds were prepared, we spread bird droppings on them.
75116: às in b’àx kətu ditè bùlkətə dəd’è udɤ̀tə bùlkətə d’ ède zə udɤ̀ta
I was like a child to them. The bride brings [them] water, the bride’s gone for water.
75123: i nə rəkà gu səd’àhme səs kòlčetə ə n’àməše məšìni n’àməše nìšto
We did the planting by hand, with stakes. There weren’t machines, there wasn’t anything.
75127: uvəžàva:me sə pàk təkà vèseli b’àme sìčku zvenòto
We respected one another, and were happy like that, all of us together.
75134: i d’è də znàm v’èče̥ pudìr’ə jà sɤzdàdəw simèjstvu de̝cà
What do I know? Later on I made a family – children:
75140: mumčètu mi nè e užènetu mə mumìčetu sə užèni
My boy isn’t married, but the girl got married,
75142: i n’àkədè sə səbìra:me po brigàdə ili pə s’èki si gu zìmə
We’d get together somewhere [to work] in brigades, or each one would do it for himself.
75146: mi kətu stənà: v’èki mumà zə žènet’e mɤžɤ̀ mi dòjde
When I got to be of marriageable age, my [future] husband came
75151: vɤf s’èlo də mə ìskə i ə dòjdaa
to the village to seek me [in marriage], and they came –
75156: pràtia togàə i svətòvnici t’èə xòdea pu dvàmə trìmə čuvèkə
at that time they sent matchmakers, two or three people would come
75162: də kəndərdìsvət bəštɤ̀tə mumɤ̀tə t’à kojàtu ìskə
to persuade the father and the daughter. A girl who is willing –
75165: pr’əstànuvə b’àgə b’èz də kàže nə màjkə i nə bəštà
she’ll elope, run off without telling her mother or her father.
75166: mə kujàtu i i ni ìskə təkà t’à slùšə kvòtu i kàžət
But a girl who didn’t want it like that, would listen to what they told her.
75168: i kəto rešìme či i sə žènim večertɤ̀ dòjdaa tùkə ut sèltu
And when we decided we’d get married, those from the village came here in the evening.
75170: dòjdaa vəf nàs nàšte sə pudgòtvia màndžə xl’àp tugàə n’àməše fùrnə
They came to us [where] ours had prepared snacks and bread (there weren’t ovens then).
75174: i jà səm sə prigòtv’ələ tàm drèite štòtu i stàvəm bùlkə
And I had prepared my clothing, because I’m going to be a bride.
75179: dòjdaa svatòvnicite̝ dunèsaa sèdem òsem altɤ̀na na ednò però
The [future] in-laws came, and brought seven or eight gold pieces on a feather –
75183: kìtkə l’ə bèše però li bèše d’è də znàm
it was either a bouquet or a feather, how should I know –
75186: pìtaə mə tì ìskəš li gu ìskəm gu sètn’a pìtət i n’ègu
and asked me, “Do you want him?”. “I want him”. Then they asked him as well,
75189: i tòj vìkə i às ku ne gɤ̀ ìskəm n’àmə də dòja
and he said, “If I hadn’t wanted her, I wouldn’t have come.”
75193: i hàjde àjde čestìtu svàtoe čestìtu svàt tòj rəkòsət sə
So OK, let’s go, congratulate the [new] in-laws, they shake hands with one another.
75197: čestìtət i nàs i s’àdət vèke nìj sm’ə vèke užèneti slàgət tugàə
They congratulate us too, and sit down. Now we’re married, and then they set out
75201: də vičèr’ə tàm idɤ̀t gɤrm’ɤ̀t či vèke bùlkətə sə užènilə i
the food for supper. People eat and make noise, because the bride is now married.
75206: tugà e às tɤ̀j b’àx əmə pò nəpr’èt ə ne sɤ̀ ìdvəli
And I was there too, but earlier on they didn’t come [to the new home yet],
75208: čàk kugàtu pràjat svàdbətə às ìməx čìnkə dvà m’èscə səm òdilə às
not even when they celebrated the wedding. I had an aunt, for two months I went
75211: səs n’ègə t’à ne dòjde vɤv nàs də spì ne gɤ̀ ìskət
[places] with her. She didn’t come to sleep at our house, they didn’t want her.
75213: čàk nə svàdbətə kət sə nəprài svàətə drùgətə vèčer
[So] even when they celebrate the wedding, it’s the next evening after the wedding.
75216: pək às večertɤ̀ mə užèniə i drùgija d’èn pu plàdne mə duvèdəə tùkə
In my case, they married me in the evening, but only brought me here the next afternoon.
75218: mə prez mòjo vrème gu n’àməše vèke tvà n’àštu
In my time they didn’t do such things any more.
75220: i sètne tàm kət sə nəsròči vèke svàdbətə gud’èš pràjət
And then, when they decide on a wedding, they fix the betrothal.
75224: òd’ət zìmət nə bùlkətə drèiti tugàə n’àməše kəm’òni təkìvə ràbuti
They go and get the bride’s clothing. Back then there weren’t trucks and such.
75227: s karùci̥ti̥ ìdət z’èmət drèiti čeìzə nəfɤ̀rgəd gu tùkə
They come with carriages to take [her] clothing; [then] they spread it out here
75230: and [everyone] looks to see how much dowry the bride has.
75231: [Какво се правеше в деня преди сватбата?]
[What did they do on the day before the wedding?]
75236: u sɤ̀butə gud’èžə vič’ərtɤ̀ e brɤsnèltə i drùgija d’èn səbàlən
The betrothal is Saturday. In the evening is the shaving [of the groom]. The next morning
75241: pàk ə pràjət inò xurò às nə m’ène zəbràiw dɤ̀l sə pràili
they dance again. I forget whether they did this for me,
75244: əmə pòmn’ə gu tvà vìkət mu medenìci̥ tùr’ət dvà trì kərvàjə
but I remember [the custom]; it’s called the honeycake. They lay out 2-3 ritual buns.
75249: ìma tərp’èzə igràjət pàk kraj t’èa kərvài medenìci i pòsl’e
There’s a festive table. They dance again, by these buns and honeycakes, and then –
75250: nìe n’àməme čèrkvə tùkə vəf sèlu vìkət pòpə
We don't have a church here in the village, they [have to] call in a priest,
75253: tòj ud drùgu sèlu bèše̝ duvàdə venčàvə nə tùkə vəf.kɤ̀šti
he was from another village. He comes, and marries us here in the house.
75257: i nəpràjət vɤ̀nkə ednà tərpèzə tàm d’èt sə kàn’ət
And they set up the festive table outside, where they’ve invited [guests],
75259: i òrətə nəs’àdət idɤ̀t igràjət kətu nə svàdbə
and people sit there, they eat and dance. Like at a wedding!
75261: a brɤs nə brəsnèlata kvò se e pràilu
And the – the shaving? How was that done?
75264: əmi pàk sə igràe kətu ubrɤ̀snət tàm zèt’ə mu nəpràjət ədèt’ə
Well, they dance again when they shave the groom, they perform the custom.
75268: i zəvàt’ət də igràjət igràjət dukət kəndìsət dukɤ̀t sə stəmnì
Then they start to dance, and dance until they drop, until it gets dark.
75272: raskaži tòčno kàk e kvò pretstavl’àva brɤsnèlata
Tell me exactly what the shaving consisted of.
75278: əmi brəsn’èltə ubrɤ̀snəd zèt’a pulèjət mu də sə umìi i xuròtu pòčvə
The shaving – they shave the groom. They pour water to wash him, and the dance starts.
75283: mùzikətə pòčvə də svìri nə xurò i zəvàtət də igràjət vèč hurò
The music starts to play dance tunes, and they start to dance the round dance,
75286: i tvà e brəsn’èltə sìčkutu svɤ̀rdzənu də ìmə veselbà
and that’s the shaving. It’s part of the overall [goal], to be joyous.
75289: tò e tvà nəpràiš unuvà nəpràš ə də ìmə n’èštu
You [do some of] this and [some of] that, so as to make this happen.
75290: [Какво се прави в седмицата след сватбата?]
[What do you do during the week after the wedding?]
75293: u sr’àdə pund’èlnik nòsim bùltu ftòrnik gu nòsim u sr’àdə
By Wednesday – we wear the veil on Monday, we wear it on Tuesday. On Wednesday
75295: kumɤ̀ tr’àə dòjde də ti̥ fɤ̀rli bùltu̥ sutr’əntɤ̀ i d’èverə
the godfather is supposed to come in the morning to remove the veil. The best man [comes]
75299: i kojàt bìlə mɤ̀škə bubulɤ̀čkə t’à nòsi ennà hùrkə s enà kəd’èlkə
and the one who was the groom’s “little bug” brings a distaff filled with wool
75305: vr’ət’ènu i zəprìdə nə dèverə zəprìdə nə bùlkətə kəd’èlkətə
and a spindle. She spins up the wool for the best man, she spins for the bride,
75309: tòj i gə dàvə i hùrkətə̥ i kətu dòi p’ètəkə
and he gives her the distaff. And when Friday comes,
75312: u p’ètək večertɤ̀ ot’ùvəme nə pòvrənki mu vìkət
we go on Friday evening to what they call the ritual visit.
75317: sikɤ̀rvətə tùkə pàj m’èsi idìn kərvàj drùgu̥ səm gu zəbràilə
The mother-in-law again kneads up a ritual bun. As for the rest, I’ve forgotten
75322: gd’è kvò bèše i ut’ùvəmi da kàžem vɤf mòjti xòrə večertɤ̀ sɤ̀buttə
where it all was. And we go to tell my people on Saturday evening
75325: də ni mɤ̀ svàrilə tùkə də səm si nə màjčinijə dvòr
that they mustn’t find me here, that I [must] be inside my mother’s yard.
75330: i sɤ̀butə več’ərtɤ̀ drùgətə vèč’ər sreštu nid’èl’ə sə vrɤ̀štəmi tùkə̥
So Saturday evening, the next evening before Sunday – we come back here.
75332: às ennò vrème̝ òt n’àməm bràt’ə n’àməm s’èstri ə b’àh
In the old days, because I didn’t have brothers or sisters, I was –
75334: če nə grɤ̀p səs kubìlkətə z bəkɤ̀rte nə grɤ̀p nòs’ə udà
I had to go with a yoke on my back, and to carry water in copper pails.
75339: kət si nəsəd’à enà sərìčkə zəlèjə sì gu pàk
I plant a row, then I water it; and then
75342: pà si nəsəd’à enà sərìčkə pà si gu zalèjə
I plant another row, and water it too.
75343: màjkə mi i bəštà mi sə nə drùgə ràbuta
My father and mother are off doing other work.
75345: às kò də pràjə nə m’ène̝ tvà mi dàvət
What can I do? This is [the work] I’ve been given.
75347: s’ètne drùgijə d’èn t’è kətu dòjət mə pàk nə grɤ̀p
And the next day, when they came, again [the pails go] onto my back
75350: vudɤ̀tə gə nòsim màlku pò dəl’èč əmə n’àməše̝ pudìr’e vèče
so as to carry water, this time further off. But there wasn’t any. So
75354: zè:me nə kàci də slàgəme̝ vudɤ̀ta i təkà si gu zìma:me
we took barrels to gather the water, and that’s how we brought it
75356: si gu səd’àhme i kətu stàne zə bràne̝ kupàl si gu
and planted [the tobacco]. And when it came time for harvest, it was hoed
75357: nə rəkà b’èz də sə orè b’èz nìštu i kəto stàne
by hand, without plowing or anything. When it’s time
75359: zə bràne̝ pɤ̀rvətə mu rəkà gə berèm udòlu pu n’àkolko listà
for the first picking, we gather a few leaves from below,
75361: i kato gu premìnem edìnija pɤ̀t tò e tugàə pu kòlku
and we go one time through the entire field, however much [it is] –
75365: dvà trì d’ekərə t’ùn se e səd’àlu ə pə kuìt
we had planted two or three decares of tobacco, but those
75367: sə mnògu xòrə tèə səd’ɤ̀t pò mnògu t’ut’ùn pək nìi
who have more people to work plant much more tobacco. But we
75368: pò màlku t’ut’ùn màlku hòrə smi pò màlku t’ut’ùn
were less people, so planted less tobacco.
75369: i tugàə vèči pɤ̀rvətə rəkà kətu gu mìnem ftòrətə rəkà vèči
And when the first picking is finished, we go through on the second one.
75372: kəd zəvàne də nəžilt’àvə pàk pòčvəme də gu berèm
We begin to pick the leaves when they've started to turn yellow,
75375: pàk pu dv’è trì licà ùž də stàvə pò xùbəf
again two or three leaves at a time, so they stay good-looking.
75378: əmə gu nìžem nə gub’èrki i nə kənàp i pòsle
Then we thread them on needles, and on cords, and after that
75382: si pràəm ràmki nə ràmkiti ili nàj nəpr’èt nə sərɤ̀ci̥
we make frames, and [put these threads] on the frames. No, first [we put them] on poles
75389: sərɤ̀citi i səs ə šùmə càriičenə go nəvɤ̀rzvəme̝ i nəpràenə skèl’ə
and tie the poles [to the frames] with corn husks. Then a scaffolding is made
75393: i nə tàə skèl’ə nər’àdəme sərɤ̀ci̥ti̥ i kugàtu vəlì dɤ̀š
and we line up the poles on the scaffolding. When it rains,
75398: ìməme pə skèl’ə put sùšinə ə tàm pək nəpràenə sərɤ̀citi gi zìməme̝
we have the scaffolding to keep things dry. Then we take these poles
75402: pu dvà pu dvà sɤrɤ̀ka i gi nòsime̝ tàm idìn du drùk
and line them up by pairs, one next to another,
75406: idìn du drùk tɤ̀j gi nər’àda:me̝ tugàə enò vr’ème
one next to another, and that’s how we lined them up in the old days.
75411: pə seàšnutu l’èsnə ràbutə zəvìəd gu s najlòna i àjd’e
Now it’s all simple: you just cover them with a plastic sheet, and that’s it.
75413: i tugàvə təkà b’èše̝ i pòsl’e pək priz zìmata
But that’s how it was back then. During the winter,
75418: kato zème̝ vèče də pàdət məglìti sə zème̝m i pòčvəme
when the fog starts to come in, we get ready and start
75422: də gu pràəm kətu vìdim če stàvə mèk zəpòčvəme də gu pràəm
to process [the tobacco]. When we see they’re soft, we start to make it [into bundles]
75426: nə kul’àntu̥ si gu pràəm nə ilpiz’ètə i tugàə gu vɤ̀rzva:me̝
[using] our knees [for support]. We make it into bundles, and tie them up
75430: səs càreičenə šùmə i gu nəpràim takà nə d’ènkuve̝ gulèmi
with corn husks, and make them into large bales.
75436: nə vɤ̀strep pu pràilnutu n’è nə d’ènk əmi nə vɤ̀strep nəpràim
Or more like a pile. We make them not into bales but into storage piles.
75440: i pudìre vèče kətu dɤ̀t čùlui tugàvə gu zìməme i gu pràəm
And then, after they give us pieces of burlap to cover them, we take and make them
75442: nə d’ènkuve̝ rəzvɤ̀rzvame go ot ə šùmətə i im gu dàəme̝
into bales. We untie [the leaves] from the corn husking, and give them
75444: i məžètu gu pràət nə d’ènkuve̝
to the men [who] make them into bales.
75447: əmi enò vrème̝ nìj kət òde:me nə učilìštu tùkə òde:me
In the old days, when we went to the school here, we went [only]
75450: du četvɤ̀rtu udelènie i pòsle zəvənà:me də òdim vəf mədr’èc
through fourth grade, and then we started to go to [school] in Mŭdrets.
75454: əmə kətu òdɛme vəf mədr’èc nìe n’àma:me obùfki tugàə n’àməše nìštu̥
But when we went to Mŭdrets, we didn’t have shoes; there wasn’t anything.
75460: əmi z’èmət nə inì cərùlki ni napràjət i səs čuràpiti du kul’enàtə
So they got us these sandals, with socks [only] to the knees.
75466: du tàm ni b’àxə čuràpi̥te enò vrèm kulinàtə ni červ’èni t’è
That’s where our socks came to in the old days. Our knees were all red [from the cold],
75467: zə zətvà nə bul’ɤ̀t seà əmə kvò də gi nəpràim
and that’s why they hurt [so much] now, but what can we do for them?
75474: i tugàvə ùča:me̝ bɤ̀lgərski mətimàtikə v’èruučènie trùduvu fizìčesku
Back then we studied Bulgarian [language], math, catechism, shop, physical education –
75481: ni mòə də si spòmn’ə drùgi kəkvì pridmèti sme ùčili
I can’t remember what other subjects we studied.
75485: əmə nə mène mətemàti̥kə̥tə mi vər’èše mnògu əmə nəlì n’àməw pərì
For me, I was really good at math, but since I didn’t have any money,
75489: i n’àməše i kòj də mə pudɤ̀ržə tə nɤ̀l səm zimàlə
and there was nobody to support me – I even [had to] take
75493: i xranìcə às mnògu ni ùča:f əmə mə pàk
[my own] food – I didn’t learn a lot. But [even though]
75496: ne mì dàvəə də četà mnògu mə pàk zimàh səs čètiri
I wasn’t allowed to study much, I still got a fairly good grade.
75497: raskažì mi za živòtə si ot detìnstvo
Tell me about your life, from childhood onwards.
75501: əmi ut detìnstvu kwò d ti rəspràvəm nìe b’à:me mnògu bràduve
From childhood – what to tell you? We were many brothers,
75504: p’èt bràt’ə i dv’è sestrì s’èdem pərčètə às səm nàj màlkija
five brothers and two sisters: seven “chunks”. I was the youngest.
75507: i kàktu stənà səmìčək vèči sìčkiti si utìdaa ut tòu sv’àt
As it turned out, I’m alone [now]; all of them have already departed this world.
75510: xòdeh nə učilìšto ùčeše mi sə mnògo tugàvə bèše təkà
I went to school, and really wanted to learn. But back then it was like this:
75511: idìn bràt urè drùk pək drùgi ràbuti vɤ̀rši ə drùk pək
one brother does the plowing, another did other jobs, and yet another
75514: pəsè ufcèti i às kətu si vɤ̀rnə ud učìlištu kətu rɤ̀t
pastured the sheep. And when I got back from school it was my turn
75521: òdim də zəbìrəme̝ mərìti màjkiti nə àgneàta də sùčət tugàə təkà bèši̥
to go [help] gather up the ewes, the mothers of suckling lambs. That’s how it was then.
75525: ni gì čàkəə t’àh večertɤ̀ də si dòət əmi è po obət
They didn’t wait till evening for [the ewes] to come, rather it was in the afternoon,
75528: dvà trì čəsɤ̀ tr’àvə si dòət àgneàtə də ne uglədn’àvət mnògu
around two or three o’clock that they must come, so the lambs wouldn’t get too hungry.
75531: pribirèm gi səs dukàrəme gi du sèlu sàmu màjkiti kətu sùčət àgneatə
We collect them, and drive them to the village – just the mothers that are suckling lambs.
75533: i posle gi iskàrvəme pək tàm du pul’ànətə du du s’èlutu ni s
Then we take them back to the meadow near our village –
75536: kràjə živèem nə s’èloto iskàrəme i tàm pəsɤ̀t jàgəncàtə i màjkiti m
we live at the edge of the village – and the lambs graze together with their mothers.
75538: pəsɤ̀t dukət sə stɤ̀mni i kətu dòət drùgiti i sə pribìrəmi
They graze until it gets dark, and when the others come we [all] go home.
75542: tuvà bèši inɤ̀ta ràbutə čubənlɤ̀kə pòsle kətu i zəvɤ̀rši
That was one thing I did, working as a shepherd. So later when I finished –
75546: àz zəvɤ̀rših sèdmi klàs n’àmə kədè də ìdə kvò də pràa
I finished seventh grade, and there was nowhere to go, nothing to do,
75547: kòj žə mə izdɤ̀ržə də ìdə də ùčə n’àštu i
nobody to support me to study anything further.
75550: i b’àh merəklìjə mnògu zə ufcèti əmə mnògu gi ubìčəh žuvòtnite dè
And I was really keen on sheep. I liked animals a lot, in fact.
75552: nè sàmu ufcèti sìčki živòtni gi ubìčəh mnògu i pòčna:
I liked not only sheep but all animals, a lot. And I began
75556: də pəsɤ̀ òfci pəsɛ̀h nàšti i nə kumšìiti tàm n’àkui drùgi
to pasture sheep. I pastured ours, and the neighbors’, and those of some others.
75558: də də ne sɤ̀ sàmu s nàšti dè i s pəs’àhme gi
Not just ours then. So we pastured them.
75560: kvò də ti rəspràvəm pòsle nə kɤ̀rɤ mi nəpràia tàm è təkòvu
What can I tell you – later they made for me, up in the fields, this –
75563: səjà dètu mu vìkəmi nìe eli kušàrə a təkà kušàrə
“saya” (sheepfold), as we call it. A “kushara” (sheepfold), yes – a “kushara”.
75566: i tàm pròletnu vrème kət se zəpruletì tuvà vrèmi si tàm du kušàrətə
And in the spring, when the weather turns to spring, you’re up at the sheepfold,
75570: tàm gi pəs’èm ufcète̝ tàm mi nòsət l’ab də jàm
and pasture the sheep there. They bring me up bread to eat.
75571: u sèlu n’àmə u sèlu sàmu gà se preublìčəm n’àkvu
[I’m] not in the village at all, only when I go to change clothes or such,
75575: ilì pək ku ìmə n’àkvu təkòvu də rčèm vilìgden gerg’òvden
or when there’s some occasion such as Easter or St. George’s Day.
75578: kətu dòjde n’àkuj bràt pò gulèmiti b’à sè žèneni
Then one of my older brothers would come – they were all married,
75582: às səm nàj màlkijə ne b’àh žènin dè i də mə smen’ɤ̀t
I was the youngest and was unmarried – to take my place
75584: i də də ìdə i às də izl’èjə tàm də glèdəm mumìti [laughter]
so I could go down to the village to feast my eyes on the girls! [laughter]
75590: ufcèti idnò vrèmi gi pàze:me bès kòčuviti gi udlɤ̀ča:me utlɤ̀kəni kòčuviti
In the old days we kept them separate from the rams. The rams were kept apart
75594: dù pitkòvden pitkòvden stàə nə dvàese i sèdmi uktòmvri
until St. Petko’s Day. St. Petko’s Day is on October 27th.
75598: tugàə gi pùskəme ufcète də sə mɤ̀rl’ət ufcèti vèči̥ də sə zəplòdɤt
Then we allow the sheep to breed so they will get pregnant,
75602: štòtu də sə uàgn’ət dvàese i ftòri fevruàri tuvà màrt
so they will lamb on the twenty-second of February – I mean March.
75604: gà sə stòpli pò rànu stud’ènu àgneàtə ne mòəd də rəstɤ̀t
When it’s warm. Earlier than that [it’s] cold, and the lambs can’t grow –
75608: ìskə uslòvia i tugàə gi pùsnə i kət sə zəplòd’ət ufcète̝ vèče̝
you need good conditions. So I breed them. After the sheep are impregnated,
75611: prez zìmətə tè pòčvəd də sə àgn’ət tugàva na dvàese i ftòri màrt
[they carry it] throughout the winter, and then begin to lamb on March 22nd.
75612: pòčvəd də sə àgn’ət pàk sme nə kušàrətə gi iskàrvəme tàm
They begin to lamb, and we’re up at the sheepfold. We take them there
75614: i pəs’èm gi tàm àgəncàtə ufcèti nòs’ət ni xl’àp tàm pribìrət
and pasture the sheep and lambs. They bring us bread there and take [stuff] back.
75617: kòledə nə gerg’òvden tr’àvə də zəkòlim àgənce tuvà bèše zəkòn tugàvə
On Christmas and St. George’s Day we slaughter lambs, that was the rule then
75620: zə sèl’ənite dè nàj xùbəvutu àgne səs nə gerg’òvden že dòət
for villagers. The best lamb would be for St. George’s day. They’d come up:
75625: še gu z’èmət tàm bràtt’ə mi pò gul’àmiti i kàrət
my older brothers would get [the lamb]. They then take it [down],
75631: zəkòl’əd gu pràəd gu c’àlu gu pečàə vəf fùrni
they slaughter it and prepare it. People roasted lambs whole in the outdoor oven –
75638: ìməše s’èlski fùrni təkìva tàm pu zə n’àkulku kumšìi sə zberɤ̀t
there were these village ovens that several neighbors would share –
75644: i gu nəpɤ̀ln’ət àgnetu kətu gu uderɤ̀t sàmu mu izvàd’əd drebulìiti udvɤ̀tre
and they stuff the lamb after they skinned it, only removing the entrails.
75648: drùgutu gu pɤ̀lnea tàm səs urìs səs nàj rəzlìčni ràbuti tàm
They fill the other [parts] with rice and different things,
75650: səs percà li s kəkvòtu štè də e i gu slàgət
with leeks, or whatever there was, to put in there.
75655: zəšìjəd gu pàk i gu slàgəə vəf fùrnətə də sə upičè
Then they sew it up again, and put it in the oven to roast.
75658: i nə gerg’òvden c’àlutu s’èlu sə səbìrə:me̝ nə pluštàt
On St. George’s Day we’d gather, the entire village, on the village square.
75659: ìmə idìn gul’àm pluštàt c’àlutu s’èlu tàm sə səbìrət nòs’ət àgneàtə
There’s a big square where the entire village gathers. They bring in the lambs –
75664: c’àl:te àgnetə gi nòs’ət tàm i pòpə mìni i gi up’àvə
they bring the entire lamb roasts there, and the priest comes by to bless them.
75666: i sìčkiti mu dàvət pu inò pərčè nə pòpə
and everyone gives a piece [of his lamb] to the priest.
75671: emi kətu mìni pòpə upèi ə àgneàtə
So when the priest comes and blesses the lambs
75674: i drùgiti pòčnət xàpnət tàm sìčkiti i pòčvət vèči visilbìti
then all the others start to eat, and the revelry begins.
75677: mùzikə ìmə svìr’ət igràjət xurà tugàə təncùvəne n’àməše kvòt segà
Musicians play, people dance the round dance. There wasn’t [any of] today’s dancing,
75682: tèə ràbuti tànci mànci təkùu n’àmə sàmu xurà rəčinìci prài xurà
these fancy dance things they do [now]. Only round dance, rŭchenitsa, line dances.
75688: e tvà sə igràeše nə vrèmetu du vičirtɤ̀ tàə visilbà
That’s how they danced in the old days. Till evening – this revelry
75689: bèše̝ du večertɤ̀ i vičirtɤ̀ sə pribìrət òrətə sèki fkɤ̀šti si
went on till evening, and then everyone went home, each to his house.
75690: [And what kind of a holiday was St. George’s Day?]
75693: emi pràət gerg’òvden bèše pràznik nə čubà nə ufčàr’ə
Well, when they celebrate St. George’s Day, it’s shepherds –
75696: ilì nə pəstìr’ə dè dètu̥ gu tòj s’à dàže gu iskàrvət
it’s really the holiday of shepherds, but now they’ve dressed it up as
75697: i tàm nə svetì g’òrgi pràznik əmə i səbìrət sə tàm xòrətə
this “holiday of St. George”. People gather together,
75699: idɤ̀t i pìjət igràjət xurà rəčenìci du vičirtɤ̀ i vičirtɤ̀ vèče
they eat and drink and dance the round dance and rŭchenitsa until evening,
75704: kət sə mrɤ̀kni sìčku sə pribìrə šòt tugàə n’aməše̥ təkìi nòšni ràbuti
and when it gets dark everyone goes home because they didn’t have this night life then,
75708: də xòd’ət è pu c’àlə vèčir mlàdi n’àmə təkɤ̀və ràbut
[like now] when young people go out all night. There weren’t such things then.
75712: [Какво правите, когато започнат да се раждат агнетата?]
[What do you do when lambs begin to be born?]
75718: tò kətu pòčni də sə àgni fs’àkə ufcà dòlu gòri i znàm
When the ewes start to lamb, I know for each one of them more or less
75723: ə dàttə kugàtu e umɤ̀rlenə i kə kòj dèn tr’àvə sə uàgni
the date when it was bred, and thus the day it should lamb.
75727: i gə nəbl’udàvəme̝ i kətu dòe vrème tàm pu pumògnem i
We watch [that one] and when the time comes we help it.
75732: uàgni sə tùrim dèm nə àgnitu də si sùči
When one lambs, we give it the lamb to suckle,
75736: nàj nəprèd də zəsùči xùbəvičku nə n’àkui è
to suckle really good first off. In some cases, though,
75739: təkìvə se àgn’ət pò umərlùšeni ne sì ne ìskəd də sùčət
the lambs are just born feeble, and they don’t want to suckle on their own,
75743: əmə nìj gi pumɤ̀čim tàm pun’àu ku nè sùči li ti sə
so we push these ones to suckle. But if it just won’t suckle for you,
75747: dədèm s ləžìčkə ml’àku sàmu i sàmu də gu putsìlim
we give it milk with a spoon. Just enough for it to get strong,
75750: i də mòi vèč kət sə səvzèmi i də pòčne
to be able to manage. And when it comes into its own it begins
75754: də si sùči səmò i si vərì pudir màjkətə i sùči si
to suckle on its own, then it goes along with its mother and suckles.
75755: [Какво правите, когато агнетата започнат да растат?]
[What do you do when the lambs start to grow?]
75756: è kətu puràsnət àgəncàtə vèče zə ufc’èti gi iskàrvəme vèči
When the lambs start to grow, we take the sheep up on their own
75758: nə nòšnu vrèmi də gi pəsèm àgneàtə gi udlɤ̀čim i gi udbìvəme̝
to pasture them at night. We separate the lambs from them, and wean them
75759: də də n sùčət vèči pòčvəme də duìm màjkite im
so that they stop suckling, and we can begin to milk their mothers.
75762: ml’àkutu nəlì nəpràim sìrni də jədè̝m ml’àku kìselu pr’àsnu
After all, we [need] milk to make cheese to eat, yogurt and fresh milk [to drink].
75763: i ufcèti òde:me nòšnu vrèmi də gi pəsèm tugàə
And back then, we’d take the sheep to pasture them during the night.
75765: The sun goes down, and off we go with them.
75771: c’àlə vèčer du səbà:ləm səbà:ləm nəpečè li slɤ̀ncitu tè tr’àvə sə pribìrət
All night, up to morning. In the morning when the sun gets strong they must return
75773: vəf kušàrətə pàg gi izduìm i nìe l’àgəme də spìm
to the sheepfold. We milk them again, and then we lie down to sleep.
75776: i t’è ležɤ̀t c’àl dèn i drùgətə vèčir pàk sɤ̀štə ràbut
They lie there all day, and then the next evening the same thing
75780: sə puftàr’ə dè təkà si gi pəs’àhme̝ ufcèti tugàə n’àməši kət sià
repeats. That’s how we pastured them then. Not like now,
75782: priz denɤ̀ də gi pəsɤ̀t tugàə vèčer sàmu vèčer
when they pasture them during the day. Back then only at night.
75784: pičè li slɤ̀nci ufcà ni pəsèš
If the sun is strong, you don’t pasture the sheep.
75786: kakvì bòlesti i li ku e ìmalo po ofcète i kàk ste gi lekùvali
What kinds of illnesses did sheep have, and how did you treat them?
75790: emi tuvà bèši bulestɤ̀ zə tuvà zə mitìlə tugàə i zəxrànvəme
Well, there was this illness called distoma (liver-fluke), and we force-feed them –
75794: kàzvəme gu zəhrànim gi dàvəmi im tə c’àlə sìčkite òrə
we call it force-feeding [them when] we give them – everyone [did this],
75795: tuvà bèši zəkòn zìməmi im xàpuvi ut vitirinàrniti lèkəri i gi dàvəme
it was the law – we get pills from the veterinarian and give them the pills.
75801: kətu im didèm du vičirtɤ̀ ni gì pùskəme də pəsɤ̀t
When we give them these pills, we don’t let them out at night to graze.
75803: nəprìmer dn’èskə sutrintɤ̀ dədèm xàpuviti du vičirtɤ̀ ne gì pùskəme də pəsɤ̀t
For instance if we give them the pills this morning, this evening we don’t let them out.
75807: a s kvò ste sa oblìčali ofčàrskoto obleklò kakvò e
And how did you dress? What was shepherds’ clothing like?
75819: cərvùli svìnski cərvùli bèli nàvuštə čèrni vɤrvì nəvìti təkà è tùkə
Sandals. Sandals of pigskin, white leg-wrappings, black cords wound about up to here –
75821: i nə krɤ̀z gi pràime n’àkuku pɤ̀ti əmi bèli čèrni vrɤ̀fki nàvuštə tàm
we tie them crossed over several times. So black and white cords, leg-wrappings,
75826: cərvùli tuvà səs patùri òdexme pòjəs zəvìt è gul’àm pòjəs ukulu krɤ̀sta
sandals, baggy trousers – we go about with a belt, a large belt around the waist.
75828: ubl’àkəni zdràvu štòtu nə kɤ̀rə mòi tə fàni i dɤ̀š
We’re dressed sensibly, because out in the fields you can get caught in the rain,
75830: mòi tə fàni i studènu sìčku i iməmi gul’àmi jəmurlùci mu vìka:mi
you can get caught in the cold, or anything. We have these big  – we called them cloaks.
75834: təkɤ̀u kəčùlkə əmə nìe mu vìkəmi jəmurlùk ut tvà tùrskə dùmə
Like hoods, but we call it a “yamurluk” (cloak). That’s a Turkish word –
75836: tuvà jəmurlùk izglèždə è t’à tə zəvìvə səs n’ègə c’àlu
it seems that “yamurluk” is [Turkish]. And it covers you up completely,
75839: səs kəčùlətə nə gləvɤ̀tə utprède kət sə zəvìjš i tòpli mnògu
with the hood on your head, and bound up in front. It keeps you really warm.
75841: tìə b’àə vàl’əni tugàvə i vàl’əə i stàvə dibèl plətɤ̀
They were made of felt. Back then they fulled the cloth and it got very thick,
75847: i ni prupùskə i dɤ̀š ne prupùskə i v’àtər
it kept out the rain and kept out the wind.
75849: [What kind of sheep did you raise?]
75853: m’èsnə puròdə ufcè tugàva si b’àa bəlkànski ufcè nàši si̥
There was [just] the local type of sheep then, our Balkan sheep.
75857: b’àə sè təkìvə dɤ̀lga vɤ̀lna òstrə vɤ̀lnə i t’à
They were all with long, sharp wool. That’s their wool.
75878: nər’èt sìčki gi up’àvə nərɤ̀s’uvə gi tàm i gi up’àvə
He blesses them one after another, sprinkles them [with holy water] and blesses them,
75989: And I sang songs to them.
75993: red, green, blue, black – and we'd mix the colors.
76142: tùk sәm sә umɤ̀žilә f tɤ̀s kɤ̀štә̥
I got married here, in this house.
76144: әmә sәm puràsnәlә pàk f tùj s’èlu
And I also grew up in this village.
76148: s’èlutu si s’è e s’èlu ubàči ìmәši pɤ̀lnɤ
The village is still a village. But there was full –
76155: sim’èjni sigà tùk šә vìdiš kɤ̀štičkә àj tùkә ši ìmә òrә
[Of] families. Now you’ll see a small house – here there’ll be some people,
76160: ə ìmәm dәšter’ɤ̀ t’à žuv’èe vəf grədɤ̀ әmә si ìdәt
I have a daughter. She lives in town, but they’ll come
76164: f nid’èl’en d’èn tùkә si dòdәt sɤ̀but’en d’èn nid’èl’en d’èn
here on Sunday. They come on Saturdays and Sundays
79703: dɤ̀t mu pu inò pərčè sìčki nə pòpə
each one gives a piece to the priest,
85643: storì me bòže prestorì a sɤndɤ̀kɤt na kon’à a a kṛ̀sɤt
transform me! Make my coffin into a horse, and the cross
86057: pròsti nè učeni ama ìnače ìmaše terikàt xòra nògu
Simple and uneducated [they may be], but there were a lot of clever folk
86111: ama ìnače pәmetlìjә pә znàči mòže da ti kàže
but they were smart. They could tell you
86113: [laughter] zә kәkvà rabòta òdiš tì po drùgo òdiš li à
What are you here for? You here for some other thing?
86114: I’m here for this sort of thing.
86115: For this – he’s here for this.
86119: èxèj pu stutìnә òfci sәm gledàl
Oho! I’ve looked after a hundred sheep or so.
86120: è i kàk kugà gi kàk stàvә tàa rabòta
Hah. And how – when do you – how does this work go?
86124: cèlata gudìna da mi ob’asnìš cèlata godìna
Throughout the year. Take me through the whole year,
86128: prìmerno kәt se zәjàgn’әt tàm kәtu zèmәd dә sә mɤ̀rl’әt
for instance, from the time they lamb up to the time they breed [again] –
86132: mi mi tuvà e glèdәj sә pru prolettà nәprìmer
Well, it’s – you see, in the spring, for instance,
86137: kәtu se zәjàgnәt ujàgnәt se tò o kәm ə dvàesti màj dә kàžeme
when they lamb, that happens around the twentieth of May.
86144: bizàәt cìcәt àgnetata slèt tovà i predòjva:me kәtu i predòime
The lambs suckle, and after that we milk the sheep. When we’ve done that,
86148: sabèreme i jàs ìәm dә kàžem pedesè mәznìki tì ìmәž dvàese
we gather them up. Let’s say I have fifty to milk and you have twenty,
86152: drùgijo ìma pèd drùgijo dèset i i sɤbèreme nә ednò mèsto
Another has five, another has ten. So we gather them in one place,
86156: trìsta òfci trìsta maznìci i tàmoka znàči kato i sabèreme
three hundred sheep, three hundred to milk, and then after we’ve gathered them
86160: we take measure, we do the reference milking.
86163: tәkà ne u ne znàe da pìše nә knìgә dә kàžeme
They didn’t, you know, know how to write or [read] books, let’s say, thus
86165: kәkvò e bìlu pres stàro vrème kәkvò sә kàk komìti kәkvò
how it was in the old days, what the insurgents [did],
86168: tùrci štò sә kәdè sә prәìli kәkvò sә prәìli
what the Turks were, what they did and where,
86171: kàk sә se krìli od nìx’ kàk
how they – how [people] hid from them, how –
86177: hm e štò dә ti kàža àzeka
Hm. Well, what should I tell you?
86182: trèbva dә mi zәdàeš vәpròs tә әku mògә dә ti udguvòra
You have to put a question to me, and if I can I’ll answer you.
86184: emi nà è kakvò e bìlu ednò vrème
Well, then, how was it in the old days?
86186: kɤ̀k se e zәselìlu sèloto znàeš li
How was the village settled – do you know that?
86187: sèlutu se e zәselìlu znàči tvà e tùka a bìlu puštin’àk
The village was settled – well, it used to be a wasteland here.
86206: nè e imàlu xòra odnačàloto ama tovà e predì trìsta četiristòtini godìni imә
No people at first. But that was three or four hundred years ago,
86210: i ud nèkәde sa nadošlì nèkoj xòra zaselìli sa se
and then some people arrived from somewhere and they settled,
86215: i postepènno postepènno se̝ uveličìlu selòto selòto e stavàlo znàči
and gradually, gradually the village grew, and the village got to be
86218: dokɤm šeesè sedemdesè kɤ̀šti a saà sme trìese semèjsva
some sixty or seventy houses. But now there are just thirty families of us.
86230: saà se rәspil’àa xòrәtә sè tèrәt àrno tèrɤt ùbәvu mèsence obèseno
Now people’ve dispersed, looking for a better life, meat for the taking.
86242: è әmi sèki izmɤ̀zvә nèguvite i i mèrime
Well, each one milks his sheep dry, and we measure
86246: kòj kòj kòlku mu pùštәt i nә kilòtu putfɤ̀rl’әme nәprìmer
how much each one gives, and ascribe it by kilos. For instance
86250: nә ednò kilò putfɤ̀rl’әme trìese kìlə dә mu se dàdәt
thirty kilos are ascribed [to an owner] for each kilo in the reference milking.
86260: prez letòtu mɤzničàre si ì̥mә̥še̥ ufčàre dvàmә li trìmә li ke mɤ̀zәt
During the summer there were milkers. Two or three shepherds do the milking
86266: mәzničàre se tìjә kәžùvәt mәzničàre i nəli tijə dòat i mәzàt i
These were called “milkers”, and they do the milking.
86270: i nә tebeka nә prèmɤzu kòlku ti e došlò
So then whatever came out to be your share at the reference milking
86273: dvè kìlә ti e dušlò pu trì vèdrә dә kàžem
[if] it came out to be two kilos, then you’d take three pails, let’s say.
86276: nìa vèdrә gu vìka:me vedròtu sәbìra dvanàese kìlә
We called them pails; a pail can take [up to] twelve kilos.
86333: әhә ìskɤd znàči sɤs màlko rəbòta nògu pәrì dә zìmәt
Yup. They want to bring in a lot of money for [very] little work.
86336: i saà tùka nèma takà trɤ̀sɤt pu pètrič trɤ̀sɤt pu sòfija
No such thing here now, they’re looking [for work] in Petrich, in Sofia –
86337: kɤdè li nèma xòra ut ut selòtu
there’s hardly anywhere without people from [our] village.
86339: sèkade ìmә pu bɤlgàrija sèkuj tèra
They’re all over Bulgaria, all looking [for work].
86340: While you in the old days –
86342: What kind of work did you do in the old days?
86346: Animal husbandry, agriculture! Looking after livestock,
86349: i zemledèlie si sèeme rɤ̀š uvès càrevička krɤtòfki
and agriculture, you know. We grow rye, oats, “tsarevichka” (corn), potatoes –
86350: ama vìe ne mù vìkaxte càrevička
86352: i tì zè dә go izmètaš
you’ve taken to twisting [your speech] about.
86357: še govòriš kàkto trèva pu stàrutu ki
[I want you to] talk in the old way, you see?
86361: jà jàs ti kәžùvәm misìrka әki ti kàžә
Well, if I say “misirka” to you, if I talk [that way]
86365: tì še mi tì še mi guvòriš pә às še tɤ rәzbìrәm
You just – you just talk to me, and I’ll understand you.
86371: às kɤdètu ne tè rәzbìrәm še tә pìtәm
And whenever I don’t understand you, I’ll ask.
86379: ùtre dòjde drùgiju trètijo pètijo tìja od ufčàreto aku sə trìmə
tomorrow another, a third, a fifth – If there are three shepherds,
86383: naprìmer tìjə se tìjə sə èdnəkvi i i trìmәtә nәprìmer idìn ìmә
for instance, they’re – the three are equal, but [of them] one would be
86388: kәtu zà čaùš odgovòrnik nàči nә stàdutu̥ sè ednò kәtu odgovòrnik nә stàduto
as if in charge, responsible for the flock. Yes, responsible for the flock.
86391: i drùgite òn kәtu vòdi tàmoka nәprìmer kato mèrɤt tuvà mlekòto mèri se
and he’d lead the others there, when they are measuring the milk,
86393: òn go mèri zapìsva si tàm ama ne zapìsvaa sәs tәkòvә
he’d measure it and write it down. But they wouldn’t write with [pen and paper],
86396: ami òdi tàm nә ednà bùka tәkà sәs sәs nòškata
he’d go over to a beech tree and then with a little knife
86398: si prài ednì čertìčki nèšto znàči
he’d make these slashes, you know?
86405: mlèku znàči trì kìlә ti e bìlu trì vèdra ke ti dàәt
Of milk. So if you had three kilos, they’ll give you three pails
86406: trìese kìlә ke ìmәš mlèku tì dә zìmәš drùgijo drùgijo
and you’d have thirty kilos of milk to take. Then the next, the next,
86409: i tuvà kàrә znàči edìn mèsec ili dvà mòže dә otkàrә
and that would go on for a month, or it could go on for two [months].
86414: izdàde se mlekòtu mlekòtu nә xòrәtә se izdàde pòsle si i rәzlàčvәt
The milk gets distributed to people, and then they separate out [the sheep].
86416: sèkoj si zìmә nèguvite kòj kàk si i i gledàl
Each takes his own, whoever had looked after which ones
86422: glèda si i cèlu lètu sobìrәt sènu [unclear]
They look after them all summer, gather hay [for them]
86424: à tàm tàm što gò pìšaa
Oh, [you mean] where they “wrote” it down?
86431: à tuà gu tovà se kažùvaše ràbuški ràbuš ràbuz znàči i [match strikes]
Ah that! That was called a tally.
86433: às ə kәtu saà vèke cèlu lèto sobirà:me sèno
Like now, already we’ve gathered hay throughout the whole summer.
86439: tɤ̀j i kɤdè gi mɤzète òfcite
So. Now, where do you milk the sheep?
86441: sәbirà:me štà šùmә dàbuva dәbìci znàči ìmә kurìi
We’ve been gathering oak leaves, oak branches – there are groves, you know.
86447: әmi ufcìte si se nәpràvә tɤ̀rla tәkòa košàrka si se napràva
Well, for the sheep, they make a pen, a sheepfold gets made.
86454: sèkoj ke zәgràdi si prez zimàtә ufčàru si e ufčàr
Each one fences off [an area] in the winter. That’s what shepherds do,
86455: ne sàm pušàč ne iskam košà košàra se napràva znàči
No thanks, I don’t smoke. So they make a sheepfold,
86459: and that’s where they milk them.
86461: rәbutnìcite kòj e vәzmòžen dè kòj kòj mòže dә glèdә
workers, whoever is able, whoever can look after them.
86467: kàk sɤ c’àlutu tɤkà ut c’àlәtә tәrlɤ̀ gi gònite ednà pu ednà
How do you [get them] all in the fold? You drive them one by one?
86470: nè ednà po ednà tè si se napràva utprèd znàči ìsxut vrәtìčka
Not one by one. They make this outlet in front, a little gate.
86477: dvè trì vratìčki kato sèdnat trìma mazničàre na stòluvetu
Two or three little gates where three milkers sit on stools.
86479: à nә nə stòluvetu jà sam na tòja stòl
Right. So [we’re] on stools. I’m on this stool,
86482: tì si na tòja tùa a a ofcète vrɤvàt pomeždu nàs
you’re on that one there, and the sheep pass between us.
86497: o o odzàt tùka kәtu e trɤ̀lata znàči ìma si pokaričàr
In the back here by the sheepfold there’s the driver.
86498: Right, and what does he do?
86502: bàčo stòje znàči odzàt i gòn’uva i znàči za da vrɤvàt ofcìte
The sheep owner stands behind and drives the sheep so they move [straight]
86505: da vrɤvàt za òti k’i izlègәt nèkoj pa mo
– move straight, because otherwise one might get out and –
86506: pa onìja nèma da izlègәt tò i ne mòže dә stàne
But this way they won’t escape [unmilked], it won’t happen,
86514: tàm è tè si vrɤvàt sàmi si vrәvàt tùka otprèt e pà zagràdeno
So they move along by themselves, it’s blocked off in front,
86517: tɤ̀rla ìma pàg zә dә ne izlègәt kato se izmɤ̀zat premèrɤt mlekòto
the pen is there so they don’t get out during the milking. The milk is measured,
86520: zakùsɤt ne znàm štò i hàjde pùštәt i tòja dèn
they have some sort of breakfast, then OK, let them go! and the rest of the day
86522: So. When did you shear the sheep?
86526: ufcìte se strigàd znàči ud girg’òvden znàči kәm šèsti desèti màj
Sheep are shorn around St. George’s day, the sixth or tenth of May.
86536: kòj ne mòže dә glèdә nèmaa kato saà sàm sәm
And those who couldn’t didn’t have any. Like now, I’m alone
86541: ne mògә dә glèәm à enà kuzà glèdәm sàmu tùka
and I can’t look after them. I just have one goat here.
86545: sàmi si pәsɤ̀t tàm nә tɤ̀rlәtә
[the sheep] graze by themselves in the pen.
86548: i tovà t’àsnoto mèsto tàm dèto minàvat kàk se kažùva
And what do you call that narrow area that they move along,
86549: kàrәm ә pu mèn ne à glèdәm әmi òdi pu mèn
I bring it along; I don’t even look after it, it just comes along with me,
86558: dobrè a tòo tàm dètu e nàj glàvnijә kәt sә prài prèmlәs
OK. Now back to when they note the yield. The head person [there],
86564: Huh? Don’t you call him “bach” (sheep owner)?
86567: è è bàč ә әmә znàči nәlì ti kәžùvәm
Well, sure, sheep owner. Didn’t I tell you
86571: kәtu se putfɤ̀rli mlekòtu nәprìmer dnèskә bәčùvәm àzeka
about ascribing milk [at the reference milking]? Today I’d be sheep owner,
86576: sràga se kә nә stràgata po nàči tovà e sràga ponèže minàvat
It’s called “straga”, the place where they pass by
86577: әku sɤ pòveče òfci ili pòveče mɤzničàre trì čètiri stòla ìma
If there are more sheep or more milkers, there’ll be three or four stools,
86578: dә kàžeme әku sә pò màlku trì stòla ìma
for instance; if there are less, then there’ll be three stools.
86581: sèdnɤt abe tòčno tәkà sàmu če stòluvetu kàg dә ti opìsvәm
They sit – just how, on these stools, how to describe [this] to you?
86584: tò stòlu znàči se napràvә sè ednò
It’s a stool, it’s made, well –
86591: sɤz bàzi sɤs čìmuve si gu nәpràvәt tәkà otprède è tәkà pudìgneno
They make it with chunks of sod. It’s built up in front like this,
86596: è kәtu tuvà sә dìgnәti nәgòre i tuvà tàmuka kәtu izlìzәt ufcìte
Like this, built up high, at the spot where the sheep come out,
86599: àh nә sràgәtә dә ne mòž də utèče ufcàtə znàči nә sràgәtә
in the “straga” so that any one sheep can’t run away, there in the “straga”.
86602: pres sràgәtә minàvәt à kәtu prez vrәtàtә saà tùka nәprìmer
They pass through the “straga”. It’s like passing through a gate, for instance,
86603: sàmo če pò tèsno e tәkà
except it’s more narrow, just enough …
86605: … for a sheep to pass through.
86607: They pass through one at a time.
86609: òti aku sә tìjә trìmәtә tàm mɤzničàre dә kàžem
So if there are three milkers there, for instance,
86612: tòj a fàšta tàә i i ә izdòje izmɤ̀ze a drùgijo drùgata
one grabs a sheep and milks it dry, and the next another,
86616: n nìe nә ednàk ne mòš ne də i izmɤ̀zeme jàs pùštәm tàa
and we can’t milk them all at once. I release one,
86619: tì lòviž drùgәtә drùgәtә i tàm si pustojànu vrɤvì si
you grab another, then another, and it’s a constant move through.
86624: nә sràgәtә si vrɤvàt pustujànnu òfci òti edìnu pùštә
The sheep keep on moving through the “straga”, since one releases,
86626: drùgiju lòvi znàči tò se brɤ̀že stàvә tàmoka što sə
another grabs, and it all gets done quickly like that.
86628: aha i tovà dèto dèto se sɤbìra mlekòto nә ufcàtә
Uh huh. And this – where the sheep’s milk accumulates –
86633: The pail is down below the …
86637: dèto tovà tò dèto go mɤzèš
… below the thing that you milk.
86639: vɤf ә vәf tuvà što go mɤzèš ml’àkutu le
in the – in the thing where you get the milk?
86641: à nә ufcàtә tuvà dètu se sɤbìrә
On the sheep, where it accumulates –
86643: à ìmeto ìme se kàzva ìme
A, udder! It’s called an udder.
86646: vìme vìme ìme ìme ufcàtә jà kuzàtә znàči ìmetu kugà [laughter]
“vime”, “ime” (udder) on the sheep. And look at the goat! Yes, udder. When [laughter] –
86652: strìženetu e [laughter] ìmә si tәkìi speciàlni krɤklìzi ili mòže sәs nòžnici
Shearing! [laughter] Well, there are special shears, or maybe with scissors,
86657: Scissors of the sort that tailors …
86663: terdzìite što sà i s tәkvìi mòže ә pә ìmә si
… old-time tailors [use], you can do it with those, but there are also
86664: i drùgi kɤrklìzi bàš speciàlni zә strìžene si ìmәše tugàj kәrklìzi
other shears. There were these shears specially [made] for shearing back then.
86668: sòpneš a ufcàtә znàči sòpneš à sèdneš sì i sì ә
You hobble the sheep, you hobble, sit by it and –
86674: às ustrìgvәx pu četìreese tòa dèn nàči kәtu sèdnә
I used to shear forty sheep a day. I would sit down [to it]
86676: ut sutrintà du òbet četìrese ke ostrìžem tùkə ə pə
in the early morning, and by noon I’d shear forty of them. But,
86677: a pa ìma nèkoj pa pèd dèset òfci ìmә pòveče ne mòže
but there’s some who would [shear] five or ten sheep, and couldn’t do more.
86681: kòj kòj kàk ìmә fàtkә bɤ̀rza fàtkә ìmә nèkuj
Each has his own approach, some [do it] quickly –
86683: әhә e kàk se kәžùvә tàә vɤ̀lnә dètu ә strižèš ud ednà ufcà
Uh huh. Now how do you call the wool that you’ve shorn from a single sheep?
86690: emì mì ustrìženә vɤ̀lnә znàči vɤ̀lnә ustrìgvә tòlku vɤ̀lnɤ znàči
Well, the shorn wool, that is, wool that’s been shorn, just wool.
86692: How much do they shear from a single sheep?
86693: o ot ednà ufcà zavìsi ufcìte kәkvì sә
From one sheep, well it depends what kind of sheep they are.
86697: àku àku ti sә glèdә әku ti si i gledàl ùbәu
If– if you’ve taken good care of them,
86700: ud ufcà mòžeš dә nәstrìžeš dә kàžem trì kìlә dvè kìlә
you can get two or three kilos of wool from shearing a sheep
86704: nò obiknovènno šìleta tovà ti onovà ti po kilò i polovìna vɤ̀lna i
but from yearlings, this and that, it’s usually a kilo and a half of wool.
86708: sìčkәtә vɤ̀lnә ednàkvә li e dèto jә ustrìgvәš
Is all wool the same, from everywhere that you shear it?
86767: tìjә nàš nàšte òfci tugàj i sɤgà sә me̝ronòsəni saà ìma
Our sheep then (and now) are the Merino sort. Now we have
86772: znàči krәstòsәni se ә tugàj bèa na nàšte čèrnә vɤ̀lnә i bèlә vɤ̀lnә
crossbreeds. But then ours had both black and white wool.
86774: How do you call the black kind?
86779: à à à čèrnә si vɤ̀lnә znàči čèrnәtә vɤ̀lnә ә tùrәš uddòlu vәf tuvà
Well, black wool is – you put the black wool below in this [place],
86784: bèlәtә uddèlnu kәtu a nòsiš nә vlәčàrkә ženìte predàt
and [you put] the white separately, take it to the carder, women spin,
86787: tàm čèpkɤt nòsi se nә vlәčàrkә izvlàči se
they comb it, take it to the carder and it gets carded.
86793: izmèsi se kɤdèli pràat à pòsle pràea grɤ̀dnici
they mix it, ready it for distaffs, and then later they made shawls.
86795: kòj kәkvò ìskә tәkò si pràeše znàči od nìx
Each one made whatever they wanted from it.
86798: a tàә mrɤ̀snәtә vɤ̀lnә kàk se kažùvә
And how do you call the dirty wool?
86800: mrɤ̀snәtә nèprànәtә nèprànәtә vɤ̀lnә nәlì tr’àvә se ispère
Dirty, unwashed. The unwashed wool. It has to get washed, right?
86802: hm onà ke se ispère sìčkәtә ne mòže dә ìmә mrɤ̀snә vɤ̀lnә
Yes, you have to wash all of it. You can’t have dirty wool.
86808: emi tò à emi tò e nà e sìčkәtә sèrava kugà a strižème
Well, well, - Ah, right! All of it is greasy when we shear it.
86812: kogà se strižè sìčkә sә kәžùvә tàa nè e pèrena
When it’s [just] shorn one says “This one isn’t washed [yet].”
86813: sèrava e vɤ̀lnata nè e pèrena
It’s greasy wool, it’s not washed.
86816: prudàvәš a nәprìmer na nèkuj ìska da mi a kùpi
You sell it, for instance, to someone [who] wants to buy it from me,
86818: ke te pìta kәkvà ti e vɤ̀lnata pèrena ili nèpèrena
he’ll ask you what kind your wool is, washed or unwashed.
86819: à sèrava si e vɤ̀lnata nàči punèže nè e
Ah, it’s greasy wool, you see, because it’s not –
86823: nè e ispèreno ot sèrata ot a tovà sɤdɤ̀rža tàmoka nèšto takà
it hasn’t been cleansed of grease, it [still] contains this –
86827: kato lèpi se znàči zә vɤ̀lnata ako ne jà ispèreš
this sticky [stuff]. That’s [how] wool [is] if you don’t wash it.
86830: ә kәtu če ispèreš tì pòsle čìsta stàva
Then after you wash it, it becomes clean.
86832: әmi ə tùka ut korèmo dèto tovà
But down by stomach, the part …
86834: okolo pokraj ìmeto pokraj glavàta kàk se
… around the udder, around the head, how ..
86836: how do you call that wool?
86838: nè pòtstrik se kažùva tovà znàči ako a si takòva
… those – that’s called skirting. That is, if it’s –
86840: dokato nè e tàa okàpva ako ako nì e u ustrìžeš
if you don’t – it falls off if you don’t shear it in time.
86842: nә vrème po korèmo ke okàpe tàa vɤ̀lna ponèže kato òdɤt
in time the wool will fall off of the stomach, because when they move around,
86845: à tùka is trɤ̀nite is pàproteka kàk òdɤt tò okàpva
when they move around hereabouts among thorns and ferns, it falls off.
86848: a pa kòj e tirikàt pәk pò ràno dә si jә isčìni
But someone who’s a clever one will dye it earlier,
86855: i si i pustrìže pu korèmo znàči ka a potsтrìže po opàškata
And you shear it off the stomach, and shear it around the tail,
86858: tùka kraj šìjata ke a potstrìže i slet edin mèsec
and here around the neck you’ll shear it. And a month later
86861: ke a strìže vèke ke i svàli runòto nàči
you’ll shear [the rest] and remove the fleece.
86863: ami ot ot šìleta ot jàgneta kàk se kәžùva tàa vɤ̀lna
And how do you call the wool you get from lambs and yearlings
86869: aà na tèp ti e kažuvàl nèkoj tìzeka
Hah, someone has told that to you [no doubt].
86871: a pa takòva kàk se naričat kato sa màlki
And how do you call them when they are little?
86872: kàk mu vìkaš na na kato rodì ofcàta màlko kàk otnačàlo
How do you call the young of a sheep, when it’s just born?
86874: emi emi tә àgәnce jàgne mu vìkame
86875: jàgn’e i pòsle kàk kakvò stàva
86877: ka kato ponagolemèe šìleta i vìkame šìleta
When it gets a bit bigger, we call them “shileta” (yearlings)
86878: ama na kòj na mɤ̀škite na žènskite
For which, the males or the females?
86880: i mɤ̀ški i žènski se vìkat šìleta znàči tàagodìšnite
Both males and females are called yearlings, the ones born in the same year.
86884: znàči prolètnite jàgništa se vìkat segà šìleta dogodìna vèke
That is, lambs born in the spring are called yearlings up to a year.
86887: And in their second year [they are called] “dzviski” (hoggets)
86892: And is the male [also] called a hogget?
86896: mɤ̀škoto se vìka dzvizò dzvìze znàči znàči po šilèto štò e dzvìze
The male [hogget] is called “dvzizo”. So after the yearling comes the hogget.
86899: tovà e dzvìze tovà e màtor tovà e stàr kòč
That’s the hogget, [then] there’s the “mator” [young ram], then the old ram.
86902: à e màtor trètata gudìna znàči kato fàneše
It’s a “mator” in its third year, when it’s just begun –
86903: And then it’s an old ram after –
86904: sta stàr kòč nàt trì gudìni tòa e stàr kòč sta
It’s an old ram after three years. That’s [when it gets to be] an old ram
86907: stàr kòč ili stàr bràf mòeš da go kàeš
An old ram, or you could also call it an old head.
86911: i i kakvò sә nèšto po rogìte pràexte li im
And what – did you do something with their horns?
86917: nè ste gi vìli tәkà dә sә krәsìvi də təkòvә
You didn’t bend them somehow, so they’d look nicer –
86921: àj [laughter] a be kòj ti u nèkoj kәtu ìmaš naprìmer a
Ho! [laughter] How did you – ? If you have one, for instance –
86924: kato às togàj kàk ìmax stò òfci nèkoj meraklìja ama na nèkoe
if someone had a hundred sheep like I did, and was particularly keen on one –
86925: koè e pò ùbavo jàgne nalì koè e pò ùbavo jàgne
if one lamb is prettier, then with the prettier lamb
86929: vrɤ̀zvaa im se rogòveto takà kato sa vìžda òšte malènko
they would bind up its horns when it was still small.
86933: ke mu i vrɤ̀zvәž za da izlègat nagòre i se vìka tovà kačòr
You’d bind its horns, so they grow straight; that’s called a “kachor” (stag-lamb)
86937: ә kәtu mu vrɤ̀zeš rogòveto i izlègәt nәgòreka znàči pràvo
When you bind its horns so they grow tall, that is, straight …
86940: nagòre a nè nastranì tovà se vìka kačòr znàči
… upwards, and not to the side. That’s called a “kachor”.
86942: è tòo ìma kačòr znàči kačòr si e napravìl
And then you’ve got a “kachor”. One’s made himself a “kachor”
86946: znàči ovènčeto ovnèto se vìka tàm dzvizàra se vìka kačòr
So a ram there is called “dzvizar”, [I mean] a “kachor”.
86949: And what do you tie [on the horns]?
86952: emi sɤs e sɤs edin konèc sɤs edna vrɤfčìca znàči
Well, a thread, or some sort of tie,
86956: à ut tìa kònopeto što sà ke nәprài edna vrɤvìčka znàči
or some hemp cord like they make now. Some small tie
86961: ke ke i vrɤ̀ze tùkə rugòveto i rugòveto ke trɤ̀gnɤt nanagòre
that you put on the horns, and the horns will grow up straight
86964: a nè nasranì òt na kòčoveto sa nastranì nәlì nә
nd not to the side. Because on rams they grow to the side –
86968: nәstrәnì sɤ àrno ama kato i vrɤ̀zeš na jàgnence òšte
to the side. Fine, but if you tie them when it’s still a lamb,
86973: kәkè se pudàat ròkčetata kәtu i vrɤ̀zeš tәkà i gi stègneš nәlì
as soon as its horns appear, if you tie them and tighten them,
86976: i tè trɤ̀gvat nanagòre i tàa gudìnә ke iskàra dә kàžeme
then they’ll grow straight up. This year, for instance,
86979: petnàese sàntima ròk drùgata godìna iskàrva òšte dèset pòsle
we had horns of fifteen centimeters, and the next year ten more.
86981: əm nèkuj iməše pu pò màlko ponèže pò udebel’àvat se nagòre
Some have less, but they get thicker as they grow up.
86984: kòlko zastarèva tòlko tòlko pò udebel’àva se kәm takòvata znàči
The older they get, the thicker [the horns], and so it goes
86987: i nògu ne mòže da iskàrame ftòrata trètata gudìna četvrɤ̀tata pa ìč
and we can’t get much height: the second, third, fourth year, and nothing
86988: togàj ke iskàraa  tòlko znàči pèt sàntima
They would only get five centimeters.
87098: ami kàg gi belèžexte ufcète belèžexte li gi da gi poznàvate
So how did you mark sheep? Did you mark them in a way to recognize them?
87099: Well, each one had a mark.
87167: i i štò sa kàzva tṛnjàne
So why – why is [the village] called Tŭrnyane [“Thorn-place”]?
87170: Because there used to be a lot of thorns.
87172: … up to your ankles. And in the winter, mud.
87177: gṛ̀sti ò sejàle sme gṛ̀sti i koto gi posèeme ednì sa belì
Oh yes, we sowed hemp. When you sow hemp, some [plants] are white,
87180: a drùgite ngi vìkame černì gṛ̀sti čɤ̀rnite pràvɤt sème
and we call the others black hemp. The black ones make seeds.
87193: a bèlite nèma iskàrvat i bèreme naprèt bèlite
But the white ones don’t. We harvest the white ones first ...
87236: i gi kàrame na rekàta ta gi tòpime
... and take them to the river to soak them.
87241: i pòsle koto okìsnat gi izvàdime i [laughter] vìkame mɤ̀neme
After they’re well-soaked we take them out and [laughter] (as we say) we swingle [them].
87244: dà kà sa kàzva tòo ùret dèto sa mɤ̀nat gṛ̀stite
Yes. What do you call the device that swingles hemp?
87249: è takà dḷ̀go i takà i u sredàta koto nòš
It’s this long, and in the middle [there’s something] like a knife.
87252: dà i a pòsle kato se
87253: po i po i pòsle kato ostàne tavà gi vlàčime
And then – we card what is left over.
87261: na grebenèca pràvime povèsmata i sɤ jà ne sɤ̀m prèla
With the carding comb we make a distaff-ful and – I haven’t spun [it],
87263: ama bàbičkite sa prèle za osnòva pa sme si tkàle
but the grannies have spun it for the warp, and then we’ve woven.
87270: za postìlki na krevàta nè e imàlo i po zemjàta da po
… to spread on beds. And there weren’t [things to spread] on the ground.
87273: a za tɤkàneto a sə se ispòlzva nalì osnòva i vɤ̀tɤk
So for weaving they use the warp, right? And the woof.
87274: kəto màlka si xodìla sìgurno sɤs ə govedàrka
When you were little, you probably went out as a cowherdess.
87276: belèk na tovà na ušìte se prài belèk
A mark – they make a mark on the ears.
87277: And how do they do that?
87278: a a tuvà sìgur me zapi èj tìze
And this surely – Hey, you’re recording me!
87279: He’s recording you; he’s recording you.
87287: na ofcàta tovà pretstavl’àva ušèto sà nèkoj ìma nàči
That means on the sheep’s ear. There are some [people], you know –
87291: jà ot tùka takà ke otsèčem dìp màlko i se vìka tovà izbrɤ̀ska
I make a little slanted cut here, and we call that “izbrŭska” (slant-cut).
87296: na dèsnotu kakòf ti e be belègo na dèsnotu ušè e izbrɤ̀ska
What’s your mark on the right ear? On the right ear it’s a slant-cut.
87298: drùgo drùgiju pәk po otprèt ìma
But another will [make it] in front.
87303: otprèt ràbuška a takà kato prevìeš ušènceto nalì
[He’ll make] a notch in front. So when you fold the ear over,
87304: i sɤs ednì pà sɤs nòžnici stàva tovà ili sɤs krɤklìzi
and then – it’s done with scissors, or with shears –
87309: otsèčneš dìp tovà se otcèpva dìp po màlkinko
you slice of a little bet and you get a “swallowtail” cut here.
87311: po màlko ama sèkoj č’e znàe belègo kakòf mu e znači
Very little, but [enough] so each one knows which mark is his.
87313: na dèsnoto ušè ti e belègo ràbuška otprèt ràbuška
So you’ve got a mark, a “rabushka” (notch) on the right ear. A notch in front.
87315: na lèvoto ušè ti e belègo odzàt ràbuška nalì odzàt se vìka
And on the left ear you’ve got a mark, a notch in the back. It’s called “the back”
87316: kato ušèto kato e takà ot tàzi stranà
when the ear is like this, on this side.
87338: ot kḷčìšta da rečèm ot ə
… [made] from tow, let’s say, from, uh, ...
87341: ot konòp a mòže da e ot vɤ̀lna
... from hemp – and it can be from wool –
87344: әm nè konòpenoto si e sàmo ot konòp
Ah, no. For hempen [fabric] it can only be from hemp.
87347: a za vḷ̀nata sàmo od vḷ̀nata sa tɤčɤ̀t
And for wool, they can weave only from [a warp made of] wool.
87349: and then [the kinds of] felt, for …
87351: a tùka stàrite xòra kək kək f kakvì drèxi vabèni sa nosìli
What – what kind of felt clothing did old people here wear,
87357: a pa otprèt se vìka pa prèdnata stranà
and [the notch] in the front part is called “the front”.
87361: [So it’s called] a slant-cut when it’s in back –
87362: o odzàt izbrɤ̀ska i otprèt mòže izbrɤ̀ska pa i otprèt ìma i izbrɤ̀ska
A slant-cut in the back, but you can also have a slant-cut in the front.
87363: ponèže tìja vɤf selòto sa znàči nògu nògu rètko trèbva da se slùči
Because it should happen very, very rarely that in one village
87367: na edìn belèg da sà mòjo belèk i tvòjo da se sravnàva
people should [all] use the same mark, that mine should be just like yours,
87370: osòbeno ako sa komšìi òti nèma da si i poznàete
especially if we are neighbors. Because otherwise you wouldn’t recognize them.
87371: nèkoj i poznàvat nògu ama nèkoj pa ne mòe gi poznàvat
Some would recognize them but others wouldn’t be able to.
87372: ako nè e belègo ne mòe gi poznàvat ke se zakàrat
If not for the mark they wouldn’t recognize them, and then they’d quarrel
87374: tì ke go vìkaš tvòje jàs ke go vìkam mòje [laughter]
You’ll say it’s yours, I’ll say it’s mine [laughter],
87375: and we might get into a fight!
87379: i drùgi drùg drùgi ìmaše li drùgi bèlezi
And other – were there other kinds of marks?
87380: nè na drùg belèk ìma kogà se sɤbìrat na tovà
No. Well [yes], there’s another mark when you gather at –
87385: na bačìjata na màndrata tùk è gòo kogà se mɤzàt
At the dairy farm, up there where they do the milking,
87390: kugà i sәbìrәt prez letòto sә dә tәkòva ìma katràn’
when they gather them there in the summer. They use pitch.
87392: ìmaše ednò vrème katràn’ znàeš li kәtu si
In the old days there was pitch (I bet you know that too!)
87397: i sɤs katràn’u i belèguvàme katràn’u i gu tùriš
And we mark them with pitch. You put it –
87399: na edìn ke e pres krɤ̀stu pràva čertà na drùgiju
One would make a straight line on [the sheep’s] back, another
87401: ke e ot srәnàtә nә drùgiju i tòo sèki znàe nàči
would [make it] on the side, and another – and each one will know
87409: dà koto se istɤkɤ̀t sɤ dɤdɤ̀t na vajàvica kàzvame
Yes. And after it’s woven, it’s given to the fulling mill, [as] we call [it] …
87416: na vajavičàr i kato gi donesɤ̀t i tàm gi bojadìšat
To the fuller. And when they take it, and dye it there ...
87435: tkàla sɤm i navòtki tkàla sɤm i kvò mu vìkame litò
I’ve woven by “navotki” (patterns), and I’ve woven what we call two-ply, ...
87439: i četvòrno s čètiri nìštelnika z dvà nìštelnika z dvà nìštelnika litò
... and four-ply, with four heddles. With two heddles – two heddles is two-ply; ...
87444: a po prèpis tɤkàla li si
And you’ve woven according to a “prepis” (pattern)?
87447: i tәkàla sɤm navòtka tovà navòtka se kàzva
I’ve woven by a “navotka” (pattern). It’s called “navotka”.
87452: And I’ve done weaving by patterns. My mother –
87454: mòjta màjka sè vìkaše bòže màle jà sɤm dṛ̀ta pa
My mother always said “Goodness sakes, I’m old and
87456: ne ne ùmem da da navàdam navòtka i tì kà znàeš
I don’t know how to weave according to a ’navotka’. How did you know
87459: a onò pro pep po prèpiska
87465: kakòf katràn’ ke e složìl nә ufcète
what kind of pitch [marking] he’ll have put on his sheep.
87470: i tàm i ofčàreto znàәd znàči pu kәtràn’u punèže
And the shepherds up there know, you see, by the pitch [marks]
87473: nә grɤbò se slàgә seà dèka se glèda nәlì
that were put on the backs [of the sheep]. Because it’s visible, right?
87476: i tìja è kato a vìdi à tàa e
and when they see one, they’ll say “Ah, that sheep [belongs]
87479: na èdi kòj si tòa kәtràn’ e nә tòa fil’ànkišìjәtә
to so and so, that kind of pitch mark designates that person.”
87485: ami a drùgi nèmaše li drùgi belèzi pu pu uxòtu
So – weren’t there any other marks on, on the ear?
87488: You didn’t punch [holes] in the ear?
87493: nè dùpčәt i saà vek’e kәt stәnà stupànstvutu tùrәt im
No, they don’t make punches. When the collective farm came, they used
87496: nèkәkvi dzәmbì tàm kәtu i jàs ne sàm vidèl
some sort of punches. But I never saw [any of that].
87499: So only the slant-cut and the notch.
87501: dà izbrɤ̀ski ràbuški znàči otprèt odzàd znàči àku tì e
Yes, slant-cuts and notches, in front or in back, so if you’ve got …
87505: dìp cèpnenko nèkoj pa mòže belègu dә mù e
