… a cut at a slant – but then someone could [also] make his mark
87510: nә vrɤ̀u nә ušèncetu saà sàmu tәkà e cèpnenku rәscàpeno
on top of the ear, with only a little bit cut out.
87516: I don’t know anything else [about that].
87518: navadàla sɤm navadàla sɤm tkàla sɤm sàmo če
I’ve woven by a pattern, woven by a pattern, except that
87523: ne sɤ̀m moža umejàla ne sɤ̀m znajàla da si prevṛ̀zvam
I couldn’t – I didn’t know how to tie it on.
87526: nalì koto go osnovèš i tùriš na krosnòto da go prevṛ̀žeš
You know, when you warp it and put it on the beam, to tie it on.
87529: svekṛ̀va mi i màjka mi sa mi prevṛzvàle
My mother-in-law and my mother would do that for me.
87532: And they would get the weaving started.
87535: i da pòčneš pòsle pa tì
For you to begin, and then you –
87592: But which – what kind of thorns?
87594: e tùka po selòto nè e bilò tәkà sɤ̀ga tùka ìma asfàl
Here in the village it wasn’t like that – now there’s asphalt here.
87596: tùka a bilò kəto mìnat kòlata sɤz volòvete
[Back then] it was like when oxcarts pass by.
87599: nè e imàlo prevòzni srèstva togàva
There wasn’t any mechanized transport then.
87605: i kato minàvat lètno vrème pepeltɤ̀ do tùka
And when they go by in the summer there’s dust up to here, …
87610: i tṛ̀n’e e imàlo tùk po trotoàrete nasèkɤde tie
And there were thorns there along the sidewalks, everywhere these –
87612: i às pòmnim kogà e bilò tṛ̀n’eto
Even I remember when there were thorns [here].
87613: [laughter] ama tò ə nalì tṛ̀n’e kato ž ә
[laughter] But this – isn’t [a matter of] thorns like …
87616: … the one that’s called Jerusalem thorn?
87619: nè nè è nalì ìma ednò bàbin zɤ̀p ìma ednò
No, no. There’s this – caltrop, you know? This –
87626: a nè e dràkata i tìja
87630: And so they called [the village] Thorn-place.
87632: vìe ste žɤnàli na rɤkà nalì
You all used to reap by hand, didn’t you?
87636: na rɤkà sme žɤnàle kòj kòlko zèmja e imàl sme z ožɤ̀nale
We reaped by hand. However much land anyone had, we reaped
87639: sìčko na rɤkà i sa vràle sa vṛšàle sa sɤs kòn’e
everything by hand. And [people] threshed – they would thresh with horses.
87640: But I don’t know that [from personal experience].
87642: nìe sme vràle sɤs mašìni tìja
87646: That’s how they call them, threshers?
87652: koto se ožɤ̀ne dokàrat tìja mašìni
When you finish reaping, they bring in these machines.
87655: ìmaše ednì vɤršìni mašìni gi kàzvat levàtor
There were these kinds of threshing machine they call a grain elevator.
87658: a koto vṛšè takà pàda dòle a pòsle dokàraa sɤs k’ùnci
When you thresh, [the grain] falls down, and then they drive it with steampipes.
87660: And when you thresh – [then] the straw –
87662: vṛvì dә na dalèče pò na dalèče i tam sɤ z zbèreme
The belt [connecting the machines] goes far, farther, and then we get together …
87666: pràvime pà kladn’à ot ot slàma
87670: i prez zimàta a prekà nìe tè tùk nadi sèlo
And then in winter we take it – we [live] here above the village –
87672: sme pravìle prez zimàta sèki si a kàra ìməme
We did it [there]; during the winter each one brings it – we have –
87674: sèki si ìma volòve kòla òfci
Each one has oxen, oxcarts, sheep –
87677: And in the winter [we put out] a ground cover …
87679: …for the animals [to protect them from winter frost].
87750: What do you grow in the garden?
87758: a da da mi kàžeš li kàk vɤršète
And – and can you tell me how you thresh?
87765: è tùka upkòlim s kulàtә prevòzim snòpetu nәpràim xɤrmàn
Well, we drive the cart around, bring in the sheaves and make a threshing floor.
87767: How is a threshing floor made?
87769: ama zèmem tә gu ub’ɛ̀lim ìmame si nìe xәrmàn si ìmәme
Well, we set to and clear it. We’ve got a threshing floor [already],
87772: ubàče gu b’ɛ̀lime òbәl xәrmànә ub’ɛ̀lime gu
but we clear it. A threshing floor is round. We clear it –
87776: We [clear off] the grass with a small hoe.
87781: trevɤ̀tә mu b’ɛ̀lim trevɤ̀tә mu b’ɛ̀lime izrìneme gu isčìstime gu izmet’ème gu
We clear off the grass, shovel it out, clean it, sweep it,
87788: turìme wòdә ә zberème òlski lәjnà ot guèdәtә ut vòluvetu
pour water [over it]. We gather manure from oxen and cattle
87792: i tùrim tә gu zәmàžeme̥ sèa sìpem òdә nәprɤ̀skәme gu
and put that down, and smear it [around]. Then we pour water [on it], sprinkling it.
87794: xodìla li si u u granìtovo kvò mu vìkaxa pò ràno
Have you been to Granitovo? What did they used to call it?
87800: I’ve gone to the village celebration.
87803: emi no tùka tùka ùčea ot kalùger ə tìe učenìcite tùka ùči
Well, they studied here – pupils from Kaluger studied here.
87806: i kàk sa učìle tìja decà u òsɤm časɤ̀ da sɤ tùka
And how these children studied! They had to be here at eight in the morning,
87808: pres tovà tùka nagòre mu vìkat bùjaka pa čèren pɤ̀t
coming across – they called it  Buyak up there – [on] a dark road,
87812: pa snèk àjde kogà e sùxo snèg vijàlica onì pòčvad
and snow. When it’s dry snow [it’s different, but] in blizzards, they start
87816: zәmàžemè gu i kәd gu zәmàžeme i drùgijә dè̝n še vɤršème
We smear it all, and when we’ve smeared it we’ll thresh the next day.
87820: zìmәme sfɤ̀rl’әme snòpetu tùkә vәf xәrmànәt
We take the sheaves and thrown them onto the “xarman” (threshing floor) –
87823: gùvnutu pu pràvu gùvnu mu vìkame
Actually it’s the “guvno” (threshing floor). We call it “guvno”.
87824: Is that how you call it?
87828: gùvnu i nasàdame gu nәsәdìme c’àlu i tùrime dikànetu
“Guvno”. We put it down. [When] we’ve put it all down, we lay the threshing board [on the sheaves].,
87831: i vòluvetu bìul’:etu̥ kәkòtu ìmә kòtu sme ìmәli
And then the oxen, water buffalo – whatever there is, whatever we had –
87834: i hi fprègnemè i tòj fàti tә òzi jà sèdam
we harness them up, and [my husband] starts to drive them and I sit
87837: nә dikànetә kàrәm i sprɤ̀ kàrәm i sprɤ̀
on the threshing board. I steer it forward and stop, steer it forward and stop –
87847: i gu nәserè zәmàže dikàn’әtә i nәberèš snòpjetu
And it shits and smears the threshing board. And you gather up the sheaves.
87849: What’s at the bottom of the threshing board?
87854: Right, and what sort are they?
87858: kәtu kàmen’ tò ednò tәkòvә pretstәvl’àvә
Like a stone. They’re like something of that sort.
87864: širòku utprèk’ i kòlkutu prәstìte dә mìnәt tәkà
Wide in front, [wide] enough for fingers to pass through, like this.
87868: tàm gu tùrime nә dikàn’ә dәrvò e dikàn’ә dәrvò nәpràeno sì
We put it there on the threshing board. It’s wood, made of wood.
87873: nәglәbènu pri cìgan’e gu dadɤ̀t tә im nәpràjәt dikàn’әtә
Hollowed out, by gypsies. People give them [the wood], and they make threshing boards for them.
87877: tәkòәt krèmen’:te̥ tә i nәpràjәt i nìe tùva pòčneme i vɤršè̝me
They ready the flintstones, and make up the threshing board. Then we begin the threshing.
87882: kәtu gu svәršème vɤršème ubrɤ̀štәme sәs vìlә nәprèš
When we thresh, we toss [the sheaves] about, first with a pitchfork
87885: sètne z bandrɤ̀k sètne s lupàta
then with a “bandrŭk” (large hayfork), and then with a shovel.
87892: sәz zɤ̀bi sɤz zɤ̀bi èj tәkà č’ètiri zɤ̀bә
With prongs, with prongs. Like this, four prongs.
87901: pɤ̀ru s vìlәtә vìlәtә znàete kəkvò e edìn čatàl
First with the pitchfork. You know what a pitchfork is? It’s a fork.
87904: z dvà ednì zìmәt pràvu uts’àkәni ut
With two. [For] some they take [tree branches] cut directly [in that form] from …
87912: We spread [it] all about with the pitchfork.
87914: rәstɤ̀rs’әme gu s vìlәtә i go i pòsle pudìre ubrɤ̀štәme
We spread it all about with the pitchfork and after that we turn it over
87917: pә s lupàtә s lupàtә dɤ̀rvena tәkàvә
with the shovel, with this wooden shovel
87922: dә se ubɤ̀rne klәsɤ̀t udgòre kәtu vәrɤ̀d dikànetu dә gu uvɤrhɤ̀t
So the ears will turn upwards when the threshing board goes to thresh them.
87928: i kәtu gu uvɤrhɤ̀t se svɤršè zèmeme tugàvә tә gu zberè̝me
And when they thresh it all out, when it’s done, we take them and then gather them up,
87930: and make it all into a pile. [unintelligible]
87935: nәpràime gu nә sòr i kәd gu nәpràime nә sòr
We make it all into a pile, and when we have made the pile,
87939: smetè̝me hәrmànә tә pòčneme ubɤ̀rneme se nә v’ɛ̀terә
we sweep out the threshing floor, and then begin to turn it over in the wind,
87942: i fɤ̀rl’әme v’ɛ̀eme z bɤ̀ndrәkә tɤ̀j
and throw [it up]. We winnow [it] with the “bandrŭk” (large hayfork).
87945: v’ɛ̀eme v’ɛ̀eme udv’ɛ̀eme gu kәd gu udv’ɛ̀eme tә gu isčìstime
We winnow and winnow it, and when we finish winnowing we clean it out
87947: nә zɤ̀rnu nè mlògu čìstu dè uddelìme gu ut slàmәtә
into grain. [It still] isn’t very clean [yet], we need to separate it from the straw.
87950: slàmәtә ә tìkәme f pl’ɛ̀vn’әtә a pәk žìtutu pòčneme
We shove the straw into the hayloft, and for the wheat, we begin
87955: tùvә s lupàtәtә pruv’àvәme gu iščìstuvәme gu
to winnow it out with the shovel, we keep on cleaning it up.
87957: če kəd gu prov’ɛ̀eme tə gu iščìstime ut slàmata kətu se iščìsti
And when we winnow it and clean out the straw, when it’s clean
87960: ìmәme dɤrmòn’ i prez dәrmòn’әt tùrimè i
we’ve got a “dermon” (large sieve). And we put it through the large sieve
87966: tɤ̀rsime i vudɤ̀ i slet tuvà sètne pәk nә rәšètu
We shake it too and after that put it through a grate.
87968: ustàtәkәt tәkà dètu ustàne dә nè e prez dәrmòn’әt
The remainder – what’s left that didn’t go through the “dermon”,
87970: We shake it through the grate.
87974: i pòsle gu tùrime f čuvalàta i gu vәrzème
And then we put it in sacks and tie it up,
87976: and take it over to the shed.
88040: da vreštɤ̀t da vìkat pə ìdɤt po dvaesetìna decà od gòre
to shriek and shout – there’s about twelve children up there.
88042: e tùka meždu tìja dvàta hɤ̀lma
88045: predì ìmaše kolàrski pɤ̀t i se izlìza tòčno na granìtovo
There used to be a carter’s trail, leading straight to Granitovo.
88047: da pò drùgo li govòrat tàm
Yes. Do they speak differently there?
88052: za kvò si zabelèzala da e razlìčno ot tùka od bèla nèkoja
What have you noticed that’s different from here, from Bela? Some –
88053: pa mì smo ofčarè pa tè tekà
Well, we are shepherds (Torlak sound of word), and they –
88059: hə a skòml’a skòml’a kato koi
88066: kato nàze da skòmja tùka dɤ̀lgo.polè tìja
Like us, yes. Skomlya here, Dŭlgo Pole, those –
88069: tùk od blìskite sàmo kalùger i orèšec govòrat turlàški drùgite si
Of the areas close by, only Kaluger and Oreshets speak Torlak. The others –
88071: orèšec ə i sèloto i i ga to gàrata gàrata
Oreshets – both the village and the station –
88072: sìgurno sa došlì ot ràzni selà tàm da rabòtat
[people] have probably come from different villages to work
88074: in the railway authority or something.
88078: pa to ìmaše i jà ne znàm kvò ìmaše tàm
And there used to be – I don’t know what there used to be there.
88084: There was a state factory there, right?
88093: za pruizvod za prerabòtka na lavandùla
… for the production and processing of lavender.
88114: na vrèmeto ot rekàta sìgurno ste polivàli ili kvò ìma li
In the old days you probably irrigated from the river or such.
88119: a ìmaše tàm kɤdè pòmpenata stàncija ìmaxme gradìni i tàm s rasàžda:me sìčki
There was – we had gardens by the pump station, transplanted everything there.
88122: mòjto pa tvòjto pa na narèt po dvèsta mètra tàm
Mine, then yours, two hundred meters’ [long], all in a row –
88126: kòlko po màlko i tàm sàde:me pipèra tàm polìva:me
maybe a bit less – and we planted peppers there, and irrigated them.
88127: tùka sàmo kartofi sàdexme a pòsle oddòle onàa gradìna
[but] here we only planted potatoes. Then there was that garden below
88131: na ednì naši bratofčèdi u vèlingràt tè ne ìdvat vèče tùka
[belonging] to some cousins in Velingrad. They don’t come here anymore,
88138: oklekovèja vìkad zemì go i go rabotì jà dokɤdè mòžex gu rabòtex
They went lame and said “You take it and work it.” So I did, as long as I could,
88140: sɤ̀štətə bàbə kəd’èt ti rəspràvəm bàbə kàp’če
The same granny I was telling you about, Granny Kapcha –
88143: ama sɤ̀ga sè sɤm izdàla bagàža če go ostàim màj
but now I’ve lost my strength, and I’ll probably be letting it go.
88144: I’ve been hearing that for five years [now].
88147: It’s the fifth year I’ve heard this.
88150: I keep [meaning] to leave it, but –
88155: mә dà è pa to dòle ràvno ìnače tùka plàmen nasàdi
Well yes. It’s flat down there, as opposed to here [where] Plamen planted
88158: do kràja lòze u brèga dòle ràvno ta nasàdim domàti
vineyards along the hillside. It’s flat below, so [that’s where] I grow tomatoes,
88159: a few peppers, and that’s it.
88161: kogàto b’àx màlɤk pòmn’ә če pròsto pri bàba mi i d’àdo
When I was little I remember that when my grandmother and grandfather –
88166: a tàm tɤ a trevà bèše gol’àm problèm zaštòto pròsta nìšto ne ras
– that grass was a big problem because nothing grew –
88170: sàmo sàmo tre sàmo trevà zaštò
88172: a kakvò s pràvite s trevà
And what – what do you do with the grass?
88177: è pa plàmen prɤ̀ska ili kupìl e kosàčka kòsime isfṛ̀game gòrime
Well, Plamen sprayed, he bought a mowing machine, we mow it, toss it, burn it.
88179: nèkoga trevàta sme sɤbìrale za živòtnite a segà
Earlier we used to gather the grass for the animals, but now –
88180: But now they don’t gather it.
88184: ìmam pèt ku sèdam kokòški tovà e cèloto imàn’e [laughter]
I’ve got five – seven hens, and that’s it. Our entire holdings!
88186: And she knows them all by name.
88188: kət se pensionìrax i stàrec ә stàreca bèše sàm ostànal tùka
When I retired, and the old man was alone here,
88190: vèče bòlen ne mòže mɤžɤ̀ mi go pensionìra tovà bèše pokràj prevràta
already ill and unable. They pensioned my husband off just before the changes,
88191: i òn se pensionìra mlàt dojdè tùka cɤ jà òšte rabòteše
he retired young and came here, alas. I was still working,
88194: dòjdem si u pètɤk večertɤ̀ štò na pednèvna kogà u sɤ̀bota
I’d come Friday evening because I was on a five-day schedule. So on Saturday –
88198: ò znàeš li če sɤm se cenìl za ofčàr abe kәg bòže
[he said] “You know, I got hired as a shepherd.” “Ah, my God,
88199: kakɤ̀f ofčàr če bɤ̀deš tì be tàm edìn čovèk mu dàl
what kind of a shepherd will you be?” A man there had given him
88201: ednà ofcà i àgne da mu xòdi na redɤ̀
a ewe and a lamb [and asked him] to take his turn
88227: nə uf za ofcìte za ofčàr što onìja dṛ̀t
as shepherd for the sheep, because that one [was] old
88229: i ne mòže i mu dàl tàa ofca i àgneto
and couldn’t [manage]. So he gave him that ewe and the lamb.
88232: dobrè dojdò drùgata nedèl’a tàa ofcà bilà imàla bliznèta
Fine. I came the following Sunday and that ewe had birthed twins
88233: tòj kupìl i drùgoto àgne da nè e àgneto sàmo
He bought the other lamb too, so it wouldn’t be just one lamb,
88238: da sa dvè àgənca što ofcàta u zarèdata tàm àgneto dòm bleì
so there’d be two lambs, with the ewe out on rounds and the lamb home bleating.
88242: dvè zavɤ̀di tovà dojdò si otìšɤl u četvṛ̀tɤk na pazàr
So he made it two. I came, and he went on Thursday to market
88245: i kupìl čètiri prasèta [laughter] ne ednò ne čètiri onì mɤ̀nenki
and bought four piglets [laughter]. Not one, not – but four! And tiny.
88249: onì dvè umrèe dvè ustànae i otogàva vèče ne kupùva òn prasè
Two of them died, two remained. And after that he never bought pigs again.
88250: jà òdim tì idì i kupì prasè e kvò da pràim vìka
I go. “You go and buy a pig!” “Well, what am I going to do?” he said –
88253: no òn mlàt pensionèr kvò da pràim da sedìm tùka te tekà
he’s young and retired. “What should I do? Just sit here like that
88258: da nìšto da se ne zanimàvam ugovòril s ednà mòja bratofčètka
and not have anything to do?” He came to an agreement with a cousin of mine –
88261: onìja ìmat žènsko telè če go kùpi da glèda kràva
they keep a cow – that he’d buy it and raise cows.
88266: sìčkite togàva razvàlia tèkezesètata i nazìmae no kràvi no òfci
They broke up all the collective farms then, and people got cows, sheep,
88268: no sìčko svèkɤr mi ne dàva i dùma da ne stàva
[a bit of] everything. My father-in-law wouldn’t allow it. “No way!
88273: vìe nèma da zìmate a sme dàle unèle u tèkezesèto
You’re not going to get [them]. We gave it all over to the collective farm,
88275: i kràva i junìca i nè i dùma da ne stàva ne dàva
both the cow and the heifer – No! No way.” He wouldn’t allow it.
88277: ako sàkate da me umòrite tovà ne mòže da bɤ̀de tekà
“If you want to kill me, it can’t be this way.”
88280: òn ne vèrvaše če se razvàli tèkezesèto i če stàne
He didn’t believe that the collective farms would fail, and that things would be
88283: kvò e segà i mòja mɤ̀ž zemà telèto če čùvame go tùka
the way they are now. So my husband bought the calf, and we’re raising it here.
88287: òn jà slet čètiri gòdini se pensionìra tamɤ̀n kad dojdò
He – Four years later I retired, and just when I came [home]
88290: no golèma junìca če se zaplòdi kàe sɤ̀ga i če se otèli
“The heifer’s big; it will [soon] be bred,” he said, “and now it will calve.”
88292: i če ìmame mlèko dobrè i če pràat obòra ja
and we’ll have milk.” Fine. They’ll make a stable. I –
88294: tì č ìdeš da go pasèš da go pasèm tàm na
“You’ll go pasture it.” So I’ll pasture it there
88296: nadi lìnijata na košàrata mu vìkame ama rèče tì se vàrdi
above the railway track, at the sheepfold, as we call it. “But watch out,” he said
88300: što onò pokìmva da te ne zbodè abè hә ә vàn’o
that it doesn’t gore you, because it shakes [its head].” “Ah, but – Vanyo,
88302: da me ne bùtne nèma da te bùtne tì kà
won’t it butt me?” “It’s not going to butt you, you just –
88306: sɤs sindžìra če kìmaš no jà ja vòdim sɤs sindžìra a òn stoì
you’ll shake it with the chain.” So I lead it with the chain and it stays
88309: e tùka na na baìra a jà natàm vèče zamìna obikòli
there on the hill. And I’ve already started to go around
88311: če fànem nagòre brèga a tò ìma edìn vìr takɤ̀f i kosìtri
and make my way up the slope, where there’s a deep pool and swampgrass –
88314: iskàralo trevojàk i o òn ottùka vìka òdi li òdi pìta
a lot of grass has grown up there. And he calls from there, asking “Is it walking?”
88316: è i kato mu čù glasɤ̀ i kato sècna onàja kràva
And when it heard his voice, that cow pulled [me],
88319: i kato me sècna i jà se fɤrlì u onìja vìr
And when it pulled me, I plunged into that pool
88320: a tò ìma zelèno takòvo ne znàm kvò se kàzva
And there’s this green stuff there, I don’t know how you call it –
88322: Hey Plamen, how do you call that?
88331: mɤ̀h fanàlo očilàta mi fṛknàe jà ispùšti kràvata junìcata onà izbèga
Moss all over, my eyeglasses flew off, I let go the cow, the heifer, and it ran off.
88334: a jà se pl’osnà kato žàba u onìja vìr i cèlata onovà zelènoto
And I was sputtering like a frog in that pool, all covered with that green.
88337: očilà nèmam kɤdè se cèlata sɤm zelèna òn bṛ̀zi vìka
No idea where my glasses are, I’m green all over, he hurries over and says
88340: màle ako e zavìla sindžìrɤ na rɤkàta če mi otkìne rɤkàta
“Oh my!” If the chain had gotten wound around my hand it would have cut it off.
88344: do dojdè tàm ìzmɤ̀kna me iz onìja vìr vṛnà se
He came there, they pulled me out of that pool, and I went home.
88349: oblèko se tùka omì se òn a izvède gòre i ja pajvanìsa
I washed and got changed, he took [the cow] up above and hobbled it.
88352: i jà sedìm sɤs stòla do n’èa da se ne skubè
And I’m sitting on a chair by it so it won’t break loose.
88354: pasèm [laughter] sedìm tàm čèkam onì pravìa tùka kvò pravìa
I pasture it [laughter], sit there and wait, they did what they did
88357: na obòra dojdè ta a prìbra tovà sɤm ja pàsla
at the stable. He came and took it [after] I’d pastured it that much.
88361: bodèše onàja kràva ùžaz bèše i na kràe
That cow gored [people], it was horrible! And finally
88366: i n’ègo go zbòde ta sɤz zòr go otɤrvàme
it gored him as well, and we extricated him with difficulty.
88370: tà a prodàdome došlè da a kupùvat ednì tṛgòfci ot montànsko nègde
So we sold it. Some merchants came from the Montana region to buy it
88372: edìn dè se perčì ò jà kòlko kràvi sɤm karàl
One was bragging: “Oh, I’ve handled so many cows,
88379: pa sɤm doìl vrɤ̀zvaše a da ja izdòi onà rìta
and milked [them too].” He tied it to milk it and it kicked out,
88382: ne dàva da pripàri do n’èja jà če gə i
it didn’t allow him to get near. “I’ll [handle] it and [I’ll]” –
88384: òn mu vìka gošò ə ne mòže takà dàj da zèmme
he said to him, “Gosho, we can’t have this. Let’s take –”
88387: òn nòseše ednà tojàga debèla mɤžɤ̀ mi da se odbran’àva
He had a thick club. My husband, [acting] to defend himself
88388: od n’èja nèma nèma nè màni tàa tojàga i zavèl ja dòle
from it, [said] “Don’t, don’t! Drop that club!” So he took the cow down
88392: kɤdè stopànstvoto ìma visòko ta da ja kàčɤt na kamiòna
to the center of the [old] collective farm to load it onto the truck.
88395: i onàja kràva kato go izletì i go pòtpre na ednò dṛ̀vo
But that cow went for him and pushed him up against a tree,
88398: na čerèšata dìp če mɤžɤ̀ mi si nosìl tàja tojàga
smack up against a cherry tree. And my husband now had this club
88400: pòčva da ja bìe po glavàta to go ostàila
and started to beat the cow on the head with it, and it let go.
88405: ta i onìja bèše po bòlnica mu sčupìla ednò rebrò
And the other guy landed in the hospital, [the cow] had broken his rib.
88407: ne im li rèžat na takìva tovà ne im li rèžat
Don’t they cut these – don’t they cut their –
88411: e kòj e imàlo do tovà segà u tovà vrème li znàeš
Well, who ever [needed] that back then? You know [how it was]
88418: pri prevràta i kɤdè razzìmame tìe kràvi kɤdè stanàme grat gràtski sèl’ani
at the changes, how we took away the cows when we became “urban peasants”.
88421: There’s so much we didn’t understand.
88424: onà pak mòe si go bùtne i z glavà sìgurno
Still, it could have butted him with its head.
88426: pa dà onà kato si e nejèlo si e i kat
Well yes, because it was bad-tempered, and when –
88431: àz bex mnògo protìf tìja kràvi togàva
I was very much against those cows at the time,
88433: i katò mi se obàdixa ednà vèčer da mi kàžat
and when they called me one evening to tell me
88436: če butàla tàtko tùka i u bòlnica vìkam e saà pàla kolàta
that it had butted Dad and he’s in the hospital, I fired up the car,
88439: ìdvam zastrèlvam kràvata i se pribìram če ùtre sɤm na ràbota
I’m about to come, shoot the cow, return home, and go to work the next day.
88442: ama mòže da odèreš i da i zèmeš mesòto
But you could have skinned it and taken the meat.
88445: òn se òn se ràdvaše takà u ə nèma kvò da prài
He was – he was happy [with it] and couldn’t do anything else.
88447: ìde u košàrata pri n’èja i ja češàl po rogìte
He went to the pen where it was and scratched it on the horns.
88450: i tè kàzvat če ne e trebvàlo da ja čèša a òn
They say he oughtn’t to have scratched it, but he
88454: i se radvàl i ja češàl po rogìte i onà za tovà bòla
caressed it and stroked it on the horns, and that’s why it gored [someone].
88459: pa pòsle kupìme drùga pa èdna se òbesi
Later we bought another, and it got strangled.
88460: pa à pa drùga i tàa kɤdè tàa kɤdè ja prodàdo jà
and then another, and that one I had to sell,
88462: ako ìmaše kòj da mi nabàvja sèno nèmaše da ja dadèm
If there’d been someone to get me hay I wouldn’t have sold it.
88465: pèt šès kràvi sme pre prekàrale kato tàa kràva sè ednò
We had five or six cows, [but none] like that one
88466: sàmo ne mòžeše da govòri ja vṛvìm i onà vɤrvì slet mène
The only [thing] it couldn’t do was speak. I go along, it comes after me,
88471: nèma da vòdim nèma da kàram àjde pèpo tùka àjde nasàm
I don’t need to lead it or drive it. “Come on, Pepa, come this way.”
88474: àj sedìm da ja pasèm trɤ̀gvam si onà trɤ̀gva po mène
I sit down to pasture it, and when I get up to go it comes after me.
88478: sèdnem da ja dòim ne dòim u čàša tùrnem kòfata tùka
[When] I sit down to milk it, I don’t milk into the glass, I put the bucket here –
88483: i bèše sɤs šès sìsi ot pètata ìmaše mlekò mɤžɤ̀ mi
It had six teats. There was milk in the fifth, [but] my husband
88486: sè vàrdeše da ne dòi pètata da si dòi čètiri tò tečè
kept constant watch to not milk the fifth, to milk the four. Such a flow!
88492: nèkoj pɤ̀t ìdeme sùtrin onò podjàlo kato ležàla tòja kɤdè ja zemàl
We’d go in the morning, it’s all wet where [the cow] lay. The guy who took it
88494: i po trìes kilà mlèko e d doìl na dèn
milked it and got thirty kilos of milk a day.
88497: na dèn i i nìe sme doìli po trìes kilà si nòsime
A day! We also milked and got thirty kilos
88501: bès kɤrmìlka bes mnògo bèše làkoma na pàša ùžaz bèše
without additional fodder. [That cow] was greedy at pasture, a terror!
88506: sìčko edèše sɤrcèto me bolèše za onàja kràva zavèdo ja dòle
It ate everything. My heart ached for that cow. I took it down
88508: onà stèlna slet ednà dvè sèdmici če se otèli [cough]
[when] it was pregnant, ready to give birth in one or two weeks [cough].
88511: i tòa došɤ̀l sɤz bùs i ja bìjat da a
and then this guy came on the bus and they beat the cow so that
88514: ja ja vòdim za kapìstrata što onà od drùgite bèga
I would lead it with a halter, because it ran off from the others.
88517: i ja bìjat da se ukàči vɤ̀tre onà nèšte
They beat it to make it climb up inside but it didn’t want to.
88519: jà se rèko čèkaj jà če se ukàčim onà če dòjde
I said, “Wait a minute, if I climb up it will come
88522: po mène lelè onà če te zgàzi kàk če me zgàzi
after me.” “Oh my, it will trample you!” “How would it trample me?!”
88526: sàmo kato ja t àjde pèpke jèla bàbo onà nàkolenči na tovà
Only – “Come on, Pepka, come with granny.” It knelt down onto it
88533: i pòsle tòo ja ispùštil drùgata godìna ta se najàla sɤz žìto
Then they neglected it, and the next year it gorged on wheat,
88537: a tàa kàk se obèsi kɤdè se obèsila
And the one that got strangled, how did that happen?
88538: è pà vṛzàl e mɤžɤ̀ mi [cough] do edìn brèk
Well, my husband had tied it up near the slope,
88542: i no te tekà izgorèla trevàta i onà se pṛzòlila nadòle
but the grass had burned off there, and it slid down
88544: i nè e možlà da se vɤ̀rne nagòre iz brèga
and couldn’t climb back up the slope.
88548: tò se opɤ̀nalo sidžìma i se obèsila
It got caught in the rope and got strangled.
88550: i takà stanàme sèl’ani ò bòže tà òfci
That’s how it was. We became peasants. Oh, those sheep!
88553: pèt òfci dva.trinàes jàgɤnci sìčkite bliznìli ednà trì
Five sheep, twelve or thirteen lambs – Each one had twins, some [even] three.
88559: ùžas nanesèm u štàjgi tùka gi natùram zimàta studèno
Horrible! I bring them here and I put them in crates, it’s cold in the winter.
88565: natùram gi u štàjgi no dòktora veterinàrnija minàvaše na provèrka
I put them in crates, and the veterinarian would come by for checkups,
88569: zìmat krɤ̀f na kràvite islèdvat tàm kvò pràat ofcìte gledat a
they take blood from the cows to analyze it, and look at the sheep,
88572: lèle jà me sràm vìkam jà glèj nanèla sɤm tìja jɤ
Oh, but I’m ashamed! Look how I’ve put these –
88576: no takà vìka se glèda stòka no nì se izàgn’e
But he said that’s how you look after livestock. But they lamb
88579: za dvà trì dèna po dvè po dvè onò mɤ̀nenko mòkro
for two or three days, and then two by two, tiny, wet,
88583: vɤ̀nka mrɤ̀zne tàm studèno natùrala sɤm štàjgi i sɤm gi narèdila tùka
and it’s freezing cold outside, so I’ve put them in crates and kept them here.
88839: tè tùj sɤm se rodìla do gròbišteto tè tùj izràsla
I was born here, near the cemetery, and grew up here.
88841: è tàm imàlo tùrska ìža jà u n’ù sɤm se rodìla
There’s a little Turkish house over there, I grew up in it.
88844: a tàm pòsle baštà mi nəpraìl do polovìn
My father built it – [well,] half of it.
88846: glèj seà onì àjde ob’asnète i
Look here, they – go ahead, explain to her [why you’ve come].
88849: došlì sme màlko da govòrime po torlàški
We’ve come to talk a bit in Torlak [dialect].
88854: I’m from Vŭrbovo (in the Torlak region), but –
88857: onì tàm nèma màlko sɤm zabovarìl
They don’t  – I’ve forgotten a little.
88861: No, they don’t speak so much that way over there. [laughter]
88863: e onò u sèko selò no u stàk’ofci jàle
Thе [speech] is [different] in each village, for instance in Stakevtsi  –
88866: gdè e krečimìr i onì ìmamo hɤ [laughter]
[And] where Krechimir is, even they say “imamo”. [laughter]
88870: mì dùmamo vrèvimo oni dùmamo gḷčimò el oràtimo el
In the meaning “we talk”, we say “vrevimo”, they say “glčimo”, or “oratimo”, or
88872: [laughter] da ni raskàžeš za ednò vrème pòmniš li predì stopànstvoto
[laughter] Tell us about the old days. Do you remember before collective farms,
88873: čàsnoto kogà bèše kvò ste rabotìli
when it was private (ownership), what work you did [then]?
88874: a predì predì stopànstvoto jà sɤm četìrese i pṛ̀vi nàbor a nàči
Before – before collective farms. I’m of the birth year ’forty-one, which means
88875: tovà si e bilò čàk pedesè pedesèt slet pedesè i ftòra
that was already in ’fifty, after that, ’fifty-two
88876: mòže da e bilò amà pà da pà pòsle dà
88878: e pa kvò sme rabotìli orèš kòpaš ə kvò si sàdiž
What did we do? You plow, you dig, you plant the way [you do]
88881: gradìnu sɤ̀ga tì a i takà ìde se u pol’èto
[in] your garden now. You go out in the field,
88882: pa se orè za kukurùs pa za žìto pa za zòp
you plow for corn, for wheat, for oats,
88884: šoto ot tovà ni e bilò xranàta prez zìmata
because that was our “hrana” (food) during the winter.
88885: jà màlko i mèšam nalì vìdiš
I’m mixing [my speech] a bit, you see.
88888: xà da rečèm jedèn’eto ama sedèla sɤm trì dɤ̀na u gràt
Ha, let’s say “jeden’e” (food). I’ve just been three days in the city…
88891: pòveče štò pòsle nalì dojdè učìlišteto i tekà sèki se spas’àva sàm
…more [actually]. Then came school, and then each one fends for himself.,
88892: jà sam imàla sàmo màjka i baštà što ə màjka mi e
I had only mother and father, my mother was –
88895: baštà i e bìl u lòm kofčèznik tàm
Her father [worked] in Lom, there he was the paymaster,
88897: as they call them in the military.
88900: obàče se razbolèl’ i onà kat se rodìla òn bìl umrèl
But then he took ill, and he had died by the time she was born.
88903: ja kažì ednò vrème kàk sèexte
Tell [us] how you used to sow in the old days.
88906: a ednò vrème po tì kàza če po nìvata sè ste bilì
You said that in the old days you were constantly out in the fields,
88910: tì se umòri sìgurno umòrihme te səs prìkaski
You’re probably tired; we wore you out with chatting.
88914: a detè kat se ròdi kvò se kogà go a a
And when a child is born, what – when do you –
88916: tùka kogà praìa tovà tèkezesè imàlo li e da gònat òrata
When they set up the collective farm here, did it happen that they forced people
88921: čùl sɤm ako nè e ofčàra ofcàta ne ne puš pùšta mlèko à
I’ve heard that if the shepherd isn’t present the sheep won’t give milk.
88924: What was it [like] back during the private ownership [era]?
88928: baštà trèto detè ə nali karàlo karàlo oženìlo se
My father was the third child, he went along a while and then got married,
88930: te tùj za siràče i onò nèmaš kòj da ti pomògne
and to an orphan, so you don’t have anyone to help you out.
88933: mì tè tìja trìmata jà kat sɤm se rodìla pŗ̀voto detè
So there’s the three of us. I was the first born.
88935: štò mì smo im bilì trì ama bràtče mi umrèlo pòsle
There were three of us, but my little brother died
88936: na trì gòdin no i togàva bèše tekà ə nèma dòktur
at three years of age. There weren’t doctors then.
88939: a jà se razbolè ot skarlatìnu òn n’èga go ùlovi po mène
I had taken ill with scarlet fever, and he got it from me.
88942: što jà sɤm bilà pò golèmška i sem sɤm uspèla nalì
The fact that I was bigger was why I managed
88945: da se spasìm onò pràznici togàva se mnògo praznùvaše
to survive. And holidays – people celebrated a lot then.
88947: svì pràznici ivànovden dragànof tàm nàj nalì znàeš kvò si e
All the holidays: St. John’s Day, St. Dragan’s Day, [etc.] You know how it is ...
88951: po kalendàr tè i da četìš če vìdiš nali svè im tə takòva
... on the calendar, you can read it and see all of them there.
88953: ìmaxa o izvinj’àvajte ìmaxa òrata konè
People had – oh excuse me! – people had horses (standard form) …
88960: ahà sɤs ə nalì sɤs fajtòn sɤs ə takòva i òn če
Uh huh, [and would get around] by carriage, and he would –
88962: trèbe da ga kàraš čovèka da ti zakàra bòlnija u takòva
that’s how you would take someone, take a sick person in that,
88964: u belogračìk imàlo e čàsni dòktore nè e imàlo tegàj
to Belogradchik [where] there were private doctors. There wasn’t
88965: segà bòlnica ne pòmnim mòž da si e amà sìgurno
a hospital. I don’t remember now, maybe there was. But probably
88968: e pòsle pràena ne znàm i tè tekà spasjàvamo se samì
it was built later, I don’t know. Anyway, we look after ourselves.
88973: i màjka jùtrom če omèsi kravàjčence štò xɤ svàki pùt
Mother will mix up buns in the morning – well [not] every time
88975: nè e imàlo i bràšno i tegàj onà če omèsi če ùzne
did we even have flour! But she’ll mix it up, she’ll take
88979: ako ìma sìren’ke če ponesèmo štò pa mì ne smò imàli
cheese if we had some, we’ll take it – But we didn’t have –
88981: kat nèmaš bàbu i dèdu tì ne mòe čùvaš i živòtni što onì
when you don’t have grandparents you can’t even look after the animals.
88982: nalì tì da ìdež da rabòtiš n’ì trèbe da gi glèda nèkoj
That is, when you must go to work, somebody has to look after them.
88984: i togàva ìdemo è tùj blìzo podi selò ìmamo n’ìvu
And then we’d go – here near the village we have a field.
88987: ìdemo i se vṛ̀nemo da poedèmo dòm mì smo bèdni bilì
We’d go [there] and then come back home to eat. We were poor,
88989: nèma da se pràim na bogàtu i sɤ̀k sɤm si
I’m not going to pretend I was rich. And now I’m the same.
88991: But I’ve got a rich soul,
88998: a mòže i pò skròmno dàže a jà mnògo skròmno živèem
Well, I can [live] more modestly. I live a very modest life.
89001: tovà sìčko koè mi e od rodìtelite obzavèždanija nèmam
Everything I have is from my parents. I don't have any household appliances,
89004: è segà pèrem na rɤkà e štò pa za mèn si
even now I wash clothes by hand, and what is it to me
89007: če si opèrem nèma da cèl dɤ̀n sɤm svobòna [laughter]
that I’ll do my washing [this way]? I won’t – I’m free all day! [laughter]
89010: glèdam si gradìnku i tegàj ìdemo od tàm do podi selò
I look after my garden. Back then we’d go outside the village
89013: da si porabòtimo nèšto onò nalì znàeš i togàva si imàlo zàvis
to work a bit. Back then, you know, there was envy –
89018: kòj imàl pòmoš òn te ne vèrva nalì dùmu sìtija glàdnija ne vèruje
whoever had help didn’t trust you. As they say – the sated disbelieves the hungry.
89021: a tè tekà i tegàj tùka komšìe amà ìma bàba dèda
Yes, that’s it. So there were neighbors, but they had grandparents,
89022: pa òfci pa kozì pa a mì nèma kvò màjka dùma
sheep, goats. We didn’t have much, but mother said,
89025: nèma da kazùete a mì naprài kìselo ə kosàčko kìselo
“Don’t talk about it.” And we – she’d make pepper-cucumber soup ...
89029: sɤs sùvu sùvu čùšku i ako imàlo kràstavica ama onò
... with dry – dry peppers, and if there was cucumber, but
89032: kràstavica odàvna ovòl’ke nèma nèmu kadà i da da ga pol’èvamo
they haven’t had cucumbers this big for a long time. No time to water them.
89035: pràte me mène onò ja detè rečèm pol’àla sɤm ga
They send me, and [I was] a child, I’d say I’ve watered them,
89036: ama kakò sɤm ga pol’àla jà sàma si znàm [laughter]
though the way I’ve watered them, only I know! [laughter]
89040: i tegàj pòsle pòčva vèče da se pribìra nalì kat okòpamo svè
And then you start to gather in everything you’ve hoed.
89042: ìdemo baštà mi prài dòm sɤz dvète rùk’e a mì də
We’d go – my father built a house with his own two hands – and we’d
89046: unesèmo tùglete če nèma nèma kòj da pomògne i tegàj
bring in bricks because there wasn’t – wasn’t anyone to help. And then
89048: ìdemo s màter mi da kòpamo jà sɤm bilà sìgurno trèto četvṛ̀to
we’d go with mother to dig. I was probably in third or fourth grade.
89051: sɤs n’ù ìdem da kòpam a kvò sɤm kopàla pa
I’d go with her to hoe, and what I hoed up, well –
89054: ò pa tegàj sɤm se sìgurno naučìla jàle jòš ùmem [laughter]
I certainly learned how, and I still know how … [laughter]
89057: da kòpam i jòšte kòpam i tegàj onà rečè nèma da kazùete
… to hoe, and I still hoe! And back then, she said, "Don’t tell [people]
89061: kvò smo jèli à mì pokùsamo ot kosàčkoto kìselo i
what we eat." So we nibble on [our] pepper-cucumber soup and –
89064: ako ìma drùgo bèbe onò uvṛ̀zano u l’ùl’kutu odzàt
And if there’s another baby it’s bound up in a cradle on your back.
89066: tì znàeš li kvò e l’ùl’ka
Do you know what a cradle is?
89073: à takà ama sàmo če e pò dḷ̀ško nalì
89077: što e bèbe tùreno tàm ga zanesèmo vṛ̀žemo tàm na nèkakvo dṛ̀vo
.. because a baby’s been stuffed into it. We carry it there and tie it on some tree.
89082: àko e uzèlo da òdi onì iskòpu bàbkutu pa ga tùre
If the child has begun to walk, they dig out a hole and put it
89084: da sèdne dòle onò če pìka li kvò če prài
to sit there so it can pee or do whatever,
89085: te tàm če sedì što onà trèbe da i u rabòti tòj
and it’ll sit there, because its mother has to work.
89086: pa če pòsle nèma lèp ə zìmata kvò da se edè
Otherwise there won’t be bread or anything to eat in the winter.
89088: pòčva da se pribìra a tovà da se žn’è
Everyone starts to gather – that is, to reap
89090: wheat, oats, rye – [we do it] all by ourselves.
89095: tè i tòj da kàem znàeš li kvò e sṛ̀p znàeš
Ah, I’ll talk about that. Do you know what a sickle is?
89098: dà pa sɤz dṛ̀vo tùj dṛ̀škata
89102: da ne ubìva i tḁkà navedèš se i rezè rèžeš ednò
… so it won’t hurt [you]. And you lean down to cut, you cut this –
89105: ə è pa no si ìma ə ìma si no jà ìmam nègde
Uh, well, it’s got –  I’ve got one somewhere,
89107: ama nèznam gdè sɤm ga turìla
but I don’t know where I put it.
89111: dṛ̀vena dṛ̀ška tùreno nalì tovà onò e takà sṛ̀pa
A wooden handle, attached to this, and the sickle is like this, ...
89116: i togàva ə tùk ìma ednò ɤ kɤdè napràeno onò tovà
And then there’s this thing that’s made –
89118: pa vìš li kàk sa se izobret’àvali òrata da da
See how clever people are, what they have invented
89120: da gim e pò lèsno što kòj znàe kvò e bilò odnačàlo
to make their lives easier! Who knows what it was like at the beginning –
89122: nùmem da kàžem nalì kɤ jà predì da se ròdim
I can’t say, it was before I was born,
89124: ama takà si e bilò z godìni i tegàj žn’èmo žn’èmo
but it’s been that way for years. And then we reap, and reap,
89127: a pà pà da ga vṛ̀žeš pà da ga zdèneš na snòp
and then – then you gather it up and make it into sheaves,
89129: prài se ednò vɤžè pàk ə ot ə tovà od žìtoto
and you make a “vŭzhe”, a cord of the wheat itself [to tie the sheaf].
89131: kvò jùže jùže li mu vìkate
What [did you say]? Do you call it “yuzhe”?
89135: tòčno takà jùže ama sɤ ìde načɤ̀ska da se naprài
Exactly that, a “yuzhe”. And one goes at night to make it,
89138: što onò kato grèe sḷ̀nceto onò se napečè i ne mòže
since when the sun shines it will get hot and one can’t –
89139: no trèbe da è da è
it needs to be – to be …
89144: dà màlko da ìma takòva i pòsle se vṛ̀že
Yes, to be a little like that. And then it gets tied off,
89146: pà ga sɤbìramo na tekà se dène pa pòsle pa pòčva
and we gather it up, and put it [in piles], and then they begin
89148: do ə vṛšìdbata i se pòčva a màjkata kojàto e nalì
[with] the threshing. They begin – And then mother, or whoever
89151: ili če ìma žetvarè kòj ìma po pòveče a argàti
[will be feeding] the reapers, when there are additional hired hands…
89156: da mu pomògnu što òrata nèkoj sa imàli u u salàš
… to help out, because some people had – In Salash
89158: bogàti mnògo nè e imàlo sɤz ə živòtni pòveče
there weren’t many rich people. Mostly people had animals,
89160: a imòt do devedesè pa do stò dèkara dalì e stigàl nèkoj
but someone might have managed holdings of 90 to 100 decares.
89163: mòže da e imàlo dè sɤs takìva pò stranìčni nalì
There might have been some like that, with holdings on the side.
89167: i tegàj kvò če napràe prekàrvu ili si pomàgu kòj ìma pòveče nalì
And then they take – or help the one who has more –
89168: tàm ìma na dùmamo gùvno tàm sìčki si kàra si
Everyone goes to what we call the “guvno” (threshing floor).
89169: sèki si dène kato mu dòe rèt da vṛšè i pòsle
Each puts his in when his turn comes to thresh, and then
89171: ednì si pomàgu a ženàta ostàne dòm da ugòtvi če pa trèbe
some help others. But women stay home to cook, because it’s necessary
89174: da ìma da da gi xràni tìja kɤdè sa na mašìnite
to have enough to feed all the people [working] on the machines
89176: što onò nalì kakò bèše əm sɤs lakombìl bèše nalì tekà bèše
like that one. What was it?  It was the one called a “locomobile”, right?
89180: i vṛšàčkata i vṛšàčkata i togàva si pomàgat kòj òče dè
And the thresher. People help with the thresher – if they want (that is).
89182: što no i sɤ̀ga smo si takìva mì smo ə bɤ̀lgarete individualìsti
We’re still like that, we Bulgarians are “individualists”.
89185: dàj da si govòrimo če sme
89187: takìva i sɤ̀k smo si takìva ɤ vìdite li
… that way. And we still are. See,
89192: ə kat òtide u čužbìna ispɤln’àva sìčki pravilà
when [a Bulgarian] goes abroad he follows all the rules.
89194: à kat e u bḷgàriju si prài kvò sàka
But when he’s in Bulgaria he does whatever he wants.
89196: ne vìdite li če e takà
Don't you see it’s like that?
89199: i kato če go prài na inàt
It’s as if he does it out of pure stubbornness.
89201: ta tì pòmniš vɤršàčkite kato dojdòa a predì tòj predì tòj
So you remember when threshing machines came in. But before that,
89204: kvò kvò e ə kogà nè e imàlo vɤršàčki a kòni
what [was it like] when there were no threshers but [just] horses?
89206: a ne mòm da ti kàem pa sìgurno sɤ ga buvàli
Ah, I can’t say. Probably they pounded it.
89208: pa sìgurno onò ne mòže drùgo
Well surely! It couldn’t be any other way.
89210: no onò drùg nàčin nè e imàlo kato i tegàj se pribìra
There wasn’t any other way. So now when it all got gathered in,
89213: pa àjde pri da pribèru žìto pa àjde dṛ̀va da se nabàve
[we say,] "Let’s gather in the wheat, and then let’s go get wood,
89214: če pa ìde zìma i tè tekà i pos
because winter is coming." And there it is.
89215: s kvò če gi kàru tìja dṛ̀va
What will they [use] to bring in the wood?
89218: s kvò gi kàru tìja dṛ̀va tùj u ìžu
How do they bring the wood to the house?
89219: o sèki si e nè sèki ama pòvečeto sa imàli
Oh, everybody had – not everybody, but most people had
89221: volòve ili kràvi i kòla sèki trèbe da si ìma dobìtɤg
oxen or cows and a cart. Everyone has to have livestock
89223: zɤ dɤ mòže da si pribère kòj če ti ìde da ti
in order to bring things in. Who is going to come
89224: da te slùša mòže da otìde àma ako ti e bràt el
to do you favors? Someone might come if he’s your brother, ...
89228: inàče trùdna ràbota i i tè tekà i se pribìra z
Otherwise it’s hard work. So you bring [things] in,
89232: zimninà kvò ìma i sèki ako ìma živòtni šùma šùma se sèklo
winter forage, whatever there is. Whoever has animals goes out to cut foliage
89235: esentɤ̀ tàm u goràta a takòva ə na na plàstove nalì
in the autumn, up there in the woods, and [piles it up] in layers.
89236: Just like you put down hay, ...
89239: tekà i šùmata dàže zìmata kòj imàl mnògo živòtni po osɤmdesè kozì
... that’s how you store the winter foliage if you had many animals. Eighty goats
89240: dèda mi na mène ama on u drùga kɤ̀šta ostanàl
my grandfather had, but he lived in another house.
89241: sa imàli òsɤm po osɤmdesè kozì i osɤmdesè òvce
They had eight – eighty goats and eighty sheep.
89246: onò jàz màlko probà pòsle kadà stanùmo pensionèri a ə sɤsipìja
I tried that out a bit when we retired, but [we were] ruined.
89247: vèrno ìmaš ìmaš jàgn’e ìmaš ə mlekò ìmaš sìren’e amà
It’s true that if you have a lamb you’ve got milk and cheese, but
89249: trèbe sèki dɤ̀n i da te mòkri i da e studenò tì otòdiš
you need to be at it every day, to go out in the damp and cold.
89252: To go out and milk them.
89256: a bè nò trèbe gi napasèš ta da mḷzèş
Well, you have to pasture them if you’re going to milk them!
89260: [laughter] inàče nèma a mḷzèš i tekà ìmaš si jàgn’ence ìmaš si kokòščice
[laughter] Otherwise there’s nothing to milk! But [if] you’ve got a lamb, hens,

Otherwise I haven’t gone anywhere else. There’s no other [thing] I can

89749: na tòj mèsto se sɤbère cèlo salò si kàra tàm snòpeto

89812: nè ama tovà e bilò u stop u stopànstvoto sabère su svì

89835: That’s right, [to know] how much is yours.

and put a cover on top. We cover it with a brick, or it can be a stone,

89934: tùrnem òšte ednà tèžes i ga ostàim nò si se doiscèdi

89944: u ednà tavà ìmamo si tavà odèlno i ga narèdim tàm

90593: ne sɤ̀m pravìlḁ jà bulgùr ìma ednì òra sa pravìle ama
I haven’t made bulghur. Some people have made it but

90606: ami sedènki sedènki pràveme seden kotò dòjde svèti ilìja svèti

90608: koto e si tòj e na ftòri àvgust
when – that’s on the second of August.
90613: St. Elias’s day, on the second.

St. Elias’s day. They pronounced it to be the twentieth of July
90616: ònia.dènka li kvò jà si go znàm na ftòri

90625: popòvete i tè nèmat ràbota ta

90627: nèmat ràbota ma a da promenìm a pa da ne pràim
They’ve nothing [else] to do “Let’s change it!” So we can’t put on

and they go to someone’s celebrations [even though] life is expensive now.

Life is expensive now. So what – what were you saying?

90649: a nìe nə òdene òjde:me i na òbet edè:me koto žɤ̀neme nèkoj

90665: za svetùčkata t’à ìska da kàže na kakvò nè na tòka

90682: slàgame ò predè:me si na mèsečina èkstra nìe tè si

90692: You won’t wear [the clothing from it].
90695: ama ne gì li pràexte po kɤ̀štite ili na vɤ̀nka na megdàn’a

90697: na megdàn’a na vɤ̀nka mòže i po kɤ̀štite koto sa zazimèe

90699: i po kɤ̀štite a koto e vɤ̀n bèreme se tàm ženorlìa doòdat

90701: ženì momì zàedno nèma koto segìkana da nèma ženì

90702: ženìte sa poznàvat i si predɤ̀t i tìja si glèdame

90706: mɤ̀že ìma si dečurlìga i tìja si ràbotea pri nàs

90707: əmhəm pa i da ne vɤ̀ ostàvat samì s ergènite
Aha, so as not to leave you alone with the bachelors.

Mhm. But we say, “There’s no such thing”.
90709: kàzvaj za nèkoga tì segà màni
Tell about the old days! Let the present go.
90710: e za nèkogi nèma ni takòva
Well, in the old days there wasn’t any such thing,

I’m telling him about that! Back then that’s how we did work bees.

Yes, different. A house party is different, a woman can’t do [her own] work.

There are many men, and she’s alone, so she calls the house party, and we spin.
90723: ta i predèm napredèm i po dvè trì vretèna i t’à

She calls us to the house party and we would go.
90730: əhə tovà znàči da da pomàgaš na n’àkoj
Aha, that means that you’re helping someone.
90737: sedènkata sì e da se grìžiš za tèbe si sèki da
At the work bee you’re concerned for yourself, each one.

90797: če si kṛ̀stiš na sestrà na bràt na svèkɤr na svekṛ̀vu

90814: dɤšteràta a sinɤ̀t mi e zapisàl na baštù mu
[for] my daughter and recorded the name of his father [for] my son.
90815: [He was alone] because his father had died.

90823: tàm da mu četì kvò da

and they christened it in the church.
90837: a sinɤ̀t mi tùka ga kṛštavàmo dòma tàm u tùja kɤ̀štu

90848: dà òn pa nè e kumunìs

90876: and one made “miyane” (wheat and egg casserole).
90879: [laughter] kažì za pòpa i za kumɤ̀ [laughter]
Tell about the priest and the godfather.
90881: a dà tovà e tovà e interèsno dovɤršì za pòpa
Yes, that’s interesting. Finish up [the story] about the priest.
90883: ɤ i pòpɤt nejtè da ga kṛštàva i sède
Well, the priest hadn’t wanted to do the christening, and sat down,
90885: ama da če obèduje i òn dòma
but he’ll eat [with us] at home.

So the godfather and the priest drank brandy together, both got fairly drunk,
90895: pa kà si zapojàše i kùm i pòp ta si pojàše

90914: ama ednì nèče da se pìšu
90918: aha kulàci gi kàžu ama òn i mòjɤt svèkɤr

90920: se nejtè pìše vednɤ̀ga [laughter] dèda na milènu

90935: a kato se nàpravi tekezèto i se pisàše

There was a bakery, an enormous reading room, stores –

But we set up the reading room later. I worked at the reading room

and ten days to me. But he couldn’t work them all, since he worked in the mines,

so I had to work them [too]. Closer on they made the bakery.
90959: prèt čitàlišteto fùrn’a bèše ìmaemo tùka vùrn’u u selò

And I worked twenty days there too. But now – who would work
90963: bes pàre ta da mu dàvaš èj nàdnicata da mu e [laughter]

We worked in the mine, in Pernik, on this –  there –
90975: na ùlei ednò sigà si ga spòmn’am vɤ̀tre
in the chutes. I remember now [how it was down] inside
90978: [where] they got the charcoal out of there.
90985: u mìnata u k’umùrɤt idòmo da rabòtimo besplàtno mladèži
We young people went down to work in the charcoal mine, for free.
90986: sà kòj če ti rabòti bes pàre nìkoj

what labor was seen, what struggle was seen, during that time!

91004: a tùka gi rasturìše sìčko rasturìše a nìe smo ga pravìli
but here they wrecked it, they tore everything down. And we had built
91007: i kancelàriju tùka pravìmo gòre u tèkezèto hm vlačìla sɤm pèsɤk
an office up there in the collective farm. I had dragged [bags of] sand,
91014: əm cimènt bìemo da napràvimo ednà ubavin’à napravìmo gòre pe
we mixed cement by hand, to build nice stuff up there, but
91016: rasturìše svè nalì tikà tikà došlì vremenà tekvìja vremenà
