92171: kà stàde stopànstvoto dva.trinàes li bèxme pedesè i sèdma li bèše
when the collective farms came, or maybe we were 12 or 13. Was it in ’57?
92174: dva.trinàez gòdin pa žn’èmo onì ni se ràdvat dèka
[Yes,] twelve or thirteen years old. And we reaped, they were happy with us,
92175: sɤs sestrà mi nèma ednà pò màlka èm bèxme
me and my sister. One wasn’t smaller than the other, we were
92181: mnògo ednàkvi čèrni kosìčki ednàkvi drèški jèlate bìzete bìzete
very much alike: black hair, the same clothes. “Come on, twins, twins!”
92183: da da ne nì nè bliznàci a bìzete da dòjdu bìzete
They didn’t [call] us “bliznatsi” (twins) but “bizete” (twins). “Let the twins come
92187: da ni pòžn’u nìe de decà ama otìdemo da ràduemo se
to reap for us.” We were kids, but we went, and were happy.
92190: če ti dadè [laughter] dvàese stotìnki če ti dadè ednò šekerčè
“I’ll give you [laughter] twenty stotinki, I’ll give you a cube of sugar.”
92194: is pàzuku bàba izvàdi onò pəžɤltèlo ama [laughter] se zaràdvaš
And Granny pulls it out of her bosom, tarnished, but [laughter] you’re happy
92196: če ti e dàdəl nèkoj nèšto
92198: kato se žn’e kàk se rèdɤt tìja kɤdè a
How do people line themselves up when they reap?
92200: mɤčìl se e naròdɤt takà e bilò položènieto takà si è
People had it hard. That was the situation, that’s how it is.
92257: By handfuls, handfuls, the reaping maidens.
92262: ìma li nèkoja kojà e nàj naprèt
Is there someone who’s up at the head?
92265: po sta po staršinà tekà go ako pò ne žn’è onà sàmo prožìn’a
The one with seniority. She doesn’t reap much, just marks out the reaping area.
92268: nalì u stopànstvoto nèmaše kombàjni pṛ̀vete godìne
There were no harvesters in the first years of the collective farms, you know,
92271: žn’èmo žèmo nàruku i onà si sàmo prožìn’a po
we reaped and reaped by hand, and she just directs the reaping on –
92272: tovà se kàzva pòstat kɤdè sme
that’s called the reaping track, [the place] where we were.
92273: pòstat li kɤdè trèbe edìn da go tekvòj
Reaping track, where one needs to –
92278: kɤdè sme tŗgnàli da žɤ̀neme na na rèdɤt kato sme se naredìli
The way we were lined up when we set out to reap in a row.
92280: tovà vìkame da iskàrame tàa pòstat i če počìvame
We say, we’ll get through this reaping track and then we’ll rest.
92283: tàa si sàmo prožìn’a do kɤdè e da ne gà iskrìvi
She just keeps track enough so the line doesn't get crooked.
92287: čèla se ožèni za krìv mùš
[People say] she would marry a crooked man!
92292: [laughter] a nìe osòbeno kràjnite kɤdè sa vṛtìš i se umòriš
[laughter] And those of us at the ends [of the line] turn around a lot and get tired.
92296: ma ot štò se umorìste a be vìkam stojàmo ta se umorìmo
“What tired you [all] out?” [she said]. “Well,” I say, “we stood here and got tired.
92299: tì vìkam sàmo prožìn’aš naprèd ama nìe vṛtìmo
You”, I say, “only mark out the track in front, but we [have to] turn
92305: ot sredùtu na kràjɤt nàj vèče ama sɤl da rabòtiš žn’eš
from the middle to the end the most." But one must only work and reap.
92310: tùramo rukòl’k’e po nàs ako nèma mùžje da onì otìdu na kosìdbu
We put handfuls behind us if there aren’t men to [help]; they go off to mow.
92312: nìje vṛzùjemo ednùš hm zmijà pod rukòl’k’e i ponèže jà sɤm bilà
Once we were tying [sheaves] and – a snake under the handfuls. So since I was
92317: nàj bestràšna mène me òkaju da tèpam a pa tèpajte
the most fearless, they called me to kill it. “So kill it!”
92321: zaštò mène me òkat ìmaše mèsnosti kɤdè pɤk ostàne sèno nepribràno
Why do they call me? There were places where the hay remains ungathered,
92327: ùtreden obezàtelno če nàjdemo zmijù kəkvòto i rukòl’k’a ako nèšto ni fàne dɤ̀ž
and the next day we’re sure to find a snake. And if there’s rain [on] the handfuls,
92329: i ne mòže da gi vṛ̀žemo pod rukòl’k’ete naòdimo zmìje
and we can’t tie them off, then we find snakes underneath the handfuls
92334: ili u u žìtoto sa nèma segà tàa u sɤrvàjver i u kḷ̀cnula
or in the wheat, but not now. It bit that [woman on the TV show] “Survivor”:
92339: ta u odraskàla ta lèle ùžas mòre umrè nènčo vodeničàrov
it scratched her and [she shouted], “Oh horrors! Noncho Vodeničarov died!”
92342: na edɤ̀n sɤrvàjver tùka edìn mnògo dobɤ̀r od bḷgàrija
[He’s] one of the Bulgarian [actors] on “Survivor”, very good.
92347: uš ga manàxa sedam òsem gòdin nemà sɤrvàjver segà pàj onà bèše
And they let it go, there’s been no “Survivor” seven-eight years and now –
92354: mnògo silnə igràč sìlen igràč ama e na pùstinijat òstrɤf kḷ̀cnu
He was a great actor, a great actor. But it bit her on a desert island.
92358: ta takà sme mɤčìli i sme rabotìli pòsle pràimo kṛ̀sci od əm
And so. We suffered and worked and then made cruciforms from –
92361: nìe odnesèmo se od ə od snòpjeto napràimo kṛ̀sci
We carry them off and make cruciform of the sheaves.
92365: zdènemo gi ùbavo da gi vètɤr ne razdùva da gi ne sobòri
We stack them up nicely so the wind won’t pull them apart when it blows.
92368: i pòsle min’ùju sɤs kolà li če e s kamiòne li če
And then they come by with carts or with trucks
92370: da prekàraju da se vṛšè takà e bilò u u žètvata
to take them off to be threshed. And that’s how it went with harvest.
92372: vɤršìdba s kvò səs kòn’i sɤs dòma sɤs volòve i
What did you thresh with? Horses, oxen? At home?
92374: amì ìmaše vèče počnàxa u stò u dòma
Well, there was – they already began to – at home –
92377: sɤs volòve i sɤx lè sɤs lesè
with oxen and with – with a “lesa” (wattle harrow).
92383: ot prùk’eve de [cough] baštà mi e na dvè dṛ̀ve màlko poiskrìvena naprèt
From branches. [cough] My father [took] two pieces of wood, slightly curved in front,
92386: turìl si gi e da se ə iskrìvi i ot leskòvi prùk’e
and made them curve [more]. Then from these hazelwood branches
92389: e isplèl da ìma dèka da ìde nò za sèden’eto
he wove something to make a place for sitting,
92391: decàta da sedìme tàm da težìme da se pò bṛ̀že
for us kids to sit there, to add weight to make it [go] faster.
92394: a kòj ìma kon’ì sɤs kon’ì se vṛšè stòdžer vṛ̀že se ə južè
Whoever had horses would thresh with horses. There’s a pole, you tie a rope
92396: i se sɤs kon’ì vṛšè a nìe sɤs volòve i sɤs lesè
and thresh with horses. We, with the oxen and the wattle harrow,
92399: vṛšèmo vṛšèmo vṛšèmo pretrìšamo dvà puti trì puti pretrìšamo
thresh, thresh, thresh, shake it twice, shake it three times,
92402: da stàne na slàmu da izlèzne žìtoto i pòčnemo i na
to make it into straw, so the wheat will emerge, and then we begin,
92407: obèremo slàmutu ka u ukàramo u plèvn’u i pòčnemo da umìtamo
we gather up the straw, take it to the loft, and start to sweep out
92411: žìtoto ta da vèemo da iskàramo [laughter] da iskàramo plèvutu
the wheat so we can winnow it, to make it [laughter] so the chaff
92413: od ednà od ednù strànu žìtoto ne znàm a be kòlko e
is on one side and the wheat on the other. How much it –
92416: mnògo e bìl tèžɤk živòtɤt ama ama to bèše vèselo
It was really hard work, but – but it was happy.
92420: nezavìsimo ot sìčko bèše bèše vèselo ìdem kà otnesèmo àmbar
Regardless of everything it was a happy [time]. We carry [it] to the barn
92423: ta sìpemo žìto imèemo si àmbar s presèci za žìto za ečmìk
and pour off the wheat. We had a barn with sections for wheat, and barley
92426: za ovɤ̀s za za limɤ̀c smo sàmo ednùš dvà puti li sejàli
and oats, and – well, we only sowed spelt once or twice
92429: nè e bil u presèk lèču smo si sejàli lèču
so there wasn’t a section for it. Ah, and lentils! We sowed lentils.
92433: kà naròdi le [laughter] ama izlèze li visokà ta ju uskubèmo
When it bears [laughter], it grows high, and we pluck it.
92438: skubèmo natvàrimo na kolàta otkàramo na gùvno ta a očùkamo
We pluck it, load it on the cart, take it to the threshing floor and pound it,
92443: odvèemo i lèča pasùl’ pàj i pasùl’ smo si br bràli
winnow it, and [you’ve got] lentils! Ah, and we also gathered beans
92446: s kolà mnògo se ne ràdžuje a i s kolà čùkanemo
with the cart, they don’t give much fruit – And we’d pound [them]
92448: na gùvno s màjku i tekà se mnògo trùd se e polagàl
at the threshing floor with mother, and so. A lot of labor was expended
92450: i se e proizveždàlo tovà ednòto vrème sà smo mnògo speciàlni
and [a lot] got produced back then. Now we’re “specialized”!
92453: i sìčko da ni e [laughter] nagotòvo pa nì e skùpo
Everything is [laughter] readymade for us, but it’s expensive.
92455: But – so what if it’s expensive.
92456: a lèča na kvò mestò se sèe
And what sort of area are lentils sown in?
92459: lèčata i ovɤ̀sɤt ìskat ta takòva pò sùxo
Lentils and oats need it to be drier.
92465: kato è otsrèšta kato takòva kamenìsto̥
Like that place over there, that rocky area.
92469: prìmerno mesnostà kàk je i ovɤ̀sɤt je xub ùbav ama hm
A place like that, for example. And oats are nice, but
92470: pàj se pò ìska da e pò na ùbavo mèsto na
they are even more particular [about] a nice place [to grow].
92472: mòže edin da izlèzne ta edvà ga žn’èš ùbavo
You can get one [plant], so you can hardly reap it properly.
92475: a ednò tṛ̀glo ta dvàes sàntima i svè skubèmo ako ne mòže
If it stops at twenty centimeters we need to pluck it if you can’t –
92477: da ne mòže go òžn’eš onò sàku i slàma da ìma nàšite
if you can’t reap it. Our people want to have straw as well.
92481: òti ovsènata slàma e nàj ùbava a ičmènata da ne sì
because straw from oats is the nicest. But for barley straw, don’t be
92484: na gùvnoto če te prisṛbì i kudè ne si pomislìl [laughter]
on the threshing floor – you’ll itch in places you never thought of! [laughter]
92487: o tovà e mnògo stràšno ečmìkɤt kvò da
92494: pòpɤt nèma tùka ìmaše pòp ama počìna
No priest. There was a priest here, but he died…
92502: mnògo odàvna tùka doòdi edìn ot tṛ̀n kɤdè opslùžva cèlata opštinà
…a long time ago. [Now] one comes by from Trŭn, he serves the entire district.
92504: to stanà segà stàde da ne òkaš pòp nì za umrèlo
But that stopped. Now we don’t call a priest [at all], not for a death,
92505: nì za əh sìčko stanà i da dòjde si s kolà čovèk
not for anything. The guy would come by in a car –
92507: pa da ga ne òkaš zaštòto
Well, you don’t call him because –
92515: skupotìja stotàrka ti zìma da dòjde da po opèe mɤrtvècɤt stotàrka
The expense! He charges you a hundred to come chant over a corpse. A hundred!
92517: a ednò vrème za kvò če go òkneš
What did you call him for in the old days?
92520: pa pàj go òkaše sɤ̀što za umrèloto ga òkaše
Well, they called him for the same, they called him when someone died.
92523: ama òn min’ùješe ednò vrème bes pàre ta svèteše vòdu
But back then he would come by for free, and bless the water
92527: na svì pràznici ama mu vṛ̀liš u kotlèto jà dvàes stotìnki
for all the holidays. You’d either throw twenty stotinkas in his kettle,
92529: jà dadèš pasùl’ dadèš kvò ìmaš od dòma i ne sàka če čo
or you’d give him beans or whatever you had at home, and he wouldn’t ask –
92531: àjde be màmo vikàla si go doma da ni kṛ̀sti
Ah, but Mom – you called him to the house to christen us.
92534: è pa kṛštavàla sɤm vi ama jà ne pòmnim da sɤm plat
Yes, I christened you, but I don’t recall that I –
92537: ne znàm kòlko sɤm platìla za kṛštan’è
I don’t know how much I paid for the christening.
92542: tùja si o kṛstì kudè živèexme predì da dòjdemo tùka
I christened him here, [that is, at] the place we lived before coming here.
92545: momčèto go kṛstìxme si tùka bèxme na kvàrtira
We christened the boy here. We were living in rented quarters,
92549: pòsle tovà strupàme sedemdesè i devèta godìna izokàmo pòb dòma
[but] then we threw this [place] together in 1979, and called the priest to the house.
92554: zgrejàmo vòdu òn pištà pištà pištà ùplaši se ot popàtoga [laughter]
We heated water, the child screamed & screamed, he took fear of the priest! [laughter]
92556: We weren’t able to christen it.
92559: Are you [trying to] peen the scythe?
92565: I don’t know how to mow.
92572: stìga be jà mògu da kòsim ženà ne umèe da kòsi
Ha, stop it! I, a woman, can mow, and this guy doesn’t know how!
92574: è pa tì si učìla jà ne sɤ̀m se učìl
Well, you learned how, I didn’t.
92581: əm dvàmata mi bràk’a ama edɤ̀n me ùči onà vìka
Um, [of] my two brothers, one of them taught me. “She,” he said,
92583: trèbe da znàe svè edɤ̀nijɤt vìka òti u ne odvedèš
needs to know everything”. The other said, “Why don’t you take her
92587: na počìfku òti u ne odvedèš na morè no a ùčiš
on holiday, why not take her to the sea rather than teach her
92589: kvò da kòsi e pa rekòx onò trèbe svè da znàm
how to mow?” And I said I need to know everything.
92591: jà sɤm bilà nasòčena za mùško ama tè sɤm otišlà u žènsko
I should have been a man, but I ended up a woman.
92594: mɤ̀ška ràbota sìčko mi se oddàva
Men’s work suits me, all kinds of it.
92600: i da zakovèm i da odrèžem trùd tèško e tèško e
To forge, to chop – it’s hard. It’s hard ...
92604: da se rabòti sɤs sekìru i sɤs ə teslù i sɤs svè
... to work with an axe and an adze, and all,
92607: ama mògu da ga da nè e kato mùškata napràva
but I can – It’s not like a man’s work,
92610: a pà i mògu da svṛ̀šim nèšto ràbotḁ
but I can manage some [of that] work.
92613: a kòseneto e mùška ràbota takà li
Mowing is man’s work, isn’t it?
92616: mùška e mùška zaštòto e tèško
92621: ta takà ta tàtko mnògo i sɤs sinɤ̀t xùbavo kòsi
Indeed. Well, Dad together with his son mows nicely.
92625: ama trèbe se xùbavo naklèpa mnògo bṛ̀zo sɤs klepàn’e na kosùtu
But you have to peen it well. [It goes] very fast when the scythe is peened.
92629: tovà e majstorìjata da a naklèpaš xùbavo ìma si čukàlo oddòle
It’s a real art to peen it well. There’s a small anvil below
92632: se pobìe i sɤs čukčè koèto ne mòže sèko čukčè
that you stick [into the ground]. Then the hammer. Not any kind of hammer,
92635: čukčè za kovàn’e na kosù onò e od dvète stranì takòva širòko
but a hammer for forging a scythe. It’s broad on both sides.
92638: nèma da e s ednòto da se kovè s ednòto da se čùka
You can’t have one for forging and another for hammering.
92641: i kat se načùka sinɤ̀t mnògo ùbavo ama ama kato ne bṛ̀za
And when my son hammers, it’s very nice. But not if you hurry.
92644: kà se nakovè kosàta mòže da naòstriš i pèt pùti da kòsiš
When you pound the scythe [right] you can sharpen it and mow five times
92646: i ùbavo kòsi ne tì dṛ̀pa i mnògo nìsko amà
and it mows nicely, doesn’t push you, and [reaches] low, but –
92649: tì spomenà za krɤštanè tùk ste praìli
You mentioned christening. Did you do it here?
92651: e pa kṛ̀štan’è ama kṛštavàmo si
Ah, christening. Yes we christened [our children].
92653: kàk se kàk se prài kṛštanè
92655: e pa tovà ti vìkam zgrèemo si vòdu òn ne nòsi tovà
Well, I was telling you. We heat the water. He doesn’t bring that
92657: za kṛštan’èto ako ìdeš u cṛkvu če se
for christening. If you go to the church
92659: tàm ìma si sùd za vodùtu u korìto si zgrèemo vòdu
there’s a vessel there for water. We heat water in a washtub,
92661: i ga tùrimo pa si a miròsva si go pa si govòri
and put the child – he anoints it and speaks,
92664: pa si obikàl’a pa kṛ̀snicata kojà e màjkata kojà e
then they go around [the altar], then the godmother and the mother –
92665: dàde mi go evrèjče dàvam ti go xristijànče
“You gave me a Jewish child, I give you a Christian child.”
92667: a màjkata ne prisɤ̀stva mène ne dàdoše da sɤm pri kṛštan’èto
The mother doesn’t attend. They didn’t let me come to the christening.
92670: da mi ga dadù pòsle xrìstianče a jà sɤm im go dalà evrèjče
so as to give me the Christian child [after] I’d given them the Jewish one.
92676: a tùka zab takòva koprìneno eli červèno eli zelèno o kṛpè zabràtka
Here – something silken, either red or green, a cloth – A headscarf!
92680: zabràtka i onà sɤz dantèlki tùka na za zakeràči se
A headscarf, the kind with lace. You tie it here [behind your head],
92684: eli se tùka pòd brada no pòveče se zakeràči i tùka se
or else here under the chin, but mostly here behind your head.
92691: tovà jašmàkɤ za lètno vrème bèlo ot tenzùxɤt kɤdè kàzvam za cedìlkata
The veil is for summer. White, of cheesecloth, like I was saying for straining.
92695: lètno vrème da ne nì e tòplo si nòsexme jašmàci
For summer, so we wouldn’t be hot, we would wear veils,
92697: od bèlite od bèloto plàtno tenzùx se kàzva
white [ones], of white fabric. It’s called cheesecloth.
92699: i si sìčko sɤz bèli kṛ̀pi po polèto
Everyone in the fields had white cloths on
92701: da ne tè udàri od gòre svetì ilìja [laughter]
so you won’t be struck from above by St. Elias! [laughter]
92709: màni às ə umìram od grɤmotèvici ot tovà ot tovà nèma stràx
Forget it. I’m deathly afraid of thunderbolts. I have no fear
92713: da mi mìne zmijà če utèpem jadòsuje me i se plàšim
of a snake crossing my path, I’ll kill it. It angers me and frightens me
92716: no če ja utèpam ama ot tovà nèma kɤdè da se skrìem
but I will kill it. But from that [other] there’s no place to hide.
92719: skrìem se krìem krìem nògo me e osòbeno kato xòdex
I [want to] hide, to hide, most especially when I was out
92722: da ìde sɤs stòkutu lèle nèma kudè da pobègneš skrìeš se
with the livestock. Oh my, nowhere to run to! You hide
92725: pod nèkɤde u nèkoja tṛnìca da ne sì od podi dṛ̀vo
under something, in some thistle-bush, so you’re not under a tree –
92726: In a pot on the hearth. [unclear]
92728: mòre utepà ednà godìna ednù gòdin màk’a mi bèše ofčàrka
One of them struck one year [when] my mother was a shepherdess,
92731: ta ùtepa deset òfce jà kàže ìdem da gi dìdzam
and it killed ten sheep. I said I’ll go pick them up,
92735: onò tò kət od ofcète vùnata bèa prodavàli me
and when [I did that] they sold the wool from the sheep
92738: jà kàže padà po ofcète i didzà gi i padà
I told [them] I fell [while going] after the sheep, lifted them, fell
92743: i tè tekà i idòše ta gi izòše da izèdoše tèpanete
and they went and ate them – they ate the ones that had been killed
92749: ot ə mɤln’àta nèmaše vìka òblaci be oddèka izlèze pustin’àkɤt
by lightning. No clouds, she said – where did this damned thing come from?
92752: ta se utreštà ta ni rèče pòtepa e sega štò da napràim
Thunder everywhere, she said, it battered us good. So what to do?
92755: slagàli li sa nèkoj pɤ̀t sekìru tè takà
Did you sometimes put an axe like this,
92757: nagòre s òstroto da ne vàli
with the sharp edge up so that it wouldn’t rain?
92760: da ne da ne ma da sɤ̀pre dɤ̀žɤt turàli smo i tùramo
To not – to not – to stop the rain? We did, and we do.
92797: i nòž zabìemo da sɤ̀pre dɤ̀žɤt i sekìru obṛ̀čamo sɤs
And we thrust a knife [in the ground] to stop the rain, and whet the axe with –
92798: i onà vìka ama vìe ama dobrè be màmo òn vìka
And she says, “But you – but fine, Mama,” he says,
92801: tì si ùškim mlàda ženà kakvò vìka dobrè še go spreš li
“You’re supposedly a young woman.” “What?” she says. “OK, will you stop it?”
92804: vìkam nèma ostanàlo e povèrie i às tìčam i slàgam kato
I say, “No, the belief has remained.” And I run and put it –
92808: bìemo prenèsi ga prenèsi ga prenèsi ga
We beat [and say] “Carry it off, carry it off, carry it off!”
92814: svìn’e su stiskàli da da pištù da ne
They shut up the pigs so they won’t shriek, [and prevent it]
92816: da sɤ̀pre olomanìjata ama onò si e i stràšno nèkoj pɤt
from stopping the storm. But it’s frightening sometimes.
92818: kàk kato poglèdneš kòlko e rasadìl si u svèt pipèr
Like when you look to see how many – you’ve planted lots of peppers,
92822: a kato pòčne da kḷ̀ca ka pòčne da vṛ̀l’a gḷ̀ta pṛ̀vo detè
and when they begin to sprout, when it starts to storm, the first child swallows –
92826: koè e pṛvàče gḷ̀ta pṛ̀voto zṛ̀no koè vìdi da sɤ̀pre gradùškata
the child that’s oldest swallows the first bud it sees so as to stop the hail.
92830: ako si pṛ̀v u na màk’u gḷ̀taš eli
If you’re the first [child] of a mother, you’ll swallow it, right?
92832: nìe ne smè igràli peperùda vìe mòže da ste igràli
We never did the “peperuda” (rainmaking ritual) dance, maybe you did.
92840: kàk kàk stàva tàa ràbota kakvò se
And how does this happen, what do –
92843: dɤ oblečù se devojčetìja u tɤ̀nki ròklički sɤz
Girls get dressed up in thin little dresses,
92849: napràvat si venčèta od zelenìš i sɤs tòčat vodà plìskat se
they make wreaths out of greenery and pour water, sprinkle it:
92851: They get wet as they dance.
92853: mòkrat se ta da predizvìkat ə dɤ̀ž da zàjde
They get wet so as to cause it to start raining,
92856: kogà je po zag segà nèšte da ga naprài
when it’s – Now they don’t want to do it,
92859: ta da mu se poklàn’až do zemjàta da celùneš
to lean down to the ground and kiss it.
92862: nèma da da go napràvim devòjčeto a da naprèd decàta
A girl [will say] "I won’t do that [now]." But earlier, children
92866: i na làzarica i na i na əm ù e na varvàra
on St. Lazar’s day and on, um, St. Barbara’s day,
92870: na tìja zìmnite pràznici niko sveti nikòla
and these winter holidays, St. Nicholas’s day –
92876: boksàva i varvàra xòdexme na varvàra s kòšničèta mòjta sɤm ja praštàla
On Boksava and St. Barbara’s we went with baskets, as I sent my [daughter].
92879: kòj ti dadè lèšta kòj bobᵊ kòj ošavᵊ
Some give you lentils, some give you beans, some dried fruit.
92882: togàva bèxa zaklàli prasètata vèče i dàvaxa sušenìci
They’d already slaughtered pigs at that point, and were giving sausages.
93287: ɛhɛ̀ əmə pìl’ci hi nəpətìsəhə sìn učukòvət jə drèbənkite pìlci sə
Ah, but the birds attacked them, son! They nibbled them. Little tiny birds they are,
93395: za dètstvoto li tr’àva da ti kàžem dètstvoto
Childhood? I should tell you [about] my childhood?
93399: a sɤm go karàla mnògo dobrè mnògo bème siromàsi
It was very good. We were very poor –
93400: nìe sme čètiri sestrì i edìn bràt takà i ama
we were four sisters and one brother. That’s [how it was]. But
93402: kogà bème takòva dòma kogà si bèxᵊ za bɤ̀dni.vèčer
When we were at home, when I was there for Christmas Eve,
93410: na krɤštan’è glèdaj segà kakvò bèše togàva krɤštan’èto kato pràvixme
At christenings – look here, [I’ll tell you] how it was back then. When we christened
93412: tàtko si dòjdeše od mìnata i togàva go ne vìkaxa prèmii
Dad would come from the mine. At that time they didn’t call it bonus pay,
93415: a go vìkaja tantièmi im dàvaxa tantièmi parì i òn če dòjde
they called it extra-bonus. They gave them extra-bonus pay. And he’ll come
93418: uprègna volòvete ti znàeš što è volòve pa tùra ednà lèsa
harnessed up oxen (you know what oxen are [right?]), and put on a wattle harrow.
93422: zèma: petlìte i gi kòl’a da si sì i zatvorìl
They take [their] roosters and slaughter them. You needed to have locked them up!
93425: jà s što sàm naròt višlà u na borìs pɤ̀rvi
[Whereas] I’ve seen [all sorts of] people:  Boris I,
93427: da sà ùbavi decà nè nèma ùbavi decà a jà im kàžex
[who] are beautiful children. No, there’s no beautiful children [there]. I told them
93433: i sìte da smè u seftè čoràpi plèteni i kato izvàdi pogàčata
and we were all wearing newly knitted socks. And when she brought out the bread,
93436: na čìf i tèk znàeš li što è čìf i tèk
“chift i tek” (odds & evens). Do. you know what “chift i tek” is?
93440: kato ogìno da sà bèše mnògo vèselo
so they’ll be like the fire. It was very joyous.
93443: ma pres pràgo òn če e odvɤ̀nka jà če sàm odvɤ̀tre
over the threshold: he’ll be outside, and I’ll be inside.
93445: You know what “trotters” are, don’t you?
93447: što tì rabòta tìja rabòtnici tùka da pùši i da pijà
What do these workers do for you here, [other than] smoke and drink?”
93465: nìe na nàšte si decà segà i i segà go ne xarèsvam
our children – I don’t like [how they do] it now –
93466: a nìe kato pràvixme krɤštan’è òšte prèdnijo dèn
[but back then] we began the christening already the day before.
93467: si prigòtvime sìčko i kumovète si gi vìkneme
We get everything ready, and we call the godparents
93468: i si i prigòtvime dàrove na kumovète
and prepare gifts for the godparents.
93469: jà sɤm si gu prigotvìla rodòpski odejàla togàva
I prepared [as a gift] the thick Rhodope blankets, [since]
93470: bèše na mòdata rodòpski odejàla čeršàvi sìčko i če prigòtvime
Rhodope blankets were the fashion then. Sheets too, everything. We’ll prepare,
93471: i kumò če dòjde̝ i če go vòdi detèto u čèrkvata
and the godfather will come, and take the child to the church.
93472: i kato se vɤ̀rne kumò ot čèrkvata i mi dadè detèto
And when the godfather returns from the church he gives me the child
93473: i kàže tì mi go dàde evrèjče òn go e krɤstìl vèče detèto
He says, “You gave me a little Jew” – he’s already christened the child
93474: u čèrkvata i go nòsi vìka tì mi go dàde evrèjče
in the church and is carrying it – he says, “You gave me a little Jew,
93475: jà ti go dàvam xristijànče nàči go e krɤstìl
and I give you a little Christian.” Which means he has christened it.
93476: i kato go e krɤstìl i vìnagi trèbe da ìma pačà
And after he’s christened it we always have to have trotters.
93478: /laughter/ takà i kumò zème panìcata sɤs pačàta i ja narèže takà
/laughter/ Well, then the godfather takes a panful of trotters, and slices it up
93479: i tùri krɤ̀s i pɤ̀rvo na detèto če tùri na čelcèto
and makes the sign of the cross. First he’ll put it on the child’s forehead
93480: i vìka i pà rečè do trì pati
and say – and he says this up to three times:
93482: tì mi go dàde xristijànče jà ti g
“You gave me a little Christian, and I – [that is]
93483: tì mi go dàde evrèjče jà ti go dàvam xristijànče
You gave me a little Jew and I give you a little Christian.”
93484: i kato ti go dadè i go razvìje i mm
And he gives it to you, and unwraps it,
93485: i kato sa go tàm kapàli i ako se e detèto naakàlo
since they’ve washed it there. And if the child has pooped,
93486: òn ə nalì ìma čeršàfče togàva xavlìja i ja dadè
he’s got, you know, sort of sheet, a bath towel, and gives that over.
93487: i ti dadè pɤ̀pčeto da go fɤ̀rliš nèkade togàva go fɤ̀rl’exa
And he gives you the [tied-off] umbilical cord to throw somewhere. Back then they threw it –
93488: bàbite go fɤ̀rlixa u gradìnata ta da e oràč i kopàč
grannies threw it into the garden, so [the child would] be a ploughman and hoer,
93489: a sàa go fɤ̀rl’a: u učìlišteto̥
but now they throw it into the school[yard].
93491: i go fɤ̀rl’aa i togàva se jadè i pìe i muzi
They’d throw it out, and then there is food and drink and music –
93492: bez mùzika nè e bilò i se kumò posrètne
nothing happened without music. They greet the godfather
93493: sɤs kùm sɤs mùzika i se ispràšta sɤs mùzika
with music, and they send him off with music.
93495: bèše vèse̥lo̥ dà i togàva kumò se dàri dar’àva se
It was merry. Yes. And then they gift the godfather. He’s gifted with
93496: òdglado čoràpi gàšti rìza sìčko pižàma kakvò e rèdno
socks, pants, shirts, everything, [even] pajamas. Whatever is appropriate.
93497: bès čeršàf ne sè dàva togàva se brodìraxa čeršàvi
And no gifting without sheets; back then they embroidered sheets,
93498: čeršàvite če dàvaš i è tàa dalà čeršàvi
and you’ll gift sheets. This [young woman] gave sheets.
93499: a koì sa pa mlàdi nevèsti kogà se klàn’axa to ednà
The ones who are young brides, when they bowed [to their elders], and one –
93500: tì klan’àla li si se ne sì nè ne me lɤ̀ži ne sì
Did you bow then? No, you didn’t. Don’t lie now, you didn’t!
93502: nalì kato se ožèn’a i kogà idaa u čèrkva bàbite gi vòda
So when they get married, and they go to church (the grannies lead them),
93503: vàra: žìto sɤs càrevici i kojà e nàj pɤ̀rva nevèsta
the [brides] cook up grain and corn. And the bride that is first
93504: tàa če e nàj dobrè a kojà e naj odzàde
will be the most successful, and the one furthest back
93505: onà e u k’umùr i če e zlè i pogàčite gi slàga:
is “blackened”, she’ll have it the worst. So they put out the ritual breads,
93506: kojà e nàj ùbava pogàča tàa če e nàj ùbava nevèsta
and the one [who made] the nicest ritual bread is [considered] the prettiest bride.
93507: ta jàze bèx ne i ràno ìda è òše u trì časò
And I was – They go early, already at three o’clock
93508: ìde u čèrkvata ta bìe kambànata ta ìdexa
she goes to the church, the bells ring out, and they [all] went,
93509: i nalì sɤz bèli kɤ̀rpi nalì znàeš kakvò se klàn’axa
with white towels. You know how they would bow, don’t you?
93511: nè prijàtno si bèše i te takvìa mi ti ràboti
No. It was very nice. And there were [other] such things, you know.
93512: i u čèrkvite bèše žìto nòsexa na ìmen dèn žìto na ivànovden
They carried [ritual] grain [dishes] into the church, on name days, on St. John’s Day.
93513: na jordànovden žìto se nòseše u čèrkvata sɤs càrevica odgòrekḁ
[And] on St. Jordan’s Day, they carried in the grain [dish] with corn on top.
93515: a segà zèmali po ednò kutiščè bonbòni i gi mɤrzì
And now they apparently just take a little box of candy each, and even that’s a bother.
93516: i pogàča se mèseše̥ pogàčḁ e osvèn pa samokòfski znàeš li
And they made ritual breads. Other than the Samokov type, do you know
93517: kvì pogàči nòsexḁ te takvìja segà è či segà na čèrkvata
what kinds of ritual bread they carried in? Now in the church
93518: na ràmoto kogà ni bèše jà ne vidòx pogàča ženà
when it was in the lowlands, I haven’t seen a single woman
93519: da e omesìla ama što porɤ̀čaž be òmesi be na čèrkvata
making her own ritual bread. Why do you order out? Make your own for the church!
93520: na na òsmi noèmvri ni e togàva i togàva ìma vìnagi
On the eighth of November back then there always were
93521: po trì pòpa u nàšta čèrkva mnògo e ùbavo togàva
three priests in each of our churches. It was really nice then.
93522: i ot daskalòvo doòždaja mnògo bèše ùbavo
People would come even from Daskalovo, it was very nice.
93524: a tàa godìna nèznam dalì sa išlì jà ne idòx
But this year I don’t know if they went. I didn’t go,
93525: pràvo da ti kàža bèx po sòfija i ne sɤ̀m odìla
to tell you the truth; I was in Sofia and didn’t go.
93527: i kazàx na ta se karàx pa i na kmèto
And I said – I had an argument with the village mayor.
93528: rèko kmète ma jà idì so po drùgite sèla da vìdite
I said, “Hey mayor – go around other villages, and you’ll see
93529: nàšite gròbišta sa nàj lòši zaštò ama ìmaž dvàma rabòtnici
[that] our graveyards are the worst [maintained]. Why? You’ve got two workers.
93531: ama ne pijà abe takà e dùmata jà rèko slùšaj da ti kàžem
“They don’t drink,” [he said]. “Well, that’s the talk,” I said. “Listen up!
93532: jà gi èbni jà segà ìde zadùšnicḁ jà neka ìda ta iščìstat
Give them a push! All Souls Day is coming, they’d better go and clean things up!”
93533: ta kato išlì da iščìstat nàšio gròp nàj ùbavo iščistìli go
And they went there to clean, and our grave got cleaned the best.
93534: vèrni go no go iščistìli pa ni ukradnà nìe go zagradìme
It’s true that they cleaned it, but they also robbed us. We had barricaded it off
93535: sɤs ə pɤ̀sno sɤs takàva ogràda go zagradìme̥ mòl’a ti se
with [unclear] we made a kind of fence around it. And would you believe it,
93536: da ni otkàča: vratèto da go ukràdna zaštò pìtam se za kakvò
they just detached the little gate and stole it. Why, I wonder – what for?
93540: i če donesè mnògo parì togàva i kato dòjde tàtko
and bring [with him] a lot of money. And when Dad came,
93543: i če dòjde kato si dòjde i màma prigotvìla pogàčite
when he came, Mom had made holiday ritual breads,
93545: če stàpime u pòdnica znàe li momìčeto što e pòdnica nè
we’d step in the “podnitsa” (baking dish). Does the girl know what’s a “podnitsa”? No.
93548: če stàpime ta da nèmame vàški da ne nì jadà krakàta
We’d step [there] so we wouldn’t have lice gnawing at our legs,
93550: da ne sì ni sɤrbà i tàtko če dòjde i če
so we wouldn’t be itching. And Dad will come and –
93552: da se kato dòjde i če unesè kòš sɤs slàma
and when he comes he brings in a basket of straw.
93555: i kato dòjde kòšo sɤs slàma i jà postèlim
And when this basket of straw arrives, I spread it out
93558: u odajàta go vìkaxme nèma stài nèma tovà golèma odajà ìmaxme
in the chamber, [as] we called it. No [separate] rooms, we had this big chamber,
93560: i pèd decà i kato unesè tovà i màma turì ošàvo
and five children. When he brings it in, Mama puts down the dried fruit compote,
93562: če tùri svè prigòtveno sìčko i na sìte i tùri svèšti
she puts all that had been prepared, for everyone, and then puts candles down.
93563: na segà sàmo na pogàčite slàga: svèšti
Now people put candles just on the ritual breads ...
93566: a nàj e vàžno bilò da slòžiš na kompòto i na pogàčḁtḁ
... but [then] the most important was to put them on the compote and on the breads.
93568: i màma na sìte si slàgaše bèdni sme bilì
And Mom put them on everything. We were poor,
93571: i kato se večèra i màma iznesè u u reštò žìto
And after supper, Mom brings out a sieve with wheat,
93576: naturàla jàbɤlki turìla òrexi i lèšnici i če igràeme
[in which] she’d put apples, and walnuts, and hazelnuts, and we’d play
93578: ama òn donesèše parì i takà i če se večèra
but he had brought money, and so we could have [a good] supper.
93580: i tovà ne znàeš nàči /laughter/ takà ako e čifᵊ dvè sa
Ah, you don’t know that either! /laughter/. Well, if it’s “chift”, it’s two –
93581: ako sa tèk trì sa òrexi
and if it’s “tek”, it’s three – walnuts.
93583: i takà krìe i kato pogòdi bràt mi sìčko sìčko mi zème
So he hides them, and when my brother guesses, he takes all of mine,
93586: pa pòčneme da revème i kato se navečèrame
and we began to howl. So after we finish supper ...
93588: tovà i vìnagi na bɤ̀dni.vèčer bez lokùm nè e bilò
... and always – Christmas Eve was never without Turkish delight.
93591: dà takà e bilò na vrème
Yes. That’s how it was back then.
93592: i takà i če večèrame no nìkoj nè stàva
And so we’d have supper, and nobody gets up
93593: dodèka sìte se ne navečèrame ta kato se
until everyone had finished with supper, so that when
93598: kvàčkata kato vòdi pìl kato se izvɤ̀di pìlita da se izvedà
the hen brings out its chicks, it will bring them out [all together].
93621: navednɤ̀š stàvame nə izvednɤ̀š i slàmata ležìme
Then all at once we get up [from the table] and lie down [to sleep] on the straw.
93623: koè e na takà legnàlo kato prasètata u i sùtrin
Each one lay down in whatever way, like piglets [together], and in the morning
93626: kojà e gotvìla č ìde u čèrkva a mažjète če zèma žìto
whoever did the cooking will go to church. And the men will take grain,
93629: i na pòrtata če tùra žìto da fàna: vrapčè
they’ll put grain at the doorstep in order to catch sparrows.
93631: i kato dòjde t i nìkoj nèma da zakùsva dode
And when she comes – nobody will have any breakfast
93633: dodèka ne dòjde ženàta ot čèrkvata i ulòva vrapčè
until the woman comes from the church and they’ve caught a sparrow.
93636: i na sìte dadà od vrapčèto da lìtne od nègo
And they give each one the sparrow to let it fly off from him
93637: ta da ìm e lèko i togàva se jadè
so they’ll [all] be light [like a sparrow]. And then everyone eats.
93639: i če se jadè i togàva mɤžèti izlìzaja
And we’ll eat, and then the men go out.
93643: zimàja slàmata i pràva venčèta i tùraja na drɤfčètata
They take the straw and make wreaths; they’d put them on small trees.
93644: i togàva se pàli drùgata slàma i se obikàl’a
Then they set fire to the rest of the straw, and everyone walks around it
93645: ta momìčetata da sà vèseli i bòdri
so that the girls will be joyous and high-spirited,
93765: pa da ti kàžem bème mnògo pa edìnni siromašìja
let me tell you, we were quite united. Poverty –
93769: na màma svekɤ̀rvata bèše màštexa i i oddelà oddelìa oddelìa gi
Mom’s mother-in-law was a stepmother, and they separated them
93772: ot ə strinàrite i màma vìka da sakàx na svekɤ̀rva mi
from her aunt’s people and Mom said – “I asked my mother-in-law,
93775: i onà mi vìka dàde kàlenite togàva sa bilì tèndžeri nə
and she said  – she’d given [me] clay – back then pans were [of clay]
93778: i vìka s sestrà ti sčupì vìka tè e golèmata ə tèndžera
and she said, your sister broke, she said, the big pan
93780: i vìka ne nèma ot kə štò da edète
and said there – there won’t be anything to eat from.
93785: i togàva nèmaše ùbavi ràboti zèma ot tàa xartìja napràvat le
There weren’t any fancy things back then, they took paper to make [decorations].
93934: pa vìka vi sìpem u ednì mɤnènki panicèta pa se kàrate
So she said, I’ll dish out [food] in tiny pans and you fight it out."
93936: i bèše pa vèselo da ti kàže̥m̥ a siromašìja
It was joyous, let me tell you, even in poverty.
93941: ot krapèc kɤdè issilìa jazovìro krapèc tì znàeš i takòva
And when they resettled [people to build] the dam in Krapets – you know Krapets? –
93945: dòjdeha ot tàmoka i kàraxa čerèši sɤs ə košòve i nìe siromàsi
they came from there bringing cherries in baskets. And we [were] poor.
93946: nèma ot kɤdè a tàtko bòg da go pròsti u mìnata rabòti
No resources. Father, God rest his soul, worked in the mine,
93947: po cèla sèdmica go nèma i màma vìka dèca tè
and was gone the whole week. So Mom said, “Children, see
93949: čerešàro e došɤ̀l ama če edète čerèši tovà e vìka takòva
the cherry-man has come, so you’ll eat cherries.” But then she said,
93953: čèrvi ìma jà vìka s tìja parì če vi kùpim orìz
“There’s worms,” and said, “With this money, I’ll buy rice,
93955: da vi napràvim jàdene i te tekà bèše
and make food for you.” And that’s how it was,
93958: siromašìja kòlko si sàkaš na vrèmeto kakvò bèše kogà se žn’èše
all the poverty you could want back then. When they reaped,
93961: i nèmaše kon’è nèmaše tàja ə tìja takòva fàbriki da se rabòta
there weren’t horses, there weren’t any of these factories to process things.
93964: i znaš kakvò se vɤršèše kato nasàda: tovà žitòto da se vɤršè
And you know how they threshed? They lay the grain down to thresh it,
93968: pòrta i nìe decàta se nakàčime na nèja ta da se s smàčka žìtoto
[Like] a gate. And we kids climbed up on it top to [help] smash the grain.
93970: te tekà bèše i pòsle vejàčka ìmaše nàraka ti znàeš sìgurno
That’s how it was. And then there was a hand-held winnower, you know that surely,
93973: i vejàčkata i koì sa pò visòki če sa gòreka
a winnower. And the ones who were taller were up above –
93977: da ne tì e xlàdno nèšto da iznesèm elèče
Aren’t you cold? Should I bring you something, a vest?
93981: i koì sa pò visòki gòre če pùska: žìtòto ednì ogrìbaja
And the taller ones above would drop the grain down. Some raked [it]
93983: ednìte pa na plèvata koì mràzime decà gi tùrime
and others would be down with the chaff. We put the kids we hated [down there]
93987: /laughter/ ma tekà bèše i takà pòsle pa odrasnàme
/laughter/ Well, that’s how it was! And later when we grew up,
93990: i kòj nakadè vìdi kato odrasnàme i màma na vrèmeto ne dàvaše
when we grew up, each went wherever they wanted. Mom back then didn’t allow [us]
93993: da se mnògo òdi i stàra ni bèše kɤ̀štata dèdoto ni dàde
to go out much. Our house was old, Grandpa had given it to us,
93996: i màma nèma bravà da se zakl’ùči a onà tùreše ednò dɤ̀rvo
and Mom didn’t have a lock on the door. So she would put a piece of wood,
93998: pa tùri mašà nalì znàeš što e mašà
she’d put the “masha” (fire tongs), you know what “masha” is, don’t you?
94001: /laughter/ à segà /laughter/ i tùri mašàta ta kato se pribèreme
/laughter/. Ah well. /laughter/ So she put up the “masha” so that when we got home
94003: da znàe kogà sme se pribràli ìnače vìka nèma da vi pùštim
she’d know what time we got home. Otherwise, she said, I won’t let you out [at all].
94006: ne nì dàvaše sega ne dɤržà na na tòa mo moràl
She wouldn’t allow it. Now people don’t care much about this – “morals”,
94010: togàva se mnògo dɤržèše i jà si ojdòx čèsna
but back then they cared a lot. So I went [to be married] in an “honorable” state.
94012: kato si ojdòx čèsna i svekorò togàva pa nèmaše so štò
And when I was married “honorably”, my father-in-law – back then there wasn’t
94014: nèšto da kupiš pedesè i i ftòra godìna se oženìx nèma nìšto
anything to buy with. In [nineteen] fifty-two [when] I got married there was nothing.
94015: pa ottùka zèmeme maslò sìren’e ta nòsime na sòfija
So we take butter and cheese from here and bring it to Sofia [to sell]
94019: ta da ni kùpa: bèx ednà snàa bèše ìmax etɤ̀rva dè
so they could buy us [things]. I was the only daughter-in-law; I had a sister-in-law
94021: ama mène me pò me obìčaše svekorò s səs svekɤ̀rvata
but my father-in-law liked me more. As to my mother-in-law –
94023: se ne uvažàvax ama so svekorò če ìde če zème sìren’e
I didn’t get along with her. But my father-in-law would go and take cheese,
94025: če zème maslò i č ìde da mi kùpi koprìna
he’d take butter, and he’d go to buy me silk
94026: da si napràvim ròkl’a i svàdbata če se napràvi
so I could make a dress. And there’ll be a wedding.
94027: po trì dèna se pràveše svàdba razbìraš li
Weddings used to last three days. Do you understand?
94030: teferìč se pràveše tì mož da znàeš əm
They’d have a “teferich” (staff for a processional flag), you maybe know –
94031: i teferìč znàeš li kakvò e
do you know what a “teferich” is?
94033: nè nàči kato e svàdbata u nedèl’a onì u sɤ̀bota
No. So then the wedding itself is on Sunday. On Saturday they –
94037: se sobèra momìčetata i če pèja i zèma ə čimšìri
the unmarried girls get together and sing, and take boxwood staffs.
94043: napràvae i odgòre na teferìčo tùra jàbɤlka pa igràeja pa pèja
They make the flagstaff, put an apple on top, and dance and sing.
94047: i posle kato dòjde i sutrintà zetovète če dòjda zèma: tovà čemšìrite
Then the next morning the groomsmen come and take the boxwood staffs.
94051: znàmeto zèma i č ìda da kràdna petlìte po komšìite kòj ne zatvòri
They take the flag, and go steal roosters from neighbors who don’t lock them up.
94054: nìkoj ne znàe dèka svàdbata se pràvi trèbe da se
Nobody – everyone knows that a wedding is on, and that one must
94057: da se zatvàraa kokòškite i kato se pokàn’i kumò
lock up all the chickens. And when they go to invite the godfather –
94059: ìda ta go kàn’a kumò sɤs ə mùzika sos sìčko i dòjde kumò
they go to invite the godfather with music and everything. And the godfather comes –
94062: kato dòjde kumò ot čèrkvata i se vrɤ̀šta: kato se vɤ̀rna
when the godfather comes from the church, when they [all] come back,
94064: ednà edìn kanàt se slòži kanàt tì go znàeš ot karùcite
they take a “kanat” (cart board) and lay it out. You know, from a carriage.
94065: nalì si znàeš kakvò e kanàt ne znàeš
You know what a “kanat” is, don’t you? [I suspect] you don’t.
94067: i tùra ednà čèrga kato tùra čèrgata i tùra
And they put a rug on it. When they put down the rug, they put down
94070: edìn kotèl vodà i cvet’à u kotèlo tùreja i nevèstata
a cauldron of water, and they’ve put flowers in the cauldron. And the bride
94073: da rìtne tovà kotèlo i da fɤ̀rli cvetjàta pres ə pres kɤ̀štata
kicks the cauldron and throws the flowers over the house.
94076: ta da ìma kolko sa cvet’àta tòlko decà da ìma
And however many flowers [she throws], that’s how many children she’ll have.
94080: i svekorò fàne s a snaàta i ja vɤrtì nèkolko pɤ̀ti okol nègo
And the father-in-law takes the daughter in law and spins her several times around him
94081: ta da ne bèga snaàta da sedì dòma da go slùša
so the daughter-in-law won’t run off, so she’ll stay at home and obey him.
94082: bèše mnògo interèsni ràboti ìmaše i takà i bèše mnògo vèselo
[They did] a lot of interesting things, and it was very joyous.
94085: i bèše ùbavo è pa kato se sɤbèrexme i komšìi ta smèx
And it was nice. When we got together with neighbors, there was a lot of laughter.
94088: te seà tàa komšìk’a ot on ot ònija dèn dojdè
Just now my neighbor came by, the day before yesterday.
94092: òjde i si dòjde po norvègija bèše segà vìka
She’d gone and returned; she’d been in Norway. “Now,” she said,
94095: če si dòjdem komšìk’ata tè dvà dèna nìkakva a nèma
“I’ll be back.” But for two days there’s no sign of my neighbor.
94097: nè nè ne sɤ̀m sɤglàsna mnògo lòši stanàme xòrata
No, no, I don’t agree [with how things are these days]. We’ve all gotten very bad.
94099: ìdexme po žìvata vodà odìla li si na žìvata vodà
We would go to the “living water”. Have you gone for living water?
94104: kato kàzax žìvata vodà ta kosàta mi pojdè nagòre
When I said “living water” my hair stood up on end.
94106: plàstexme odgòreka po trì pɤti sme išlì nagòre pa ìdeme
We were stacking hay up there. We went up there three times. We all go,
94112: govedarjè pa ofčarjè pa pèexme pa ìdeme nalì idòme na xolàndija
cowherds, shepherds, and we’d sing and go around. We went to Holland
94113: po predì kòlko godìni bèše tùka pèexme i igràeme i č ìdeme
some years back. There we sang and danced, and we’d go –
94116: i po klàdnica ìdexme ə kadè li ne sè lùtaxme i igràeme
And we went to Kladnitsa – we went all over the place, and danced.
94118: i onìa ot xolàndija ni mnògo bèa aresàli ta idòme po
And the people from Holland liked us a lot, and we went around –
94122: pa kòlko vrème ojdòme tòčno na dvanàesti dekèmvri
How long were we there? It was exactly on the twelfth of December
94127: dɤšter’àta ìmaše roždèn dèn tava go onà na trinàesti ta ojdòme
that my daughter had her birthday, so we went on the thirteenth,
94130: i za bɤ̀dni.vèčer si dojdòme pòsle onì tùka dooždàa
and came back on Christmas Eve. Later they came here.
94133: ama jà n’ìn’oto ne gò xarèsax da ti kàžem
But to tell you the truth, I didn’t like their [life] there.
94135: tàmoka nèma xlepᵊ nìe sme si tùka bɤ̀lgarite na xlèp
They don’t have any bread [to speak of] there. We Bulgarians are big on bread.
94137: tàmoka è če vìdiš ednà felìja če ti dadà če vìdiš sòfija
There, when they give you bread it’s a single slice. But in Sofia!
94144: smèj se smèj se takà bèše
Go ahead and laugh, [but] that’s how it was.
94148: i na mèso nìe ne smè s takà sviknàli a onì kato dojdòa
And meat! We’re not that used to [eating meat]. But when they came
94151: nìe drùgojàče napravìme rèkox na dèdoto jà slušaj da ti kàža
we did things differently. I said to Grandpa, “Listen, I’ll tell you.”
94154: tè mèn mi bèa trì ženì u sèlo tùka gi tùrex
They were three women here in the village with me, and I placed them
94157: na ednò mèsto òšte ne bème natàm oprajàli kɤ̀štata
in the same spot. We hadn’t yet put the house in order.
94161: vɤpròsa če gi pribràx i jàden’e ìmaše mnògo obìčax
But the point is that I took them, and fed them. I liked it a lot.
94167: sèka vèčer po ednà butìlka mas mastìka pìexa da im e slàtko
Every evening they drank a bottle of ouzo – more power to them!!
94168: tovà sam tovà ìskax i tovà sam davàla
That’s what I wanted, and that’s what I gave them.
94172: ama zakòl’ame jagnèto i jadèxme i bèa dovòlni do skòro ìmaše
And we slaughtered a lamb and ate it, and they were content. Recently
94173: pa ednà komšìk’a ne idè na xolàndija a onì ispratìli
a neighbor of ours didn’t go to Holland, and they sent [her back]
94177: ednò šàlče takà pròsto za uvažènie čùdim se što sàkaš pa
a shawl, just a mark of respect. I wonder what you want [I said to]
94180: tì kàka dèno tì ne sì odìla nìkəde i nìšto ne znàeš
my] sister Dena. You haven’t gone anywhere and you don’t know anything.
94185: i na ezar jòsif ako znàeš ə kadè e na càro kal’àskata
and Exarch Joseph, if you know where that is, at the emperor’s carriage.
94186: zn nìšto ne znàeš i tìja ràboti tì nìšto ne znàete
You don’t know these things, you don’t know anything.
94189: sɤdèbnata palàta znàeš li kadè e
The Palace of Justice, do you know where that is?
94196: à takà fli flizàla li si dòleka u mazèto kadè sa golemcìte miž
Ah, OK. Have you gone in below, to the cellar where the big shots [hang out]?
94198: ne mòž da si flizàla tàm ne dàva ne mè lɤ̀ži̥
[No,] you can’t have gone there, it’s not allowed. Don’t lie to me,
94201: ne sì flizàla a nìa otsrèšta ìdexme jàlovico bèše tàm pazàč
you haven’t been. But we went across from there, Yalovitso was the guard.
94203: ìdeme ama se sabùeme ìdeme na kafè tàmoka i rečème
We went there, took our shoes off, went to the café there and said,
94205: jà me pùšti da vìdim kal’àskata na càro kadè e bilà
“Let me see the emperor’s carriage, where it was,
94207: kakvò e bilò sìčko tàmoka ìdexme ta glèdaxme jà sam màlko naxàlna
what it was like.” We went and saw everything there. I’m a little pushy
94209: po tìja ràboti nè da sam naxàlna pròsto ìskax da da razberèm
about these things. Well, not so much pushy, I just wanted to know
94211: kakvò e bilò štò e bilò i ìdexme i nasèkade
how it was and what it was. We went everywhere,
94213: nasèkade sam odìla i vìtoša ednà ìmaxme prijàtelka u
I’ve gone all over. To Vitosha, we had a friend there.
94216: pa pòsle ojdòx rabotìx u dèckata gradìna šesnàese godìni rodìteli
And then I went and worked 16 years at a kindergarten. Parents –
94219: kòlko si sàkaš odìx nasèkade sam odìla na koprìvštica
as many as you want. I went all over, I’ve gone to Koprivshtitsa
94221: kòlko pɤ̀ti tàm ni snimàa i nèma značènie kakvò i da bilò
many times. They took our photos there, no matter for what reason,
94224: ìmam òšte vèstnici da ti gi pokàža kakvà snìmka ìmam
I still have the newspapers and can show you the photo I have.
94226: nèma da kàžeš deka sɤm jà bilà takà i idòme pa
You wouldn’t know that it was me! And we went again
94228: u koprìvštica tàm ni aresàa za u xolàndija ta idòme
to Koprivshtitsa. The [Dutch] liked us there, and we went to Holland.
94230: i u xolàndija kato ìdexme ne ìm aresàx živòto im ne aresàx
But when we went to Holland I didn’t like their – I didn’t like their life.
94232: mnògo vodà da ìdex u dèckata gradìna decàta im žɤ̀lti kato
Too much water! We went to a kindergarten, their children are yellow like –
94233: ne mòg da ti gi kàžem ispìeni decà nè kato nàšte
I can’t describe them to you Washed-out children, not like ours,
94237: ìmaše ednà prevɤr ja im kazùex ùoči ne vì xarèsvam živòto̥
there was a – I told them straight to their faces, “I don’t like your life.”
94239: u vòda živèja tì ne išlà li si tàm da vìiš kakvò e
They live in water. Have you gone there to see what it’s like?
94241: kɤ̀štiti sa im u vodà ne sì odìla na vètrenata vodenìca
Their houses are in the water. You haven’t gone. At a windmill
94246: ta stòexme ta vìkax na ženìte à da zèmeme pèsag
[where] we were standing I said to the women, “Let’s take some sand
94248: da si izmàžem kɤ̀štata ìdexme po cèla nòš
so I can plaster my house!" We were out аll night long.
94249: e što bèše ùbavo vèselo bèše da znàeš
Ah, it was nice. It was happy, you know?
94647: tùkə ìməši i vərenìci gur’àə vàr s’èki d’èn tùkə minàvət
There were lime pits here too, they burned lime. Every day there would pass by here
